title: Preface
content: Preface Logic and Proof is volume F1 of the series. It is followed by Sets, Relations, and Cardinality.

title: Connectives and Derivations
content: Connectives and Derivations Section 1.1 opens with two arguments that every integer with an even square is even. Every sentence in both is true, and yet only one is a proof. The other, Argument B, starts from “n is even”, reaches “n^2 is even”, and then announces the reverse. Spotting the flaw once it is pointed out is easy. Naming it, so that the same flaw can be caught in an argument we have never seen, needs an answer to a harder question: when is a list of true sentences a proof? The motivating problem of this chapter is to name exactly what is wrong with Argument B, and the answer arrives in Section 1.5. This chapter and the next build the calculus that answers the question. A proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule. We first learn to read such chains, with no logic in them at all, and then learn the rules one at a time, for “and”, “implies”, and “or”, each defined by a small pattern of lines and practiced in many short derivations and in proofs about numbers. Chapter 2 does the same for “not”, “iff”, and proof by contradiction, and shows how to find derivations systematically; Chapter 3 asks whether the rules are right (@thm-soundness, @thm-completeness); Chapter 4 adds “for every” and “there exists”; Chapter 5 turns derivations back into the prose mathematicians write. What you need. School algebra only: the rules of signs, adding and multiplying inequalities, and the facts that every integer is even or odd and every real number is nonnegative or negative. They are used as facts in examples; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves the order facts from the axioms for the real numbers. No earlier chapter is needed. Time. About 35 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 50 hours for everything. Roadmap - Statements and connectives. The language: what a statement is, the five connectives and the constant \bot, the main connective of a statement, and the sequent as a claim about the form of an argument. - Derivations. The format of a derivation, with no logic yet: numbered lines, premises, a justification on every line, and rule schemas, practiced on two borrowed facts about inequalities. - Conjunction. The first two rules of logic, \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E}, and the two directions of reasoning: from the goal backwards and from the premises forwards. - Using an implication. The rule \rulename{{\to}E}, modus ponens, and chains of implications found forwards and backwards; why its converse pattern is not a rule. - Proving an implication. The rule \rulename{{\to}I} and the box: assumptions, their scope, repetition, and the full definition of a derivation. - Or, introduced. The rule \rulename{\vee I}, which loses information but never truth, and the habit of postponing a disjunctive goal. - Using or: proof by cases. The rule \rulename{\vee E}, two boxes ending in the same line, the laws of “or”, and case proofs about absolute values. Named moves - Read the skeleton off the goal. The goal’s main connective chooses the introduction rule: \wedge gives two subgoals, \to a box, \vee a choice to postpone. - Use a premise by its main connective. Its elimination rule says what you may do with it: take a conjunction apart, feed an implication its hypothesis, split a disjunction into cases. - Open a box, close a box. An assumption lives exactly as long as its box. - Work from both ends. Premises at the top, the goal at the bottom; fill the gap from both sides. - Postpone a disjunction. Choose a side of a goal P \vee Q only when that side is in hand. - Cases end in the current goal. Both boxes of \rulename{\vee E} close on the statement you are trying to reach.

title: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content:
Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument This is where the book starts, and it starts with a question every reader of mathematics eventually asks: when is an argument a proof? A proof is not a list of true sentences, and it is not an argument that merely sounds convincing. This section takes the first steps towards a precise answer. It says what the sentences of a proof are, how they are built from smaller ones, and what it means for two arguments to have the same form, which is the thing logic studies. Two arguments about squares Recall that an integer n is even when n = 2k for some integer k, and odd when n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. (The word “some” has rules of its own, which come in Chapter 4; here we use it as school algebra does.) Here is a fact about integers that Chapter 2 proves properly, once the rules for “not” are in place. For every integer n, if n^2 is even, then n is even. Read the following two arguments for it. Each is written in the style of a textbook proof, and each sentence in each of them is true. Argument A. Suppose n is odd, say n = 2k + 1 for an integer k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1, so n^2 is odd, and therefore n^2 is not even. So an odd n never has an even square. Since every integer is even or odd, an integer with an even square must be even. Argument B. Suppose n is even, say n = 2k for an integer k. Then n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2), and 2k^2 is an integer, so n^2 is even. Hence if n^2 is even, then n is even. Argument A is a correct proof. Argument B is not, although none of its sentences is false. It starts from “n is even” and arrives at “n^2 is even”. That is a perfectly good proof of a different statement: “if n is even, then n^2 is even”. The claim asks for the journey in the opposite direction, from the square back to the number, and the last sentence of B announces a conclusion that the argument never reached. Seeing this is easy once it is pointed out. Saying in general what went wrong is harder, and that is what this chapter and the next are for. To name the error we need to know what the rules of proof are, and before that, what they act on. So we start with the smallest pieces: the sentences a proof is made of. Statements A proof is written in sentences, but not every sentence can appear in one. “Is 91 prime?” cannot be a step of an argument, because it asserts nothing; neither can “Let us now turn to the case n = 0.” The sentences that can serve as steps are the ones that make a claim. A statement is a sentence that is either true or false. [Statement] A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, and not both. In words: a statement makes a claim, and the claim is either correct or incorrect. The definition asks that one of the two is the case. It does not ask that we know which one. A statement whose truth nobody has settled is still a statement. [Statements and nonstatements] Decide which of the following are statements. 1. 7 is a prime number. 2. 0.999 > 1. 3. There are infinitely many primes p for which p + 2 is also prime. 4. Is 2^{11} - 1 prime? 5. x > 2. 6. 3 > 2. (a) This is a statement, and it is true. (b) This is a statement, and it is false. A false sentence is as much a statement as a true one. (c) This is a statement. It is the twin prime conjecture, and at the time of writing nobody knows whether it is true. It is certainly true or false, which is all the definition asks. (d) This is a question, so it is not a statement. The sentence “2^{11} - 1 is prime” is a statement, and a false one, since 2^{11} - 1 = 2047 = 23 \cdot 89. (e) This is not a statement. Whether it is true depends on what x is: it is true when x = 3 and false when x = 0, and as written nothing says which. Such a sentence is called an open sentence. (f) This is the sentence of (e) with x replaced by 3, and it is a true statement. Items (e) and (f) differ by one symbol, and the difference is the whole point. The open sentence x > 2 becomes a statement in two ways. We can put a number in for x, as in (f). Or we can say which x we mean in some other way, as in “for every real number x, x > 2” (a false statement) or “for some real number x, x > 2” (a true one). The words “for every” and “for some” are the quantifiers, and they are the subject of Chapter 4. Mathematics is full of open sentences, and we cannot wait until Chapter 4 to use them. So this chapter adopts a convention. When an example says “let x be a real number” and then talks about x, the letter x names one fixed number, not further specified. Every sentence about that x is then a statement, true or false according to which number x is. “Let x be a real number with x > 2; then x^2 > 4” is an argument about one number, which happens to work whatever the number is. Chapter 4 explains why an argument of that kind proves a statement about every x at once. The book reserves the words “proposition” and “theorem” for proved results, so it calls the sentences of logic statements. Other books call them propositions, which is where the name propositional logic, for what this chapter and the next study, comes from. The connectives Most statements in mathematics are built from smaller ones. “0 < x and x < 1” is built from “0 < x” and “x < 1” with the word “and”. “If n^2 is even, then n is even” is built from two statements with “if … then”. The words that do the building are the connectives. A statement built from smaller statements by a connective is compound; one that is not is atomic. For this chapter, “x > 0” is atomic: it has an inner structure, a number and an order, but no connective joins parts of it. We write P, Q, R, S for statements whose inner structure we are ignoring. They stand for arbitrary statements, atomic or compound. There are five connectives. In the last column of the table, x is a real number, P is “x > 0”, and Q is “x < 1”. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Symbol Name Read Example --------------------- --------------- -------------------- ------------------------------------- P \wedge Q conjunction P and Q x > 0 and x < 1, that is, 0 < x < 1 P \vee Q disjunction P or Q x > 0 or x < 1 P 	o Q implication if P, then Q if x > 0, then x < 1 P \leftrightarrow Q biconditional P if and only if Q x > 0 if and only if x < 1 
eg P negation not P x is not positive, that is, x \le 0 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ To the five connectives we add one statement with no parts at all, written  ot and read “contradiction”. It stands for a statement that is false however things stand: 0 = 1 will do. A proof that reaches  ot has shown that the situation it was working in cannot occur. That is the heart of proof by contradiction, and Chapter 2 gives  ot its rules. In P 	o Q, the statement P is the hypothesis (or antecedent) and Q the conclusion (or consequent). English has many ways of saying P 	o Q: “P implies Q”, “Q if P”, “Q whenever P”, “P only if Q”, “P is sufficient for Q”, and “Q is necessary for P” all say the same thing, and the exercises ask you to see why. “If and only if” is often shortened to iff. Several English words become \wedge: “but”, “although”, and “while” all assert both parts, and add a tone of contrast that logic ignores. “2 is prime but not odd” is a conjunction. So is “neither … nor”, in disguise: “9 is neither even nor prime” asserts that 9 is not even and that 9 is not prime, which is 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q with P: “9 is even” and Q: “9 is prime”. Chained inequalities are conjunctions in disguise too. 0 < x < 1 abbreviates (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), and a \le b \le c abbreviates (a \le b) \wedge (b \le c). The symbol \le itself hides a disjunction: a \le b means (a < b) \vee (a = b). And a 
e b is the negation 
eg(a = b). All three facts are used often in the sections that follow. In theorem statements the book writes \Rightarrow and \iff, as mathematicians usually do, and in running prose it says “implies” and “if and only if”. The arrows 	o and \leftrightarrow are kept for the formal derivations that start in the next section. Nothing but typography separates the two pairs. In everyday English, “or” is often exclusive: “soup or salad” on a menu means one but not both. In mathematics, P \vee Q is inclusive: it is true when P is true, when Q is true, and when both are. For a real number x, “x \ge 0 or x \le 0” is true whatever x is; at x = 0 both parts are true, and that does not spoil it. An exclusive “or” must be said in full: “P or Q, but not both”, which is (P \vee Q) \wedge 
eg (P \wedge Q). The word “if” means different things in a theorem and in a definition. In a theorem, “if P, then Q” is one direction only: “if n is divisible by 4, then n is even” is true, and its converse is false at n = 2. In a definition, “a number is even if it is twice an integer” is meant as “if and only if”: a number that is not twice an integer is not called even. Section 2.4 explains this convention of language. Translating a sentence Translating into symbols is a skill of its own, best learned slowly, in three steps. Find the atomic statements, the smallest pieces that make a claim, and give each a letter. Find the connectives, whatever English words carry them. Then decide how the pieces group. Take “if 12 is divisible by 3 and by 4, then 12 is divisible by 6”. The atomic statements are P: “12 is divisible by 3”, Q: “12 is divisible by 4” and R: “12 is divisible by 6”. English lets “12 is divisible by” be said once and shared; logic writes each piece in full. The words “if … then” carry 	o, and “and” carries \wedge. The hypothesis is everything between “if” and “then”, so the statement is (P \wedge Q) 	o R, not P \wedge (Q 	o R). The second reading would claim P outright, and the English sentence claims nothing outright: it only says what follows from what. A second example shows a connective hidden inside a word. Let x be a real number, and read “x is nonzero, and if x is positive, then so is x^3”. With Z: “x = 0”, P: “x > 0” and C: “x^3 > 0”, “nonzero” is 
eg Z, and the whole sentence is 
eg Z \wedge (P 	o C). Letters that recall their statements, as here, often help; a letter is only a name. In both examples the English word order is a poor guide to the grouping. When in doubt, ask of each connective: which two statements does it join? Reading a statement: precedence and the main connective Connectives can be combined without limit, and a string of symbols is only useful if it can be read in one way. Consider 
eg P \wedge Q. Does it deny P and then assert Q, or does it deny the whole of P \wedge Q? These are different claims. With P: “n is even” and Q: “n > 0”, the first says that n is odd and positive, while the second says only that n is not a positive even number, which n = -4 satisfies. Parentheses settle every such question, and a few conventions let us drop the ones that would only add clutter. 1. 
eg binds most tightly: it applies to the smallest complete statement that follows it. So 
eg P \wedge Q means (
eg P) \wedge Q, and to deny P \wedge Q we write 
eg(P \wedge Q). 2. \wedge and \vee bind more tightly than 	o and \leftrightarrow. So P \wedge Q 	o R means (P \wedge Q) 	o R. 3. 	o groups to the right: P 	o Q 	o R means P 	o (Q 	o R). The book usually writes these parentheses anyway. 4. In a mixture of \wedge and \vee, or of 	o and \leftrightarrow, the parentheses are always written. We never write P \wedge Q \vee R. Convention (3) is the natural one: a statement “if P, then if Q, then R” is common, and (P 	o Q) 	o R, whose hypothesis is itself an implication, is rare. Chapter 3 turns “a statement built from letters by connectives” into an exact definition (@def-formula) and proves that every such statement can be read in only one way (@thm-unique-readability). In this chapter we parse by eye. The conventions only decide where parentheses may be dropped. The next definition names the one piece of information that reading a statement is for. [Main Connective] The main connective of a compound statement is the connective applied last when the statement is built up from its parts. An atomic statement has no main connective. The main connective is found by undoing the construction from the outside. Take 
eg(P \wedge Q) 	o R . By convention (1), the 
eg applies only to the parenthesized P \wedge Q; by convention (2), the 	o takes everything to its left as its hypothesis. So the last step joined 
eg(P \wedge Q) and R with 	o, and 	o is the main connective. Its hypothesis 
eg(P \wedge Q) has main connective 
eg, applied to P \wedge Q, whose main connective is \wedge. The construction can be drawn as a tree, with the main connective at the root and the letters at the leaves. Reading the tree from the top: the statement is an implication; its hypothesis is a negation; what is negated is a conjunction. Reading from the bottom retraces how the statement was built. A one-symbol change moves the root: in 
eg(P \wedge Q 	o R) the parentheses make the whole implication the thing denied, and the main connective is 
eg. Here is a second statement taken apart the same way, this time with every step said aloud: P \vee Q 	o R \wedge S . There is no 
eg, so convention (1) does nothing. By convention (2), \vee and \wedge bind before 	o, so the statement is (P \vee Q) 	o (R \wedge S), and its main connective is 	o. The hypothesis P \vee Q has main connective \vee and the conclusion R \wedge S has main connective \wedge. With x a real number, P: “x > 1”, Q: “x < -1”, R: “x^2 > 1” and S: “x^4 > 1”, it reads: if x > 1 or x < -1, then x^2 > 1 and x^4 > 1. The main connective is not grammar for its own sake. It is the first thing to find when a proof has to be written, because it decides how the proof begins. To prove “if 0 < x < 1, then x^2 < x”, whose main connective is 	o, a proof starts “Suppose 0 < x < 1.” To prove “x^2 + 1 > 0 and x^2 + 1 
e 0”, whose main connective is \wedge, a proof has two parts, one for each side. Section 1.3 gives this habit a name, each later section of this chapter adds to it, and Section 2.6 turns it into a method for finding proofs. Find the main connective of each statement. 1. 
eg P \vee Q 2. 
eg (P \vee Q) 3. (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) (a) \vee: by convention (1) the 
eg applies only to P, so the statement is the disjunction of 
eg P and Q. (b) 
eg: the parentheses make the whole disjunction the thing denied. (c) \wedge: each parenthesized implication is complete, and the last step joins them with “and”. The form of an argument Here are two short arguments, one about integers and one about real numbers. If n is odd, then n^2 is odd. And n is odd. So n^2 is odd. If x > 2, then x^2 > 4. And x > 2. So x^2 > 4. They are about different things, and yet they are the same argument. Write P for “n is odd” and Q for “n^2 is odd” in the first, and P for “x > 2” and Q for “x^2 > 4” in the second. Both then read: from P 	o Q and P, conclude Q. What makes the step correct has nothing to do with odd numbers or squares. It depends only on the shape of the premises, on the fact that one of them is an implication and the other is its hypothesis. That shape is the argument’s form, and the part of the argument that lives in the letters is its content. Logic studies the forms of arguments, not their content. Separating the two has a payoff. Once a form has been shown to be correct, every argument of that form is correct, whatever its content; we check the form once and use it forever. The notation for a claim about forms is the following. [Sequent] Let P_1, \dots, P_n and Q be statements, where n \ge 0. The sequent P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q is the claim that Q can be derived from P_1, \dots, P_n by the rules of logic. The statements P_1, \dots, P_n are its premises and Q is its conclusion. When n = 0 we write \vdash Q. The symbol \vdash is called the turnstile, and P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q is read “P_1 to P_n prove Q”. A sequent is not an argument, and it is not true merely because its conclusion is true: it claims that a certain kind of object, a derivation from those premises to that conclusion, exists. The next section says what a derivation is, and so exactly when the claim holds. It is proved the way any existence claim is proved, by exhibiting one. The two arguments above both have the form P 	o Q, \ P \vdash Q , and the rule ulename{{	o}E} of Section 1.4 says that this sequent holds. The case n = 0 is the degenerate one, and it matters. \vdash Q claims that Q can be derived from no premises at all: that the rules alone produce it. Such statements exist, and Section 1.5 derives the first of them. Which of the following arguments has the same form as “If n is divisible by 6, then n is divisible by 3. And n is divisible by 6. So n is divisible by 3”? 1. If n is divisible by 4, then n is even. And n is even. So n is divisible by 4. 2. If x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0. And x > 0 and y > 0. So xy > 0. The given argument has the form P 	o Q, \ P \vdash Q. (i) does not. With P: “n is divisible by 4” and Q: “n is even”, it has the form P 	o Q, \ Q \vdash P: the second premise is the conclusion of the implication, not its hypothesis. This form is not correct, and n = 2 shows it. The first premise is true for every integer, since a multiple of 4 is 4k = 2(2k); the second is true, since 2 is even; yet 2 is not divisible by 4. (ii) has the same form, with P the compound statement “x > 0 and y > 0” and Q the statement “xy > 0”. A letter may stand for a compound statement. Each connective, two rules We now come to the idea that organizes this chapter and the next. Think about what a mathematician does with the word “and”. There are exactly two things to do with it. - To prove a statement of the form P \wedge Q, prove P and prove Q. - To use a statement of the form P \wedge Q that is already known, take either half. Nobody needs to be taught these two moves. They are also, and this is the point, all there is to know about “and” for the purpose of writing proofs. Every other fact about \wedge, such as that P \wedge Q and Q \wedge P say the same thing, follows from the two moves, as Section 1.3 shows. The first move is called the introduction rule for \wedge, written ulename{\wedge I}, because it is how a \wedge gets into a proof. The second is the elimination rule, ulename{\wedge E}, because it is how a \wedge is taken apart. The table below is an informal preview. Section 1.3 states these two rules exactly, as patterns of lines. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule What it allows You write --------------------- ------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------- ulename{\wedge I} from P and Q, conclude P \wedge Q “We have shown x > 0 and x < 1. Hence 0 < x < 1.” ulename{\wedge E} from P \wedge Q, conclude P; also Q “Since 0 < x < 1, in particular x > 0.” --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every connective works the same way. Each comes with introduction rules, saying how to prove a statement with that main connective, and elimination rules, saying what a statement with that main connective lets us conclude. The rules for \wedge come in Section 1.3, those for 	o in Sections 1.4 and 1.5, and those for \vee in Sections 1.6 and 1.7. The rules for 
eg,  ot, and \leftrightarrow, and one more rule for proof by contradiction, which stands apart from the others, are the subject of Chapter 2. Two slogans summarize the plan. Each connective comes with a way to prove it and a way to use it. A proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule. The rules are chosen so that they never lead from true statements to a false one. For \wedge this is plain: if P and Q are both true, so is P \wedge Q, and if P \wedge Q is true, so is P. Chapter 3 proves it for every rule at once (@thm-soundness); the theorem is called soundness. The second slogan is what makes a proof possible to check. Finding a proof may need an idea. Checking one needs none: go through it line by line and ask of each line which rule produced it and whether that rule was applied to lines that really are there. A reader who has lost the thread of a long argument can always fall back on that question, and it is the question to ask of Argument B. In Part 0 we ask it out loud; Chapter 5 shows how the same rules run silently underneath ordinary written proofs. The order of these chapters differs from that of many logic books, which begin with truth tables: tables listing, for instance, when P 	o Q is true. There, the row “if P is false, then P 	o Q is true” has to be accepted as a convention, and it looks arbitrary. Here, that fact comes out of how proofs work (Section 2.1), and the tables arrive in Chapter 3, which proves that the rules and the tables agree (@cor-derivable-iff-valid). We can now say what we will make of Argument B. Its claim has the form Q 	o P, with Q: “n^2 is even” and P: “n is even”, and B’s reasoning runs from P to Q. Section 1.5 names the error as a misuse of the rule for proving an implication: B began from the conclusion P where the rule asks it to begin from the hypothesis Q. And to repair B without new ideas, one would have to pass from “if n is even, then n^2 is even” and “n^2 is even” to “n is even”, the form P 	o Q, \ Q \vdash P of the Quick check above. Chapter 3 proves that this pattern cannot be derived from the rules at all: no derivation leads from P 	o Q and Q to P (@cor-refuting-row). What comes next The rest of this chapter is built to a pattern, and knowing the pattern in advance makes the sections easier to read. Section 1.2 says what a derivation looks like and how to read one. It uses no logic at all. Its only rules are two facts about inequalities, borrowed for practice, so that the format can be seen on its own: numbered lines, premises at the top, and a justification on every line. Each of Sections 1.3 to 1.7 then introduces one rule, except that Section 1.3 introduces the pair of rules for “and”, which are so simple that the two are one idea. The rule is defined by its pattern, a small picture of the lines it needs and the line it writes. The pattern is read clause by clause, since each clause is there for a reason and each is broken by some tempting mistake. Then come several derivations with the new rule, from the smallest possible to a few lines longer, and each is preceded by an Idea that says why each rule was chosen. Each section also shows its rule at work in a proof about numbers, where the rule is usually invisible. The Ideas ask two questions, again and again, and it is worth learning them now. - What does the goal’s main connective ask for? The statement we are trying to reach decides the last step of the derivation, and so its overall shape. - What does an available line’s main connective let me do? A statement we already have decides what we can get out of it. The first question works backwards, from the bottom of a derivation; the second works forwards, from the top. Section 1.3 gives the two directions their names, and every later section adds its rule to one of them: an introduction rule answers the first question, an elimination rule the second. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of a statement. Is “10^{100} + 1 is prime” a statement? For a real number x, is “x^2 - 1 = 0” a statement? Is “0^2 - 1 = 0”? 2. With P: “n is even” and Q: “n is prime”, write “n is prime but not even” in symbols. 3. Find the main connective of P \wedge Q 	o 
eg R, and write the statement with all its parentheses. 4. True or false, with a reason: if P and Q are both true, then P \vee Q is false. 5. Let x and y be real numbers. Write the form of the argument “x > 0 and y > 0; so y > 0 and x > 0” as a sequent, saying what each letter stands for. 6. Which of \wedge, \vee, 	o is the main connective of (P \vee Q) \wedge (Q 	o R)? Using the preview table of “Each connective, two rules”, say what a proof of this statement must do, and name the rule that Section 1.3 will state for it. (a) A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, and not both (@def-statement). Yes: 10^{100} + 1 is a definite integer, so it either is prime or is not. The definition does not ask us to know which. With x fixed, as in this chapter’s convention, “x^2 - 1 = 0” is a statement about that one number: true if x is 1 or -1, false otherwise. Without the convention it would be an open sentence. The sentence “0^2 - 1 = 0” is a statement outright, and it is false, since 0^2 - 1 = -1. (b) Q \wedge 
eg P. The word “but” is a conjunction. (c) Convention (2) groups P \wedge Q before 	o acts, and convention (1) lets 
eg take only R. So the statement is (P \wedge Q) 	o (
eg R), and its main connective is 	o (@def-main-connective). (d) False. The mathematical “or” is inclusive, so P \vee Q is true when both parts are true. (e) With P: “x > 0” and Q: “y > 0”, the form is P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P (@def-sequent). Section 1.3 derives it. (f) \wedge: each parenthesized part is complete, and the last step joins them with “and”. So a proof of it has two parts: it proves P \vee Q, and it proves Q 	o R. The rule that puts the two parts together is ulename{\wedge I}. This is the first question of “What comes next”, asked before any rule has been stated exactly: the goal’s main connective decides the last step. B. Practice [B1: Translating analysis] Translate each sentence into symbols, using the atomic statements given. You do not need to know what the words mean; only the grammar matters. 1. “f is continuous at a but not differentiable there”, with C: “f is continuous at a” and D: “f is differentiable at a”. 2. “If the sequence (a_n) converges, it is bounded”, with V: “(a_n) converges” and B: “(a_n) is bounded”. 3. “x is rational or irrational”, with R: “x is rational”. (A real number is irrational when it is not rational.) 4. “The set F is closed if and only if its complement is open”, with K: “F is closed” and U: “the complement of F is open”. (a) C \wedge 
eg D. “But” asserts both parts, and “not differentiable there” is the negation of D. (b) V 	o B. The pronoun “it” refers to (a_n), so the conclusion is the statement B. (c) R \vee 
eg R. “Irrational” means “not rational”, so the second part is 
eg R, not a new atomic statement. (d) K \leftrightarrow U. [B2: Parsing] For each statement, insert all the parentheses that the conventions allow us to omit, and name the main connective. 1.

eg P) 	o Q, main connective 	o. (b) (P \vee (

eg R), main connective \leftrightarrow. Each 
eg applies to the single letter after it, and \vee binds more tightly than \leftrightarrow. (c) (

eg P, which is the smallest complete statement following it. (d) P 	o (Q 	o (
eg R)), main connective the first 	o. By convention (3), 	o groups to the right. The statement P \wedge Q 	o R is (P \wedge Q) 	o R: “if x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0”. It is true for all real x and y, since the product of two positive numbers is positive. C. Going deeper [C1: “Only if” and “unless”] Let P and Q be statements. 1. Explain why “P only if Q” means P 	o Q, and not Q 	o P. (Ask: which situation would make “P only if Q” false?) 2. Explain why “P unless Q” means 
eg Q 	o P. 3. Let x be a real number. Decide whether each sentence is true for every real x. Justify your answer, giving a value of x that makes it false where there is one. - “x^2 = 4 if x = 2.” - “x^2 = 4 only if x = 2.” - “x^2 > 0 unless x = 0.” (a) “P only if Q” says that P does not happen without Q. It is broken exactly when P holds and Q fails. That is also exactly when P 	o Q is broken: an implication promises Q whenever P, and the promise fails only when P holds without Q. So the two say the same thing. By contrast, Q 	o P is broken when Q holds and P fails, a different situation. For example, “a number is divisible by 4 only if it is even” is true, while “a number is even only if it is divisible by 4” is false (take 2). (b) “P unless Q” says that P holds in every situation except possibly those where Q holds. So once we know that Q fails, we may conclude P, which is 
eg Q 	o P. For instance, “the equation ax = 1 has a solution unless a = 0” says: if a 
e 0, then ax = 1 has a solution. (c) The first sentence is (x = 2) 	o (x^2 = 4). It is true for every x: when x = 2, x^2 = 4, and when x 
e 2 it promises nothing. The second is (x^2 = 4) 	o (x = 2), the same two parts in the opposite direction. It is false for x = -2, where x^2 = 4 but x 
e 2. The third is 
eg(x = 0) 	o (x^2 > 0), by (b). It is true for every x: a nonzero real number is positive or negative, and in both cases its square is positive. The first two sentences differ by one word, and they are implications in opposite directions. Confusing them is exactly the mistake of Argument B at the start of this section. [C2: Necessary and sufficient] Let x be a real number. 1. Write “x > 1 is sufficient for x^2 > 1” and “x > 1 is necessary for x^2 > 1” as implications. 2. Decide which of the two is true for every real x, and give a value of x that makes the other false. 3. Find a condition on x, written with \vee, that is both necessary and sufficient for x^2 > 1. You may use that x^2 > 1 exactly when \abs{x} > 1, where \abs{x} is x if x \ge 0 and -x if x < 0. (a) “P is sufficient for Q” means that P is enough to guarantee Q, that is, P 	o Q. “P is necessary for Q” means that Q cannot hold without P, that is, Q 	o P. So the two sentences are (x > 1) 	o (x^2 > 1) and (x^2 > 1) 	o (x > 1). (b) The first is true for every x: if x > 1, then x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 1 \cdot x = x > 1, where multiplying x > 1 by the positive number x keeps the inequality. The second is false for x = -2: then x^2 = 4 > 1, but x < 1. (c) (x > 1) \vee (x < -1). It is sufficient: if x > 1, then \abs{x} = x > 1, and if x < -1, then \abs{x} = -x > 1; either way x^2 > 1. It is necessary: if x^2 > 1, then \abs{x} > 1, and \abs{x} is x or -x, so x > 1 or -x > 1, the latter meaning x < -1.

title: 1.2 Derivations: Premises, Lines and Justifications
content: Derivations: Premises, Lines and Justifications The previous section stated a slogan: a proof is a chain in which every line is a premise, an assumption, or one application of a rule. This section makes part of that slogan exact, the premises and the lines that apply a rule; assumptions wait until Section 1.5. It says what such a chain looks like on the page, how each line carries its reason, and how anyone can check the chain without understanding its subject. It introduces no rule of logic. Its only rules are two facts about inequalities, borrowed for practice, so that the format of a derivation can be learned on its own. Checking a chain without understanding it Here is a chain of inequalities between fractions: 0 < \tfrac{1}{3} < \tfrac{1}{2} < 1 . It is read as three claims, 0 < \tfrac13, \tfrac13 < \tfrac12, and \tfrac12 < 1, and a reader who accepts them concludes 0 < 1. What justifies that conclusion? Not a picture of the number line, and not a feeling that the numbers go up. The justification is one fact, used twice: if a < b and b < c, then a < c. From 0 < \tfrac13 and \tfrac13 < \tfrac12 it gives 0 < \tfrac12. From 0 < \tfrac12 and \tfrac12 < 1 it gives 0 < 1. What must a reader know to check those two steps? Nothing about fractions, and nothing about what < means. It is enough to see that the two inequalities used in each step have the same expression in the middle, and that the new inequality joins the outer two. A clerk who had never seen a number could do it, provided the clerk can compare symbols. That is the sense in which a proof can be checked without being understood: a proof is correct when every step matches its pattern, and matching is mechanical. The rest of this section writes such chains in the format that the whole of Part 0 uses, with every reason on the page. Everything here is about the format. The logic starts in Section 1.3. Two rules about numbers, for practice We borrow two facts about real numbers and use them as rules. Every reader knows them, so attention can go entirely to the format. - Tr (for “transitivity”, or chaining): from a < b and b < c, write a < c. - Sh (for “shift”): from a < b, write a + c < b + c, for any number c. These are facts about numbers, not rules of logic. They are used as rules in this section and its exercises only. When a later proof adds 1 to both sides of an inequality, that is a step of school algebra, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves the facts behind such steps from the axioms for the real numbers. Rule schemas A rule is applied by matching, and to match we need something to match against. That something is a small picture of the lines the rule needs and the line it writes. A rule is a pattern: given these lines, you may write that line. [Rule Schema] A rule schema is a pattern of lines: given lines and boxes at the top, possibly none, and exactly one new line at the bottom, whose justification names the rule and cites the given lines and boxes. Line numbers in a schema are written i, j, k. The letters in the pattern stand for arbitrary expressions of the right kind, and a use of the rule replaces them consistently: the same letter by the same expression, symbol for symbol, everywhere it occurs. A line is justified by the rule when it and the lines it cites, with their numbers, are an instance of a schema of the rule: the pattern with every letter replaced in this way. The schema of \mathrm{Tr} is Here a, b, c stand for expressions for numbers. In words, clause by clause. - Given lines at the top, one new line at the bottom. The schema of \mathrm{Tr} has two given lines, i and j, and one new line, k. The given lines may sit anywhere above line k, in either order, and need not be next to each other or to line k. The drawing puts them together only because a drawing has to put them somewhere. - The justification cites the given lines. “\mathrm{Tr} \ i, j” says that line i plays the part a < b and line j plays the part b < c. The order of the citation assigns the parts, not the order of the lines on the page. - Letters are replaced consistently, symbol for symbol. The middle letter b occurs in both given lines, so it must be replaced by the same expression in both: the same string of symbols, not merely the same number. This is the clause a careless step breaks. - Nothing else is required. There is no condition on what the expressions mean, how large they are, or whether the given lines are true. An instance first. Take i = 3, j = 5, k = 6, and replace a by 0, b by \tfrac12, and c by 1. The pattern becomes: line 3 is 0 < \tfrac12, line 5 is \tfrac12 < 1, and line 6 is 0 < 1, justified “\mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 5”. So if lines 3 and 5 of some list say exactly those things, line 6 may say 0 < 1 with that justification. Now a noninstance, by a minimal change. Keep line 3 as 0 < \tfrac12, and let line 5 be \tfrac13 < 1. Is “6. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 5” justified? Line 3 forces b to be \tfrac12, and line 5 forces b to be \tfrac13. The letter b cannot be both, so these lines are not an instance of the schema. Line 6 is true, but \mathrm{Tr} was not applied, so the line has no justification. The schema of \mathrm{Sh} has one given line: Its letter c occurs only in the new line, so it may be replaced by any expression; consistency asks only that the same expression is added on both sides. From y < 5 the rule may write y + 1 < 5 + 1 or y + x < 5 + x, but not y + 1 < 5 + 2. Nor does it write y + 1 < 6: that is a different string of symbols. A logical rule with a letter that occurs only in its new line appears in Section 1.6. Why define rules this way? Because a rule applied by matching can be checked by someone who knows nothing about the subject. The schema turns “this step is obviously fine” into “this step matches that pattern”, a claim anyone can test. Every rule of logic in the following sections is given in this form, and the definition was worded so that none of them needs a new one: Section 1.5 adds given boxes, cited as ranges of lines, and a rule of Chapter 4 has no given lines at all. From the next section on, the letters in a schema are Greek: \varphi, \psi, \chi (phi, psi, chi) stand for arbitrary statements, just as a, b, c stand for expressions for numbers here. Replacing them works the same way, with parentheses put around a compound statement where it is needed. For example, if a schema has the given lines \varphi and \psi and the new line \varphi \wedge \psi, then the three lines P \to Q, R, and (P \to Q) \wedge R are an instance of it, with \varphi replaced by P \to Q and \psi by R. The middle expression must match exactly, symbol for symbol. The step “0 < \tfrac24 and \tfrac12 < 1, so 0 < 1” is tempting, because \tfrac24 = \tfrac12 and every line in it is true, but it is not an application of \mathrm{Tr}: the two middle expressions are different strings. A checker who had to notice that they are equal would need arithmetic, and the point of a schema is that a checker needs nothing. Compare symbols, not values. Derivations without boxes A single application of a rule is one step. A proof strings steps together, and each step may use what earlier steps produced. The next definition says exactly how. [Box-Free Derivation] Fix a list of rules, each given by schemas. A box-free derivation is a finite list of numbered lines 1, 2, \dots, n, where n \ge 1, each carrying one statement and a justification, such that: 1. the first lines, possibly none and possibly all, are premises, justified by nothing; a short horizontal rule is drawn under the last premise; 2. every later line is justified by one rule of the list, citing earlier lines, and it and the cited lines form an instance of a schema of that rule. The premises of the derivation are its premise lines, and its conclusion is its last line. In words. Clause (i) says where a derivation starts: with the statements it is given. They are not proved, and they need no reason; they are the assumptions the whole derivation works under. Clause (ii) says how it goes on: each further line is one step of one rule, and the only lines it may use are ones already written. The word “earlier” is the only condition on which lines may be cited for now. Section 1.5 adds assumptions made inside boxes, and then “earlier” is refined to “available”: an earlier line may become unusable once the box it sits in has closed. The layout is always the same. Line numbers run down the left, statements sit in the middle, and each justification is on the right: the rule’s name, then the cited line numbers, in the order the schema assigns them. A vertical bar runs down the left of the statements, and a short horizontal rule under the last premise separates what is given from what is derived. The bar does no work yet. From Section 1.5 on, a box draws a second, shorter bar, and the bars beside a line show which assumptions it depends on. The degenerate case is worth a look. A single premise line, with nothing after it, satisfies both clauses: clause (i) holds, and clause (ii) has no lines to speak about. So it is a derivation, and its premise is its conclusion. First derivations Here are three derivations with \mathrm{Tr}, each with the reasoning that found it. The reasoning is the part to watch: a derivation on the page runs from the top down, but it is rarely found that way. [Chaining] Let x, y, u, v, w, z be real numbers. Using the rule \mathrm{Tr} only, write a box-free derivation of each conclusion from the given premises. 1. Premises 0 < x, x < y, y < 1; conclusion 0 < 1. 2. The same premises in the order y < 1, 0 < x, x < y; the same conclusion. 3. Premises u < v, w < z, v < w; conclusion u < z. (a) Idea. The premises form a chain 0 < x < y < 1, in which each link shares its right end with the next link’s left end. So we work forwards, from what we have: chain the first two links at their shared middle x, then chain the result with the third link at the shared middle y. Read it back line by line. Lines 1–3 are the premises. Line 4 says: lines 1 and 2 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr}, line 1 as a < b and line 2 as b < c, with a, b, c replaced by 0, x, y; so we may write 0 < y. Line 5 says the same of lines 4 and 3, with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. The letters are replaced afresh at each use: the b of line 4 has nothing to do with the b of line 5. (b) Idea. The same chain, found the same way. Only the line numbers change. Line 5 is justified “\mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 1”: line 4 is cited first because it plays the part a < b, although line 1 comes first on the page. The justification, not the position, says which line plays which part. (c) Idea. This time the chain is scrambled, so we work backwards, from what we want. The goal u < z can come from \mathrm{Tr} only if we have some u < m and m < z for a single expression m. Which m? The only premise starting with u is u < v, so try m = v. Then u < v is a premise, and the remaining need is v < z: a new, smaller goal. Ask the same question of it. It can come from \mathrm{Tr} with some v < m' and m' < z; the only premise starting with v is v < w, and with m' = w the second need, w < z, is a premise too. The search has reached the premises, and the derivation is its record, written forwards. The search could have started instead from w < z, the premise ending in z: with m = w it needs u < w, which is \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3, and then u < z is \mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 2. That is a different correct derivation. A sequent usually has many, and any one of them establishes it. Part (c) is the first goal-directed search in the book: we asked what the goal needs, turned the need into smaller goals, and stopped when every goal was a premise. Parts (a) and (b) went forwards from the premises instead. From Section 1.3 on, the Ideas do both with the rules of logic, and name the two directions. Line 1 of a derivation is 0 < x and line 3 is x < 1. Which is correct: “4. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3” or “4. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 1”? The first. With the citation “1, 3”, line 1 plays a < b and line 3 plays b < c: a is 0, b is x in both lines, and c is 1, so the new line a < c is 0 < 1. With “3, 1”, line 3 would play a < b and line 1 would play b < c, so b would have to be 1 (from line 3) and 0 (from line 1) at once. What a derivation proves A derivation shows that its conclusion follows from its premises. This is exactly what the sequent of @def-sequent claimed, so the claim can now be made exact. [Derivable] Let \Gamma be a list of statements \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, where n \ge 0, and let \psi be a statement. We say \psi is derivable from \Gamma, and write \Gamma \vdash \psi , if there is a derivation, using the rules of logic, whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi. We write \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi for \Gamma \vdash \psi, and \vdash \psi when \Gamma is empty. In words, four remarks. 1. The sequent is now an exact claim. \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi is the sequent of @def-sequent, and it holds exactly when a derivation of the required kind exists. It is proved by exhibiting one. 2. Which derivations? Until Section 1.5, “derivation” means a box-free derivation (@def-box-free-derivation). Section 1.5 widens the word to allow boxes, and the definition is then read with the wider notion. Nothing proved before changes: a box-free derivation is still a derivation. 3. Not every premise must be used. A derivation may ignore some statements of \Gamma, and it may even have no premise lines at all. It may not use a premise that is not in \Gamma. 4. Relative to a list of rules. The symbol \vdash always refers to a list of rules. From Section 1.3 on, it is the rules of logic introduced so far; adding a rule never destroys a derivation, so a sequent once derived stays derived. Here there are no rules of logic yet, so we name the rules we mean: “\Gamma \vdash \psi with \mathrm{Tr}”, or “with \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}”. For instance, part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation shows 0 < x, \ x < y, \ y < 1 \vdash 0 < 1 with \mathrm{Tr}. In the derivations of the next sections, the capital letters P, Q, R, S stand for arbitrary statements, as in Section 1.1. A derivation written with them proves not one sequent but infinitely many at once, one for each way of putting statements in for the letters. Chapter 3 makes this precise. What sequent “with \mathrm{Tr}” does part (c) of @exm-chaining-derivation show? u < v, \ w < z, \ v < w \vdash u < z with \mathrm{Tr}. The premises of the derivation are lines 1–3, and its last line is u < z. [Derivations, simplest first] Decide whether each of the following is a derivation, and if so, what it shows. 1. The single line 1 \quad P \quad \text{premise}. 2. The empty list, with no lines at all. 3. The derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation, for the list of rules consisting of \mathrm{Tr} alone. (a) Yes. Its only line is a premise, so clause (i) of @def-box-free-derivation holds, and clause (ii) has no lines to speak about. Its last line is P. It shows P \vdash P: every statement is derivable from itself. No rule was used, so this holds whatever the list of rules is. (b) No. The definition asks for n \ge 1 lines, and a derivation must have a last line to be its conclusion. So the empty list derives nothing. In the same way, a list with no premises can never get started with \mathrm{Tr}, \mathrm{Sh}, or any rule that cites at least one line: its first line would have to cite an earlier line, and there is none. Every rule met before Section 1.5 cites at least one line, so until then \vdash \psi holds for no \psi. Section 1.5 changes that. (c) Yes. Lines 1–3 are premises, with the rule drawn under line 3: clause (i). Line 4 cites lines 1 and 2, which are earlier, and lines 1, 2, 4 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr} with a, b, c replaced by 0, x, y. Line 5 cites lines 4 and 3, which are earlier, and lines 4, 3, 5 are an instance with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. So clause (ii) holds for both later lines. The premises are the three premise lines and the conclusion is 0 < 1. A premise is given, not proved. A derivation shows that its conclusion follows from its premises, and \Gamma \vdash \psi says nothing about whether the statements in \Gamma are true. From the false premises 1 < 0 and 0 < -1, the rule \mathrm{Tr} gives 1 < -1. That is a correct derivation with a false conclusion. What a correct derivation guarantees is conditional: if the premises are true, and the rules never lead from true lines to a false one, then the conclusion is true. Reading a derivation Finding a derivation may need an idea, as part (c) of @exm-chaining-derivation did. Checking one never does. For each line after the premises, ask three questions. 1. Which rule? Name the rule the justification cites, and check that it is on the list of rules. 2. Do the cited lines and this line form an instance of that rule’s schema? Find the replacement of the letters: read it off the cited lines in the order the citation gives them, and check that every letter gets the same expression each time it occurs, and that the new line is what the pattern then says. 3. Are the cited lines earlier? Each cited number must be smaller than the number of the line doing the citing. A line that passes all three is correct, whatever it says and whether or not it is true. Here is the check run on part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Rule Cites Instance (the letters’ values) Earlier? -------------- -------------- -------------- -------------------------------- --------------- 1–3 premises — — — 4 \mathrm{Tr} 1, 2 a: 0; b: x; c: y 1, 2 < 4: yes 5 \mathrm{Tr} 4, 3 a: 0; b: y; c: 1 4, 3 < 5: yes --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every line passes, so the list is a derivation. Section 1.5 extends this table, when “earlier” becomes “available”. Finding a derivation may need an idea; checking one never does. A line can fail one question and pass the others. The next example breaks a correct derivation in two ways, each time with the smallest change that does it. [Not a derivation] Each list below is the derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation with one change. Say which of the three questions of “Reading a derivation” fails, and at which line. 1. The statements of lines 4 and 5 are swapped, and each keeps its justification. 2. Line 5 is justified “\mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 4” instead of “\mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 3”. (a) The list is the following. Line 5 passes all three questions, exactly as line 4 did before. Line 4 passes the first two: lines 5, 3, and 4 are an instance of \mathrm{Tr} with a, b, c replaced by 0, y, 1. It fails the third, because it cites line 5, which is not earlier. So the list is not a derivation. (It would also be useless if it were one: its last line is now 0 < y, not 0 < 1.) (b) Line 5 is now “0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 4”. Lines 3 and 4 are earlier, so the third question passes, and the rule is named, so the first passes. The second fails. The citation makes line 3, y < 1, play a < b, so a is y and b is 1; and it makes line 4, 0 < y, play b < c, so b is 0. The letter b cannot be both 1 and 0, so there is no instance. The lines are the right ones in the wrong roles. Change (b) shows why the citation order is part of the justification, and change (a) why the order of the lines is. Exercise C2 below asks what would go wrong if a line were allowed to cite a later one. How this looks in a mathematical proof A proof about sequences might contain the line 0 < \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac{1}{n} \le 1 \qquad \text{for } n \in \nZ_{>0} . It asserts three links: 0 < \frac{1}{n+1}, \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac1n, and \frac1n \le 1. A reader who takes from it a claim about its two ends, 0 < 1, performs two steps in silence. The first is one application of chaining: 0 < \frac{1}{n+1} and \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac1n give 0 < \frac1n. The second joins 0 < \frac1n with \frac1n \le 1, and it is not \mathrm{Tr}: the line \frac1n \le 1 has \le, not <, so the lines do not match the schema. It is a different pattern, “from a < b and b \le c, write a < c”, another true fact about numbers. That is exactly why a justification must name the pattern it uses. “By the chain” does not say which one. Written chains like this one are everywhere in analysis, and they are derivations with the justifications left off. Nobody writes the justifications out in a real proof about numbers. But a reader checking a hard chain does what the table of “Reading a derivation” does: for each step, which fact, applied to which earlier lines. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the definition of a box-free derivation, and of \Gamma \vdash \psi. 2. Fill in the justifications of the following derivation, which uses \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}. 3. Is the following list a derivation with \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}? If not, name the line and the clause of @def-box-free-derivation that fails. “1. 0 < x, premise. 2. x < 1, premise. 3. 0 + 1 < 1 + 1, \mathrm{Sh} \ 4. 4. 0 < 1, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2.” 4. What sequent “with \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}” does the derivation of (b) show? 5. True or false, with a reason: if \Gamma \vdash \psi with \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}, and every statement in \Gamma is true, then \psi is true. (a) A box-free derivation, relative to a list of rules, is a finite list of numbered lines, at least one, each with a statement and a justification, in which the first lines are premises, justified by nothing, and every later line is justified by one rule of the list, citing earlier lines, so that it and the cited lines form an instance of a schema of that rule (@def-box-free-derivation). And \Gamma \vdash \psi means that there is a derivation whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi (@def-derivable). (b) Line 4: \mathrm{Tr} \ 2, 3, with a, b, c replaced by x, y, 5. Line 5: \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 4, with a, b, c replaced by 1, x, 5. Line 6: \mathrm{Sh} \ 5, with a, b replaced by 1, 5 and c by 2. No other justification works: for line 5, the only earlier lines of the form 1 < \dots and \dots < 5 that share a middle are lines 1 and 4. (c) No. Line 3 cites line 4, which is not earlier, so clause (ii) fails at line 3. Every line is an instance of its rule: lines 4, 3 form an instance of \mathrm{Sh} with c replaced by 1, and lines 1, 2, 4 an instance of \mathrm{Tr}. The only fault is the order. (d) 1 < x, \ x < y, \ y < 5 \vdash 1 + 2 < 5 + 2 with \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}. (e) True. Both rules lead from true lines to true lines: if a < b and b < c are true, so is a < c, and if a < b is true, so is a + c < b + c. Go down the derivation: the premises are in \Gamma, so they are true, and each later line comes from earlier, true lines by one of the two rules, so it is true too. Hence the last line, \psi, is true. This is soundness in miniature: Chapter 3 proves it for the rules of logic (@thm-soundness), and makes “go down the derivation” a proof by induction. B. Practice [B1: Shift, then chain] Let x, y, z be real numbers. Using \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh}, derive x + 1 < z from the premises x < y and y + 1 < z. Remember that \mathrm{Sh} writes a + c < b + c literally: no simplification of an expression is a step of the derivation. Then say in one sentence how you found the step that uses \mathrm{Sh}. Line 3 is \mathrm{Sh} on line 1 with a, b, c replaced by x, y, 1. Line 4 is \mathrm{Tr} on lines 3 and 2 with a, b, c replaced by x + 1, y + 1, z; the middle y + 1 is the same string in both cited lines. The step was found backwards: the goal needs a middle expression, premise 2 ends in z and suggests y + 1, and the missing link x + 1 < y + 1 is premise 1 shifted by 1. [B2: Instances] A derivation begins with the premises 1.\ \ 0 < x, \qquad 2.\ \ x < 3, \qquad 3.\ \ 3 < y . Determine which of the following candidate lines 4 are justified. Justify your answer: for each justified one, give the replacement of the letters; for each other one, say which clause of @def-rule-schema fails. 1. 0 < 3, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2. 2. x < y, \mathrm{Tr} \ 2, 3. 3. 0 < y, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3. 4. 0 + 2 < x + 2, \mathrm{Sh} \ 1. 5. x + 1 < 3 + 2, \mathrm{Sh} \ 2. 6. x + y < 3 + y, \mathrm{Sh} \ 2. (a) Justified: a, b, c are 0, x, 3. (b) Justified: a, b, c are x, 3, y. (c) Not justified. Line 1 makes b the expression x, and line 3 makes it 3: the middle letter is not replaced consistently. The line can be derived in two steps (0 < 3 by \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2, then 0 < y from that line and line 3), but not in this one. (d) Justified: a, b, c are 0, x, 2. The rule writes 0 + 2, not 2. (e) Not justified. The left side forces c to be 1 and the right side forces c to be 2; the letter c is not replaced consistently. The statement x + 1 < 3 + 2 is even true whenever line 2 is, but \mathrm{Sh} does not write it. (f) Justified: a, b, c are x, 3, y. The letter c may be replaced by any expression, including one with a letter in it. [B3: How many steps a chain takes] 1. Write the chain 0 < \tfrac14 < \tfrac13 < \tfrac12 as a derivation, with its three links as premises and the conclusion 0 < \tfrac12, using \mathrm{Tr}, forwards from the first link as in part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation. 2. A chain e_0 < e_1 < \dots < e_m has m \ge 1 links. Forward chaining, as in (a), writes the links as premises and then joins the first link with the next, again and again. How many applications of \mathrm{Tr} does it use to reach e_0 < e_m? (a) (b) m - 1. Each application takes the line e_0 < e_k reached so far and the next link e_k < e_{k+1}, and writes e_0 < e_{k+1}, so it absorbs one more link. The first link needs no application, and each of the other m - 1 links needs one. In (a), m = 3 and there are 2 applications; when m = 1, the single premise is already the conclusion. No cleverer derivation does better: every derivation of e_0 < e_m from the links with \mathrm{Tr} uses at least m - 1 applications. We do not prove this here; the proof is an induction, the method of Chapter 3 (@ax-induction), and nothing in the book depends on it. C. Going deeper [C1: A bad rule] Add to \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh} a third rule, \mathrm{Flip}: from a < b, write b < a. 1. Derive 1 < 0 from the premise 0 < 1, using \mathrm{Flip}. 2. Explain why a checker following “Reading a derivation” would accept your derivation. 3. What property do \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh} have that \mathrm{Flip} lacks? (a) (b) Line 1 is a premise. Line 2 names a rule on the list, cites line 1, which is earlier, and lines 1, 2 are an instance of the schema of \mathrm{Flip} with a replaced by 0 and b by 1. All three questions pass. The checker never asks whether a line is true, only whether it matches a rule, so a bad rule is invisible to it. (c) \mathrm{Tr} and \mathrm{Sh} never lead from true lines to a false one (A1(e)). \mathrm{Flip} does: from the true line 0 < 1 it writes the false line 1 < 0. With such a rule, a derivation from true premises could end anywhere, so checking is only as good as the rules checked against. Chapter 3 proves that the rules of logic have the good property, and calls it soundness (@thm-soundness). [C2: Find the error] A student offers the following list as a derivation of 0 < 4 with \mathrm{Tr}. 1. Is 0 < 1, \ 1 < 2, \ 2 < 3, \ 3 < 4 \vdash 0 < 4 with \mathrm{Tr}? 2. Is the list a derivation? If not, name the line that fails and the clause of @def-box-free-derivation it breaks. 3. The two lines “1. 0 < 0, \mathrm{Tr} \ 2, 2” and “2. 0 < 0, \mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 1” would each pass the first two questions of “Reading a derivation”. Use them to explain why a line may cite only earlier lines. (a) Yes. Swap lines 5 and 6 and renumber: Each later line cites earlier lines and is an instance of \mathrm{Tr}, with middles 1, 2, 3. So the student’s conclusion is derivable (and true). (b) No. Line 5 cites line 6, which is not earlier, so clause (ii) fails at line 5. Every line is an instance of \mathrm{Tr}: lines 6, 3, 5 with middle 2; lines 1, 2, 6 with middle 1; lines 5, 4, 7 with middle 3. So the only fault is the order. That the conclusion is true and derivable does not repair the list: a derivation must meet the definition line by line. (c) Line 1 cites line 2 twice, and line 2 cites line 1 twice. Each is an instance of \mathrm{Tr} with a, b, c all replaced by 0: from 0 < 0 and 0 < 0, write 0 < 0. So if lines could cite later lines, these two lines would justify each other, in a loop that rests on no premise, and the false statement 0 < 0 would be derivable from nothing. Requiring cited lines to be earlier rules out every such loop: following the citations backwards from any line, the numbers go down, so they must end, and they can end only at premises. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: says the conclusion is derivable and gives a correct derivation (every line an instance, every citation earlier). - 3: names line 5 as the faulty line and the broken clause: a cited line must be earlier. - 1: notes that the other lines are instances of \mathrm{Tr}, so the order is the only fault. - 3: explains with the loop why later citations cannot be allowed: the two lines justify each other, rest on no premise, and give a false line. Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the list a derivation because its conclusion is true; blaming line 7, which cites line 5, an earlier line.

title: 1.3 Conjunction: the Rules for And
content: Conjunction: the Rules for And Section 1.2 set up the format of a derivation and practiced it on two toy rules about numbers, which the book now puts away. This section introduces the first two rules of logic, one for proving a statement of the form “P and Q” and one for using it. Both are defined by their schemas, in the sense of @def-rule-schema, and every derivation below is checked against those schemas and nothing else. The rules are so simple that we can spend the section on something harder: how to find a derivation. Two questions will organize every search in Part 0, and they appear here for the first time: what does the goal ask for, and what do the lines we already have allow? A conjunction in disguise Much of analysis is written in chains such as 0 < x < 1. As Section 1.1 observed, the chain is a conjunction in disguise: it says 0 < x and x < 1, that is, (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1). Watch what proofs do with it. A proof that uses 0 < x < 1 usually needs only one half at a time. “Since 0 < x < 1, in particular x > 0, so we may divide by x.” The proof takes the conjunction apart and keeps the piece it wants. A proof that proves 0 < x < 1 must prove both halves. It shows 0 < x, then shows x < 1, and then writes “hence 0 < x < 1”. Nothing else will do: one half is not the whole claim. Section 1.1 previewed these two moves in a table, informally. Here they become rules, stated as patterns of lines, so that a derivation using them can be checked by matching, exactly as Tr was matched in Section 1.2. The two rules Recall from @def-rule-schema that a schema has given lines at the top and exactly one new line at the bottom, whose justification names the rule and cites the given lines. From this section on, the letters in a schema are the Greek letters \varphi (“phi”), \psi (“psi”) and \chi (“chi”), and each stands for an arbitrary statement. A use of the rule replaces each Greek letter by one statement, the same statement everywhere the letter occurs. To prove “\varphi and \psi”, prove each; to use it, take either. [Rules for Conjunction] The first schema is the rule \rulename{\wedge I} (and-introduction). The second and third are the two forms of the rule \rulename{\wedge E} (and-elimination), one writing the left conjunct and one the right. Read the schemas clause by clause. \rulename{\wedge I}, the given lines. Two lines, \varphi and \psi, must stand earlier in the derivation. They may be anywhere above line k, in either order, with other lines between them; the schema draws them next to each other only to save space. \rulename{\wedge I}, the order of the citation. The justification “\rulename{\wedge I} i, j” puts the statement of line i on the left of the new conjunction and the statement of line j on the right. So the citation, not the position of the lines, decides the order of the conjuncts: if line 3 is Q and line 2 is P, then “\rulename{\wedge I} 3, 2” writes Q \wedge P, and “\rulename{\wedge I} 2, 3” writes P \wedge Q. \rulename{\wedge I}, the degenerate case. Nothing says that i and j are different lines. With i = j, the letters \varphi and \psi are replaced by the same statement, and the rule writes \varphi \wedge \varphi. It is a silly line, and a legal one. \rulename{\wedge E}, one conjunction, either conjunct. One given line, whose statement is a conjunction \varphi \wedge \psi. The rule writes one conjunct per application: to get both halves, apply it twice, on two lines, each citing the same conjunction. That is why the rule has two schemas and not one schema with two new lines. \rulename{\wedge E} looks only at the main connective. To apply \rulename{\wedge E} to a line, we must see the line’s statement as \varphi \wedge \psi, and that means its main connective (@def-main-connective) must be \wedge. The two conjuncts are then the two parts that this \wedge joins, and nothing smaller. Take (P \wedge Q) \wedge R. Its main connective is the second \wedge, so the replacement is \varphi \coloneqq P \wedge Q, \qquad \psi \coloneqq R , and one application of \rulename{\wedge E} writes P \wedge Q or R. It does not write P, and it does not write Q. Getting to Q takes a second application, to the new line P \wedge Q. What the rules do not say. They say nothing about what \varphi and \psi mean. A line is justified by \rulename{\wedge I} or \rulename{\wedge E} when it and the lines it cites are an instance of a schema (@def-rule-schema), and that can be seen by looking at symbols. \rulename{\wedge E} reaches one layer at a time. From line 1, (P \wedge Q) \wedge R, the line “Q — \rulename{\wedge E} 1” is not an instance of either \rulename{\wedge E} schema, because line 1’s conjuncts are P \wedge Q and R. The line is wrong as a justification even though Q does follow; the repair costs one line, P \wedge Q by \rulename{\wedge E} 1 first, then Q from it. Which statements can \rulename{\wedge E} write, in one application each, from the line (P \wedge Q) \wedge (R \wedge S)? Only P \wedge Q and R \wedge S. The main connective is the middle \wedge, so \varphi is P \wedge Q and \psi is R \wedge S. Each of P, Q, R, S needs a second application, to one of those two lines. Line 2 is P \wedge Q and line 5 is R. Which line does “\rulename{\wedge I} 5, 2” justify, and which does “\rulename{\wedge I} 2, 5” justify? “\rulename{\wedge I} 5, 2” justifies R \wedge (P \wedge Q), and “\rulename{\wedge I} 2, 5” justifies (P \wedge Q) \wedge R. The first line cited becomes the left conjunct, and a compound statement placed inside a conjunction keeps its brackets. Why these rules. They are exactly the two moves of the opening paragraph, “prove both” and “use either”, and nothing more. Section 1.1’s slogan said that each connective comes with a way to prove it and a way to use it; for \wedge, the way to prove it is \rulename{\wedge I} and the way to use it is \rulename{\wedge E}. Why they are safe. If the given lines are true statements, so is the new line: if \varphi and \psi are both true, so is \varphi \wedge \psi, and if \varphi \wedge \psi is true, so is each conjunct. Chapter 3 proves this property for every rule of the calculus at once, and calls it soundness (@thm-soundness). Two directions of reasoning A derivation has premises at the top and its goal, the conclusion we want, at the bottom. Between them is a gap, and finding a derivation means filling the gap. There are two places to start. From the goal. Ask: what is the goal’s main connective? If it is \wedge, the last line can be written by \rulename{\wedge I}, and then the goal \varphi \wedge \psi splits into two subgoals, \varphi and \psi, each to be reached on some line above. This is goal-directed reasoning. It works backwards, from the bottom of the gap upwards, and its first question is which introduction rule builds the goal’s main connective. From the premises. Ask: what are the main connectives of the lines we already have? A line whose main connective is \wedge can be taken apart by \rulename{\wedge E}, and each conjunct becomes a new line to work with. This is premise-directed reasoning. It works forwards, from the top of the gap downwards, and its first question is which elimination rule uses the line’s main connective. Work from both ends: take the premises apart, and build the goal from its parts. The derivation is finished when the two ends meet: when every subgoal read off the goal is a line obtained from the premises. Section 1.2 already found one derivation backwards, from the goal u < z of part (c) of @exm-chaining-derivation; the toy rule Tr played the part that introduction rules play from now on. Each later section of this chapter adds one rule to one of the two lists (an introduction rule to the goal-directed list, an elimination rule to the premise-directed one), and Section 2.6 collects the lists into a method. First derivations In each example below, the Idea says, for each line, whether it was found from the goal or from a premise. [Three warm-ups] Give a derivation of each sequent. 1. P, \ Q \vdash Q \wedge P. 2. P \vdash P \wedge P. 3. P \wedge Q \vdash Q. (a) Idea. The goal Q \wedge P has main connective \wedge, so, goal-directed, its last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals Q and P. Both subgoals are premises, so the two ends meet at once. The citation is “2, 1”, because Q, on line 2, must be the left conjunct. Written “\rulename{\wedge I} 1, 2”, the line would have to be P \wedge Q. (b) Idea. The goal is again a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge I}, with the subgoals P and P. One premise meets both. This is the degenerate case i = j of \rulename{\wedge I}. (c) Idea. The goal Q is a letter, with no main connective, so the goal suggests no rule. The premise has main connective \wedge, so, premise-directed, take it apart; its right conjunct is the goal. Line 2 is the second form of \rulename{\wedge E}, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q. The three derivations are box-free derivations in the sense of @def-box-free-derivation, with \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E} as the list of rules: premises first, and every later line an instance of a schema whose given lines are earlier. By @def-derivable they show the three sequents. When the goal is a letter, as in (c), only the premises can suggest a step. When every subgoal is a premise, as in (a) and (b), the premises need no taking apart. The next derivation needs both ends. The first result is that the order of a conjunction does not matter. [Conjunction Commutes] P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P. Write the premise at the top, the goal at the bottom, and leave a gap (left picture; the lines carry the numbers they will have at the end). Start from the goal. Its main connective is \wedge, so the last line will be \rulename{\wedge I}, and we need P and Q on earlier lines (right picture: two subgoals, not yet justified). Now start from the premise. Its main connective is \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} gives P and gives Q. That closes the gap: the pieces the goal asks for are the pieces the premise supplies. The following is a box-free derivation with the single premise P \wedge Q and last line Q \wedge P. Lines 2 and 3 are the two forms of \rulename{\wedge E} applied to line 1, and line 4 is \rulename{\wedge I} applied to lines 3 and 2, in that order, so line 3 becomes the left half. By @def-derivable, P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P. Read back in words, the derivation is a short paragraph: We are given that P and Q. In particular P holds, and in particular Q holds. So Q and P both hold. Each sentence is one line, and each “in particular” is one application of \rulename{\wedge E}. Nothing in the derivation looks at what P and Q say. With P: “0 < x” and Q: “x < 1” it turns “0 < x and x < 1” into “x < 1 and 0 < x”; with any other two statements it does the same. Because the letters stand for arbitrary statements, one derivation written with letters proves every such instance at once. The second result is that the grouping of a conjunction does not matter either. It needs the premise taken apart in two layers. [Conjunction Is Associative] (P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R). From the goal: its main connective is the outer \wedge, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with the subgoals P and Q \wedge R. The second subgoal is itself a conjunction, so it is again \rulename{\wedge I}, with the subgoals Q and R. The goal-directed search stops at the letters P, Q, R. From the premise: its main connective is also an outer \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} gives P \wedge Q and R. The line P \wedge Q is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge E} again gives P and Q. The premise-directed search also stops at the three letters, and the ends meet there. Since \rulename{\wedge E} reaches one layer at a time, the premise must be peeled in two rounds. The following is a box-free derivation with the single premise (P \wedge Q) \wedge R and last line P \wedge (Q \wedge R). Lines 2 and 3 apply \rulename{\wedge E} to line 1, with \varphi \coloneqq P \wedge Q and \psi \coloneqq R. Lines 4 and 5 apply \rulename{\wedge E} to line 2, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q. Line 6 applies \rulename{\wedge I} to lines 5 and 3, and line 7 applies \rulename{\wedge I} to lines 4 and 6, with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q \wedge R. By @def-derivable, (P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R). The lines could come in other orders. Line 3 could come after lines 4 and 5, for instance, since it is used only at line 6. What cannot move is the dependence: every line must come after each line it cites. The converse, P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \wedge R, is derived the same way, peeling the premise’s inner conjunction on the right instead of the left; Exercise B1 asks you to write it out. With both directions, the brackets in a chain of conjunctions carry no information, which is why the chain 0 < x < 1 < y is written without any. A line is not used up A line of a derivation is a statement that has been established. Citing it does not consume it: it can be cited again, by as many later lines as need it. The derivation of P \wedge Q, \ R \vdash (P \wedge R) \wedge (Q \wedge R) shows this. From the goal: \rulename{\wedge I} at the bottom, with subgoals P \wedge R and Q \wedge R; each is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge I} again, with subgoals P, R and Q, R. From the premises: \rulename{\wedge E} on line 1 gives P and Q, and R is already a premise. Both subgoals that need R cite the same line 2. Line 2 is cited by lines 5 and 6, and line 1 by lines 3 and 4. In a written proof this is the everyday “we use the hypothesis x > 0 again”. Take everything apart, rebuild in the new order The last derivation of the section rearranges four letters: (P \wedge Q) \wedge (R \wedge S) \vdash (S \wedge Q) \wedge (P \wedge R). From the premise: two layers of \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} twice on line 1 and then twice on each of the two new lines, which leaves the four letters on lines 4 to 7. From the goal: two layers of \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge I} builds S \wedge Q and P \wedge R from the letters and then joins them. There is nothing to choose; the only care needed is the order of each citation. The recipe visibly does not depend on these particular letters or brackets. Take the premise apart with \rulename{\wedge E} until only letters remain, then build the goal from the letters with \rulename{\wedge I}, inside out. It works whenever the premise and the goal are both built from letters by \wedge alone and every letter of the goal occurs in the premise, whatever the bracketing and the order on either side. So “\wedge is commutative and associative” is, in the end, the observation that \rulename{\wedge E} can always take a conjunction down to its letters and \rulename{\wedge I} can always build one back up. (Chapter 3’s completeness theorem, @thm-completeness, gives another reason, from the truth tables.) How this looks in a mathematical proof Real proofs mix the logical rules with facts about their subject. The rules supply the joints; the facts supply the content. [A product of numbers in the unit interval] Let x and y be real numbers with 0 < x < 1 and 0 < y < 1. Show that 0 < xy < 1, and name the rule behind each logical step. The hypothesis 0 < x < 1 is the conjunction (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1). By \rulename{\wedge E} we have 0 < x and x < 1 separately, and likewise 0 < y and y < 1. Since x > 0 and y > 0, the product xy is positive. Since y < 1 and x > 0, multiplying by x gives xy < x; together with x < 1 this gives xy < 1. These steps are school algebra, not logic. Finally, from 0 < xy and xy < 1, \rulename{\wedge I} gives (0 < xy) \wedge (xy < 1), which is 0 < xy < 1. As a derivation, the same proof reads as follows. Lines 7 and 8 are justified “algebra”: each is a step by a fact about numbers used as a rule, exactly as Tr was used in Section 1.2, and not a rule of logic. Line 7 uses “a product of two positive numbers is positive”; line 8 uses “multiplying an inequality by a positive number keeps its direction”, then the pattern of Tr. The facts about numbers supply the content of the solution; the rules supply the joints, taking statements apart and putting the pieces back together.
