The goal-directed reading is visible in the prose too: “show 0 < xy < 1” is a conjunction, so the solution sets itself two subgoals, and it says “finally” when the two meet. Common errors The warning above covered \rulename{\wedge E} applied through a layer. Two more errors are common. \rulename{\wedge E} applies only to a line whose main connective is \wedge. The line (P \wedge Q) \to R contains a \wedge, but its main connective is \to, so “P — \rulename{\wedge E} 1” is illegal. With x a real number, P: “x > 0”, Q: “x > 1” and R: “x^2 > 1”, the premise “if x > 0 and x > 1, then x^2 > 1” is true for every x, yet at x = -1 the line x > 0 is false. The illegal step leads from a true premise to a false line, so no rule that allowed it could be safe. The third error is a mismatch between the citation and the line. Suppose line 3 is Q and line 2 is P, and someone writes “P \wedge Q — \rulename{\wedge I} 3, 2”. The statement P \wedge Q is fine, and it does follow from lines 2 and 3. But “\rulename{\wedge I} 3, 2” names line 3 as the left conjunct, so the line it justifies is Q \wedge P. A checker compares the line with the citation and rejects it; the repair is to write “2, 3”. This looks pedantic, and it is the point: a justification that says something false about the line it justifies cannot be checked by matching, and then nothing can be checked by matching. What the rules sound like Every rule is something mathematicians already say. The table pairs each rule of this section with the sentence that uses it in a written proof and, for readers who meet a proof assistant, with the Lean code that performs it (h.1 names the left half of a hypothesis h). Nothing later depends on the last column. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean --------------------- --------------------------------------- ------------------------- \rulename{\wedge I} “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor \rulename{\wedge E} “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Section 1.4 adds the first rule for “implies”, and the table grows with each new rule. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the three schemas of @def-rules-conjunction from memory, and name the rule of each. 2. Which statements does one application of \rulename{\wedge E} give from the line P \wedge (Q \wedge R)? 3. True or false, with a reason: \rulename{\wedge E} may be applied to the line P \wedge Q \to R. 4. In the derivation in the proof of @prp-and-associative, why must line 2 come before line 4? 5. Fill in the justifications (i)–(iv) of the following derivation. (a) See @def-rules-conjunction: \rulename{\wedge I} has given lines i: \varphi and j: \psi and new line k: \varphi \wedge \psi, cited “\rulename{\wedge I} i, j”; the two forms of \rulename{\wedge E} each have the given line i: \varphi \wedge \psi and the new line k: \varphi, respectively \psi, cited “\rulename{\wedge E} i”. (b) P, or Q \wedge R. The main connective is the first \wedge, so \varphi is P and \psi is Q \wedge R. (c) False. By the conventions of Section 1.1, \wedge binds more tightly than \to, so the line is (P \wedge Q) \to R, whose main connective is \to. It is not of the form \varphi \wedge \psi. (d) Line 4 is P, obtained by \rulename{\wedge E} from line 2, P \wedge Q. A rule may cite only earlier lines (@def-box-free-derivation), and P cannot be obtained from line 1 in one step, since line 1’s conjuncts are P \wedge Q and R. (e) (i) \rulename{\wedge E} 1; (ii) \rulename{\wedge E} 1; (iii) \rulename{\wedge E} 3; (iv) \rulename{\wedge I} 4, 2. B. Practice [B1: The other grouping] Give a derivation of P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \wedge R. For each line, say whether you found it from the goal or from the premise. From the goal: \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals P \wedge Q and R, and P \wedge Q by \rulename{\wedge I} from P and Q. From the premise: \rulename{\wedge E} gives P and Q \wedge R, and \rulename{\wedge E} on Q \wedge R gives Q and R. Lines 2–5 were found from the premise, lines 6–7 from the goal. With @prp-and-associative, each of (P \wedge Q) \wedge R and P \wedge (Q \wedge R) is derivable from the other. [B2: Annotating a proof] Let x and y be real numbers. Here is a proof. Let 1 < x < 2 and 3 < y < 4. Then 4 < x + y < 6. Write out the proof in full, naming each use of \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{\wedge I}, and marking the steps that are school algebra rather than logic. The hypotheses are the conjunctions (1 < x) \wedge (x < 2) and (3 < y) \wedge (y < 4), and the goal is (4 < x + y) \wedge (x + y < 6). By \rulename{\wedge E}, four times, we have 1 < x, x < 2, 3 < y, and y < 4 separately. Adding 1 < x and 3 < y gives 1 + 3 < x + y, that is, 4 < x + y (school algebra: two inequalities in the same direction may be added). Adding x < 2 and y < 4 gives x + y < 6 (school algebra again). Finally \rulename{\wedge I} joins 4 < x + y and x + y < 6 into 4 < x + y < 6. As a derivation it has the same shape as the one in @exm-product-in-unit-interval: two premises, four \rulename{\wedge E} lines, two lines justified “algebra”, and one \rulename{\wedge I} line. [B3: Which lines are instances?] A derivation begins as follows. Determine which of the following candidates for line 4 are correct. Justify your answer. 1. P — \rulename{\wedge E} 1. 2. R — \rulename{\wedge E} 1. 3. (Q \wedge R) \wedge S — \rulename{\wedge I} 3, 2. 4. S \wedge (Q \wedge R) — \rulename{\wedge I} 3, 2. 5. Q — \rulename{\wedge E} 3. (a) Correct: the first form of \rulename{\wedge E} with \varphi \coloneqq P and \psi \coloneqq Q \wedge R. (b) Incorrect. Line 1’s conjuncts are P and Q \wedge R; R lies one layer deeper. “R — \rulename{\wedge E} 3” would be correct. (c) Correct: \rulename{\wedge I} with line 3 on the left and line 2 on the right, \varphi \coloneqq Q \wedge R and \psi \coloneqq S. (d) Incorrect. The citation “3, 2” puts line 3 on the left, so it justifies (Q \wedge R) \wedge S, not S \wedge (Q \wedge R). “\rulename{\wedge I} 2, 3” would be correct. (e) Correct: the first form of \rulename{\wedge E} with \varphi \coloneqq Q and \psi \coloneqq R. C. Going deeper [C1: What conjunction cannot do] Show that no box-free derivation whose only premise is P \wedge Q, and whose only rules are \rulename{\wedge I} and \rulename{\wedge E}, has a line whose statement contains the letter R. Deduce that, with these two rules, P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge R cannot be shown. [Hint 1] Suppose some line does contain R, and look at the first such line. [Hint 2] That first line is not a premise. Which rule wrote it, and which letters can that rule write? Suppose, for a contradiction, that some line of such a derivation contains R. The derivation has finitely many lines, so there is a first such line; call it line k. Every line before line k is free of R. Line k is not a premise, because every premise is P \wedge Q, which does not contain R. So line k is justified by one of the two rules, citing earlier lines (@def-box-free-derivation). If it is \rulename{\wedge I}, citing lines i and j, then its statement is \varphi \wedge \psi, where \varphi and \psi are the statements of lines i and j. Both are earlier than k, so neither contains R, and neither does \varphi \wedge \psi. If it is \rulename{\wedge E}, citing line i, then its statement is one conjunct of the statement of line i: a part of it. Line i is earlier than k and free of R, so the part is free of R too. Either way line k does not contain R, which contradicts the choice of k. So no line contains R. In particular no such derivation has the last line P \wedge R, and P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge R cannot be shown with these rules. The argument, “look at the first bad line; it cannot be a premise, and no rule can create it from good lines”, is an argument by induction on the lines of a derivation. Chapter 3 makes such arguments exact (@thm-strong-induction); the proof of @thm-soundness is one. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: considers a first line containing R, and says why a first one exists (finitely many lines); or, equally, goes down the derivation line by line, showing each line free of R because every line it cites is. - 2: rules out a premise. - 2: \rulename{\wedge I} case: the new line is built from the statements of two earlier, R-free lines. - 2: \rulename{\wedge E} case: the new line is part of an earlier, R-free line. - 2: concludes that no line contains R, and so that P \wedge R is never a last line. Fatal errors (0 for the step): arguing about one particular derivation instead of every derivation; arguing that R is “not true” instead of about which symbols the rules can write. [C2: A shortcut through two layers] A student offers the following derivation of P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash Q \wedge P. 1. Is line 2 an instance of a schema of \rulename{\wedge E}? Justify your answer. 2. Is the conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. 3. The step at line 2 never leads from a true line to a false one. Why must a checker still reject it? 4. State, as a schema, a rule \wedge\mathrm{E}^{*} that would allow line 2. Show that every use of \wedge\mathrm{E}^{*} in a derivation can be replaced by two uses of \rulename{\wedge E}. (a) No. To match line 1 with \varphi \wedge \psi, we must read \varphi and \psi off line 1’s main connective, which is the first \wedge: \varphi is P and \psi is Q \wedge R. So \rulename{\wedge E} writes P or Q \wedge R, and Q is neither. (b) Yes. Insert the missing layer. (c) A derivation is checked by matching each line against the schemas of the rules on the list, and line 2 matches none. A checker that also accepted steps that “obviously follow” would need to understand the statements, and then its verdict would be only as reliable as that understanding. The steps that seem obvious are the ones nobody looks at twice, and they are where unnoticed errors live. (This item is not a find-the-error exercise in the usual sense: the step has no counterexample, since it never leads from truth to falsehood. It is simply not a step of this calculus.) (d) One such rule, in schema form: Suppose line k of a derivation is \psi, justified “\wedge\mathrm{E}^{*} i”, with line i the statement \varphi \wedge (\psi \wedge \chi). Replace line k by two lines: first \psi \wedge \chi, justified \rulename{\wedge E} i (the second form, with the conjuncts \varphi and \psi \wedge \chi), then \psi, justified by \rulename{\wedge E} citing that new line (the first form, with the conjuncts \psi and \chi). Renumber the later lines, and every citation of them, up by one; a later citation of line k now cites the second new line, which carries the same statement \psi. Every other line is unchanged and still cites earlier lines. Doing this for each \wedge\mathrm{E}^{*} line, one at a time, gives a derivation with the same premises and last line that uses only \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{\wedge I}. A rule that can always be replaced in this way adds convenience and no new power; Section 2.3 calls such a rule a derived rule. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) no, reading \varphi and \psi off the main connective of line 1. - 2: (b) yes, with a correct derivation. - 2: (c) checking is by matching the schemas; a step that is not an instance is rejected, whether or not it is true. - 2: (d) a correct schema, one given line and one new line. - 2: (d) the replacement by two \rulename{\wedge E} lines, with the renumbering of later citations. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming the conclusion is not derivable; offering a counterexample to line 2.

title: 1.4 Using an Implication: Modus Ponens
content: Using an Implication: Modus Ponens Section 1.3 gave the two rules for “and”. This section gives one rule for “implies”: the rule that uses an implication already in hand. Proving an implication needs a new device, an assumption with a boundary, and that is the subject of Section 1.5. Using one needs nothing new, and it is what a proof does every time it applies a theorem. The rule is short; the work of the section is to see exactly what it allows and what it does not, and to find chains of implications both forwards and backwards. Four cards Before the rule, a puzzle about what “if … then” says. Four cards Each of four cards has a whole number on one side and a color on the other. They lie on a table showing 6, \qquad 7, \qquad \text{red}, \qquad \text{green} . Someone claims: if a card shows an even number on one side, then its other side is red. Which cards must be turned over to find out whether the claim is true of these four cards? Decide before reading the solution. The claim is an implication about each card: if its number is even, its color is red. Take the cards one at a time and ask whether the hidden side could show that the claim is false. The claim is false for a card exactly when that card has an even number and is not red. The card showing 6. Its number is even, so the hypothesis of the implication holds, and the claim says its other side is red. If that side is green, the claim is false. This card must be turned. The card showing 7. Its number is odd, so the hypothesis fails, and the claim says nothing about this card. Whatever its color, the card cannot contradict the claim. Leave it. The red card. Its color is the conclusion of the implication. If its number is even, the card fits the claim; if its number is odd, the card still fits, since the claim says only what even cards look like and nothing about which cards are red. No hidden number can contradict the claim. Leave it. The green card. If its number is even, it is an even card that is not red, and the claim is false. This card must be turned. So the answer is the 6 and the green card. Many people, asked this, choose the 6 and the red card. The 6 is right. The red card is the tell: choosing it means reading the claim as if it also said “if a card is red, then its number is even”, which is the converse. An implication and its converse are different claims, and the claim here is only the first. The two cards that matter are the two ways an implication meets a case. The 6 shows the hypothesis, and an implication together with its hypothesis gives its conclusion: that is the rule of this section. The red card shows the conclusion, and an implication together with its conclusion gives nothing: that is the most important thing the rule does not allow. The green card shows that the conclusion fails; saying exactly what follows from that needs the rules for “not”, and Section 2.3 returns to this card with the rule behind it, called modus tollens. The rule An implication fires on its hypothesis, and gives its conclusion. [Implication Elimination] This rule is called \rulename{{\to}E} (implication-elimination, or modus ponens). Read the schema clause by clause, as we read those of @def-rules-conjunction. Two given lines. One line is an implication \varphi \to \psi, the other is \varphi. Both must stand earlier in the derivation; they may be anywhere above line k, in either order. Reading the implication. To see a line as \varphi \to \psi, its main connective (@def-main-connective) must be \to. Then \varphi, the hypothesis, is everything that this \to joins on its left, and \psi, the conclusion, is everything on its right. In (P \wedge Q) \to R, the hypothesis is P \wedge Q and the conclusion is R. In P \to (Q \to R), the hypothesis is P and the conclusion is Q \to R, itself an implication. The hypothesis must match exactly. Line j must be the statement \varphi, symbol for symbol: the letter \varphi occurs in both given lines, and a use of the rule replaces it by the same statement in both (@def-rule-schema). A part of \varphi will not do, and neither will a statement that “says the same thing”. From (P \wedge Q) \to R and Q \wedge P, the rule gives nothing, although Q \wedge P and P \wedge Q are each derivable from the other (@prp-and-commutes); the hypothesis must first be rebuilt, in the right order, by \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{\wedge I}. The new line is the conclusion, and only the conclusion. The rule writes \psi, the whole of what stands right of the main \to. If \psi is Q \wedge R, the rule writes Q \wedge R, and getting Q takes one more line, by \rulename{\wedge E}. The citation. We cite the implication first and the hypothesis second: “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j”, as in the schema. Unlike the citation of \rulename{\wedge I}, the order here cannot change the new line, since only \psi can come out; the fixed order just makes every \rulename{{\to}E} line read the same way. A degenerate case. The statements \varphi and \psi may be the same. From P \to P and P, the rule writes P, which was already there. The line is legal and useless. Why this rule. It is what “by Theorem so-and-so” means. A theorem of school algebra says: if a < b and b < c, then a < c. Take its instance with a = \sqrt{2}, b = 1.5, and c = 2 (passing from “for all a, b, c” to one instance is a rule of its own, which Chapter 4 states; here we take the instance as given): \bigl( (\sqrt{2} < 1.5) \wedge (1.5 < 2) \bigr) \to \sqrt{2} < 2 . We know \sqrt{2} < 1.5, because 1.5^2 = 2.25 > 2, and we know 1.5 < 2. Then \rulename{\wedge I} builds the hypothesis (\sqrt{2} < 1.5) \wedge (1.5 < 2), and \rulename{{\to}E} gives \sqrt{2} < 2. Every application of a theorem has this shape: check the theorem’s hypotheses, assemble them into exactly the theorem’s hypothesis, and fire. Why it is safe. If \varphi \to \psi is true and \varphi is true, then \psi is true; that is what “if \varphi, then \psi” asserts. Chapter 3 proves this for the rule as part of the soundness theorem (@thm-soundness). Why nothing more. From \varphi \to \psi alone, \rulename{{\to}E} cannot fire: an implication by itself asserts neither its hypothesis nor its conclusion. And \rulename{{\to}E} does not run backwards: from \varphi \to \psi together with its conclusion \psi, it gives nothing about \varphi. That pattern, \varphi \to \psi, \ \psi \ \text{ therefore } \ \varphi , is called affirming the consequent, and it is the red card of the puzzle. It is not an instance of \rulename{{\to}E}, because the second given line of \rulename{{\to}E} must be the hypothesis \varphi, and here it is the conclusion \psi. It can lead from true premises to a false conclusion: the Quick check on the form of an argument in Section 1.1 took “if n is divisible by 4, then n is even” and “n is even” at n = 2, both true, where “n is divisible by 4” is false. It is also the step that would repair Argument B of Section 1.1. Chapter 3 proves more: no derivation of P \to Q, \ Q \vdash P exists at all, whichever rules of Chapters 1 and 2 it uses (@cor-refuting-row). Affirming the consequent looks like modus ponens and is not. Let x be a real number. “If x > 2, then x^2 > 4” is true for every x, and at x = -3 we have x^2 = 9 > 4; but x > 2 is false there. From an implication and its conclusion, nothing follows about the hypothesis. Line 1 is P \to (Q \to R). What does \rulename{{\to}E} give from line 1 and a line Q? And from line 1 and a line P? From line 1 and Q: nothing. The main connective of line 1 is the first \to, so its hypothesis is P, and Q does not match it. From line 1 and P: the conclusion Q \to R. A second application, to Q \to R and the line Q, would then give R. At this point an implication can be used but not proved. A derivation can write an implication only by taking it out of a line that already contains it: \rulename{\wedge E} applied to (P \to Q) \wedge R, or \rulename{{\to}E} applied to P \to (Q \to R) and P. No rule so far builds a new \to. Section 1.5 gives the rule that does. Chains of implications With \rulename{{\to}E}, a derivation can pass along a chain: from P and P \to Q to Q, from Q and Q \to R to R, and so on. Such a chain can be found from either end. Forwards, from the premises. An available implication (for now, one on an earlier line) whose hypothesis is also available can fire: \rulename{{\to}E} writes its conclusion, which becomes available in turn and may be the hypothesis of another implication. Keep firing until the goal appears. This is premise-directed reasoning, as in Section 1.3: the premise’s main connective, \to, picks the elimination rule that uses it. Backwards, from the goal. Suppose the goal is \psi. Look among the available lines for an implication whose conclusion is \psi, say \varphi \to \psi. If there is one, it is enough to reach \varphi: then \rulename{{\to}E} writes \psi. So \varphi becomes the new goal, and we repeat. This is goal-directed reasoning, but of a new kind. In Section 1.3 the goal’s main connective chose an introduction rule. Here the goal may be a letter, with no main connective at all, and it still directs the search: it tells us which implication to look for. The two directions meet in the middle, when a line reached forwards is a goal reached backwards. In written mathematics the backward step has a standard phrase, “to show \psi, it suffices to show \varphi”, and Chapter 5 collects it with the other phrases that stand for rules. The premises are P, P \to R, Q \to S, and R \to S, and the goal is S. Search backwards: which implications could give the goal, and which of them leads to a derivation? Two premises have conclusion S: Q \to S and R \to S. The first makes Q the new goal, and no line is Q or has conclusion Q, so that branch is a dead end. The second makes R the new goal; P \to R has conclusion R, and its hypothesis P is a premise. So the derivation is R by \rulename{{\to}E} from P \to R and P, then S by \rulename{{\to}E} from R \to S and R. A backward search may branch, and a branch that stalls is abandoned for the next one. Chains of implications Give a derivation of each sequent. 1. P \to Q, \ P \vdash Q. 2. P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash R. 3. P \wedge Q, \ P \to (Q \to R) \vdash R. 4. (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P, \ Q \vdash R. 5. (P \to Q) \wedge (R \to S), \ P \wedge R \vdash Q \wedge S. (a) Idea. There is nothing to choose: the premises are an implication and its hypothesis, and the rule fires once. This is the sequent that Section 1.1 said \rulename{{\to}E} makes true, and now it is shown: a derivation with these premises and this last line exists. (b) Idea, forwards. The premise P \to Q has its hypothesis P available, so it fires and gives Q. Now Q \to R has its hypothesis available, so it fires and gives R, the goal. Idea, backwards. The same derivation can be found from the other end. The goal R is a letter. Which available implication has conclusion R? Only Q \to R, so it suffices to reach Q (left picture: the goal at the bottom, its new subgoal Q above it). Which implication has conclusion Q? Only P \to Q, so it suffices to reach P; and P is a premise, so the gap closes (right picture). Both searches write the same five lines. The forward search wrote each line as soon as it could; the backward one wrote the last line first and worked up. In a derivation this small they cost the same. Exercise B3 has a case where they do not. (c) Idea. The goal R is a letter. From the goal: the only line that mentions R is P \to (Q \to R), but its conclusion is Q \to R, not R; the R sits one implication deeper. From the premises: P \wedge Q is a conjunction, so take it apart by \rulename{\wedge E}, giving P and Q. Now P is exactly the hypothesis of P \to (Q \to R), whose main connective is the first \to, so it fires and gives Q \to R. This new line is an implication whose hypothesis Q is available, so it fires too. Line 6 is the first line in this chapter where \rulename{{\to}E} fires on an implication that was itself written by \rulename{{\to}E}, not given as a premise. A line is a line, however it was obtained. (d) Idea. This time the goal leads. The goal R is the conclusion of (P \wedge Q) \to R, so it suffices to reach its hypothesis P \wedge Q. That subgoal is a conjunction, so, goal-directed as in Section 1.3, it comes from \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals P and Q, and both are premises. Compare (c). There the implication took its two hypotheses one at a time, P \to (Q \to R), and the conjunction was a premise to be taken apart. Here the implication takes both hypotheses at once, (P \wedge Q) \to R, and the conjunction is a subgoal to be built. The content is the same; the brackets decide which rules the derivation uses. (Section 1.5 shows that each of the two implications is derivable from the other.) (e) Idea. Both ends at once. From the goal: Q \wedge S is a conjunction, so its last line is \rulename{\wedge I}, with subgoals Q and S. From the premises: both are conjunctions, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes each apart, giving P \to Q, R \to S, P, and R. The two ends meet through \rulename{{\to}E}: P \to Q fires on P and gives the subgoal Q, and R \to S fires on R and gives the subgoal S. Lines 3–6 came from the premises, line 9 from the goal, and lines 7–8 are where the two searches met. Each derivation in the example is a box-free derivation (@def-box-free-derivation) with \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E}, and \rulename{{\to}E} as its rules, so by @def-derivable each shows its sequent. In each, the Idea chose a rule for a reason that can be stated: the goal’s main connective, an available line’s main connective, or an available implication whose conclusion is the goal. Checking a line of modus ponens Finding a chain can take some searching; checking one never does. For a line justified “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j”, the questions of Section 1.2 (which rule? is it an instance? are the cited lines earlier?) become four small ones: 1. Are lines i and j earlier than this line? 2. Is the main connective of line i a \to? If so, read off \varphi (its left side) and \psi (its right side). 3. Is line j exactly \varphi, symbol for symbol? 4. Is this line exactly \psi? Here is the check run on the lines of (c) above that use \rulename{{\to}E}, and on a tempting wrong line, “R — \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 4”, that a hurried reader might write instead of lines 5 and 6. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Cites \varphi, \psi read off line i Line j is \varphi? Line is \psi? -------------- -------------- ------------------------------- -------------------- ----------------------- 5: Q \to R 2, 3 P, Q \to R yes (P) yes 6: R 5, 4 Q, R yes (Q) yes wrong: R 2, 4 P, Q \to R no (Q is not P) no (R is not Q \to R) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The wrong line fails twice: it feeds line 2 the wrong hypothesis and takes out a part of the conclusion. Both failures come from reading P \to (Q \to R) as though its hypothesis were Q and its conclusion R. The main connective settles it: the first \to is the one applied last, so everything after it, Q \to R, is the conclusion. How this looks in a mathematical proof Let x be a real number with x > 2. Suppose we know two facts of school algebra: - if x > 2, then x^2 > 4 (since x > 2 > 0, multiplying x > 2 by x gives x^2 > 2x, and 2x > 4); - if x^2 > 4, then x^2 + 1 > 5 (add 1 to both sides). A written proof that x^2 + 1 > 5 takes one sentence: Since x > 2, we have x^2 > 4, and so x^2 + 1 > 5. As a derivation, with the two facts and the hypothesis as premises, it reads as follows. Each piece of the sentence is one line. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Sentence ----------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------- 3 “Since x > 2, …” (the hypothesis) 4 “… we have x^2 > 4, …” (\rulename{{\to}E}, firing the first fact) 5 “… and so x^2 + 1 > 5.” (\rulename{{\to}E}, firing the second fact) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The sentence never mentions lines 1 and 2. That is normal: when an implication is a known theorem or a fact of school algebra, writers leave it unstated and write only “since … we get …”. Each “since \varphi, \psi” in a proof is one application of \rulename{{\to}E} to an implication that the reader is trusted to supply. When a proof is hard to follow, writing the unstated implications down is often how one finds a gap: either the implication is false, or its hypothesis was never established. Common errors The warning above was about the wrong given line: the conclusion in place of the hypothesis. The other common error is a hypothesis that is only partly there. \rulename{{\to}E} needs the whole hypothesis. From (P \wedge Q) \to R and P alone, it gives nothing. This is the commonest slip in analysis: “f is continuous, so by the theorem f attains a maximum”. The theorem meant (proved in Part I) has a second hypothesis, that f is defined on a closed bounded interval, and without it the conclusion fails: f(x) = x on the open interval (0, 1) is continuous and has no largest value, since \frac{a + 1}{2} is a larger value than a for every a in (0, 1). A near relative is a hypothesis in the wrong order, as in the clause-by-clause reading: Q \wedge P is not the hypothesis of (P \wedge Q) \to R. The repair is two \rulename{\wedge E} lines and one \rulename{\wedge I} line, and Exercise B1 asks for it. What the rules sound like The table of Section 1.3 grows by one row. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean --------------------- --------------------------------------- ------------------------- \rulename{\wedge I} “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor \rulename{\wedge E} “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2) \rulename{{\to}E} “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” exact h hp --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In the Lean column, h is the implication and hp the proof of its hypothesis; h hp applies the one to the other, which is modus ponens. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the schema of \rulename{{\to}E} from memory. 2. Lines 1 and 2 of a derivation are P \to (Q \wedge R) and P. Which of the following can line 3 be, by one application of \rulename{{\to}E}? Q \wedge R; Q; R \wedge Q; P \to Q. 3. In @exm-wason-selection, why is the red card not worth turning? 4. True or false, with a reason: from lines P \to Q and Q \to R, \rulename{{\to}E} gives P \to R. (a) Given lines i: \varphi \to \psi and j: \varphi; new line k: \psi, justified “\rulename{{\to}E} i, j” (@def-rule-implication-elimination). (b) Only Q \wedge R, the conclusion of line 1. The line Q needs a further \rulename{\wedge E}, and R \wedge Q two further \rulename{\wedge E} lines and a \rulename{\wedge I} line. The line P \to Q is not the conclusion of line 1, so \rulename{{\to}E} cannot write it. (c) The claim is “even \to red”, and the red card shows the conclusion. An odd number behind it would not contradict the claim, which says nothing about which cards are red; an even number would fit it. Inferring anything about its number from its color would be affirming the consequent. (d) False. \rulename{{\to}E} needs an implication and a line that is its hypothesis. The hypothesis of Q \to R is Q, and P \to Q is not Q; the hypothesis of P \to Q is P, which is not a line. So \rulename{{\to}E} does not apply at all. (The sequent P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to R does hold, but its derivation needs the rule of Section 1.5.) B. Practice [B1: Two chains] Give a derivation of each sequent. For each, say which step you found first, and whether it came from the goal or from a premise. 1. P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to (R \wedge S) \vdash S \wedge Q. 2. (P \wedge Q) \to R, \ Q \wedge P \vdash R. (a) The first step found was from the goal: S \wedge Q is a conjunction, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals S and Q. Then from the premises: P \to Q fires on P and gives Q, and Q \to (R \wedge S) fires on Q and gives R \wedge S, which \rulename{\wedge E} takes apart. Line 4 is cited twice, by line 5 and by line 7. (b) The first step found was from the goal: R is the conclusion of line 1, so it suffices to reach P \wedge Q exactly. The premise Q \wedge P is not it. So take the premise apart and rebuild in the right order. [B2: Two facts and a number] Let x be a real number. Take as premises the two facts “if 0 < x < 1, then x^2 < x” and “if x^2 < x, then x^3 < x^2”, and the hypothesis 0 < x < 1. Derive x^3 < x^2, naming the rule on each line. Then write the argument as one or two sentences of prose. The hypothesis 0 < x < 1 is the conjunction (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), which is exactly the hypothesis of the first fact, so the first fact fires on it at once. In prose: Since 0 < x < 1, we have x^2 < x, and therefore x^3 < x^2. Both facts are true for every real x: if 0 < x < 1, multiplying x < 1 by x > 0 gives x^2 < x; and if x^2 < x, then x(x - 1) < 0, so x > 0, and multiplying x^2 < x by x gives x^3 < x^2. [B3: Which premises are needed?] Find a derivation of P, \ P \to Q, \ P \to R, \ R \to S, \ S \to U, \ Q \to T \ \vdash \ T , and list the premises it uses. Explain why a backward search finds the needed premises faster than a forward one here. Search backwards. The goal T is the conclusion of Q \to T only, so it suffices to reach Q. The goal Q is the conclusion of P \to Q only, so it suffices to reach P, a premise. It uses premises 1, 2, and 6. The others are never cited, which is allowed: a derivation need not use every premise (@def-derivable). Deleting lines 3–5 and renumbering gives a derivation of P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to T \vdash T. A forward search fires every implication whose hypothesis is available, relevant or not: from P it writes Q and R, then S from R, then U from S, and T from Q — five new lines, three of them useless. The backward search looks only at implications whose conclusion is the current goal, and at each stage exactly one qualifies, so it writes only the two lines the derivation needs. C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Here is an argument, followed by the derivation its author offers for it. If 10 is divisible by 6, then 10 is even. And 10 is even. So 10 is divisible by 6. With D: “10 is divisible by 6” and E: “10 is even”: 1. Name the line that fails, and say why it is not an instance of the schema of \rulename{{\to}E}. 2. Show that the step can lead from true premises to a false conclusion. 3. What new statement about divisibility can be correctly derived from the two premises with the rules so far? (a) Line 3. The schema needs, besides the implication \varphi \to \psi, a line that is its hypothesis \varphi. Matching line 1 gives \varphi \coloneqq D and \psi \coloneqq E, so the second cited line would have to be D; line 2 is E, which is \psi. The line affirms the consequent. (b) This instance already does. The first premise is true, because every multiple of 6 is even (6k = 2(3k)); the second is true, since 10 = 2 \cdot 5; and the conclusion is false, since 10 = 6 \cdot 1 + 4 leaves remainder 4 on division by 6. So the step at line 3 leads from two true premises to a false line, and no safe rule can allow it. (c) None. \rulename{{\to}E} cannot fire, since no line is the hypothesis D; \rulename{\wedge E} has no conjunction to take apart; and \rulename{\wedge I} only joins the premises into conjunctions such as (D \to E) \wedge E, which say nothing the premises did not. The premises tell us nothing about whether 10 is divisible by 6, which is why the conclusion had to be smuggled in. [C2: Both ends] Consider the sequent P \to (Q \to R), \ S \to P, \ S \wedge Q \ \vdash \ R \wedge S . 1. Describe a search for a derivation in words, in three parts: what the goal asks for; what the premises give; where the two meet. 2. Write the derivation, naming the rule on every line. [Hint 1] Two premises have main connective \to and one has \wedge; the goal has \wedge. Write down what each main connective lets you do. [Hint 2] The goal splits into R and S. Which available implication could end in R, and after how many firings? (a) From the goal: R \wedge S is a conjunction, so the last line is \rulename{\wedge I} with subgoals R and S. The only line mentioning R is P \to (Q \to R), whose conclusion is Q \to R; so R needs Q \to R and Q, and Q \to R needs P. From the premises: S \wedge Q splits by \rulename{\wedge E} into S and Q; then S \to P fires on S and gives P. Where they meet: S is at once a subgoal and a piece of the premise; P, reached forwards, is the hypothesis the backward search asked for; and Q, from \rulename{\wedge E}, is the last hypothesis R needs. (b) The derivation, with the rule on every line: Line 4 is cited twice, by line 6 and by line 9. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: from the goal, splits R \wedge S into the subgoals R and S for a final \rulename{\wedge I}. - 2: takes S \wedge Q apart by \rulename{\wedge E}. - 3: fires S \to P, then P \to (Q \to R), then Q \to R, each \rulename{{\to}E} citing an implication and exactly its hypothesis. - 2: the final \rulename{\wedge I}, with the citation order giving R \wedge S. - 1: the three-part description names where the searches meet. Any other correct derivation earns the same points step for step (its lines may come in another order, as long as each cites only earlier lines). Fatal errors (0 for the step): \rulename{{\to}E} on P \to (Q \to R) with Q (the wrong hypothesis); affirming the consequent anywhere.

title: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box Sections 1.3 and 1.4 gave three rules. \rulename{\wedge I} builds a conjunction; \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E} take a line apart or use it. With them we can use an implication, but we cannot prove one. Most theorems are implications, so this is the gap that matters most. This section fills it with the rule \rulename{{\to}I}. The rule asks us to do something new: to assume a statement we do not know, inside a boundary that says where the assumption holds. The boundary is a box. Boxes change what an earlier line may cite, so at the end of the section we can say exactly what a derivation is. Supposing something we do not know Here is a small theorem about a real number x. If x > 2, then x^2 > 4. The proof everyone would write goes like this. Suppose x > 2. Then x > 0, so multiplying x > 2 by x gives x^2 > 2x. Also 2x > 4. Hence x^2 > 4. Then, often without saying it: this proves that if x > 2, then x^2 > 4. Look at the first sentence. We do not know that x > 2. The number x is arbitrary, and it may well be 0. So “suppose x > 2” asserts nothing. It opens a temporary world, one in which x > 2 holds, and asks what else holds there. Inside that world, the sentences “x^2 > 2x”, “2x > 4”, and “x^2 > 4” are true. Outside it they are not: at x = 0 all three are false. Only the last sentence of the proof leaves the temporary world. What it carries out is not “x^2 > 4” but the implication “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4”, and that is true for every real x. None of the rules so far can do this. \rulename{\wedge I} writes a conjunction, and \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E} write a piece of a line that is already there. So with those three rules, an implication can stand on a line only as a premise or as a piece of an earlier line. To prove “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” from nothing, we must be allowed to suppose. A supposition is only safe if it has a boundary. Without one, the proof above could go on: “… Hence x^2 > 4. So x^2 > 4 for every real x.” That is false at x = 0. The error is not in any computation; it is that a sentence from inside the temporary world was used outside it. A derivation draws the boundary as a box. The assumption opens the box: it is written with a vertical bar to its left and a short horizontal rule under it. Every line derived under the assumption carries the same bar. When the box closes, the bar stops, and exactly one thing leaves: the implication from the assumption to the box’s last line. To prove “if \varphi, then \psi”, assume \varphi in a box, reach \psi inside it, and close the box. The introduction rule for implication Here is the rule, as a pattern. The given part is now a box, not a line, and the rule cites it as a range of lines. Beside it, for reference, is the rule \rulename{{\to}E} of @def-rule-implication-elimination, so that the two rules for “implies” stand in one place. [Rules for Implication] The left schema is the rule \rulename{{\to}I} (implication-introduction); the right one is \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination). In \rulename{{\to}I}, the line \varphi is an assumption, which opens the box, and the assumption is discharged when the box closes. The line \psi is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi and \psi stand for any statements, replaced consistently, and i, j, k for line numbers. The drawing says most of the rule. Read it clause by clause. 1. Open a box whose first line is the assumption \varphi. The assumption may be any statement: true or false, related to the premises or not. Its justification is simply “assumption”. The price of assuming anything we like is the box. 2. Inside the box, work as usual. Every rule may be used. A line inside may cite the assumption, the lines derived inside the box so far, and the lines above the box that are still in force: the premises, and earlier lines that are not inside a box that has already closed. 3. The last line of the box is \psi. It must be a line of this box itself, not a line of some further box opened inside it. (The drawing cannot show this, which is why the definition says it in words.) 4. Close the box, and write \varphi \to \psi on a later line outside it, in practice the very next line. The justification cites the whole box as the range \lines{i}{j}, from its assumption to its last line, not its lines one by one. 5. After the box closes, nothing inside it may be cited again. The assumption is discharged, and everything derived under it goes with it. Only the implication leaves. Clause 5 is the boundary of the temporary world. The subsection “Derivations, precisely” below turns it into an exact rule about which lines a line may cite. The degenerate case is i = j: a box of one line, whose assumption is also its last line. Then \psi is \varphi, and the rule writes \varphi \to \varphi. Nothing in the rule asks the box to contain more than its assumption. Why the rule is right. The implication \varphi \to \psi claims only that \psi holds whenever \varphi does. The box shows exactly that: starting from \varphi, and from facts that hold anyway, the rules lead to \psi. Chapter 3 proves that every rule, \rulename{{\to}I} included, never leads from true premises to a false conclusion (@thm-soundness). Why the box closes. The lines inside hold only under the assumption. If the assumption is false, as x > 2 is at x = 0, they may be false too. Closing the box is what stops them being used where the assumption is not in force. A first box: implication is transitive The first result proved with a box is the chaining of implications. Section 1.4 used chains of implications forwards, firing each on a hypothesis already in hand. Here the hypothesis is not in hand, and we still want the chain. [Implication Is Transitive] P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to R. Start from the goal. Its main connective is \to, so the last line will be \rulename{{\to}I}, and that needs a box that opens with P and ends with R. Inside the box, the new goal is R. Reason backwards: R is the conclusion of the premise Q \to R, so \rulename{{\to}E} gives it once Q is on a line. And Q is the conclusion of P \to Q, so \rulename{{\to}E} gives it from P, which the box has just assumed. The following derivation has premises P \to Q and Q \to R, and last line P \to R. Line 3 opens a box with the assumption P. Lines 4 and 5 apply \rulename{{\to}E} inside it, each citing a premise and a line of the box. Line 5, R, is the last line of the box. Line 6 closes it and writes P \to R, citing the box \lines{3}{5}. By @def-derivable, this proves the proposition. Read the drawing once more. The bar that starts at line 3 stops after line 5. The statements P, Q, and R on lines 3–5 were never established outright; they hold inside the temporary world where P is assumed. Only P \to R stands outside, next to the premises. Now give the letters some content. Let x be a real number, and let P : x > 3, \qquad Q : x^2 > 9, \qquad R : x^2 > 4 . The premise P \to Q holds: when x > 3, we have x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 3x > 9. The premise Q \to R holds because 4 < 9: if x^2 > 9, then x^2 > 4. With the premises in hand, lines 3–6 become a paragraph, one sentence per line. Line Sentence ------ ------------------------------------------------ 3 Suppose x > 3. 4 Since x > 3 implies x^2 > 9, we get x^2 > 9. 5 Since x^2 > 9 implies x^2 > 4, we get x^2 > 4. 6 Hence, if x > 3, then x^2 > 4. A practiced writer would compress this to “if x > 3, then x^2 > 9 > 4”: the same derivation with its joints hidden. When a proof is hard to follow, expanding it back into this form is how one finds the gap. The same result holds with the two premises joined into one, (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash P \to R. Two \rulename{\wedge E} lines take the premise apart first (premise-directed), and the rest is the derivation above, renumbered. The box opens with P, the hypothesis of the goal P \to R. That choice is forced, and getting it backwards is the most common misuse of the rule. The box of \rulename{{\to}I} opens with the hypothesis of the implication to be proved, never with its conclusion. Argument B of Section 1.1 had to prove Q \to P, with Q: “n^2 is even” and P: “n is even”. It opened its box with P, the conclusion, and reached Q. Every line inside that box is correct. But a box from P to Q gives P \to Q, the converse, and B’s last sentence announced Q \to P. That names the error of Argument B, as Section 1.1 promised: B used \rulename{{\to}I} with the box opened at the wrong end. The implication B needed, from the square back to the number, is a genuine theorem, and Chapter 2 proves it. Derivations, precisely Section 1.2 defined a derivation without boxes (@def-box-free-derivation): every line after the premises applies a rule to earlier lines. With boxes, “earlier” is no longer enough. In the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive, line 5 is earlier than any line we might add after line 6. If a line 7 could cite line 5, it could write R outside the box, and the derivation would claim that R follows from the premises alone. That is the “x^2 > 4 for every x” error of the first subsection. So the full definition is mostly about which earlier lines are still available. A derivation is a list of lines in which every line is a premise, an assumption that opens a box, a repetition of a line still in force, or the result of one rule applied to lines and boxes that are still available. [Derivation] Fix a list of rules. A derivation is a finite list of numbered lines 1, 2, \dots, n, each carrying one statement and a justification, together with a set of boxes. A box is a block of consecutive lines whose first line is an assumption. Any two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other. A box ends at one of its lines and is closed after it. The last line of the derivation lies outside every box. The scope rule. Line i is available at line k if i < k and every box containing line i also contains line k. A box is available at line k if it ends before line k and the boxes other than itself that contain it are exactly the boxes containing line k. A line may cite only lines and boxes available at it. Every line is exactly one of the following: 1. a premise; the premises are the first lines, above every box, with a short rule under the last of them; 2. an assumption, which may be any statement, and opens a new box; 3. a repetition of the statement on a line available at this one, justified “R” and the line repeated; 4. the conclusion of one rule of the list, applied to lines and boxes available at this one, such that this line and the cited lines and boxes form an instance of the rule’s schema. Clause (D3) is the rule \rulename{R} (repetition), whose schema is where line i must be available at line k. In words, clause by clause. (D1) Premises are the givens; they hold throughout, and they are available at every later line, since no box contains them. (D2) We may assume anything, but the assumption opens a box, and that is the price. (D3) A statement already established, and still in force, may be written again. (D4) Everything else is one step of one rule, applied to material that is still in force. The scope rule is the definition’s real content. Line i is available at line k when every assumption that line i was derived under is still in force at line k. So: - a line in no box is available at every later line; - a line inside a box is available further down that box, and inside every box opened within it; - once its box closes, the line is available nowhere. Open a box, close a box: an assumption lives exactly as long as its box. A closed box, cited as a whole by \rulename{{\to}I}, must sit directly in the part of the derivation where the citing line is. The citing line may not lie outside a box that contains the cited box (that box has closed too), nor inside a further box opened after the cited box ended. Well defined. Whether a line is available is decided by looking at the boxes; nothing about the meaning of the statements enters. Checking a derivation stays mechanical. Nothing earlier changes. A derivation with no boxes is a box-free derivation of @def-box-free-derivation for the same rules with \rulename{R} added: with no boxes, “available” means just “earlier”. So every derivation of Sections 1.2–1.4 is a derivation in the new sense, and @def-derivable is read from now on with this definition. The sequent \Gamma \vdash \psi still means: there is a derivation whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi. Its last line lies in no box, so it depends on the premises and on nothing that was merely assumed. Two more words will be needed in Chapter 3, where the rules are proved trustworthy (@thm-soundness). The length of a derivation is its number of lines. The context of a line is the list of the premises together with the assumptions of every box containing that line: the statements the line depends on. The context of the last line is just the premises, since the last line lies in no box. Repetition. Most rules may cite an available line directly, so \rulename{R} is rarely needed. It is needed when a rule wants a statement as a line of a particular box: \rulename{{\to}I} wants its \psi as a line of the box itself (clause 3 of the reading). The typical use copies a line into a box opened below it. Line i is available at line k exactly when every box containing line i contains line k; in this drawing, line i is in no box that has closed, so the copy is legal. The worked example @exm-first-boxes below uses it. A box that is never closed cannot end a derivation. If the last line of a list is still inside a box, it depends on an assumption that was never discharged, and @def-derivation does not count the list as a derivation at all. “Suppose x > 2. Then x^2 > 4”, with nothing after it, proves nothing about x: the implication is the only thing the supposition was allowed to produce, and it was never written. How to check a derivation Section 1.2 checked a line by asking which rule it uses, which lines it cites, and whether they are earlier. With boxes the third question becomes: are they available here? For each line after the premises, ask: 1. Which rule? Name it. An assumption opens a box; \rulename{R} repeats; every other line applies one rule. 2. Which lines or boxes does it cite, and do they form an instance of the rule’s schema? \rulename{{\to}E} cites an implication and exactly its hypothesis; \rulename{{\to}I} cites one box, whose assumption and last line must be the two sides of the implication written. 3. Are they available here? Apply the scope rule to each cited line and box. Finding a derivation may need an idea; checking one never does. Here is the check run on the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive. The last column lists the context of each line. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Which rule? Cites Available? Context -------------- ----------------------------------------- -------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- --------------------- 1, 2 premises (D1) — — P \to Q, Q \to R 3 assumption (D2); opens the box 3–5 — — P \to Q, Q \to R, P 4 \rulename{{\to}E}: Q from P \to Q and P 1, 3 1 is in no box; 3 is in box 3–5, which contains 4 P \to Q, Q \to R, P 5 \rulename{{\to}E}: R from Q \to R and Q 2, 4 2 is in no box; 4 is in box 3–5, which contains 5 P \to Q, Q \to R, P 6 \rulename{{\to}I}: P \to R from the box box 3–5 the box ended at 5; neither it nor 6 lies in another box P \to Q, Q \to R -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every line passes, and the last line lies in no box. The context column shows the temporary world: it grows by P at line 3, and shrinks back at line 6. An assumption used outside its box Now watch the scope rule catch an error. Take the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive and add one line, as a careless writer might. [A line cited from a closed box] Is the following a derivation? If it were, what would it show? No. Lines 1–6 are the derivation of @prp-implication-transitive, and line 7 claims to be a repetition (D3). Line 5 lies inside the box \lines{3}{5}, and that box does not contain line 7. By the scope rule, line 5 is not available at line 7, and (D3) repeats only an available line. So line 7 is illegal. If it were allowed, the list would show P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash R, and that would be a disaster. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 3”, Q: “x > 2”, R: “x > 1”. Both premises are true whatever x is. At x = 0 the conclusion x > 1 is false. A step that leads from true premises to a false conclusion cannot be a step of proof. The error is easy to see in a drawing, where the bar visibly stops after line 5. In prose there is no bar, and the same error hides. The assumption of a closed box is gone, and so is everything derived from it. Here is a typical slip. “Suppose x > 1. Then x^2 = x \cdot x > 1 \cdot x > 1. Hence x > 1 implies x^2 > 1. Moreover x^3 = x \cdot x^2 > 1, so x^3 > 1.” The sentence “Hence …” closed the box. The last sentence still uses x > 1 and x^2 > 1, and so it asserts x^3 > 1 with no hypothesis, which fails at x = 0. The repair is to keep the box open until everything that needs x > 1 is done, and to conclude “if x > 1, then x^2 > 1 and x^3 > 1”. In the derivation below, which of lines 3 to 7 may cite line 2 individually? Lines 3, 4, and 5. They lie in the box \lines{2}{5}, the only box containing line 2, so line 2 is available to each of them. Line 6 cites the box \lines{2}{5} as a whole, which is what \rulename{{\to}I} requires; it does not cite line 2 by itself, and could not, since line 6 is outside the box. Line 7 may not cite line 2 either, for the same reason. More boxes: from nothing, and one inside another The next three derivations are short, and each shows one new feature of boxes. [First boxes] Find a derivation of each sequent. 1. \vdash P \to P. 2. \vdash P \to (Q \to P). 3. P \to (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (P \to R). (a) Idea. The goal is an implication, so open a box with its hypothesis P; the box must end with P. The assumption is already P, so the box can end at once: this is the degenerate case of \rulename{{\to}I}. Line 1 is an assumption (D2) and opens the box \lines{1}{1}, whose last line is P. Line 2 cites that box, which ended before line 2 and, like line 2, lies in no other box. There are no premises, so this shows \vdash P \to P. It is the first statement in the book derivable from no premises. Section 1.2 observed that nothing could be: every rule of Sections 1.3 and 1.4 (@def-rules-conjunction, @def-rule-implication-elimination) cites at least one line, so a derivation using only them needs a first line, and that line must be a premise. A box is what escapes: its first line is an assumption, and the assumption is discharged before the end. (b) Idea. Read the goal from the outside in. Its main connective is the first \to, so open a box with P; the new goal is Q \to P, again an implication, so open a box with Q inside the first. The inner box must end with P. The statement P is already available, on line 1, but \rulename{{\to}I} wants it as a line of the inner box itself. That is the job of \rulename{R}. Line 3 is legal: the only box containing line 1, the box \lines{1}{4}, also contains line 3. The boxes are nested, and the inner one closes first. No line cites line 2 on its own: the assumption Q is never used, and nothing in \rulename{{\to}I} requires it to be. An implication whose conclusion is already known holds whatever its hypothesis. (c) Idea. The goal Q \to (P \to R) asks for a box with Q and, inside it, a box with P ending in R. Inside both boxes, work from the premise: its main connective is the first \to, with hypothesis P, so \rulename{{\to}E} fires on the assumption P and gives Q \to R. That implication fires on the assumption Q and gives R, the inner goal. Line 5 cites line 2 from inside the inner box: every box containing line 2 (only \lines{2}{6}) contains line 5. So the order of two hypotheses does not matter. For real numbers a and x, the derivation turns “if a > 0, then (if x > 1, then ax > a)” into “if x > 1, then (if a > 0, then ax > a)”. In (b) and (c) the goal told us which boxes to open, and in which order: the outermost \to of the goal gives the outermost box. This is the goal-directed move of this section. An implication goal opens a box with its hypothesis; the new goal is its conclusion. Two hypotheses, or one at a time A theorem with two hypotheses, “if x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0”, is often written with one hypothesis at a time: “let x > 0; then, if y > 0, xy > 0”. The two forms are (P \wedge Q) \to R and P \to (Q \to R). Each can be derived from the other, so a writer may use whichever reads better. [Two Hypotheses or One at a Time] (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \to R), and P \to (Q \to R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R. Try it first (ten minutes): for the first claim, which boxes will you open, and in which order? The tempting first move is premise-directed: use (P \wedge Q) \to R at once. But \rulename{{\to}E} needs P \wedge Q on a line, and at the start nothing is on a line except the premise. So start from the goal. Its main connective is the first \to, so open a box with P; the new goal Q \to R is again an implication, so open a box with Q inside the first. Now both P and Q are available, \rulename{\wedge I} builds P \wedge Q, and the premise fires. For the second claim the goal (P \wedge Q) \to R asks for one box, with P \wedge Q; take the assumption apart and feed the halves to the premise one at a time, P first because it is the premise’s outer hypothesis. Before reading on: in the first derivation, which lines may line 4 cite, and why may line 6 cite the box 3–5 but not line 5 on its own? For the first claim, the following is a derivation with premise (P \wedge Q) \to R and last line P \to (Q \to R). Line 4 may cite lines 1, 2, and 3: line 1 lies in no box, the only box containing line 2 (the box \lines{2}{6}) contains line 4, and both boxes containing line 3 contain line 4. Line 6 may cite the box \lines{3}{5}, because that box has ended and both it and line 6 lie in the box \lines{2}{6} and in no other. Line 6 may not cite line 5 on its own, because the box \lines{3}{5} contains line 5 and not line 6. For the second claim, the following is a derivation with premise P \to (Q \to R) and last line (P \wedge Q) \to R. Every line cites line 1, which lies in no box, or lines of the box \lines{2}{6} from inside it. By @def-derivable, the two derivations prove the two claims. In the first derivation the boxes are nested, and the inner one closes first: an assumption made later is discharged earlier. That is the general pattern, forced by @def-derivation, since two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other. Read mathematically, the first claim turns “if x > 0 and y > 0, then xy > 0” into “if x > 0, then (if y > 0, then xy > 0)”, and the second turns it back. The two forms say the same thing, one hypothesis at a time or both at once. Section 2.4 gives a name and a symbol to a pair of statements that, like these two, can each be derived from the other. To show Q \wedge R \vdash (P \to Q) \wedge (S \to R), does the derivation need one box or two? Two. The goal’s main connective is \wedge, which opens no box, so the goal splits into the two implications P \to Q and S \to R (goal-directed \rulename{\wedge I}). Each is proved by \rulename{{\to}I}, with its own box, opened by its own hypothesis. Inside each box, \rulename{\wedge E} on the premise gives the half that box needs. The two boxes are disjoint: the first closes before the second opens. Line 8 may cite lines 4 and 7, which lie in no box. What the rule sounds like Every rule is something mathematicians already say. The table adds the rules of this section to those of Sections 1.3 and 1.4: the sentence that performs the rule in a written proof and, for readers who meet a proof assistant, the Lean code that does the same. Nothing later depends on the last column. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ------------------- --------------------------------------- ------------------------- \rulename{{\to}I} “Assume P. … Hence Q.” intro hp \rulename{R} “As shown above, P.” exact hp ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The sentence for \rulename{{\to}I} is the one to watch. “Assume P” opens a box, and “hence Q” is its last line. The closing line, “so P implies Q”, is usually left unsaid in written mathematics. It is still there: the box closes whether or not anyone says so. It is also the line Argument B got wrong. Chapter 5 turns sentences like these into a dictionary between derivations and prose. Every derivation in this section was built from the rules alone, and each repeated in full whatever it needed. Section 2.3 lets a sequent already derived be used as a single line of a later derivation; until then, a derivation that needs an earlier result must repeat its steps. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Consider the following derivation, whose justifications are missing. 1. Write the schema of \rulename{{\to}I} from memory, and state the condition that the drawing cannot show. 2. Fill in the justifications (i), (ii), (iii), and say what the derivation shows, written with \vdash. 3. Which of lines 1–5 are available at line 6? What is the context of line 5? 4. Someone extends the derivation by a line 7, the statement R justified by \rulename{{\to}E} 6, 3. Is the result a derivation? If not, name the clause of @def-derivation that line 7 breaks. 5. In the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry, why is line 4 available at line 5? And why is the inner box closed before the outer one? 6. In the same derivation, which rule produces line 5, and which lines does it cite? (a) The schema is the left one in @def-rules-implication: a box from an assumption \varphi on line i to a line \psi on line j, and then \varphi \to \psi on line k, justified \rulename{{\to}I} \lines{i}{j}. The condition the drawing cannot show: \psi is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. (b) (i) \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 3; (ii) \rulename{{\to}E} 4, 2; (iii) \rulename{{\to}I} \lines{3}{5}. The derivation shows P \to (Q \to R), \ Q \vdash P \to R. (c) Lines 1 and 2. Lines 3, 4, and 5 lie in the box \lines{3}{5}, which does not contain line 6. (The box \lines{3}{5} as a whole is available at line 6, which is why (iii) may cite it.) The context of line 5 is P \to (Q \to R), Q, P: the two premises and the assumption of the one box containing it. (d) No. Line 6 is available at line 7, but line 3 is not: it lies in the box \lines{3}{5}, which does not contain line 7. So line 7 applies a rule to a line that is not available, which (D4) forbids. (e) Line 4 lies in two boxes, \lines{2}{6} and \lines{3}{5}, and both contain line 5; so by the scope rule line 4 is available at line 5. The inner box \lines{3}{5} lies inside the outer box \lines{2}{6}, and two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other, so the inner box must end first. Read off the goal: the inner box proves Q \to R, which is the last line the outer box needs. (f) \rulename{{\to}E}, citing line 1, the implication (P \wedge Q) \to R, and line 4, its hypothesis P \wedge Q. B. Practice [B1: Swapping inside an implication] Show that \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (Q \wedge P) by a derivation. Then write the argument as a paragraph of prose, one sentence per line. The goal has main connective \to, so the derivation opens a box with P \wedge Q and must end it with Q \wedge P. Inside, the goal is a conjunction, whose halves \rulename{\wedge E} supplies from the assumption. It has no premises, and its last line lies outside the box, so it shows \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (Q \wedge P). In prose: Assume P and Q. In particular P holds, and in particular Q holds. Hence Q and P both hold. This proves that if P and Q, then Q and P. Compared with @prp-and-commutes, the premise P \wedge Q has become an assumption, and the conclusion has become an implication that depends on nothing. [B2: An assumption that is not used] 1. Show that Q \vdash P \to Q, and say which line needs repetition. 2. Show that \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (R \to Q). 3. Let x be a real number. Write the instance of (a) with Q: “x^2 \ge 0” and P: “x > 5” as an English sentence, and say which hypothesis its proof never uses. (a) The goal is an implication, so open a box with P; its last line must be Q. Line 3 needs repetition: \rulename{{\to}I} wants Q as a line of the box \lines{2}{3} itself. It is legal because line 1 lies in no box. (b) Two implications, so two nested boxes: one with P \wedge Q, and inside it one with R. Line 4 is legal: the only box containing line 2 also contains line 4. (Applying \rulename{\wedge E} to line 1 inside the inner box works as well.) (c) “x^2 \ge 0; therefore, if x > 5, then x^2 \ge 0.” The hypothesis x > 5 is never used: its box only repeats what was known. [B3: Unwinding an absolute value] 1. Show that P \to Q, \ P \to R \vdash P \to (Q \wedge R). 2. Let x be a real number. Use (a) to deduce “if \abs{x - 2} < 1, then 1 < x < 3” from the two facts “if \abs{x - 2} < 1, then x > 1” and “if \abs{x - 2} < 1, then x < 3”. Write the resulting argument as prose. (a) The goal is an implication, so assume P, and reach Q \wedge R by getting each half. The assumption on line 3 is cited twice, by lines 4 and 5: a line is not used up when it is cited. (b) Take P: “\abs{x - 2} < 1”, Q: “x > 1” and R: “x < 3”. The two facts are the premises P \to Q and P \to R, and Q \wedge R is 1 < x < 3. The derivation in (a), with these statements put in for the letters, is a derivation of P \to (Q \wedge R) from the two facts. In prose: Suppose \abs{x - 2} < 1. Then x > 1 by the first fact, and x < 3 by the second. Hence 1 < x < 3. This proves that \abs{x - 2} < 1 implies 1 < x < 3. [B4: Putting a derivation in order] Here are nine lines, each a statement with its justification. Seven of them, in the right order and with the right boxes, form a derivation of P \to (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (P \to R). Give the order, and say where each box opens and closes. Then say why each of the other two lines cannot be used. 1. P \to R, by \rulename{{\to}I} on the box from P to R. 2. Q, assumption. 3. R, by \rulename{{\to}E} from Q \to R and Q. 4. R, by \rulename{R}, repeating the line R of (iii), written directly below (i). 5. P \to (Q \to R), premise. 6. Q \to (P \to R), by \rulename{{\to}I} on the box from Q to P \to R. 7. R, assumption, opening the box for the \rulename{{\to}I} that proves P \to R. 8. Q \to R, by \rulename{{\to}E} from P \to (Q \to R) and P. 9. P, assumption. The order is (v), (ii), (ix), (viii), (iii), (i), (vi), with one box opened by (ii) and closed after (i), and a second box inside it, opened by (ix) and closed after (iii). This is the derivation of @exm-first-boxes (c). It is the only admissible order. The premise (v) comes first. The last line (vi) needs a box from Q to P \to R, so (ii) opens a box whose last line is (i). Line (i) needs a box from P to R, which must lie inside the box of Q, since (i) is a line of that box; so (ix) opens the inner box, whose last line is (iii). Inside it, (viii) needs the premise and (ix), and (iii) needs (viii) and (ii). Opening the box of P first and the box of Q inside it would not do: the inner \rulename{{\to}I} would then give Q \to R, and the outer one P \to (Q \to R), the premise again. (iv) cannot be used where it is placed. Directly below (i), the inner box has closed, and line (iii) lies inside it; so (iii) is not available there, and (D3) repeats only an available line (the scope rule of @def-derivation). It is the error of @exm-illegal-citation. (v) cannot be used. \rulename{{\to}I} proves P \to R from a box opened by P, the hypothesis. A box opened by R would prove an implication with hypothesis R: the converse error of Argument B. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: a line from a closed box] A student wants to show (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash (P \to (Q \to R)) \wedge (Q \to (P \to R)), and offers the following derivation. Lines 1–7 are the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry. 1. Find the first illegal line, and name the clause of @def-derivation that it breaks. 2. Is the student’s conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. 3. The student defends line 10: “at line 10, both P and Q are assumed, exactly as they were at line 5, so R holds there too.” Explain why @def-derivation does not accept this defense, and show by an instance with real numbers that the move “repeat a line of a closed box” cannot be allowed. [Hint 1] For (a), check each line’s citations against the scope rule; for (b), keep the student’s idea and change one step. [Hint 2] For (b), inside the box of P at line 9, the assumptions Q (line 8) and P (line 9) are both available. What did lines 4 and 5 do with such a pair? (a) Line 10 is the first illegal line. It claims to repeat line 5 by (D3), but line 5 lies in the boxes \lines{2}{6} and \lines{3}{5}, and neither contains line 10. So line 5 is not available at line 10, and (D3) allows repeating only an available line. Lines 1–9 are correct, and lines 11–13 would be correct if line 10 were. (b) Yes: the sequent is derivable. Replace line 10 by two lines that do inside the new boxes what lines 4 and 5 did inside the old ones. Every box containing line 8 or line 9 contains line 10, and line 1 lies in no box; the other lines check as before. The student’s derivation was wrong and its conclusion right: a flawed argument can have a true conclusion. (c) Availability is about boxes, not about which statements happen to be assumed. The boxes \lines{8}{11} and \lines{9}{10} of the student’s derivation are new boxes; that their assumptions repeat those of the old boxes gives line 10 no access to what was derived inside the old ones. And the move, once allowed, can be used anywhere. Used outside every box, as a line 8 “R, R 5” after lines 1–7, it would derive (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash R. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 2”, Q: “x > 3” and R: “x > 1”. The premise “if x > 2 and x > 3, then x > 1” is true whatever x is, and at x = 0 the conclusion x > 1 is false. A move that leads from a true premise to a false conclusion cannot be a step of proof. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: names line 10, because line 5 lies in boxes that do not contain it. - 3: gives any correct derivation of the sequent, every citation available. - 1: says the conclusion is derivable although the argument is wrong. - 3: explains that availability depends on boxes, not on repeated assumptions, with an instance where the move leads from a true premise to a false conclusion. Fatal errors (0 for the step): naming line 5 or line 9; claiming the sequent is not derivable; refuting the conclusion instead of the move. [C2: A hypothesis inside a hypothesis] Show that (P \to Q) \to (P \to R) \vdash P \to (Q \to R). Then say, in one sentence, why the premise cannot be used until a third box is opened. [Hint 1] Read the boxes off the goal. The premise’s hypothesis is P \to Q: what would you need to derive it? [Hint 2] Which rule proves an implication, and what does that rule need? The goal P \to (Q \to R) asks for a box with P and, inside it, a box with Q whose last line is R. The premise gives P \to R as soon as we have P \to Q, and P \to R with the available P gives R. So the task is to derive P \to Q inside the box of Q, and that takes a third box. Line 5 is a legal repetition: both boxes containing line 3 contain line 5. Line 8 may cite line 2 because the box \lines{2}{9}, the only box containing line 2, contains line 8. The premise’s hypothesis is the implication P \to Q, which \rulename{{\to}E} needs on an available line, and an implication is derived by \rulename{{\to}I}, which needs a box of its own. (That box assumes P again although line 2 already did: \rulename{{\to}I} needs the box, not new information.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: opens a box with P and inside it a box with Q, read off the goal. - 3: derives P \to Q inside the box of Q by a box whose last line is Q. - 2: obtains P \to R, then R, by \rulename{{\to}E} on available lines. - 2: closes the boxes inner first, each \rulename{{\to}I} citing an available box. - 1: the sentence says P \to Q must be a line, hence needs a box. Fatal errors (0 for the step): citing a line outside the box that contains it; writing P \to Q with no box. [C3: Exit check: a derivation and its prose] 1. Write a derivation of P \to Q, \ (Q \to R) \wedge (R \to S) \vdash P \to S, with every line justified. 2. Let x be a real number, and take P: “x > 5”, Q: “x > 4”, R: “x^2 > 16”, S: “x^2 > 9”. Say why each premise is true for every real x. Then write your derivation as fluent prose about x, one sentence per step. (a) Premise-directed first: the second premise is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes it apart. Goal-directed next: the goal is an implication, so open a box with its hypothesis P, and reach S by firing the three implications in turn. Lines 1–4 lie in no box, so they are available inside the box \lines{5}{8}; line 9 cites that box, which has ended, and neither it nor line 9 lies in another box. (b) The premise P \to Q holds because 5 > 4: if x > 5, then x > 4. For Q \to R: if x > 4, then x > 0, so x^2 = x \cdot x > 4x > 16. For R \to S: if x^2 > 16, then x^2 > 9, since 16 > 9. So both premises (the second a conjunction of two true implications) hold for every real x. In prose: We know that x > 5 implies x > 4, that x > 4 implies x^2 > 16, and that x^2 > 16 implies x^2 > 9. Suppose x > 5. Then x > 4. Hence x^2 > 16, and so x^2 > 9. This proves that if x > 5, then x^2 > 9. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: takes the conjunctive premise apart by two \rulename{\wedge E} lines (inside or outside the box). - 2: opens a box with P (not S) and closes it on S, a line of that box. - 2: three \rulename{{\to}E} steps, each citing an implication and exactly its hypothesis, every cited line available. - 1: the closing \rulename{{\to}I} cites the box as a range. - 3: prose with one sentence per step, “suppose” for the assumption, and a closing sentence stating the implication. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a box opened with the conclusion S (the converse error); citing a line of the box after it has closed.

title: 1.6 Or, Introduced
content: Or, Introduced Sections 1.3 to 1.5 gave the rules for “and” and “implies”. With them we can take a conjunction apart, fire an implication on its hypothesis, and prove an implication by opening a box. This section starts on the third connective of the chapter, “or”. It gives the rule that proves a disjunction, \rulename{\vee I}, and a habit that goes with it: when the goal is a disjunction, commit to one of its sides only when that side is in hand. Near its end it meets a goal that the rules still cannot reach, and that goal is the question the next section answers. Throwing information away on purpose Suppose a proof has just shown that a real number x satisfies x > 0, and the definition it is checking asks for x \ge 0. Every writer takes the step “so x \ge 0” without a pause. Look at what the step does. Section 1.1 noted that the symbol \le hides a disjunction, so x \ge 0 is the statement (x > 0) \vee (x = 0) . The step turns a statement into a disjunction of which it is one side. The step loses something. “x > 0” tells us that x is not 0; “x \ge 0” no longer does. A proof that takes the step throws information away, and it does so on purpose: the definition asks for the weaker statement, and the stronger one is not in the form it asks for. The same move appears whenever a known fact has a disjunction as its hypothesis. School algebra says that if a = 0 or b = 0, then a \cdot b = 0. To use this on a product whose first factor we know to be 0, we must hand the fact its hypothesis, “a = 0 or b = 0”. What we have is only “a = 0”. So again the step goes from one side to the whole disjunction, and only then does the fact fire. Both steps are instances of one rule. This section states it as a pattern, reads the pattern clause by clause, and then uses it in two ways: when the goal is a disjunction, and when a premise needs one. The rule of or-introduction To prove a disjunction, it is enough to prove one of its two sides. The rule is defined, like every rule since Section 1.3, by its schema (@def-rule-schema). The Greek letters stand for arbitrary statements, and i, k for line numbers. The rule has two forms, one for each side, so it is printed as two schemas. [Or-Introduction] The rule given by these two schemas is called \rulename{\vee I} (or-introduction). In words, clause by clause. - One given line. Line i holds a statement \varphi, which may be any statement at all, and it must be available at line k, in the sense of the scope rule of @def-derivation: an earlier line, not inside a box that has already closed. The justification “\rulename{\vee I} i” cites that one line. There is no box: \rulename{\vee I} is a one-step rule, like \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{{\to}E}. - Either side. The new line is a disjunction with \varphi as one of its two sides: on the left in the first schema, on the right in the second. Both forms have the same name, and the justification does not say which was used; the shape of the new line shows it. - Any other side. The letter \psi appears in no given line. It stands for any statement at all. It need not be true, it need not have been mentioned before, and it need not have anything to do with \varphi. This is the rule’s one surprising clause. No earlier rule has it: \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\wedge E}, \rulename{{\to}E}, and \rulename{{\to}I} all build their new line out of statements that already stand on the lines or boxes they cite. - Consistent replacement. As @def-rule-schema requires, \varphi is replaced by the whole cited statement, symbol for symbol.
