If line 3 is P \wedge Q, then \rulename{\vee I} 3 may write (P \wedge Q) \vee R, with \varphi replaced by P \wedge Q and \psi by R. The brackets matter: the main connective of the new line (@def-main-connective) must be the \vee that the rule introduces. Here is an instance. Let x be a real number, and suppose line 4 of some derivation is x > 0. Then each of the lines (x > 0) \vee (x = 0), \qquad (x = 0) \vee (x > 0), \qquad (x > 0) \vee (x < -7) may be written as a later line, justified by “\rulename{\vee I} 4”. The first and third use the first schema, with \psi replaced by x = 0 and by x < -7; the second uses the second schema. The third line is silly, and it is correct: it is true whenever line 4 is, and nothing in the rule asks the added side to be useful. The degenerate case is \psi equal to \varphi. From P the rule writes P \vee P, and then the two schemas give the same line. It is a legal step, and the next section uses the statement P \vee P once. Now three nonexamples, each a small change of an instance. Take line 1 to be the statement named in each, and line 2 the line shown. - From P, the line “P \wedge Q — \rulename{\vee I} 1” is not an instance. The new line of \rulename{\vee I} is a disjunction, and the main connective of P \wedge Q is \wedge. - From Q \vee P, the line “P \vee Q — \rulename{\vee I} 1” is not an instance. With \varphi replaced by Q \vee P, the two schemas give (Q \vee P) \vee \psi and \psi \vee (Q \vee P). In both, the cited statement is one whole side of the new line, and Q \vee P is not a side of P \vee Q. Whether P \vee Q follows from Q \vee P at all is the question at the end of this section. - From P \vee Q, the line “P — \rulename{\vee I} 1” is not an instance. It runs the rule backwards, from a disjunction to one of its sides. Why this rule. In mathematics “or” is inclusive (Section 1.1): \varphi \vee \psi is true when \varphi is true, when \psi is true, and when both are. So \varphi \vee \psi is true whenever \varphi is, whatever \psi says. The rule is this first clause read as a permission. It is also the only rule of the chapter so far whose new line is a disjunction built on the spot. The other rules can produce a disjunction only by copying a line that already is one (\rulename{R}), or by cutting one out of a bigger line, as \rulename{\wedge E} cuts a side out of a conjunction and \rulename{{\to}E} the conclusion out of an implication. That is why, below, every derivation that needs a disjunction it cannot cut out of a line reaches for \rulename{\vee I}. Why it is safe. If the given line is true, the new line is true, whatever \psi is, by the inclusive reading. What the step loses is information: a reader of \varphi \vee \psi can no longer tell which side holds. Chapter 3 proves that derivations built from the rules of this chapter and the next never lead from true premises to a false conclusion (@thm-soundness); for \rulename{\vee I} the reason is the sentence just given. \rulename{\vee I} loses information, never truth. \rulename{\vee I} runs one way only. From \varphi it gives \varphi \vee \psi; from \varphi \vee \psi it gives nothing, and in general \varphi does not follow from \varphi \vee \psi at all. The phrase “in particular” belongs to \rulename{\wedge E}, not to “or”. For a concrete failure, let x be a real number: “x \ge 0 or x < 0” is true whatever x is, and “in particular x \ge 0” is false at x = -1. Do not read “or” as “one but not both” when checking a step. From x = 2, \rulename{\vee I} gives “x = 2 or x \le 5”, although at x = 2 both sides are true. The step is correct: the disjunction is inclusive, and the rule never claims that the added side is false. Let x be a real number, and suppose line 1 of a derivation is x = 2. Which of the following may line 2 be, justified by one application of \rulename{\vee I} to line 1? 1. (x = 2) \vee (x = 3). 2. (x = 3) \vee (x = 2). 3. (x = 2) \vee (1 = 0). 4. x \ge 2. (i) Yes, by the first schema, with \psi replaced by x = 3. (ii) Yes, by the second schema. (iii) Yes, by the first schema, with \psi replaced by the false statement 1 = 0. The line is true, since its left side is, and it is useless; the rule allows it. (iv) Only once x \ge 2 is written out as (x > 2) \vee (x = 2), the disjunction that the symbol \ge hides (Section 1.1). In that form it is an instance of the second schema, with \varphi replaced by x = 2. A checker who matches symbols sees the difference, which is why a derivation writes the disjunction out. A disjunction as a goal Section 1.3 asked two questions before writing any line: what is the goal’s main connective? (goal-directed reasoning, from the bottom up) and what are the available lines’ main connectives? (premise-directed reasoning, from the top down). Each rule so far added an answer. A conjunction as a goal splits into two subgoals, both needed (\rulename{\wedge I}); an implication as a goal opens a box (\rulename{{\to}I}, @def-rules-implication). Now \vee joins the list of goals. If the goal is \varphi \vee \psi, its last line can be \rulename{\vee I}, and then the subgoal is \varphi or \psi: one of the two, of our choosing. That choice is new. A conjunction’s two subgoals are both needed, so there is nothing to choose; here only one side is needed, and a wrong choice can leave us working towards a statement that does not follow from what we have. A goal P \vee Q from the premise Q shows the danger in miniature: choose P, and the new subgoal P cannot be reached from Q at all: with P false and Q true, a derivation would lead from a true premise to a false conclusion, and Chapter 3 proves that no derivation does (@thm-soundness). So the goal-directed step for \vee comes with a caution: Postpone a disjunction: choose a side of a goal \varphi \vee \psi only when that side is in hand. “In hand” means that the side stands on an available line, or is plainly one step away. Until then, work from the premises: take conjunctions apart, fire implications, open the boxes the goal asks for, and look at what appears. When one side of the goal turns up, the choice has been made for us. Here are four derivations, in order of difficulty. Each Idea says, for each rule, whether it was chosen by the goal or by a premise. [Derivations with or-introduction] Show that: 1. P \vdash P \vee Q, and P \vdash Q \vee P; 2. P \wedge Q \vdash P \vee Q; 3. P \to Q \vdash P \to (Q \vee R); 4. (P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \to (R \vee S)). (a) Idea. The goal is a disjunction, and one of its sides, P, is the premise: in hand from the start. The only choice is which schema, and the goal decides it: P sits on the left of P \vee Q and on the right of Q \vee P. In the first, line 2 is the first schema with \varphi replaced by P and \psi by Q; in the second, it is the second schema with the same replacement. The letter Q appears in no premise. That is the clause “any other side” at work. (b) Idea. The goal P \vee Q is a disjunction, and neither side stands on a line yet, so we postpone it. Premise-directed: the premise’s main connective is \wedge, so \rulename{\wedge E} takes it apart. After that, both sides of the goal are in hand, and either choice finishes. The left derivation chose the left side (first schema); the right one chose the right side (second schema). Both are correct, and the choice was free precisely because both sides were in hand. That will not usually be so. (c) Idea. The goal’s main connective is the outer \to; the \vee sits inside its conclusion. Goal-directed: open a box with the hypothesis P, and the new goal inside it is Q \vee R, a disjunction, so we postpone it. Premise-directed: the premise P \to Q is an implication whose hypothesis P is now on a line, so \rulename{{\to}E} fires and gives Q. The left side of the goal is in hand; \rulename{\vee I} takes it, and \rulename{{\to}I} closes the box. Line 3 cites line 1, which lies in no box, and line 2, the assumption of the box that contains line 3. Line 4 is a line of the box itself, so \rulename{{\to}I} may cite the box \lines{2}{4}. (d) Idea. The goal has two arrows at the top of its structure, P \to (Q \to \cdots), so, as in @prp-curry, we open two nested boxes, first P, then Q; the inner one will close first. The innermost goal is R \vee S: postpone. Premise-directed: the only line that mentions R is the premise (P \wedge Q) \to R. Its hypothesis is P \wedge Q, which is not on any line, but both of its halves are: the two assumptions. So \rulename{\wedge I} builds it, \rulename{{\to}E} fires, and R is in hand. Then \rulename{\vee I}, and the two boxes close. This derivation uses every rule of the chapter so far except \rulename{\wedge E} and \rulename{R}. Line 4 cites line 2, from the outer box, which is still open at line 4. Line 5 cites line 1 from inside two boxes: a line in no box is available everywhere below it. Line 7 is a line of the outer box itself, which is why \rulename{{\to}I} at line 8 may cite \lines{2}{7}. Derivation (c) is where the habit of postponing pays. Suppose that, inside the box, we had committed at once to the goal’s right side, planning to reach Q \vee R from R. The box would then need R itself, from the premise P \to Q and the assumption P alone. The instance in the next warning makes both of these true and R false, so no derivation reaches R from them (a derivation never leads from true lines to a false one, which Chapter 3 proves: @thm-soundness). The plan was dead from its first step. Choosing a side of a disjunctive goal too early turns a reachable goal into an unreachable one. In (c), the goal inside the box is Q \vee R. A writer who opens with “we show R” has set out to prove, from P \to Q and P, the statement R; with x a real number, P: “x > 2”, Q: “x > 1” and R: “x > 3”, the premise and the assumption hold at x = 2.5, and R fails there. Keep the goal as the whole disjunction until one side appears on a line. Manufacturing a hypothesis In every derivation so far, \rulename{\vee I} produced the goal, or the goal of a box. It has a second use. A premise whose hypothesis is a disjunction can fire only when that disjunction stands on a line, exactly as written (the matching clause of @def-rule-implication-elimination). If one side of it is in hand, \rulename{\vee I} builds the whole hypothesis. [A disjunctive hypothesis splits into two implications] Show that (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R). Idea. Goal-directed: the goal is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge I} splits it into two subgoals, P \to R and Q \to R, and each is an implication, so each gets its own box. Inside the box of P, the goal is R. Premise-directed: the only line that mentions R is the premise, and \rulename{{\to}E} on it needs its hypothesis P \vee Q on a line. We have P, one side of that hypothesis. So \rulename{\vee I} manufactures P \vee Q, and the premise fires. Here \rulename{\vee I} is chosen not because the goal is a disjunction (the goal is R) but because a premise’s hypothesis is one. The box of Q is the same, with the other schema. Line 3 uses the first schema of @def-rule-disjunction-introduction (P on the left), line 7 the second (Q on the right). Both produce the same statement P \vee Q, the one the premise asks for. The two boxes are separate: the second opens after the first has closed, and nothing in it cites a line of the first. Line 10 cites lines 5 and 9, which lie in no box. This is the first place in this section where \rulename{\vee I} manufactures the hypothesis of a premise, and it will not be the last: the product example below, and several exercises, do the same. Weakening is how a strong fact is fed to a rule, or a theorem, that asks for a weaker one. In mathematical terms, the derivation says that a theorem with a hypothesis “P or Q” splits into two theorems. Let x be a real number, and suppose we know “if x \ge 0, then x^3 \ge 0”, that is, “if x > 0 or x = 0, then x^3 \ge 0”. Then we know “if x > 0, then x^3 \ge 0” and “if x = 0, then x^3 \ge 0”. The way back, from the two implications to the single one with the disjunctive hypothesis, needs the rule of the next section; it is derived there. In the derivation of @exm-or-hypothesis-split, line 3 could not have been skipped by letting line 4 cite line 2 directly, as “R — \rulename{{\to}E} 1, 2”. Why not? \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination) needs the implication on one cited line and its hypothesis, exactly, on the other. The hypothesis of line 1 is P \vee Q, and line 2 is P, which does not match it symbol for symbol. Line 3 writes the hypothesis out, and only then does line 1 fire. A goal we cannot reach yet The most obvious fact about “or” is that the order of its sides does not matter: P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. Try to derive it with the rules so far. The goal Q \vee P is a disjunction, so we postpone it and look at the premise. Its main connective is \vee, and no rule so far takes a disjunction apart. \rulename{\wedge E} needs a conjunction and \rulename{{\to}E} an implication; \rulename{\wedge I}, \rulename{\vee I}, and \rulename{R} may cite P \vee Q, but only to copy it or to build something larger around it. So the premise gives us nothing, and neither side of the goal ever comes into hand. We can get this far, though. Each side of the premise, assumed in a box, leads to the goal: This is a correct derivation, with a disappointing last line: it shows P \vee Q \vdash Q \to (Q \vee P), and line 1 is never cited. (A derivation need not use every premise, @def-derivable.) What we would like is to put the three lines 1, 4, and 7 together: one of P, Q holds, and either one leads to Q \vee P; so Q \vee P. That is a proof by cases, and none of the rules so far performs it. With them we cannot find a derivation of P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. The missing move is to use a disjunction, as \rulename{\wedge E} uses a conjunction and \rulename{{\to}E} uses an implication. The next section gives the rule that does this, and with it the six-line derivation that this attempt lacks. How this looks in a mathematical proof In written mathematics \rulename{\vee I} is almost always silent. Here are the two steps of the opening, written out as derivations. [A product with a zero factor] Let a and b be real numbers, and take as known the school fact “if a = 0 or b = 0, then a \cdot b = 0”. Prove that if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0, naming the rule behind each step. Then write the step from x > 0 to x \ge 0 as a derivation. The goal is an implication, so the proof supposes a = 0 (a box). Inside, the fact needs its hypothesis “a = 0 or b = 0”, which \rulename{\vee I} manufactures, as in @exm-or-hypothesis-split. In prose, with each step’s rule in brackets: Suppose a = 0. Then a = 0 or b = 0 [\rulename{\vee I}]. So, by the school fact, a \cdot b = 0 [\rulename{{\to}E}]. Hence, if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0 [\rulename{{\to}I}]. As a derivation, with the school fact as the premise: A written proof would say “if a = 0, then a \cdot b = 0 by the fact”, and leave out the words “a = 0 or b = 0”. The derivation shows what that sentence leaves out: a box, a weakening, and one use of the fact. For the second step, let x be a real number with x > 0. Written out, x \ge 0 is (x > 0) \vee (x = 0), and the step is one application of the first schema: Line 2 is x \ge 0, written out. Every “so x \ge 0” after x > 0, every “so \abs{t} \le 1” after \abs{t} < 1, and every “so n is even or n > 5” after “n is even” is this rule. A reader who checks a proof line by line should see it, even where the writer did not name it. It is a step that never leads from a truth to a falsehood, and it is also the step that explains why a conclusion can say less than the proof knew. What the rules sound like Since Section 1.3, each rule has had a row in a table that pairs it with the sentence a written proof uses for it and, for readers who meet a proof assistant, with the Lean code that performs it. Here is the row for \rulename{\vee I}; nothing later depends on the last column. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ------------------- --------------------------------------- ---------------------------- \rulename{\vee I} “So P or Q holds.” left (or Or.inl hp); right ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrase is different from the “in particular” of \rulename{\wedge E} on purpose. “In particular” announces that a part is being taken out of something bigger; “so P or Q” announces that something bigger, and weaker, is being built. Chapters 2 and 4 add rows for the remaining rules, and Chapter 5 turns the table into a dictionary between derivations and prose. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the two schemas of @def-rule-disjunction-introduction from memory, and say which letter in them may stand for a statement that appears in no earlier line. 2. Which of the following sentences, taken from proofs about a real number x or real numbers a, b, use \rulename{\vee I}? For each of the others, name the rule it uses. - “We have x < 3, so x \le 3.” - “We found that a = 0. So a = 0 or b = 0, and therefore a \cdot b = 0.” - “Since 0 < x < 1, in particular x < 1.” - “Since \abs{x - 2} < 1 implies 1 < x < 3, and \abs{x - 2} < 1, we get 1 < x < 3.” 3. True or false, with a reason: \rulename{\vee I} may introduce a side that is false. 4. To show Q, \ (P \vee Q) \to (Q \to R) \vdash R, which rule writes the first line after the premises, and what is that line? Why is that rule used, although the goal is not a disjunction? (a) From a line i holding \varphi, a line k holding \varphi \vee \psi, justified “\rulename{\vee I} i”; and, from the same line, a line k holding \psi \vee \varphi, with the same justification (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction). The letter \psi appears in no given line: it may be any statement. (b) The first uses \rulename{\vee I}: x \le 3 is (x < 3) \vee (x = 3), and its left side is in hand. The second uses \rulename{\vee I} to build “a = 0 or b = 0” from its left side, and then \rulename{{\to}E} on the fact about products, as in @exm-product-zero. The third uses \rulename{\wedge E}: 0 < x < 1 is (0 < x) \wedge (x < 1), and the sentence takes out its right half. The fourth uses \rulename{{\to}E}, with the implication first and its hypothesis second. (c) True. The added side \psi may be any statement, false ones included, as in the line (x = 2) \vee (1 = 0) of the Quick check after the definition. The new line is still true whenever the cited line is, because “or” is inclusive: one true side is enough. (d) The rule is \rulename{\vee I}, by its second schema, and line 3 is P \vee Q, from line 1. It is used because a premise’s hypothesis is a disjunction. The goal R occurs only in the premise (P \vee Q) \to (Q \to R), and \rulename{{\to}E} fires on that premise only when P \vee Q itself stands on a line. Only its right side Q is on a line, and \rulename{\vee I} turns it into P \vee Q. Then Q \to R follows by \rulename{{\to}E} 2, 3, and R by \rulename{{\to}E} 4, 1. The move is the one of @exm-or-hypothesis-split, where \rulename{\vee I} builds a premise’s hypothesis. B. Practice [B1: Committing to a side] Show that P \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (R \vee S), and that P \vdash (Q \vee P) \vee R. For each derivation, say at which line you committed to a side of a disjunctive goal, and why that was safe. For the first, the goal is an implication, so open a box with Q; the goal inside is R \vee S, which we postpone. Premise-directed, \rulename{\wedge E} takes out Q \to R, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires on the assumption Q. We committed at line 5, to the left side R, and only after line 4 had put R on a line. The other conjunct of the premise, P, is never used. For the second, the goal (Q \vee P) \vee R is a disjunction whose left side, Q \vee P, is itself a disjunction, and P is one side of that. Line 2 uses the second schema (P on the right) and line 3 the first, with \varphi replaced by Q \vee P. We committed twice, at lines 2 and 3, and both times the side was in hand: at line 2 the side P was the premise, and at line 3 the side Q \vee P was line 2. Choosing the side R at the outer level would have left the subgoal R, which the premise P cannot give. [B2: The last line] A search for P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to (S \vee R) has reached the stage below; only the last line is missing. Name the move, then complete it. The move is the one read off the goal: an implication goal opens a box with its hypothesis, and the box is closed by \rulename{{\to}I} once its last line is the implication’s conclusion. The box opened with P at line 3, and its last line, line 6, is S \vee R, the conclusion of the goal. So line 7 closes the box: Line 7 cites the box as the range \lines{3}{6}, not its lines one by one. Inside the box, the disjunction S \vee R was postponed until R came into hand at line 5; the side in hand was the right one, so line 6 uses the second schema. [B3: A theorem with a weaker hypothesis] Let x be a real number, and take as known the school fact “if x \ge 1, then x^2 \ge x”. Prove that if x > 1, then x^2 \ge x. Write the proof as a derivation whose premise is the school fact, with x \ge 1 written out as a disjunction, and then as two or three sentences of prose. Written out, x \ge 1 is (x > 1) \vee (x = 1), so the premise is an implication whose hypothesis is a disjunction. The goal is an implication: open a box with x > 1. Inside, \rulename{\vee I} manufactures the premise’s hypothesis, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires. In prose: Suppose x > 1. Then x \ge 1, so x^2 \ge x by the fact. Hence if x > 1, then x^2 \ge x. The words “then x \ge 1” are line 3. For instance, at x = 3 the conclusion reads 9 \ge 3. C. Going deeper [C1: Which new rules are safe?] Suppose someone proposes new rules for the derivations of this chapter. Let x be a real number. 1. Take the rule “from \varphi \vee \psi, write \varphi”. Starting from the premise “x \ge 0 or x < 0”, which is true for every real x, derive with it a line that is false at x = -1. 2. \rulename{\vee I} adds a side \psi that may be any statement at all. Explain why it can never lead from a true line to a false one. 3. Is the rule “from \varphi, write \varphi \wedge \psi, for any statement \psi” safe in the same sense? Justify your answer with an instance. (a) With \varphi replaced by x \ge 0 and \psi by x < 0, the proposed rule turns the premise into the line x \ge 0. At x = -1 the premise is true, since -1 < 0, and the line -1 \ge 0 is false. So the rule can lead from a true line to a false one. (b) Suppose the cited line \varphi is true. The new line \varphi \vee \psi (or \psi \vee \varphi) is true when at least one of its sides is true, because “or” is inclusive (Section 1.1), and its side \varphi is true. So the new line is true, whatever \psi is. The truth or falsity of \psi never enters. (c) No. The new line \varphi \wedge \psi is true only when both sides are, and \psi is arbitrary. With \varphi replaced by x = -1 and \psi by x \ge 0, at x = -1 the cited line is true and the new line, “x = -1 and x \ge 0”, is false. The contrast with (b) is the whole difference between \vee and \wedge: a disjunction needs one true side, so an arbitrary second side is harmless; a conjunction needs both, so it is not. That is why \rulename{\wedge I} asks for both sides on lines. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) applies the proposed rule to the premise to get x \ge 0, and checks at x = -1 that the premise is true and the new line false. - 3: (b) argues from the inclusive meaning of “or”: one true side makes the disjunction true, whatever the other side is. - 3: (c) answers no, with an instance in which \varphi is true and \varphi \wedge \psi is false. - 1: (c) names the difference: a conjunction needs both sides true. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), a premise that is false at x = -1; in (b), an argument that assumes \psi is true; in (c), “safe” on the grounds that \varphi is true. [C2: Predicting the manufacture] 1. Show that (P \vee Q) \to (R \wedge S) \vdash P \to S. 2. Show that (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R. 3. In each derivation, which rule built the hypothesis of the premise? Could you have predicted, from the premise’s main connective and the shape of its hypothesis alone, that this rule would be needed? (a) The goal is an implication: open a box with P; the goal inside is S. The only line mentioning S is the premise, whose conclusion R \wedge S contains it; to use the premise, \rulename{{\to}E} needs P \vee Q, built from P by \rulename{\vee I}. Then \rulename{\wedge E} takes out S. (b) The goal is an implication: open a box with P \wedge Q; the goal inside is R. The premise fires on P \vee Q. The assumption gives P by \rulename{\wedge E}, and \rulename{\vee I} builds P \vee Q. Taking Q at line 3 instead, and building P \vee Q by the second schema, works equally well. (c) In both, \rulename{\vee I} built the hypothesis (line 3 in (a), line 4 in (b)), and in both it could be predicted. The premise’s main connective is \to, so the premise is used by \rulename{{\to}E}, which needs its hypothesis P \vee Q on a line of its own, exactly. That disjunction occurs only inside the premise, as its hypothesis, and no rule takes the hypothesis out of an implication (\rulename{{\to}E} gives the conclusion). So it had to be built, and the only rule of the chapter so far that builds a disjunction is \rulename{\vee I}. The one question left was which side would be in hand; in (b) the conjunction P \wedge Q offered both.

title: 1.7 Using Or: Proof by Cases
content: Using Or: Proof by Cases The previous section met a goal the rules could not reach: from P \vee Q, derive Q \vee P. The rules could build a disjunction (\rulename{\vee I}, @def-rule-disjunction-introduction), but none of them could use one. This section gives the rule that uses a disjunction, \rulename{\vee E}. It is the most familiar move in mathematics after “suppose”: the split into cases, “if x \ge 0, then …; if x < 0, then …”. It is also the last rule of this chapter. We use it to reach the stalled goal, to prove the laws that let “and” and “or” be rearranged, and to prove three facts about absolute values; the section ends with all the rules of the chapter on one page. A proof that needs two cases The absolute value of a real number is defined in two cases: \abs{x} \coloneqq \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 . \end{cases} Suppose we want to prove that \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y} for all real numbers x and y. There is no single computation to do. Which formula gives \abs{xy} depends on the sign of xy, and that depends on the signs of x and y. Yet once the signs are fixed, each case is one line: if x \ge 0 and y < 0, for instance, then \abs{xy} = -xy = x \cdot (-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. So the proof we want has the shape “every real number is \ge 0 or < 0; in the first case …; in the second case …; so in every case …”. The rules so far cannot say this. The attempt at P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P at the end of Section 1.6 met the same wall from the other side. It derived that each side of the premise, assumed in a box, leads to the goal: lines 4 and 7 there were P \to (Q \vee P) and Q \to (Q \vee P). What it lacked was a rule to say “one of P, Q holds, and either one leads to Q \vee P; so Q \vee P”. No rule of \wedge or \to takes a statement “\varphi or \psi”, which does not say which side holds, and still reaches a definite conclusion. That is the job of the elimination rule for “or”. The rule of or-elimination To use “\varphi or \psi”, reach your goal from \varphi, and reach it again from \psi. The definition block states both rules for disjunction, so that the pair stands in one place: the new rule first, and then the two schemas of \rulename{\vee I} recalled from Section 1.6. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), the Greek letters stand for arbitrary statements and i, j, k, l, m, n for line numbers. [Rules for Disjunction] The first schema is the rule \rulename{\vee E} (or-elimination, or proof by cases); the other two are \rulename{\vee I}, as in @def-rule-disjunction-introduction. In \rulename{\vee E}, each line \chi (line k and line m) is a line of its box itself, not of a box inside it. In words, clause by clause. - The disjunction. Line i holds a disjunction \varphi \vee \psi, available at line n. The cases are not ours to invent: they are the two sides of a disjunction we already have, as a premise, an assumption, or a line derived earlier. Writing “Case 1 … Case 2 …” does not create it. - Two boxes. The first box opens with the left side \varphi as its assumption, the second with the right side \psi. They are separate: the second opens after the first has closed, and the drawing shows a break in the vertical bar between them. So, by the scope rule of @def-derivation, no line of the second box may cite a line of the first. The disjunction does not tell us which side holds, so we must be ready for both, and each case’s assumption is in force only inside its own box. - The same last line. Both boxes end in the same statement \chi, and in each box \chi is a line of that box itself, not of a box opened inside it. The rule then writes \chi a third time, outside both boxes, where neither \varphi nor \psi is assumed. That is honest only because \chi was reached whichever case holds. - Three citations. The justification “\rulename{\vee E} i, \lines{j}{k}, \lines{l}{m}” cites the disjunction first, then the box of the left side, then the box of the right side, each box as a range. Both boxes must be available at line n: closed, and sitting directly in the part of the derivation where line n is (@def-derivation). - Any conclusion. The statement \chi need not mention \varphi or \psi. It is whatever we are trying to reach. The next subsection says how to choose it. The degenerate case is a box of one line, whose assumption is already \chi. Nothing in the rule asks a box to contain more than its assumption, just as nothing in \rulename{{\to}I} did (@exm-first-boxes). The second derivation below has two such boxes. A case may use only its own assumption. Here is the error in its usual form. Let x be a real number, and split on “x \ge 0 or x < 0”. Case x \ge 0: then \abs{x} = x. Case x < 0: since x \ge 0, again \abs{x} = x. So \abs{x} = x. The second case cites the assumption of the first, whose box has closed, which the scope rule forbids. The conclusion is false at x = -1. Cases end in the current goal Section 1.3 set up two questions: what is the goal’s main connective? and what are the available lines’ main connectives? Section 1.6 answered the first for \vee: postpone a disjunctive goal until one side is in hand. Now we can answer the second. A disjunction on an available line invites \rulename{\vee E}: split on it. What should the two boxes end in? The rule leaves \chi to us, and the choice is always the same. It is the current goal: whatever we are trying to reach at the point where the split is made. That may be the goal of the whole derivation, or a subgoal inside other boxes. The boxes of the split end in it, and the \rulename{\vee E} line that closes the split then writes it outside both boxes, exactly where it was wanted. Cases end in the current goal. The two habits fit together. Faced with a goal \varphi \vee \psi and an available disjunction \alpha \vee \beta, do not choose a side of the goal yet: split on \alpha \vee \beta first. Inside each case the current goal is still \varphi \vee \psi, but now a new line is in hand, the case’s assumption, and it may be one side of the goal. Then choose, and the choice may be different in the two boxes. This is exactly how the stalled goal of Section 1.6 goes. [First derivations with “or”] Show that P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P, and that P \vee P \vdash P. Idea. For the first: the goal Q \vee P is a disjunction, and neither side is in hand, so we postpone it. The premise is a disjunction, so we split on it; the current goal is Q \vee P, so both boxes will end there. In the box of P, the right side of the goal is in hand, and \rulename{\vee I} takes it; in the box of Q, the left side is, and \rulename{\vee I} takes that. The choice of side differs between the boxes, and each is safe because it is made inside its own case. The two boxes are separate: the break in the vertical bar between lines 3 and 4 shows where the first closes and the second opens. Line 3 uses the second schema of \rulename{\vee I} (P on the right) and line 5 the first (Q on the left). Both boxes end in Q \vee P, and line 6 cites the disjunction on line 1 and the boxes \lines{2}{3} and \lines{4}{5}. Compare the stalled attempt of Section 1.6: its two boxes are these two boxes, and line 6 is the step it could not take. For the second, the goal is P, and the premise is a disjunction, so we split. Both cases are already the goal, so each box consists of its assumption alone. This is the degenerate case split, in which the two cases are the same case. The box \lines{2}{2} is a legal box whose last line is P, a line of that box itself, and so is \lines{3}{3}. Change one line of the first derivation and it stops being a derivation. Suppose the second box stops at its assumption Q, and the last line still claims Q \vee P: Everything cited exists and is available: the disjunction, a box opened by P, a box opened by Q. What fails is the clause about the last lines. The box \lines{4}{4} ends in Q, the box \lines{2}{3} ends in Q \vee P, and \rulename{\vee E} needs one statement that ends both. The repair is the missing line 5 of the correct derivation. A derivation contains a line P \vee Q and a box opened by P that ends in R. No box is opened by Q. Which clause of \rulename{\vee E} stops us writing R? What single change to the derivation would allow it? The clause “two boxes”: the rule needs one box opened by each side of the disjunction, and the box opened by Q is missing. Adding a box opened by Q whose last line is R (a derivation of R from Q and the lines available there) allows \rulename{\vee E}, citing the disjunction and both boxes. Why is the rule built like this? Drop the second box, and from “x \ge 0 or x < 0” and a derivation of \abs{x} = x from x \ge 0 we could conclude \abs{x} = x for every real x, which fails at x = -1. Allow the two boxes to end in different statements \chi_1 and \chi_2, and ask what may be written after them: all we honestly know is “\chi_1 or \chi_2”. That is already reachable with the rule as it stands, by \rulename{\vee I} at the end of each box, turning both last lines into \chi_1 \vee \chi_2 (exercise B3 carries this out). So the rule asks for one common last line and loses nothing. The next derivation splits on a disjunction that is not a premise but an assumption, opened because the goal asked for it. [Cases on a hypothesis are two implications] Show that (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \to R. Idea. Goal-directed: the goal is an implication, so we open a box with its hypothesis P \vee Q, and the current goal inside is R. Premise-directed: the assumption just made is a disjunction, so we split on it, and both case boxes end in the current goal R. In the case P, the premise’s main connective is \wedge; \rulename{\wedge E} takes out P \to R, and \rulename{{\to}E} fires on the case’s assumption. The case Q is the same with the other half of the premise. Line 9 closes the split inside the outer box: it cites line 2 and the boxes \lines{3}{5} and \lines{6}{8}, all of which sit directly in the box \lines{2}{9}, as line 9 does. Line 9 is a line of the outer box itself, so \rulename{{\to}I} at line 10 may cite \lines{2}{9}. Lines 4 and 7 cite line 1, which lies in no box. Section 1.6 derived the converse, (P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R), in @exm-or-hypothesis-split, using only \rulename{\vee I}. So each of the two statements is derivable from the other: cases on a hypothesis are two implications. This is how mathematicians prove “if P or Q, then R”: they prove “if P, then R” and “if Q, then R”. To show that an integer which is one more, or three more, than a multiple of 4 is odd, one treats the two forms separately, and the derivation above is the reason that is enough. Laws of “or” Case splits are not only about numbers. The same two rules prove the laws that let us rearrange “and” and “or”. The first says that “and” distributes over “or”, in both directions. [Distributivity] P \wedge (Q \vee R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R), and (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) \vdash P \wedge (Q \vee R). Try it first (ten minutes): derive the first sequent. Which rule will give its last line, and which disjunction will you split on? The natural first attempt reads the goal: it is a disjunction, so end with \rulename{\vee I} and aim at one side, say P \wedge Q. That needs Q on a line, and the premise offers only P and Q \vee R; nothing turns Q \vee R into Q. The other side fails the same way. So the goal must be postponed, and the attempt shows why: the premise holds a disjunction, Q \vee R, and neither of its sides is known. Premise-directed, then: \rulename{\wedge E} takes the premise apart into P and Q \vee R, and we split on Q \vee R, both cases ending in the current goal (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R). In the case Q, the side P \wedge Q is one \rulename{\wedge I} away, and \rulename{\vee I} weakens it to the whole goal; the case R builds the other side. In the second sequent the premise itself is the disjunction, so we split on it at once; each case is a conjunction containing P, and \rulename{\vee I} turns its other half into Q \vee R. Before reading on: in the first derivation, which line does each box end on, and why must the two be the same? For the first sequent, the following is a derivation with premise P \wedge (Q \vee R) and last line (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R). Lines 5 and 8 may cite line 2, which lies in no box and so is available everywhere below it. Both boxes end in the goal, lines 6 and 9, as \rulename{\vee E} at line 10 requires. For the second sequent, the following is a derivation with premise (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) and last line P \wedge (Q \vee R). This proves both sequents. The answer to the prompt: the boxes end on lines 6 and 9, both (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R). They must be the same statement because line 10 writes that statement outside both boxes, where neither Q nor R is assumed, and that is honest only if it was reached in each case. In the second derivation, line 8 derives P a second time instead of citing line 3. It has to: line 3 lies in the box \lines{2}{6}, which has closed, so line 3 is not available at line 8. Each case must earn its own P. For a real number x, take P: “x \ne 0”, Q: “x > 0” and R: “x < 0”. The first sequent then reads: a nonzero number that is positive or negative is a positive nonzero number or a negative nonzero number. The law is dull in words, which is as it should be. Its use is in derivations, where it moves a case split from inside a conjunction to the outside, and in the laws of sets, where “and” and “or” become intersection and union. The next derivation shows a case split inside a case: \rulename{\vee E} applied within one box of another \rulename{\vee E}. [Regrouping a disjunction] Show that P \vee (Q \vee R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \vee R. Idea. The goal is a disjunction, and no side of it is in hand: postpone. The premise is a disjunction: split on it, with both boxes ending in the current goal (P \vee Q) \vee R. The case P is two weakenings: first to P \vee Q, then to the goal. The case Q \vee R is itself a disjunction, and neither Q nor R is known; so, inside that box, we split again, and the inner boxes end in the same current goal. In the inner case Q the goal is two weakenings away, and in the inner case R one. Before reading on: which disjunction does the inner \rulename{\vee E} cite, and which box must contain it? Line 11 is the inner case split. It cites the disjunction on line 5, the assumption of the outer box it sits in, and the boxes \lines{6}{8} and \lines{9}{10}, all of which sit inside the box \lines{5}{11}, as line 11 does. Line 12 is the outer case split. Its second box is \lines{5}{11}, whose last line, line 11, is a line of that box itself and not of a further box inside it, as @def-rules-disjunction requires. That is why line 11 is needed at all: without it, the box \lines{5}{11} would end inside the inner box \lines{9}{10}. From a skeleton to a proof about numbers Almost every proof by cases in analysis has the same skeleton. A known fact supplies the cases, and each case is handled by a separate argument, a small lemma that turns the case’s assumption into the goal. As a derivation, with the fact and the two lemmas as premises: The idea behind it is the whole method of this section at its simplest. The goal R is atomic, so the goal suggests nothing. Premise-directed, the disjunction on line 1 is split, both boxes ending in the current goal R. In each box the matching lemma fires on the case’s assumption. (@exm-cases-on-hypothesis did the same with the two lemmas packed into one conjunction, and inside a box.) In a proof about real numbers, the disjunction is usually a fact about the order. The facts about \le and the absolute value used below are school algebra: every real number a satisfies a \ge 0 or a < 0; the rules of signs for products; adding two inequalities of the same direction. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves all of them from the axioms of an ordered field. Here we take them as known. In the language of this chapter, “every real number a satisfies a \ge 0 or a < 0” is a supply of disjunctions: for each number we meet, it gives a line (a \ge 0) \vee (a < 0) that \rulename{\vee E} may cite. The first example is the smallest, and it is written twice: as a proof in which every step carries its rule in brackets, and as a derivation. [A number is at most its absolute value] Let x be a real number. Prove that \abs{x} \ge x, by cases, labeling each step with its rule. The goal \abs{x} \ge x is the disjunction (\abs{x} > x) \vee (\abs{x} = x), and neither side is known for every x (the first fails at x = 1, the second at x = -1), so we postpone it. The fact “x \ge 0 or x < 0” is a disjunction to split on. In prose: We have x \ge 0 or x < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case x \ge 0. By the definition of the absolute value, \abs{x} = x [\rulename{{\to}E}]. So \abs{x} \ge x [\rulename{\vee I}]. Case x < 0. By the definition, \abs{x} = -x, and -x > 0 > x; so \abs{x} > x [\rulename{{\to}E}], which is the school-algebra fact “if x < 0, then \abs{x} > x” used on the case’s assumption. So \abs{x} \ge x [\rulename{\vee I}]. In either case \abs{x} \ge x, so \abs{x} \ge x. As a derivation, with the order fact, the definition’s first clause, and the school-algebra fact about negative numbers as premises, and with \abs{x} \ge x written out: It is the skeleton above, with a weakening at the end of each box: line 6 takes the right side of the goal (second schema of \rulename{\vee I}) and line 9 the left side (first schema). Each case took the side it had in hand. At x = 3, the first case applies and line 6 reads 3 > 3 or 3 = 3; at x = -2, the second applies and line 8 reads 2 > -2. The next two examples are longer, and in each the case split is doing real work. [The absolute value of a product] Let x and y be real numbers. Prove that \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}. We use that \abs{a} = -a whenever a \le 0: for a < 0 this is the definition, and for a = 0 both sides are 0. The number x satisfies x \ge 0 or x < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Inside each case, y \ge 0 or y < 0, and we argue by cases again. Case x \ge 0, y \ge 0. Then xy \ge 0, so \abs{xy} = xy = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x \ge 0, y < 0. Then xy \le 0, so \abs{xy} = -xy = x \cdot (-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x < 0, y \ge 0. Then xy \le 0, so \abs{xy} = -xy = (-x) \cdot y = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Case x < 0, y < 0. Then xy > 0, so \abs{xy} = xy = (-x)(-y) = \abs{x}\abs{y}. Each inner case split reaches \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}, so each outer case does, and hence the equation holds. The structure is two uses of \rulename{\vee E}, one inside each box of the other: two outer boxes (the sign of x), each containing two inner boxes (the sign of y), and every one of the four inner boxes ending in the same equation, the current goal. The second and third cases needed the remark about a \le 0. When x = 0 and y < 0, the product is 0, not negative, and without the remark the case would have a hole at exactly that point. A case split need not be the obvious one. The triangle inequality has an equally short proof with two cases, if we split on the sign of the right quantity. [The triangle inequality by cases] Let x and y be real numbers. Prove that \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. First, every real number a satisfies a \le \abs{a} and -a \le \abs{a}. This is itself a proof by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]: if a \ge 0, then \abs{a} = a, so a \le \abs{a}, and -a \le 0 \le a = \abs{a}; if a < 0, then \abs{a} = -a, so -a \le \abs{a}, and a < 0 < -a = \abs{a}. Now x + y \ge 0 or x + y < 0, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case x + y \ge 0. Then \abs{x + y} = x + y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, adding x \le \abs{x} and y \le \abs{y}. Case x + y < 0. Then \abs{x + y} = -x - y = (-x) + (-y) \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, adding -x \le \abs{x} and -y \le \abs{y}. Both cases reach \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, so it holds. Two case splits appear here, one after the other rather than one inside the other. The first proves a small lemma for an arbitrary number a, both halves at once, and its first half, a \le \abs{a}, is @exm-abs-at-least-x again. The second uses both halves of the lemma, for a = x and for a = y. Splitting on the sign of x + y instead of the signs of x and y is what saves two cases: the absolute value in the goal is \abs{x + y}, and its sign is the only one the goal’s left side cares about. A case split must cover every possibility. A common faulty proof of the triangle inequality treats “x \ge 0 and y \ge 0” and “x < 0 and y < 0”, checks both, and stops. The disjunction of these two cases is not a fact: x = 1, y = -1 satisfies neither. So there is no line \varphi \vee \psi for \rulename{\vee E} to cite, and the rule was never legally applied. The missing mixed-sign cases are the interesting ones: at x = 1, y = -1 the inequality reads 0 \le 2, and it is strict. The warning is about the first thing \rulename{\vee E} cites. The disjunction must itself be on an available line, derived or known, before the boxes are opened. Cases must exhaust, and a split that silently drops a value is a missing case in disguise. “Every real x satisfies x > 0 or x < 0” is false: x = 0 satisfies neither. A proof that splits into x > 0 and x < 0 cites a disjunction that is not available, and proves nothing about x = 0. The true disjunctions are “x \ge 0 or x < 0”, and “x > 0, or x = 0, or x < 0”. Cases may overlap, however. “x \ge 0 or x \le 0” is true for every real x, and x = 0 lies in both cases. Nothing in \rulename{\vee E} forbids this: the rule asks that the goal be reached in each case, not that the cases be disjoint. (This is the inclusive “or” of Section 1.1.) Each of the following begins a proof that x^2 \ge 0 for every real number x. Which case splits are exhaustive, so that \rulename{\vee E} may be applied? 1. Case x \ge 0; case x < 0. 2. Case x > 0; case x < 0. 3. Case x \ge 0; case x \le 0. (i) Exhaustive: every real number is \ge 0 or < 0. (ii) Not exhaustive: x = 0 is in neither case, so the disjunction cited is false. The claim is still true at 0, but this split never proves it there. (iii) Exhaustive. The cases overlap at x = 0, which does no harm: x^2 = 0 \ge 0 is reached in both. What the rules sound like Here is the row of the rule, phrase, and Lean table for \rulename{\vee E}. As before, the last column is for readers who use a proof assistant, and nothing depends on it. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------- \rulename{\vee E} “Case 1: P. … so R. Case 2: Q. … so R. In either case, R.” Or.elim h (or cases h) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrase has three parts, and a written proof often drops the first: “we argue by cases” without saying which disjunction supplies them. When the disjunction is a standard fact (“x \ge 0 or x < 0”), that is harmless. When it is not, the reader should ask for it, because it is the line the rule cites first. The rules of this chapter This chapter has introduced six rules, one or two at a time, and the structural clause \rulename{R}. Here they are on one page, as schemas. Letters in the number column stand for line numbers; every cited line must be available (@def-derivation), and each box rule needs the box’s last line as a line of that box itself. Conjunction (@def-rules-conjunction): \rulename{\wedge I}, and the two forms of \rulename{\wedge E}. Implication (@def-rules-implication): \rulename{{\to}E} and \rulename{{\to}I}; and repetition, clause (D3) of @def-derivation. Disjunction (@def-rules-disjunction): the two forms of \rulename{\vee I}, and \rulename{\vee E}. Each rule is also a move in the search for a derivation. Read by the goal’s main connective, the introduction rules say how a goal is built: that is the move read the skeleton off the goal. Read by an available line’s main connective, the elimination rules say how that line is used: use a premise by its main connective. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Main connective As the goal (goal-directed) As an available line (premise-directed) ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \wedge two subgoals, one per side; finish with \rulename{\wedge I} take it apart with \rulename{\wedge E} \to open a box with the hypothesis; the new goal is the conclusion; close with \rulename{{\to}I} fire it with \rulename{{\to}E} once its hypothesis is on a line, or make the hypothesis a subgoal \vee postpone; choose a side with \rulename{\vee I} when that side is in hand split with \rulename{\vee E}; both boxes end in the current goal -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- And here is the full rule, phrase, and Lean table for the chapter, assembled from the rows of Sections 1.3 to 1.7. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean --------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ ---------------------------- \rulename{\wedge I} “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor \rulename{\wedge E} “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2) \rulename{{\to}E} “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” exact h hp \rulename{{\to}I} “Assume P. … Hence Q.” intro hp \rulename{R} “As shown above, P.” exact hp \rulename{\vee I} “So P or Q holds.” left (or Or.inl hp); right \rulename{\vee E} “Case 1: P. … so R. Case 2: Q. … so R. In either case, R.” Or.elim h (or cases h) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The rules for “not”, for \bot, and for “if and only if”, the rule for proof by contradiction, and the method that turns the table of moves above into a way of finding derivations are the subject of Chapter 2. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the rule \rulename{\vee E} as a schema, and name the three things its justification cites. 2. For each sentence, taken from a proof, name the disjunction that supplies the cases and the statement both cases end in. - “If n is even, then n^2 + n = n(n + 1) is even; if n is odd, then n + 1 is even and so is n(n + 1). Either way, n^2 + n is even.” - “Both possibilities for the sign of t give t^2 \ge 0.” 3. Let n be an integer. True or false, with a reason: “If n is even, then n^2 is even. Since every integer is even or odd, n^2 is even” is a correct proof by cases that n^2 is even. 4. The following is offered as a derivation of P \vee Q, \; P \to R \vdash R. Name the line that is not justified and the clause of @def-rules-disjunction it violates. 5. In the first derivation of @prp-distributivity, which line is the disjunction that \rulename{\vee E} cites at line 10, and where did it come from? Why does each box end in (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) rather than in P \wedge Q and P \wedge R? 6. In the same derivation, why does line 6 use \rulename{\vee I} to put P \wedge Q on the left? Could line 6 have been (P \wedge R) \vee (P \wedge Q)? (a) The schema is the first one of @def-rules-disjunction: from a line i holding \varphi \vee \psi, a box \lines{j}{k} opened by \varphi, and a box \lines{l}{m} opened by \psi, each ending in the same statement \chi as a line of its own, a line n holding \chi. The justification “\rulename{\vee E} i, \lines{j}{k}, \lines{l}{m}” cites the disjunction and the two boxes. (b) In the first, the disjunction is “n is even or n is odd”, and both cases end in “n^2 + n is even”. In the second, it is “t \ge 0 or t < 0” (the sentence does not say it, and a careful reader supplies it), and both cases end in t^2 \ge 0. (c) False. The disjunction “n is even or n is odd” does not say which side holds, so \rulename{\vee E} needs a second case, reaching “n^2 is even” from “n is odd”, and the argument has none. Here the second case cannot be supplied: at n = 1 the number n^2 = 1 is odd, so the claim itself is false. (d) Line 5. \rulename{\vee E} needs two boxes, one opened by each side of the disjunction (the clause “two boxes”); line 5 cites only the box opened by P, and no box opened by Q exists. Nothing available reaches R from Q either, so the gap cannot be filled from these premises. An instance shows the claim itself fails (informally: a derivation never leads from true premises to a false conclusion, which Chapter 3 proves: @thm-soundness): for a real number x, take P: “x > 1”, Q: “x < 1”, R: “x > 0”. At x = -1 both premises hold and R does not. (e) Line 3, Q \vee R, obtained from the premise by \rulename{\wedge E}. Each box must end in the current goal, (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R), because line 10 writes one statement, the same one that ends both boxes; boxes ending in P \wedge Q and P \wedge R would end in different statements, and \rulename{\vee E} could not be applied to them. (f) Line 6 must be the current goal exactly, since both boxes end in it and line 10 writes it. The goal (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) has P \wedge Q as its left side, so line 6 uses the first schema of \rulename{\vee I}. The line (P \wedge R) \vee (P \wedge Q) is also an instance of \rulename{\vee I} on line 5 (the second schema), but it is a different statement: the first box would then end differently from the second, whose last line 9 is (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R), and \rulename{\vee E} could not cite both boxes. B. Practice [B1: The other distributive law] Show that (P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R) \vdash P \vee (Q \wedge R). Hint: after taking the premise apart, you will need a case split inside a case. The goal is a disjunction with no side in hand, so we postpone it. The premise gives two disjunctions. Split on P \vee Q, both cases ending in the goal. In the case P, the goal is one weakening away. In the case Q, we still lack R, so we split on P \vee R inside that box: its case P weakens as before, and its case R combines with Q. Line 10 cites line 6, the assumption of the enclosing box, which is still open at line 10. Line 12 cites line 3, which lies in no box. Splitting on P \vee R first, with the roles of Q and R exchanged, works equally well. [B2: The larger of two numbers] For real numbers a and b, let \max(a, b) \coloneqq a if a \ge b, and \max(a, b) \coloneqq b if a < b. Prove that \max(a, b) \ge a and \max(a, b) \ge b. Hence deduce that \max(a, b) \ge \frac{1}{2}(a + b): the larger of two numbers is at least their average. We have a \ge b or a < b, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]; the current goal is the conjunction “\max(a, b) \ge a and \max(a, b) \ge b”. Case a \ge b. Then \max(a, b) = a. So \max(a, b) \ge a, since a = a and \ge allows equality [\rulename{\vee I}]; and \max(a, b) = a \ge b. So both hold [\rulename{\wedge I}]. Case a < b. Then \max(a, b) = b. So \max(a, b) = b > a, which gives \max(a, b) \ge a [\rulename{\vee I}]; and \max(a, b) = b \ge b [\rulename{\vee I}]. So both hold [\rulename{\wedge I}]. In either case \max(a, b) \ge a and \max(a, b) \ge b, so both hold. Adding the two inequalities gives 2\max(a, b) \ge a + b, and dividing by 2 > 0 gives \max(a, b) \ge \frac{1}{2}(a + b). For instance, \max(3, -5) = 3 \ge -1 = \frac{1}{2}(3 + (-5)). [B3: Two cases, two conclusions] 1. Show that P \vee Q, \; P \to R, \; Q \to S \vdash R \vee S. 2. Use (a) to prove: for every integer n, n^2 is a multiple of 4 or n^2 is one more than a multiple of 4. You may use that every integer is even or odd. (a) The goal is a disjunction: postpone. Split on P \vee Q. In each case the matching implication gives one of R, S, and \rulename{\vee I} weakens it to the common last line R \vee S, the current goal. (b) Take P: “n is even”, Q: “n is odd”, R: “n^2 is a multiple of 4”, S: “n^2 is one more than a multiple of 4”. The premise P \vee Q is the fact we may use. For P \to R: if n = 2k for an integer k, then n^2 = 4k^2. For Q \to S: if n = 2k + 1, then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 4(k^2 + k) + 1. By (a), R \vee S. For instance, 6^2 = 36 = 4 \cdot 9 and 7^2 = 49 = 4 \cdot 12 + 1. C. Going deeper [C1: The reverse triangle inequality] Let x and y be real numbers. Prove that \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert \le \abs{x - y} by splitting into the two cases \abs{x} \ge \abs{y} and \abs{x} < \abs{y}, using in each case the triangle inequality of @exm-triangle-inequality-cases. Then explain why these two cases exhaust all possibilities, and why a split on the signs of x and y would need four cases. [Hint 1] The triangle inequality bounds \abs{u + v}. Write x as a sum of two numbers whose absolute values appear in the goal. [Hint 2] In the case \abs{x} \ge \abs{y}, the left side is \abs{x} - \abs{y}. Start from x = (x - y) + y. We use two school facts: for real numbers a, b, either a \ge b or a < b; and \abs{-a} = \abs{a} for every real a (if a \ge 0 then -a \le 0, so \abs{-a} = a; if a < 0 then -a > 0, so \abs{-a} = -a = \abs{a}). By the first fact, \abs{x} \ge \abs{y} or \abs{x} < \abs{y}, and we argue by cases [\rulename{\vee E}]. Case \abs{x} \ge \abs{y}. Then \abs{x} - \abs{y} \ge 0, so \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert = \abs{x} - \abs{y}. By @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to the numbers x - y and y, \abs{x} = \abs{(x - y) + y} \le \abs{x - y} + \abs{y} , so \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y}, which is the goal in this case. Case \abs{x} < \abs{y}. Then \abs{x} - \abs{y} < 0, so \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert = \abs{y} - \abs{x}. By @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to y - x and x, \abs{y} = \abs{(y - x) + x} \le \abs{y - x} + \abs{x} , so \abs{y} - \abs{x} \le \abs{y - x} = \abs{-(x - y)} = \abs{x - y}. Both cases reach the goal, which proves the inequality. The two cases exhaust all possibilities because they are the two sides of the disjunction “a \ge b or a < b” with a = \abs{x}, b = \abs{y}, and that disjunction holds for all real numbers. The split was chosen by the goal: the outer absolute value is of \abs{x} - \abs{y}, and its formula depends only on the sign of that difference. A split on signs would decide \abs{x} and \abs{y} separately: x \ge 0 or x < 0 gives the formula for \abs{x}, and inside each case y \ge 0 or y < 0 gives the formula for \abs{y}. That is a case split inside each box of another, with 2 \cdot 2 = 4 inner boxes, as in @exm-abs-product-cases. Fewer would not do for that method: with only the sign of x fixed, \abs{y} still has no formula. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states the disjunction \abs{x} \ge \abs{y} or \abs{x} < \abs{y} and says it holds for all reals. - 3: in the first case, removes the outer absolute value correctly and derives \abs{x} - \abs{y} \le \abs{x - y} from the triangle inequality for (x - y) + y. - 3: in the second case, the same with the roles exchanged, including \abs{y - x} = \abs{x - y}. - 2: explains the four sign cases as a split inside each case of another. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert = \abs{x} - \abs{y} in both cases; applying the triangle inequality to a difference as if \abs{u - v} \le \abs{u} - \abs{v}. A proof that squares both sides instead, or splits on signs, earns the 6 points of the two middle lines if every case is complete. [C2: Find the error] Here is a proof, by four cases, that \abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} for all real numbers x and y. Case 1: x \ge 0. Then \abs{x} = x. Case 1a: y \ge 0. Then \abs{y} = y, and \abs{x - y} is x - y or y - x. Since x - y \le x \le x + y and y - x \le y \le x + y, we get \abs{x - y} \le x + y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}. Case 1b: y < 0. Then \abs{y} = -y, and x - y > 0, so \abs{x - y} = x - y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}. Case 2: x < 0. Then \abs{x} = -x. Case 2a: y \ge 0. Then \abs{y} = y, and x - y < 0, so \abs{x - y} = y - x = \abs{y} + \abs{x}. Case 2b: y < 0. Then \abs{y} = -y. Since x \ge 0 and y < 0, we have x - y > 0, so \abs{x - y} = x - y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, because x \le \abs{x} and -y = \abs{y}. All four cases give \abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. 1. Is the statement true? 2. Find the line that is not justified, and name the rule whose conditions it breaks. 3. Show with specific numbers that the step fails. 4. Repair Case 2b. (a) Yes. For instance, it follows from @exm-triangle-inequality-cases applied to x and -y, since \abs{-y} = \abs{y} (shown in the solution of @exr-disjunction-and-cases-c1). So the question is not whether the conclusion holds but whether this argument proves it. (b) The sentence “Since x \ge 0 and y < 0, we have x - y > 0” in Case 2b. The assumption x \ge 0 is the assumption of Case 1. In derivation terms, it opens the first box of the outer \rulename{\vee E}, and Case 2b lies inside the second box, which is opened by x < 0. Once the first box has closed, its lines are not available (the scope rule of @def-derivation), so Case 2b may not cite x \ge 0: the rule broken is \rulename{\vee E}, whose second box may use only its own assumption and the lines available outside both boxes. The sentence is the reasoning of Case 1b copied into Case 2b, where its assumption is no longer in force. So the box of Case 2 does not reach the goal from the lines available to it, and the final \rulename{\vee E} has no right to cite it. (c) Take x = -3 and y = -1, which is Case 2b. Then x - y = -2, which is not > 0, and \abs{x - y} = 2 \ne -2 = x - y. The conclusion of Case 2b still holds here (2 \le 3 + 1), but the step used to reach it is false. (d) In Case 2b, x < 0 and y < 0, so \abs{x} = -x and \abs{y} = -y. The number \abs{x - y} is x - y or y - x. Since x < 0, we have x - y < -y = \abs{y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. Since y < 0, we have y - x < -x = \abs{x} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. So in either case \abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}, using only the assumptions of Case 2b. [C3: Exit check: a distributive law, rule by rule] Derive (P \wedge Q) \vee (R \wedge Q) \vdash (P \vee R) \wedge Q, naming the rule and the cited lines on every line. Then say which steps would change if the premise were (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) and the goal P \wedge (Q \vee R), and which would stay the same. The goal is a conjunction, but neither of its sides is on a line, and the premise is a disjunction, so we split on the premise first; both cases end in the current goal (P \vee R) \wedge Q. In each case, \rulename{\wedge E} takes the assumption apart, \rulename{\vee I} builds P \vee R from the side in hand, and \rulename{\wedge I} builds the goal. Line by line: 1 is the premise; 2 is the assumption of the first case; 3 and 4 are \rulename{\wedge E} on line 2; 5 is \rulename{\vee I} on line 3, first schema; 6 is \rulename{\wedge I} on lines 5 and 4, in that order, so that P \vee R is the left conjunct; 7 is the assumption of the second case; 8 and 9 are \rulename{\wedge E} on line 7; 10 is \rulename{\vee I} on line 8, second schema; 11 is \rulename{\wedge I} on lines 10 and 9; 12 is \rulename{\vee E}, citing the disjunction on line 1 and the boxes \lines{2}{6} and \lines{7}{11}, both of which end in the goal as lines of their own. No line of the second box cites the first. With premise (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) and goal P \wedge (Q \vee R), the shape stays the same: a split on the premise, \rulename{\wedge E} twice in each box, one \rulename{\vee I} and one \rulename{\wedge I} in each box, and \rulename{\vee E} at the end. What changes is which part is weakened and where it goes. The common conjunct is now P, and the parts that differ between the cases are Q and R; so the \rulename{\vee I} lines build Q \vee R (from Q in the first box, first schema; from R in the second, second schema), and the \rulename{\wedge I} lines cite the line holding P first, since P is now the left conjunct of the goal. That derivation is the second one of @prp-distributivity. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: splits on the premise by \rulename{\vee E}, with two boxes opened by its two sides. - 2: in each box, takes the assumption apart by \rulename{\wedge E} into both conjuncts. - 2: in each box, uses \rulename{\vee I} to build P \vee R from the side in hand, with the correct schema. - 2: in each box, builds the goal by \rulename{\wedge I}, so that both boxes end in the same line, the goal. - 2: the \rulename{\vee E} line cites the disjunction and both boxes as ranges, and the final sentences name the changed steps (the \rulename{\vee I} lines, now building Q \vee R, and the order of the \rulename{\wedge I} citations). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a line in one box citing a line of the other box; a conclusion drawn inside one box only and then used outside it. A second route is also correct: split the premise twice, once ending both boxes in P \vee R and once ending both in Q, and then join the two results by \rulename{\wedge I} outside every box (14 lines). Its points map as follows: 2 for either split with two boxes opened by the premise’s sides; 2 for the \rulename{\wedge E} lines in the boxes; 2 for the \rulename{\vee I} sides; 2 for the final \rulename{\wedge I}, with the boxes of each split ending in the same line; 2 for the citations and the final sentences. [C4: The second half] A search for Q \vee R, \ Q \to (P \to S), \ R \to S \vdash P \to S has written the premises and opened one box; the rest is blank. The finished derivation has 11 lines. Name the move, then complete it. [Hint 1] Inside the box, what is the current goal, and which available line is a disjunction? [Hint 2] Inside the box the goal is S, and no available line gives S at once. What can you do with the one disjunction available? The moves are two. First, the box of line 4 was read off the goal: P \to S is an implication, so the box opened with P, and its current goal is S; it will be closed by \rulename{{\to}I}. Second, inside it, the available disjunction Q \vee R (line 1, in no box, so available inside the box) is split, and both case boxes end in the current goal S. In the case Q, line 2 fires to give P \to S, which fires on line 4; in the case R, line 3 fires. Line 7 cites line 4, the assumption of the outer box, which contains line 7. Line 10 is a line of the box \lines{4}{10} itself (the case boxes have closed), so \rulename{{\to}I} may cite that box at line 11. Splitting outside the box instead, with both case boxes ending in P \to S, is also a correct derivation of the sequent; it does not complete the lines given, because it would split before line 4, not after. R. Review [R1] Let f be a function and [a, b] an interval. Take the atomic statements C: “f is continuous on [a, b]”, B: “f is bounded on [a, b]” and I: “f is integrable on [a, b]”; you need not know what the words mean. Translate the argument “If f is continuous on [a, b] and bounded there, then f is integrable on [a, b]. f is bounded on [a, b]. f is continuous on [a, b]. So f is integrable on [a, b] and bounded there.” into a sequent, and derive it. The sequent is (C \wedge B) \to I, \ B, \ C \vdash I \wedge B: three premises and a conclusion, as in @def-sequent. The goal is a conjunction, so it splits into the subgoals I and B. B is a premise. The only line that mentions I is the first premise, whose hypothesis C \wedge B is built by \rulename{\wedge I} (@def-rules-conjunction) from two premises; then \rulename{{\to}E} (@def-rule-implication-elimination) gives I. Line 4 cites line 3 first, so that C is the left conjunct, as in the hypothesis of line 1; the hypothesis must match exactly. Line 2 is cited twice, at lines 4 and 6: a line is not used up by being cited. [R2] Show that (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R), \ P \wedge S \vdash R \wedge S, and say in one sentence which step you found by working backwards from the goal. Premise-directed, both premises are conjunctions and are taken apart by \rulename{\wedge E} (@def-rules-conjunction); goal-directed, the goal R \wedge S splits into R and S, and S is already in hand. For R, work backwards as in @exm-implication-chains: Q \to R is available, so Q becomes the subgoal; P \to Q is available, so P does; and P is in hand. The chain of lines 7 and 8 was found backwards, from the subgoal R to Q to P, and written forwards. [R3] Is \vdash (P \wedge (P \to Q)) \to (Q \vee R)? Justify your answer. Yes. The goal’s main connective is the outer \to, so the move is to open a box with its hypothesis P \wedge (P \to Q) (@def-rules-implication). Inside, the current goal is Q \vee R, which we postpone. The assumption is a conjunction, so \rulename{\wedge E} gives P and P \to Q; \rulename{{\to}E} gives Q; now the left side of the goal is in hand, and \rulename{\vee I} (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction) takes it. The derivation has no premises, so it shows \vdash (P \wedge (P \to Q)) \to (Q \vee R). The look-alike start fails: the statement contains \vee, and one might begin with \rulename{\vee I} on the whole goal. But the goal’s main connective is \to, not \vee, so \rulename{\vee I} cannot produce it; and even inside the box, choosing a side of Q \vee R before Q is on a line would have left the subgoal R, which nothing supplies.

title: Negation, Classical Logic and Finding Derivations
2.1 Contradiction: Using a Negation
content:
Contradiction: Using a Negation Chapter 1 gave rules for “and”, “implies”, and “or”, and not one of them mentions “not”. Yet written proofs are full of sentences such as “this is impossible”, “this case cannot occur”, and “which contradicts what we assumed”. This section gives the two rules that use a negation: the first says exactly what a clash between two lines is, and the second says what a clash buys. The rule that proves a negation is the subject of the next section. A case that cannot occur Here is Argument A of Section 1.1, told as a proof by cases. Let n be an integer whose square is even. Every integer is even or odd, so there are two cases. If n is even, we are done. If n is odd, then n^2 is odd; but n^2 is even, and no integer is both, so this case cannot occur. Hence n is even. Chapter 1 has a rule for a proof by cases: ulename{\vee E} of @def-rules-disjunction. It asks for a disjunction and two boxes, one opened by each disjunct, and both boxes must end on the same line, the goal. In the argument above the goal is “n is even”. The first box reaches it at once. The second box does not reach it at all. It reaches “impossible”, and then simply declares itself finished. Two things are missing, and no rule of Chapter 1 supplies them. - A way to record the impossibility: the lines “n^2 is even” and “n^2 is odd”, together with “no integer is both”, should produce a line that says “contradiction”. - A way to close the impossible box with the goal: from the line “contradiction”, the box should be allowed to write “n is even”, so that both boxes end on the same line and ulename{\vee E} applies. Section 1.1 introduced the symbols for both. The connective 
eg forms the negation 
eg\varphi, read “not \varphi”. The constant  ot, read “contradiction”, is a statement that is false however things stand. There they were symbols only. The two rules below give them their first uses. The rules for a clash The rule for recording a clash has a simple content. The statement 
eg\varphi says that \varphi fails, so a derivation that has both \varphi and 
eg\varphi available is working in a situation that cannot occur. The rule writes this down as the line  ot. A second rule then says what such a line is good for. A statement and its negation clash; from a clash, anything follows. [Rules for Contradiction] The left schema is ulename{
eg E} (not-elimination): if \varphi and 
eg\varphi stand on lines i and j available at line k, write  ot, citing both, the unnegated line first. The right schema is ulename{ ot E} (contradiction-elimination, or ex falso): if  ot stands on a line i available at line k, write any statement \varphi, citing line i. As with every rule of Chapter 1, the letters \varphi and i, j, k follow @def-rule-schema: \varphi stands for one statement, the same one wherever it occurs in the schema, and i, j, k for line numbers. Let us read the two schemas clause by clause. ulename{
eg E}, the given lines. There are two, and they must be exactly \varphi and 
eg\varphi: the second is the first with one 
eg written in front of the whole of it, symbol for symbol. It is not enough that the second line “contradicts the first in spirit”. The lines x < 1 and x > 1 cannot both hold, but neither is the negation of the other as written, so they are not an instance of the schema. (The warning below shows how to turn them into one.) ulename{
eg E}, availability. Both lines must be available at line k, in the sense of the scope rule of @def-derivation: each is earlier than k, and not inside a box that has already closed. They may stand in either order on the page. The citation fixes their roles: “ulename{
eg E} i, j” says that line i is \varphi and line j is 
eg\varphi. ulename{
eg E}, the new line. It is  ot and nothing else. The rule does not write the goal, or 
eg\varphi again, or anything else; it records the clash and stops. What to do with the clash is the business of the second rule. Splitting the work this way keeps each rule to one step, and it lets the next section aim at the line  ot as a goal in its own right. ulename{ ot E}, the given line. One line,  ot, available at line k. ulename{ ot E}, the new line. Any statement at all, chosen by the writer. Like the second disjunct in ulename{\vee I} (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction), the statement \varphi occurs in no given line: it need not be related to anything above, and it may itself be a negation, or  ot again. Two more observations complete the reading. First, ulename{ ot E} is the elimination rule of  ot: it says how a line  ot is used. There is no introduction rule of its own for  ot. Other rules can pass a  ot along (ulename{ ot E} may write it again, and ulename{{	o}E} writes it from \varphi 	o  ot and \varphi), but each of them needs  ot already written in a line it uses. Apart from being assumed, the only way a line  ot first appears is by ulename{
eg E}: it is the one rule whose new line is always  ot, from lines in which  ot need not occur. So ulename{
eg E} plays two parts at once: it is the way a negation is used, and it is the way  ot is produced. Second, why is ulename{ ot E} honest? A rule should never lead from lines that hold to a line that fails. A line  ot can stand only in a part of a derivation where the premises and the open assumptions cannot all hold together, at least when the  ot was written by ulename{
eg E}, from some \varphi and 
eg\varphi that were both available there; that the rules which only pass a  ot along keep this property is part of what Chapter 3 checks in proving @thm-soundness. In such a place there is no situation in which the conclusion of ulename{ ot E} would have to be checked, so it cannot be caught failing. Chapter 3’s soundness theorem turns this remark into a proof. Which of these pairs of lines are, as written, an instance of the given lines of ulename{
eg E}, and in which order must each be cited? The pairs are (i) Q \wedge R and 
eg(Q \wedge R); (ii) 
eg P and 
eg
eg P; (iii) P 	o Q and 
eg P 	o Q. (i) Yes, with \varphi = Q \wedge R; cite the line Q \wedge R first. (ii) Yes, with \varphi = 
eg P: the second line is 
eg(
eg P). Cite 
eg P first, then 
eg
eg P. (iii) No. The main connective of 
eg P 	o Q is 	o (@def-main-connective), so it is not a negation at all; the 
eg applies to P alone. The negation of P 	o Q would be 
eg(P 	o Q). Clashes in school mathematics. In derivations about numbers, the clash usually comes from a school fact written as a negation. For real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b and a \ge b holds, so a \ge b says the same as 
eg(a < b), and we use them interchangeably. So a line x^2 < 0 and the school fact x^2 \ge 0, written as 
eg(x^2 < 0), give  ot by ulename{
eg E}. The symbol a 
e b means 
eg(a = b), by definition. And the fact “no integer is both even and odd” is a negation of a conjunction, 
eg(E \wedge O) with E for “n is even” and O for “n is odd”. It clashes only with a line E \wedge O, which ulename{\wedge I} builds from separate lines E and O. A clash must have the exact shape \varphi, 
eg\varphi. The lines x < 1 and x > 1 are not yet a clash. To make them one, write x > 1 as 
eg(x \le 1) (for real numbers, x > 1 holds exactly when x \le 1 fails), and get x \le 1 from x < 1 by ulename{\vee I}, since x \le 1 means (x < 1) \vee (x = 1). And some pairs that look opposed do not clash at all: x \ge 1 and x \le 1 both hold at x = 1. ulename{ ot E} does not run backwards. From  ot we may write \varphi, or 
eg\varphi, or anything; but from \varphi alone no rule writes  ot. If it could, the true line x = 1 would give  ot, and then ulename{ ot E} would give the false line x = 2. First derivations with a clash The five derivations below grow in difficulty. Each Idea says why each rule was chosen, in the two directions Chapter 1 used: from the goal (what does the goal’s main connective ask for?) and from the premises (what does an available line’s main connective let us do?). This section adds one question to each list. From the goal: when nothing produces the goal, can a clash produce it? From the premises: an available negation 
eg\varphi is used in exactly one way, by ulename{
eg E}, so it asks for \varphi. [The first clashes] Show that (a)  ot \vdash P, and (b) P \wedge Q, \ 
eg Q \vdash R. (a) is the rule ulename{ ot E} itself, the degenerate case with no clash to find. In (b), the first premise is a conjunction, so the premise-directed move takes it apart by ulename{\wedge E}. Its half Q and the premise 
eg Q are exactly a pair \varphi,
