eg\varphi. The goal R has nothing to do with the premises: no rule builds it from them. Only ulename{ ot E} can write it, and ulename{ ot E} needs a line  ot, which the clash supplies. (a) Two lines: the premise, and one application of ulename{ ot E}. (b) Five lines. Line 4 cites line 3 first because line 3 plays \varphi and line 2 plays 
eg\varphi, with \varphi = Q. The half P of the first premise is never used; a derivation need not use every premise (@def-derivable). The next result is the pattern of (b) with nothing extra around it. We state it as a proposition, because later sections cite it. [Contradictory Premises Prove Anything] P, \ 
eg P \vdash Q. The premises are a clash as they stand, so ulename{
eg E} writes  ot at once, and ulename{ ot E} writes the goal, which nothing else could produce. The derivation has premises P and 
eg P and last line Q. This proves the proposition. In the next derivation the clash happens inside a box, and the rule ulename{ ot E} writes the box’s goal. [Vacuous Implication] 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q. The goal is an implication, so the goal-directed move of Chapter 1 (ulename{{	o}I}, @def-rules-implication) opens a box with its hypothesis P; the new goal is Q. Nothing available mentions Q, so no rule can build it. But inside the box, the assumption P and the premise 
eg P clash, and ulename{ ot E} writes the box’s goal Q. This is the section’s goal-directed move: when nothing produces the goal, look for a clash. The derivation has premise 
eg P and last line P 	o Q. Line 3 may cite line 1, which lies in no box. This proves the proposition. Line 4 is the line that makes the box close properly: ulename{{	o}I} needs the box to end on Q, as a line of that box itself, and ulename{ ot E} put it there. In the next example no clash is lying about. It has to be made. [Manufacturing the other half of a clash] Show that 
eg(P \vee Q) \vdash P 	o R. As before, the goal P 	o R opens a box on P, and the new goal R occurs nowhere else, so a clash must write it. Inside the box there is no 
eg P to clash with. The only negation available is the premise 
eg(P \vee Q), and the premise-directed question says what it asks for: the line P \vee Q. That line is one ulename{\vee I} away from the assumption P. So the clash is manufactured: the unnegated half of the premise becomes a subgoal, and ulename{\vee I} is chosen not because the goal is a disjunction but because the premise’s clash needs one. Six lines. Line 4 cites line 3 as \varphi and line 1 as 
eg\varphi, with \varphi = P \vee Q. In words: if neither P nor Q holds, then P cannot hold, so an implication with hypothesis P is true whatever its conclusion. The mirror image, with Q as the hypothesis, is exercise B1. The last derivation of this section is the pattern of the opening argument: a case split in which one case is impossible. [An impossible case] Show that P \vee Q, \ P 	o R, \ 
eg R \vdash Q. The goal Q is a letter, so the goal gives no introduction rule to aim at. The premises do: P \vee Q is a disjunction, and Chapter 1’s premise-directed move for a disjunction is ulename{\vee E}, with two boxes that both end in the current goal Q. The box of Q ends as soon as it opens: its assumption is already the goal. The box of P cannot reach Q honestly, because nothing in it produces Q. So we look for a clash: P feeds the premise P 	o R, and R clashes with 
eg R. The box ends on Q by ulename{ ot E}. This is the second new move: an impossible case closes itself. Nine lines. The second box consists of its assumption alone, a one-line box, just as in the derivation of P \vee P \vdash P in @exm-disjunction-first-derivations: its last line is its first line, and that line is Q, which is what ulename{\vee E} needs. The two boxes are separate, so line 7 could not cite line 8, and nothing in the second box could cite lines 4–7. Look at line 7 of this derivation again. The box of P is a case “that cannot occur”, and line 7 is the sentence “so there is nothing to prove”: the case is closed with whatever the other case reaches. Every proof by cases with an impossible case has this line somewhere, usually unwritten. The impossible case must be impossible from what is available in its own box. A clash with a line of a sibling box, or of a box that has already closed, is a scope error (@def-derivation), even when the clash “looks right”. In @exm-impossible-case the clash in the box of P uses line 5, from that box, and the premise on line 3; neither lives in another box. Exercise C2 shows the error and what it can prove. The moves of this section, in one place. Goal  ot: find a clash. Look for \varphi and 
eg\varphi among the available lines; if only 
eg\varphi is there, make \varphi a subgoal. An impossible case closes itself. In a case split, a case that reaches  ot ends by ulename{ ot E} on the current goal. The next section adds a way to reach the goal  ot deliberately, by assuming something. How the rules look in a mathematical proof We can now prove the fact of Argument A in Section 1.1, with every rule named. Three school facts about integers enter as premises. An integer n is even if n = 2k for some integer k, and odd if n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. And: 1. every integer is even or odd; 2. no integer is both even and odd; 3. the square of an odd integer is odd. The third is a computation. If n = 2k + 1 for an integer k, then n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1 , and 2k^2 + 2k is an integer, so n^2 is odd. Taking “an integer k with n = 2k + 1” and working with it is a step about “there exists”; the rules for such steps come in Chapter 4, and here we use the step as school algebra. [Even Square, Even Number] Let n be an integer. If n^2 is even, then n is even. The hypothesis “n^2 is even” hands us nothing to compute with: it says n^2 = 2j for some integer j, and no algebra turns that into a statement about n. The word “odd” does hand us something, since n = 2k + 1 can be squared. So we split on (E1) and show that the odd case is impossible: there (E3) makes n^2 odd, which clashes with the hypothesis through (E2). The impossible case then closes itself. Suppose n^2 is even [	ext{assumption for } ulename{{	o}I}]. By (E1), n is even or n is odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case n even. This is the goal. Case n odd. By (E3), n^2 is odd [ulename{{	o}E}]. So n^2 is both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}]; this contradicts (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]. So this case cannot occur, and in it n is even [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases n is even [ulename{\vee E}]. This proves that if n^2 is even, then n is even [ulename{{	o}I}]. The logic of the proof fits in a derivation. Write E for “n is even”, O for “n is odd”, S for “n^2 is even”, and T for “n^2 is odd”. Then (E1) for n is E \vee O, (E2) for n^2 is 
eg(S \wedge T), and (E3) for n is O 	o T; these are the premises. Each line is one sentence of the proof. Line Sentence of the proof ------ -------------------------------------------------- 1–3 (E1) for n, (E2) for n^2, (E3) for n 4 Suppose n^2 is even. 5 Case n even. (A one-line box: it is the goal.) 6 Case n odd. 7 By (E3), n^2 is odd. 8 So n^2 is both even and odd, 9 which contradicts (E2). 10 So this case cannot occur, and in it n is even. 11 In both cases n is even. 12 This proves that if n^2 is even, then n is even. Line 8 cites line 4, the assumption of the outer box; it may, since the box \lines{4}{11} contains line 8 (@def-derivation). Two steps of the proof are not in the derivation: passing from the facts (E1)–(E3), which are about every integer, to their instances for this n and this n^2; and naming the k of (E3). Both are quantifier steps, and Chapter 4 gives their rules. Which sentence of the proof of @thm-square-even-implies-even is the rule ulename{ ot E}, and what does it write? The sentence “So this case cannot occur, and in it n is even”, line 10 of the derivation. It cites the line  ot (line 9) and writes E, “n is even”, which is the goal of the case, so that the box of O ends on the same line as the box of E. Every rule in this proof is a primitive rule: ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{\vee E}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{
eg E}, and ulename{ ot E}. The next section uses the theorem twice, to prove that no rational number has square 2. Section 2.3 reads the same proof again with shorter steps, as mathematicians usually write it, “by the contrapositive”. Vacuous truth We can now settle the question that makes many readers distrust logic. Is the sentence if x^2 < 0, then x = 7 true, for a real number x? The hypothesis never holds, and the conclusion has nothing to do with it. Everyday intuition is unsure what to say. The rules are not unsure. [An implication with an impossible hypothesis] Let x be a real number. Show that if x^2 < 0, then x = 7. The goal is an implication, so open a box with x^2 < 0, aiming at x = 7. Nothing produces x = 7, so look for a clash: the school fact x^2 \ge 0 is 
eg(x^2 < 0), which clashes with the assumption. This is exactly the derivation of @prp-vacuous-implication, with P read as “x^2 < 0” and Q as “x = 7”. With the school fact as the premise: In prose: suppose x^2 < 0; this contradicts x^2 \ge 0; so this case cannot occur, and in it x = 7; hence if x^2 < 0, then x = 7. We wrote out all five lines rather than citing @prp-vacuous-implication as a single step. Using an already proved sequent as one line of a new derivation is a genuine new permission, and Section 2.3 grants it; until then, a derivation repeats the steps. An implication whose hypothesis cannot hold is called vacuously true. Nothing about it was decided by convention. It is forced by two rules that each look harmless: ulename{{	o}I}, which proves an implication by assuming its hypothesis, and ulename{ ot E}, which closes an impossible case. Everyday language agrees. A friend says: “if you finish the exercises by Friday, I will buy you lunch”. You do not finish them. Whatever your friend does on Friday, the promise has not been broken. A promise never tested is never broken. Vacuous truth is not a curiosity; it is what makes case splits work. In @exm-impossible-case, line 7 closed the impossible case by ulename{ ot E}, and line 10 of the derivation of @thm-square-even-implies-even did the same. When Chapter 3 gives each connective a truth table (@def-truth-value), the rows of 	o with a false hypothesis are the ones these two rules force. Chapter 4 meets the same phenomenon in another dress: a statement about “every element of the empty set” is true, because there is no element to test. “True” is not “useful”. The statements “if x^2 < 0, then x = 7” and “if x^2 < 0, then x 
e 7” are both true, and neither says anything about x or about 7. Likewise “if n is an even prime greater than 2, then n = 17” is true and empty. When a hypothesis turns out to be impossible, suspect the hypothesis; do not believe the conclusion. What the rules sound like Here are the rows of the rule, phrase and Lean table for this section’s rules. The last column is for readers who use a proof assistant; nothing depends on it. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------- ulename{
eg E} “…, which contradicts …” exact hn hp (goal False) ulename{ ot E} “This case cannot occur.” “So there is nothing to prove.” exfalso ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- In Lean the two steps are often taken together: absurd hp hn closes any goal from a proof hp of P and a proof hn of 
eg P, which is ulename{
eg E} followed by ulename{ ot E}, and the tactic contradiction finds such a pair by itself. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the schemas of ulename{
eg E} and ulename{ ot E} from memory. 2. Match each sentence, taken from proofs, with the rule it uses, ulename{
eg E} or ulename{ ot E}: “But n was assumed odd, and we have just shown it is even”; “In this case x^2 < 0, which is impossible, so there is nothing to prove”. 3. True or false, with a reason: ulename{ ot E} lets us write  ot from any line. 4. In @exm-impossible-case, why is the second box only one line long? 5. In the derivation after @thm-square-even-implies-even, why does line 8 need line 4, and why may it cite it? (a) ulename{
eg E}: from a line i with \varphi and a line j with 
eg\varphi, both available, write  ot at line k, citing i, j. ulename{ ot E}: from an available line i with  ot, write any statement \varphi at line k, citing i. The two schemas are those of @def-rules-contradiction. (b) The first is ulename{
eg E}: “odd” and “even” clash through (E2), and the sentence records the clash. The second is ulename{ ot E}: “impossible” records a clash (an ulename{
eg E} against x^2 \ge 0, left unsaid), and “there is nothing to prove” closes the case with whatever the case needs. (c) False. ulename{ ot E} runs from  ot to any statement, not from any statement to  ot. ulename{ ot E} needs a line  ot to start from. The rule that records a clash as  ot is ulename{
eg E}, and it needs two lines \varphi and 
eg\varphi. (d) The box is opened by Q, and Q is already the goal of both boxes. So the box’s first line is also its last line, which is all ulename{\vee E} asks of it. (e) Line 8 is S \wedge T, built by ulename{\wedge I} from S and T; line 4 is the only line that says S. It may cite line 4 because the only box containing line 4, the box \lines{4}{11}, also contains line 8 (the scope rule of @def-derivation). B. Practice [B1: Two clashes] 1. Show that 
eg(P \vee Q) \vdash Q 	o R. 2. Show that (P 	o Q) \wedge 
eg Q, \ P \vdash 
eg R, and say why ulename{ ot E} may write a negation. (a) As in @exm-manufactured-clash, with Q in place of P: the box of Q manufactures P \vee Q by ulename{\vee I} on the other side. (b) Take the first premise apart, fire the implication on the second premise, and clash. Line 7 is an instance of ulename{ ot E} with \varphi = 
eg R: the schema allows any statement in place of \varphi, and a negation is a statement. [B2: An even successor] Let n be an integer. Prove that if n + 1 is even, then n is odd, by cases on (E1) with one case shown impossible. Tag each step with its rule, as in the proof of @thm-square-even-implies-even. Suppose n + 1 is even [	ext{assumption for } ulename{{	o}I}]. By (E1), n is even or n is odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case n even. Write n = 2k with k an integer. Then n + 1 = 2k + 1, so n + 1 is odd, by the definition of odd. So n + 1 is both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}]; this contradicts (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]. So this case cannot occur, and in it n is odd [ulename{ ot E}]. Case n odd. This is the goal. In both cases n is odd [ulename{\vee E}]. This proves that if n + 1 is even, then n is odd [ulename{{	o}I}]. The step “n even, so n + 1 odd” plays the part that (E3) played in the theorem: it is the implication fired by ulename{{	o}E} inside the impossible case. Here the impossible case is the first one, and the other case is the goal. [B3: Two vacuous promises] Let x be a real number. Prove that if x^2 + 1 \le 0, then x > 100; and that if x^2 + 1 \le 0, then x < -100. Write each as a derivation with one premise, a school fact, and explain why the two statements together are no paradox. The school fact is x^2 + 1 > 0, true for every real x since x^2 \ge 0 gives x^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0. For real numbers, x^2 + 1 > 0 says the same as 
eg(x^2 + 1 \le 0). The first derivation is the pattern of @exm-vacuous-square: The second is the same, with x < -100 on lines 4 and 5: ulename{ ot E} may write any statement. No real number is both greater than 100 and less than -100. That is no paradox, because neither implication ever applies: its hypothesis holds for no real x. Both are vacuously true, and both say nothing about x, as the warning on vacuous truth says. C. Going deeper [C1: A disjunct that cannot hold] 1. Show that P \vee (Q \wedge 
eg Q) \vdash P. 2. What does (a) say about the statement “x > 0, or x = 1 and x 
e 1”, for a real number x? (a) The premise is a disjunction, so split it by ulename{\vee E}, with both boxes ending in the goal P. The box of P is a one-line box. The box of Q \wedge 
eg Q is impossible: ulename{\wedge E} gives a clash, and ulename{ ot E} closes the case. (b) With P: “x > 0” and Q: “x = 1”, the statement is P \vee (Q \wedge 
eg Q), since x 
e 1 is 
eg(x = 1). By (a), it gives x > 0. So the second disjunct adds nothing: a disjunct that can never hold is an impossible case, and it closes itself. (Conversely, x > 0 gives the whole statement by ulename{\vee I}, so the two say the same thing.) [C2: A clash that escaped its box] A student wants to show 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q and writes: 1. Is the sequent 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q derivable? 2. Find the first line that is not justified, and name the clause of @def-derivation it breaks. 3. Show that the move made at that line can lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. 4. Write a correct derivation. (a) Yes: it is @prp-vacuous-implication. The conclusion is true; the question is whether this argument proves it. (b) Line 4. It cites line 3, which lies inside the box \lines{2}{3}, and that box has closed before line 4. By the scope rule of @def-derivation, a line inside a closed box is not available. (Lines 1–3 are fine: a box may close without a rule discharging it, although nothing then leaves it. Lines 5–7 would be fine if line 4 were.) (c) Lines 1–4 alone would “derive” 
eg P \vdash Q by the same move. Read P as “x > 0” and Q as “x = 7”, and take x = -1. The premise 
eg(x > 0) is true, and the conclusion x = 7 is false. So the move “write, outside a box, what a closed box’s  ot would allow” can lead from a true premise to a false line. The line  ot on line 3 holds only under the assumption P; once the box closes, that assumption is gone, and so is the clash. (d) Move the ulename{ ot E} inside the box, where the clash is: Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: answers (a) yes, citing @prp-vacuous-implication or giving a derivation. - 3: names line 4 as the first failure and the scope rule (a line inside a closed box is not available) as the clause broken. - 3: gives a counterexample to the step, not only to some conclusion: a reading of P, Q under which lines 1–4 go from a true premise to a false line. - 2: a correct derivation, with every citation available. Fatal errors (0 for the step): blaming line 7 or line 6 (they are correct once line 4 is); saying that ulename{ ot E} itself is the error.

title: 2.2 Proving a Negation
2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content:
Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules Section 2.1 closed an impossible case by hand, and Section 2.2 proved negations by hand, one box at a time. By now the same few patterns keep coming back: the impossible case of @exm-impossible-case, and a box that turns a known implication round. Mathematicians give such patterns names (“by contraposition”, “since P fails, Q”) and use them in one breath. This section proves three of them once, from the rules we have, and then allows each to be used as a single line. The one new thing is that permission: a derived rule. A box that keeps coming back Here are two short arguments from different corners of mathematics. Let n be an integer whose square is not even. Suppose n is even. Then n^2 is even, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence n is not even. Let x be a real number with x^2 < 1. Suppose x \ge 1. Then x^2 \ge x \ge 1, which contradicts x^2 < 1. Hence x < 1. The subjects differ; the steps are the same. Each has a known implication (“if n is even, then n^2 is even”; “if x \ge 1, then x^2 \ge 1”), and a fact saying that the implication’s conclusion fails. Each then opens a box on the implication’s hypothesis, fires the implication inside it by ulename{{	o}E}, meets the clash with ulename{
eg E}, and closes the box by ulename{
eg I} (@def-rules-negation). (For reals, x^2 < 1 and x < 1 are the exact negations of x^2 \ge 1 and x \ge 1.) The same four lines appear whenever an implication is used backwards, from the failure of its conclusion to the failure of its hypothesis. A mathematician does not write these four lines. She writes “since n^2 is not even, n is not even”, or “by contraposition”, and moves on: the lines are the same every time. But a derivation is checked line by line against the rules, and “by contraposition” is not one of the rules. What licenses the short form? First we derive the pattern once, as a sequent, with the rules we have. Then we say exactly when a sequent already derived may be used as a single line. Modus tollens, from the rules we have The pattern of the two arguments is: from an implication and the negation of its conclusion, infer the negation of its hypothesis. [Modus Tollens] P 	o Q, \; 
eg Q \vdash 
eg P. Read the skeleton off the goal. The goal 
eg P is a negation, and Section 2.2’s move for a negated goal is a box opened on what is negated, here P, with goal  ot. Inside the box, look for a clash (Section 2.1’s move for the goal  ot). The premise 
eg Q will clash with Q, so Q is the subgoal, and the premise P 	o Q gives it from the box’s own assumption. The following is a derivation with premises P 	o Q and 
eg Q, and last line 
eg P. Line 5 cites the premise on line 2, which lies in no box and so is available everywhere below it. The box \lines{3}{5} ends in  ot as a line of its own, so ulename{
eg I} closes it on line 6. This proves the proposition. The name is Latin for “the mode that takes away”: denying the conclusion takes away the hypothesis. Its partner, from P 	o Q and P to Q, is ulename{{	o}E}, traditionally modus ponens, “the mode that puts” (@def-rule-implication-elimination). The derivation uses ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg E}, and ulename{
eg I}, and nothing else. A second form of the same fact packs the two premises into one implication. It is the form in which mathematicians state it: an implication implies its contrapositive. [Contrapositive] P 	o Q \vdash 
eg Q 	o 
eg P. The goal is an implication, so Chapter 1’s first goal-directed move applies: open a box with its hypothesis 
eg Q, and the new goal is 
eg P. That goal is a negation, so open a second box, on P, inside the first. Inside both boxes we are exactly where the proof of @prp-modus-tollens was: P and P 	o Q give Q, which clashes with 
eg Q. The following is a derivation with premise P 	o Q and last line 
eg Q 	o 
eg P. Line 5 may cite line 2, because the only box containing line 2, the box \lines{2}{6}, also contains line 5 (the scope rule of @def-derivation). The inner box closes on line 6, a line of the outer box itself, and line 7 closes the outer box. This proves the proposition. The statement 
eg Q 	o 
eg P is called the contrapositive of P 	o Q. Like modus tollens, its derivation uses only the rules so far: ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg I}, and ulename{
eg E}. The passage back, from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P to P 	o Q, is a different matter; the warnings below return to it. Now compare the two derivations. Lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens are, line for line and citation for citation, lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-contrapositive: P, then Q by ulename{{	o}E}\ 1, 3, then  ot by ulename{
eg E}\ 4, 2, then 
eg P by ulename{
eg I}\ \lines{3}{5}. And they are the four lines of the two arguments that opened this section. Writing them out every time buries the argument in bookkeeping. What a derived rule is A sequent that has been derived may be used as a rule. This is what a mathematician does when she writes “by Lemma 3”: the lemma was proved once, and each use of it is a single step. For derivations we must say exactly what that step may do. [Derived Rule] Let \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi be a sequent, written with statement letters, that has already been derived earlier in the book. In a later derivation, replace each letter in \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, \psi by a statement, the same statement for every occurrence of the same letter. If lines i_1, \dots, i_n, all available at line k, hold the resulting instances of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, we may write the resulting instance of \psi on line k. The justification names the result and cites i_1, \dots, i_n. A sequent used in this way is a derived rule. For example, @prp-modus-tollens becomes the rule ulename{MT}: In words: a proved sequent is a new rule. Its premises become the cited lines, its conclusion the line written, and its letters the metavariables of a schema (@def-rule-schema). Read the definition clause by clause. 1. “Already derived.” The sequent must have been derived before the line that uses it: earlier in the book, and never inside its own derivation. A derivation that used a sequent to derive that same sequent would prove nothing. 2. “Replace each letter … the same statement for every occurrence.” The letters of a derived sequent stood for arbitrary statements all along (@def-derivable), so they may be replaced by any statements, provided the replacement is uniform. From (A \wedge B) 	o C and 
eg C, the rule ulename{MT} gives 
eg(A \wedge B), with \varphi replaced by A \wedge B and \psi by C. Chapter 3 makes this replacement exact, under the name substitution. 3. “Available at line k.” The scope rule of @def-derivation still governs every citation. A derived rule may not reach into a closed box, just as a primitive rule may not. 4. “The resulting instance of \psi.” The rule writes the conclusion, with the same replacement, and nothing else. The derived rule does not open or close any box of the derivation that uses it. We give the derived rules of this section short tags: ulename{MT} for @prp-modus-tollens, ulename{CP} for @prp-contrapositive, and, once it is proved below, ulename{DS} for @prp-disjunctive-syllogism. Every other derived sequent is a derived rule too, cited by its name: the five lines written out in @exm-vacuous-square, for instance, are now one line citing @prp-vacuous-implication. Convenience, not power. A derived-rule line abbreviates a stretch of derivation that we could write out in full. To expand it, repeat each cited line by (D3) of @def-derivation, then copy the derivation of the sequent below the repetitions, with its letters replaced, its premises replaced by the repetitions, and its line numbers shifted. Every citation inside the copy points inside the copy or to a repetition, all in the current box, so every citation is available. The copy’s boxes close before its last line, which is the instance of \psi. If the copy itself uses derived rules, expand those lines in the same way; this stops, because each derivation cites only results proved before it. So whatever can be derived with derived rules can be derived with the primitive rules alone. The degenerate case is a sequent with nothing done to its premise, P \vdash P, whose derivation is the single premise line (part (a) of @exm-derivations): as a derived rule it copies an available line, which repetition already does. The first use with content is modus tollens proved a second time, with ulename{CP} as a rule. The premise P 	o Q invites ulename{CP}, and its conclusion 
eg Q 	o 
eg P is an implication whose hypothesis is the other premise. Line 3 is the instance of @prp-contrapositive with P and Q replaced by themselves; line 4 is modus ponens on it. Written out in full, line 3 would become a repetition of line 1 followed by lines 2–7 of the derivation of @prp-contrapositive. This is honest because @prp-contrapositive was derived from the primitive rules, not from @prp-modus-tollens: the chain of derived rules ends in primitive rules, without a loop. A derived rule must match its sequent exactly, under one uniform replacement of letters. From P 	o Q and 
eg R, ulename{MT} gives nothing: no single statement in place of \psi turns the pair into \varphi 	o \psi and 
eg\psi. Equally, from P 	o 
eg Q and Q, ulename{MT} gives nothing yet: it needs the negation of the conclusion, 
eg
eg Q, and Q is not that line. (Here ulename{
eg I} would give 
eg
eg Q first, as in @exm-double-negation-introduction, and then ulename{MT} applies.) Likewise ulename{DS}, as stated below, refutes the left disjunct; applied blindly to P \vee Q and 
eg Q, it does not match. Disjunctive syllogism: the impossible case, filed The second pattern is the impossible case of Section 2.1. Every integer is even or odd; this one is not odd; so it is even. A disjunction, one side refuted, the other side left. [Disjunctive Syllogism] P \vee Q, \; 
eg P \vdash Q. This is @exm-impossible-case with a simpler clash. There, the case P produced R by ulename{{	o}E}, which clashed with 
eg R. Here the case P clashes with the premise 
eg P at once. So: split the premise P \vee Q by ulename{\vee E}, both boxes ending in the current goal Q. The Q box is its own assumption. The P box cannot reach Q honestly, so it reaches a clash and closes by ulename{ ot E}: an impossible case closes itself. The following is a derivation with premises P \vee Q and 
eg P, and last line Q. The two boxes \lines{3}{5} and \lines{6}{6} are separate. The second consists of its assumption alone, which is already the statement Q that ulename{\vee E} needs. This proves the proposition. Set the derivation beside that of @exm-impossible-case. Both split P \vee Q into the same two boxes, and in both the Q box is one line long. Inside the P box, two lines reached  ot there (lines 5–6) and one line does here (line 4); then ulename{ ot E} closes the box in the same way. From now on this whole stretch is one line, tagged ulename{DS}. The rule as stated refutes the left disjunct. To refute the right one, first put the disjunction in the other order; that, too, is now one line, since @exm-disjunction-first-derivations derived P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P. (Exercise B1 derives the mirror image directly.) [Derived rules in use] 1. Show that P 	o Q, \; Q 	o R, \; 
eg R \vdash 
eg P, and then write the derivation out with primitive rules only. 2. Show that P \vee Q, \; 
eg P, \; Q 	o R \vdash R. Idea. A derived rule is a premise-directed shortcut: a line \varphi 	o \psi with a line 
eg\psi invites ulename{MT}; a disjunction with one side refuted invites ulename{DS}. This is the move this section adds to the search for derivations: before opening a box by hand, ask whether a derived rule takes the step at once. (a) Work backwards from the goal 
eg P. The premise P 	o Q would give it by ulename{MT} if 
eg Q were available. And 
eg Q comes by ulename{MT} from Q 	o R and 
eg R. So ulename{MT} is used twice, the second time on the conclusion of the first. Line 4 is the instance with \varphi replaced by Q and \psi by R; line 5 the instance with P and Q. In primitive rules, each ulename{MT} line becomes its four lines, as in lines 3–6 of the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens: a box on the hypothesis, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{
eg I}. This natural expansion has eleven lines. The literal expansion of @def-derived-rule adds a repetition of each cited line and is longer; the natural one cites the available lines directly. (b) The disjunction P \vee Q has its left side refuted by 
eg P, so ulename{DS} gives Q, and then Q 	o R fires. Expanded, line 4 becomes the seven lines of the derivation of @prp-disjunctive-syllogism, with a case split on line 1 and the case P closed by ulename{ ot E}. Which derived rule of this section, if any, gives a new line in one step from each pair of available lines? (i) P 	o Q and 
eg Q. (ii) P \vee Q and 
eg P. (iii) P \vee Q and Q 	o R. (iv) P 	o 
eg Q and Q. (i) ulename{MT} gives 
eg P. (ii) ulename{DS} gives Q. (iii) None: nothing is known about the case P. (iv) None in one step: ulename{MT} needs the negation of the conclusion 
eg Q, which is 
eg
eg Q, not Q. A ulename{
eg I} box gives 
eg
eg Q from Q first, as in @exm-double-negation-introduction, and then ulename{MT} gives 
eg P. Modus tollens on numbers, and the green card In a mathematical proof, ulename{MT} is the step “since the conclusion fails, the hypothesis fails”. Here it is with numbers. [Modus tollens on numbers] Let x be a real number with x^2 \le 4. Use the implication “if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” to show that x \le 2, naming the derived rule. Take P: “x > 2” and Q: “x^2 > 4”. The implication is P 	o Q. (It holds because x > 2 > 0 gives x^2 = x \cdot x > 2x > 4.) The hypothesis x^2 \le 4 is 
eg Q, since for real numbers x^2 \le 4 and x^2 > 4 are exact negations of each other. By ulename{MT} (@prp-modus-tollens), 
eg P, that is, 
eg(x > 2), which is x \le 2. The same step settles the card most people leave on the table in @exm-wason-selection (Section 1.4): the cards show 6, 7, red, and green, and the claim is “if a card shows an even number on one side, then its other side is red”. For the green card, let E be “this card’s number is even” and R “its color side is red”. The claim, for this card, is E 	o R. The card shows green, so 
eg R. If the claim holds, ulename{MT} gives 
eg E: the hidden number must be odd. Turning the card tests exactly that line: an even number there would give E, and with 
eg R and E 	o R, ulename{{	o}E} and ulename{
eg E} would reach  ot. The red card offers only R, and from E 	o R and R no rule gives anything about E; that was Section 1.4’s affirming the consequent. So the green card must be turned and the red one need not be. Modus tollens is the step people skip. ulename{CP} turns the claim into its contrapositive 
eg R 	o 
eg E, “a card whose color is not red has an odd number”, which carries the claim’s content to the green card; Section 2.5 derives the passage back, so the two say the same. The converse R 	o E, “a red card has an even number”, is a different claim, and the card rule never made it. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof @thm-square-even-implies-even (Section 2.1) says that for an integer n, if n^2 is even then n is even. Section 2.1 proved it by cases, with the odd case shown impossible and closed by ulename{ ot E}. Here is the same theorem argued as mathematicians usually write it, with the derived rules doing the work. We use the facts (E1)–(E3) of Section 2.1: every integer is even or odd; no integer is both; the square of an odd integer is odd. [Even square, even number, by contraposition] Let n be an integer. Prove that if n^2 is even, then n is even, using ulename{CP} and ulename{DS}, and label each step with its rule. Idea. The hypothesis “n^2 is even” hands us nothing to compute with, while “n is odd” hands us n = 2k + 1. So we turn (E3) round by ulename{CP}: a number whose square is not odd is not odd itself. Then (E1), with one side refuted, leaves “even” by ulename{DS}. Suppose n^2 is even [	ext{assumption for } ulename{{	o}I}]. If n^2 were odd [	ext{assumption for } ulename{
eg I}], it would be both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}], contradicting (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]; hence n^2 is not odd [ulename{
eg I}]. By (E3), if n is odd then n^2 is odd, so by contraposition, if n^2 is not odd then n is not odd [ulename{CP}]. Hence n is not odd [ulename{{	o}E}]. By (E1), n is even or odd, so n is odd or even [	ext{or commutes}], by the exchange of disjuncts of @exm-disjunction-first-derivations used as a derived rule. Since n is not odd, n is even [ulename{DS}]. This proves that if n^2 is even, then n is even [ulename{{	o}I}]. With E: “n is even”, O: “n is odd”, S: “n^2 is even”, T: “n^2 is odd”, and the three facts as premises, the skeleton is this derivation. Line 11 is @exm-disjunction-first-derivations used as a derived rule, so that line 12 refutes the left disjunct, as ulename{DS} requires. Compare this with the twelve-line derivation after @thm-square-even-implies-even in Section 2.1. There, line 11 split on (E1) at once, and the odd case, lines 6–10, got T from (E3), built S \wedge T, clashed with (E2), and closed by ulename{ ot E}. Here the same work is spread over named steps. The ulename{
eg I} box on lines 5–7 does the clash with (E2), which there was lines 8–9. Lines 9 and 10, ulename{CP} and ulename{{	o}E}, abbreviate a box that assumes O, gets T by (E3), as line 7 did there, and clashes with line 8. Line 12, ulename{DS}, abbreviates a case split on the disjunction with the case O closed by ulename{ ot E}, as lines 5–11 did there. The short version reads the way people talk. Notice also what the argument never does. It feels like “suppose not”, and written out in full it does contain one: ulename{CP} assumes that n is odd, reaches  ot, and concludes that n is not odd. What it never does is assume that n is not even and conclude from a contradiction that n is even. Every negation in it is introduced; none is removed. The difference will matter in Section 2.5. Common errors A derived rule may be used only after its sequent has been derived, and never inside its own derivation. A “derivation” of @prp-contrapositive that justifies one of its lines by ulename{CP} proves nothing: it assumes what it sets out to show. Exercise C2 is an example, and Section 2.6 returns to the error in general. The converse of the contrapositive is a different sequent. ulename{CP} passes from P 	o Q to 
eg Q 	o 
eg P; it does not pass from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P back to P 	o Q. Try it: in a box on P the goal is Q, a letter with no negation, and the natural box, on 
eg Q, reaches  ot and so closes to 
eg
eg Q, not Q. Section 2.5 derives the passage back with a new rule. That no derivation with the rules so far exists is true, but we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. “Suppose x \ge 0” inside a proof framed “Assume x^3 < 0; we show x < 0” is not the contrapositive. It is a box on the negation of the goal x < 0, and closing such a box on the unnegated goal needs the rule of Section 2.5. The contrapositive route replaces the frame: prove “if x \ge 0, then x^3 \ge 0”, and ulename{CP} turns it into “if x^3 < 0, then x < 0”, since x^3 < 0 and x < 0 are the exact negations of x^3 \ge 0 and x \ge 0. What the rules sound like Here are the rows of the rule, phrase, and Lean table for this section’s derived rules. As before, the last column is for readers who use a proof assistant, and nothing depends on it. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean --------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------- ulename{MT} “Since Q fails, so does P.” mt h hnq ulename{CP} “We prove the contrapositive: suppose not Q; … so not P.” mt ulename{DS} “P is impossible, so Q.” h.resolve_left hnp ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @def-derived-rule in your own words, including what “already derived” and “the same statement” require. 2. Here is a derivation that uses ulename{MT}. Rewrite it with primitive rules only. 3. True or false, with a reason: “
eg Q 	o 
eg P follows from P 	o Q by ulename{CP}, so P 	o Q follows from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P by ulename{CP}.” (a) If a sequent has been derived earlier (not inside the derivation that uses it), then in a later derivation we may replace its letters by statements, each letter by one statement everywhere it occurs, and, when available lines hold the resulting instances of its premises, write the resulting instance of its conclusion on one line, citing the sequent and those lines. (b) Line 3 becomes a box on R, then ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{
eg E}, and ulename{
eg I}: (c) False. ulename{CP} is the sequent P 	o Q \vdash 
eg Q 	o 
eg P. Applied to 
eg Q 	o 
eg P, with P replaced by 
eg Q and Q by 
eg P, it gives 
eg
eg P 	o 
eg
eg Q, not P 	o Q. The passage from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P to P 	o Q is the converse, a different sequent; Section 2.5 derives it with a new rule. B. Practice [B1: The other disjunctive syllogism] 1. Show that P \vee Q, \; 
eg Q \vdash P by a derivation from the primitive rules. 2. Let x be a real number with x^2 = 1 and x > 0. You may use that x^2 = 1 implies x = 1 or x = -1. Deduce that x = 1, naming the result you use. (a) As in @prp-disjunctive-syllogism, with the roles of the boxes exchanged: now the case Q is the impossible one. (b) Since x^2 = 1, we have x = 1 or x = -1. Since x > 0 and -1 < 0, we have x 
e -1. By part (a), with P: “x = 1” and Q: “x = -1”, used as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule), we conclude x = 1. This is the derivation of @prp-contrapositive. It is the only admissible order. The premise comes first. (i) needs a box from

(The whole derivation is also pointless: line 3 alone is already the goal.) (b) The derivation of @prp-contrapositive, from the primitive rules: Yes: a line “

[C3: Exit check: labeling a proof] Here is a proof that for an integer n, if n^2 is odd, then n is odd. Suppose n^2 is odd.
