title: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content:
Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says One connective is still without rules: “if and only if”. Theorems say “n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd”, and every definition, though written with a plain “if”, is used as an “if and only if”. Section 1.1 warned that “if” means different things in a theorem and in a definition, and promised an explanation. The one new thing here is the pair of rules for \leftrightarrow; the rest of the section (provable equivalence, the layout of an “iff” proof, the convention about definitions, chains of equivalences) is what the rules are used for. The rules for “if and only if” “P if and only if Q” combines “P if Q”, which is Q 	o P, with “P only if Q”, which is P 	o Q, as @exr-statements-and-connectives-c1 explains. A proof of it travels both ways; a use of it, either way. An implication is proved by a box, opened on the hypothesis and closed on the conclusion (@def-rules-implication); an “if and only if” needs two such boxes. An “if and only if” is two implications, and proving it takes two proofs. [Rules for the Biconditional] The first schema is the rule ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} (iff-introduction); its two assumptions are discharged when their boxes close, and each box’s last line (\psi in the first, \varphi in the second) is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. The two schemas below it are the two forms of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (iff-elimination). As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi and \psi stand for any statements, replaced consistently, and i, j, k, l, m for line numbers. Read the rules clause by clause. 1. Two boxes. ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} needs two available boxes: one opened by \varphi and ending in \psi, the other opened by \psi and ending in \varphi, each last line a line of its own box. Each is exactly the box ulename{{	o}I} would need for one direction. Their order does not matter, but both must be there: a single box from \varphi to \psi proves \varphi 	o \psi and nothing more. 2. Separate boxes. The boxes are siblings, not nested, so nothing in the second may cite a line of the first (the scope rule of @def-derivation). Each direction is a proof on its own. 3. Citation. The justification cites both boxes as ranges, as in ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}\ \lines{2}{4}, \lines{5}{7}. 4. Elimination, either way. From \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi and \varphi on available lines, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} writes \psi; from \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi and \psi, it writes \varphi. It is modus ponens in whichever direction we need, citing the biconditional first. First derivations with iff The section’s goal-directed move: a goal \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi opens two boxes, one on each side, and each box’s goal is the other side. [An iff read both ways] 1. Show that P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash Q \leftrightarrow P. 2. Show that P \leftrightarrow Q, \; 
eg Q \vdash 
eg P. (a) Idea. The goal is an iff, so the last line is ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, and we need a box from Q to P and a box from P to Q. Each box’s goal is one ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} away: the premise crosses from its assumption to the other side. Line 3 uses the second form of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (right to left), line 5 the first. (b) Idea. The goal 
eg P is a negation, so open a box on P and aim at  ot (Section 2.2). Inside, the premise P \leftrightarrow Q turns P into Q, and Q clashes with 
eg Q. This is the derivation of @prp-modus-tollens with ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} on line 4: if two statements are equivalent and one fails, so does the other. The rules say nothing that the two implications do not say. The next result makes this exact. [An Iff Is Two Implications] P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P), and (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. Each goal chooses its rule. For the first, the goal is a conjunction of two implications: ulename{\wedge I} needs both, and each is built in its own ulename{{	o}I} box, crossing the premise with ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} inside. For the second, the goal is an iff: open its two boxes. The premise is a conjunction, so take it apart first (premise-directed), and cross each box with one of its halves by ulename{{	o}E}. For the first claim, the following is a derivation with premise P \leftrightarrow Q and last line (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P). For the second claim, the following is a derivation with premise (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) and last line P \leftrightarrow Q. Lines 2 and 3 lie in no box, so both boxes may cite them. This proves both claims. So \leftrightarrow could have been an abbreviation for (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P). We keep it as a connective with its own rules, so that every connective is proved by an introduction rule and used by an elimination rule. [Negating both sides of an iff] Show that P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q. Idea. The goal is an iff, so there are two boxes, one opened by 
eg P and reaching 
eg Q, the other the reverse. Each box’s goal is a negation, so each contains a ulename{
eg I} box: the goal-directed move applied twice, one inside the other. Inside the inner box, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} crosses from one side of the premise to the other, and the result clashes with the outer assumption. Each half is part (b) of @exm-iff-symmetric, run inside a box. Line 5 cites line 2, the assumption of the outer box, still open there. The two halves are mirror images. The derivation uses only the rules of this section and of Sections 2.1–2.2. Its converse, 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, is also derivable, with the rule of Section 2.5: in the box of P it must produce the positive statement Q, and the natural box, on 
eg Q, closes to 
eg
eg Q, not Q. That no derivation avoids the new rule is true, but we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. Section 2.5 sets the converse as an exercise. Provable equivalence @prp-iff-two-implications is a pair of sequents, one in each direction. It is not the first such pair: @prp-curry and @prp-distributivity are pairs too. When two statements can each be derived from the other, either may stand in for the other in any derivation, and the situation deserves a name. Two statements are provably equivalent when each can be derived from the other. Provable Equivalence Statements P and Q are provably equivalent, written P \dashv\vdash Q, if P \vdash Q and Q \vdash P. In words: there is a derivation with premise P and last line Q, and another with premise Q and last line P. The symbol is the turnstile of @def-derivable written twice, back to back; two derivations prove the claim. The degenerate example is P \dashv\vdash P: the one-line derivation of part (a) of @exm-derivations serves in both directions. A first real example is P \vee Q \dashv\vdash Q \vee P: @exm-disjunction-first-derivations shows P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P, and the same derivation with the letters exchanged shows the converse. By the same exchange, part (a) of @exm-iff-symmetric gives P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash Q \leftrightarrow P. A minimal change gives a one-way street. @exm-double-negation-introduction derived P \vdash 
eg
eg P, but the converse, 
eg
eg P \vdash P, would have to remove two negations, and no rule met so far removes one. So we cannot claim P \dashv\vdash 
eg
eg P: the clause “Q \vdash P” is the one missing. (It holds once Section 2.5 adds its rule; that it cannot hold without that rule is true, and Chapter 3 proves it: @thm-raa-independent.) Likewise @prp-contrapositive derives 
eg Q 	o 
eg P from P 	o Q, but not yet the reverse. The connective \leftrightarrow and the relation \dashv\vdash are two sides of one idea; the next result makes the link exact, and shows that \dashv\vdash behaves as an equivalence should. [Provable Equivalence and the Biconditional] For all statements P, Q, R: 1. P \dashv\vdash Q if and only if \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q; 2. P \dashv\vdash P; if P \dashv\vdash Q, then Q \dashv\vdash P; and if P \dashv\vdash Q and Q \dashv\vdash R, then P \dashv\vdash R. Everything here moves whole derivations around. To prove \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, the two boxes of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} are the two given derivations, with their premises turned into the boxes’ assumptions. To use \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, write out its derivation and apply ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. For transitivity, run one derivation into the next: the last line of the first is the premise of the second. We use one observation twice. Let D be a derivation, and copy its lines, in order and with their numbers shifted, to some place in another derivation, with every line of the copy inside the same boxes as that place. Then every citation inside the copy is still available: if line i of D is available at line k of D, every box of D containing line i contains line k, and the boxes added around the copy contain both lines. Closed boxes cited in D are handled the same way. So each copied line is justified by the same rule as before. (\Rightarrow) in (a). Suppose P \vdash Q and Q \vdash P, by derivations D_1 and D_2. Build a derivation with no premises as follows. Open a box with the assumption P and, below it, copy D_1, turning each of its premise lines P into a repetition of the assumption by (D3) of @def-derivation. By the observation, the copy is justified, and its last line Q is a line of the box itself, since the last line of D_1 lies in none of D_1’s boxes. Close the box. Open a second box with Q, copy D_2 in the same way, and close it on P. Then ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} on the two boxes gives P \leftrightarrow Q. So \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. (\Leftarrow) in (a). Suppose \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, by a derivation D with no premises. For P \vdash Q, start with the premise P, copy D below it, and write Q by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} from the last line of the copy, P \leftrightarrow Q, and line 1. Both cited lines lie in no box, so both are available. For Q \vdash P, do the same with premise Q, using the other form of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. So P \dashv\vdash Q. (b) The one-line derivation consisting of the premise P shows P \vdash P, in both directions, so P \dashv\vdash P. Symmetry holds because @def-provable-equivalence says the same thing about P, Q as about Q, P. For transitivity it is enough to show that P \vdash Q and Q \vdash R give P \vdash R, since the reverse direction is the same statement with P and R exchanged. Take a derivation D_1 of Q from P, and below its last line copy a derivation D_2 of R from Q, turning each premise line Q of D_2 into a repetition of the last line of D_1. That line lies in no box, so it is available everywhere below it, and by the observation the rest of the copy is justified. The result has premise P and last line R. This proves the proposition. Part (a) says that one derivation of P \leftrightarrow Q from no premises carries the same information as two derivations, one each way. Part (b) says that \dashv\vdash can be used like “=” in a calculation: chains of provable equivalences run either way and join end to end. Here are equivalences derived so far. Each row gives two derived rules (@def-derived-rule), one in each direction. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Provable equivalence Derived in ----------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- P \wedge Q \dashv\vdash Q \wedge P @prp-and-commutes, with the letters exchanged for the converse P \vee Q \dashv\vdash Q \vee P @exm-disjunction-first-derivations, likewise (P \wedge Q) 	o R \dashv\vdash P 	o (Q 	o R) @prp-curry P \wedge (Q \vee R) \dashv\vdash (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) @prp-distributivity (P 	o R) \wedge (Q 	o R) \dashv\vdash (P \vee Q) 	o R @exm-cases-on-hypothesis and @exm-or-hypothesis-split P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o P) @prp-iff-two-implications P \leftrightarrow Q \dashv\vdash Q \leftrightarrow P @exm-iff-symmetric (a), with the letters exchanged ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The fourth row is distributivity of \wedge over \vee as a provable equivalence. Some familiar laws are not in the table, because the text has derived them in one direction only; associativity of \vee is one (@exm-disjunction-regroup). A sequent in one direction is not an equivalence. P \wedge Q \vdash P holds by ulename{\wedge E}, but P \vdash P \wedge Q does not: take P: “2 > 1” and Q: “1 > 2”, and the premise is true while the conclusion is false. (A derivation never leads from true premises to a false conclusion; Chapter 3 proves this, @thm-soundness.) Before writing \dashv\vdash, check that both derivations exist. Proving an iff: two directions In a written proof, the two boxes of ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} become two paragraphs: (\Rightarrow) assumes the left side and reaches the right, (\Leftarrow) the reverse. Neither may borrow the other’s assumption: they are two separate boxes. The first example completes the story of parity. We use the facts (E1)–(E3) of Section 2.1: every integer is even or odd; no integer is both even and odd; the square of an odd integer is odd. [Odd Square, Odd Number] Let n be an integer. Then n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd. Two boxes. Forwards is (E3). Backwards, “n^2 is odd” gives nothing to compute with, so split on (E1) and show the even case impossible, as in @exm-impossible-case. (\Rightarrow) This is (E3). (\Leftarrow) Suppose n^2 is odd [	ext{assumption for the second box}]. By (E1), n is even or odd, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. If n is odd, we are done. If n is even, say n = 2k with k an integer, then n^2 = 2(2k^2) is even; so n^2 is both even and odd [ulename{\wedge I}], which contradicts (E2) [ulename{
eg E}]. So this case cannot occur, and n is odd in it too [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases n is odd. This proves the theorem [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}]. With the derived rules of Section 2.3, (\Leftarrow) fits in one breath, “n cannot be even, since then n^2 would be even; so n is odd”: ulename{
eg I} with (E2), then ulename{MT}, then ulename{DS} on (E1). The next example is about real numbers, and its two directions do different work. Each hypothesis is needed: dropping either one breaks one of the two directions, as the remark after the proof shows. [Squaring Preserves Order] Let x and y be real numbers with x \ge 0 and y \ge 0. Then x \le y \iff x^2 \le y^2 . Forwards, multiply x \le y by x \ge 0 and by y \ge 0, and chain. Backwards, nothing undoes squaring without square roots, so we split instead: either x \le y, which is the goal, or y < x. In the second case the forward argument, run with a strict inequality, gives y^2 < x^2, which clashes with the hypothesis: an impossible case, closed by ulename{ ot E}. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x \le y. Multiplying by x \ge 0 gives x^2 \le xy, and multiplying by y \ge 0 gives xy \le y^2. Hence x^2 \le y^2. (\Leftarrow) Suppose x^2 \le y^2. For real numbers, x \le y or y < x, and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. If x \le y, we are done. If y < x, then x > y \ge 0, so x > 0. Multiplying y < x by x > 0 gives xy < x^2, and multiplying y < x by y \ge 0 gives y^2 \le xy. Hence y^2 < x^2, which contradicts x^2 \le y^2 [ulename{
eg E}]; so this case cannot occur, and x \le y holds in it [ulename{ ot E}]. In both cases x \le y. This proves the theorem [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}]. Each hypothesis has a job. The direction (\Rightarrow) needs x \ge 0, and fails without it: x = -2, y = 1 gives x \le y but x^2 = 4 > 1 = y^2. (Its proof also multiplied by y \ge 0, but there y \ge 0 already follows from y \ge x \ge 0.) The direction (\Leftarrow) used only y \ge 0, and fails without it: x = 1, y = -2 gives x^2 = 1 \le 4 = y^2 but x > y. A payoff comes at once. For a, b \ge 0, apply @thm-squares-order to x = \sqrt{a} and y = \sqrt{b}: \sqrt{a} \le \sqrt{b} if and only if a \le b. Taking square roots preserves order, a fact used constantly in estimates. (That square roots of nonnegative numbers exist is a school fact here; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it from the least upper bound axiom.) Here is a proof of the statement “for a real number x, x^2 = 1 if and only if x = 1 or x = -1”. If x = 1, then x^2 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1. If x = -1, then x^2 = (-1)(-1) = 1. This proves the claim. Which direction has been proved, and which is missing? Supply the missing one. The proof assumes the right side, “x = 1 or x = -1”, splits it into its two cases, and reaches x^2 = 1 in both. So it proves (\Leftarrow), by ulename{\vee E}. The direction (\Rightarrow) is missing. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x^2 = 1. Then (x - 1)(x + 1) = x^2 - 1 = 0. A product of real numbers is zero only if one of the factors is zero, so x - 1 = 0 or x + 1 = 0, that is, x = 1 or x = -1. A proof of an iff can prove one direction twice and look complete. For “n is odd if and only if n^2 is odd”, a proof that shows “if n is odd, then n^2 is odd” and then “if n^2 is not odd, then n is not odd” has proved (\Rightarrow) and its contrapositive (@prp-contrapositive), which is (\Rightarrow) again. The direction (\Leftarrow), “if n^2 is odd, then n is odd”, is still missing; its contrapositive would be “if n is not odd, then n^2 is not odd”. Before writing “this proves the theorem”, check that one paragraph assumes each side. What a definition says Here is a definition written the way this book and most others write definitions. A function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is strictly increasing if, for all real numbers x and y, x < y implies f(x) < f(y). Grammatically the sentence is an implication, “f is strictly increasing if [condition]”, and read as a theorem it would allow only one move, from the condition to the term. But a definition is not a theorem. It introduces a new term, and the new term means exactly the condition: no more, since nothing else was said about the term, and no less, since the condition is all the term was made to express. So the definition is used in both directions, as an \leftrightarrow between the term and the condition, and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} is how it is used. In a definition, “if” means “if and only if”. This is a convention of mathematical language, not a rule of logic. Some books write “iff” or :\Leftrightarrow in definitions; this book, like most, writes “if” and puts the term defined in bold, which signals that the “if” is an “iff”. Here it is used three ways. The words “for all real numbers x and y” are a quantifier, whose rules come in Chapter 4; here we use them informally. [A definition used in both directions] 1. Show that f(x) = 3x - 5 defines a strictly increasing function f \colon 
R 	o 
R. 2. Suppose g \colon 
R 	o 
R is strictly increasing. Show that g(1) < g(2). 3. Show that h(x) = x^2 does not define a strictly increasing function h \colon 
R 	o 
R. (a) Let x and y be real numbers with x < y. Multiplying by 3 > 0 gives 3x < 3y, and subtracting 5 gives 3x - 5 < 3y - 5, that is, f(x) < f(y). So f satisfies the condition, and by the definition, read from right to left, f is strictly increasing [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}]. (b) Since g is strictly increasing, the definition, read from left to right, says that x < y implies g(x) < g(y) for all real x and y [ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}]. Taking x = 1 and y = 2, and using 1 < 2, we get g(1) < g(2) [ulename{{	o}E}]. (c) Suppose h were strictly increasing [	ext{assumption for } ulename{
eg I}]. By the definition read from left to right, as in (b), -1 < 0 would give h(-1) < h(0), that is, 1 < 0, which is false [ulename{
eg E}]. So h is not strictly increasing [ulename{
eg I}]. Part (a) uses the definition from the condition to the term; parts (b) and (c) use it from the term to the condition. A definition read only as an “if” would permit (a) and nothing else. The convention is for definitions only. In a theorem, “if” means “if”, one direction. A familiar theorem of calculus, proved in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 7, says: if f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. Its converse is false. The function f(x) = \abs{x} is continuous at 0, but it is not differentiable there, since its graph has a corner: the quotient \abs{h}/h is 1 for h > 0 and -1 for h < 0. Reading a theorem’s “if” as “iff” means proving its converse without a proof, which is the error of Argument B in Section 1.1. Chains of equivalences “The following are equivalent: (a), (b), (c)” means that any two of the three are equivalent: three iff statements, or six implications. Three implications suffice, if they go round in a cycle: 	ext{(a)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(b)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(c)} \Rightarrow 	ext{(a)} . Once the cycle is proved, any condition leads to any other by following the arrows round. Here is the derivation behind that sentence. [Proving Equivalence by a Cycle] P 	o Q, \; Q 	o R, \; R 	o P \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q. Likewise, from the same three premises, Q \leftrightarrow R and R \leftrightarrow P are derivable. The goal is an iff, so there are two boxes. From P, one step along the cycle reaches Q. From Q, the cycle reaches P the long way round, through R: a backward chain of ulename{{	o}E}, as in Section 1.4. The other two equivalences need no new work, because the three premises do not change when the letters are rotated. The following is a derivation with the three premises and last line P \leftrightarrow Q. Now replace P, Q, R throughout by Q, R, P respectively. The premises P 	o Q, Q 	o R, R 	o P become Q 	o R, R 	o P, P 	o Q, the same three statements in a different order, and every line remains justified by the same rule. So the renamed derivation derives Q \leftrightarrow R from the same premises. Rotating once more gives R \leftrightarrow P. This proves the proposition. In a cycle every condition reaches every other along the arrows; longer cycles work the same way. Two arrows back and forth are not a cycle through three conditions. Proving (a) \Rightarrow (b) and (b) \Rightarrow (a) shows that (a) and (b) are equivalent and says nothing about (c): no arrow enters or leaves it. For a real number x, take (a) “x > 0”, (b) “2x > 0”, and (c) “x > 1”. Both arrows between (a) and (b) are true, and (c) is not equivalent to them: x =  rac{1}{2} satisfies (a) and (b) but not (c). Every condition in the list must lie on the cycle. [Three descriptions of the unit interval] Let x be a real number. Prove that the following are equivalent. 1. 0 < x < 1. 2. x^2 < x. 3. x > 0 and 1/x > 1. By @prp-equivalence-cycle it suffices to prove (a) \Rightarrow (b) \Rightarrow (c) \Rightarrow (a). (a) \Rightarrow (b). Suppose 0 < x < 1. Multiplying x < 1 by x > 0 gives x^2 < x. (b) \Rightarrow (c). Suppose x^2 < x. First, x > 0: otherwise x \le 0, and then x \le 0 \le x^2, so x \le x^2, which contradicts x^2 < x. (In rules: we have x \le 0 or x > 0; the first is refuted by a ulename{
eg I} box, and ulename{DS} (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism) leaves the second.) Since x > 0, we may divide x^2 < x by x, which gives x < 1, and then divide x < 1 by x, which gives 1 < 1/x. So x > 0 and 1/x > 1. (c) \Rightarrow (a). Suppose x > 0 and 1/x > 1. Multiplying 1 < 1/x by x > 0 gives x < 1. So 0 < x < 1. The order of the cycle was a choice, made so that each arrow was short: (b) \Rightarrow (c) carried the only case split. The reverse cycle would also do, with different arrows to prove. What the rules sound like The rows for this section’s rules complete the table for the connectives; Section 2.6 collects the rules in one place. The Lean names in the last column come from the two fields of an iff, mp (“modus ponens”, left to right) and mpr (right to left). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Rule You write Lean ------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------- ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} “(\Rightarrow) Suppose P. … so Q. (\Leftarrow) Suppose Q. … so P.” constructor ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} “Since P holds if and only if Q does, and P holds, so does Q.” h.mp hp / h.mpr hq ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State the rules ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, and the definition of P \dashv\vdash Q. 2. For a real number x \ge 0, consider “x^2 = x if and only if x = 0 or x = 1”. Write the directions (\Rightarrow) and (\Leftarrow) as implications. Which one would a proof begin with “Suppose x^2 = x”? 3. True or false, with a reason: from the definition “an integer n is even if there is an integer k with n = 2k” and the fact that 10 is even, we may conclude that 10 = 2k for some integer k. 4. True or false, with a reason: from the theorem “if x > 1, then x^2 > 1” and the fact that x^2 > 1, we may conclude that x > 1. (a) ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}: from a box \varphi \dots \psi and a box \psi \dots \varphi, both available, write \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi. ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}: from \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi and either side, write the other (@def-rules-biconditional). P \dashv\vdash Q means P \vdash Q and Q \vdash P (@def-provable-equivalence). (b) (\Rightarrow): if x^2 = x, then x = 0 or x = 1. (\Leftarrow): if x = 0 or x = 1, then x^2 = x. The direction (\Rightarrow) begins “Suppose x^2 = x”, since it assumes the left side. (c) True. A definition’s “if” means “if and only if”, so the definition may be used from the term “even” to the condition, by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. (Indeed k = 5.) (d) False. A theorem’s “if” is one direction only, and the conclusion would be its converse. The converse fails at x = -2: x^2 = 4 > 1 but x < 1. B. Practice [B1: Iff is transitive] Show that P \leftrightarrow Q, \; Q \leftrightarrow R \vdash P \leftrightarrow R. The goal is an iff, so we open two boxes: P to R, and R to P. In each, the premises are used as bridges, one after the other, by ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. Lines 4 and 8 use P \leftrightarrow Q in opposite directions, as do lines 5 and 7 with Q \leftrightarrow R. [B2: A parity equivalence] Let n be an integer. Prove that n is even if and only if n + 3 is odd. (\Rightarrow) Suppose n is even, say n = 2k with k an integer. Then n + 3 = 2k + 2 + 1 = 2(k + 1) + 1, and k + 1 is an integer, so n + 3 is odd. (\Leftarrow) Suppose n + 3 is odd, say n + 3 = 2j + 1 with j an integer. Then n = 2j - 2 = 2(j - 1), and j - 1 is an integer, so n is even. This proves the equivalence. [B3: Strict inequalities] Let x and y be real numbers with x \ge 0 and y \ge 0. Deduce from @thm-squares-order and @exm-iff-negations that x < y if and only if x^2 < y^2. You may use that, for real numbers a and b, a < b holds exactly when b \le a fails. Apply @thm-squares-order with the roles of x and y exchanged, which is allowed since both are nonnegative: y \le x if and only if y^2 \le x^2. By @exm-iff-negations, with P: “y \le x” and Q: “y^2 \le x^2”, used as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule), we get: y \le x fails if and only if y^2 \le x^2 fails. By the fact quoted, the left side says x < y and the right side says x^2 < y^2. This proves that x < y if and only if x^2 < y^2. C. Going deeper [C1: Divisibility by six] For integers d and n, write d \mid n if n = dk for some integer k. Let n be an integer. Prove that the following three conditions are equivalent, by a single cycle of three implications. 1. 6 \mid n; 2. 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n; 3. 6 \mid n^2. You may use @thm-square-even-implies-even and part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3. [Hint 1] Choose the order of the cycle so that each arrow is short. The two results you may use both pass from a square to the number itself. [Hint 2] Try (i) \Rightarrow (iii) \Rightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (i). The last arrow is the one that needs an idea: the two halves of (ii) must be used together, not one at a time. We prove (i) \Rightarrow (iii) \Rightarrow (ii) \Rightarrow (i), which suffices by @prp-equivalence-cycle. (i) \Rightarrow (iii). Suppose n = 6k. Then n^2 = 36k^2 = 6(6k^2), so 6 \mid n^2. (iii) \Rightarrow (ii). Suppose n^2 = 6j. Then n^2 = 2(3j) is even, so n is even by @thm-square-even-implies-even, that is, 2 \mid n. Also n^2 = 3(2j), so 3 \mid n^2, and by part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3, 3 \mid n. Hence 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n [ulename{\wedge I}]. (ii) \Rightarrow (i). Suppose 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n, and write n = 3b with b an integer. The integer b is odd or even. If b were odd, then n = 3b would be odd: writing b = 2c + 1 gives 3b = 6c + 3 = 2(3c + 1) + 1. But n is even, and no integer is both, so this case cannot occur [ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}]. Hence b is even, say b = 2c, and n = 6c, so 6 \mid n. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: names a cycle through all three conditions and cites @prp-equivalence-cycle (or proves the needed implications explicitly). - 2: (i) \Rightarrow (iii) by computation. - 3: (iii) \Rightarrow (ii), citing @thm-square-even-implies-even for the factor 2 and part (a) of @exr-negation-and-contradiction-b3 for the factor 3. - 4: (ii) \Rightarrow (i), combining the two factors correctly (ruling out b odd, or n = 3n - 2n, or otherwise). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “cycle” that omits a condition; using “2 \mid n and 3 \mid n gives 6 \mid n” without proof; using “6 \mid n^2 implies 6 \mid n” as known. Any other cycle through the three conditions earns full marks if each of its arrows is proved: 1 point for the cycle and its citation, and 3 points for each of its three arrows. [C2: Dropping a hypothesis, and repairing the statement] 1. Suppose only y \ge 0 is assumed in @thm-squares-order, and x is an arbitrary real number. The remark after it says that (\Leftarrow) survives. Which steps of its proof use y \ge 0, and why is x \ge 0 never needed? Refute (\Rightarrow) with a new pair. 2. Prove that for all real numbers x and y, \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if x^2 \le y^2. Hint: for (b), apply @thm-squares-order to the right pair of numbers. (a) The proof of (\Leftarrow) uses y \ge 0 twice: for x > 0 from x > y, and for y^2 \le xy. Its other multiplication is by the derived x > 0, so x \ge 0 is never used. For (\Rightarrow), take x = -3, y = 1: x \le y and y \ge 0, but x^2 = 9 > 1 = y^2. (b) Let x and y be real numbers. Then \abs{x} \ge 0 and \abs{y} \ge 0, so @thm-squares-order applies to the pair \abs{x}, \abs{y} and gives \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if \abs{x}^2 \le \abs{y}^2. Finally \abs{x}^2 = x^2, since \abs{x} is x or -x and (-x)^2 = x^2, and likewise \abs{y}^2 = y^2. This proves that \abs{x} \le \abs{y} if and only if x^2 \le y^2.

title: 2.5 Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules
content:
Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules Every rule so far either builds a statement or takes one apart. The rules for negation are no exception: ulename{
eg I} (@def-rules-negation) builds 
eg\varphi from a box that opens with \varphi and ends in  ot, and ulename{
eg E} (@def-rules-contradiction) uses 
eg\varphi against \varphi. Yet in three places this chapter has stopped one step short of a goal. This section adds the one rule that takes a negation away, reductio ad absurdum. It then derives from it the classical laws that mathematics uses without noticing, and shows that three of them are one principle in three forms. Two boxes that look alike Here are two arguments that a mathematician would both call “proof by contradiction”. The first is the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational. It fixes a rational number r, supposes r^2 = 2, reaches a contradiction, and concludes that r^2 
e 2. In the language of @def-rules-negation, it opens a box with the assumption P (“r^2 = 2”), reaches  ot inside it, and closes the box to get 
eg P. That is ulename{
eg I}. The second is an argument of a kind that analysis uses constantly. [A number below every positive number] Let x be a real number with x \ge 0, and suppose that x \le \varepsilon for every real number \varepsilon > 0. Prove that x = 0. Suppose, for a contradiction, that x 
e 0. Since x \ge 0 and x 
e 0, we have x > 0. Then \varepsilon \coloneqq x/2 is a real number with \varepsilon > 0, so the hypothesis applies to it and gives x \le x/2. Subtracting x/2 from both sides gives x/2 \le 0, and multiplying by 2 gives x \le 0. This contradicts x > 0. Hence x = 0. (The step “the hypothesis applies to it” uses a rule for “every”, which Chapter 4 makes precise. The facts about \le are school algebra, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 derives from axioms.) Look at its shape. The box opens with the assumption 
eg P, where P is “x = 0”, reaches  ot, and closes to give P. If we tried to justify the last line by ulename{
eg I}, we would get the negation of the box’s assumption, 
eg
eg P: “it is not the case that x 
e 0”. That is not P. The two arguments put their negations in different places. ulename{
eg I} puts a 
eg into the conclusion; the second argument takes one out. Where the rules so far stop short The second argument is not a curiosity. Three times already in this chapter a derivation has stopped short in the same way: it reached a negation where the goal was not one. 1. Section 2.2 warned against the argument “suppose x is not positive; …; hence x is positive”. The box opens with 
eg(x > 0) and reaches  ot, so ulename{
eg I} gives 
eg
eg(x > 0), and no rule so far gets from there to x > 0. 2. In @exr-derived-rules-c1, the premises P 	o Q and 
eg P 	o R led to 
eg(
eg Q \wedge 
eg R), “not both Q and R fail”, and not to Q \vee R. 3. Section 2.4 noted, after @exm-iff-negations, that its converse, 
eg P \leftrightarrow 
eg Q \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q, resists the rules so far. The natural box on 
eg Q, inside the box of P, closes to 
eg
eg Q, not Q. Try the smallest case, P from 
eg
eg P. The goal P is a letter, so no introduction rule applies: the goal-directed moves have nothing to say. The premise 
eg
eg P is a negation, and a negation can be used only by ulename{
eg E}, against the statement it negates, 
eg P. So we assume 
eg P in a box. The box reaches  ot at once, and ulename{
eg I} closes it with 
eg
eg P: the premise again. Every attempt goes round this circle. In fact no derivation of P from 
eg
eg P uses only the rules of Chapter 1 and Sections 2.1–2.4. That is a claim about all derivations, and no search can prove it. Chapter 3 proves it (@thm-raa-independent), by reading statements with more than two truth values. For the other two stalls the same is true, but we state it without proof, and nothing in this book depends on it. Here we name the missing step and add it as a rule. Reductio ad absurdum To prove \varphi, it is enough to show that “not \varphi” leads to a contradiction. Reductio ad Absurdum This is the rule ulename{RAA} (reductio ad absurdum, “reduction to the absurd”). The line 
eg\varphi is an assumption, which opens the box and is discharged when the box closes. The line  ot is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi stands for any statement and i, j, k for line numbers. Read the rule clause by clause. 1. The assumption is the exact negation of the goal. To prove \varphi, the box opens with 
eg\varphi: the negation of the whole of \varphi. If \varphi is Q \vee R, the box opens with 
eg(Q \vee R), not with 
eg Q \vee R. 2. The box must reach  ot, as a line of the box itself: a  ot inside a smaller box depends on a further assumption, as in ulename{
eg I}. 3. The result is \varphi itself, not 
eg
eg\varphi, which ulename{
eg I} would give from the same box. This clause is the whole content of the rule. 4. The box closes, its assumption is discharged, and the justification cites the box as a range \lines{i}{j}. In words: the box is a thought experiment in which \varphi fails. If the experiment ends in  ot, then \varphi cannot fail, and ulename{RAA} lets us write \varphi. Set the new rule beside ulename{
eg I}: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Rule The box opens with The box ends with After the box ------------------- -------------------- ------------------- ----------------- ulename{
eg I} \varphi  ot 
eg\varphi ulename{RAA} 
eg\varphi  ot \varphi ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ The rows differ only in where the 
eg sits, and that small difference makes ulename{RAA} different in kind. Every other primitive rule is the introduction or the elimination rule of one connective (ulename{ ot E} counts as the elimination rule of  ot), and repetition is a clause of @def-derivation, not a rule for a connective. ulename{RAA} belongs to no connective. It applies to every statement \varphi, whatever its main connective, and even to a letter, which has none. For one kind of goal the new rule is never needed at the last step. Suppose the goal is itself a negation 
eg\psi. An ulename{RAA} box for it opens with 
eg
eg\psi. Replace it by a ulename{
eg I} box that opens with \psi; inside it, derive 
eg
eg\psi from \psi by the three lines of @exm-double-negation-introduction (a box on 
eg\psi that clashes with \psi); then continue as the ulename{RAA} box did, citing that line wherever the ulename{RAA} box cited its assumption. The box still ends in  ot, and ulename{
eg I} closes it with 
eg\psi. So the last step of a derivation of a negation never needs ulename{RAA}, though steps inside its box still may. ulename{RAA} earns its place on the other goals. The assumption that opens an ulename{RAA} box must be the exact negation of the goal. To prove x \le 1 by contradiction, assume x > 1, since for real numbers “not x \le 1” says x > 1. Assuming x \ge 1 instead is a common slip. It is not the negation: x = 1 satisfies both x \le 1 and x \ge 1. A box opened with x \ge 1 cannot honestly reach  ot while x = 1 is possible, so a “contradiction” that seems to be reached hides an error. A box opens with the assumption 
eg(x < 0) and reaches  ot, as a line of the box itself. Which of the following may be written after it closes, and by which rule? (i) x < 0; (ii) 
eg
eg(x < 0); (iii) x \ge 0. (i) By ulename{RAA}: the box opened with the negation of x < 0. (ii) By ulename{
eg I}: ulename{
eg I} writes the negation of the box’s assumption, and the assumption is 
eg(x < 0). (iii) By neither. For real numbers x \ge 0 says the same as 
eg(x < 0), which is exactly the statement the box has refuted. The move: when stuck, assume the negation of the goal Chapter 1 and Sections 2.1–2.4 built two lists of moves. From the goal: its main connective chooses an introduction rule and so a box or two subgoals. From the premises: each available line’s main connective chooses the elimination rule that uses it, and a goal  ot asks for a clash. The new rule adds one move, for the moment when both lists are used up. We are stuck at a gap when the goal-directed moves give nothing (the goal is a letter, or a disjunction with neither side in hand) and no premise-directed move brings the goal closer. Then open an ulename{RAA} box on the negation of the goal. The new goal is  ot, so we hunt for a clash, and the box has given us one more line to clash with: 
eg\varphi itself. When stuck, assume the negation of the goal, and hunt for a clash. The move is a last resort, not a first one. Section 2.6 explains why it never does harm and still comes last. Four of the five derivations below reach the moment of being stuck, and their Ideas say where; the first shows the rule at its smallest. Five derivations with the new rule The degenerate case. The smallest use of ulename{RAA} proves P from P. There is nothing to find: the premise is the goal. The derivation is here only to show the rule at its smallest. The box opens with 
eg P, and the one line it needs,  ot, comes from the clash of the assumption with the premise. It is legal and pointless, since line 1 already is the goal. It is the purest case of a pattern that turns up in real proofs: a contradiction box whose assumption does nothing except clash with a line we already had. The warnings at the end of this section return to it. The stall, resolved. The next result is the one on which we got stuck. [Double Negation] For every statement P: 1. P \vdash 
eg
eg P, by a derivation that does not use ulename{RAA}; 2. 
eg
eg P \vdash P, by a derivation that uses ulename{RAA}. In (a) the goal 
eg
eg P is the negation of 
eg P, so the goal-directed move of Section 2.2 opens a ulename{
eg I} box with 
eg P, and the premise clashes with it at once. In (b) the goal P is a letter, so no introduction rule applies. The only premise is a negation, which can only clash; the attempt above showed that clashing it inside a ulename{
eg I} box leads back to the premise. We are stuck, so we assume the negation of the goal: an ulename{RAA} box on 
eg P. The premise clashes with it at once. (a) This is the derivation of @exm-double-negation-introduction (a), which uses the rules of @def-rules-negation alone; we repeat it to set it beside (b). (b) An ulename{RAA} box on 
eg P: Line 3 applies ulename{
eg E} to the statement 
eg P on line 2 and to its negation 
eg
eg P on line 1. This proves both parts. In both derivations, lines 2 and 3 form a box that opens with 
eg P and reaches  ot by a clash with line 1. Only the rule that closes the box differs, and with it the last line. So the two directions are not mirror images: one needs only the rules for 
eg, and the derivation of the other uses the new rule. Nonexample by minimal change. Change only the last line of (a), from 
eg
eg P to P, keeping the justification ulename{
eg I}\ \lines{2}{3}. Lines 1–3 still check. What fails is the conclusion of ulename{
eg I}, which must be the negation of the box’s assumption, here 
eg
eg P. To write P, the justification must be ulename{RAA}. From now on both parts are derived rules in the sense of @def-derived-rule. A line 
eg
eg\varphi may be justified by “ulename{
eg
eg I} i”, citing a line \varphi, and a line \varphi by “ulename{
eg
eg E} i”, citing a line 
eg
eg\varphi. The first stall of the list above is now one line: from 
eg
eg(x > 0), ulename{
eg
eg E} gives x > 0. Contraposition, backwards. @prp-contrapositive derives 
eg Q 	o 
eg P from P 	o Q with the rules for 	o and 
eg alone. In practice we use it the other way round. To prove “if n^2 is even then n is even”, one may prove “if n is not even then n^2 is not even”, and the step from that back to the original goes from 
eg Q 	o 
eg P to P 	o Q. [Converse of the Contrapositive] For all statements P and Q, 
eg Q 	o 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q. The goal is an implication, so the goal-directed move opens a box with P, and the new goal is Q, a letter. The premise needs 
eg Q before it gives anything, and 
eg Q is nowhere; the box’s assumption P is a letter and cannot be taken apart. We are stuck at Q, so we assume its negation, 
eg Q. That is exactly what the premise wanted: ulename{{	o}E} gives 
eg P, which clashes with the P of the outer box, and ulename{RAA} closes the inner box with Q. The derivation is: Line 5 may cite line 2 because line 2 lies in a box that is still open. ulename{RAA} enters at line 6. This proves the proposition. So contraposition behaves like double negation: going from P 	o Q to 
eg Q 	o 
eg P needs no ulename{RAA}, and our derivation of the way back uses one ulename{RAA}. That no derivation of the way back can avoid it is true, but we state it without proof. When Q is itself a negation, the inner goal is a negation, and by the paragraph after @def-rule-raa that ulename{RAA} can be replaced by ulename{
eg I}. Excluded middle. Every integer is even or odd. Every real number is \ge 0 or < 0. The purely logical form of such facts is the law P \vee 
eg P, which the next result derives from no premises at all. [Excluded Middle] For every statement P, \vdash P \vee 
eg P. The goal is a disjunction, so Section 1.6’s move postpones it: choose a side only when that side is in hand. But there are no premises, so no premise-directed move applies, and neither side can be derived on its own (informally: P may be true or false; Chapter 3 makes this exact). We are stuck, so we assume the negation of the whole goal, 
eg(P \vee 
eg P), which says that neither side holds, and hunt for a clash. The new line can clash only with P \vee 
eg P, which ulename{\vee I} builds from either side. So we manufacture a side, as in @exm-manufactured-clash. If P held, then P \vee 
eg P would hold, against the assumption; so 
eg P, by ulename{
eg I}. But then P \vee 
eg P holds after all, and that is the final clash. The derivation is: The derivation has no premises, so it shows \vdash P \vee 
eg P. ulename{RAA} is used once, at line 8. This proves the proposition. The assumption of line 1 is used twice, at lines 4 and 7. The first use refutes P; the second uses that refutation. Excluded middle now becomes a derived rule with no premises: a line \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi may be written anywhere, for any statement \varphi, justified by ulename{LEM} with no line cited. Pasting in the eight lines above would replace it. Its use is proof by cases on a statement. To derive \chi, derive it once in a box that assumes \varphi and once in a box that assumes 
eg\varphi, and combine the two boxes with the line \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi by ulename{\vee E}. The paragraph after De Morgan’s laws below uses it that way, and so does part (b) of the result after them. A law with no negation. The last of the five is a law in which 
eg does not occur at all. [Peirce’s Law] For all statements P and Q, \vdash ((P 	o Q) 	o P) 	o P. Try it first (ten minutes): use the goal-directed and premise-directed moves of the earlier sections on this goal until they stall. eg P we are stuck at the goal Q, so we argue for it by ulename{RAA}, using the premise: Line 7 cites line 5, the assumption of the enclosing case box, which is still open: the legal version of what the student wanted. [C3: Exit check: a classical disjunction] Derive \vdash P \vee (P 	o Q) using the primitive rules only (those of Chapter 1, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, and ulename{RAA}), with no derived rule, so neither ulename{LEM} nor ulename{
eg
eg E} as a single line. Name the rule on every line, and say which line is classical. The search. The goal is a disjunction, so we postpone it; there are no premises, so no premise-directed move applies; and neither side is derivable on its own (P may be false, and P 	o Q is false when P is true and Q false). We are stuck, so we assume the exact negation of the goal, 
eg(P \vee (P 	o Q)), and hunt for a clash. The assumption can clash only with P \vee (P 	o Q), which ulename{\vee I} builds from either side. The side P 	o Q is an implication, so we open a box on P with the goal Q. Inside it, ulename{\vee I} gives P \vee (P 	o Q) from P, which clashes with the assumption, and ulename{ ot E} writes Q. So P 	o Q holds, ulename{\vee I} gives the goal, and that is the second clash. Lines 1 and 2 are assumptions, of the ulename{RAA} box and of the ulename{{	o}I} box; every other line names its rule on the right. The classical line is line 9; every other rule used is a rule for a connective. The shape is that of @prp-excluded-middle: there the inner box closed by ulename{
eg I} to give 
eg P; here it ends with ulename{ ot E} and closes by ulename{{	o}I} to give P 	o Q. A second correct route first derives P \vee 
eg P by the eight lines of @prp-excluded-middle, written out, and then splits on it: in the case P, ulename{\vee I} gives the goal; in the case 
eg P, a box on P clashes with 
eg P, ulename{ ot E} writes Q, ulename{{	o}I} gives P 	o Q, and ulename{\vee I} the goal. Its classical line is the ulename{RAA} inside the written-out excluded middle. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: an ulename{RAA} box opened with 
eg(P \vee (P 	o Q)), the exact negation of the goal. - 3: an inner box on P that reaches  ot by ulename{\vee I} and ulename{
eg E} against the outer assumption, and then Q by ulename{ ot E}. - 2: P 	o Q by ulename{{	o}I}, then P \vee (P 	o Q) by ulename{\vee I}, and the second clash. - 2: ulename{RAA} closes the outer box, and it is named as the classical step. - 1: every citation is available. The second route earns the same points, step for step: 2 for the written-out excluded middle opened correctly (its ulename{RAA} box on 
eg(P \vee 
eg P)); 3 for the box on P in the case 
eg P, closed by ulename{ ot E}; 2 for ulename{{	o}I}, the two ulename{\vee I} lines, and the ulename{\vee E}; 2 for naming the ulename{RAA} inside excluded middle as the classical step; 1 for availability. Fatal errors (0 for the step): opening the outer box with anything but 
eg(P \vee (P 	o Q)); closing the outer box by ulename{
eg I} (that gives 
eg
eg(P \vee (P 	o Q))); a line justified by ulename{
eg
eg E} or ulename{LEM} taken as a rule, which the item excludes.

title: 2.6 How to Find a Derivation
content:
How to Find a Derivation We now have every rule for the connectives. Checking a derivation is mechanical, as @def-derivation makes it: for each line, which rule, which lines, and are they available. Finding one is not, since an assumption may be any statement at all. Yet every Idea in Chapters 1 and 2 found its derivation with the same handful of moves. This section introduces no new rule. It collects those moves into one method, puts them in order, says why the order is right, and then watches the method work: on four searches that succeed, one that fails, and one mathematical goal. It ends with every rule in one place. The moves so far Each section since Section 1.3 has added a move, either to the list read off the goal (goal-directed: which introduction rule builds the goal’s main connective?) or to the list read off the premises (premise-directed: which elimination rule uses an available line’s main connective?). Here they are together, with the section where each first appeared. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The situation The move First met ----------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------- goal \varphi \wedge \psi two subgoals, \varphi and \psi, joined by ulename{\wedge I} Section 1.3 resource \varphi \wedge \psi take it apart by ulename{\wedge E} Section 1.3 resource \varphi 	o \psi fire it on \varphi by ulename{{	o}E}; if \varphi is missing, make it a subgoal Section 1.4 goal \varphi 	o \psi a box opened with \varphi, with the new goal \psi Section 1.5 goal \varphi \vee \psi postpone; choose a side only when it is in hand Section 1.6 resource \varphi \vee \psi two cases, each ending in the current goal Section 1.7 goal  ot find a clash, or manufacture one; an impossible case closes itself by ulename{ ot E} Section 2.1 goal 
eg\varphi a box opened with \varphi, with the new goal  ot Section 2.2 a pattern with a name use the derived rule as one line (ulename{MT}, ulename{DS}, …) Section 2.3 goal \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi two boxes, one for each direction Section 2.4 stuck assume the negation of the goal (ulename{RAA}), or split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi (ulename{LEM}) Section 2.5 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Eleven moves is a lot to hold in mind at a blank page. The method below turns them into an order of attack. To state it we need a name for a derivation that is only half written. Partial derivations A search builds a derivation from the outside in: the last line first, then the boxes the goal asks for, then the lines in between. What exists halfway is not yet a derivation, but it is close to one. [Partial Derivation] A partial derivation is a list of lines laid out as a derivation (@def-derivation), except that some stretches of lines are still missing. Each missing stretch is a gap, drawn as a row \vdots. The line just below a gap is its current goal; it is already written, but it has no justification yet, since the lines of the gap are to supply one. The lines available at the current goal, in the sense of @def-derivation, are the gap’s resources. In words: every line that has been written is a premise, an assumption, a current goal, or a line justified by a rule from lines and boxes available to it; the boxes are nested and closed as in any derivation; only the gaps are missing. A search starts with a single gap, below the premises and above the conclusion, and each step replaces a gap by lines, boxes, and smaller gaps. It ends when no gap is left, and then the partial derivation is a derivation. The degenerate partial derivation is the starting point of every search: the premises, one gap, and the goal. Its resources are the premises. The snapshots in the worked searches below are all partial derivations; a line carries the number it will have in the finished derivation, so that snapshots can be compared, and a line whose place is not yet fixed carries no number. On paper you would number the lines at the end. Nonexample. Take a snapshot and leave one of its boxes open at the bottom, so that the conclusion sits inside the box. That is not a partial derivation, even though every line is correct so far: @def-derivation asks that every box close and that the last line lie outside every box, and a gap cannot repair that, since filling a gap adds lines only above its current goal. In the second snapshot of @exm-search-distribute below, the second gap has the current goal  ot on line 11. List its resources. Lines 1, 7, 8, and 9: the premise P 	o 
eg Q, the line 
eg(P \wedge Q), and the assumptions Q and P of the two boxes that contain the gap. Line 7 lies in no box and above the gap, so it is available, though this gap will not need it. Lines 2–6 are not resources: they lie in a box that has closed. The method Work from both ends: let the goal choose the boxes, let the premises choose the eliminations, and meet in the middle. Searching for a derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi. 1. Set up. Write the premises \Gamma at the top and \varphi at the bottom, with one gap between. 2. Goal-directed step. Take the main connective of the current goal (@def-main-connective) and set up its introduction rule: - \psi \wedge \chi: two gaps, with goals \psi and \chi (Section 1.3); - \psi 	o \chi: a box opened with \psi; inside it, the new goal is \chi (Section 1.5); - 
eg\psi: a box opened with \psi; inside it, the new goal is  ot (Section 2.2); - \psi \leftrightarrow \chi: two boxes, one from \psi to \chi and one from \chi to \psi (Section 2.4); - \psi \vee \chi: postpone; do not choose a side yet (Section 1.6), unless the disjunction is being manufactured for a clash with its own negation (step 4), when either side may be chosen (see below). Repeat while the current goal is a \wedge, 	o, 
eg, or \leftrightarrow. 3. Premise-directed step. Take the main connective of a resource and apply its elimination rule: ulename{\wedge E} freely (Section 1.3); ulename{{	o}E} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} when the other statement they need is a resource, or can be made a new goal (Sections 1.4 and 2.4); ulename{\vee E} by opening two boxes, one per disjunct, each ending in the current goal (Section 1.7). A derived rule may do the work of several lines (Section 2.3): a resource \psi 	o \chi with 
eg\chi available gives 
eg\psi by ulename{MT}; a resource \psi \vee \chi with 
eg\psi available gives \chi by ulename{DS}. 4. Clash. If the current goal is  ot, look for a pair \chi, 
eg\chi among the resources, or make \chi the new goal for some resource 
eg\chi and manufacture it, starting again at step 2 for that goal. Whatever the current goal, if the resources clash, write  ot and then the goal by ulename{ ot E}: an impossible case closes itself (Section 2.1). 5. Stuck. Use ulename{RAA}: open a box with the negation of the current goal, whose new goal is  ot; if that gives nothing, try the same with a goal further out whose box contains the stalled gap. Or use ulename{LEM} on a well-chosen statement \chi, and split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi by ulename{\vee E}. Then return to step 3 (Section 2.5). When no gap is left, number the lines and check the derivation as @def-derivation says. The steps are listed in the order in which to try them, and the order has reasons. The goal-directed steps lose nothing. Suppose the goal \psi 	o \chi is derivable from the resources \Gamma at all, by some derivation D. Then \chi is derivable from \Gamma together with \psi: add \psi to the premises of D (@def-derivable asks only that the premises belong to the list), and append the line \chi by ulename{{	o}E}, citing the last line of D and the premise \psi. So opening a box on \psi never turns a derivable gap into an underivable one. With ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{
eg E}, or ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} as the appended line, the same argument covers \wedge, 
eg, and \leftrightarrow. That is why step 2 may be applied without thinking. Choosing a side of \vee can lose everything. A disjunction can be derivable when neither side is. From P \vee Q the goal Q \vee P is derivable (@exm-disjunction-first-derivations), but P \vee Q does not say which side holds, so a last line ulename{\vee I} from Q, or from P, leaves a gap that cannot be filled (Chapter 3 makes “cannot” exact, @cor-refuting-row). Choosing a side is safe only once the resources decide it, typically inside a case of ulename{\vee E}, or when the disjunction is being manufactured for a clash (step 4) with a resource that is its negation: then the resources derive  ot as soon as they derive the disjunction, and from  ot every statement, either side included, by ulename{ ot E}. Step 5 also loses nothing, and still comes last. If \varphi is derivable from the resources, then  ot is derivable from them together with 
eg\varphi, by one appended ulename{
eg E}; so an ulename{RAA} box is always safe. A split on \chi \vee 
eg\chi is safe too, since each case only adds a resource. Step 5 comes last because the goal  ot gives step 2 nothing to work with, because a good \chi must be chosen, and because a derivation that did not need the classical step reads worse with it (the costume of Section 2.5). For each goal, with no premises, name the first rule the method aims for and the box or gaps it sets up. 1. 
eg(P \wedge 
eg P) 2. (P \vee Q) 	o (Q \vee P) 3. (P 	o Q) \wedge (Q 	o (P 	o Q)) 4. P \vee 
eg(P \wedge Q) (a) ulename{
eg I}: a box opened with P \wedge 
eg P, goal  ot. (b) ulename{{	o}I}: a box opened with P \vee Q, goal Q \vee P; that goal is a disjunction, so it is postponed, and step 3 uses the new resource P \vee Q by ulename{\vee E}. (c) ulename{\wedge I}: two gaps, with goals P 	o Q and Q 	o (P 	o Q), each then a box. (d) Step 2 postpones the disjunction, and with no premises steps 3 and 4 have nothing to use, so the search is at step 5 at once. ulename{LEM} on P works: in the case P, ulename{\vee I} gives the left side; in the case 
eg P, a ulename{
eg I} box on P \wedge Q clashes (its ulename{\wedge E} gives P) and gives 
eg(P \wedge Q), and ulename{\vee I} gives the right side. Splitting the goal We now run the method. The first search uses only steps 2, 3, and 4. It is the full version of the chapter’s main move, read the skeleton off the goal, then work from both ends, which comes back twice in the exercises with parts left blank. [Splitting the goal, then using the premise] Find a derivation of P 	o 
eg Q \vdash 
eg(P \wedge Q) \wedge (Q 	o 
eg P). Step 1. The premise on top, the goal at the bottom, one gap. The resources of the gap are the premise alone. Step 2, first pass. The goal’s main connective is \wedge, so it splits into two gaps, with goals 
eg(P \wedge Q) and Q 	o 
eg P, joined at the end by ulename{\wedge I}: Step 2, again. Both new goals have a connective, so step 2 applies to each. The goal 
eg(P \wedge Q) asks for a ulename{
eg I} box opened with P \wedge Q and ending in  ot. The goal Q 	o 
eg P asks for a ulename{{	o}I} box opened with Q; inside it the goal 
eg P asks, in turn, for a ulename{
eg I} box opened with P. Every gap now has the goal  ot, and step 2 has nothing more to do: Steps 3 and 4, first gap. The resources are lines 1 and 2. Step 3 splits line 2 into P and Q by ulename{\wedge E}. Now P is the hypothesis of line 1, so ulename{{	o}E} gives 
eg Q. Step 4 finds the pair Q, 
eg Q. Steps 3 and 4, second gap. The resources are lines 1, 7, 8, and 9, and line 7 is not needed. ulename{{	o}E} on lines 1 and 9 gives 
eg Q, which clashes with line 8. Both gaps close: What the method did. The goal-directed steps wrote nine of the fourteen lines, every box among them, before the premise was used; the premise-directed steps wrote four, lines 3, 4, 5, and 10. The premise itself was used once in each gap, by the same ulename{{	o}E}. Line 10 cites line 1 from inside two boxes, which is legal because line 1 is a premise and so is available everywhere below it. Notice how little thinking the search needed. Step 2 is mechanical, and it did most of the work: by the time the premise was consulted, each gap was small, with the goal  ot and two or three resources. That is the typical shape of a successful search: the goal fixes the skeleton, and the premises fill in the flesh. Cases must end in the goal When the goal gives nothing, the premises must. The next search is driven by a disjunction among the premises. [Proof by cases, found by the method] Find a derivation of P \vee Q, \ P 	o R, \ Q 	o R \vdash R. The goal R is a letter, so step 2 has nothing to do. Step 3 looks at the resources. ulename{{	o}E} on P 	o R needs P, and making P a new goal is hopeless: from P \vee Q we know that one of P, Q holds, not which. The disjunction itself is the resource to use, by ulename{\vee E}, with two boxes that each end in the current goal R: Inside the first box, P is a resource, so ulename{{	o}E} on line 2 closes the gap at once; the second box is the same with line 3: This is the pattern that Section 1.7 called the skeleton of almost every proof by cases (compare @exm-cases-on-hypothesis, which packages the same two boxes into one implication). The method found it without being told. Why the boxes end in the current goal. ulename{\vee E} (@def-rules-disjunction) gives, after the two boxes, their common last line and nothing else. A box that ends in anything but the current goal leaves that goal still to be reached, and two boxes that end in different statements cannot be combined at all. The word current matters: had the goal been S 	o R, step 2 would first open a box on S, the current goal inside it would be R, and the two case boxes, opened inside the box of S, would end in R, not in S 	o R. Postponing a disjunction The third search has a disjunction as its goal. It shows why step 2 postpones one, and how a dead end can name the statement to split on. [Choosing a side too early] Find a derivation of P 	o (Q \vee R) \vdash (P 	o Q) \vee (P 	o R). The tempting start. The goal is a disjunction, and it is tempting to choose a side at once, say P 	o Q, and finish with ulename{\vee I}. The new goal is an implication, so we open a box on P; then ulename{{	o}E} gives Q \vee R, and ulename{\vee E} splits into the cases Q and R, each to end in the current goal Q. The first case ends at once. The second is a dead end: In the case R the resources are P 	o (Q \vee R), P, Q \vee R, and R, and none of them yields Q: no resource has Q as a conclusion except Q \vee R, which is already split, and nothing clashes. Choosing the right side instead fails in the mirror image, in the case Q. In fact neither side follows from the premise alone: with P and Q true and R false the premise is true and P 	o R is false, and with P and R true and Q false the premise is true and P 	o Q is false. (Chapter 3 turns such rows into proofs that no derivation exists: @cor-refuting-row.) The diagnosis. Each case of the dead end knew which side it wanted: the case Q wanted P 	o Q, and the case R wanted P 	o R. But those cases were opened inside the box of P, too late to choose the side of a disjunction that stands outside it. The side must be decided before any box is opened, and the premise does not decide it. Steps 2–4 are used up: we are at step 5. The dead end also names the statement to split on. If Q holds, the left side is easy. If Q fails, then from P the premise gives Q \vee R with its left side refuted, and ulename{DS} gives R. So we use ulename{LEM} on Q, and each case gets the whole goal: Now each case decides the side. In the case Q, the goal is P 	o Q: a box on P whose last line repeats Q. In the case 
eg Q, the goal is P 	o R: a box on P, then Q \vee R by ulename{{	o}E}, then R by @prp-disjunctive-syllogism used as a derived rule, citing Q \vee R and 
eg Q. Then ulename{\vee I}, on the correct side each time: What the method did. Step 2 postponed the goal, the tempting start broke that rule, and its dead end showed both why the rule exists and what to do instead. Line 5 repeats line 3 because ulename{{	o}I} needs Q as a line of the box of line 4 itself. ulename{LEM} on P, the first split one thinks of, also succeeds, but less well: in the case P the premise gives Q \vee R, and a second ulename{\vee E}, with two more implication boxes, is needed inside it; the finished derivation has 22 lines against these 14. Do not choose a disjunct early. A goal \psi \vee \chi tempts us to pick a side and prove it, and the choice usually fails, as the first attempt above did: neither P 	o Q nor P 	o R follows from the premise. Postpone the \vee goal, use the resources first, and choose a side only inside a case that decides it. When nothing else works The fourth search reaches step 5 in the other form, ulename{RAA}, and then needs steps 2 and 4 inside the box. [A search that reaches step 5 at once] Find a derivation of 
eg(P \leftrightarrow Q) \vdash P \vee Q. Steps 1–4. The goal is a disjunction, so step 2 postpones it. The one resource is a negation, and a negation can be used only in a clash (step 4), which needs the goal  ot; the goal is P \vee Q. Neither side is in hand: the premise says only that P and Q differ, not which one holds. Steps 2–4 have nothing to offer. Step 5. We assume the negation of the goal. The new goal is  ot, and the gap has one more resource: Step 4 inside the box. The resources are two negations, 
eg(P \leftrightarrow Q) and 
eg(P \vee Q), and no pair clashes yet. So we choose a statement to manufacture: P \leftrightarrow Q, to clash with line 1, or P \vee Q, to clash with line 2. The second is the goal we started from, a disjunction of two letters with no side in hand, so aiming at it leads back to the start. So we choose P \leftrightarrow Q, and it is a biconditional, so step 2 sets up two boxes: The two small gaps. In the first, the resources are lines 1, 2, and 3, and the goal Q is a letter that no resource produces. But the resources clash once a line is manufactured: ulename{\vee I} builds P \vee Q from line 3, which clashes with line 2, and ulename{ ot E} writes Q (step 4: an impossible case closes itself). The second gap is the mirror image: What the method did. Step 5 came first, because nothing else applied, and after it steps 2 and 4 did the rest: step 4 chose which clash to aim for, step 2 read the two boxes off P \leftrightarrow Q, and step 4 closed each box with a manufactured clash and ulename{ ot E}. In words: suppose neither P nor Q holds; then each of them implies the other, since neither can hold at all; so P \leftrightarrow Q, against the premise. The assumption of line 2 is used twice, at lines 5 and 9. A split by ulename{LEM} on P also works, but less well: in the case 
eg P the goal side Q is a letter that the resources do not give, and the search is stuck there a second time. The derivation of Peirce’s law in Section 2.5 (@prp-peirce) was found by the same method, and it adds one detail to step 5. There, step 2 opened a box with the goal P, step 3 made P 	o Q a subgoal, step 2 opened a box on P with the goal Q, and the search stalled at Q. Assuming 
eg Q at the stalled gap gives nothing new: a clash with 
eg Q needs Q, the stalled goal itself. Assuming 
eg P one level out does, because the new resource 
eg P is available in every gap inside its box, including the stalled one. That is why step 5 says to try a goal further out when the current one gives nothing. A search that fails The method is not a machine that always succeeds. Here it fails, and the failure is instructive. Try P 	o Q \vdash Q 	o P. Step 2 opens a box on Q with the goal P: The goal P is a letter. Step 3: ulename{{	o}E} on line 1 needs P, the goal itself. Step 4: nothing clashes, and there is no negation among the resources to aim at. Step 5, ulename{RAA}: assume 
eg P; the only negation among the resources is now 
eg P, and a clash with it needs P, the goal again. ulename{LEM} on P: the case 
eg P needs P again. ulename{LEM} on Q: the case 
eg Q clashes with line 2, and the case Q is where we started. Step 5 at the goal further out, an ulename{RAA} box on 
eg(Q 	o P) around the whole search: a clash with it needs Q 	o P, the goal again, and step 2 opens the same box on Q with the same goal P. Every route returns to one gap, “P from P 	o Q and Q”. That is affirming the consequent (Section 1.4), the step that would repair Argument B. But notice what we have not shown. A search that fails proves nothing about derivations in general. An assumption may be any statement at all, by the assumption clause of @def-derivation, so there are infinitely many derivations to consider, and a cleverer one might exist. To show that no derivation of Q 	o P from P 	o Q exists, we need a different tool. That is the question this chapter leaves open. We show that something is derivable by exhibiting a derivation; how could we ever show that something is not? Chapter 3 answers it (@cor-refuting-row). It gives each statement a truth value and proves that the rules never lead from true premises to a false conclusion; the assignment with P false and Q true, which makes P 	o Q true and Q 	o P false, then settles this search for good. A mathematical goal The method reads the frame of a proof off the goal whether the statements are letters or facts about numbers. In ordinary mathematics its payoff is that the first and last sentences of a proof, and its division into parts, are fixed before any mathematics is done. [Building a skeleton] Let m and n be integers. Prove that if mn is odd, then m is odd and n is odd. The skeleton. The main connective is “if … then”, so step 2 opens a ulename{{	o}I} box: “Assume mn is odd. … Hence m is odd and n is odd.” The new goal is a conjunction, so step 2 again: two separate proofs, one that m is odd and one that n is odd. Each is a letter as far as logic can see, and the one resource, “mn is odd”, cannot be taken apart. So step 3 brings in facts we can compute with: “if m is even then mn is even” is one, and ulename{CP} (@prp-contrapositive) turns it into “if mn is not even then m is not even”, which the resource can feed. Then “every integer is even or odd” and ulename{DS} finish. The proof. Assume mn is odd. We show that m is odd and that n is odd. First, if m is even, say m = 2k with k an integer, then mn = 2(kn) is even. By the contrapositive (@prp-contrapositive), if mn is not even, then m is not even. Now mn is odd, so it is not even, since no integer is both; hence m is not even. Since every integer is even or odd, m is odd, by @prp-disjunctive-syllogism. Exchanging the roles of m and n in the previous paragraph shows that n is odd. Hence m and n are both odd. What the method did. It fixed the first sentence, the two paragraphs, and the last sentence; the only computation is mn = 2(kn). No step uses ulename{RAA}: the classical-looking move from “m is not even” to “m is odd” is disjunctive syllogism on the fact that every integer is even or odd. (The phrase “say m = 2k” names a witness, which is a rule for “there exists” from Chapter 4.) Do not assume what you want to prove. To derive a goal \varphi, it is tempting to open a box with \varphi. The box reaches \varphi at once, but after it closes it gives \varphi 	o \varphi, not \varphi, and its assumption is gone. An assumption is useful when the goal asks for it: the hypothesis of an implication (step 2), the negated goal of ulename{RAA} (step 5), a disjunct of a resource (step 3). Opening the box on the conclusion of an implication is the converse error of Argument B in Section 1.1. The rules in one place This is the reference sheet for Chapters 1 and 2: every primitive rule as its schema, with the label that defines it. As in every schema (@def-rule-schema), \varphi, \psi, \chi stand for any statements, replaced consistently, and i, j, k, \dots for line numbers. Each box rule needs the box’s last line as a line of that box itself, not inside a further box, and every cited line or box must be available (@def-derivation). Conjunction (@def-rules-conjunction): ulename{\wedge I}, and the two forms of ulename{\wedge E}. Implication (@def-rules-implication): ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{{	o}E}. Disjunction (@def-rules-disjunction): the two forms of ulename{\vee I}, and ulename{\vee E}, whose two boxes end in the same statement \chi. Contradiction and negation (@def-rules-contradiction, @def-rules-negation): ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E} (which may write any statement \varphi), and ulename{
eg I}. Biconditional (@def-rules-biconditional): ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, which works in both directions. Reductio ad absurdum (@def-rule-raa), the one classical rule, and repetition, clause (D3) of @def-derivation, which copies an available line into the current box. Derived rules.
