title: Truth, Soundness and Completeness
content:
Truth, Soundness and Completeness Chapters 1 and 2 built a calculus of derivations, and with it we can show that a sequent holds: write a derivation. What we cannot yet do is show that a sequent does not hold. Section 2.6 searched for a derivation of P 	o Q \vdash Q 	o P, and every route stalled; but a search that fails proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist somewhere. The motivating problem of this chapter is to prove that no derivation of q 	o p from p 	o q exists, however long and however clever. The answer is to give formulas a meaning. A valuation makes each atom true or false, a truth table computes the value of every formula from its atoms, and \Gamma \models \psi says that every valuation making the premises true makes the conclusion true. Two theorems then tie meaning to derivation. Soundness: whatever can be derived is true in every row where the premises are true; so a single row with true premises and a false conclusion proves that no derivation exists. Completeness: whatever is true in every such row can be derived; so the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 are enough. To state and prove these theorems we first make formulas into mathematical objects, and we meet induction, on the natural numbers and on the shape of a formula, because both theorems are proved by it. These are the book’s first proofs about proofs, and its first long proofs. The chapter ends with normal forms, the constructive content of completeness. What you need. Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for every connective, the definition of a derivation with its boxes and its scope rule (@def-derivation), derived rules (@def-derived-rule), and the classical rules of Section 2.5, above all the law of excluded middle (@prp-excluded-middle). The arithmetic and order of the natural numbers are used as school facts. Time. About 40 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 55 hours for everything. Roadmap - Formulas as objects. The exact definition of a formula, parse trees, subformulas and height, the shorthand of Chapter 1 as a translation, and why a derivation stays a derivation when formulas are put in for its atoms. - Induction on numbers and on formulas. The principle of induction, strong induction, and structural induction, and with them the proofs that every formula is read in only one way and that a definition by one clause per connective defines exactly one thing. - Valuations and truth tables. Truth values for atoms, the value of every formula computed along its parse tree, and why a table with 2^n rows tells everything about a formula with n atoms. - Tautologies, entailment, and equivalence. The semantic counterpart \Gamma \models \psi of a sequent, tautologies and satisfiability, the standard equivalences, and what may be replaced or substituted without changing truth. - Soundness. The rules never lead from truth to falsehood, proved by induction on the lines of a derivation; so one refuting row shows that a sequent has no derivation. - Completeness. Every truth-table consequence of finitely many premises has a derivation: the rules prove their own truth tables, one row at a time, and excluded middle glues the rows together. - Normal forms and adequate connectives. Every formula is equivalent to one in disjunctive and in conjunctive normal form; validity read off a conjunctive normal form; which sets of connectives can express everything. Named moves - Induction on the shape of a formula. Prove it for atoms and  ot; prove it for each connective, assuming it for the parts. - Define by recursion on formulas. One clause per way of building a formula; unique readability makes the definition well defined. - Refute with one row. A valuation making every premise true and the conclusion false proves \Gamma 
vdash \psi, by soundness. - Induction on the lines of a derivation. To prove that every derivable sequent has a property, show that every rule preserves it. - Split on an atom. With p \vee 
eg p and ulename{\vee E}, prove the goal once assuming p and once assuming 
eg p.

title: 3.1 Formulas as Objects
content:
Formulas as Objects Chapter 2 ended on a question that no derivation can answer. We show that a sequent holds by writing a derivation of it; but how could we show that one does not hold, that no derivation of Q 	o P from P 	o Q exists, however long and however clever? This chapter answers the question, and the answer is a theorem about every derivation of every formula. A theorem about every formula needs, first of all, an exact description of what a formula is. This section gives it. It defines formulas, draws them as trees, names their parts, and says how the shorthand of Chapters 1 and 2 fits in. Nothing is yet proved about all formulas at once; the tool for that is the next section’s. Why formulas must become objects Here is the theorem that Section 3.5 proves, stated loosely: If \psi can be derived from premises \Gamma, then \psi is true in every situation in which all the premises are true. Read it as a mathematician reads a statement about all integers. “For every integer n, n^2 - n is even” can be proved only by someone who knows what an integer is: every integer is even or odd, and each kind can be handled. A proof needs a way to take hold of an arbitrary object of the kind the statement is about. The loose theorem above is about arbitrary derivations, and a derivation is a list of formulas, so the proof will need a way to take hold of an arbitrary formula. Chapters 1 and 2 never needed one. There we read statements by eye: we found the main connective of 
eg(P \wedge Q) 	o R (@def-main-connective) by looking, and we drew its tree by hand. That is fine for one statement at a time. It is useless for a claim about all statements, because “all the strings we would recognize as statements” is not a description anyone can reason from. So we now do for formulas what Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 will do for the real numbers: say exactly which objects we mean, in a form that later proofs can use. The description has three parts. First, the alphabet, the symbols formulas are written with. Second, the formation rules, which say how formulas are built. Third, a closing clause saying that nothing else is a formula. The third is the one that is easy to forget and that makes everything else work. The alphabet Formulas are strings of symbols. A string is a finite list of symbols written one after another, and its length is the number of symbols in it. The symbols are these. - Atoms: p, q, r, p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots, infinitely many of them. Each atom is one symbol: p_1 is a single symbol whose name happens to carry a subscript, not the two symbols p and 1. - The constant  ot, read “contradiction”, as in Chapter 1. - The connectives: 
eg (the only one that takes one part) and \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow (the binary connectives, which take two). - The parentheses ( and ). An atom plays the part that a letter played in Chapters 1 and 2: a statement whose inner structure we ignore. In those chapters the letters were capitals, P, Q, R, and they stood for arbitrary statements, atomic or compound. From now on we keep two kinds of letter apart, because the theorems of this chapter need the difference. - An atom p, q, r, \dots is a symbol of the language. It occurs in formulas. - A metavariable \varphi, \psi, \chi (phi, psi, chi) is a name we use when talking about formulas: “let \varphi be a formula”. It never occurs in a formula. The definition below says exactly how the building goes. It is an inductive definition: it names the starting pieces, names the ways of building new formulas from old, and then closes the door on everything else. A formula is a string built from atoms and  ot by the connectives, one step at a time, with a pair of parentheses around every binary step. Without (F4), clauses (F1)–(F3) would be satisfied by far too many collections of strings. The collection of all strings contains every atom and  ot, and is closed under writing 
eg in front and under wrapping two strings with a connective in parentheses; so (F1)–(F3) alone cannot tell us that p \wedge 	o q is excluded. Clause (F4) says the formulas are only those strings that the building steps reach. In the language of sets, which Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 introduces properly, the formulas are the smallest collection of strings closed under (F1)–(F3). Without the parentheses in (F3), a string could be read in two ways. Take p \wedge q \vee r. Built one way, it is “p \wedge q” joined to r by \vee; built the other way, it is p joined to “q \vee r” by \wedge. The two constructions have different parse trees (defined below), and they say different things: if p is false and r is true, then “p and q, or r” is true, because r is, while “p, and q or r” is false, because p is. (Section 3.3 makes “true under an assignment of values” exact; the everyday reading of Chapter 1 is enough here.) With the parentheses of (F3) the two constructions give two different strings, ((p \wedge q) \vee r) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad (p \wedge (q \vee r)) , and the ambiguity disappears. The next section proves that it disappears for every formula: a formula can be built in only one way (the unique readability theorem of Section 3.2). Why not parentheses around a negation too? Nothing would break, but nothing would be gained. The symbol 
eg always stands in front of what it negates, so 
eg\varphi can be read in only one way without help. Keeping the official language as lean as possible makes the proofs about it shorter. Why atoms, and not sentences like “x > 0”? Because the theorems of this chapter are about forms, and the form of an argument is what remains when the content of its atomic statements is forgotten (Chapter 1’s slogan: logic studies the forms of arguments). An atom is a statement reduced to a name. A formula is a string of symbols, and questions about formulas are questions about strings. “Is (p \wedge p) the same formula as p?” has the answer no: the first has length 5 and the second length 1, even though they always have the same truth value (Section 3.3 gives the means to check this). Sameness of formulas is letter-for-letter identity; sameness of meaning is a different relation, which Section 3.4 names. Parse trees A formation sequence records how a formula was built, but it is a list, and a list hides the shape of the building. Chapter 1 drew the shape as a tree, with the main connective at the top (the tree after @def-main-connective). We now make that drawing official. A parse tree is a formula’s construction drawn upside down: the last step at the root, the atoms at the leaves. [Parse Tree] A parse tree for a formula is defined along the clauses of @def-formula. 1. For an atom or  ot: a single node, labeled by that atom or by  ot. 2. If T is a parse tree for \varphi, then the tree whose root is labeled 
eg and has T hanging below it as its only subtree is a parse tree for 
eg\varphi. 3. If T and T' are parse trees for \varphi and \psi, then the tree whose root is labeled \circ, with T hanging below it on the left and T' on the right, is a parse tree for (\varphi \circ \psi). The leaves are the nodes with nothing below them; a branch is a path from the root down to a leaf. In words: (T1) is the tree of a formula that was not built at all, a single node. (T2) puts a new root 
eg on top of an existing tree. (T3) joins two existing trees under a new root carrying the connective, keeping left and right apart, because (p 	o q) and (q 	o p) are different formulas. Parentheses do not appear in a parse tree: their only job in the string was to show the grouping, and the tree shows the grouping by its shape. Every formula has a parse tree. Take a formation sequence of the formula and build a tree for each entry in turn: an atom or  ot gets (T1), and an entry 
eg\chi_j or (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) gets (T2) or (T3) from the trees already built for the earlier entries. The tree built for the last entry is a parse tree for the formula. Could a formula have two different parse trees? That would happen if one string could be built in two different ways, as p \wedge q \vee r could if parentheses were not written. Section 3.2 proves that it never happens (the unique readability theorem); until then we say “a parse tree”. After that section, every formula has exactly one, and we speak of the parse tree. Subformulas and height Each node of a parse tree is the root of the part of the tree below it, and that part is itself a parse tree, built by the same clauses, for a formula. The formulas that arise in this way are the pieces a formula is built from. [Subformula] The subformulas of a formula \varphi are the formulas whose parse trees hang from the nodes of a parse tree for \varphi: for each node, the formula of which the part of the tree from that node downwards is a parse tree. The formulas at the children of the root are the immediate subformulas of \varphi. So the subformulas of \varphi include \varphi itself (at the root) and each atom that occurs in \varphi (at the leaves). A formula of the form

Replace each atom of a derivation by a formula, the same formula at every occurrence of the same atom, and all such replacements at once. The result is again a derivation. Here is why. First, each line becomes a formula. Replacing atoms by formulas in a formula \chi gives a formula: take a formation sequence of \chi, write in front of it a formation sequence of each formula put in for an atom, and replace the atoms inside the old entries. Each old entry that was an atom has become the last entry of one of the sequences written in front; each old entry built by (F2) or (F3) is now built by the same clause from the replaced versions of the same earlier entries. So the new list is a formation sequence, and its last entry is the replaced \chi. Second, each line is still justified. Each line of the old derivation was a premise, an assumption, a repetition, or an instance of a rule’s schema (@def-derivation, clauses (D1)–(D4)). Being an instance means: the line and the lines it cites are the schema with its metavariables replaced by certain formulas. The schema’s own symbols are connectives,  ot and parentheses, never atoms, so replacing atoms in the lines is the same as replacing atoms inside those certain formulas. The new lines are therefore the same schema with its metavariables replaced by the new formulas: an instance of the same rule. Third, nothing about citations changes. The line numbers, the boxes, and which line cites which are untouched, and whether a line or a box is available depends on nothing else (@def-derivation, the scope rule). eg q)). 2. Write the official formula for: p 	o q \vee r 	o 
eg p and 
eg p \wedge q \leftrightarrow r. (a) p \wedge q 	o r 	o p. The outer pair goes by rule 1; (p \wedge q) loses its pair because \wedge binds more tightly than 	o (rule 3); (r 	o p) loses its pair because 	o groups to the right (rule 4). 
eg(p \vee q) 	o 
eg p \wedge 
eg q. The outer pair goes; the pair around 
eg p \wedge 
eg q goes by rule 3. The pair after the first 
eg stays: without it, rule 2 would make the 
eg apply to p alone. (b) (p 	o ((q \vee r) 	o 
eg p)). Rule 3 groups q \vee r first; rule 4 then makes the first 	o the main connective, with conclusion ((q \vee r) 	o 
eg p). ((
eg p \wedge q) \leftrightarrow r). Rule 2 makes 
eg apply to p alone; rule 3 groups 
eg p \wedge q before \leftrightarrow. C. Going deeper [C1: Forgetting the grouping convention] Suppose we forgot rule 4 of the shorthand, so that p 	o q 	o r 	o s could stand for any official formula obtained by inserting parentheses into it. 1. List every official formula it could stand for, and draw the shape of each parse tree. 2. How many are there? Say how the count is found, by splitting at the main connective. 3. Which of them is the one rule 4 chooses? [Hint 1] The main connective is one of the three arrows. Choose it first. [Hint 2] Write c_n for the number of groupings of a chain of n atoms, and find c_1, c_2 and c_3 first. (a) The main connective is one of the three arrows; what lies on each side is then grouped in every possible way. - Main connective the first arrow: p on the left, and q 	o r 	o s on the right, grouped in one of two ways. This gives (p 	o (q 	o (r 	o s))) and (p 	o ((q 	o r) 	o s)). - Main connective the second arrow: (p 	o q) on the left and (r 	o s) on the right, each grouped in one way. This gives ((p 	o q) 	o (r 	o s)). - Main connective the third arrow: p 	o q 	o r on the left, grouped in one of two ways, and s on the right. This gives ((p 	o (q 	o r)) 	o s) and (((p 	o q) 	o r) 	o s). Their parse trees have the root 	o in each case: in the first two, the leaf p on the left and a tree of height 3 on the right (a right-leaning chain, or a left-leaning one); in the third, two trees of height 2 side by side; in the last two, a tree of height 3 on the left and the leaf s on the right. (b) There are 5. Write c_n for the number of groupings of a chain of n atoms joined by one binary connective. A chain of one or two atoms has one grouping: c_1 = c_2 = 1. For three atoms the main connective is the first or the second arrow, and the side with two atoms has one grouping: c_3 = c_1 c_2 + c_2 c_1 = 2. For four atoms, choosing the main connective splits the chain into a left part of k atoms and a right part of 4 - k atoms, for k = 1, 2, 3, and the two parts are grouped independently: c_4 = c_1 c_3 + c_2 c_2 + c_3 c_1 = 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 . The three terms are the three bullets of (a). (c) Rule 4 groups to the right, so the main connective is the first arrow and its right side is grouped to the right again: (p 	o (q 	o (r 	o s))), the first formula of the list. The numbers 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, \dots produced by this splitting are the Catalan numbers; they grow quickly: a chain of eleven atoms joined by ten connectives already has 16{,}796 readings. Parentheses, or a fixed convention, are not pedantry.

title: 3.2 Induction on Numbers and on Formulas
content:
Induction on Numbers and on Formulas Section 3.1 made formulas into objects: strings built from atoms and  ot by five clauses, and by nothing else. There are infinitely many of them, and the theorems this chapter is heading for are about all of them. This section supplies the tool for proving anything about infinitely many objects at once. It is induction, first on the natural numbers, where it is familiar, then on formulas, where it takes the form this chapter uses again and again. With it we prove that every formula can be read in only one way, and that a definition given one clause per connective defines exactly one thing. One argument for infinitely many cases Here is a claim about every formula: every formula has as many left parentheses as right ones. It is believable. The clause (F3) of @def-formula adds one of each, and the other clauses add none. But the claim is about infinitely many strings, and checking them one by one never ends. The belief already contains the shape of a proof. Every formula is reached by finitely many building steps from atoms and  ot (clause (F4)). The starting pieces have no parentheses, so they have equally many of each kind. Each building step turns formulas that balance into a formula that balances. So, step by step along any formation sequence, balance is never lost, and every formula balances. Exactly the same shape appears with numbers. To show that some property holds for every natural number, show that it holds for 0, and that it passes from each number to the next. Every natural number is reached from 0 by finitely many steps of “add one”, so the property is never lost. This is induction. We state it for numbers first, because it is simpler there, then prove the version for formulas from it. Two words about language before we start. Statements such as “for every n \in 
N, …” and “there is a k with …” are used in this section in their everyday sense, as Chapters 1 and 2 used them. Their rules of proof are the subject of Chapter 4, and nothing here needs more than the everyday reading. Likewise, a “collection” of formulas or numbers is meant in its everyday sense; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 treats sets properly. As in the rest of the book, 
N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} starts at 0, and the arithmetic and order of the natural numbers are used as school facts. The principle of induction A property of natural numbers is an open sentence P(n) about a natural number n, such as “n^2 \ge n” or “2^n > n”: for each particular n it becomes a statement, true or false (compare the open sentence x > 2 of @exm-statements, which became a statement once x was fixed). If a property holds for 0, and passes from each number to the next, then it holds for every number. [Principle of Induction] Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that 1. P(0) holds, and 2. for every n \in 
N, if P(n) holds, then P(n + 1) holds. Then P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. In symbols (the quantifier symbols are Chapter 4’s; here they abbreviate the words): \Bigl( P(0) \ \wedge \  orall n \in 
N \  igl( P(n) 	o P(n + 1)  igr) \Bigr) \ 	o \  orall n \in 
N \ P(n) . In words: hypothesis (i) is the base case. Hypothesis (ii) is the inductive step, and inside it, the assumption “P(n) holds” is the induction hypothesis. The step is one implication, proved once, for a number n about which we assume nothing except that it is a natural number with P(n). The conclusion is about every natural number at once. Its status. We take @ax-induction as a basic property of 
N, given and not proved, in the same way that Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes the least upper bound axiom as a basic property of 
R. It is, in a precise sense, what the three dots in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} mean: the natural numbers are what we reach from 0 by adding one, again and again, and nothing else. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 proves that it is equivalent to the well-ordering principle (every nonempty collection of natural numbers has a least element), and the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 derives it from the axioms of set theory. Nothing in this book depends on those two routes; every later use cites this principle. Dominoes. The usual picture is a row of dominoes, one for each natural number. The base case knocks over the first. The inductive step says that each domino, if it falls, knocks over the next. Then every domino falls. The picture carries the one point that matters: the step must work for every n, the first transition from 0 to 1 included. A single domino standing too far from the next stops the whole row, however well the others are placed. Not an infinite derivation. From P(0) and the step we could derive P(1) by ulename{{	o}E}, then P(2), and so on; each single P(n) has a finite derivation, n lines long or so. But no finite derivation contains all of them, and “and so on” is not a rule. The principle of induction is what licenses the passage, in one step, from the two hypotheses to “for every n”. It is a rule about 
N, not a rule of logic. The step as a box. In the language of Chapter 1, the inductive step is proved by a ulename{{	o}I} box. We fix a natural number n, knowing nothing about it except what the step allows, and open a box assuming P(n); inside the box we reach P(n + 1); closing the box gives the implication. The passage from “this n was arbitrary” to “for every n” is a rule for “for every”, and Chapter 4 states it. For now, “let n \in 
N” means what Chapter 1 made it mean (Section 1.1): one fixed number, not further specified. Starting from another number. Often a property is claimed only from some b \in 
N on, as in “for every n \ge 1”. Then it suffices to prove P(b), and, for every n \in 
N with n \ge b, that P(n) implies P(n + 1). Indeed, apply @ax-induction to the property Q(m): “P(b + m) holds”. Its base case Q(0) is P(b), and its step from Q(m) to Q(m + 1) is the step from P(b + m) to P(b + m + 1), where b + m \ge b. So Q(m) holds for every m \in 
N, and every natural number n \ge b is b + m for the natural number m = n - b. We call this induction started at b; it is @ax-induction applied to Q. Here is the first proof by induction, with every part labeled. [A sum of products of neighbors] Prove that for every natural number n \ge 1, 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + \dots + n(n + 1) =  rac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3} . Let P(n) be the displayed equation. Its left side is the sum of the n terms k(k + 1) for k = 1, \dots, n, so the left side for n + 1 is the left side for n plus the one new term (n + 1)(n + 2). Before proving anything, test small cases. For n = 1, 2, 3 the left side is 2, 2 + 6 = 8 and 8 + 12 = 20, and the right side is  rac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3} = 2,  rac{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4}{3} = 8 and  rac{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5}{3} = 20. The claim is plausible. It starts at n = 1, so we use induction started at 1 (see above). Base case. For n = 1 the left side is the single term 1 \cdot 2 = 2, and the right side is  rac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3} = 2. So P(1) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1, and suppose P(n) holds (the induction hypothesis). Then  egin{aligned} 1 \cdot 2 + \dots + n(n + 1) + (n + 1)(n + 2) &=  rac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3} + (n + 1)(n + 2) \ &=  rac{(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3)}{3} , \end{aligned} where the first equality is the induction hypothesis and the second takes out the common factor (n + 1)(n + 2), leaving  rac{n}{3} + 1 =  rac{n + 3}{3}. The last expression is the right side of P(n + 1). So P(n) implies P(n + 1). Conclusion. By @ax-induction, started at 1, P(n) holds for every natural number n \ge 1. Notice where the induction hypothesis entered: exactly once, to replace the sum of the first n terms by a closed expression. A proof by induction that never uses its induction hypothesis is either not an induction or is hiding a gap. The inductive step of an inequality usually has a second ingredient besides the hypothesis: a crude estimate that finishes the job. [An inequality by induction] Prove that 3^n \ge 2n + 1 for every n \in 
N. Let P(n) be “3^n \ge 2n + 1”. Base case. 3^0 = 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1, so P(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose 3^n \ge 2n + 1. Then 3^{n + 1} = 3 \cdot 3^n \ge 3(2n + 1) = 6n + 3 \ge 2n + 3 = 2(n + 1) + 1 , where the first inequality multiplies the induction hypothesis by the positive number 3, and the second uses 6n \ge 2n, true because n \ge 0. So P(n + 1) holds. Conclusion. By @ax-induction, 3^n \ge 2n + 1 for every n \in 
N. The estimate 6n + 3 \ge 2n + 3 throws away a great deal. That is typical: the step needs only to reach P(n + 1), not to reach it tightly, and a generous estimate that is obviously true is better than a sharp one that needs its own proof. The inductive step must hold for every n, including the first transition. Try to prove “2^n \ge n^2 for every n \in 
N”: the base case 1 \ge 0 holds, and the step 2^{n + 1} = 2 \cdot 2^n \ge 2n^2 \ge (n + 1)^2 looks fine, but its last inequality holds only for n \ge 3, so the steps from 0 to 1, from 1 to 2 and from 2 to 3 are not covered. The claim survives the first two gaps (at n = 1, 2 \ge 1, and at n = 2 both sides are 4), but it is false at n = 3, where 2^3 = 8 < 9 = 3^2; it is true again from n = 4 on. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 shows a famous “proof” that fails in the same way at its very first step, from 1 to 2. Strong induction Sometimes the step from n to n + 1 is the wrong shape. The immediate parts of a formula (\varphi \circ \psi) are shorter than it, but not by exactly one symbol; a natural number may be best understood through a smaller one that is not its predecessor. In such cases we want to assume the property not just for n, but for every smaller number. If a property holds for n whenever it holds for all smaller numbers, then it holds for every number. Strong Induction Let P(n) be a property of natural numbers. Suppose that for every n \in 
N: if P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n, then P(n) holds. Then P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. This form is also called course-of-values induction: the hypothesis may use the whole course of values P(0), \dots, P(n - 1), not just the last one. Its induction hypothesis is stronger (we assume more), so its step is easier to prove; the theorem says we lose nothing by it. There seems to be no base case. There is one, hidden. For n = 0, the hypothesis says: if P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0, then P(0) holds. No natural number is less than 0, so “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0” is vacuously true: for each k \in 
N, the implication “if k < 0, then P(k)” has a false hypothesis, and an implication with a false hypothesis holds (@prp-vacuous-implication, 
eg P \vdash P 	o Q). So at n = 0 the hypothesis of the theorem hands us P(0) outright. In practice, the proof of the step usually treats small n separately, and that is where the base cases live. Strong induction is ordinary induction applied to a stronger property. Let Q(n) say “P(k) holds for every k \le n”. Then Q(n) is exactly the hypothesis the theorem needs at n + 1, since the numbers below n + 1 are those up to n; so the theorem’s hypothesis moves us from Q(n) to Q(n + 1). Ordinary induction on Q does the rest, and Q(n) contains P(n). Suppose the hypothesis of the theorem holds. For n \in 
N, let Q(n) be the property “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k \le n”. We prove Q(n) for every n by @ax-induction. Base case. No natural number is less than 0, so P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < 0, vacuously. By the hypothesis of the theorem at n = 0, P(0) holds. The only k \in 
N with k \le 0 is 0, so Q(0) holds. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose Q(n). The natural numbers k < n + 1 are exactly those with k \le n, since no natural number lies strictly between n and n + 1. So Q(n) says that P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n + 1, and the hypothesis of the theorem at n + 1 gives P(n + 1). A natural number k \le n + 1 satisfies k \le n or k = n + 1, and P(k) holds in both cases. Hence Q(n + 1). By @ax-induction, Q(n) holds for every n \in 
N. Given n \in 
N, Q(n) applied to k = n gives P(n). This proves the theorem. In the proof of @thm-strong-induction, to which property is @ax-induction applied, and why is it not applied to P(n) itself? To Q(n): “P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k \le n”. Applied to P(n) itself, ordinary induction would give us only P(n) as induction hypothesis, while the hypothesis of the theorem at n + 1 asks for P(k) at every k \le n. The property Q carries exactly that information from one step to the next. The first use shows the typical shape: the step splits into a few small cases, handled directly, and a general case that reaches back further than one. [Threes and fives] Prove that every natural number n \ge 8 is a sum of threes and fives: n = 3a + 5b for some integers a, b \ge 0. Ordinary induction is awkward here. From n = 3a + 5b we cannot easily reach n + 1: we would have to trade some threes for fives or the other way round, and there may be none of the kind we want to trade. Going back three steps is easy instead: if n - 3 is a sum of threes and fives, add one more three. So we use strong induction. For n \in 
N, let P(n) be “if n \ge 8, then n = 3a + 5b for some integers a, b \ge 0”. Let n \in 
N, and suppose P(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < n. We show P(n). Case n < 8. Then the hypothesis “n \ge 8” of P(n) is false, and P(n) holds vacuously. Cases n = 8, 9, 10. Directly: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3 \cdot 3, 10 = 5 \cdot 2. Case n \ge 11. Let k = n - 3. Then k \ge 8, so k \in 
N, and k < n. By the induction hypothesis P(k), there are integers a, b \ge 0 with n - 3 = 3a + 5b. Then n = 3(a + 1) + 5b, with a + 1 \ge 0 and b \ge 0. In every case P(n) holds. By @thm-strong-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N: every n \ge 8 is a sum of threes and fives. The three direct cases are the base cases. They are needed because the general case reaches back three steps: for n = 8, 9, 10, the number n - 3 is 5, 6, 7, which is below 8, and there the induction hypothesis P(n - 3) is vacuous and gives us nothing. The bound 8 cannot be lowered: 7 is not a sum of threes and fives, since neither 7 nor 7 - 5 = 2 is a multiple of 3. Structural induction We return to formulas. The formation sequence of a formula plays the part that “0, 1, 2, \dots” plays for numbers: every formula is reached from atoms and  ot by finitely many uses of the clauses. So a property of formulas can be proved in the same two parts. A property of formulas is a statement P(\varphi) about a formula \varphi, true or false for each particular formula: “\varphi has as many left as right parentheses”, “\varphi contains the atom p”. If every atom and  ot has a property, and each way of building a formula passes the property from the parts to the whole, then every formula has it. Structural Induction Let P(\varphi) be a property of formulas. Suppose that 1. P(p) holds for every atom p, and P( ot) holds; 2. for every formula \varphi, if P(\varphi) holds, then P(
eg\varphi) holds; 3. for all formulas \varphi, \psi and each binary connective \circ, if P(\varphi) and P(\psi) hold, then P((\varphi \circ \psi)) holds. Then P(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. In words: (i) is the base case, one for each kind of formula of length one. (ii) and (iii) are the inductive steps, one for each building clause of @def-formula, and inside them “P(\varphi) and P(\psi)” is the induction hypothesis, assumed for the immediate parts of the formula being built. There are six cases in all when the four binary connectives are counted separately; often the four are handled at once, with \circ left unspecified. Take any formula and a formation sequence ending in it. Walk along the sequence: each entry is an atom or  ot, which has the property by (i), or is built from earlier entries, which have it already, by (ii) or (iii). “Earlier entries, any of them” is exactly the shape of strong induction, applied to the position in the list. Suppose (i)–(iii) hold, and let \chi be a formula. By @def-formula (F4) there is a formation sequence \chi_1, \dots, \chi_m with \chi_m = \chi. For i \in 
N, let Q(i) be the property “if 1 \le i \le m, then P(\chi_i) holds”. We prove Q(i) for every i \in 
N by @thm-strong-induction. Let i \in 
N, and suppose Q(k) holds for every k \in 
N with k < i. If i = 0 or i > m, then Q(i) holds vacuously. So let 1 \le i \le m. By the definition of a formation sequence, one of three things is true. - \chi_i is an atom or  ot. Then P(\chi_i) holds by (i). - \chi_i = 
eg\chi_j for some j < i. Then 1 \le j \le m, and Q(j) gives P(\chi_j). The entry \chi_j is a formula (every entry of a formation sequence is one, Section 3.1), so (ii) applies and gives P(\chi_i). - \chi_i = (\chi_j \circ \chi_l) for some j, l < i and a binary connective \circ. Then 1 \le j, l \le m, and Q(j) and Q(l) give P(\chi_j) and P(\chi_l), both entries are formulas, and (iii) gives P(\chi_i). So Q(i) holds. By @thm-strong-induction, Q(i) holds for every i \in 
N; in particular Q(m) gives P(\chi_m), that is, P(\chi). Since \chi was an arbitrary formula, this proves the theorem. The proof uses strong induction, because an entry of a formation sequence may be built from any earlier entries, not only from the one just before it. A tempting alternative is induction on the height of a formula: prove the property for all formulas of height 1, then for height h + 1 assuming it for smaller heights. That route is circular here. The height was defined through “the” parse tree (@def-height), and a formula has only one parse tree only because of the unique readability theorem below, whose proof uses structural induction. Inducting on the position in a formation sequence needs nothing but @def-formula. A structural induction must cover every clause, the base case  ot and the step for 
eg included. Try to prove “every formula contains an atom”: it holds for atoms, and the steps for 
eg and for (\varphi \circ \psi) keep it, since the atoms of the parts are atoms of the whole. But the case  ot fails, and so does the claim:  ot, 
eg ot and ( ot 	o  ot) contain no atom. A proof that “forgets”  ot proves something false. Which clause of @def-formula makes step (ii) of @thm-structural-induction necessary? Give a property of formulas that holds for every atom and for  ot, passes from \varphi and \psi to (\varphi \circ \psi) for every binary connective, and yet fails for some formula. Clause (F2), which builds 
eg\varphi from \varphi: step (ii) is the step for that clause. Without it, the formulas made by (F2) would be missed. One such property: “\varphi is an atom, or is  ot, or begins with (”. Atoms and  ot have it, and every formula (\varphi \circ \psi) begins with (, whatever its parts are. But 
eg p does not have it. So (i) and (iii) alone do not prove a property of every formula; the property fails exactly at a formula made by the forgotten clause. Counting parentheses Our first structural induction proves the claim this section began with, together with two refinements: one that the next theorem needs, and one that Exercise C1 uses. We count parentheses in strings, and for this some words about strings. An initial segment of a string s is the string of the first k symbols of s, for some k with 0 \le k \le the length of s. For k = 0 it is the empty string, with no symbols; for k equal to the length it is s itself. An initial segment is proper if it is shorter than s. The excess of a string s is \operatorname{ex}(s) \coloneqq (	ext{number of } ( 	ext{ in } s) - (	ext{number of } ) 	ext{ in } s) . So a left parenthesis has excess 1, a right parenthesis -1, and any other symbol 0; and the excess of a string written as two strings one after the other is the sum of their excesses, since the counts add. For example, \operatorname{ex}(\,(p \wedge (q\,) = 2: after reading (p \wedge (q we are inside two pairs of parentheses that have not yet closed. That is the picture to keep: the excess of an initial segment is the depth we are at when we have read that far. [Parenthesis Count] Let \chi be a formula. 1. \operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 0: \chi has as many left as right parentheses. 2. Every initial segment u of \chi has \operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 0. If moreover \chi has the form (\varphi \circ \psi) and u is proper and nonempty, then \operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 1. 3. For every occurrence of a binary connective in \chi, the initial segment of \chi that ends just before that occurrence has excess at least 1. In words: (a) is balance. (b) says that reading a formula from the left, we never close more parentheses than we have opened, and that inside a formula (\varphi \circ \psi) we stay at depth at least 1 until the very last symbol. (c) says that no binary connective lies outside all parentheses. Part (a) is the fact we set out to prove; (c), with (a), is what the unique readability theorem needs, and (b) shows that no proper initial segment of a formula is a formula (Exercise C1). The steps for (b) and (c) use (a) for the parts, so the three are proved together. Induction on the shape of a formula, all three parts at once. For 
eg\varphi, the extra 
eg changes no count. For (\varphi \circ \psi), list its initial segments by where they stop: before anything, inside \varphi, at the connective, inside \psi, at the end. Each is “(” followed by pieces whose excess the induction hypothesis controls. We prove, by @thm-structural-induction, that every formula \chi has the property P(\chi): “(a), (b), and (c) hold for \chi”. Atoms and  ot. The formula is one symbol, not a parenthesis. (a) Its excess is 0. (b) Its initial segments are the empty string and the formula itself, both of excess 0; and it does not have the form (\varphi \circ \psi), which has length at least 5. (c) It contains no binary connective. Negation. Let \varphi be a formula with P(\varphi); we show P(
eg\varphi). (a) \operatorname{ex}(
eg\varphi) = 0 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) = 0, by (a) for \varphi. (b) An initial segment of 
eg\varphi is either empty, of excess 0, or 
eg followed by an initial segment u' of \varphi, of excess \operatorname{ex}(u') \ge 0 by (b) for \varphi. The formula 
eg\varphi begins with 
eg, so it does not have the form (\varphi' \circ \psi'), and the second sentence of (b) says nothing about it. (c) A binary connective in 
eg\varphi lies in \varphi, and the initial segment of 
eg\varphi before it is 
eg followed by the initial segment of \varphi before it, whose excess is at least 1 by (c) for \varphi. Binary connectives. Let \varphi, \psi be formulas with P(\varphi) and P(\psi), let \circ be a binary connective, and let \chi = (\varphi \circ \psi). (a) \operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 1 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) + 0 + \operatorname{ex}(\psi) - 1 = 0, by (a) for \varphi and for \psi. (b) Every initial segment of \chi is of exactly one of the following five kinds, and its excess is as shown: - the empty string: excess 0; - ( followed by an initial segment u' of \varphi: excess 1 + \operatorname{ex}(u') \ge 1, by (b) for \varphi; - (\varphi\,\circ: excess 1 + \operatorname{ex}(\varphi) + 0 = 1, by (a) for \varphi; - (\varphi\,\circ followed by a nonempty initial segment v' of \psi: excess 1 + 0 + \operatorname{ex}(v') \ge 1, by (a) for \varphi and (b) for \psi; - \chi itself: excess 0, by (a) for \chi. All five have excess at least 0. The proper nonempty ones are those of the middle three kinds, and they have excess at least 1. (c) An occurrence of a binary connective in \chi is the connective \circ between \varphi and \psi, or lies in \varphi, or lies in \psi. Before \circ stands (\varphi, of excess 1. Before an occurrence in \varphi stands ( followed by the initial segment of \varphi before it, of excess at least 1 + 1 = 2 by (c) for \varphi. Before an occurrence in \psi stands (\varphi\,\circ followed by the initial segment of \psi before it, of excess at least 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 by (a) for \varphi and (c) for \psi. In all three cases the excess is at least 1. So P(\chi) holds. By @thm-structural-induction, every formula has the property P, which proves the lemma. The proof of (c) gave more than (c) states, and the next proof uses the extra.
