eg\wedge-formulas inside the property. [Hint 2] Let P(\varphi) be “if \varphi is a 
eg\wedge-formula, then \operatorname{nodes}(\varphi) > \operatorname{neg}(\varphi)”. The immediate parts of a 
eg\wedge-formula are 
eg\wedge-formulas. For a formula \varphi, let P(\varphi) be: “if \varphi is a 
eg\wedge-formula, then \operatorname{nodes}(\varphi) > \operatorname{neg}(\varphi)”. We prove P(\varphi) for every formula \varphi by @thm-structural-induction; for a 
eg\wedge-formula it is the claim. The immediate parts of a 
eg\wedge-formula are 
eg\wedge-formulas, since every symbol of a part is a symbol of the whole. Atoms. \operatorname{nodes}(p) = 1 > 0 = \operatorname{neg}(p).  ot, and the connectives \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow. The formulas  ot and (\varphi \circ \psi) with \circ one of \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow are not 
eg\wedge-formulas, so for them P holds vacuously, whatever the clauses chosen for them. Negation. Suppose P(\varphi), and let 
eg\varphi be a 
eg\wedge-formula. Then \varphi is one, so \operatorname{nodes}(\varphi) > \operatorname{neg}(\varphi) by P(\varphi), and adding 1 to both sides gives \operatorname{nodes}(
eg\varphi) > \operatorname{neg}(
eg\varphi). Conjunction. Suppose P(\varphi) and P(\psi), and let (\varphi \wedge \psi) be a 
eg\wedge-formula. Then \varphi and \psi are, so \operatorname{nodes}(\varphi) > \operatorname{neg}(\varphi) and \operatorname{nodes}(\psi) > \operatorname{neg}(\psi). Adding the two inequalities and then 1, \operatorname{nodes}((\varphi \wedge \psi)) = \operatorname{nodes}(\varphi) + \operatorname{nodes}(\psi) + 1 > \operatorname{neg}(\varphi) + \operatorname{neg}(\psi) = \operatorname{neg}((\varphi \wedge \psi)) . (Since the counts are integers, each hypothesis gives at least 1 to spare, so the left side exceeds the right by at least 3.) By @thm-structural-induction, P(\varphi) holds for every formula, which proves the claim. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states the property for every formula, in a form that covers exactly the 
eg\wedge-formulas, with the recursive counts. - 1: atom case. - 2: negation case, from the hypothesis for \varphi, after checking that \varphi is a 
eg\wedge-formula. - 3: conjunction case, using the hypotheses for both parts. - 2: names the induction principle and says why  ot and the other connectives are harmless (vacuous). Fatal errors (0 for the step): applying the hypothesis to the formula being proved; a conjunction case that uses one part only and says “similarly” for the other.

title: 3.3 Valuations and Truth Tables
content:
Valuations and Truth Tables Sections 3.1 and 3.2 made formulas into objects: every formula is built from atoms and  ot by the connectives in exactly one way, and so a function on formulas can be defined one clause per connective. So far a formula is only a string of symbols. It says nothing, and it is neither true nor false. This section gives formulas a meaning. We say what it takes to fix the truth or falsity of every atom, and then compute the truth value of every formula from the values of its atoms, one connective at a time. The result is the truth table, the second way of looking at a formula that Chapters 1 and 2 kept promising. Throughout, formulas are those of @def-formula, with atoms p, q, r, p_1, p_2, \dots, and we use Chapter 1’s shorthand for them (outer parentheses dropped, the usual precedence, 	o grouped to the right), as Section 3.1 allows. Reading a table off the rules Before any definition, a question. Suppose we want to call each statement true or false, and we want the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 to be safe: whenever the lines a rule cites are true, the line it writes is true. How must “true” behave for each connective? The rules answer almost completely. This subsection is motivation only; nothing later rests on it, and Section 3.6 makes it exact. Conjunction. Take statements \varphi and \psi. If both are true, ulename{\wedge I} writes \varphi \wedge \psi from them, so \varphi \wedge \psi must be true. If \varphi \wedge \psi is true, ulename{\wedge E} writes \varphi and writes \psi, so both must be true; turned around, if either of them is false, then \varphi \wedge \psi must be false. All four combinations of values are settled:  egin{array}{cc|c} \varphi & \psi & \varphi \wedge \psi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} Here \mathrm{T} stands for “true” and \mathrm{F} for “false”. Contradiction. The rule ulename{ ot E} writes any statement from  ot. If  ot were ever true, ulename{ ot E} would lead from a true line to every statement, false ones included. So  ot must be false, always. Negation. The rule ulename{
eg E} writes  ot from \varphi and 
eg\varphi. Since  ot is false, \varphi and 
eg\varphi are never both true: if \varphi is true, 
eg\varphi is false. And @prp-excluded-middle derives \varphi \vee 
eg\varphi from no premises at all, so at least one of the two is true: if \varphi is false, 
eg\varphi is true. Negation flips the value. Implication. The rule ulename{{	o}E} writes \psi from \varphi 	o \psi and \varphi. So in the combination “\varphi true, \psi false”, the implication cannot be true: that is the one row where \varphi 	o \psi is false. The other three rows are forced by derivations. @prp-vacuous-implication derives P 	o Q from 
eg P, so whenever P is false (and 
eg P therefore true), P 	o Q must be true, whatever Q is. And P 	o Q is derivable from Q alone (@exr-proving-an-implication-b2 (a) of Section 1.5): so whenever Q is true, P 	o Q must be true. That settles the rows with P false (by the first derivation) and the row with both true (by the second). The vacuous rows of 	o, “if P is false, then P 	o Q is true”, are often presented as a convention to be swallowed. Here they are forced by ulename{ ot E}, the rule that closes an impossible case, exactly as Section 2.1 said they would be. The rows of \vee and \leftrightarrow can be read off their rules in the same way, and Exercise C1 below asks for a sharper version of the argument for 	o. We now turn the answers into a definition. Valuations A formula such as p \wedge 
eg q cannot be true or false on its own, because p and q are atoms: letters with no content. What decides its value is a choice of which atoms are true. We need a word for one such choice. A valuation is one possible situation, described by saying which atoms are true and which are false. [Valuation] A valuation v assigns to every atom p exactly one of the two truth values \mathrm{T} and \mathrm{F}. We write v(p) for the value it assigns to p, and say that p is true under v if v(p) = \mathrm{T}, false under v if v(p) = \mathrm{F}. In words: a valuation answers, for each atom separately, the question “true or false?”, and it answers every such question. Two valuations are equal when they give every atom the same value. Nothing links the values of different atoms: v(p) and v(q) may be chosen freely, and that freedom is the whole point. Some valuations, simplest first. - The all-T valuation gives every atom the value \mathrm{T}; the all-F valuation gives every atom \mathrm{F}. They are the two extreme cases, and both will return as tests. - The valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{T}, v(q) = \mathrm{F} and v(r) = \mathrm{F} for every other atom r. This is the typical way to describe a valuation: give the values of the few atoms we care about, and fix the rest once and for all. - A valuation may treat infinitely many atoms differently: v(p_n) = \mathrm{T} for odd n and v(p_n) = \mathrm{F} for even n, with every other atom false. Formulas are finite, so no formula will ever see more than finitely many of these values. Making this precise is the job of the lemma in the next subsection but one. Nonexample. “p is true” and “p is false” together do not describe a valuation: the definition asks for exactly one value per atom. And a list that gives p the value \mathrm{T} and says nothing about the other atoms is not a valuation either, since it fails “every atom”. We never need more than such a partial list, but we complete it (by \mathrm{F}, say) so that the definition applies. The value of a formula A valuation fixes the atoms. The value of every other formula should then follow, computed from the values of its parts by the tables of the first subsection. Since formulas are built by the clauses of @def-formula, this is a definition by recursion. The value of a formula is computed from the bottom of its parse tree upwards, one connective at a time. [Truth Value of a Formula] Let v be a valuation. The truth value v(\varphi) of a formula \varphi under v is defined by recursion on \varphi: 1. for an atom p, v(p) is the value the valuation assigns to p; and v( ot) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}; 2. v(
eg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, and v(
eg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}; 3. v(\varphi \wedge \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}; otherwise \mathrm{F}; 4. v(\varphi \vee \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} or v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} (or both); otherwise \mathrm{F}; 5. v(\varphi 	o \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}; otherwise \mathrm{T}; 6. v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if v(\varphi) = v(\psi); otherwise \mathrm{F}. We say \varphi is true under v, or v makes \varphi true, if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}; otherwise \varphi is false under v. Clauses (V2)–(V6) say that the value of a compound formula depends only on the values of its immediate parts, and they are summed up in the tables of the five connectives:  egin{array}{c|c} \varphi & 
eg\varphi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} \qquad  egin{array}{cc|cccc} \varphi & \psi & \varphi \wedge \psi & \varphi \vee \psi & \varphi 	o \psi & \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} Read them clause by clause. (V1): an atom has the value the valuation gives it, and  ot is false under every valuation. (V2): negation flips. (V3): a conjunction needs both parts. (V4): a disjunction needs at least one part; “or” is inclusive, as the rule ulename{\vee I} of Section 1.6 already said, so the row with both parts true gives \mathrm{T}. (V5): an implication is false in exactly one case, a true hypothesis with a false conclusion. (V6): a biconditional says the two sides agree. The columns for 
eg, \wedge and 	o, and the value of  ot, are the ones the first subsection read off the rules. Section 3.6 proves that every row of every table is, in a precise sense, a derivable sequent. Well defined. Clause (V1) gives a value to every atom and to  ot, and each of (V2)–(V6) gives a rule computing the value of a compound formula from the values of its immediate parts. By @thm-structural-recursion, such clauses define exactly one function on all formulas. This is what Section 3.2 was for. Without unique readability a formula could be split into immediate parts in two ways, and the two splittings could give two values. The string p \wedge q \vee r, with no parentheses and no convention, shows the danger: its two readings are (p \wedge q) \vee r and p \wedge (q \vee r), and under a valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{F} and v(r) = \mathrm{T}, v igl( (p \wedge q) \vee r  igr) = \mathrm{T}, \qquad v igl( p \wedge (q \vee r)  igr) = \mathrm{F} . In the first, p \wedge q is \mathrm{F} and r is \mathrm{T}, so the disjunction is \mathrm{T}. In the second, q \vee r is \mathrm{T} but p is \mathrm{F}, so the conjunction is \mathrm{F}. A formula of @def-formula carries its parentheses, and has one value. [Computing a value] Let v be a valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{T} and v(r) = \mathrm{F}. Compute v(\varphi) for \varphi = (p \vee 
eg q) 	o (q \wedge r) . Work from the leaves of the parse tree up to its root, one node at a time, each time using one clause of @def-truth-value. List the subformulas so that each comes after its immediate parts: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Subformula Clause Value ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------ ------------------------------------ p, q, r (V1) \mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F} 
eg q (V2): v(q) = \mathrm{T} \mathrm{F} p \vee 
eg q (V4): both parts \mathrm{F} \mathrm{F} q \wedge r (V3): v(r) = \mathrm{F} \mathrm{F} (p \vee 
eg q) 	o (q \wedge r) (V5): the hypothesis is \mathrm{F} \mathrm{T} ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ So v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. The last step did not need the value of q \wedge r: a false hypothesis makes an implication true whatever its conclusion is. Computing by hand, one may stop a branch as soon as its value is decided. Nonexample. The rule “every formula gets the value \mathrm{T}” agrees with the all-T valuation on every atom, but it is not the truth value of @def-truth-value under any valuation. It breaks (V1) at  ot, and it breaks (V2) at 
eg p, where p and 
eg p would both be \mathrm{T}. The truth value under the all-T valuation is the function that (V1)–(V6) produce from it, and it makes 
eg p false. Values do not distribute over connectives the way symbols seem to. The value of 
eg(p \wedge q) is not computed by negating p and q and keeping the \wedge: under a valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{T} and v(q) = \mathrm{F}, the formula 
eg(p \wedge q) is \mathrm{T} (since p \wedge q is \mathrm{F}), while 
eg p \wedge 
eg q is \mathrm{F} (since 
eg p is \mathrm{F}). Always follow the parse tree: the main connective is applied last. Let v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{T}, v(r) = \mathrm{T}. What is v igl( (p \vee q) 	o 
eg r  igr)? \mathrm{F}. Bottom up: p \vee q is \mathrm{T}, by (V4), since q is \mathrm{T}; 
eg r is \mathrm{F}, by (V2); and an implication with a true hypothesis and a false conclusion is \mathrm{F}, by (V5). Only the atoms of a formula matter A valuation fixes infinitely many values, but a formula contains only finitely many atoms. We expect the value of a formula to depend only on the values of its own atoms. That is the fact that makes truth tables finite, and it is our first proof by structural induction about meaning. Recall from Section 3.2 that \atoms(\varphi), the set of atoms occurring in \varphi, is defined by recursion: \atoms(p) = \{ p \} for an atom p, \atoms( ot) is empty, \atoms(
eg\varphi) = \atoms(\varphi), and the atoms of \varphi \circ \psi, for each binary connective \circ, are those of \varphi together with those of \psi. Two valuations v and w agree on a set of atoms if v(p) = w(p) for every atom p in it. [Coincidence Lemma] Let \varphi be a formula, and let v and w be valuations that agree on \atoms(\varphi). Then v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). Structural induction on \varphi, with the property “for all valuations v, w that agree on the atoms of \varphi, v(\varphi) = w(\varphi)”. At an atom, the two valuations agree by hypothesis. At a compound formula, both values are computed by the same clause from the values of the immediate parts, and the parts have fewer atoms to disagree on, so the hypothesis for the parts applies. We apply @thm-structural-induction to the property C(\varphi): for all valuations v and w that agree on \atoms(\varphi), v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). Atoms. Let p be an atom and let v, w agree on \atoms(p) = \{ p \}. Then v(p) = w(p), which is C(p).  ot. By (V1), v( ot) = \mathrm{F} = w( ot) for all valuations v, w. So C( ot) holds. Negation. Assume C(\varphi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(
eg\varphi). Since \atoms(
eg\varphi) = \atoms(\varphi), they agree on \atoms(\varphi), so v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) by C(\varphi). By (V2), v(
eg\varphi) is determined by v(\varphi) and w(
eg\varphi) by w(\varphi) through the same rule, so v(
eg\varphi) = w(
eg\varphi). This proves C(
eg\varphi). Conjunction. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \wedge \psi). Every atom of \varphi is an atom of \varphi \wedge \psi, so v and w agree on \atoms(\varphi), and v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) by C(\varphi). In the same way v(\psi) = w(\psi) by C(\psi). By (V3), v(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, that is, exactly when w(\varphi) = w(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, that is, exactly when w(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T}. Hence v(\varphi \wedge \psi) = w(\varphi \wedge \psi), which is C(\varphi \wedge \psi). Disjunction. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \vee \psi). As in the previous case, v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V4), v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when one of v(\varphi), v(\psi) is \mathrm{T}, that is, when one of w(\varphi), w(\psi) is \mathrm{T}, that is, when w(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}. So C(\varphi \vee \psi). Implication. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi 	o \psi). Again v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V5), v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{F} exactly when v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and w(\psi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{F}. So C(\varphi 	o \psi). Biconditional. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let v, w agree on \atoms(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi). Again v(\varphi) = w(\varphi) and v(\psi) = w(\psi). By (V6), v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi), that is, when w(\varphi) = w(\psi), that is, when w(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \mathrm{T}. So C(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi). Every clause of @def-formula has been covered, so by @thm-structural-induction, C(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. This proves the lemma. The four binary cases are the same argument four times: the values of the parts agree, and one clause turns equal inputs into equal outputs. Here they are written out so that the pattern can be seen in full; later proofs write such a repeated case once, and say which cases it stands for. Two consequences. First, to know v(\varphi) we need only the values of v on the finitely many atoms of \varphi: if \varphi has n atoms, it has at most 2^n different “situations”, one for each way of giving its atoms the values \mathrm{T} and \mathrm{F}. (Each atom has two choices, and the choices are independent, so the number of ways doubles with each new atom: 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^n. This count is itself a small induction on n, by @ax-induction.) Second, the extra atoms a valuation happens to fix are irrelevant: two valuations that differ only on atoms not in \varphi give \varphi the same value. Let \varphi = p 	o (q \vee p). Two valuations v and w agree on p and q but disagree on r and on every p_n. What does @lem-coincidence say about v(\varphi) and w(\varphi)? Does it say anything about v(\varphi \wedge r) and w(\varphi \wedge r)? \atoms(\varphi) = \{ p, q \}, and v, w agree there, so v(\varphi) = w(\varphi). For \varphi \wedge r the atoms are p, q, r, and the valuations disagree on r, so the lemma does not apply. Indeed the values can differ: \varphi is true under every valuation (if p is true, so is q \vee p), so v(\varphi \wedge r) = v(r) and w(\varphi \wedge r) = w(r), which differ. Truth tables @lem-coincidence says that a formula’s value is decided by finitely many choices, and so it can be tabulated once and for all. A truth table lists the value of a formula in every possible situation, one row per way of giving its atoms values. [Truth Table] Let \varphi be a formula and let p_1, \dots, p_n be a list of distinct atoms that includes every atom of \varphi. A row is an assignment of a truth value to each of p_1, \dots, p_n. The truth table of \varphi (on p_1, \dots, p_n) lists, for each of the 2^n rows, the value v(\varphi) for a valuation v that agrees with the row on p_1, \dots, p_n. We say \varphi is true (or false) in the row. Well defined. Two things must be checked. Existence: every row comes from a valuation, for instance the one that gives p_1, \dots, p_n the row’s values and every other atom \mathrm{F}. Independence of the choice: two valuations that agree with the same row agree on p_1, \dots, p_n, hence on \atoms(\varphi), so by @lem-coincidence they give \varphi the same value. Without the lemma, “the value in a row” would not make sense, since a row says nothing about the infinitely many other atoms. The list p_1, \dots, p_n is allowed to contain atoms that do not occur in \varphi; then pairs of rows that differ only there show the same value. This freedom lets us compare several formulas in one table, over the atoms of all of them, and Section 3.4 does that constantly. When \varphi has no atoms at all, as 
eg ot or  ot 	o  ot do, the list may be empty, and the table has 2^0 = 1 row: such a formula has the same value under every valuation. Conventions. The atom columns come first. The rows are listed with \mathrm{T} before \mathrm{F}, the last atom alternating fastest: for two atoms, TT, TF, FT, FF. In practice we add a column for each subformula, building up to \varphi in the order of the parse tree, as in @exm-value-down-the-tree, but now for every row at once. [The truth table of modus ponens] Make the truth table of ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q on p, q, and read off from it what ulename{{	o}E} does. Columns for the two atoms, then for each subformula in turn:  egin{array}{cc|ccc} p & q & p 	o q & (p 	o q) \wedge p & ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The third column is (V5): \mathrm{F} only in the row TF. The fourth is (V3) applied to the third column and the p column: \mathrm{T} only in the first row. The last is (V5) again, with the fourth column as hypothesis and q as conclusion: the hypothesis is false in rows 2–4, so those rows are \mathrm{T}, and in row 1 the conclusion q is \mathrm{T}. So the formula is true in every row. Read as a statement about ulename{{	o}E}: the only row in which both given lines p 	o q and p are true is row 1, and in that row the line the rule writes, q, is true as well. The rule never leads from true lines to a false one, at least when its lines are atoms. Section 3.5 proves this for every rule and every formula. Now a table built column by column for a biconditional, whose two sides Chapter 2 related by derivations. [An implication and its contrapositive] Make the truth table of (p 	o q) \leftrightarrow (
eg q 	o 
eg p).  egin{array}{cc|ccccc} p & q & p 	o q & 
eg q & 
eg p & 
eg q 	o 
eg p & (p 	o q) \leftrightarrow (
eg q 	o 
eg p) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The columns p 	o q and 
eg q 	o 
eg p are identical: each is \mathrm{F} only in row 2. For 
eg q 	o 
eg p that is the row where the hypothesis 
eg q is \mathrm{T} and the conclusion 
eg p is \mathrm{F}, that is, q false and p true, which is the same row TF. So the biconditional is \mathrm{T} in every row. Compare Chapter 2. There @prp-contrapositive derived 
eg Q 	o 
eg P from P 	o Q with the rules for implication and negation, and @prp-contrapositive-converse derived the way back with a derivation that uses ulename{RAA}. The table sees no difference between the two directions; it only sees that the two columns agree. What a table can and cannot tell about derivations is the subject of Sections 3.5 and 3.6. A table with n atoms has 2^n rows, so three atoms give 8 and five give 32. Often we do not need all of them. [Working backwards from F] Find every row in which \varphi = (p 	o q) 	o  igl( p 	o (q \wedge r)  igr) is false: first with the full table on p, q, r, then without it. The full table.  egin{array}{ccc|cccc} p & q & r & p 	o q & q \wedge r & p 	o (q \wedge r) & (p 	o q) 	o (p 	o (q \wedge r)) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The formula is false in exactly one row, row 2: p and q true, r false. Backwards from F. An implication is false in exactly one way, by (V5): hypothesis true, conclusion false. Apply that to the main connective of \varphi, and then to whatever it forces. 1. \varphi is \mathrm{F} exactly when p 	o q is \mathrm{T} and p 	o (q \wedge r) is \mathrm{F}. 2. p 	o (q \wedge r) is \mathrm{F} exactly when p is \mathrm{T} and q \wedge r is \mathrm{F}. 3. With p true, p 	o q is \mathrm{T} exactly when q is \mathrm{T}. 4. With q true, q \wedge r is \mathrm{F} exactly when r is \mathrm{F}. Each step was forced, so there is exactly one row making \varphi false: p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{F}. Four short steps replace eight rows. The second method has a name in this book: working backwards from F. Assume the formula is false, and ask what each part is forced to be, starting from the main connective. Implications and disjunctions are false in only one way, and conjunctions are true in only one way, so they force values; a false conjunction, a true disjunction, or a true implication leaves a choice, and then we split into cases. If the forcing ends in a contradiction (some atom would need both values), the formula is false in no row. If it ends in a consistent assignment, that assignment is a row making the formula false, and the cases that were split give all such rows. A truth table sees only the connectives. Everything inside an atom is invisible to it. The statement “for every real x, if x > 2, then x^2 > 4” is true, but its propositional form, with the atoms a: “x > 2” and b: “x^2 > 4”, is a 	o b, which is false in the row with a true and b false. That row cannot happen for real numbers, and the reason lies in algebra, not in the connectives. Likewise “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N such that …” is a single atom for a truth table, with two rows and nothing to compute. Chapter 4 looks inside atoms. Why does @def-truth-table need @lem-coincidence? What would go wrong in a table for p \vee q if the value of p \vee q could depend on the atom r? A row gives values to the listed atoms only, and many valuations agree with it, differing on the other atoms. The table records “the” value of the formula in the row, so all those valuations must give the same value; @lem-coincidence guarantees it. If v(p \vee q) could depend on r, the row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{F} would contain valuations giving different values, and there would be no single entry to write. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Make the truth tables of 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) and of (p \vee q) 	o p. 2. Make the truth table of p \leftrightarrow 
eg p. Is it true in any row? 3. Compute the value of (p 	o  ot) \vee ( ot 	o p) under the all-F valuation, and under the all-T valuation. 4. How many rows has the truth table of a formula on the atoms p, q, r, s? 5. True or false, with a reason: if v(p) 
e w(p), then v(p 	o (q 	o p)) 
e w(p 	o (q 	o p)). (a)  egin{array}{cc|ccc} p & q & 
eg q & p \wedge 
eg q & 
eg(p \wedge 
eg q) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} \qquad  egin{array}{cc|cc} p & q & p \vee q & (p \vee q) 	o p \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The first formula has the same column as p 	o q: false only in row TF. (b) In the row p = \mathrm{T}, 
eg p is \mathrm{F}, and in the row p = \mathrm{F}, 
eg p is \mathrm{T}; the two sides always differ, so by (V6) the formula is \mathrm{F} in both rows. It is true in no row.  egin{array}{c|cc} p & 
eg p & p \leftrightarrow 
eg p \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} (c) The disjunct  ot 	o p has a false hypothesis, since v( ot) = \mathrm{F} under every valuation (V1), so it is \mathrm{T} by (V5), and the disjunction is \mathrm{T} by (V4). This holds under both valuations (and under every other). (d) 2^4 = 16. (e) False. The formula p 	o (q 	o p) is true under every valuation: if v(p) = \mathrm{F}, the hypothesis is false; if v(p) = \mathrm{T}, the conclusion q 	o p has a true conclusion. So v and w give it the value \mathrm{T} however they differ. @lem-coincidence says that agreement on the atoms forces agreement on the formula; it says nothing in the other direction. B. Practice [B1: Backwards from F] For each formula, work backwards from F to find every row on its atoms in which it is false, or show that there is none. 1.  igl( (p \vee q) \wedge ((p 	o r) \wedge (q 	o r))  igr) 	o r. 2.  igl( p 	o (q 	o r)  igr) 	o  igl( (p 	o q) 	o (p 	o r)  igr). 3.  igl( (p 	o r) \vee (q 	o r)  igr) 	o  igl( (p \vee q) 	o r  igr). 4.  igl( (p 	o q) \wedge (q 	o r)  igr) 	o (r 	o p). (a) Suppose the formula is \mathrm{F}. Then r is \mathrm{F}, and the hypothesis is \mathrm{T}, so each of p \vee q, p 	o r, q 	o r is \mathrm{T} (V3). With r false, p 	o r true forces p = \mathrm{F}, and q 	o r true forces q = \mathrm{F}. Then p \vee q is \mathrm{F}, a contradiction. So the formula is false in no row. It is the table’s version of proof by cases: if r follows from each of p and q, and one of them holds, then r holds. (b) Suppose it is \mathrm{F}. Then p 	o (q 	o r) is \mathrm{T} and (p 	o q) 	o (p 	o r) is \mathrm{F}; the latter forces p 	o q to be \mathrm{T} and p 	o r to be \mathrm{F}, and the last forces p = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{F}. Then p 	o q true with p true forces q = \mathrm{T}. Now p 	o (q 	o r) has a true hypothesis and the conclusion q 	o r, which is \mathrm{F} (true q, false r), so it is \mathrm{F}, a contradiction. False in no row. (c) Suppose it is \mathrm{F}. Then (p \vee q) 	o r is \mathrm{F}: r = \mathrm{F} and p \vee q is \mathrm{T}. And (p 	o r) \vee (q 	o r) is \mathrm{T}: with r false, p 	o r is \mathrm{T} exactly when p = \mathrm{F}, and q 	o r exactly when q = \mathrm{F}; so at least one of p, q is \mathrm{F}. Together with p \vee q true: exactly one of p, q is \mathrm{T}. This leaves a choice, so split. The formula is false in exactly two rows: p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}, r = \mathrm{F} and p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{F}. Check the first: q 	o r is \mathrm{T}, so the hypothesis is \mathrm{T}; p \vee q is \mathrm{T} and r is \mathrm{F}, so the conclusion is \mathrm{F}. (d) Suppose it is \mathrm{F}. Then r 	o p is \mathrm{F}: r = \mathrm{T}, p = \mathrm{F}. The hypothesis must be \mathrm{T}: p 	o q is \mathrm{T} because p is \mathrm{F}, and q 	o r is \mathrm{T} because r is \mathrm{T}, whatever q is. Nothing forces q. So the formula is false in exactly two rows: p = \mathrm{F}, r = \mathrm{T}, and q either value. [B2: Counting atoms, the last step blank] Call a formula binary-built if it is built from atoms by the four binary connectives only, so that neither 
eg nor  ot occurs in it; the immediate parts of a binary-built formula are again binary-built. Define by recursion (@thm-structural-recursion) the number \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) of atom occurrences and the number \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) of binary connectives:  egin{aligned} \mathrm{occ}(p) &= 1, & \mathrm{occ}(\varphi \circ \psi) &= \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) + \mathrm{occ}(\psi), \ \mathrm{bin}(p) &= 0, & \mathrm{bin}(\varphi \circ \psi) &= \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1, \end{aligned} for every atom p and every binary connective \circ. (For  ot and 
eg give both functions any values; they play no part below.) Here is a proof, by @thm-structural-induction, that every binary-built formula \varphi has \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) = \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + 1 . The property is C(\varphi): if \varphi is binary-built, then \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) = \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + 1.  ot and negation. Neither  ot nor a formula 
eg\varphi is binary-built, so C holds for them: its “if” is never met. Atoms. \mathrm{occ}(p) = 1 = 0 + 1 = \mathrm{bin}(p) + 1. Conjunction. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let \varphi \wedge \psi be binary-built. Then \varphi and \psi are binary-built, so  egin{aligned} \mathrm{occ}(\varphi \wedge \psi) &= \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) + \mathrm{occ}(\psi) =  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + 1  igr) +  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1  igr) \ &=  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1  igr) + 1 = \mathrm{bin}(\varphi \wedge \psi) + 1 . \end{aligned} Disjunction and biconditional. The computation is the same with \vee, and with \leftrightarrow, in place of \wedge. Implication. ______ Name the move, then complete it. The move is induction on the shape of a formula (@thm-structural-induction): the case for a compound formula uses the property for its immediate parts, and nothing else. Implication. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let \varphi 	o \psi be binary-built. Its immediate parts \varphi and \psi are binary-built, so \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) = \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + 1 and \mathrm{occ}(\psi) = \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1. Hence  egin{aligned} \mathrm{occ}(\varphi 	o \psi) &= \mathrm{occ}(\varphi) + \mathrm{occ}(\psi) =  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + 1  igr) +  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1  igr) \ &=  igl( \mathrm{bin}(\varphi) + \mathrm{bin}(\psi) + 1  igr) + 1 = \mathrm{bin}(\varphi 	o \psi) + 1 , \end{aligned} which is C(\varphi 	o \psi). All clauses of @def-formula are covered, so @thm-structural-induction gives C(\varphi) for every formula, and in particular the equation for every binary-built formula. For instance (p 	o q) \wedge (p \vee r) has four atom occurrences (p counted twice) and three binary connectives. [B3: A table for a named pattern] Make the truth table of  igl( (p \vee q) \wedge 
eg p  igr) 	o q, and say which derived rule of Chapter 2 it corresponds to, as @exm-truth-table-modus-ponens did for ulename{{	o}E}.  egin{array}{cc|cccc} p & q & p \vee q & 
eg p & (p \vee q) \wedge 
eg p & ((p \vee q) \wedge 
eg p) 	o q \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} True in every row. The only row in which both p \vee q and 
eg p are true is row 3, and there q is true. This is disjunctive syllogism, ulename{DS} (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism): from P \vee Q and 
eg P, infer Q. C. Going deeper [C1: The rows of implication are forced] Pretend we do not know the table of 	o. Say only that there is some table: a rule t giving a truth value t(a, b) for each pair of truth values a, b, with v(\varphi 	o \psi) = t igl( v(\varphi), v(\psi)  igr) for every valuation v and all formulas \varphi, \psi. (The other connectives keep their clauses.) Suppose the two rules for implication preserve truth in the following sense. - (E) For every valuation v and all formulas \varphi, \psi: if v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} and v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}. - (I) For every list of formulas \Gamma and all formulas \varphi, \psi: if every valuation that makes all of \Gamma and \varphi true makes \psi true, then every valuation that makes all of \Gamma true makes \varphi 	o \psi true. Prove that t is the table of (V5): t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{F}, and t(a, b) = \mathrm{T} for the other three pairs. [Hint 1] Each of the four values of t is one instance of (E) or of (I), with atoms for \varphi and \psi and a well-chosen valuation. [Hint 2] For t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{T}) and t(\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F}), try (I) with \Gamma empty and \varphi = \psi = p. Let p and q be distinct atoms. t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{F}. Take a valuation v with v(p) = \mathrm{T}, v(q) = \mathrm{F}. If t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) were \mathrm{T}, then v(p 	o q) = t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{T} and v(p) = \mathrm{T}, so (E) would give v(q) = \mathrm{T}, which is false. So t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{F}. t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{T}) = t(\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{T}. Apply (I) with \Gamma empty and \varphi = \psi = p. Its hypothesis, “every valuation making p true makes p true”, holds. So every valuation makes p 	o p true. A valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{T} gives t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{T}) = v(p 	o p) = \mathrm{T}, and one with v(p) = \mathrm{F} gives t(\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{T}. t(\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}) = \mathrm{T}. Apply (I) with \Gamma the list q, \varphi = p and \psi = q. Every valuation making q and p true makes q true, so every valuation making q true makes p 	o q true. A valuation with v(p) = \mathrm{F}, v(q) = \mathrm{T} makes q true, so t(\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}) = v(p 	o q) = \mathrm{T}. No step used a value of t that had not yet been found, since the formulas in \Gamma, \varphi and \psi contain no 	o. So the only table of 	o under which both rules preserve truth is the table of (V5). Conditions (E) and (I) are what Section 3.5 proves about the rules ulename{{	o}E} and ulename{{	o}I}; the exercise shows that nothing but the standard table could have passed. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: the row (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) from (E), with a valuation making p true and q false, and the argument by contradiction. - 3: the rows (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{T}) and (\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{F}) from (I), with the hypothesis of (I) checked, and a valuation for each value of p. - 3: the row (\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}) from (I) with a nonempty \Gamma (or any other correct instance), hypothesis checked. - 1: says why the argument is not circular (no 	o in the formulas used). Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the standard table of 	o to justify a value of t; an instance of (I) whose hypothesis is not checked. [C2: Find the error] Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Let v_{\mathrm{T}} be the all-T valuation. Every formula built from atoms by \wedge, \vee and 	o only is true under v_{\mathrm{T}}. Proof. By @thm-structural-induction, with the property “if \varphi is built from atoms by \wedge, \vee, 	o only, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}”. The formulas  ot, 
eg\varphi and \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi are not built in this way, so the property holds for them. If a formula built in this way is \varphi \wedge \psi, \varphi \vee \psi or \varphi 	o \psi, then \varphi and \psi are built in this way too, so the hypothesis applies to them. (1) For an atom p, v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{T} by the definition of v_{\mathrm{T}}. (2) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V3). (3) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V4), since at least one part is true. (4) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5), because v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} and an implication with a false hypothesis is true. This covers every clause, and proves the claim. 1. Is the claim true? 2. Name the line that fails and say exactly what is wrong with it. 3. Give a formula on which the reason given in that line is false. 4. Repair the line. (a) Yes. The claim is true, and the repaired proof in (d) proves it. So no formula is a counterexample to the claim; the error is in the argument only. (b) Line (4). Its hypothesis states v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, and its reason states v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}. The reason contradicts the induction hypothesis it is supposed to use: it quotes the vacuous row of (V5), which does not apply here. The conclusion v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} is correct, but not for the reason given. (c) p 	o q. Under v_{\mathrm{T}}, v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{T}, so the stated reason “v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{F}” is false, although v_{\mathrm{T}}(p 	o q) = \mathrm{T} holds. (d) (4) If v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} and v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, then v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5), because the conclusion \psi is true, so we are not in the one row (true hypothesis, false conclusion) where an implication is false. With this line the induction is correct, and the claim follows. Section 3.7 uses this fact to show that \wedge, \vee and 	o cannot express negation. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the claim is true (with the reason: the repaired proof). - 3: names line (4), and says its reason contradicts the hypothesis v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} of that very case. - 2: a formula, such as p 	o q, on which the stated reason fails. - 3: the repair, citing the row of (V5) that actually applies (conclusion true). Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the claim false; locating the error in line (3) (at least one part true is correct) or in the handling of  ot, 
eg, \leftrightarrow.

title: 3.4 Tautologies, Entailment and Equivalence
content:
Tautologies, Entailment and Equivalence Section 3.3 gave every formula a value under every valuation, and collected the values in a truth table. One formula at a time, though, is not what Chapters 1 and 2 were about. They were about sequents: premises on the left, a conclusion on the right, and the claim that the conclusion can be derived. This section defines the counterpart of a sequent in terms of truth, \Gamma \models \psi: every valuation that makes the premises true makes the conclusion true. On the way it names the formulas that are true in every row, and the pairs of formulas that are true in the same rows. It ends with two lemmas about changing a formula, by replacing one part or by putting formulas in for its atoms, that later sections use. Tautologies and contradictions Some tables of Section 3.3 had a last column made entirely of \mathrm{T}: the formula ((p 	o q) \wedge p) 	o q of @exm-truth-table-modus-ponens, and the biconditional of @exm-table-contrapositive. Their truth does not depend on the situation. One table in Exercise A1 there, that of p \leftrightarrow 
eg p, was all \mathrm{F}. These extremes deserve names. A tautology is true for reasons of form alone: whatever the atoms mean, it comes out true. [Tautology and Contradiction] A formula \varphi is a tautology if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} for every valuation v. It is a contradiction if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F} for every valuation v. By @lem-coincidence, the value of \varphi under a valuation depends only on the row the valuation gives to the atoms of \varphi. So \varphi is a tautology exactly when its truth table has \mathrm{T} in every row, and a contradiction exactly when it has \mathrm{F} in every row. Infinitely many valuations, finitely many rows to check. Examples, simplest first. - p 	o p and p \vee 
eg p are tautologies: in the row p = \mathrm{T} both are true, and in the row p = \mathrm{F}, p 	o p has a false hypothesis and 
eg p is true. - p \wedge 
eg p and p \leftrightarrow 
eg p are contradictions: in each row one of p, 
eg p is false, and the two sides of the biconditional differ. - A formula with no atoms, such as  ot or 
eg ot, has the same value under every valuation (its table has one row). So it is either a contradiction, like  ot, or a tautology, like 
eg ot. This degenerate case is the only one in which “not a tautology” forces “a contradiction”. - Nonexample. p 	o q is neither: it is \mathrm{T} in the row TT and \mathrm{F} in the row TF. Most formulas are like this. Changing one symbol of the tautology p 	o p, to get p 	o q, loses the property: the rows in which the hypothesis and conclusion differ are no longer excluded by their being the same atom. The formulas in between also need a word, and so do lists of formulas, because a list of premises can fail to be true together even when each premise alone can be true. [Satisfiable] A formula \varphi is satisfiable if there is a valuation v with v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. A list of formulas \Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, where n \ge 0, is satisfiable if there is a valuation that makes every \varphi_i true. A formula or list that is not satisfiable is unsatisfiable. In words: a formula is satisfiable if some row makes it true, and a list is satisfiable if some single row makes all its members true at once. So a formula is unsatisfiable exactly when it is a contradiction. The empty list (n = 0) is satisfiable: every valuation makes all of its members true, since it has none to check. The list p, 
eg p is unsatisfiable, although each of its members is satisfiable: a row making p true makes 
eg p false. Satisfiability of a list is about a common row, not about each formula separately. And the list p 	o q, \ q 	o r, \ r 	o 
eg p is satisfiable, by the row with p false and q, r true (the first two have true conclusions, and the third has conclusion 
eg p, which is true); in fact p is false in every row that makes all three true. Tautologies and unsatisfiable formulas are two sides of one coin. For every formula \psi, \psi 	ext{ is a tautology} \iff 
eg\psi 	ext{ is unsatisfiable.} Indeed, by (V2) of @def-truth-value, v(
eg\psi) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}. So “no valuation makes 
eg\psi true” says “no valuation makes \psi false”, which is “every valuation makes \psi true”. Section 3.7 uses this to turn a question about tautologies into one about satisfiability. “Not a tautology” does not mean “a contradiction”. The formula p 	o q is neither: some rows make it true and some false. To show a formula is not a tautology, one row making it false is enough; to show it is a contradiction, every row must make it false. Semantic entailment Now the counterpart of a sequent. A derivation from premises \Gamma to a conclusion \psi is a promise that \psi follows from \Gamma. In terms of truth, “follows” should mean: no situation makes the premises true and the conclusion false. We want to prove, in the next two sections, that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 derive exactly the sequents that pass this test; for that we need a precise name for the test. An argument is valid when its conclusion is true in every row in which all its premises are true. Semantic Entailment Let \Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n be a list of formulas, where n \ge 0, and let \psi be a formula. We say \Gamma semantically entails \psi, and write \Gamma \models \psi , if every valuation that makes all of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n true also makes \psi true. We then also call the argument from \Gamma to \psi valid. We write \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \models \psi for \Gamma \models \psi, and \models \psi when \Gamma is empty. If \Gamma \models \psi fails, we write \Gamma 
ot\models \psi, and a valuation that makes every formula of \Gamma true and \psi false is a refuting valuation, or refuting row. Clause by clause. “Every valuation”: the condition is checked in all situations, not in the actual one; a valid argument cannot be spoiled by what the atoms happen to mean. “That makes all of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n true”: rows in which some premise is false are ignored, whatever the conclusion does there. “Also makes \psi true”: in the remaining rows, the conclusion must hold. In symbols, for every valuation v,  igl( v(\varphi_1) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ and } \dots 	ext{ and } v(\varphi_n) = \mathrm{T}  igr) \ \Rightarrow \ v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} . And \Gamma 
ot\models \psi says: there is a valuation making every premise true and the conclusion false. One refuting row is enough. Checking it. And from @exm-affirming-the-consequent’s refuting row we learn something about all instances too, but only in one direction; the next warning says which. Substitution must be uniform: every occurrence of p_i is replaced by the same \varphi_i. Replacing only the first p of the tautology p 	o p by q gives q 	o p, which is false in the row q = \mathrm{T}, p = \mathrm{F}. And the lemma runs one way only. An instance can be a tautology when the pattern is not: p \vee q is not a tautology, but its instance with 
eg p put in for q is p \vee 
eg p, which is. So a refuting row for a pattern with atoms shows that the pattern is not valid, not that every instance fails. Two questions, side by side We now have two ways of saying that \psi follows from \Gamma. They were built from different materials, and it is worth setting them next to each other before the next two sections connect them. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- \Gamma \vdash \psi \Gamma \models \psi ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- What it says there is a derivation from premises in \Gamma to \psi every valuation making all of \Gamma true makes \psi true What it is about syntax: lines, rules, boxes meaning: truth values How to show it holds exhibit one derivation check every row (or work backwards from F) How to show it fails no method yet: a failed search proves nothing exhibit one refuting row Defined in @def-derivable (Section 1.2) @def-valid-argument (this section) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Look at the fourth row. To show that something is not derivable, we would have to survey infinitely many derivations; to show that something is not valid, one row suffices. And to show that something is valid takes a finite, mechanical check, while showing it derivable may need an idea. Each column is easy exactly where the other is hard. The next two sections prove that the two columns always give the same answer. Section 3.5 proves soundness: if \Gamma \vdash \psi, then \Gamma \models \psi; so a refuting row proves that no derivation exists, which answers the question Chapter 2 ended on. Section 3.6 proves completeness: if \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi; so a successful table check guarantees that a derivation exists, even before anyone has found it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Classify each formula as a tautology, a contradiction, or satisfiable but not a tautology: p 	o (q 	o p); p \wedge 
eg(p \vee q); (p 	o q) \wedge (q 	o p); 
eg(p 	o p); (p \wedge q) 	o (p \vee r). 2. For each, decide whether it holds, and give a refuting row if it does not: p \wedge q \models p \leftrightarrow q; p \leftrightarrow q \models p \wedge q; 
eg p 	o p \models p. 3. True or false, with a reason: if \Gamma \models \psi and \Gamma \models 
eg\psi, then \Gamma is unsatisfiable. 4. True or false, with a reason: p \vee q \models p or p \vee q \models q. (a) p 	o (q 	o p): a tautology (if p is \mathrm{T}, the conclusion q 	o p is \mathrm{T}; if p is \mathrm{F}, the hypothesis is false). p \wedge 
eg(p \vee q): a contradiction (if p is \mathrm{T}, so is p \vee q, and 
eg(p \vee q) is \mathrm{F}). (p 	o q) \wedge (q 	o p): satisfiable, not a tautology (\mathrm{T} in the row TT, \mathrm{F} in TF). 
eg(p 	o p): a contradiction, since p 	o p is a tautology. (p \wedge q) 	o (p \vee r): a tautology (if the hypothesis is \mathrm{T}, then p is \mathrm{T}, so is p \vee r). (b) p \wedge q \models p \leftrightarrow q holds: the only row making p \wedge q true has p = q = \mathrm{T}, where p \leftrightarrow q is true. p \leftrightarrow q \models p \wedge q fails: the row p = q = \mathrm{F} makes p \leftrightarrow q true and p \wedge q false. 
eg p 	o p \models p holds: in the row p = \mathrm{F}, the premise 
eg p 	o p has a true hypothesis and a false conclusion, so it is false; the only row making the premise true has p = \mathrm{T}. (c) True. If a valuation made all of \Gamma true, it would make both \psi and 
eg\psi true, which (V2) forbids. So no valuation makes all of \Gamma true. (d) False. The row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T} refutes p \vee q \models p, and the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F} refutes p \vee q \models q. Each disjunct fails in some row where the disjunction holds, although in every such row one of them holds: \models must work row by row with a single conclusion. B. Practice [B1: Valid or not] Decide whether each entailment holds, by a table or by working backwards from F. If it holds, also give a derivation of the corresponding sequent with \vdash in place of \models, using the rules of Chapters 1 and 2; if it fails, give a refuting row. 1. p 	o q, \ 
eg q \models 
eg p. 2. p 	o (q \vee r), \ 
eg q \models p 	o r. 3. p 	o q \models 
eg p 	o 
eg q. 4. p \vee q, \ p 	o r, \ q 	o r \models r. (a) Holds. Backwards from F: 
eg p false means p = \mathrm{T}; 
eg q true means q = \mathrm{F}; then p 	o q is \mathrm{F}, so no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false. A derivation, with modus tollens (@prp-modus-tollens) as a derived rule: (b) Holds. Backwards from F: p 	o r false means p = \mathrm{T}, r = \mathrm{F}; 
eg q true means q = \mathrm{F}; then q \vee r is \mathrm{F}, and p 	o (q \vee r) is \mathrm{F}, contradicting the first premise. A derivation, with disjunctive syllogism (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism), which refutes the left disjunct: (c) Fails. The row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{T} makes p 	o q true (false hypothesis) and 
eg p 	o 
eg q false (
eg p true, 
eg q false). It is the pattern of the Quick check, “denying the hypothesis”, in the form of an implication. (d) Holds. Backwards from F: r = \mathrm{F}; then p 	o r true forces p = \mathrm{F}, and q 	o r true forces q = \mathrm{F}; then p \vee q is \mathrm{F}, a contradiction. A derivation by cases: [B2: A biconditional as a disjunction] Show by a truth table that p \leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \wedge q) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q). Which theorem of this chapter will guarantee, without any search, that each side can be derived from the other?  egin{array}{cc|ccccc} p & q & p \leftrightarrow q & p \wedge q & 
eg p \wedge 
eg q & (p \wedge q) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \end{array} The columns of p \leftrightarrow q and of the disjunction agree in every row, so the two formulas are equivalent: each side entails the other. The theorem that turns each entailment into a derivation is completeness, in Section 3.6: if \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. So p \leftrightarrow q \vdash (p \wedge q) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q) and its converse are both derivable, before any derivation has been written. [B3: Entailment and implication] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \varphi, \psi formulas. Prove: 1. \varphi \models \psi if and only if \models \varphi 	o \psi; 2. \Gamma, \varphi \models \psi if and only if \Gamma \models \varphi 	o \psi. We prove (b); then (a) is (b) with \Gamma empty, since \Gamma, \varphi is then the one-formula list \varphi. (\Rightarrow) Suppose \Gamma, \varphi \models \psi, and let v make every formula of \Gamma true. If v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, then v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5). If v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then v makes every formula of the list \Gamma, \varphi true, so v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} by hypothesis, and again v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T}. So \Gamma \models \varphi 	o \psi. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \Gamma \models \varphi 	o \psi, and let v make every formula of \Gamma, \varphi true. Then v makes every formula of \Gamma true, so v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T}, and v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. By (V5), an implication with a true hypothesis is true only if its conclusion is, so v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}. So \Gamma, \varphi \models \psi. Part (b) is the table’s version of ulename{{	o}I} (the direction \Rightarrow) and of ulename{{	o}E} (the direction \Leftarrow). C. Going deeper [C1: Substitution with a new connective, the last half blank] Extend the formulas by a new binary connective \mathbin{|} (“not both”, often called NAND): add to @def-formula the clause “if \varphi and \psi are formulas, so is (\varphi \mathbin{|} \psi)”, and to @def-truth-value the clause (V7) v(\varphi \mathbin{|} \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if v(\varphi) = v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}; otherwise \mathrm{T}. Assume that structural induction and recursion work for the extended formulas as before, with one more clause. A substitution \sigma of \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n for p_1, \dots, p_n is defined by the clauses in the text, with \sigma(\chi \mathbin{|} 	heta) \coloneqq \sigma(\chi) \mathbin{|} \sigma(	heta) added. Prove that if \chi is a tautology of the extended language, so is \sigma(\chi). Here is the first half of a proof. Let v be a valuation, and let w be the valuation with w(p) \coloneqq v(\sigma(p)) for every atom p. We show v(\sigma(\chi)) = w(\chi) for every formula \chi of the extended language, by structural induction. Atoms: v(\sigma(p)) = w(p) is the definition of w. Name the move, then complete it. The move is induction on the shape of a formula, now with eight cases: atoms,  ot, 
eg, and five binary connectives. The property is C(\chi): v(\sigma(\chi)) = w(\chi).  ot. \sigma( ot) =  ot, so v(\sigma( ot)) = \mathrm{F} = w( ot) by (V1). Negation. Assume C(\chi). Then v(\sigma(
eg\chi)) = v(
eg\sigma(\chi)), which by (V2) is \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\sigma(\chi)) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\chi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(
eg\chi) = \mathrm{T}. The four old binary connectives. Assume C(\chi) and C(	heta), and let \circ be one of \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow. Then v(\sigma(\chi \circ 	heta)) = v(\sigma(\chi) \circ \sigma(	heta)) is computed by the clause for \circ from the two values v(\sigma(\chi)) = w(\chi) and v(\sigma(	heta)) = w(	heta); the same clause computes w(\chi \circ 	heta) from the same two values. So they are equal. The new connective. Assume C(\chi) and C(	heta). By (V7), v(\sigma(\chi \mathbin{|} 	heta)) = v(\sigma(\chi) \mathbin{|} \sigma(	heta)) is \mathrm{F} exactly when v(\sigma(\chi)) = v(\sigma(	heta)) = \mathrm{T}, that is, when w(\chi) = w(	heta) = \mathrm{T}, that is, when w(\chi \mathbin{|} 	heta) = \mathrm{F}. This covers every clause, so C(\chi) holds for every formula. Now let \chi be a tautology and v any valuation: v(\sigma(\chi)) = w(\chi) = \mathrm{T}. So \sigma(\chi) is a tautology. Only one case is new. The proof of @lem-substitution never looked at what the clauses say, only that each computes the value of a compound from the values of its parts; any connective defined by a table passes. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: names the move and states the property v(\sigma(\chi)) = w(\chi) for all \chi. - 1: the  ot case. - 2: the 
eg case, from the hypothesis for \chi. - 2: the old binary cases, using the hypotheses for both parts. - 3: the \mathbin{|} case, with (V7) and both hypotheses. - 1: the conclusion for tautologies. Fatal errors (0 for the step): omitting the \mathbin{|} case; using w where v is meant in the conclusion. [C2: Is equivalence preserved by substitution?] Let \sigma be a substitution and suppose \varphi \equiv \psi. Is \sigma(\varphi) \equiv \sigma(\psi)? Prove it, or give a counterexample. Then suppose that De Morgan’s law (b) of @prp-standard-equivalences had been checked only for atoms, 
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q, by its four-row table. Use your answer to deduce from this, in one line, that 
eg((r 	o s) \wedge 
eg t) \equiv 
eg(r 	o s) \vee 
eg
eg t. Yes. By the paraphrase of @def-semantic-equivalence, \varphi \equiv \psi means \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi. By @lem-substitution (a), \models \sigma(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi), and by the definition of \sigma, \sigma(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \sigma(\varphi) \leftrightarrow \sigma(\psi). So \models \sigma(\varphi) \leftrightarrow \sigma(\psi), that is, \sigma(\varphi) \equiv \sigma(\psi). (Alternatively, apply @lem-substitution (b) to \varphi \models \psi and to \psi \models \varphi.) For the instance: the substitution of r 	o s for p and 
eg t for q turns the two sides of 
eg(p \wedge q) \equiv 
eg p \vee 
eg q into 
eg((r 	o s) \wedge 
eg t) and 
eg(r 	o s) \vee 
eg
eg t, so these are equivalent by the first part. Checking a law for atoms, by one small table, is therefore enough. A tempting counterexample fails for a reason worth seeing. With \sigma putting 
eg p for q, the nonequivalent formulas p and 
eg q become the equivalent p and 
eg
eg p: substitution can create equivalences. It cannot destroy one, which is what the question asks. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: reduces \equiv to a tautology \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi, or to two entailments, citing the definition. - 3: applies @lem-substitution correctly. - 2: computes \sigma(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) = \sigma(\varphi) \leftrightarrow \sigma(\psi) from the definition of \sigma. - 2: the instance, with the substitution named. Fatal errors (0 for the step): answering “no” by a pair that is not equivalent before the substitution; using a nonuniform replacement.

title: 3.5 Soundness
content:
Soundness Chapter 2 ended on a question it could not answer. Section 2.6 searched for a derivation of P 	o Q \vdash Q 	o P, and every route came back to the same gap; but a search that fails proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist. The row that refutes affirming the consequent in Section 3.4, p = \mathrm{F} and q = \mathrm{T}, finds what the search could not: it makes p 	o q true and q 	o p false. This section proves the theorem that turns such a row into a proof that no derivation exists. It is called soundness: whatever the rules derive is true in every row where the premises are true. The proof is the book’s first long proof about proofs, and it is an induction on the lines of a derivation. What must be proved, and why it is not obvious Chapters 1 and 2 checked each rule as it arrived. ulename{\wedge I} is safe because two true statements make a true conjunction (Section 1.3); ulename{{	o}E} is safe because that is what “if … then” asserts (Section 1.4). Each time, the book said that Chapter 3 would prove it “for every rule at once”. Why is that more than collecting the separate checks? The first attempt at a proof is: go down a derivation, line by line, and show that each line is true in every row in which the premises are true. For a derivation without boxes this works. Each line is a premise, or comes from earlier lines by a rule, and the rule turns true lines into a true line. But it fails at the first box. Here is the derivation of @prp-contrapositive, written with atoms: Line 3 is p, and the row p = \mathrm{F}, q = \mathrm{F} makes the premise p 	o q true and line 3 false. Line 5 is  ot, which is false in every row. So the lines inside a box are not true in the rows where the premises are true, and the first attempt collapses. Yet the derivation is correct, and its last line 
eg q 	o 
eg p is true in every row making p 	o q true (@exm-table-contrapositive). What goes wrong is that a line inside a box is not claimed on the strength of the premises alone. Line 4 says: if p 	o q, 
eg q and p all hold, then q holds. That is a true claim about rows. Every line depends on the premises and on the assumptions of the boxes around it, and a correct statement about each line must mention both. Chapter 1 gave this list a name. Derivations of formulas From now on the lines of a derivation carry formulas in the sense of @def-formula, with atoms p, q, r, \dots. Nothing in the rules changes. Every rule was stated as a schema, whose letters \varphi, \psi, \chi stand for arbitrary statements (@def-rule-schema), so it applies to formulas as it stands, and @def-derivation and @def-derivable read the same with “formula” for “statement”. As Section 3.1 said, a derivation written with Chapter 2’s letters P, Q is a pattern, and reading its letters as atoms, or as any formulas, gives a derivation of formulas. Two conventions for the rest of the section. The primitive rules are those of Chapters 1 and 2 collected in Section 2.6: ulename{R}, ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{{	o}E}, ulename{\vee I}, ulename{\vee E}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{RAA}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. The box rules among them are the five that cite a box: ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{RAA}, ulename{\vee E} and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}. The other eight, ulename{R} included, cite only lines; we call them the one-step rules. A derivation may also use derived rules such as ulename{MT} and ulename{LEM}. A line citing one abbreviates a stretch of derivation in rules proved earlier, with the letters replaced by formulas (@def-derived-rule), and Section 2.3 showed how to write it out: repeat the cited lines, then paste the derivation of the derived rule below them. Every chain of derived rules ends in primitive rules. So whenever \Gamma \vdash \psi, there is also a derivation of \psi from premises in \Gamma that uses primitive rules only. That is the only kind of derivation the proof below has to consider. The context of a line Let a derivation have lines 1, \dots, n. We write \varphi_k for the formula on line k. Recall from Section 1.5, just after @def-derivation, that the context of line k is the list of the premises together with the assumptions of every box containing line k; we write it \Gamma_k. For lists of formulas \Delta and \Delta', we write \Delta \subseteq \Delta' when every formula of \Delta occurs in \Delta'. The context of a line is everything that line depends on: the premises, and every assumption still open where the line stands. In the derivation of @prp-contrapositive above, the boxes are \lines{2}{6} and \lines{3}{5}, and the contexts are: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Formula Boxes containing it Context ----------------- ------------------- ---------------------------- ------------------------ 1 p 	o q none p 	o q 2 
eg q \lines{2}{6} p 	o q, \ 
eg q 3, 4, 5 p, q,  ot \lines{2}{6}, \lines{3}{5} p 	o q, \ 
eg q, \ p 6 
eg p \lines{2}{6} p 	o q, \ 
eg q 7 
eg q 	o 
eg p none p 	o q ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Now look at each line through its context. Line 3 is one of the formulas in its own context, so every row making the context true makes line 3 true. Line 4: every row making p 	o q and p true makes q true. Line 5: no row makes p 	o q, 
eg q, and p all true (the first and third force q), so the context is unsatisfiable and it entails even  ot (Section 3.4). Line 6: every row making p 	o q and 
eg q true makes p false. Line 7: its context is the premise, and we know p 	o q \models 
eg q 	o 
eg p. So on this derivation, every line k satisfies \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k . This is the statement that survives the boxes, and it is the one we shall prove for every line of every derivation. Two facts about contexts, read off the scope rule, do the bookkeeping. The first says that citing an available line never involves an assumption the citing line does not have. The second says exactly what the context of a box’s last line is, when the box is cited by a box rule. [Contexts in a Derivation] Let lines i, k and a \le b belong to a derivation, and let \Gamma_j denote the context of line j. 1. If line i is available at line k, then \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k. 2. If line k is justified by a box rule citing the box whose first line is a and whose last line is b, then the formulas of \Gamma_b are exactly those of \Gamma_k together with \varphi_a, the assumption of that box. We write this \Gamma_b = \Gamma_k, \varphi_a. Both parts compare two sets of boxes, since contexts differ only in the assumptions of the boxes around a line. For (a), the scope rule says that the boxes around line i are among the boxes around line k. For (b), the boxes around line b should be the cited box itself and the boxes around line k; the danger is a further box inside the cited box that also ends on line b, and the box rules forbid exactly that. (a) The premises belong to every context. Any other formula of \Gamma_i is the assumption of a box containing line i. Since line i is available at line k, every box containing line i also contains line k, by the scope rule of @def-derivation. So that assumption belongs to \Gamma_k. (b) Let B be the box from line a to line b. Since line k cites B, the box B is available at line k. By the scope rule, it ends before line k, and the boxes containing B are exactly the boxes containing line k. We find the boxes containing line b. Every box containing line k contains B, and so contains line b; and B contains line b. Conversely, let C be a box containing line b. By @def-derivation, two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other; C and B share line b, so C = B, or C contains B, or C lies inside B. The last is impossible: then line b, the last line of B, would be a line of a box inside B, and every box rule requires the last line of its box to be a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it (@def-rules-implication, @def-rules-negation, @def-rule-raa, @def-rules-disjunction, @def-rules-biconditional). So C = B, or C is one of the boxes containing B, which are the boxes containing line k. Hence the boxes containing line b are B and the boxes containing line k. The assumption of B is \varphi_a, so \Gamma_b consists of the premises, the assumptions of the boxes containing line k, and \varphi_a, which is \Gamma_k together with \varphi_a. In the derivation of @prp-contrapositive, line 6 cites the box \lines{3}{5} by ulename{
eg I}, and \Gamma_5 = p 	o q, \ 
eg q, \ p is \Gamma_6 = p 	o q, \ 
eg q with the assumption p added, as (b) says. Line 5 cites lines 4 and 2, both available there, and \Gamma_4 and \Gamma_2 are contained in \Gamma_5, as (a) says. Part (b) needs the box to be cited by a box rule. @def-derivation allows a box to end on the same line as a box inside it, and then its last line has a larger context. In the derivation below, the box \lines{2}{4} is available at line 5, but \Gamma_4 = p, \ q, \ r contains r, the assumption of the inner box, as well as q. No box rule may cite \lines{2}{4}: its last line lies inside the box \lines{3}{4}, not in \lines{2}{4} itself. (This is why the derivation of @exm-disjunction-regroup needs its line 11.) In the derivation of @prp-contrapositive above, which case of the soundness claim handles line 5? Which lines’ contexts are involved, and why does \Gamma_5 \models  ot hold? Line 5 is  ot, by ulename{
eg E} citing lines 4 and 2: a one-step rule. Lines 4 and 2 are available at line 5, so by @lem-context-inclusion (a), \Gamma_4 = p 	o q, \ 
eg q, \ p and \Gamma_2 = p 	o q, \ 
eg q are contained in \Gamma_5 = p 	o q, \ 
eg q, \ p. The claim for the earlier lines gives \Gamma_4 \models q and \Gamma_2 \models 
eg q. So a valuation making \Gamma_5 true would make both q and 
eg q true, which clause (V2) of @def-truth-value forbids. No valuation makes \Gamma_5 true, and \Gamma_5 \models  ot holds because there is no row to check. The soundness theorem We can now state the theorem that Chapters 1 and 2 kept pointing to. Soundness Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If \Gamma \vdash \psi, then \Gamma \models \psi. Try it first (ten minutes): suppose line k is \varphi 	o \psi, by ulename{{	o}I} from a box that opens with \varphi and ends with \psi. Suppose you already know that every row making the context of line k and \varphi true makes \psi true. Why is \varphi 	o \psi true in every row making the context of line k true? What happens in the rows where \varphi is false? An attempt at the ulename{{	o}I} case runs into two things. First, knowledge about the box’s last line is knowledge about rows making its own context true, which contains the assumption \varphi; that is why the claim must carry contexts, and why @lem-context-inclusion (b) is needed. Second, the rows in which \varphi is false are not covered by the box at all, and they need nothing: there \varphi 	o \psi is true by (V5). The same two moves handle every box rule. The Step roadmap: ① Prove the stronger claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every line k of a derivation in primitive rules. ② Use strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction): a rule may cite any earlier line, not only the line just above, so the hypothesis must be available for all earlier lines at once. ③ Split on how line k is justified. A premise or an assumption belongs to its own context. A one-step rule: apply the hypothesis to the cited lines, move their contexts into \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), and use one clause of @def-truth-value. A box rule: apply the hypothesis to each box’s last line, whose context is \Gamma_k plus the box’s assumption by @lem-context-inclusion (b), and argue about the rows where that assumption is true or false. ④ The last line lies in no box, so its context is the premises, all in \Gamma; adding the other formulas of \Gamma keeps the entailment. Before reading on: in the case of ulename{RAA} (Claim 3 below), where does the proof use that v(
eg\varphi) is \mathrm{F} exactly when v(\varphi) is \mathrm{T}, and which half of that fact does it use? Step 1 (reduction to primitive rules). Suppose \Gamma \vdash \psi. As shown in the subsection on derivations of formulas, there is a derivation of \psi whose premises all belong to \Gamma and which uses primitive rules only. Fix one, with lines 1, \dots, n; let \varphi_k be the formula on line k and \Gamma_k its context. Step 2 (the induction). For k \in 
N, let S(k) be the statement: if 1 \le k \le n, then \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k. We prove S(k) for every k by @thm-strong-induction. So let k \in 
N, and assume S(j) for every j < k. If k = 0 or k > n, there is nothing to prove, so let 1 \le k \le n. Every line and every box that line k cites is available at line k, and so lies before line k (@def-derivation). Hence the induction hypothesis \Gamma_j \models \varphi_j holds for every line j that line k cites, and for the last line of every box it cites. Let v be a valuation that makes every formula of \Gamma_k true. We show v(\varphi_k) = \mathrm{T}; since v is arbitrary, this proves \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k. By @def-derivation, line k is a premise, an assumption, or the conclusion of one primitive rule, and the three claims below treat these cases. Step 3 (the cases). If line k is a premise or an assumption, then v(\varphi_k) = \mathrm{T}. A premise belongs to every context. An assumption opens a box, that box contains line k, and so its assumption \varphi_k belongs to \Gamma_k. In both cases \varphi_k is one of the formulas that v makes true.
