So any order is admissible in which (iii) comes before (v), (viii), and (iv); (vii) and (i) come before (viii) and (iv); (v) comes before (ii); and (viii) and (iv) come before (ii). For instance (vii), (i), (iii), (v), (iv), (viii), (ii) is also admissible: (vii) and (i) do not mention v, and the two cases may be taken in either order. Line (vi) applies the induction hypothesis to line k itself. The hypothesis of @thm-strong-induction covers only the lines j < k; (vi) assumes what is to be proved. Line (ix) uses the context of the citing line for the box’s last line. It is false: line b lies inside the box, whose assumption \varphi is part of its context, so \Gamma_b = \Gamma_k, \varphi, not \Gamma_k. In the derivation of @exm-soundness-run, line 3 has context p \vee q, \ p, while line 6 has context p \vee q, and p \vee q \models q \vee p could not be read off from line 3 directly. C. Going deeper [C1: A safe rule and an unsafe one] 1. Add to the primitive rules a one-step rule \mathsf{X}: from a line \varphi \wedge \psi, infer \varphi \vee \psi. Show that @thm-soundness still holds for derivations that may use \mathsf{X}. 2. Add instead a one-step rule \mathsf{Y}: from a line \varphi \vee \psi, infer \varphi \wedge \psi. Show that soundness fails: name the case of the proof that breaks, give a derivation using \mathsf{Y} of a sequent with a refuting row, and give the row. [Hint 1] The proof of @thm-soundness treats one rule per case. Adding a rule adds one case to Claim 2 and changes nothing else. [Hint 2] For (b), start a derivation from the premise p, and look for a way to write p \vee q first. (a) The proof of @thm-soundness goes through with one more case in Claim 2. Every other part is unchanged: Step 1 and Step 4 do not look at the rules, @lem-context-inclusion (a) holds for any cited line, and (b) concerns only box rules, and \mathsf{X} is not one. The case \mathsf{X}. Line k is \varphi \vee \psi, citing a line i holding \varphi \wedge \psi. By (\ast), v(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T}, so v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} by (V3), and v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V4). So every line of a derivation with \mathsf{X} still satisfies \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k, and soundness holds. (b) The new case of Claim 2 fails: from v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}, (V4) gives only that one disjunct is true, and (V3) needs both. With \mathsf{Y}, this is a derivation of p \vdash q: The row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F} makes the premise true and the conclusion false, so p 
ot\models q, although p \vdash q with \mathsf{Y}. The failure is at line 3: its context is p, and the row makes p and line 2 true but line 3 false. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) says that only one case is added, and why the rest of the proof (Steps 1 and 4, @lem-context-inclusion) is unaffected. - 3: (a) the case for \mathsf{X}, using the hypothesis for the cited line through @lem-context-inclusion (a) and the clauses (V3), (V4). - 2: (b) names the failing case, with the reason (one true disjunct does not give a true conjunction). - 3: (b) a correct derivation with \mathsf{Y} and a refuting row for its sequent. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “refuting row” that makes a premise false; in (a), checking \mathsf{X} only on atoms without the context argument. [C2: Exit check: soundness] Close the section first, and write from memory. Write out, in full, the ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{
eg I} and ulename{\vee E} cases of the proof of @thm-soundness: state the claim being proved for every line, set up the induction, and prove the three cases, naming the reason for each step. The claim. Fix a derivation in primitive rules with lines 1, \dots, n, and write \varphi_k for the formula on line k and \Gamma_k for its context (@def-derivation). We prove \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every k with 1 \le k \le n, by @thm-strong-induction applied to “if 1 \le k \le n, then \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k” (for k = 0 it holds vacuously): fix k with 1 \le k \le n, assume \Gamma_j \models \varphi_j for every line j < k, and let v be a valuation making every formula of \Gamma_k true. Every line and box that line k cites lies before line k, so the hypothesis applies to the cited lines and to the last lines of the cited boxes. We show v(\varphi_k) = \mathrm{T}. ulename{{	o}I}. Line k is \varphi 	o \psi, citing the box from line a (the assumption \varphi) to line b (the formula \psi). By @lem-context-inclusion (b), \Gamma_b = \Gamma_k, \varphi. Since b < k, the hypothesis gives \Gamma_k, \varphi \models \psi. If v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, then v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5). If v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then v makes every formula of \Gamma_k, \varphi true, so v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, and v(\varphi 	o \psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V5). ulename{
eg I}. Line k is 
eg\varphi, citing the box from line a (the assumption \varphi) to line b (the formula  ot). By @lem-context-inclusion (b) and the hypothesis for line b, \Gamma_k, \varphi \models  ot. Since v( ot) = \mathrm{F} under every valuation (V1), no valuation makes all of \Gamma_k, \varphi true. As v makes \Gamma_k true, v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, so v(
eg\varphi) = \mathrm{T} by (V2). ulename{\vee E}. Line k is \chi, citing line i (holding \varphi \vee \psi) and the boxes from a to b (\varphi to \chi) and from c to d (\psi to \chi). Line i is available at line k, so \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a); v makes \Gamma_i true, and the hypothesis for line i gives v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}, so v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} or v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} by (V4). By @lem-context-inclusion (b), \Gamma_b = \Gamma_k, \varphi and \Gamma_d = \Gamma_k, \psi, and the hypothesis for lines b and d gives \Gamma_k, \varphi \models \chi and \Gamma_k, \psi \models \chi. If v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then v makes \Gamma_k, \varphi true, so v(\chi) = \mathrm{T}; if v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}, likewise by the second box. Conclusion. With the other cases, the induction gives \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every line. The last line lies in no box, so its context is the premises, which all belong to \Gamma; a valuation making \Gamma true makes the premises true, and so makes the last line \psi true: \Gamma \models \psi. egI; the split on which disjunct is true for \veeE). - 1: the conclusion for the last line. A proof that inducts on the length of the derivation instead, and handles open boxes correctly, earns the same points step for step. title: 3.6 Completeness
content:
Completeness Soundness (@thm-soundness) says that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 never lead from true premises to a false conclusion: whatever can be derived is true in every row where the premises are. That answers half of the chapter’s question. The other half is the converse. Could the rules be too weak, so that some sequent is true in every row and yet no derivation of it exists? This section proves that they are not: every truth-table consequence has a derivation. The proof reads a derivation off the truth table, one row at a time, and then glues the rows together with excluded middle. The question soundness leaves open Recall the two relations from Section 3.4. \Gamma \vdash \psi says that there is a derivation of \psi from premises in \Gamma (@def-derivable). \Gamma \models \psi says that every valuation making all of \Gamma true makes \psi true (@def-valid-argument). Soundness is the implication \Gamma \vdash \psi \ \Rightarrow \ \Gamma \models \psi . Its converse is not automatic. The rules are a list that people wrote down, and a list can leave something out. Suppose, as a thought experiment, that we struck ulename{RAA} (@def-rule-raa) from the list. Every derivation that remains is still a derivation, so soundness still holds. But the tautology p \vee 
eg p would then have no derivation (this is the optional @thm-raa-independent of Section 3.5). So a sound list of rules can be too short. The question is whether our list is long enough. Here is a sequent to keep in mind. The formula (p 	o q) \vee (q 	o p) is a tautology: if q is true then p 	o q is true, and if q is false then q 	o p is true. Chapter 2 found a derivation of it (@exr-finding-derivations-c2), but only after reaching for ulename{LEM}, and nothing in Chapter 2 promised that a derivation would be there to find. We want a theorem that promises it in advance, for every tautology and every valid sequent. We are going to prove: If \Gamma is a list of formulas and \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. The plan has two ideas, one per row and one for all the rows together. 1. One row gives one derivation. Fix a row of the truth table, that is, a valuation v. Write each atom as it stands in that row: p if v makes p true, 
eg p if v makes it false. From these signed atoms we will derive the formula \psi if \psi is true in the row, and 
eg\psi if it is false. The derivation climbs the parse tree of \psi, one connective at a time. 2. The rows are glued by excluded middle. If \Gamma \models \psi, the first idea gives \psi from \Gamma and the signed atoms of each row. Two rows that differ only at the atom p have derivations from “\ldots, p” and from “\ldots, 
eg p”. The rule ulename{\vee E} applied to p \vee 
eg p merges them into one derivation that no longer mentions p. Removing the atoms one at a time leaves a derivation from \Gamma alone. The first idea is known as Kalmár’s lemma, and gluing rows by excluded middle is the standard way to finish; the route is the classical one. We keep the premises \Gamma throughout, and we isolate the two ingredients as lemmas so that each can be checked on its own. Before either, we need a little bookkeeping about derivations. Bookkeeping: adding premises and chaining derivations In Chapter 2 we learned to use a proved sequent as a single line (@def-derived-rule): its derivation could be pasted in, with its letters replaced by formulas. The completeness proof uses this move dozens of times, so we now state exactly what it gives and check that pasting really produces a derivation. [Weakening and Cut] Let \Gamma and \Delta be lists of formulas, and let \varphi, \psi, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m (m \ge 1), and  eta be formulas. 1. Weakening. If \Gamma \vdash \psi and every member of \Gamma is a member of \Delta, then \Delta \vdash \psi. In particular, \Gamma \vdash \psi implies \Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi. 2. Cut. If \Gamma \vdash \varphi and \Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. 3. Chaining. If \Gamma \vdash \alpha_i for every i = 1, \dots, m, and \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta, then \Gamma \vdash  eta. In words: (a) extra premises never hurt; (b) a formula that has been derived may be used as a premise; (c) a sequent already proved can be applied to formulas already derived. Part (c) is @def-derived-rule for sequents: applying a proved sequent to formulas already derived, outside every box. Inside a box, Section 2.3’s expansion does the same job. Part (a) is read off @def-derivable, which asks only that the premises of the derivation belong to the list. For (b) and (c), write the derivations one after another and let the last one cite, instead of its premise \alpha_i, the last line of the derivation of \alpha_i. The only thing to check is the scope rule of @def-derivation: the last line of a derivation lies in no box, so it stays available to everything written after it. (a) A derivation witnessing \Gamma \vdash \psi has premises that belong to \Gamma, hence to \Delta, and its last line is \psi. By @def-derivable it witnesses \Delta \vdash \psi. The second sentence is the case where \Delta is \Gamma, \varphi. For (b) and (c) we prove one statement that contains both: (\ast) If \Gamma \vdash \alpha_i for every i = 1, \dots, m, and \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta, then \Gamma \vdash  eta. Part (b) is (\ast) with m = 1, \alpha_1 = \varphi and  eta = \psi. Part (c) follows from (\ast), since \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta gives \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash  eta by (a). To prove (\ast), let D_i be a derivation of \alpha_i with premises in \Gamma, for each i, and let E be a derivation of  eta with premises in \Gamma, \alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m. If the last line of E is one of its premises, then  eta is a member of \Gamma, and the one-line derivation whose only line is the premise  eta shows \Gamma \vdash  eta; or  eta is some \alpha_i, and D_i shows \Gamma \vdash  eta. Otherwise, build a list of lines F as follows. 1. First, as premises, every premise of D_1, \dots, D_m, and every premise of E that is a member of \Gamma. 2. Then the lines of D_1 that are not premises, then those of D_2, and so on up to D_m, each with its boxes. 3. Then the lines of E that are not premises, with its boxes. Renumber the lines, and change each citation as follows. A citation of a premise that is in \Gamma now cites the premise line of step 1 carrying that formula. A citation in E of a premise \alpha_i that is not in \Gamma now cites the last line of D_i; that line is not a premise of D_i, because the premises of D_i are in \Gamma and \alpha_i is not, so it was copied in step 2. Every other citation follows its line to its new number. We check that F is a derivation (@def-derivation). The premises come first and lie in no box. The boxes are those of the D_i and of E, moved as blocks, so two boxes are still disjoint or nested, each still begins with its assumption, and each line lies in exactly the boxes it lay in before. Hence a line and a box that were available at a citing line are still available there, since the boxes containing each are unchanged. A premise line of step 1 lies in no box and comes first, so it is available at every later line. The last line of D_i lies in no box (it was the last line of a derivation) and comes before every line of E, so it is available at every line of E. Each line carries the same formula and the same justification as before, citing lines with the same formulas, so it is an instance of the same rule. Finally, the last line of F is the last line of E, namely  eta, and it lies in no box. The premises of F are all in \Gamma. Therefore \Gamma \vdash  eta, which proves (\ast). The lemma is pure bookkeeping, but it is what makes “cite a proved sequent as one line” honest. From now on, when a derivation cites a sequent proved earlier as a single line, the lemma (for a line in no box) or @def-derived-rule (for a line inside a box, where the cited lines are repeated inside the box first) is the reason the result is a derivation in the primitive rules. As Section 3.5 said, soundness was proved for the primitive rules, and a line citing a derived rule abbreviates a pasted derivation; for whole derivations, part (c) is the precise form of “abbreviates”, and inside a box the pasting of @def-derived-rule is the same bookkeeping. Suppose \Gamma \vdash \alpha and \Gamma \vdash 
eg\alpha. Which part of @lem-weakening-cut, applied to which proved sequent, gives \Gamma \vdash \chi for every formula \chi? Part (c) with m = 2, \alpha_1 = \alpha, \alpha_2 = 
eg\alpha and  eta = \chi, applied to @prp-ex-falso, P, 
eg P \vdash Q, with \alpha for P and \chi for Q. The rules prove their own truth tables Each line of the truth table of a connective says something like “with \alpha true and  eta false, \alpha 	o  eta comes out false”. Read with signs, that line is a sequent: from \alpha and 
eg eta, conclude 
eg(\alpha 	o  eta). If every such sequent is derivable, then the rules know the truth tables. This is the key to the first idea of the plan. Section 3.3 began by reading the tables off the rules; the lemma below makes that reading exact: every line of every table is a derivable sequent. [Derivable Means Valid] For every list of formulas \Gamma and every formula \psi, \Gamma \vdash \psi \iff \Gamma \models \psi . In particular, whether \Gamma \vdash \psi holds can be decided by checking the 2^n rows of a truth table, where n is the number of atoms occurring in \Gamma and \psi. (\Rightarrow) is @thm-soundness and (\Leftarrow) is @thm-completeness. For the second sentence, let p_1, \dots, p_n be the atoms occurring in \Gamma and \psi. By @lem-coincidence, the values of the members of \Gamma and of \psi under a valuation depend only on its values at p_1, \dots, p_n, so \Gamma \models \psi holds exactly when it holds in each of the 2^n rows of the joint truth table. That is a finite check, and by the first sentence it decides \Gamma \vdash \psi. So a question that looks as if it needs a search through infinitely many possible derivations can be settled by a finite table. The search for a derivation may still be the quicker way to a yes, and one row is the quickest way to a no (@cor-refuting-row), but neither is needed. We defined \Gamma \vdash \psi only for a list, that is, for finitely many premises. One may allow an infinite collection \Gamma of premises and say \Gamma \vdash \psi when \psi is derivable from finitely many members of \Gamma (a derivation has finitely many lines, so it can only use finitely many). The equivalence with \Gamma \models \psi still holds for infinite \Gamma; this is the compactness theorem of propositional logic. We do not prove it, and nothing in the book depends on it. Our proof does not reach it: Step 1 needs finitely many atoms. Two roads to every answer We now have two independent ways to settle any question “is \Gamma \vdash \psi?”. Then \varphi^{v} = \alpha \vee  eta and  eta^{v} =  eta. Chaining \Sigma \vdash  eta with (\vee 2) gives \Sigma \vdash \alpha \vee  eta. - Case v(\alpha) = v( eta) = \mathrm{F}. Then \varphi^{v} = 
eg(\alpha \vee  eta), \alpha^{v} = 
eg\alpha and  eta^{v} = 
eg eta. Chaining both hypotheses with (\vee 3), 
eg\alpha, 
eg eta \vdash 
eg(\alpha \vee  eta), gives \Sigma \vdash 
eg(\alpha \vee  eta). Biconditional, \varphi = \alpha \leftrightarrow  eta. By @def-truth-value, v(\alpha \leftrightarrow  eta) = \mathrm{T} exactly when v(\alpha) = v( eta). Each case uses both hypotheses. - Case T, T. \varphi^{v} = \alpha \leftrightarrow  eta; chain \Sigma \vdash \alpha, \Sigma \vdash  eta with ({\leftrightarrow}1). - Case F, F. \varphi^{v} = \alpha \leftrightarrow  eta; chain \Sigma \vdash 
eg\alpha, \Sigma \vdash 
eg eta with ({\leftrightarrow}2). - Case T, F. \varphi^{v} = 
eg(\alpha \leftrightarrow  eta); chain \Sigma \vdash \alpha, \Sigma \vdash 
eg eta with ({\leftrightarrow}3). - Case F, T. \varphi^{v} = 
eg(\alpha \leftrightarrow  eta); chain \Sigma \vdash 
eg\alpha, \Sigma \vdash  eta with ({\leftrightarrow}4). The cases cover all four pairs of values, so in each the property holds for \varphi. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: the \vee case: the three value cases, each with the right sequent of @lem-connective-rows and only the hypotheses its premises need. - 4: the \leftrightarrow case: the four value cases, each with the right sequent and both hypotheses. - 1: names chaining (@lem-weakening-cut (c)) as the step that combines the hypotheses with the sequent. - 1: says that the cases cover every pair of values. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a sequent whose premises are not the signed parts \alpha^{v},  eta^{v} of that case. [C2: Exit check: completeness] Close the section first, and write from memory. 1. Prove @lem-atom-splitting: if \Delta, p \vdash \psi and \Delta, 
eg p \vdash \psi, then \Delta \vdash \psi. 2. Prove Step 3 of the proof of @thm-completeness in full: from the Claim of Step 2, for every valuation v, \Gamma, p_1^{v}, \dots, p_n^{v} \vdash \psi, deduce \Gamma \vdash \psi. State the statement you prove by induction, and say which principle of induction you use. [Hint 1] For (a): excluded middle and proof by cases. For (b): remove the signed atoms from the end of the list, one at a time. [Hint 2] For (b): let S(j) say “for every valuation v, \Gamma, p_1^{v}, \dots, p_j^{v} \vdash \psi”, and show that S(j) implies S(j - 1) for 1 \le j \le n. (a) Let D derive \psi from premises in \Delta, p, and E from premises in \Delta, 
eg p. Write, as premises, those of D and E that lie in \Delta; then p \vee 
eg p by ulename{LEM} (@prp-excluded-middle, a derived rule with no premises); then a box opening with p containing the nonpremise lines of D, in which citations of the premise p now cite the assumption and citations of premises in \Delta cite the premise lines; then a box opening with 
eg p, built from E in the same way; then \psi by ulename{\vee E}, citing the line p \vee 
eg p and the two boxes. (If D or E ends on a premise, its box is the assumption alone when that premise is the assumption’s formula, and otherwise the assumption followed by \psi by ulename{R}.) Every copied line keeps its boxes, now inside the new box, and cites lines still available to it. The last line of each box is \psi, as a line of that box itself, because the last line of D or E lay in no box. The two boxes and the ulename{LEM} line lie in no box, so they are available at the final line. So the result is a derivation of \psi from premises in \Delta, and \Delta \vdash \psi. (b) For 0 \le j \le n, let S(j) be: for every valuation v, \Gamma, p_1^{v}, \dots, p_j^{v} \vdash \psi. The Claim of Step 2 is S(n). The step. Let 1 \le j \le n and assume S(j). Let v be any valuation, and let v^{+}, v^{-} agree with v except that v^{+}(p_j) = \mathrm{T} and v^{-}(p_j) = \mathrm{F}. Since the p_i are distinct, both agree with v on p_1, \dots, p_{j-1}. By S(j) for v^{+} and for v^{-}, with \Delta \coloneqq \Gamma, p_1^{v}, \dots, p_{j-1}^{v}: \Delta, p_j \vdash \psi and \Delta, 
eg p_j \vdash \psi. By (a), \Delta \vdash \psi. As v was arbitrary, S(j - 1) holds. The induction. We use @ax-induction on m \in 
N with the statement T(m): “if m \le n, then S(n - m)”. T(0) is S(n). If T(m) holds and m + 1 \le n, then S(n - m) holds and j = n - m lies between 1 and n, so the step gives S(n - m - 1), which is T(m + 1). Hence T(n), which is S(0): for every valuation, \Gamma \vdash \psi. Valuations exist, so \Gamma \vdash \psi. (Inducting downwards on j, or on the number of atoms removed, is the same argument; either earns full marks.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) pastes both derivations into the two boxes of a ulename{\vee E} on p \vee 
eg p, with the premise p (or 
eg p) redirected to the box’s assumption, and says why every citation is still available. - 1: (a) cites ulename{LEM} (@prp-excluded-middle) as a derived rule. - 3: (b) sets up an induction on the number of atoms removed (or downward on j) with a statement quantified over every valuation, and names the induction principle. - 2: (b) in the step, applies the hypothesis to both valuations that differ at p_j, and notes that they agree with v on the other atoms. - 1: (b) concludes \Gamma \vdash \psi from S(0). Fatal errors (0 for the step): splitting on an atom using the Claim for a single valuation only; an induction statement that fixes v before the induction, so that the two valuations of the step are not covered by the hypothesis.

title: 3.7 Normal Forms and Adequate Connectives
content:
Normal Forms and Adequate Connectives The proof of completeness wrote each row of a truth table as a list of signed atoms p_1^{v}, \dots, p_n^{v} (Section 3.6). Join the signed atoms of one row by \wedge, and you get a formula that is true in that row and in no other. Join those formulas, one for each row where a given formula \varphi is true, by \vee, and you get a formula with the same truth table as \varphi. This section turns that observation into two standard shapes for formulas, the disjunctive and the conjunctive normal form. It then reads validity off the conjunctive shape at a glance, and asks how few connectives are really needed. Conjunctions and disjunctions of many formulas Normal forms are long conjunctions and disjunctions. Section 3.4 fixed how to write them, in the paragraph on long conjunctions after @prp-standard-equivalences. For formulas \chi_1, \dots, \chi_k with k \ge 1, \chi_1 \wedge \chi_2 \wedge \dots \wedge \chi_k is the conjunction grouped to the right, \chi_1 \wedge (\chi_2 \wedge (\cdots \wedge \chi_k)), and likewise for \vee; for k = 1 it is \chi_1 itself. That paragraph proved, by induction on the number of terms, how such formulas are evaluated: for every valuation v,  egin{aligned} v(\chi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \chi_k) = \mathrm{T} &\iff v(\chi_i) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ for every } i = 1, \dots, k, \ v(\chi_1 \vee \dots \vee \chi_k) = \mathrm{T} &\iff v(\chi_i) = \mathrm{T} 	ext{ for some } i = 1, \dots, k. \end{aligned} {#eq-many-term-values} We use these two lines constantly below, and we cite them by this display. So a long conjunction is true when all its parts are, and a long disjunction when at least one is, just as the words say. Literals, clauses and the two normal forms The building blocks are the smallest formulas that still carry a sign. [Literal] A literal is an atom or the negation of an atom. So p, 
eg p, q_7 and 
eg q_7 are literals. The signed atom p^{v} of Section 3.6 is always a literal. The formulas 
eg
eg p, 
eg(p \wedge q) and  ot are not: in the first two, 
eg is applied to something other than an atom, and  ot is neither an atom nor a negation. The opposite of a literal is 
eg p if the literal is p, and p if it is 
eg p. By the clause for 
eg in @def-truth-value, a literal and its opposite take opposite values under every valuation. From literals we build two kinds of blocks and two kinds of formulas. - A clause joins one or more literals by \vee, such as p \vee 
eg q \vee r, or 
eg q alone. - A conjunct (in this section, short for “conjunctive clause”) joins one or more literals by \wedge, such as p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r, or 
eg q alone. A normal form is a formula whose connectives come in fixed layers: negations only on atoms, then one layer of one connective, then one layer of the other. [Disjunctive Normal Form] A formula has disjunctive normal form (DNF), or is in DNF, when it has the shape C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k, with k \ge 1, where every C_i joins one or more literals by \wedge. Conjunctive Normal Form A formula has conjunctive normal form (CNF), or is in CNF, when it has the shape K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k, with k \ge 1, where every K_i joins one or more literals by \vee. In words: a DNF is an “or of ands” and a CNF an “and of ors”, and in both the only negations sit directly on atoms. Read a DNF as a list of situations, any one of which makes it true; read a CNF as a list of requirements, all of which must be met. Check some formulas against the definitions, clause by clause. 1. (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (
eg p \wedge q) is in DNF: two conjuncts, each a conjunction of literals. It is not in CNF: as a conjunction of clauses it would have to be a single clause (it is not a conjunction), and a clause cannot contain \wedge. 2. (p \vee q) \wedge (
eg p \vee 
eg q) is in CNF, with two clauses, and not in DNF. 3. p \wedge 
eg q is in both: in DNF with one conjunct, and in CNF with two clauses of one literal each. Likewise p \vee 
eg q is in both. 4. A single literal, 
eg r, is in both forms: one conjunct of one literal, and one clause of one literal. This degenerate case matters, because a formula such as 
eg r must count as already normal. A nonexample by a minimal change: (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee r is in DNF, but 
eg(p \wedge q) \vee r is not in either form. Only one symbol moved, and the literal condition fails: 
eg now stands on the conjunction p \wedge q, not on an atom. The formula p 	o q is in neither form either, since 	o is not allowed at all. Why these layers? Because they are the shapes that the truth table hands us, as the next theorem shows, and because in these shapes some questions become easy: the subsection “Reading validity off a CNF” below decides validity of a CNF without a table. A literal is an atom with at most one 
eg, and nothing else. 
eg
eg p is equivalent to the literal p but is not a literal, so 
eg
eg p \vee q is not in CNF as written. Likewise  ot is not a literal, so a “normal form” containing  ot is not one; that is why the constructions below never use it. Which of the following are in CNF, and which are in DNF? (i) (p \vee 
eg q) \wedge r; (ii) 
eg(p \vee q); (iii) p \vee (
eg q \wedge r). (i) CNF, with clauses p \vee 
eg q and r; not DNF, since the conjunct would have to be the whole formula and p \vee 
eg q is not a literal. (ii) Neither: 
eg stands on a disjunction. (iii) DNF, with conjuncts p and 
eg q \wedge r; not CNF, since the one clause would contain \wedge. Reading a DNF off the truth table Take a valuation v and atoms p_1, \dots, p_n with n \ge 1, and form the conjunct of the signed atoms of the row of v, C_v \coloneqq p_1^{v} \wedge \dots \wedge p_n^{v} . For every valuation w, each p_i^{v} is true under w exactly when w(p_i) = v(p_i): if v(p_i) = \mathrm{T}, then p_i^{v} = p_i; if v(p_i) = \mathrm{F}, then p_i^{v} = 
eg p_i, which is true under w exactly when w(p_i) = \mathrm{F}. By @eq-many-term-values, w(C_v) = \mathrm{T} \iff w(p_i) = v(p_i) 	ext{ for every } i = 1, \dots, n . {#eq-row-conjunct} So C_v is true in the row of v and in no other row. It is a formula that “names” one row. [Exactly one of two] Find a formula in DNF that is true exactly when exactly one of p, q is true, and check it. The rows with exactly one of p, q true are (p, q) = (\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) and (\mathrm{F}, \mathrm{T}). Their conjuncts are p \wedge 
eg q and 
eg p \wedge q, so the answer is (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (
eg p \wedge q). Check against the table: in the row T, F the first conjunct is true; in F, T the second is; in T, T each conjunct has a false literal (
eg q, 
eg p); in F, F likewise (p, q). So the formula is true in exactly the two rows wanted. The same recipe works for any formula. [Disjunctive Normal Form] Every formula \varphi is equivalent to a formula in DNF. If \varphi has at least one atom, the DNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \varphi. List the rows where \varphi is true and disjoin their conjuncts C_v. A valuation makes the disjunction true exactly when it agrees with one of those rows, which by @lem-coincidence is exactly when it makes \varphi true. Two degenerate cases need a convention: a formula with no T-row, whose disjunction would be empty, and a formula with no atoms, which has no rows to speak of. By the paraphrase of @def-semantic-equivalence, two formulas \varphi and \psi are equivalent exactly when v(\varphi) = v(\psi) for every valuation v. Case 1: \varphi has at least one atom. Let p_1, \dots, p_n (n \ge 1) be the atoms of \varphi. A row is a choice of a value for each p_i; there are 2^n rows, and for each we fix a valuation that takes those values at p_1, \dots, p_n (and, say, T at every other atom). By @lem-coincidence, v(\varphi) depends only on the row of v. Let v_1, \dots, v_k be the fixed valuations of the rows in which \varphi is T. If k \ge 1, let D \coloneqq C_{v_1} \vee \dots \vee C_{v_k}, which is in DNF by @def-dnf, with atoms among p_1, \dots, p_n. Let w be any valuation. By @eq-many-term-values and @eq-row-conjunct, w(D) = \mathrm{T} exactly when w agrees with some v_j on p_1, \dots, p_n. If it does, then w(\varphi) = v_j(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} by @lem-coincidence. Conversely, if w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}, then the row of w is one where \varphi is T, so w agrees on p_1, \dots, p_n with the valuation v_j fixed for that row. Hence w(D) = w(\varphi) for every w, and \varphi \equiv D. If k = 0, then \varphi is F in every row, hence under every valuation. The formula p_1 \wedge 
eg p_1 is in DNF (one conjunct of two literals) and is F under every valuation by @def-truth-value. So \varphi \equiv p_1 \wedge 
eg p_1. Case 2: \varphi has no atoms. Any two valuations agree on all the atoms of \varphi (there are none), so by @lem-coincidence v(\varphi) is the same for every v. Let p be an atom. If that value is T, then \varphi \equiv p \vee 
eg p, which is true under every valuation and is in DNF (two conjuncts of one literal); if it is F, then \varphi \equiv p \wedge 
eg p. This proves the theorem. The conjuncts C_v are the signed atoms of Section 3.6 joined by \wedge. There the signed atoms of a row were premises from which \varphi^{v} was derived; here they are joined into a formula that is true in that row only. The proof is the proof of completeness with the derivations taken out. For p \wedge 
eg p we could have written  ot, which is also F under every valuation. We did not, because  ot is not a literal, and because the adequacy theorem at the end of this section reuses the construction in a language without  ot. Conjunctive normal form A DNF lists the rows where a formula is true. A CNF does the opposite: it lists the rows where the formula is false, one clause per row, each clause being false in its row and true in every other. Conjunctive Normal Form Every formula \varphi is equivalent to a formula in CNF. If \varphi has at least one atom, the CNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \varphi. Apply @thm-dnf to 
eg\varphi and negate the result: \varphi \equiv 
eg
eg\varphi \equiv 
eg(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k). Now push the 
eg inwards with De Morgan’s laws and double negation (@prp-standard-equivalences): 
eg(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k) becomes 
eg C_1 \wedge \dots \wedge 
eg C_k, and each 
eg C_i, the negation of a conjunction of literals, becomes the disjunction of the opposite literals. The proof checks the outcome directly with @eq-many-term-values, which avoids De Morgan’s laws for many terms. By @thm-dnf, 
eg\varphi \equiv C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k for some conjuncts C_1, \dots, C_k (with atoms among those of \varphi if it has any, since 
eg\varphi has the same atoms). For each i, let K_i be the disjunction of the opposites of the literals of C_i, in the same order, and let K \coloneqq K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k. Then K is in CNF, with the same atoms as C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k. Let w be a valuation. Each literal of K_i is true under w exactly when the corresponding literal of C_i is false. By @eq-many-term-values, used three times:  egin{aligned} w(K) = \mathrm{T} &\iff 	ext{for every } i, \ w(K_i) = \mathrm{T} \ &\iff 	ext{for every } i, 	ext{ some literal of } C_i 	ext{ is false under } w \ &\iff 	ext{for every } i, \ w(C_i) = \mathrm{F} \ &\iff w(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k) = \mathrm{F} . \end{aligned} Since C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k \equiv 
eg\varphi, the last line holds exactly when w(
eg\varphi) = \mathrm{F}, that is, when w(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}. So w(K) = w(\varphi) for every w, and \varphi \equiv K. Unwinding the construction: the conjuncts C_i of the DNF of 
eg\varphi are the rows where \varphi is false, and K_i is the clause that is false exactly in the row of C_i. So the CNF can be read straight off the table: one clause per F-row, built from the opposites of that row’s signed atoms. In the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}, for instance, the clause is 
eg p \vee q. A formula with no F-row gets, by the proof, the clause of a contradiction’s DNF negated, 
eg p \vee p (from C_1 = p \wedge 
eg p), which is true in every row. Alternatively, a CNF can be reached by rewriting. First replace each  ot, which is not a literal, by p \wedge 
eg p for an atom p; both are false in every row. Replace \alpha \leftrightarrow  eta by (\alpha 	o  eta) \wedge ( eta 	o \alpha) and \alpha 	o  eta by 
eg\alpha \vee  eta; push each 
eg inwards by De Morgan’s laws, and remove 
eg
eg; finally distribute \vee over \wedge, replacing \alpha \vee ( eta \wedge \gamma) by (\alpha \vee  eta) \wedge (\alpha \vee \gamma). Each step replaces a part of the formula by an equivalent one: the equivalences are  ot \equiv p \wedge 
eg p and those of @prp-standard-equivalences, which hold for arbitrary formulas, and @lem-replacement says the whole formula stays equivalent; since \equiv is transitive (Section 3.4), the steps chain. Stopping before the distribution step, and distributing \wedge over \vee instead, gives a DNF. The rewriting route is often much shorter than the table, as the next example shows, but it can also be much longer, as the warning after it shows. [Two routes to a normal form] Put \varphi = (p 	o q) 	o (
eg q 	o r) into DNF and into CNF, first from its truth table and then by rewriting. The table route. Work backwards from F (Section 3.3): \varphi is false exactly when p 	o q is T and 
eg q 	o r is F. The latter needs 
eg q true and r false, so q = r = \mathrm{F}; then p 	o q true needs p = \mathrm{F}. So \varphi has exactly one F-row, p = q = r = \mathrm{F}, as the table confirms:  egin{array}{ccc|c|c|c} p & q & r & p 	o q & 
eg q 	o r & (p 	o q) 	o (
eg q 	o r) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} The DNF of @thm-dnf has one conjunct for each of the seven T-rows:  egin{aligned} &(p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r) \vee (p \wedge 
eg q \wedge 
eg r) \ &\quad \vee (
eg p \wedge q \wedge r) \vee (
eg p \wedge q \wedge 
eg r) \vee (
eg p \wedge 
eg q \wedge r). \end{aligned} The CNF of @thm-cnf has one clause for the single F-row, built from the opposites of 
eg p, 
eg q, 
eg r: it is the single clause p \vee q \vee r. The rewriting route. Eliminate the three implications, then push the negation in:  egin{aligned} \varphi &\equiv 
eg(
eg p \vee q) \vee (
eg
eg q \vee r) \ &\equiv (
eg
eg p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \vee r) \ &\equiv (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee q \vee r , \end{aligned} using (c) of @prp-standard-equivalences three times, then De Morgan’s law (b) for 
eg(\alpha \vee  eta), then double negation (d) twice. This is already a DNF, with three conjuncts. For a CNF, distribute, by (g) together with commutativity (f) and associativity (h): (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \vee r) \equiv (p \vee q \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q \vee r). The second clause contains q and 
eg q, so it is true in every row, and a conjunction with a part that is true in every row is equivalent to its other part. So \varphi \equiv p \vee q \vee r: one clause, as the table route found. The formula p \vee q \vee r is also a DNF, with three conjuncts of one literal each. So the table’s seven conjuncts and the rewriting’s three can both be replaced by three one-literal conjuncts. Both routes are correct; they differ in length, and neither is guaranteed to give the shortest normal form. A formula has many equivalent CNFs and DNFs; “normal form” does not mean “unique form”. p \vee q \vee r and (p \vee q \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q \vee r) are both CNFs of the formula above. And the two routes have opposite weaknesses. The table route needs all 2^n rows. The rewriting route can explode at the distribution step: distributing (p_1 \wedge q_1) \vee (p_2 \wedge q_2) \vee (p_3 \wedge q_3) gives 8 clauses, one for each way of picking p_i or q_i from every conjunct, and n such conjuncts give 2^n clauses. Reading validity off a CNF A CNF is a list of requirements, all of which must hold. That makes one question easy. [Validity of a CNF] 1. A formula in CNF is a tautology exactly when every clause contains some atom together with its negation. 2. A formula in DNF is satisfiable exactly when some conjunct contains no atom together with its negation. Try it first (ten minutes): take a clause in which no atom occurs both with and without 
eg, such as p \vee 
eg q \vee r. Can you find a row that makes it false? What does that row do to a CNF containing this clause? The direction “every clause has a pair \Rightarrow tautology” is the easy one: p \vee 
eg p is true in every row, so a clause containing both is too, and a conjunction of clauses true in every row is true in every row. The attempt above is the other direction. To make a CNF false, it is enough to make one clause false, and a clause is false only when all its literals are. So set every atom of the clause against its literal: F for a plain atom, T for a negated one. The one thing that could stop us is an atom that appears both plain and negated, since it would have to be both F and T. That is exactly the pair the proposition talks about. (a) Let K = K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k be in CNF. (\Leftarrow) Suppose every clause K_i contains some atom p and its negation 
eg p. Let v be a valuation. One of p, 
eg p is true under v, by @def-truth-value, so v(K_i) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. This holds for every i, so v(K) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. As v was arbitrary, K is a tautology (@def-tautology). (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose some clause K_i contains no atom together with its negation. Define a valuation v by: v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if the literal p occurs in K_i; v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if the literal 
eg p occurs in K_i; v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} for every other atom. This is well defined, because no atom occurs in K_i both as p and as 
eg p. Every literal of K_i is false under v, so v(K_i) = \mathrm{F} by @eq-many-term-values, and hence v(K) = \mathrm{F}, again by @eq-many-term-values. So K is not a tautology. (b) Let D = C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k be in DNF. (\Leftarrow) Suppose C_i contains no atom together with its negation. Define v by v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} if p occurs in C_i, v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{F} if 
eg p occurs in C_i, and v(p) \coloneqq \mathrm{T} otherwise; this is well defined as in (a). Every literal of C_i is true under v, so v(C_i) = \mathrm{T} and v(D) = \mathrm{T} by @eq-many-term-values. So D is satisfiable (@def-satisfiable). (\Rightarrow) If every conjunct contains some p and 
eg p, then under every valuation one of these two literals is false, so every conjunct is false and so is D, by @eq-many-term-values. So D is not satisfiable. This proves the proposition. The two parts are two faces of one fact. Section 3.4 showed that a formula is a tautology exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable (after @def-satisfiable). Let D be in DNF, and let K be the CNF whose clauses are the conjuncts of D with every literal replaced by its opposite. The proof of @thm-cnf, applied to \varphi =
