Eliminate the outer implication and then the inner one, and push the negation in:  egin{aligned} (p 	o q) 	o (q \wedge r) &\equiv 
eg(p 	o q) \vee (q \wedge r) \ &\equiv 
eg(
eg p \vee q) \vee (q \wedge r) \ &\equiv (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) . \end{aligned} The last line is a DNF. Here 
eg(p 	o q) \equiv p \wedge 
eg q, since an implication is false exactly when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion false. For a CNF, distribute: (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) \equiv (p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee q) \wedge (
eg q \vee r) , and drop the clause 
eg q \vee q, which is true in every row: the CNF is (p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee r) \wedge (
eg q \vee r). (The clause p \vee r is redundant too: (p \vee q) \wedge (
eg q \vee r) is an equivalent CNF, as splitting on q shows. Either is correct.) The check. The formula is false exactly when p 	o q holds and q \wedge r fails. Its table:  egin{array}{ccc|c|c|c} p & q & r & p 	o q & q \wedge r & (p 	o q) 	o (q \wedge r) \ \hline \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \ \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{T} & \mathrm{F} & \mathrm{F} \end{array} The T-rows are T T T, T F T, T F F, and F T T. The DNF (p \wedge 
eg q) \vee (q \wedge r) is true in exactly these: p \wedge 
eg q in T F T and T F F, and q \wedge r in T T T and F T T. In each of the four F-rows the CNF has a false clause: 
eg q \vee r in T T F and F T F, p \vee q in F F T and F F F. By the table route, the DNF has four conjuncts, one per T-row, and the CNF four clauses, one per F-row, for instance 
eg p \vee 
eg q \vee r for the row T T F. Any correct DNF and CNF earns full marks; a CNF is not unique. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: eliminates 	o correctly, with 
eg(p 	o q) \equiv p \wedge 
eg q and its reason. - 3: a correct DNF. - 3: a correct CNF, by distribution carried out in full or by one clause per F-row. - 2: the check against the table, covering at least the four F-rows (or the four T-rows). Fatal errors (0 for the step): 
eg(p 	o q) rewritten as 
eg p 	o 
eg q; a “CNF” with a conjunction inside a clause. R. Review [R1] Find a derivation of p \vee q, \ 
eg(p \wedge r), \ r \vdash q. The method of Section 2.6 (@exm-search-cases shows it on a proof by cases). The goal q is an atom, so no introduction rule applies; the premise p \vee q is a disjunction, so we use it by ulename{\vee E}, with the goal q in both boxes. The case q is the goal. In the case p, nothing gives q directly, so we look for a clash: p and the premise r build p \wedge r by ulename{\wedge I}, which clashes with 
eg(p \wedge r), and ulename{ ot E} closes the impossible case (@exm-manufactured-clash). The second box is its assumption alone, which is already the goal. No ulename{RAA} is used. [R2] Let m and n be integers, and consider the argument: “m + n is even only if m and n are both even or both odd. m is even and n is odd. Therefore m + n is not even.” Translate it into a sequent, using atoms e: “m + n is even”, a: “m is even”, b: “n is even”, and decide whether the premises entail the conclusion. “P only if Q” is P 	o Q (Section 1.1, and @exr-statements-and-connectives-c1). “Both odd” is 
eg a \wedge 
eg b, since an integer is odd exactly when it is not even. So the sequent is e 	o ((a \wedge b) \vee (
eg a \wedge 
eg b)), \ \ a \wedge 
eg b \ \models \ 
eg e . Work backwards from F. A refuting row needs 
eg e false, so e = \mathrm{T}, and the second premise true, so a = \mathrm{T}, b = \mathrm{F}. In that row a \wedge b and 
eg a \wedge 
eg b are both F, so the first premise is \mathrm{T} 	o \mathrm{F}, which is F. So no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false: the entailment holds. By @thm-completeness, the sequent is also derivable. (The eight-row table gives the same answer; working backwards found the only candidate row at once.) [R3] Is (p \wedge (q \vee r)) 	o ((p \wedge q) \vee r) a tautology? Is it derivable without ulename{RAA}? A tautology. Work backwards from F (Section 3.3). The formula is false only if p \wedge (q \vee r) is true and (p \wedge q) \vee r is false. The second needs r false and p \wedge q false; the first needs p true and q \vee r true, so with r false, q true. But then p \wedge q is true. No row makes the formula false, so it is a tautology (@def-tautology). Derivable without ulename{RAA}. Completeness (@thm-completeness) says it is derivable, but not how, and its proof uses ulename{LEM} in @lem-atom-splitting, so it does not answer the second question. A search does: the goal is an implication, so a box on p \wedge (q \vee r); split it by ulename{\wedge E} and use q \vee r by ulename{\vee E}. No ulename{RAA} is used: the boxes close by ulename{\vee E} and ulename{{	o}I}. The tools: truth values (@def-truth-value) for the first question, the search of Chapter 2 for the second. The look-alike tool, completeness, answers only “derivable with all the rules”.

title: Predicate Logic and the Quantifier Rules
content:
Predicate Logic and the Quantifier Rules “x^2 \ge 0 for every real x.” “There is no largest prime.” “For every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N.” The statements of analysis are made of the words “for every” and “there exists”, and Chapters 1–3 cannot see them: to a truth table, each of these sentences is a single atom, and the argument “every positive real has a square root; 2 is positive; so 2 has a square root” has the invalid form p, q 	herefore r. This chapter adds the missing grammar (predicates, terms, and the two quantifiers) and then, exactly as Chapters 1 and 2 did for the connectives, gives the rules one per section: how to use a “for every”, how to prove one, how to prove a “there exists”, how to use one, and the rules for equality. Each quantifier rule comes with a side condition about names, and the side conditions turn out to be exactly the rules that analysts break when a \delta secretly depends on an x, or when a witness is treated as if it were arbitrary. The motivating problem is this. A function f is continuous when for every x and every \varepsilon > 0 there is a \delta > 0 that works; it is uniformly continuous when for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a \delta > 0 that works for every x. The two definitions differ only in the order of two quantifiers. Why does “uniformly continuous implies continuous” have a proof a few lines long, while its converse is false? The answer is a fact about the order in which names are introduced in a derivation, and Section 4.10 reads it off rule by rule. Along the way the chapter translates mathematical definitions into formulas, negates them quantifier by quantifier, gives formulas a meaning in models, and uses models to show that some searches for a derivation must fail. The last section, which is optional, proves that the extended rules are sound. What you need. Chapters 1–3. From Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for every connective, the definition of a derivation with its boxes and its scope rule (@def-derivation), derived rules (@def-derived-rule), the classical rules of Section 2.5, and the search method of Section 2.6, which each rule section here extends by one step. From Chapter 3: formulas as objects (@def-formula), structural induction and recursion (@thm-structural-induction, @thm-structural-recursion), truth tables, and soundness with its refuting rows (@thm-soundness, @cor-refuting-row). School arithmetic and the order of 
N, 
Z, 
Q, and 
R are used in examples as facts. Time. About 70 hours on the core track (all of A, one B, and one C per section, the exit checks); about 90 hours for everything. Roadmap - Predicates and quantifiers. Predicates, variables, and the domain; how to read “for every” and “there exists”, bounded quantifiers, and why the order of two quantifiers can change everything. - Terms, formulas, free variables, and substitution. The exact language, which letters are still holes, the operation “put t in for x” that every rule uses, and the one way it goes wrong: capture. - Using “for every”: instantiation. The rule ulename{ orall E}: a universal statement may be applied to any term, and the term is read off the goal. - Proving “for every”: let x be arbitrary. The rule ulename{ orall I} and the flagged box: prove the statement for a fresh name about which nothing is assumed. - Proving “there exists”: exhibit a witness. The rule ulename{\exists I}, and why the witness is chosen only when an available line shows it. - Using “there exists”: name a witness. The rule ulename{\exists E}, its box, and its fresh-name condition, and the first derivation that moves an \exists past a  orall (and where the reverse move breaks down). - Equality and unique existence. The rules ulename{=I} and ulename{=E}, calculation chains, “there is exactly one”, and the completed table of rules, phrases, and proof-assistant commands. - Translating mathematics. Definitions from analysis written as formulas with nested and bounded quantifiers, the bounded forms of the four rules, and the search method in one place. - Negating and moving quantifiers. “Not every” is “some not”, negation pushed inward quantifier by quantifier, and the laws that move a quantifier across a connective. - Uniformly continuous implies continuous, rule by rule. The chapter’s centerpiece: the full derivation, and the exact lines at which the converse breaks down. - Models and counter-models. A meaning for every formula, in a structure with an assignment; a counter-model as a proof that a sentence does not follow. - Soundness for predicate logic (optional). The soundness theorem of Chapter 3 extended to the quantifier and equality rules, with each side condition used in its own case. Named moves - Instantiate at the term you need (ulename{ orall E}): read the term off the goal, not off the order of the premises. - Let x be arbitrary (ulename{ orall I}): a fresh name, about which nothing is assumed. - Postpone the witness (ulename{\exists I}): choose the term only when an available line shows it. - Name the witness early (ulename{\exists E}): “choose x_0 with …”, open the box at once, and never generalize over it. - Fix, obtain, choose: ulename{ orall I}, then ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists E} on the hypothesis, then ulename{\exists I} with a term built from what is available. The shape of most proofs in analysis. - Negate quantifier by quantifier: push 
eg inward, turning  orall into \exists and back, and keep the bounds. - Refute with a model: a structure in which the premises are true and the conclusion false. - Read the dependency off the order: a variable may depend on the variables quantified to its left, and only on them.

title: 4.1 Predicates and Quantifiers
content:
Predicates and Quantifiers Chapters 1–3 built a complete account of the connectives: rules for using and proving “and”, “or”, “implies”, and “not”, a meaning for every formula through truth tables, and the theorems that the rules prove exactly what the tables say. In all of that, an atomic statement was a closed box. The statements of analysis are not boxes. “For every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N such that …” has its whole content inside, in the words “for every” and “there is” and in the letters they govern. This section opens the box. It introduces predicates, variables, the domain a statement talks about, and the two quantifiers  orall and \exists, and it teaches how to read a quantified sentence. It proves no theorem and states no rule: the four quantifier rules come one per section, in Sections 4.3 to 4.6. An argument the truth table rejects Here is an argument that nobody would doubt. Every positive real number has a square root. The number 2 is positive. Therefore 2 has a square root. It is correct in the plainest sense: if the two premises are true, the conclusion must be. Now try to check it with the tools of Chapters 1–3. The three sentences contain no connective at all, so each is atomic. Give them atoms: - p: “every positive real number has a square root”; - q: “2 is positive”; - r: “2 has a square root”. The argument has the form p, q 	herefore r. Three different atoms, and nothing connects them. The valuation that makes p and q true and r false makes both premises true and the conclusion false. So by @cor-refuting-row, p, \ q 
vdash r . No derivation, with any rule of Chapters 1 and 2, leads from p and q to r. There is no contradiction here, and it is worth seeing exactly why. @cor-refuting-row is about the form p, q 	herefore r: it says that no derivation leads from two arbitrary statements to a third, unrelated one. That is true. Our argument is correct for a reason that the form cannot see. The first premise speaks about every positive real number. The second says that 2 is one of the things the first premise speaks about. The conclusion says of 2 what the first premise said of all of them. The three statements share parts: a property (“is positive”), another property (“has a square root”), an object (2), and the word “every”. Chopped into atoms, the shared parts disappear. This is the warning of Section 3.3 come true: a truth table sees only the connectives, and everything inside an atom is invisible to it. Section 3.3 ended that warning with the remark that this chapter looks inside atoms. We now do. The first job is a vocabulary for the parts inside: the properties, the objects, and the words “every” and “some”. Section 4.3 then gives the rule that makes the argument above a derivation, four lines long. Predicates: statements with holes Chapter 1 met the sentence “x > 2” and called it an open sentence (item (e) of @exm-statements). It is not a statement, because its truth depends on what x is: it is true when x is 3 and false when x is 0. Put a number in for x and it becomes a statement. The argument of the last subsection is built from two open sentences of this kind: “x is positive” and “x has a square root”. Each has one hole, marked by x. The premise “2 is positive” is the first open sentence with 2 put into the hole; the conclusion is the second, with 2 put into its hole. The first premise does something else with the holes, which we come to in the next subsection. Open sentences are the missing parts, and they deserve a name. A predicate is a statement with holes in it; filling every hole with a name of an object gives a statement. A predicate is an open sentence with one or more marked holes. The number of holes is its arity: a predicate with one hole is one-place (or unary), with two holes two-place (binary), and so on. We write a predicate as a capital letter followed by its holes in parentheses: P(x) for “x is positive”, S(x) for “x has a square root”, D(x, y) for “x divides y”. The letters that mark the holes are variables: x, y, z, u, and in analysis also \varepsilon, \delta, N, n, and for primes and other natural numbers p, q. A constant is a name of one particular object: 0, 1, 2, or a letter a, b, c that has been given a fixed meaning. In words: a predicate says something about objects without saying which objects. The variables are placeholders, not objects. “x is positive” is about whatever will be put in for x, and until something is, it is neither true nor false. Many predicates of mathematics are written with a symbol between their two holes rather than a letter in front: x < y, x \le y, x = y, x \mid y. These are two-place predicates like any other; only the way of writing them differs. Membership x \in A, for a fixed set A, is a one-place predicate of x: “x is an element of A”. Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 develops sets and membership properly. Until then a set is understood informally, as a collection of objects (usually numbers), and nothing in this section uses more about a set A than whether a given object is an element of it. For sets A and B, A \subseteq B means that every element of A is an element of B; so A \subseteq 
R says that A is a set of real numbers. Objects can also be built from other objects: x + 1, x^2, \abs{x}, 2 \cdot y. The symbols that build them (+, squaring, \abs{\cdot}, \cdot) are function symbols, and an expression such as x^2 + 1 names an object as soon as x does. A function symbol may also be a letter, f(x). Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 defines functions as sets of pairs; here a function symbol is simply a way of naming one object in terms of others. Section 4.2 makes all of this exact, under the name term. For now, a term is any expression that names an object: a variable, a constant, or a function symbol applied to terms. Filling holes is the first way to turn a predicate into a statement. - P(2): “2 is positive”. A statement, and true. - P(-3): “-3 is positive”. A statement, and false. - D(3, 12): “3 divides 12”. True. - D(3, y): “3 divides y”. Still open: one hole is filled and one is not. It is a one-place predicate of y. - P(x^2 + 1): “x^2 + 1 is positive”. Still open, in x. (It happens to be true whatever real number x is, but that is a fact about the numbers, and the sentence still has a hole.) The last two items show that filling holes is not all or nothing. A predicate with some holes filled is a predicate with fewer holes. Only when every hole is filled, or closed in the way described next, do we have a statement. A clash of letters to keep apart. In Chapters 1 and 2, capital letters P, Q, R stood for whole statements, and Chapter 3 read them as atoms or as arbitrary formulas. In this chapter P, Q, R are predicate symbols, followed by their holes: P(x), R(x, y). A bare P or Q in this chapter, in a reference back to Chapters 1–3 or in a review exercise, is a statement letter as before. The parentheses tell the two uses apart. The small letters p, q, r were atoms in the argument that opened this section, which was written in the language of Chapter 3, and they are atoms again wherever a later section reads a formula with a truth table (Section 4.11). A formula of this chapter has no atoms (Section 4.2 replaces them by predicates with their holes), so inside one, p and q are variables, used for primes and other natural numbers. A property P(n) of natural numbers, as in the principle of induction (@ax-induction), was already a one-place predicate in this sense. Quantifiers and the domain There is a second way to turn “x is positive” into a statement, and the first premise of our argument uses it. The premise does not put a particular number into the hole of “x has a square root”. It says that the open sentence “if x is positive, then x has a square root” is true whatever real number is put in. The word “every” closes the hole without filling it. Two questions have to be answered before “whatever is put in” makes sense. What may be put in? And how many of those things must make the sentence true? The first question is answered by a domain of discourse, or domain: the collection of objects that the variables range over. For the argument above, the domain is the real numbers, 
R. In number theory it is often 
Z or 
N (in this book 
N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}, with 0). A domain always has at least one element; Section 4.11 explains why the book insists on this, and how it handles the empty set instead. The second question is answered by the quantifier. “For every” promises something of each object in the domain; “there exists” promises it of at least one. Let \varphi be an open sentence in which the variable x marks a hole (it may have other holes too). There are two quantifiers. - The universal quantifier:  orall x\, \varphi, read “for every x, \varphi”, “for all x, \varphi”, or “for each x, \varphi”. It is true when every element of the domain, put in for x, makes \varphi true. - The existential quantifier: \exists x\, \varphi, read “there exists an x such that \varphi”, “there is an x with \varphi”, or “for some x, \varphi”. It is true when at least one element of the domain, put in for x, makes \varphi true. In words:  orall x and \exists x each close the hole marked x, so they remove x from the list of holes.  orall x\, \varphi makes one claim about the whole domain at once: no element is an exception. \exists x\, \varphi claims that there is at least one element for which \varphi holds, and it does not say which, or how many. “At least one” includes the case of exactly one and the case of all of them. The word “some” in mathematics never means “some but not all”. With these, the first premise of our argument, over the domain 
R, is  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o S(x)  igr), “for every x, if x is positive, then x has a square root”. The second premise is P(2) and the conclusion is S(2). Now the shared parts are visible: P occurs in both premises, S in the first premise and the conclusion, and 2 in the second premise and the conclusion. The rule of Section 4.3 uses the first premise with x replaced by 2, giving P(2) 	o S(2), and ulename{{	o}E} finishes. Notice the 	o inside the quantifier. The premise does not say that every real number is positive and has a square root; it says that every real number which is positive has one. The subsection on bounded quantifiers below explains why a “for every” restricted to part of the domain always comes with an implication. “True” in this section, and up to Section 4.11, means what it means in ordinary mathematics: we look at the domain and ask whether every element, or some element, makes the sentence true. Section 4.11 turns this reading into a definition, with models. Until then the reading is used only to understand sentences and to decide whether they are true as statements about numbers. Every claim that a sentence can be derived from others will be proved by writing a derivation, never by this reading. The same sentence over different domains A quantified sentence is a claim about its domain, so changing the domain can change its truth value. Two examples show how. Take  orall x\, (x \ge 0), “every x is at least 0”. - Over 
N it is true: every natural number is at least 0. - Over 
Z it is false: the integer -1 is in the domain, and -1 \ge 0 is false. One element of the domain that makes \varphi false is enough to make  orall x\, \varphi false. Such an element is a counterexample. To show that the sentence is true over 
N, on the other hand, we had to say something about every natural number at once. Take \exists x\, (x^2 = 2), “some x has square 2”. - Over 
R it is true: the real number \sqrt{2} has square 2. (Its existence is a school fact here; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it from the axioms of the real numbers.) - Over 
Q it is false: that no rational number has square 2 is exactly @thm-sqrt2-irrational. One element that makes \varphi true is enough to make \exists x\, \varphi true. Such an element is a witness. To show that the sentence is false over 
Q, on the other hand, a theorem about every rational number was needed, and Chapter 2 proved it by contradiction. The two quantifiers are mirror images. For  orall, a single counterexample refutes and a general argument confirms. For \exists, a single witness confirms and a general argument refutes. Section 4.9 makes the mirror exact: “not every x satisfies \varphi” says the same as “some x fails \varphi”. Over which of the domains 
Z_{>0} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}, 
Z, 
R is the sentence \exists x\, (x + x = x) true? Give a witness where it is true, and a reason where it is false. Only x = 0 satisfies x + x = x, since subtracting x from both sides gives x = 0. So the sentence is true over 
Z and over 
R, with the witness 0. It is false over 
Z_{>0}, which does not contain 0: every n \in 
Z_{>0} has n + n > n, since n > 0. (Over 
N = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\} it would be true, again with the witness 0.) Reading a quantified sentence Quantified sentences are read from the outside in: the first quantifier governs everything after it, and inside it may sit another quantifier, a connective, or a predicate. Reading aloud slowly, one symbol at a time, is the most reliable way to understand one. Here are three, simplest first. [Reading three sentences] Read each sentence aloud, say what it claims, and decide whether it is true over the domain given. 1.  orall x\, (x^2 \ge 0), over 
R. 2. \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \le y), over 
N. 3. 
eg\exists p\,  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) \wedge  orall q\, (\mathrm{Prime}(q) 	o q \le p)  igr), over 
N, where \mathrm{Prime}(p) is the one-place predicate “p is prime”. (a) “For every x, x^2 is at least 0.” The claim is about every real number, and it is true: the square of a real number is never negative (a school fact about signs: x \cdot x is a product of two numbers of the same sign, or 0). (b) “There is an x such that for every y, x \le y.” Unpack from the outside. The outer quantifier \exists x asks for one natural number x. What must be true of it is the inside,  orall y\, (x \le y): every natural number y is at least x. So the sentence says that 
N has a least element. It is true, with the witness x = 0: every natural number is at least 0. (c) The outer symbol is 
eg, so the sentence denies what follows. What follows is \exists p\, (\dots): there is a p that is prime and such that every prime q is at most p. Such a p would be a largest prime. So the sentence says “there is no largest prime”. It is true: this is the ancient theorem that there are infinitely many primes. Nothing in this book depends on that theorem; here it is only something to read. Notice the shape inside (c):  orall q\, (\mathrm{Prime}(q) 	o q \le p), “every prime is at most p”, has an implication under the  orall. It speaks about primes only, and the implication is how a “for every” is restricted to them. The next subsection makes this a rule of writing. The sentence in (b) has two quantifiers, and they come in a definite order: first \exists x, then  orall y. The order matters, and the subsection “The order of quantifiers” below is about it. First, restricted quantifiers. Bounded quantifiers Mathematics rarely says “for every real number”. It says “for every \varepsilon > 0”, “for every x \in A”, “there is an n \ge N”. The quantifier ranges over a part of the domain, described by a condition. There is no new quantifier for this; the condition is written into the sentence with a connective. Which connective turns out to matter. A “for every” restricted to a condition is an implication; a “there exists” restricted to a condition is a conjunction. [Bounded Quantifier] Let A be a set, x a variable, and \varphi an open sentence. The bounded quantifiers are the abbreviations  egin{aligned}  orall x \in A \; \varphi \quad &	ext{stands for} \quad  orall x\, (x \in A 	o \varphi), \ \exists x \in A \; \varphi \quad &	ext{stands for} \quad \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi). \end{aligned} In the same way, for a term a in which x does not occur,  orall x > a \; \varphi stands for  orall x\, (x > a 	o \varphi) and \exists x > a \; \varphi for \exists x\, (x > a \wedge \varphi), and likewise with \ge, <, \le in place of >. In words: “for every x in A, \varphi” means “for every x whatsoever, if x is in A, then \varphi”. “There is an x in A with \varphi” means “there is an x that is in A and satisfies \varphi”. The condition x \in A, or x > a, is the bound. A bounded quantifier is not a new symbol of the language: it is shorthand, and every statement about it is a statement about the formula it stands for. The display after @ax-induction, in Section 3.2, used  orall n \in 
N as an abbreviation of the words “for every natural number n”. It was already this bounded form:  orall n \in 
N\;  igl( P(n) 	o P(n + 1)  igr) stands for  orall n\,  igl( n \in 
N 	o (P(n) 	o P(n + 1))  igr). Why 	o under  orall, and \wedge under \exists. Try the other choices and see what they say. Take the domain 
R, the set A = \{1, 2\}, and the open sentence x > 5. - “Every element of A is greater than 5” is false: 1 is not. The correct form  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x > 5) is false too, with the counterexample x = 1, which is in A and not greater than 5. The wrong form  orall x\, (x \in A \wedge x > 5) says that every real number is in A and greater than 5. It is false as well, but for a reason that has nothing to do with A’s elements: x = 0 is not in A. Change A to \{6, 7\} and the correct form becomes true while the wrong one stays false. - “Some element of A is greater than 5” is false for A = \{1, 2\}. The correct form \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge x > 5) is false too: no real number is both in A and greater than 5. The wrong form \exists x\, (x \in A 	o x > 5) is true, with the witness x = 0: since 0 
otin A, the implication “if 0 \in A then 0 > 5” has a false hypothesis and is true (vacuous truth, the phenomenon behind @prp-vacuous-implication). So a  orall with \wedge inside claims too much: it says the whole domain lies in A. An \exists with 	o inside claims too little: anything outside A is a witness. Neither says what was meant. An existential quantifier with an implication directly inside, \exists x\, (\alpha 	o  eta), is almost always a mistranslation. Over 
R, “some element of \{1, 2\} exceeds 5” is false, but \exists x\, (x \in \{1, 2\} 	o x > 5) is true, because x = 0 makes the hypothesis false. When you write \exists and then 	o, check whether you meant \wedge. One domain per formula. The logic of this book has a single domain for all the variables of a formula. Mathematics often mixes kinds of objects in one sentence: in “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N \in 
N such that for every n \ge N, …”, the letter \varepsilon is a real number, while N and n are natural numbers. The convention is: the domain is the larger kind (here 
R), and the smaller kind enters as a bound (\exists N \in 
N,  orall n \in 
N). So the sentence begins  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \dots  igr), and n ranges over real numbers that happen to be required, by the bound, to be natural numbers. A sequence (a_n) becomes a function symbol a, with a(n), written a_n, the n-th term. Its values at real numbers that are not natural numbers are never used, because a is only ever applied to variables bounded by n \in 
N. We state this convention once, here; every translation in this chapter follows it. The empty set. Bounded quantifiers make sense even when the bound is never satisfied. Let \emptyset be the empty set, the set with no elements (Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 introduces it properly), so that x \in \emptyset is false for every x. -  orall x \in \emptyset \; \varphi stands for  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi). For every x, the hypothesis x \in \emptyset is false, so the implication is true. The sentence is true, whatever \varphi says. For example, “every element of \emptyset is greater than 5” and “every element of \emptyset is less than 5” are both true. - \exists x \in \emptyset \; \varphi stands for \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset \wedge \varphi). No x makes the first conjunct true, so the sentence is false, whatever \varphi says. Section 2.1 met this phenomenon for implications: a statement whose hypothesis never holds is true, and says nothing. A universal statement about the elements of an empty set is true for the same reason, because there is nothing to test. This is the reading; Section 4.4 derives the universal half with the rules. “Every element of A has property \varphi” does not imply “some element of A has property \varphi”. It fails when A is empty: “every element of \emptyset is greater than 5” is true, and “some element of \emptyset is greater than 5” is false. The step from “every” to “some” needs an element, and the bound can remove all of them. The order of quantifiers A sentence with two quantifiers of different kinds can change its meaning completely when they are swapped. This is the single most important fact about reading quantifiers, and the definitions of analysis depend on it. [Swapping two quantifiers] Over the domain 
R, compare 	ext{(i)} \ \  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad 	ext{(ii)} \ \ \exists y\,  orall x\, (x + y = 0) . Read each aloud, and decide which is true. (i) “For every x there is a y with x + y = 0”: every real number has an additive inverse. It is true. Given any real x, the number y = -x satisfies x + y = x + (-x) = 0. (ii) “There is a y such that for every x, x + y = 0”: one single number y is an inverse of every real number at once. It is false. Whatever real number y is proposed, take x = 1 - y; then x + y = 1 
e 0. So no y works. The two sentences have the same letters, the same quantifiers and the same equation. Only the order differs. In (i), the y may be chosen after x is known, so it may depend on x: the witness -x is a different number for each x. In (ii), y must be chosen first, once and for all, and then it must work for every x that comes after. What makes the pair work as an example? Two properties, and any other pair with the same shape would do as well. First, for each x separately there is a suitable y. Second, no one y is suitable for all x together, because each y serves only one x (here, only x = -y). Quantifiers as a game. The difference in @exm-quantifier-order-sum can be felt by reading a sentence as a game between two players. The reading applies to a sentence whose quantifiers all stand at the front, unnegated, followed by an inside with no quantifiers, as in (i) and (ii); a bounded quantifier such as  orall \varepsilon > 0 counts, its bound being checked with the inside. The challenger chooses a value for each  orall variable and tries to make the sentence false. The defender chooses a value for each \exists variable and tries to make it true. They move in the order in which the quantifiers are written, left to right, and each player sees every move made so far. When all variables have values, the inside is checked. The sentence is true exactly when the defender has a way of playing that wins against every choice of the challenger. A quantifier under a 
eg, or in the hypothesis of an implication, changes sides: 
eg  orall x\, \varphi is played as \exists x\, 
eg \varphi, with the defender moving. Section 4.9 proves the laws that push a 
eg inward in this way. - In (i), the challenger moves first and picks some x. The defender sees x and answers y = -x. The defender always wins. - In (ii), the defender moves first and must commit to some y without knowing x. The challenger sees y and answers x = 1 - y. The challenger always wins. Read the dependency off the order: a variable may depend on the variables quantified to its left, and only on them. In (i), y is to the right of x, so the choice of y may use x. In (ii), y is to the left, so it may not. Sections 4.4 to 4.6 will show this same dependence as a fact about the boxes of a derivation, and Section 4.10 shows that it is the whole difference between continuity and uniform continuity. When swapping is harmless. Two quantifiers of the same kind may be swapped.  orall x\,  orall y\, \varphi and  orall y\,  orall x\, \varphi both say that \varphi holds for every choice of the pair; in the game, the challenger makes both moves, and the order of the challenger’s own moves gives nothing away. Likewise \exists x\, \exists y\, \varphi and \exists y\, \exists x\, \varphi both say that some pair works. Section 4.4 derives the first swap with the rules. For quantifiers of different kinds, one direction is always safe: if one y works for every x, then for every x some y works (the same one). Section 4.6 derives this, \exists y\,  orall x\, \varphi to  orall x\, \exists y\, \varphi, and @exm-quantifier-order-sum shows that the other direction fails. Over the domain 
N, swap the two quantifiers in “for every n there is a prime larger than n”, that is, in  orall n\, \exists p\,  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) \wedge p > n  igr). Read the result aloud. Is it true? The swapped sentence is \exists p\,  orall n\,  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) \wedge p > n  igr): “there is a prime that is larger than every natural number”. It is false. Whatever p is proposed, take n = p: then p > n is false, so the inside fails. (The original sentence is true; it is another form of the theorem that there are infinitely many primes, which we do not use.) As in @exm-quantifier-order-sum, the original lets the prime depend on n, and the swapped sentence demands one prime for all n at once. Words that hide quantifiers English marks quantifiers loosely, and mathematical English has habits that hide them altogether. Three traps are worth naming now, before they cause trouble in a translation. The word “any” can mean “every” or “some”, and only the sentence around it decides. “Any x in A is positive” means every element of A is positive:  orall x \in A\; (x > 0). “If any x in A is positive, then A is nonempty” means if some element is positive: \exists x \in A\; (x > 0) 	o \dots. When you meet “any”, rewrite the sentence with “every” and with “some”, and keep the one that says what was meant. Hidden universal quantifiers. A theorem stated as “if n is even, then n^2 is even” has no quantifier word in it, and yet it is not about one number. It means: for every integer n, if n is even, then n^2 is even. A letter that is not introduced anywhere, in the statement of a theorem, is read with a “for every” in front. Chapter 5 names this convention and lists the others that written mathematics relies on. When translating, put the hidden quantifier back first. An implication inside \exists. This is the warning after @def-bounded-quantifier, and it deserves repeating because it comes up in translations of analysis: “there is an N such that, if n \ge N, then …” is not the shape of the sentence displayed under One domain per formula above, where the implication n \ge N 	o \dots sits under  orall n \in 
N. The implication belongs under a  orall: “there is an N such that for every n, if n \ge N, then …”. What comes next We can now read quantified sentences and decide, as mathematicians, whether they are true. We cannot yet reason with them in the sense of Chapters 1 and 2: there is no rule for using a “for every”, for proving one, for proving a “there exists”, or for using one. Section 4.2 first makes the language exact, because the rules will need to say precisely what “put 2 in for x” means. Sections 4.3 to 4.6 then give the four rules, one per section, in the same way as Chapters 1 and 2 gave the rules for the connectives. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Read each sentence aloud, and say over which of the domains 
N, 
Z, 
R it is true: (i)  orall x\, (x + 1 > x); (ii) \exists x\, (x + 1 = 0); (iii)  orall x\, \exists y\, (y < x); (iv) \exists x\, (2 \cdot x = 1); (v)  orall x\, (x \cdot x \ge x). 2. With domain 
R, which of the following translates “some element of A is negative”? (i) \exists x\, (x \in A 	o x < 0); (ii) \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge x < 0); (iii)  orall x\, (x \in A \wedge x < 0). For each of the two others, say what it claims instead. 3. What is the arity of the predicate “x + y = z”, and how many holes does “3 + y = z” have left? 4. True or false, with a reason:  orall x \in \emptyset \; (x 
e x) is true. (a) (i) “For every x, x + 1 is greater than x.” True over all three domains: adding 1 always gives a larger number. (ii) “There is an x with x + 1 = 0.” The only solution is x = -1. False over 
N, which does not contain -1; true over 
Z and 
R, with the witness -1. (iii) “For every x there is a y smaller than x.” False over 
N: for x = 0 there is no natural number y < 0. True over 
Z and 
R: given x, take y = x - 1. (iv) “There is an x with 2x = 1.” The only solution is x =  rac{1}{2}. False over 
N and 
Z, true over 
R with the witness  rac{1}{2}. (v) “For every x, x \cdot x is at least x.” True over 
N: if x = 0, then x \cdot x = 0 = x; if x \ge 1, then x \cdot x \ge 1 \cdot x = x. True over 
Z: an integer is either at least 1, as before, or at most 0, and then x \cdot x \ge 0 \ge x. False over 
R: the counterexample x =  rac{1}{2} has x \cdot x =  rac{1}{4} <  rac{1}{2}. (b) (ii) is the translation (@def-bounded-quantifier: \wedge under \exists). (i) is true as soon as some real number lies outside A, since that number makes the implication vacuously true; so it can be true when no element of A is negative (for A = \{1\}, say). (iii) claims that every real number is in A and negative, which is false whatever A is (take x = 0). (c) It has three holes, x, y, z, so it is three-place. Filling x with 3 leaves two holes, y and z. (d) True. It stands for  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o x 
e x). For every x the hypothesis x \in \emptyset is false, so the implication is true, even though its conclusion x 
e x is false for every x. B. Practice [B1: Ordered quantifiers] Determine which of the following sentences are true over the domain given. Justify your answer: give the witness a true \exists asks for (as a function of the earlier variables, if there are any), or the counterexample that refutes a  orall. 1.  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), over 
N. 2.  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 1), over 
N. 3. \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \cdot y = y), over 
R. 4.  orall x\, \exists y\, (y \cdot y = x), over 
R. (a) True. Given any natural number x, the natural number y = x + 1 satisfies x < y. The witness depends on x, which the order  orall x\, \exists y allows. (b) False. The challenger chooses x = 2. Then x + y = 1 forces y = -1, which is not a natural number; every natural y gives 2 + y \ge 2. So for x = 2 no y works. (For x = 0 and x = 1 the witnesses y = 1 and y = 0 do exist, so the challenger must choose with care.) (Over 
Z the sentence would be true, with y = 1 - x.) (c) True, with the witness x = 1: for every real y, 1 \cdot y = y. The witness is chosen first and does not depend on y, as the order \exists x\,  orall y demands. (d) False, with the counterexample x = -1: for every real y, y \cdot y \ge 0 > -1, so no y has y \cdot y = -1. [B2: Order matters] Give an example of a two-place predicate R(x, y) on the domain 
N such that  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) is true and \exists y\,  orall x\, R(x, y) is false. Check both claims. Take R(x, y): “y > x”.  orall x\, \exists y\, (y > x) is true. Given any natural number x, the natural number y = x + 1 satisfies y > x. \exists y\,  orall x\, (y > x) is false. Whatever natural number y is proposed, take x = y: then y > x is false. So no y is greater than every x. Any answer must have two properties, and a different answer can be checked against them. 1. Every x has a partner: for each x \in 
N there is at least one y with R(x, y). 2. No y is a partner of every x: for each y \in 
N there is at least one x with R(x, y) false. For example, “y 
e x” also works: each x has the partner x + 1, and each y fails to be a partner of x = y. So does “y \ge x”: each x is its own partner, and each y fails to be a partner of x = y + 1. A predicate that does not work is “y \ge 1”: property 1 holds, but property 2 fails, because y = 1 is a partner of every x, so \exists y\,  orall x\, (y \ge 1) is true. C. Going deeper [C1: A least element] Decide whether \exists x\,  orall y\, (x \le y) is true over each of the domains 
N, 
Z, [0, 1] and (0, 1]. Give the witness where it is true, and where it is false show that every proposed x is defeated by some y. The sentence says that the domain has a least element: one x that is at most every element y. Over 
N: true, with the witness x = 0. Every natural number y satisfies 0 \le y. Over 
Z: false. Let x be any integer. The integer y = x - 1 satisfies y < x, so x \le y fails. No integer is least. Over [0, 1]: true, with the witness x = 0. Every y \in [0, 1] satisfies 0 \le y, by the definition of the interval. Over (0, 1]: false. Let x \in (0, 1], so 0 < x \le 1. The number y =  rac{x}{2} satisfies 0 <  rac{x}{2} < x \le 1, so y \in (0, 1] and y < x; hence x \le y fails. The defeating y depends on the proposed x, which is allowed, because in the game the challenger chooses y after seeing x. The last two domains differ by a single point, 0, and that point is exactly the least element of [0, 1]. Removing it leaves a set with no least element, although every element of (0, 1] is still at least 0. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 returns to this distinction between a least element and a greatest lower bound. [C2: The wrong connective] Take the domain 
R. 1. The sentence “every element of A is positive” is mistranslated as  orall x\, (x \in A \wedge x > 0), and “some element of A is positive” as \exists x\, (x \in A 	o x > 0). For each mistranslation, give a set A \subseteq 
R for which it has a different truth value from the English sentence. 2. Show that the first mistranslation is false for every set A \subseteq 
R, and the second is true for every set A \subseteq 
R. What does this say about how much each one tells us about A? (a) Take A = \{1\} for the first. “Every element of \{1\} is positive” is true. The mistranslation claims that every real x is in \{1\} and positive; x = 0 is neither, so it is false. Take A = \{-1\} for the second. “Some element of \{-1\} is positive” is false, since its only element is negative. The mistranslation is true, with the witness x = 0: since 0 
otin \{-1\}, the implication “if 0 \in A, then 0 > 0” has a false hypothesis and is true. (b) For the first, let A \subseteq 
R be any set. The real number x = 0 does not satisfy x > 0, so it does not satisfy x \in A \wedge x > 0, whatever A is. It is a counterexample to the  orall, so the sentence is false. For the second, let A \subseteq 
R be any set, and consider the real number x = 1. The conclusion 1 > 0 is true, so the implication 1 \in A 	o 1 > 0 is true whether or not 1 \in A. Hence x = 1 is a witness, whatever A is, and the sentence is true. So neither mistranslation tells us anything about A at all: the first is false and the second is true, whichever set A is. A sentence whose truth value does not depend on A cannot express a property of A. This is the precise sense in which the wrong connective “claims too much” under  orall and “too little” under \exists. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: a set for the first mistranslation, with both truth values checked. - 2: a set for the second mistranslation, with both truth values checked, and the implication at the witness justified (its hypothesis is false, or its conclusion is true). - 3: for the first, for an arbitrary A, a real number (the same for every A, or chosen by cases covering every A) that fails x \in A \wedge x > 0, with the check. - 3: for the second, for an arbitrary A, a witness (the same for every A, or chosen by cases covering every A) at which x \in A 	o x > 0 holds, with a reason that covers every A (its conclusion is true, or a check in every case). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a witness or counterexample that depends on A in (b) without a case split covering every A; reading \exists x\, (x \in A 	o x > 0) as “some element of A is positive”.

title: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content:
Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution Section 4.1 read quantified sentences the way a mathematician does, by eye. That was enough to understand them, and it is not enough to reason with them. Each quantifier rule of Sections 4.3 to 4.6, and the rule for using an equation in Section 4.7, has the form “put the term t in for the variable x in the formula \varphi”, written \varphi[t/x], and a rule has to say exactly which symbols change and which do not. This section makes the language of Section 4.1 exact, in the way Section 3.1 made the propositional language exact, and then defines the operation \varphi[t/x]. The one new thing is substitution, together with the single way in which it can go wrong, called capture. Terms, formulas, and free variables are the smaller definitions it needs, and each comes just before it is used. Which letters are holes Three sentences, over the domain 
N: - “x > 2” is not a statement. It is the open sentence of item (e) of @exm-statements, true for some values of x and false for others. - “ orall x\, (x^2 \ge 0)” is a statement, and a true one. The letter x still appears, but the quantifier has closed its hole: the sentence does not ask which x we mean. - “ orall x\, (x \ge y)” is neither true nor false as it stands. It is true when y is 0 (every natural number is at least 0) and false when y is 1 (the number 0 is not at least 1). It is an open sentence in y, although it begins with a quantifier. So the question “is this a statement?” is not answered by looking for quantifiers. It is answered by asking which letters are still holes. In the third sentence x is closed by  orall x and y is open. The open letters will be called free, and the closed ones bound. Here is why the difference matters for reasoning. Over 
N, the sentence \exists y\, (y 
e x) is an open sentence in x, and it is true for every x: given x, the number y = x + 1 differs from it. Now suppose that we want to say the same thing about a particular number named by another letter, and we put y in for x without thinking. The result is \exists y\, (y 
e y), “some number differs from itself”, which is false. Nothing about numbers went wrong. The y that we put in landed inside the scope of \exists y, and the quantifier took hold of it: the new y was meant to name a number from outside, and it has become the quantifier’s own placeholder. This is capture. Capture is the one trap of substitution, and the rules of Sections 4.3 to 4.7 substitute at almost every step. So we need exact answers to three questions: what the expressions are that can be put in; which occurrences of x get replaced; and when putting t in for x is safe. (A remark on the choice of example. The formula  orall y\, (y 
e x) looks just as natural, and putting y in for x there gives  orall y\, (y 
e y). But  orall y\, (y 
e x) is false for every x already, since y = x is a counterexample, and a false sentence turned into a false sentence shows nothing.) Terms Section 3.1 described the propositional language by its alphabet and its formation rules. The language of predicate logic has more symbols, of more kinds. - Variables: x, y, z, u, with subscripts x_0, x_1, y_0, \dots, and in analysis also \varepsilon, \delta, N, n, k, L, and for primes and other natural numbers p, q. There are infinitely many, so that a fresh one is always available. Each is one symbol. - Constant symbols, such as 0, 1, 2, a, b, c. (A letter may be a constant in one language and a function symbol in another: in a language with a sequence, a is the sequence’s one-place function symbol, as below, and not a constant.) - Function symbols, each with a number of places n \ge 1, its arity: f and g, the arithmetic symbols +, \cdot and - (two places), and - in front of a number, halving \cdot/2, squaring and \abs{\cdot} (one place). The one-place and the two-place minus are different symbols written alike; the number of terms they are applied to shows which is meant. - Predicate symbols, each with an arity n \ge 1: P, Q, R, S, <, \le, >, \ge, \mathrm{Prime}, and \in A for a fixed set A (one place, as in Section 4.1). - Equality =, which every language has. - The constant  ot, the connectives 
eg, \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow of Chapter 3, and the quantifier symbols  orall and \exists. - Parentheses (, ), and the comma. Which constant, function, and predicate symbols are available depends on the subject. For the argument of Section 4.1 we need the constant 2 and the one-place predicate symbols P and S. For arithmetic we need 0, 1, +, \cdot, and <. Every formula uses only finitely many symbols, and we never need to fix the whole list in advance. The first things to build are the names of objects. A term is a name of an object, built from variables and constants by function symbols. [Term] The terms are the strings given by the following clauses. 1. Every variable is a term, and every constant symbol is a term. 2. If f is a function symbol of arity n and t_1, \dots, t_n are terms, then f(t_1, \dots, t_n) is a term. 3. Nothing else is a term: a string is a term only if it is the last entry of a finite list of strings in which every entry is a variable, a constant symbol, or f(s_1, \dots, s_n) for some function symbol f of arity n and earlier entries s_1, \dots, s_n. In words: (Tm1) gives the starting pieces, the names that are not built from anything. (Tm2) applies a function symbol to as many terms as it has places, with the terms in parentheses and separated by commas. (Tm3) closes the door, exactly as clause (F4) of @def-formula did for propositional formulas: a term is something reached from variables and constants by finitely many uses of (Tm2). A variable of a term t is a variable that occurs in t. A term with no variables, such as 2 or f(c), names one fixed object once the symbols are interpreted; a term with variables, such as x + 1, names an object only once its variables have values. Shorthand. As with formulas in Section 3.1, we write terms in the familiar way and let the official form be understood. So x + y is shorthand for +(x, y), 2 \cdot y for \cdot(2, y), x^2 for the squaring symbol applied to x, -x for the one-place minus applied to x, x - y for the two-place minus applied to x and y, x/2 for halving applied to x, \abs{x} for \abs{\cdot} applied to x, and a_n for a(n), with a a one-place function symbol (the convention of Section 4.1 for sequences). The school conventions about grouping (\cdot before +, and so on) say which official term is meant. Here are terms, simplest first. - x and 2: by (Tm1). The degenerate terms, built in no steps; every argument about all terms has to handle them. - x + 1, officially +(x, 1): by (Tm2) from the terms x and 1. - f(f(c)): by (Tm2) twice, from c, for a one-place f. Its only building blocks are constants, so it has no variables. - \abs{a_n - L}, officially \abs{\cdot} igl( -(a(n), L)  igr), with the two-place minus: by (Tm2) three times, from the variables n and L. Its variables are n and L. The letter a is a function symbol, not a variable. And strings that are not terms, each by one clause: - x < 1 is not a term. It does not name an object; it says something about one. It is built with a predicate symbol, and (Tm2) uses only function symbols. It will be a formula. - f(x, y), for a one-place f, is not a term: (Tm2) applies f to exactly one term. Terms can be drawn as trees, exactly as formulas were in Section 3.1: a variable or a constant is a single node, and f(t_1, \dots, t_n) is a node labeled f with the trees of t_1, \dots, t_n below it, in order. And a term can be read in only one way. The proof is the proof of unique readability for formulas in Section 3.2 (@thm-unique-readability), with the parentheses and commas of (Tm2) doing the work that the parentheses of (F3) did there. We do not repeat it. Formulas Next, the statements and open sentences. Atomic formulas say something about terms; everything else is built from them by connectives and quantifiers. A first-order formula is built from predicates applied to terms, by the connectives and the two quantifiers. [First-Order Formula] The formulas (of predicate logic, or first-order formulas) are the strings given by the following clauses. 1. Atomic formulas. If R is a predicate symbol of arity n and t_1, \dots, t_n are terms, then R(t_1, \dots, t_n) is a formula. If t_1 and t_2 are terms, then t_1 = t_2 is a formula. And  ot is a formula. 2. If \varphi is a formula, then 
eg\varphi is a formula. 3. If \varphi and \psi are formulas, then (\varphi \wedge \psi), (\varphi \vee \psi), (\varphi 	o \psi), and (\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) are formulas. 4. If \varphi is a formula and x is a variable, then  orall x\, \varphi and \exists x\, \varphi are formulas. 5. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a finite list in which every entry is an atomic formula, or is built by (Fm2), (Fm3) or (Fm4) from earlier entries. In words, clause by clause. - (Fm1). The atomic formulas are the new starting pieces. They replace the atoms p, q, r of Chapter 3, and they have an inside: a predicate symbol and its terms. Equality is always there. The constant  ot is kept. - (Fm2), (Fm3). The connectives work exactly as in @def-formula, parentheses included. - (Fm4). The new clause. A quantifier symbol followed by a variable is put in front of a formula, with no parentheses, as

Structural induction and structural recursion (@thm-structural-induction, @thm-structural-recursion) carry over to first-order formulas with one change in the list of cases. The base case covers every atomic formula (and  ot), and there are two new building steps, from \varphi to  orall x\, \varphi and to \exists x\, \varphi, for every variable x, each with one part, like the step to 
eg\varphi. So, to prove that every formula has a property, prove it for the atomic formulas and  ot, and prove that it passes from \varphi to 
eg\varphi,  orall x\, \varphi, and \exists x\, \varphi, and from \varphi, \psi to (\varphi \circ \psi). To define a function on formulas, give one clause for each of these cases. The proofs in Section 3.2 go through word for word with the new cases added, and unique readability holds for the same reason; we use all three without repeating them. The same two principles hold for terms, with (Tm1) as the base case and (Tm2) as the one building step. Shorthand. The conventions of Section 3.1 for dropping parentheses stay, with three additions. 1. Two-place predicate symbols such as <, \le are written between their terms: x < y is shorthand for <(x, y). (When sets are themselves objects of the domain, as in Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1, \in is a two-place predicate symbol and x \in A is \in(x, A); in this chapter A is always a fixed set, so we treat \in A as one-place.) Parse trees. A parse tree for a first-order formula is drawn as in Section 3.1, with one new kind of node: a quantifier node, labeled  orall x or \exists x, with the tree of the formula it governs as its only subtree. The leaves are atomic formulas (or  ot); their terms have trees of their own, which we do not draw. Here is the tree of  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, R(x, y)  igr). The root is the quantifier node  orall x, so the formula’s main symbol is  orall x. Below it is the implication, with the atomic formula P(x) on the left and the quantifier node \exists y on the right, which governs the atomic formula R(x, y). Draw the parse tree of  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\,  orall x\, R(x, y), written in shorthand. What is its main symbol? By shorthand rule 2, each quantifier applies to the smallest formula after it, so the official formula is ( orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\,  orall x\, R(x, y)) and its main symbol is 	o. The root is 	o. Its left subtree is the node  orall x above the leaf P(x). Its right subtree is the node \exists y, below it the node  orall x, and below that the leaf R(x, y). The two  orall x nodes are on different branches. Free and bound occurrences The parse tree shows which quantifier governs which part of a formula. That is exactly what decides whether a letter is a hole. An occurrence of a variable is bound if a quantifier on that variable stands above it in the parse tree; otherwise it is free. [Free and Bound Variables] Let \varphi be a formula and x a variable. An occurrence of x in \varphi is an appearance of x inside one of the terms of an atomic formula of \varphi. (The x written just after a quantifier symbol, as in  orall x, is part of the quantifier node and is not an occurrence.) - An occurrence of x is bound if the path from its leaf up to the root of the parse tree passes through a quantifier node  orall x or \exists x, with the same variable x. The lowest such node binds the occurrence. - An occurrence that is not bound is free. - The scope of a quantifier node is the part of the tree below it: the formula it governs. - The variable x is a free variable of \varphi, or is free in \varphi, if at least one occurrence of x in \varphi is free. In words: an occurrence of x is bound when it lies in the scope of a quantifier on x; quantifiers on other variables do not bind it. If several quantifiers on x stand above it, the nearest one, the lowest in the tree, is the one that binds it. A free occurrence is a hole still open. A variable is free in a formula if it has at least one free occurrence, even if it has bound occurrences too. One more word, for the times when a variable must be new to a formula. A variable appears in \varphi if it is written anywhere in \varphi: inside a term, or just after a quantifier symbol. So y appears in  orall y\, P(x), although it has no occurrence there. A variable that does not appear in \varphi has no occurrence in \varphi, and no quantifier of \varphi is on it; every freshness condition of this chapter is stated with “appear” for that reason. [Sentence] A sentence is a formula with no free variables. A sentence is what Chapter 1 called a statement, once the domain and the symbols are fixed: every hole is closed, so it is true or false. A formula with free variables is an open sentence, true or false only once values are given to its free variables. Examples, simplest first. The domain is irrelevant to all of them: being free or bound is a matter of the string, not of what it means. -  ot and P(c) are sentences: they contain no variables at all. So is  orall x\, P(c). These are the degenerate cases. -  orall x\, (x^2 \ge 1): the single occurrence of x lies below the node  orall x, so it is bound. A sentence. -  orall x\, (x \ge y): the occurrence of x is bound by  orall x; the occurrence of y has no quantifier on y above it, so it is free. The free variables are y alone. Not a sentence. -  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, R(x, y)  igr), drawn above: both occurrences of x are bound by the root; the occurrence of y in R(x, y) is bound by \exists y. A sentence. - P(x) \wedge  orall x\, Q(x): the occurrence of x in P(x) is free (no quantifier stands above it: the  orall x governs only Q(x)), and the occurrence in Q(x) is bound. So x is a free variable of this formula, and it is not a sentence. -  orall x\, \exists x\, P(x): the occurrence of x has two quantifiers on x above it, and the lower one, \exists x, binds it. The outer  orall x binds nothing. A sentence. The recursive description. In proofs about all formulas we need “x is free in \varphi” in the form that structural induction can use, one case per clause of @def-first-order-formula. - x is free in an atomic formula exactly when x occurs in one of its terms; x is never free in  ot. - x is free in 
eg\varphi exactly when x is free in \varphi. - x is free in (\varphi \circ \psi) exactly when x is free in \varphi or in \psi. - x is free in  orall y\, \varphi, and in \exists y\, \varphi, exactly when x is a different variable from y and x is free in \varphi. Each line is read off the tree. In an atomic formula there are no quantifier nodes, so every occurrence is free. The tree of 
eg\varphi or (\varphi \circ \psi) adds a root that is not a quantifier node, so it binds nothing. The tree of  orall y\, \varphi adds the root  orall y on top of the tree of \varphi: an occurrence of x inside \varphi keeps its path, with one more node at the top, so it is free in  orall y\, \varphi exactly when it was free in \varphi and the new node is not a quantifier on x, that is, when x and y are different variables. The only case with any content is a quantifier on a variable other than x, where the substitution is passed on, and the induction hypothesis applies because x is still not free inside. The difference between the safe case and the two unsafe ones is exactly this: whether a variable of t is quantified somewhere above a free occurrence of x. A term is free for x when putting it in for x lets none of its variables be captured. [Free For] Let t be a term, x a variable, and \varphi a formula. The term t is free for x in \varphi if no free occurrence of x in \varphi lies in the scope of a quantifier  orall y or \exists y such that y is a variable of t. In words: look at each place where t will go, that is, at each free occurrence of x. Look at the quantifiers above it in the tree. If none of them is on a variable of t, the substitution is safe there. The term is free for x when it is safe at every such place. Informally: no variable of t becomes bound when t is put in. Four special cases, each immediate from the definition, cover most uses. - A term with no variables (2, c, f(c)) is free for every variable in every formula: there is no y to capture. - The variable x is free for x in every formula. A free occurrence of x never lies in the scope of a quantifier on x; if it did, it would be bound. - A variable z that does not appear in \varphi is free for every variable in \varphi: no quantifier of \varphi is on z. - If x is not free in \varphi, every term is free for x in \varphi: there are no free occurrences to check. (And then \varphi[t/x] = \varphi by the claim above.) In our examples: y is not free for x in \exists y\, (y 
e x), because the free occurrence of x lies in the scope of \exists y and y is a variable of the term y. The term y + 1 is not free for x in \exists y\, (y > x), for the same reason. And y + 1 is free for x in  orall z\, (x < z): the only quantifier above the free occurrence of x is on z, which is not a variable of y + 1. The recursive description. For induction proofs, “free for” can be read off case by case, like “free”: - t is free for x in every atomic formula and in  ot; - t is free for x in 
eg\varphi exactly when it is free for x in \varphi, and in (\varphi \circ \psi) exactly when it is free for x in both \varphi and \psi; - t is free for x in  orall y\, \varphi (and in \exists y\, \varphi) exactly when either x is not free in  orall y\, \varphi, or y is not a variable of t and t is free for x in \varphi. The first two lines hold because an atomic formula has no quantifiers and a connective node is not a quantifier. For the third: if x is not free in  orall y\, \varphi, there is nothing to check. If it is free, then y is a different variable and the free occurrences of x in  orall y\, \varphi are those in \varphi; each lies in the scope of the new root  orall y and of the quantifiers inside \varphi above it. The root is harmless exactly when y is not a variable of t, and the quantifiers inside are harmless exactly when t is free for x in \varphi. Why the definition. “Free for” is the precise condition under which \varphi[t/x] says about t what \varphi says about x. Each rule of Sections 4.3, 4.5, and 4.7 will carry it as a side condition, and Section 4.3 shows the capture example of this section turning a true premise into a false conclusion when the side condition is ignored. The definition asks for no more than it needs: a variable of t may be quantified elsewhere in \varphi, as long as no free occurrence of x lies in its scope. For instance, y is free for x in P(x) \wedge \exists y\, Q(y), and the result P(y) \wedge \exists y\, Q(y) says of y what the original said of x. Capture changes meaning, and it gives no warning: the definition of \varphi[t/x] returns a formula either way. Over

The result is  orall z\, (y + 1 < z), “y + 1 is smaller than every number”, which is what the original said about x. In  orall y\, (x < y): no. The occurrence of x lies in the scope of  orall y, and y is a variable of y + 1. The definition gives  orall y\, (y + 1 < y): “every number is larger than its own successor”. That is a sentence about no particular number at all, and a false one; the original said something about x, and the result should have said the same about y + 1. The y of y + 1 was captured. A bound variable is a placeholder, and the name of a placeholder does not matter. “Some number differs from x” can be written \exists y\, (y 
e x) or \exists z\, (z 
e x), just as \int_0^1 s^2 \, ds and \int_0^1 u^2 \, du are the same integral. So the way out is: rename the bound variable first, then substitute. Renaming. Let \varphi be a formula and y, z variables, with z not appearing in \varphi. The formula  orall z\, \varphi[z/y] is obtained from  orall y\, \varphi by renaming the bound variable y to z; likewise \exists z\, \varphi[z/y] from \exists y\, \varphi. The same may be done to a quantifier anywhere inside a larger formula. In words: change the variable after the quantifier, and change the occurrences it binds, to a letter that appears nowhere in the formula. The condition that z does not appear in \varphi does two jobs. It makes z free for y in \varphi (the third special case above), so no new z is captured by a quantifier inside \varphi. And it ensures that no free z already in \varphi is captured by the new quantifier  orall z. Without it, renaming can change the meaning:  orall y\, (y \ge z) says something about z (over 
N, that z = 0), and “renaming” y to z would give  orall z\, (z \ge z), a sentence that is simply true. Its status. Renaming is not a rule of the calculus, and we have not proved that it keeps meaning. Here is where it stands. For a renaming at the front of a formula,  orall y\, \varphi and  orall z\, \varphi[z/y] can each be derived from the other in three lines, once the rules of Section 4.4 are available; that section does it, and Section 4.6 does the same for \exists. A renaming inside a larger formula we take as a convention of this book: formulas that differ only by renaming bound variables are treated as saying the same thing. Its justification in terms of meaning follows from a lemma of Section 4.12 (@lem-term-substitution, with the variable z as the term), together with @lem-free-coincidence and an induction on the surrounding formula, which we do not carry out. Section 4.12 is optional, and nothing outside it depends on that lemma. The recipe. To put t in for x in \varphi when t is not free for x: rename each quantifier of \varphi that is on a variable of t and has a free occurrence of x in its scope, each to a different variable that appears neither in \varphi nor in t (each such step is a renaming in the sense above); then substitute. R, as intended. Which fresh letter we choose does not matter: two choices give formulas that differ only by a renaming. From now on, whenever a rule writes \varphi[t/x], it will require t to be free for x in \varphi, and if we want a t that is not, we rename first.
