N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2  igr). The term \varepsilon/2 contains the variable \varepsilon: the fixed \varepsilon of the proof, not the bound one of the hypothesis. It is free for \varepsilon in \varphi, because the only quantifiers above the free occurrences of \varepsilon in \varphi are on N and n. Section 4.3’s rule makes this step, and “\varepsilon/2 > 0” then comes from \varepsilon > 0 by arithmetic. “Take N = n.” Now suppose the proof has chosen N, so it knows \psi \ = \  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr), with N free. A tempting step is to “apply this with n in place of N”. No rule allows this: N has been chosen, not quantified, so no term may be put in for it. Writing the step out shows how badly it goes wrong, because n is not even free for N in \psi: the occurrence of N lies in the scope of  orall n. The substitution produces  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge n 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr), which says that every term of the sequence is within \varepsilon of L, a far stronger claim that does not follow. In words, the error is to let the threshold N be “the n we are looking at”, when n is the placeholder of “for all n \ge N”. A proof that needs a statement about a particular index names it with a new letter, say m \ge N, and substitutes m, which is free for n. Induction, as a formula. The display after @ax-induction in Section 3.2 used a property P(n). With substitution it can be written for any formula \varphi in which the variable n is free, as the formula \Bigl( \varphi[0/n] \ \wedge \  orall n \in 
N \,  igl( \varphi 	o \varphi[n + 1/n]  igr) \Bigr) \ 	o \  orall n \in 
N \; \varphi , where \varphi[0/n] plays the part of P(0) and \varphi[n + 1/n] the part of P(n + 1). The term n + 1 is free for n in \varphi: its only variable is n, and a free occurrence of n never lies in the scope of a quantifier on n. This is how the principle of induction reads in the language of this chapter; its status (a basic property of 
N) is unchanged. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each formula, mark each occurrence of each variable as free or bound, list the free variables, and say whether it is a sentence: (i)  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)); (ii) \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y); (iii)  orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x); (iv)  orall \varepsilon\,  igl( \varepsilon > 0 	o \exists \delta\, (\delta > 0 \wedge \delta < \varepsilon)  igr). 2. Which of the following are terms, and which are formulas, for one-place f, two-place g and two-place predicate R? (i) g(f(x), c); (ii) R(f(x), c); (iii) f(R(x, c)); (iv)  orall c\, R(c, c). 3. True or false, with a reason: if t is a variable, then t is free for x in every formula. 4. True or false, with a reason:  igl(  orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr)[c/x] is  orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(c). (a) (i) The single occurrence of x, in P(x), is bound by  orall x (the x after  orall belongs to the quantifier node and is not an occurrence); the occurrence of y in Q(y) is free (no quantifier on y). Free variables: y. Not a sentence. (ii) The occurrence of x is bound by \exists x, that of y by  orall y. No free variables: a sentence. (iii) By shorthand rule 2 this is ( orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x)). In the left part, x is bound by  orall x and y is free. In the right part, y is bound by \exists y and x is free (the  orall x governs only the left part). Free variables: x and y, each with one free and one bound occurrence. Not a sentence. (iv) Every occurrence of \varepsilon lies below  orall \varepsilon, and both occurrences of \delta lie below \exists \delta; 0 is a constant. A sentence. (b) (i) A term, by (Tm2) twice. (ii) A formula, atomic by (Fm1): the predicate R applied to the terms f(x) and c. (iii) Neither: R(x, c) is a formula, not a term, and (Tm2) applies f only to a term. (iv) Neither: (Fm4) puts a variable after  orall, and c is a constant symbol. (c) False. The variable y is not free for x in \exists y\, (y 
e x), since the free occurrence of x lies in the scope of \exists y. (A variable t is free for x when t is x itself, or when t does not appear in the formula.) (d) True. The formula is ( orall x\, P(x) \wedge Q(x)) by shorthand rule 2. The \wedge passes the substitution to both parts;  orall x\, P(x) is unchanged because its quantifier is on x, and Q(x) becomes Q(c). B. Practice [B1: Computing substitutions] Compute each substitution. Where the term is not free for the variable, say which quantifier would capture it, rename first, and then substitute. 1.  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr)[f(y)/x]. 2.  igl(  orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(x)  igr)[c/x]. 3.  igl(  orall y\, (x < y)  igr)[y + 1/x]. 4.  igl( \exists x\, (x = 2 \cdot y)  igr)[x/y]. 5.  igl( \exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(y)  igr)[x + 1/y]. (a) No quantifiers, so f(y) is free for x. Every occurrence of x is replaced: P(f(y)) \wedge R(f(y), y). The y inside f(y) and the y already in R(x, y) now stand side by side; with no quantifier around, both are the same free y, as intended. (b) By shorthand rule 2 the formula is ( orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(x)). The constant c has no variables, so it is free for x. The left part is unchanged (quantifier on x); the free x in P(x) becomes c:  orall x\, R(x, y) 	o P(c). (c) Not free for: the free occurrence of x lies in the scope of  orall y, and y is a variable of y + 1. Rename y to z, which appears nowhere:  orall z\, (x < z). Then substitute:  orall z\, (y + 1 < z). (Without renaming, the definition would give  orall y\, (y + 1 < y), which says nothing about y + 1.) (d) Not free for: the free occurrence of y lies in the scope of \exists x, and the term is x. Rename x to z: \exists z\, (z = 2 \cdot y), “y doubled is something”, then substitute: \exists z\, (z = 2 \cdot x). (Without renaming, the result would be \exists x\, (x = 2 \cdot x), “some number is its own double”, a claim about no particular number.) (e) By shorthand rule 2 the formula is (\exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(y)). The occurrence of y in y > x is bound, and the one in Q(y) is free and not in the scope of any quantifier; so x + 1 is free for y (the \exists y above the bound y is irrelevant, since that occurrence is not replaced). The result is \exists y\, (y > x) \wedge Q(x + 1). [B2: The set of free variables] For a term t, let \mathrm{Var}(t) be the set of variables of t, and for a formula \varphi, let \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) be the set of its free variables. 1. Write down clauses that define \mathrm{Var}(t) by recursion on terms and \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) by recursion on formulas, one clause for each case of @def-term and of @def-first-order-formula. 2. Use your clauses to compute \mathrm{FV} of  orall x\, (x < y) \wedge \exists y\, (y < x) and of  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = z), showing each step. (a) For terms:  egin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(x) &= \{x\} \ 	ext{ for a variable } x, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(c) = \emptyset, \ \mathrm{Var} igl( f(t_1, \dots, t_n)  igr) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_n). \end{aligned} For formulas:  egin{aligned} \mathrm{FV} igl( R(t_1, \dots, t_n)  igr) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_n), \ \mathrm{FV}(t_1 = t_2) &= \mathrm{Var}(t_1) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t_2), \qquad \mathrm{FV}( ot) = \emptyset, \ \mathrm{FV}(
eg\varphi) &= \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), \qquad \mathrm{FV} igl( (\varphi \circ \psi)  igr) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi), \ \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, \varphi) &= \mathrm{FV}(\exists x\, \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}. \end{aligned} These are the four lines of the recursive description of “free” in the text, rewritten as sets: x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) exactly when x is free in \varphi. By structural recursion (carried over to terms and to first-order formulas), each set of clauses defines exactly one function. (b) First formula. \mathrm{FV}(x < y) = \{x, y\}, so \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, (x < y)) = \{x, y\} \setminus \{x\} = \{y\}. \mathrm{FV}(y < x) = \{x, y\}, so \mathrm{FV}(\exists y\, (y < x)) = \{x\}. The conjunction gives \{y\} \cup \{x\} = \{x, y\}, which agrees with A1(a)(iii). Second formula. \mathrm{FV}(x + y = z) = \mathrm{Var}(x + y) \cup \mathrm{Var}(z) = \{x, y, z\}. Then \mathrm{FV}(\exists y\, (x + y = z)) = \{x, z\}, and \mathrm{FV}( orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = z)) = \{z\}. So the formula is an open sentence in z alone (over 
R it is true for every z: given x, take y = z - x). C. Going deeper [C1: What substitution does to the free variables] Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable and t a term, with t free for x in \varphi, and with x free in \varphi. 1. Prove that the free variables of \varphi[t/x] are the free variables of \varphi other than x, together with the variables of t: \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) =  igl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}  igr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), with the notation of B2. 2. Show, with the capture example \exists y\, (y > x), t = y + 1, that the conclusion can fail when t is not free for x. Show also, with an example of your own, that it can fail when x is not free in \varphi. [Hint 1] Structural induction on \varphi. The hypothesis “x free in \varphi” does not pass to both parts of (\varphi \circ \psi), so prove a statement that also covers formulas in which x is not free. [Hint 2] Prove, for every \varphi in which t is free for x: if x is free in \varphi, the displayed equation holds; if not, \varphi[t/x] = \varphi. Start with the same statement for terms: \mathrm{Var}(s[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) when x occurs in s. (a) Terms. Let s be a term in which x occurs. Then \mathrm{Var}(s[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). By induction on s: if s is the variable x, then s[t/x] = t and both sides are \mathrm{Var}(t). (A constant, or a variable other than x, does not contain x.) If s = f(s_1, \dots, s_n), then s[t/x] = f(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]); for each s_i containing x, the induction hypothesis gives \mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x]) = (\mathrm{Var}(s_i) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), and for each s_i not containing x, s_i[t/x] = s_i (as in the proof of the claim in the text). At least one s_i contains x, so the union over i is (\mathrm{Var}(s) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on \varphi, the statement S(\varphi): if t is free for x in \varphi, then \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) when x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi), and \varphi[t/x] = \varphi when x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\varphi). The second half is the claim proved in the text, for every \varphi; so in each case below we assume x \in \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) and prove the equation. Write E(\chi) for the set (\mathrm{FV}(\chi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t). Atomic. Let \varphi = R(s_1, \dots, s_n) with x occurring in some s_i. By the clause for atomic formulas, \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) is the union over i of the sets \mathrm{Var}(s_i[t/x]). Exactly as in the term case for f(s_1, \dots, s_n) (the result for terms for each s_i containing x, s_i[t/x] = s_i for the others, and at least one s_i containing x), this union is E(\varphi). The same for s_1 = s_2. ( ot has no free variables.) Negation. \mathrm{FV}((
eg\varphi)[t/x]) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = E(\varphi) = E(
eg\varphi), by the induction hypothesis (t is free for x in \varphi, and x is free in \varphi). Binary connective. Let x be free in (\varphi \circ \psi); then t is free for x in both parts, and x is free in at least one. If it is free in both, the induction hypothesis gives E(\varphi) \cup E(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi)). If it is free in \varphi only, then \psi[t/x] = \psi, and E(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi) = E((\varphi \circ \psi)), because x 
otin \mathrm{FV}(\psi). Symmetrically if it is free in \psi only. Quantifier. Let x be free in  orall y\, \varphi. Then y is not x and x is free in \varphi; and since t is free for x in  orall y\, \varphi while x is free there, y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t) and t is free for x in \varphi (the recursive description of “free for”). So  egin{aligned} \mathrm{FV} igl( ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x]  igr) &= \mathrm{FV} igl( \varphi[t/x]  igr) \setminus \{y\} =  igl( (\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t)  igr) \setminus \{y\} \ &=  igl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x, y\}  igr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) = E( orall y\, \varphi), \end{aligned} where the third equality uses y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t), and the last uses \mathrm{FV}( orall y\, \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{y\}. The case of \exists y is the same. This proves S(\varphi) for every formula, and (a) is its first half. (b) With \varphi = \exists y\, (y > x) and t = y + 1: \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) = \{x\}, so the equation would give \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = \{y\}. But \varphi[t/x] = \exists y\, (y > y + 1), whose set of free variables is \emptyset. The y of the term was captured, so it is not free in the result; the quantifier case of the proof fails because y \in \mathrm{Var}(t). For the second hypothesis, take \varphi = P(z) and t = y. Then x is not free in \varphi, and t is free for x (there are no quantifiers). Now \varphi[t/x] = P(z), with free variables \{z\}, while the equation would give \{z\} \cup \{y\} = \{y, z\}. Without a free x, nothing is put in, so the variables of t do not appear. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves the statement for terms, or states it and handles the variable case and the case of a compound term. - 2: sets up an induction that survives the connective case (strengthened statement, or a separate treatment of parts in which x is not free, using \varphi[t/x] = \varphi). - 3: the quantifier case, using that “free for” gives y 
otin \mathrm{Var}(t) and naming where that fact is used. - 1: the atomic and negation cases. - 2: both counterexamples in (b), each checked by computing both sides. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the equation \mathrm{FV}(\chi[t/x]) = (\mathrm{FV}(\chi) \setminus \{x\}) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t) for a part \chi in which x is not free (it fails there; see the second example in (b)); removing y from \mathrm{Var}(t) without justification. [C2: Renaming is not swapping] 1. Show that  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) and  orall y\, \exists x\, (y < x) are the same sentence up to renaming bound variables: give a sequence of renamings, each allowed by the condition of the text, leading from the first to the second. 2. Show that  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) and \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) are not the same up to renaming. Hint: what does a renaming leave unchanged? (a) A renaming needs a variable that does not appear in the formula, so the two letters cannot be exchanged in one step; go through a third letter z. 1. In  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), rename the bound x to z, which does not appear:  orall z\, \exists y\, (z < y). 2. Rename the bound y to x, which no longer appears:  orall z\, \exists x\, (z < x). 3. Rename the bound z to y, which no longer appears:  orall y\, \exists x\, (y < x). Each step renames one quantifier and the occurrences it binds, to a letter absent from the formula at that moment. The result is the second sentence. (Over 
N both say “there is no largest natural number”, in two spellings.) (b) A renaming changes only which letters are used. It does not change the parse tree’s shape, which quantifier symbol ( orall or \exists) sits at which node, or which quantifier node binds which occurrence. In  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) the root is a  orall node; in \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) the root is an \exists node. No sequence of renamings turns a  orall node into an \exists node, so no sequence of renamings leads from one sentence to the other. The two sentences also say different things: over 
N, the first is true (take y = x + 1) and the second false (for any y, take x = y). This is @exm-quantifier-order-sum again. Renaming changes the names of the placeholders; swapping changes the order in which they are chosen, and the order is what carries the meaning.

title: 4.3 Using "For Every": Instantiation
content:
Using “For Every”: Instantiation Section 4.2 made the language exact and defined the operation \varphi[t/x], “put the term t in for the variable x”, with its one hazard, capture. We can now give the first quantifier rule. It is the rule for using a universal statement: whatever holds for every object holds for the object named by any term we care to write. The rule is called ulename{ orall E}. It is the rule behind every “by the theorem, applied to x = 2”. With it alone, universal statements can be used but not proved, and the section ends at exactly that gap, which Section 4.4 fills. Applying a statement about everything Every application of a general fact to a particular case is one step of logic, and so far that step has been taken on trust. Three earlier places took it. - Section 1.4 used the theorem “if a < b and b < c, then a < c” at a = \sqrt{2}, b = 1.5, c = 2, and said that passing from “for all a, b, c” to one instance is a rule of its own, still to be stated. - In @exm-raa-zero (Section 2.5) the hypothesis was “x \le \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0”, and the proof applied it to the one number \varepsilon = x/2. - Section 4.1 opened with the argument “every positive real has a square root; 2 is positive; so 2 has a square root”, which a truth table calls invalid because it sees only three unrelated atoms. The same step happens in each: a statement about every object is applied to one object, named by a term. In the language of Section 4.2, the first premise of the square-root argument is  orall x\, (P(x) 	o S(x)), and applying it to 2 gives  igl( P(x) 	o S(x)  igr)[2/x] \ = \ P(2) 	o S(2), which is part (a) of @exm-computing-substitutions. From there ulename{{	o}E} finishes. All that is missing is a rule that licenses the first step. The rule A universal statement may be applied to any term: remove the quantifier and put the term in for the variable. [Universal Elimination] Here \varphi is a formula, x a variable, and t any term, subject to one side condition: t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Line i must be available at line k (the scope rule of @def-derivation). This rule is called ulename{ orall E} (universal elimination, or instantiation), and \varphi[t/x] is an instance of  orall x\, \varphi. In words: if a line says that \varphi holds for every x, then any later line, where that line is still available, may write what \varphi says about t. The rule cites one line and no box. Read the definition clause by clause. 1. The cited line begins with  orall x. Its main symbol must be the quantifier, with the whole of \varphi as its scope. By shorthand rule 2 of Section 4.2,  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(c) is an implication whose hypothesis is  orall x\, P(x); its main symbol is 	o, so ulename{ orall E} does not apply to it. A  orall buried inside another connective is not available to the rule until the rules for that connective have dug it out. 2. Any term. The term may be a constant (c, 2), a variable (y, or x itself), or a compound term (f(c), a - 1, \varepsilon/2). It may be a variable that already occurs elsewhere in the derivation. Nothing about the term has to be established first: ulename{ orall E} needs no line saying that t “exists” or “is in the domain”, because every term names an element of the domain. 3. Every free occurrence, by the same term. The new line is \varphi[t/x], so by @def-substitution every free occurrence of x in \varphi is replaced, and all of them by the same t. We do not choose which occurrences change. 4. Free for x. This is the condition of @def-free-for, and it is the rule’s only restriction. It forbids exactly the substitutions in which a variable of t would be captured by a quantifier of \varphi. 5. Line i is available. Line i must be available at line k (the scope rule of @def-derivation). Every rule asks this; it is not a restriction special to ulename{ orall E}. A degenerate case. If x is not free in \varphi, then \varphi[t/x] = \varphi for every term t (the claim proved in Section 4.2), and ulename{ orall E} simply removes a quantifier that bound nothing: from  orall x\, P(c) it writes P(c). Legal, and dull. One line, many uses. The cited line stays where it is, available as before. A derivation may instantiate the same universal line as often as it likes, at different terms or the same one. Worked derivation (d) below uses one premise twice. Why this rule. It says no more than the word “every”. If every object in the domain satisfies \varphi, then so does the object that t names, whichever object that is. A term always names something, since the domain is never empty (Section 4.1), so the instance always has something to be about. Why “free for”. The instance must say about t what \varphi says about x. Section 4.2 showed that when a variable of t is captured, \varphi[t/x] can say something quite different. The condition rules capture out, and the subsection on common errors below shows the rule going wrong without it. Section 4.11 states that the rule, with its condition, never leads from true premises to a false line, and the optional Section 4.12 proves it. Line 1 of a derivation is  orall x\, \exists z\, (z > x + y). For which terms t may ulename{ orall E} write (\exists z\, (z > x + y))[t/x] on line 2? Is t = y allowed? Is t = z + 1? The only free occurrence of x in \exists z\, (z > x + y) lies in the scope of \exists z, and that is the only quantifier above it. So t is free for x exactly when z is not a variable of t: any term not containing z is allowed. The term y is allowed, and gives \exists z\, (z > y + y); the variable y already occurs free in the line, and that does no harm. The term z + 1 is not allowed: it would give \exists z\, (z > z + 1 + y), where the z of the term has been captured. Nor is z itself. To instantiate at z, rename the bound z first (Section 4.2), say to w: from  orall x\, \exists w\, (w > x + y), ulename{ orall E} at z gives \exists w\, (w > z + y). Four derivations The worked derivations below use ulename{ orall E} and the rules of Chapter 1. Each has an Idea that says why each rule was chosen, continuing the search method of Section 2.6: a goal-directed step looks at the goal’s main symbol, a premise-directed step at a resource’s. The new question is the one that ulename{ orall E} raises every time: at which term? [Instantiation at work] Give a derivation of each sequent. 1.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c). 2.  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(c, c). 3.  orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ R(a, b) \vdash R(b, a). 4.  orall x\, (P(x) 	o P(f(x))), \ P(c) \vdash P(f(f(c))). (a) Idea. The goal Q(c) has no connective or quantifier, so no introduction rule produces it, and the search turns to the premises. The premise P(c) cannot be taken apart. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) begins with  orall, so it can be used only by ulename{ orall E}. At which term? The goal mentions the term c, so instantiate at c. That gives an implication whose hypothesis is a premise and whose conclusion is the goal. Line 3 is (P(x) 	o Q(x))[c/x]; the constant c has no variables, so it is free for x. Read c as 2, P(x) as “x is positive”, and Q(x) as “x has a square root” (Section 4.1 wrote S for this predicate), and the derivation is the square-root argument of Section 4.1, in the four lines promised there. The argument that truth tables rejected is derivable once the rules can see inside its sentences. (b) Idea. The premise has two quantifiers, and ulename{ orall E} removes one at a time, the outermost first: the main symbol of the premise is  orall x, and only after it is gone is  orall y the main symbol. The goal R(c, c) shows the term for both. Line 2 is ( orall y\, R(x, y))[c/x]: the quantifier  orall y is on a variable other than x, so the substitution passes through it (@def-substitution). Line 3 instantiates y at c as well. Nothing forbids putting the same term in for two different variables; “for all x and y” includes the case x = y. (c) Idea. Work backwards from the goal R(b, a). The only line that can produce it is the first premise, through an instance of its inside, R(x, y) 	o R(y, x), followed by ulename{{	o}E}. Which instance has conclusion R(b, a)? Matching R(y, x) with R(b, a) gives y \coloneqq b and x \coloneqq a. Then the hypothesis of that instance is R(a, b), which is the second premise. So the terms are read off the goal: a for x first (the outer quantifier), then b for y. A reader who matches the goal R(b, a) against the hypothesis R(x, y) instead of the conclusion R(y, x) puts b for x and a for y, and gets R(b, a) 	o R(a, b). That is a legal line, but its hypothesis is the goal itself, so ulename{{	o}E} cannot fire. Match the goal against the conclusion of the implication, since that is the part ulename{{	o}E} delivers. (d) Idea, forwards. The premise P(c) is the hypothesis of the instance of the first premise at c, so instantiating at c and firing gives P(f(c)). Now P(f(c)) is the hypothesis of the instance at f(c), so the same premise, instantiated again, fires again and gives P(f(f(c))), the goal. Idea, backwards. The goal P(f(f(c))) has the shape P(f(x)), the conclusion of the inside of the first premise, with x \coloneqq f(c). So the last ulename{ orall E} must be at the compound term f(c), and its hypothesis P(f(c)) becomes the new goal. That has the shape P(f(x)) with x \coloneqq c, and its hypothesis is the premise P(c). Line 5 cites line 1 again: a universal line can be instantiated as often as needed. Its term f(c) contains no variable, so it is free for x, and (P(x) 	o P(f(x)))[f(c)/x] is P(f(c)) 	o P(f(f(c))): every x is replaced by the whole term f(c), including the one inside f(x). An arithmetic reading: over 
N, let f(n) be n + 2, let P(n) say “n is even”, and let c be 0. The first premise says that adding 2 to an even number gives an even number, the second that 0 is even, and the derivation concludes that f(f(0)) = 4 is even. Each further step up the even numbers would cost two more lines. Reaching “every n of the form f(\cdots f(0) \cdots)” at once is a job for induction, not for this rule. In each derivation, the Idea chose the term of every ulename{ orall E} by matching: the goal, or a hypothesis still needed, has a definite shape, and the instance is chosen to have that shape. Instantiating at a term that nothing asks for is legal, and it fills a derivation with lines that lead nowhere. Checking a line of instantiation Choosing the term can take thought; checking a line never does. For a line justified “ulename{ orall E} i”, ask four questions. 1. Is line i available here (@def-derivation)? 2. Is the main symbol of line i a universal quantifier? If so, read off its variable x and its scope \varphi. 3. Is this line \varphi[t/x] for some term t? Find t by comparing the two lines at a free occurrence of x in \varphi; then check that every free occurrence of x became that same t, and that nothing else changed. 4. Is t free for x in \varphi? Run on line 5 of (d): line 1 is available, since no box contains it; its main symbol is  orall x, with scope P(x) 	o P(f(x)); comparing gives t = f(c), and both occurrences of x became f(c); and f(c) has no variables, so it is free for x. The line passes. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof Let a be a real number. A proof might say: Since y^2 \ge 0 for every real y, applying this to a - 1 gives (a - 1)^2 \ge 0, that is, a^2 - 2a + 1 \ge 0. The first half of the sentence is one ulename{ orall E}, at the compound term a - 1. The second half rewrites (a - 1)^2 by school algebra. In a derivation such a step is written as one line justified “arith”, for arithmetic: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Line Sentence ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 “Since y^2 \ge 0 for every real y, …” (the general fact) 2 “… applying this to a - 1 gives (a - 1)^2 \ge 0, …” (ulename{ orall E} at a - 1) 3 “… that is, a^2 - 2a + 1 \ge 0.” (arith) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A line justified “arith” records a fact of school arithmetic or algebra, used on the lines it cites; here the fact is that (u - 1)^2 and u^2 - 2u + 1 are the same number for every real u. It is not a new rule. Written out in full, it is a universally quantified arithmetic statement, here  orall u\,  igl( (u - 1)^2 \ge 0 	o u^2 - 2 \cdot u + 1 \ge 0  igr), taken as one more premise, instantiated by ulename{ orall E} at the term on the line (here a) and applied by ulename{{	o}E} to the cited line. That is exactly the pattern of (a) above. The book writes it as one line because spelling it out every time would bury the logic under algebra; its bound variables are letters that appear nowhere else in the derivation, and that keeps every term free for them. As in the earlier chapters, the facts of school algebra are used here as facts. Section 4.4 will turn this three-line derivation into a proof of x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0 for every real x. That needs a rule this section does not have. Common errors Three mistakes are worth seeing written out, each with a reading in which the premise is true and the offending line false. Capture. The premise  orall x\, \exists y\, (y 
e x) says, over 
N, that for every number there is a different one; it is true, since x + 1 
e x. Instantiating “at y” without looking writes this: Line 2 says that some number differs from itself, which is false. The step breaks the side condition: the free occurrence of x in \exists y\, (y 
e x) lies in the scope of \exists y, and y is a variable of the term y, so y is not free for x. This is the capture example of Section 4.2, now inside a derivation. The repair is to rename first:  orall x\, \exists z\, (z 
e x) is the same premise up to renaming, and ulename{ orall E} at y gives \exists z\, (z 
e y), “some number differs from y”, which is what was meant. ulename{ orall E} at a term that is not free for x can turn a true premise into a false line, and the definition of \varphi[t/x] gives no signal: it returns a formula either way. Over 
N, from the true  orall x\, \exists y\, (y 
e x), the “instance at y” is \exists y\, (y 
e y), which is false. Before instantiating at a term with variables, look for quantifiers on those variables inside \varphi. A buried quantifier. From the line  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(c) one may not write P(c) 	o Q(c). The main symbol of the line is 	o, and the  orall x governs only the hypothesis  orall x\, P(x). The line says “if every x has P, then Q(c)”; the false step reads it as “if c has P, then Q(c)”, which is far stronger. Over 
N, read P(x) as x \ge 1, Q(x) as x = 0, and c as 1. The line is true, because its hypothesis “every natural number is at least 1” is false (0 is not). The false step’s result, “if 1 \ge 1, then 1 = 0”, is false. Replacing only some occurrences. Over 
R,  orall x\, (x \le x^2 \vee x < 1) is true: a real x \ge 1 has x^2 = x \cdot x \ge x, and every other real has x < 1. Writing 2 \le x^2 \vee x < 1 from it replaces the first x and leaves the others. That is not \varphi[2/x], which is 2 \le 2^2 \vee 2 < 1: the substitution replaces every free occurrence. The half-replaced line still has x free, and when x names 1 it reads 2 \le 1 \vee 1 < 1, which is false. A stall Try the sequent  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) . It is plainly correct: if every x has both properties, then every x has the first. Search for a derivation. The goal begins with  orall, and no rule so far is made for proving a  orall. Apart from ulename{ ot E} (@def-rules-contradiction) and ulename{RAA} (@def-rule-raa), which reach a line only by way of a contradiction, a line beginning with  orall can only be taken out of a line or box that already contains it. So the goal-directed step has nothing to offer, and we turn to the premise. ulename{ orall E} at c gives P(c) \wedge Q(c), and ulename{\wedge E} gives P(c). The same works at d, at f(c), at any term we name. But each line is an instance. No finite list of instances is the statement  orall x\, P(x), which speaks about every object at once, including all the objects that none of our terms happen to name. So with ulename{ orall E} alone, a universal statement can be used but not proved. Leaving aside a detour through a contradiction, a derivation can write  orall x\, \psi only by taking it out of a line or box that already contains it, as line 2 of (b) took  orall y\, R(c, y) out of the premise. Section 1.4 was in the same position with implications, and Section 1.5 filled the gap with a box. Section 4.4 does the same for  orall: it proves P of one name about which nothing is known, and that box finishes this derivation in four lines. What the rule sounds like The table of Sections 1.3–1.7 and 2.1–2.5 gains a row for ulename{ orall E}. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ---------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------- ulename{ orall E} “In particular, for x = t, …”; “applying the hypothesis to t, …” h t (or specialize h t) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Written mathematics has many forms of the phrase: “in particular, for x = 3, …”; “applying the hypothesis to x_0 - 1, …”; “by the theorem with \varepsilon/2 in place of \varepsilon, …”. In the Lean column, h is the universal statement and t the term; applying h to t gives the instance, just as applying an implication to a proof of its hypothesis gave its conclusion in Section 1.4. In Lean a universal statement behaves like a function that takes a term and returns a proof of the instance. The search method: one more step The search method of Section 2.6 had a goal-directed step and a premise-directed step for each connective. Instantiation adds a premise-directed step. - A resource  orall x\, \varphi. Do not instantiate blindly. Instantiate at the term that the goal, or another resource, asks for: match the shape of the goal (or of a hypothesis still needed) against \varphi, and read off the term. If the term is not free for x in \varphi, rename the bound variables of \varphi first. Instantiating is always safe, in the sense of Section 2.6: the new line is added and nothing is lost, since the universal line stays available. What can go wrong is only that the derivation fills with instances nobody needs, as a forward search filled with useless lines in Section 1.4. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the schema of ulename{ orall E} and its side condition from memory. 2. For each pair, decide whether line 2 follows from line 1 by one application of ulename{ orall E}. If not, name the clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination that fails. - (i) Line 1:  orall x\, \exists y\, (y > x); line 2: \exists y\, (y > y). - (ii) Line 1:  orall x\, (x \cdot x \ge 0); line 2: 3 \cdot x \ge 0. - (iii) Line 1:  orall x\, P(x) 	o P(c); line 2: P(a) 	o P(c). - (iv) Line 1:  orall x\, (P(x) 	o P(f(x))); line 2: P(f(c)) 	o P(f(f(c))). 3. True or false, with a reason: from  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), one application of ulename{ orall E} gives  orall x\, R(x, c). 4. Why does ulename{ orall E} not need a line saying that the term t names an element of the domain? (a) From line i:  orall x\, \varphi, line k may be \varphi[t/x], justified “ulename{ orall E} i”, for any term t that is free for x in \varphi, with line i available at line k. (b) (i) Not legal: the term y is not free for x in \exists y\, (y > x), since the free x lies in the scope of \exists y (clause 4, capture). Over 
Z, line 1 is true and line 2 is false. (ii) Not legal: only the first x was replaced, so line 2 is not \varphi[t/x] for any t (clause 3). The instance at 3 is 3 \cdot 3 \ge 0. Line 2 still has x free, and over 
R it is false when x names -1. (iii) Not legal: the main symbol of line 1 is 	o, not  orall (clause 1); the  orall x governs only P(x). Over 
N with P(x) read as x \ge 1, c as 0, and a as 1: line 1 says “if every natural number is at least 1, then 0 \ge 1”, true because its hypothesis is false; line 2 says “if 1 \ge 1, then 0 \ge 1”, which is false. (iv) Legal: it is \varphi[f(c)/x] with \varphi = P(x) 	o P(f(x)), both occurrences of x replaced by f(c), and f(c) has no variables, so it is free for x (clause 2: any term, compound ones included). (v) False. The main symbol is  orall x, so one application removes  orall x and gives  orall y\, R(t, y) for some term t. The line  orall x\, R(x, c) would need the inner quantifier removed while the outer one stays, and the rule cannot reach inside the outer quantifier. (The sequent  orall x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash  orall x\, R(x, c) is derivable, but it needs the rule of Section 4.4.) (vi) Every term names an element of the domain: once the symbols are interpreted, a constant names one, and a compound term names the value of a function at elements. And the domain is never empty (Section 4.1). So “every element satisfies \varphi” applies to whatever t names, with nothing further to check. (Bounded quantifiers are different: to use  orall x \in A\; \varphi at t one also needs t \in A, and Section 4.8 builds that into a rule.) B. Practice [B1: Two links] Give a derivation of  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \  orall x\, (Q(x) 	o R(x)), \ P(a) \vdash R(a), and say, for each ulename{ orall E} line, which line of the search asked for its term. The goal R(a) is the conclusion of the instance of the second premise at a, so it suffices to reach Q(a); that is the conclusion of the instance of the first premise at a, so it suffices to reach P(a), a premise. Both terms come from the goal: the second ulename{ orall E} (line 6) from R(a), the first (line 4) from the subgoal Q(a). [B2: An increasing function] Read f as a function from 
R to 
R and a, b, c as real numbers. Give a derivation of  orall x\,  orall y\, (x \le y 	o f(x) \le f(y)), \ a \le b, \ b \le c \ \vdash \ f(a) \le f(b) \wedge f(b) \le f(c) , and then write the argument as one sentence of prose. The goal is a conjunction, so its last line is ulename{\wedge I}, with subgoals f(a) \le f(b) and f(b) \le f(c). Each is the conclusion of an instance of the first premise: matching f(x) \le f(y) with f(a) \le f(b) gives x \coloneqq a, y \coloneqq b, and with f(b) \le f(c) gives x \coloneqq b, y \coloneqq c. The hypotheses of the two instances are the other two premises. The premise is instantiated twice, along two different paths: once at a and b, once at b and c. In prose: Since f is increasing and a \le b, we have f(a) \le f(b), and likewise b \le c gives f(b) \le f(c). The word “increasing” carries the first premise, and the two applications of it are the two pairs of ulename{ orall E} lines. [B3: Squares are not negative] Let a and b be real numbers. Give a derivation of  orall x\, (x^2 \ge 0) \vdash (a + b)^2 \ge 0 \wedge (a - b)^2 \ge 0 . Then extend it by one line justified “arith” to a derivation of a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab from the same premise, and say which earlier line the arith line uses. The goal is a conjunction of two instances of the premise, at the compound terms a + b and a - b. Both terms are free for x in x^2 \ge 0, which has no quantifier. Lines 1–4 are the first derivation. For the second goal only line 3 is needed: (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2, so (a - b)^2 \ge 0 says a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \ge 0, and adding 2ab to both sides gives a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab. That algebra is the arith line 5. (Lines 2 and 4 are then unused, which is allowed, and deleting them leaves a three-line derivation of a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab. Line 2 would give a^2 + b^2 \ge -2ab in the same way.) C. Going deeper [C1: A partner makes a loop] A relation R is symmetric if R(x, y) gives R(y, x), and transitive if R(x, y) and R(y, z) give R(x, z). Show that in a symmetric and transitive relation, every element that is related to something is related to itself, by giving a derivation of  egin{aligned} & orall x\,  orall y\, (R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)), \ & orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\, ((R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) 	o R(x, z)), \ R(a, b) \ \vdash \ R(a, a) . \end{aligned} Explain how each term of each ulename{ orall E} was chosen. [Hint 1] The goal R(a, a) can only come from the transitivity premise. Match its conclusion R(x, z) with the goal. [Hint 2] The match gives x \coloneqq a and z \coloneqq a, and leaves y open. Which y makes the hypothesis R(a, y) \wedge R(y, a) reachable from the premises? The search. The goal R(a, a) is atomic, so it must be the conclusion of an instance of a premise. Symmetry ends in R(y, x), and its instance at a, a is R(a, a) 	o R(a, a), whose hypothesis is the goal itself: a dead end. Transitivity ends in R(x, z). Matching gives x \coloneqq a and z \coloneqq a. The variable y does not occur in the conclusion, so the goal says nothing about it; the hypothesis R(a, y) \wedge R(y, a) must decide. The premise R(a, b) offers R(a, y) with y \coloneqq b. Then the second conjunct is R(b, a), which symmetry gives from R(a, b): the instance of the symmetry premise at x \coloneqq a, y \coloneqq b (read off its needed conclusion R(b, a), as in @exm-universal-elimination-derivations (c)). The terms. Lines 7 and 9 put a in for x and for z: both read off the goal. Line 8 puts b in for y: read off the premise R(a, b), the only available fact of the form R(a, \cdot). Lines 4 and 5 put in a and b: read off the needed line R(b, a). All terms are constants, so every one is free for its variable. The hypothesis “related to something” is needed. In a symmetric and transitive relation an element related to nothing need not be related to itself: on \{0, 1\}, the relation that holds only between 0 and 0 is symmetric and transitive, and R(1, 1) fails. Without a premise like R(a, b) the search has no term for y that makes the hypothesis of line 9 reachable. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: identifies transitivity as the source of the goal and instantiates it with a for x and z. - 2: chooses b for y, with the reason (the premise R(a, b)). - 2: obtains R(b, a) from symmetry at a, b, with ulename{{	o}E}. - 2: builds the conjunction in the right order and fires the transitivity instance. - 2: every ulename{ orall E} removes the outermost quantifier of a cited line and replaces every occurrence of its variable. Fatal errors (0 for the step): removing an inner quantifier before an outer one; instantiating transitivity at a term for y for which neither conjunct of the hypothesis is available. [C2: Instantiating at the variable itself] 1. Show that  orall x\, P(x) \vdash P(x), by a derivation whose one ulename{ orall E} line you check against every clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination. 2. The reverse step, from a line P(x) to  orall x\, P(x), is an instance of no rule so far. Show that it must not be allowed without restriction: give a reading over 
Z, with x naming one particular integer, in which P(x) is true and  orall x\, P(x) is false. 3. Section 4.4 will allow the step from a line P(x_0) to  orall x\, P(x) under conditions on the name x_0: the line P(x_0) must close a special box opened for x_0, and x_0 must appear in no premise, in no assumption still in force, and not in the conclusion  orall x\, P(x). Using this description, explain why the route “ orall x\, P(x), so P(x), so  orall x\, P(x)” cannot use the letter x as the name, what it must do instead, and why no name at all will do when P(x) is itself the premise. (a) Clause 1: the main symbol of line 1 is  orall x, with scope P(x). Clause 2: the term is the variable x itself, and any term is allowed. Clause 3: P(x)[x/x] = P(x), so every free occurrence was replaced, by x. Clause 4: x is free for x in every formula (Section 4.2: a free occurrence of x never lies in the scope of a quantifier on x). Clause 5: line 1 is a premise and lies in no box, so it is available at line 2. So line 2 is legal. Its x is now free: line 2 says “P holds of whatever x names”, which is true whatever x names, since line 1 says that P holds of everything. (b) Read P(x) as “x is even” and let x name 2. Then P(x) is true, and  orall x\, P(x), “every integer is even”, is false, since 1 is odd. A rule allowing the step from P(x) to  orall x\, P(x) in general would lead from a true line to a false one. (c) With the letter x as the name, the conclusion  orall x\, P(x) contains x (the variable after the quantifier counts, which is what “appear” means), so the condition “not in the conclusion” fails, whatever else holds. The route must instantiate at a different letter instead: open the box for a new name x_0, write P(x_0) by ulename{ orall E} at x_0 from line 1, and close the box with  orall x\, P(x). Now x_0 appears nowhere in the premise  orall x\, P(x), there is no other assumption, and x_0 is not in the conclusion; every condition holds. If P(x) is itself the premise, take any name. If the name is x, the line P(x) is available but x appears in the premise and in the conclusion. If the name is some x_0 other than x, the box needs the line P(x_0), and the search finds nothing that gives it: the premise is about x, and no line mentions x_0. A stalled search proves nothing by itself, since a cleverer derivation might exist. By (b), none should exist: P(x) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) would lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. Section 4.11 turns this reading into a counter-model for the sequent P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x), with x_0 naming 2; the same reading with x naming 2 is a counter-model for P(x) \vdash  orall x\, P(x), and the soundness statement given there (proved in the optional Section 4.12) then shows that P(x) 
vdash  orall x\, P(x). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) the derivation, with each of the five clauses checked, including that x is free for x. - 2: (b) a reading with P(x) true and  orall x\, P(x) false, the value of x stated. - 3: (c) the flag x fails “not in the conclusion”; the fix instantiates at a fresh x_0 inside the box. - 2: (c) for the premise P(x): the name x fails the side condition, and for a different name the search stalls, with the pointer to Section 4.11 for non-derivability. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming the flag x is fine because x is bound in the conclusion; treating P(x) and P(x_0) as the same line.

title: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content:
Proving “For Every”: Let x Be Arbitrary Section 4.3 gave the rule for using a universal statement, and ended at a stall: from  orall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) it could derive P(c) for every term c we cared to name, but never  orall x\, P(x) itself. No list of instances is a statement about everything. This section gives the rule that proves a universal statement, ulename{ orall I}. It needs one new device, a box that carries a name instead of an assumption, and one new side condition, which turns the mathematician’s “let x be arbitrary” into something a reader can check line by line. One number we know nothing about Here is a fact of school algebra. For every real number x, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. We cannot check it number by number; there are too many numbers. The proof everyone writes takes one real number and argues about it: Let x \in 
R. Then x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2, and a square is never negative. So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. Then, often without saying so: since x was arbitrary, this holds for every real x. Chapter 1 adopted a convention for sentences like “let x be a real number”: the letter names one fixed number, not further specified (Section 1.1). It promised that Chapter 4 would explain why an argument of that kind proves a statement about every x at once. Section 2.2 met the same step at the end of the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational, passing from an arbitrary rational r to every rational; Section 3.2 met it in induction, passing from “let n \in 
N” to “for every n”. Each time the step was taken on trust. Here is why it is correct, and when it is not. The argument about x used nothing about x except that it is a real number. It never said “suppose x > 0” or “take x = 3”. So it could be repeated word for word with 0, with -7, with \pi, with any real number in place of x, and it would prove the claim for that number. One argument about a number we know nothing about is a recipe for an argument about each number, and that is what “for every” asks for. Everything depends on “nothing”. If the argument had used a fact about x that not every number has, the recipe would break for some numbers. “Let x be a real number with x > 0. Then x > 0. Since x was arbitrary, every real number is positive” is the same shape, and its conclusion is false. The step “since x was arbitrary” is legitimate only when x was arbitrary: when no premise and no assumption still in force says anything about it. The rule of this section makes that condition exact. The flagged box To prove “for every x”, take a fresh name that nothing is known about, prove the statement for that name, and generalize. In a derivation the argument about the arbitrary x is drawn as a box, as Chapter 1 drew the argument under an assumption. The box opens with no assumption at all. Instead it carries the arbitrary name, written at its top left, and is called a flagged box; the name is its flag. [Rules for the Universal Quantifier] The rule on the left is ulename{ orall I} (universal introduction, or generalization). It cites a flagged box, with flag x_0, from its first line i to its last line j, and writes  orall x\, \varphi on line k. The flag x_0 is a variable. The box’s last line j is \varphi[x_0/x], and it is a line of the flagged box itself, not of a box inside it. The side condition is on the name: at line k, - x_0 appears in no premise, - x_0 appears in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and - x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi. The rule on the right is ulename{ orall E}, as in @def-rule-universal-elimination: t is any term free for x in \varphi. In words: to prove that \varphi holds for every x, open a box flagged with a new name x_0, prove \varphi[x_0/x], “\varphi holds of x_0”, as the box’s last line, close the box, and write  orall x\, \varphi. The side condition says that x_0 really was arbitrary. What a flagged box is. @def-derivation (Section 1.5) said that a box is a block of consecutive lines whose first line is an assumption. We now extend that definition, and two things change. First, a box may be flagged: it carries a name, a variable written at its top, and a flagged box need not open with an assumption. The box of ulename{ orall I} has none; the box of the rule for using “there exists” in Section 4.6 is flagged and has one. Second, the rules that close a flagged box carry side conditions about its name, such as the one above. Everything else in @def-derivation stays word for word: two boxes are disjoint or one is inside the other, a box ends at one of its lines, and the scope rule decides which lines and boxes are available where. A flagged box with no assumption adds nothing to what is assumed; it only marks where the name is in use. Here are the two boxes side by side: the box of ulename{{	o}I} from @def-rules-implication, and the flagged box. Both draw a boundary and both are cited as a range i–j. The ulename{{	o}I} box opens with what we suppose; the flagged box opens with the name we have fixed. In the schema the flagged box begins with a gap \vdots on line i, only so that the range has a first line; in a real derivation line i is whatever the box’s first line is. When a flagged box immediately contains another box, as in the swap of two quantifiers in the examples below, the range starts at the first line of that inner box. Read the rule part by part: the flag, the three clauses of the side condition, and the last line. - The flag. Opening the box is the written “let x_0 be arbitrary”. The flag is always a variable, never a constant: a constant has a fixed meaning, while the whole point of x_0 is that it may stand for anything. The book writes flags with a subscript 0, x_0, y_0, \varepsilon_0, so that they stand out. - No premise, no open assumption (the first and second clauses). This is “we know nothing about x_0”. What is known at line k is the premises and the assumptions of the boxes still open there. If none of them mentions x_0, then nothing that was used about x_0 inside the box is special to x_0. - Not in the conclusion (the third clause). The name must not leak out. Inside the box it stood for an arbitrary object, and  orall x\, \varphi is meant to speak about all objects through the bound x. The derivation is legal, and it is correct for the reason in (b): line 3 was derived from a premise that says nothing about x_0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the left conjunct by two ulename{ orall E} lines at x_0, outside any box. - 2: a flagged box with ulename{ orall E} at the flag and ulename{ orall I} citing it. - 2: the side condition checked clause by clause: premise, open assumptions, conclusion. - 2: (b) explains that lines outside the box that do not rest on premises or assumptions about x_0 cannot make x_0 special. Alternatively, 2 for showing that renaming the box’s flag to a new letter gives a derivation that meets the stronger condition and has the same last line. - 2: (c) correct answer with the availability check for the repeated line. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that line 3 makes line 6 illegal; checking the side condition against lines that are not premises, open assumptions or the conclusion. [C2: Find the error] A student offers this proof. Claim. For every real number x, x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. Proof. (1) Let x be a real number. (2) At x = 0: 0 - 0 + 1 = 1 \ge 0. (3) At x = 1: 1 - 2 + 1 = 0 \ge 0. (4) At x = 2: 4 - 4 + 1 = 1 \ge 0. (5) So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0, and since x was arbitrary, the claim holds for every real x. 1. Is the claim true? 2. Does the argument prove it? Name the step that fails and the rule it misuses. 3. Show that the step can lead to a false conclusion: give a polynomial p for which the same checks at x = 0, 1, 2 succeed and p(x) \ge 0 fails for some real x. 4. Point to a correct proof. [Hint 1] Write lines (2)–(4) as formulas. Which terms do they mention? [Hint 2] Write the student’s proof as a derivation: open a box flagged x_0 for line (1), and write lines (2)–(4) as lines inside it. What would line (5) have to cite? (a) Yes. For every real x, x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 \ge 0, since a square is never negative. (b) No. Lines (2)–(4) are true, and line (1) opens a flagged box, “let x be arbitrary”. The error is in line (5). With \varphi the formula x^2 - 2 \cdot x + 1 \ge 0, lines (2)–(4) establish \varphi[0/x], \varphi[1/x] and \varphi[2/x]: statements about the constants 0, 1, 2. None of them is \varphi[x_0/x] for the flag. Inside the box, nothing about the arbitrary x was ever proved. The first sentence of (5), “so x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0”, has the right form: it is \varphi[x_0/x], with the student’s x as the flag. But no rule writes it: it is not a premise, an assumption or a repetition, and no rule takes \varphi[0/x], \varphi[1/x] and \varphi[2/x] to \varphi[x_0/x]. So the closing “since x was arbitrary” applies ulename{ orall I} to a box whose last line was never derived: the lines the box legally derives are all instances at constants, not the instance at the flag. Line (1) was idle: the argument never used the x it introduced. (c) Take p(x) = x(x - 1)(x - 2). The same checks succeed: p(0) = 0 \ge 0, p(1) = 0 \ge 0, p(2) = 0 \ge 0. But p(-1) = (-1)(-2)(-3) = -6 < 0, so “p(x) \ge 0 for every real x” is false. So the pattern of (5), concluding “for every x” from checks at a few constants, can lead from true checks to a false conclusion. It is not an instance of ulename{ orall I}, as (b) showed. (Section 4.11 states, and the optional Section 4.12 proves, that legal steps never lead from true premises to a false conclusion.) The claim in (a) is true for a different reason, one that the argument never gave. (d) The derivation under “How this rule looks in a mathematical proof”: inside the box flagged x_0, ulename{ orall E} applies “squares are not negative” at x_0 - 1, an arith line rewrites it as x_0^2 - 2x_0 + 1 \ge 0, and that line is \varphi[x_0/x], so ulename{ orall I} applies. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) the claim is true, with a reason (it is a square). - 3: (b) names step (5) and ulename{ orall I}; says that lines (2)–(4) are instances at constants, not the instance at the flag. - 3: (c) a polynomial that passes the three checks and fails somewhere, with both computations shown. - 2: (d) a correct proof, generalizing over a statement proved about the arbitrary x. Fatal errors (0 for the step): answering (b) with “the claim is false”; a “counterexample” in (c) that fails one of the three checks or is non-negative everywhere.

title: 4.5 Proving "There Exists": Exhibit a Witness
content:
Proving “There Exists”: Exhibit a Witness Sections 4.3 and 4.4 gave the two rules for “for every”: ulename{ orall E} uses a universal statement, and ulename{ orall I} proves one. This section starts on the other quantifier. It gives the rule that proves an existential statement, ulename{\exists I}, and the habit that goes with it: when the goal is “there exists”, do not guess the object, but wait until a line of the derivation shows it. Section 4.4 left open a sequent that no rule so far could finish,  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x); it is finished here in three lines. Showing that something exists How does a mathematician prove that there is a natural number N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100? By naming one. “Take N = 100: then 1/(N + 1) = 1/101, and 1/101 < 1/100.” Nobody asks for more, and nobody objects that N = 1000 would also have done. The proof exhibits a witness, checks that it has the property, and stops. Look at what the proof does with the witness at the end. The statement proved, “there is an N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100”, does not say which N; the 100 still in it belongs to the bound 1/100, not to N. The number was needed to establish the claim and is then forgotten: a reader of the conclusion learns that some N works, not which one. Chapter 1 used the same pattern from its first page. It recalled that an integer n is even when n = 2k for some integer k, and said that the word “some” has rules of its own, to come in Chapter 4. Here is the first of them. To show that 6 is even, take k = 3: then 6 = 2 \cdot 3. The statement “6 is even” is \exists k\, (6 = 2 \cdot k), and the proof passes from the instance 6 = 2 \cdot 3 to it. The second rule for “some”, how to use “n = 2k for some k”, is the subject of Section 4.6. There is a helpful way to see the step, which Section 4.1’s reading of \exists suggests. Over a domain with three elements named a, b, c, the sentence \exists x\, P(x) says what the disjunction P(a) \vee P(b) \vee P(c) says (grouped to the right, as in Section 3.4): at least one of the three has P. An existential is a long “or”, with one disjunct for each object of the domain. Proving a disjunction from one of its sides is ulename{\vee I} (@def-rule-disjunction-introduction), and proving an existential from one instance is the rule of this section. The analogy is only a guide (a domain such as 
N has infinitely many elements, and a formula cannot be infinitely long), but it predicts the rule’s behavior exactly: it throws information away, and it must never be run backwards. The rule of existential introduction To prove that something has a property, show that one particular thing has it. [Existential Introduction] The rule given by this schema is called ulename{\exists I} (existential introduction). Here \varphi is any formula, x any variable, and t any term, subject to one side condition: t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Line i must be available at line k (@def-derivation). In words, clause by clause. 1. One given line, no box. The rule cites one available line, as ulename{\vee I} does. Like ulename{ orall E} of Section 4.3, it opens no box and introduces no fresh name. 2. The cited line is an instance. Line i must have the form \varphi[t/x]: the formula \varphi with the term t put in for every free occurrence of x (@def-substitution). The term t is the witness. 3. The rule reads the cited line backwards. The line \varphi[t/x] is given, and \varphi is not: we choose it. In practice we look at the cited line, choose a variable x that does not appear in it (Section 4.2), and replace some of the occurrences of t by x; the result is \varphi, and \varphi[t/x] is then the cited line. If x does appear in the line, this recipe can fail (from R(x, c), marking c gives \varphi = R(x, x), and \varphi[c/x] = R(c, c) is not the line), so check directly that \varphi[t/x] is exactly the cited line. In every case check clause 5. One line is an instance of many formulas, so one line has many existential conclusions. The table below shows this. 4. Any term. The witness may be a constant (3, c), a compound term (f(c), 2k + 1), or a variable: a variable that appears elsewhere in the derivation, a fresh name of a flagged box such as x_0, or even the variable x itself. No box is needed for any of these. The rule never asks where t came from. 5. Free for x. The only restriction is the condition of @def-free-for, the same one that ulename{ orall E} carries. Its job is shown by the nonexample below. One line, several readings. Let line i be R(c, c), with R a two-place predicate symbol and c a constant. The witness is c, and c occurs twice. Each occurrence may be marked with x or left alone, and each choice is a different \varphi: ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ \varphi \varphi[c/x] (the cited line) the new line \exists x\, \varphi ----------------------- ------------------------------- ---------------------------------- R(x, c) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(x, c) R(c, x) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(c, x) R(x, x) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(x, x) R(c, c) R(c, c) \exists x\, R(c, c) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ All four are legal steps. Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x \le y” and c as 5: the cited line says 5 \le 5, and the three useful conclusions say that something is at most 5, that 5 is at most something, and that something is at most itself. Each is a true and weaker statement. The last row is the degenerate choice: \varphi has no free x, so \varphi[c/x] is \varphi (Section 4.2) and the new line \exists x\, R(c, c) quantifies over nothing. It is legal, and it says nothing that line i did not. Why this rule. Under the reading of Section 4.1, \exists x\, \varphi is true when at least one element of the domain, put in for x, makes \varphi true. If \varphi[t/x] is true, then the object that t names is such an element, so \exists x\, \varphi is true. The side condition is what makes “\varphi[t/x] says about t what \varphi says about x” correct: that was the content of “free for” in Section 4.2. Section 4.12 turns this sentence into a proof. ulename{\exists I} forgets the witness, and keeps the truth. A nonexample: capture. Let line 1 be  orall y\, R(y, y). With \varphi =  orall y\, R(x, y) and t = y, the definition of substitution gives \varphi[y/x] =  orall y\, R(y, y), which is line 1. So it is tempting to write \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) by ulename{\exists I}. Line 2 breaks the side condition: the free occurrence of x in \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, and y is the variable of the term t, so y is not free for x in \varphi. The step would be wrong. Read over 
Z with R(x, y) as “x \le y”: line 1 says that every integer is at most itself, which is true, and line 2 says that some integer is at most every integer, that is, that there is a least integer, which is false. The y put in for x was meant to name one object, and it was captured by  orall y and made to range over all of them. The witness must be written on a line. “There is an N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100: take N large enough” is not an application of ulename{\exists I}, because “large enough” is not a term, and the rule asks for an instance \varphi[t/x] on an available line. In a written proof, “large enough” is a promise to name the witness, and the promise is kept by a term such as N = 100, followed by the check that it works (1/101 < 1/100). Until then nothing has been proved. Let line 1 be 2 + 2 = 4. Which of \exists x\, (x + x = 4), \qquad \exists x\, (x + 2 = 4), \qquad \exists x\, (2 + 2 = x) may line 2 be, justified by one application of ulename{\exists I} to line 1? For each that may, name \varphi and the witness t. All three. For \exists x\, (x + x = 4), take \varphi = (x + x = 4) and t = 2: both 2’s of line 1 are marked. For \exists x\, (x + 2 = 4), take \varphi = (x + 2 = 4) and t = 2: only the first 2 is marked, and the second is written out in \varphi. For \exists x\, (2 + 2 = x), take \varphi = (2 + 2 = x) and t = 4: the witness is a different term. In each case \varphi[t/x] is exactly line 1, and \varphi has no quantifier, so t is free for x. From “for every” to “there exists” Section 4.4 left  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) open. It looks like the easiest sequent in the chapter, and it has a small puzzle in it. To use ulename{\exists I}, the goal needs an instance P(t) on a line. The premise gives an instance for every term, by ulename{ orall E}. But the sequent mentions no constant, so which term? [Every Implies Some]  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x). The following is a derivation. Line 2 is ulename{ orall E} at the term x: with \varphi = P(x), the instance \varphi[x/x] is P(x), and the variable x is free for x in every formula (Section 4.2). Line 3 is ulename{\exists I} with the same \varphi and the witness x. This proves the proposition. The puzzle is answered by clause 4 of the reading of @def-rule-existential-introduction: a variable is a term, so no constant is needed. The line P(x) has x free; it says that P holds of whatever x names. Nothing in the derivation says what that is, and nothing needs to. The same three lines prove  orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, \varphi for every formula \varphi, since \varphi[x/x] = \varphi (Section 4.2). The rules accept this derivation in any case; it leads from a true premise to a true conclusion only because every domain has at least one element, the convention of Section 4.1. Over an empty domain,  orall x\, P(x) would be true with nothing to check and \exists x\, P(x) false with no witness; the convention enters at line 2, where P(x) treats x as naming an object, and there must be one to name. Section 4.11 explains why the book keeps the convention. This does not clash with the empty set of Section 4.1, where  orall x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is true and \exists x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is false. A bounded quantifier is an abbreviation (@def-bounded-quantifier):  orall x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi), and \exists x \in \emptyset\; \varphi is \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset \wedge \varphi). The domain is still non-empty; it is the set \emptyset that has no elements. Running the three lines on the bounded premise gives ulename{ orall E} at x, the line x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi, and then ulename{\exists I} gives only \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi), an existential with 	o inside. No line x \in \emptyset is available to fire the implication, so the bounded “every implies some” is not derived, and it should not be. An existential goal: postpone the witness The search method of Section 2.6 asks two questions at each gap: what is the goal, and what are the resources? Sections 4.3 and 4.4 added a step for each side of  orall. Now \exists can be a goal. If the goal is \exists x\, \varphi, its last line can be ulename{\exists I}, and then the new goal is \varphi[t/x] for a term t of our choosing. That is the same situation as a goal \varphi \vee \psi, where ulename{\vee I} left us to choose a side, and the danger is the same. A wrong t can leave a goal that does not follow from the resources, although the existential does. Section 2.6 met the danger for \vee and answered it by postponing; the answer here is the same. Postpone the witness: choose the term t of a goal \exists x\, \varphi only when an available line shows an instance \varphi[t/x]. Until then, work on the premises and on the other goals, and watch what terms appear. Often the witness is a term that only appears late, built by ulename{ orall E} or ulename{{	o}E} from the premises. Here are four derivations, in order of difficulty, each with an Idea that says why each rule was chosen. [Derivations with existential introduction] Show that: 1. P(c) \wedge Q(c) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr); 2. R(c, c) \vdash \exists x\, R(x, c) \wedge \exists x\, R(x, x); and decide whether one ulename{\exists I} step leads from \exists x\, R(x, x) to \exists x\, R(x, c); 3.  orall x\, R(x, x) \vdash  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y); 4.  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(f(x))  igr), \ P(c) \vdash \exists y\, Q(y). (a) Idea. The goal is an existential, and the premise already is an instance of a suitable \varphi: mark both occurrences of c. One goal-directed step finishes. Here \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(x) and t = c. Marking only the first c, with \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(c), would give the legal but weaker line \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(c)), which is not the goal. (b) Idea. The goal is a conjunction, so it splits into two goals (Section 1.3), and each is an existential with the line R(c, c) as an instance, read in two different ways (the first and third rows of the table above). Line 2 uses \varphi = R(x, c) and line 3 uses \varphi = R(x, x), both with the witness c. Now the second question. From the line \exists x\, R(x, x), the step to \exists x\, R(x, c) is not an ulename{\exists I} step. The new line is \exists x\, \varphi with \varphi = R(x, c), so the cited line would have to be R(t, c) for some term t. The line \exists x\, R(x, x) is not of that form: its main symbol is \exists x, not R. The rule passes from an instance to an existential, never from one existential to another. Nor is the step safe by any other route: read over 
Z with R(x, y) as “x \cdot y = 1” and c as 0, the line \exists x\, R(x, x) is true (take x = 1), and \exists x\, R(x, c), “some integer times 0 is 1”, is false. (c) Idea. The goal is a  orall, so the step of Section 4.4 opens a flagged box with a fresh name x_0, and the new goal is \exists y\, R(x_0, y). That is an existential: postpone it and look at the premise. The premise is a  orall; instantiate it at the term the goal mentions, x_0. The result, R(x_0, x_0), shows the witness: it is x_0 itself, a variable used as a term, as x was in @prp-forall-implies-exists. Line 3 uses \varphi = R(x_0, y), the variable y, and the witness x_0; it marks the second occurrence of x_0 and keeps the first. Line 4 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag x_0 (@def-rules-universal): x_0 appears in no premise, there is no open assumption, and x_0 does not appear in line 4. The ulename{\exists I} inside the box needed no box of its own, although its witness is a fresh name. Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x \le y”: every number is at most itself, so every number is at most something. (d) Idea. The goal \exists y\, Q(y) is an existential, and no line yet has the form Q(t). Postpone, and work forwards. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) is a  orall; the only term in sight is c, so instantiate at c (Section 4.3), and ulename{{	o}E} with the premise P(c) fires. The result Q(f(c)) shows the witness: the compound term f(c). Line 5 uses \varphi = Q(y) and t = f(c). Now see what choosing the witness first would have done. The term in sight at the start is c, and “take y = c” leaves the goal Q(c). Nothing gives it: the premise speaks of Q only at terms of the form f(\dots), and Q(c) need not hold at all. Read over 
Z with P as “odd”, Q as “even”, f(x) as x + 1, and c as 3: the premises say that the successor of every odd integer is even and that 3 is odd, the conclusion says that some integer is even, and the witness the derivation finds is f(3) = 4, while Q(c) says that 3 is even. The search stalls exactly because it chose the witness before the derivation had produced it. The four Ideas share a pattern. In (a) and (b) the witness stood on a premise line from the start; in (c) and (d) it appeared only after other rules had run, and in (d) it was a term that no line mentioned at the start. Postponing costs nothing in (a) to (c), where the right witness was already a term in sight when the existential goal appeared (in (c) the goal names x_0), and it is necessary in (d), where the only term in sight at the start, c, is the wrong witness. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof In a written proof, ulename{\exists I} is the word “take”, followed by a check. “6 is even: take k = 3; then 6 = 2 \cdot 3.” Over 
Z, with one line of school arithmetic justified “arith” as in Section 4.3: Line 2 marks the 3 with k, and keeps the 6 and the 2: \varphi = (6 = 2 \cdot k). In the same way “7 is odd: take k = 3, since 7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1” is an ulename{\exists I} with \varphi = (7 = 2 \cdot k + 1). A bounded witness. Analysis states its existentials with bounds. “There is an N \in 
N with 1/(N + 1) < 1/100” abbreviates \exists N\,  igl( N \in 
N \wedge 1/(N + 1) < 1/100  igr) (@def-bounded-quantifier), so the witness must satisfy both conjuncts. Taking N = 100 is two steps: ulename{\wedge I} puts the bound and the inequality together, and ulename{\exists I} forgets the witness. Line 4 marks two of the three occurrences of 100 in line 3 and keeps the one on the right. Section 4.8 folds lines 3 and 4 into a single bounded step. The witness 100 is the least that works, since N = 99 gives 1/100, which is not less than 1/100; but the proof does not need the least witness, only one. A witness built from what is available. Often the witness is a term made from other names. To show that for every integer n there is an odd integer greater than 2n, a proof says “let n be an integer; 2n + 1 will do, since it is odd and greater than 2n”. The words “let n be an integer” open the flagged box of Section 4.4, and “2n + 1 will do” is ulename{\exists I} with the compound witness 2n + 1, as in (d) above. In general, the witness may be any term the reader can check. ulename{\exists I} runs one way only. From P(c) it gives \exists x\, P(x); from \exists x\, P(x) it gives nothing, and in particular not P(c). “Some integer is even” is true and “3 is even” is false: the existential does not say which object has the property, so it cannot be read back as a statement about a named one. Using an existential takes a rule of its own, with a box, and that is Section 4.6. What the rule sounds like Here is the row of the rule, phrase and Lean table for ulename{\exists I}; nothing later depends on the last column, and Section 4.7 collects the whole table. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ---------------------- ----------------------------------------- ----------------------------- ulename{\exists I} “Take x = t. Then …”; “2k + 1 will do.” use t (or Exists.intro t h) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrase names the witness and then checks it. A proof that names the witness without the check (“take N = 100.”) has written the line \exists x\, \varphi without the instance \varphi[t/x] it cites; the reader must supply the instance, and should be able to. The search method: one more step. Each rule section adds a step to the method of Section 2.6, and Section 4.8 collects them. - Goal \exists x\, \varphi. Postpone. Work on the premises and on other goals until an available line is an instance \varphi[t/x], with t free for x in \varphi; then ulename{\exists I}. The witness may be a compound term that appears only after other rules have run, as f(c) did in (d). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State ulename{\exists I} as a schema, with its side condition. 2. Line 1 of a derivation is R(c, f(c)). Which of the following may line 2 be, by one application of ulename{\exists I} to line 1? For each that may, give \varphi and the witness t; for each that may not, say why. (i) \exists x\, R(x, f(c)); (ii) \exists x\, R(c, x); (iii) \exists x\, R(x, f(x)); (iv) \exists x\, R(x, x); (v) \exists x\, R(f(c), x). 3. Line 1 of a derivation is  orall y\, (y \le y \cdot y). Is \exists x\,  orall y\, (y \le x \cdot x) a legal ulename{\exists I} step from line 1? Read both lines over 
Z: which is true? 4. True or false, with a reason: from the line \exists x\, P(x), one application of ulename{\exists I} gives P(c). 5. The current goal of a search is \exists x\, \varphi and no available line is an instance of \varphi. What does the search method say to do, and why not choose a witness now? (a) From \varphi[t/x] on an available line i, write \exists x\, \varphi on line k, justified “ulename{\exists I} i”. Side condition: t is free for x in \varphi. (b) (i) Yes: \varphi = R(x, f(c)), t = c; only the first c is marked. (ii) Yes: \varphi = R(c, x), t = f(c); the witness is the compound term. (iii) Yes: \varphi = R(x, f(x)), t = c; both occurrences of c are marked, and \varphi[c/x] is R(c, f(c)). (iv) No: the conclusion fixes \varphi = R(x, x), whose instances R(t, t) have equal arguments, while the arguments c and f(c) of line 1 differ. (v) No: the conclusion fixes \varphi = R(f(c), x), whose instances R(f(c), t) have f(c) as first argument, while line 1 has c there. (Read over 
N with R(x, y) as “x < y”, f(x) as x + 1, and c as 0: line 1 says 0 < 1, and (v) says that something exceeds 1, true but not by this step; (iv) says that some number is less than itself, which is false.) (c) No. With \varphi =  orall y\, (y \le x \cdot x), the formula \varphi[y/x] is line 1, so the witness would be the variable y; but the free occurrences of x in \varphi lie in the scope of  orall y, so y is not free for x in \varphi. Over 
Z, line 1 is true: for y \le 0, y \le 0 \le y \cdot y, and for y \ge 1, y \le y \cdot y after multiplying 1 \le y by y > 0. The other line is false: whatever integer x is proposed, y = x \cdot x + 1 gives y > x \cdot x. So the step would lead from a true line to a false one, which is what the side condition prevents. (d) False. ulename{\exists I} concludes an existential from an instance; it never concludes an instance. The line P(c) does not follow from \exists x\, P(x) at all: over 
Z with P as “even” and c as 3, the first is true and the second false. (e) Postpone the goal: work on the premises (ulename{ orall E} at the terms the goal mentions, ulename{{	o}E}, and so on) until a line \varphi[t/x] appears, then use ulename{\exists I}. A witness chosen now leaves the goal \varphi[t/x], which may not follow from the resources even when \exists x\, \varphi does, as “take y = c” did in @exm-existential-introduction-derivations (d). B. Practice [B1] Derive  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(x)  igr), \ P(a) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr). In the Idea, say which rule each line was chosen by: the goal or a premise. Idea. The goal is an existential: postpone it. The premise  orall x\, (\dots) is instantiated at the only term in sight, a, and ulename{{	o}E} with P(a) gives Q(a); both steps are premise-directed.
