Now the witness a is visible, and the instance the goal needs is P(a) \wedge Q(a), which ulename{\wedge I} builds. The last step is the postponed ulename{\exists I}. Line 6 uses \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(x) and the witness a. [B2] Over 
R, with the premise  orall x\,  igl( x + (-x) = 0  igr), derive  orall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0), the true sentence (i) of @exm-quantifier-order-sum. Say what the witness is, and what it depends on. Idea. The goal is a  orall: open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0 (Section 4.4); the new goal is \exists y\, (x_0 + y = 0). Postpone it, and instantiate the premise at the term the goal mentions, x_0. The line x_0 + (-x_0) = 0 shows the witness: -x_0. Line 3 uses \varphi = (x_0 + y = 0) and the witness -x_0, which contains no variable bound in \varphi. At line 4, x_0 appears in no premise, there is no open assumption, and x_0 does not appear in the conclusion, so ulename{ orall I} applies (@def-rules-universal). The witness -x_0 is built from x_0, so it depends on x_0: a different number for each x. That is legal, because ulename{\exists I} is applied inside the box, where x_0 is available as a term. It is the box picture of the game of Section 4.1: the \exists y is played after the  orall x, and may use it. [B3] Over 
Z, prove “there is an integer n with n^2 = n + 2” as a derivation whose only line not justified by a rule is one line of arithmetic justified “arith”; write n^2 as n \cdot n. Then write the proof as one sentence. The witness 2 works, since 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 2 + 2. Line 2 uses \varphi = (n \cdot n = n + 2) with the witness 2. Line 1 contains four 2’s, and \varphi marks three of them: both factors on the left and the first term of the sum on the right. The last 2 is the constant of the statement and stays. Marking all four would give \exists n\, (n \cdot n = n + n), a different statement. In one sentence: Take n = 2; then n^2 = 4 = n + 2. The witness -1 works too, since (-1) \cdot (-1) = 1 = -1 + 2; a proof needs only one. C. Going deeper [C1: The conclusion clause of for-all-introduction] The side condition of ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal) has three clauses about the flag x_0: it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at the ulename{ orall I} line, and not in the conclusion  orall x\, \varphi. Show that the third clause is needed: give a “derivation” that breaks only that clause, from a premise that is true over 
N to a sentence (@def-sentence) that is false over 
N. Check that every other step is legal. [Hint 1] The conclusion of the illegal ulename{ orall I} still mentions the flag, so it is not yet a sentence. Which rule of this section can replace a name on a line by a bound variable? [Hint 2] Start from the premise  orall x\, (x \le x), and open a flagged box with the name y_0. The illegal line. Line 3 is ulename{ orall I} with the flag y_0 and \varphi = (x \le y_0): the instance \varphi[y_0/x] is y_0 \le y_0, the last line of the box. The flag y_0 appears in no premise (line 1 has no y_0), and there is no open assumption at all. But y_0 appears in the conclusion  orall x\, (x \le y_0), so the third clause fails, and only it. The other lines are legal. Line 2 is ulename{ orall E} at the term y_0, which is free for x in x \le x since that formula has no quantifier. Line 4 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi =  orall x\, (x \le y) and the witness y_0: \varphi[y_0/y] is line 3, and y_0 is free for y in \varphi, since the only quantifier of \varphi is on x. Over 
N. Line 1 says that every natural number is at most itself: true. Line 4 says that some natural number is at least every natural number, that is, that there is a largest natural number: false, since for any y, x = y + 1 is larger. What the clause prevents. The box proved y_0 \le y_0, a fact about y_0 in which the two sides are the same name. Line 3 generalized only one side and kept the other, so it claimed that one fixed y_0 is at least every x: a claim about y_0 that the box never proved. The flag is “let y_0 be arbitrary”; it must not survive into the statement that “since y_0 was arbitrary” produces. Line 4 then shows the damage, by turning the leaked name into a witness. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: a derivation whose only illegal line is a ulename{ orall I} whose flag appears in its conclusion. - 2: checks the other two clauses at that line (no premise, no open assumption contains the flag). - 2: checks the remaining lines (here ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I}, with free-for). - 3: shows the premise true and the conclusion false over 
N, with the witness of the falsity (y + 1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a second illegal line (for instance a capture in ulename{\exists I}); a premise that is false over 
N. [C2: A witness is not a name] Explain why the rules so far (Chapters 1–2 and ulename{ orall E}, ulename{ orall I}, ulename{\exists I}) cannot derive \exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c). Go through the rules that could produce the last line P(c), and say what each would need. Then say, in one sentence, why no rule for using \exists should give P(c). The argument below is informal: it explains why every search stalls, and it does not by itself prove that no derivation exists. Section 4.11 gives a model in which the premise is true and P(c) is false. With the soundness theorem stated there (and proved in the optional Section 4.12), that model shows no derivation exists. Which rules could write P(c). The line P(c) is atomic, so no introduction rule writes it: ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{{	o}I}, ulename{\vee I}, ulename{
eg I}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists I} all write a line whose main symbol is their own connective or quantifier. The remaining rules take P(c) out of something larger: ulename{\wedge E} needs a conjunction with P(c) as a side; ulename{{	o}E} needs an implication \psi 	o P(c) and \psi; ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} a biconditional with P(c) as a side; ulename{\vee E} a disjunction and two boxes each ending in P(c); ulename{ orall E} a universal  orall x\, \psi with \psi[c/x] = P(c); ulename{ ot E} the line  ot; ulename{RAA} a box from 
eg P(c) to  ot; and ulename{R} the line P(c) itself. The derived rules of Chapter 2 abbreviate derivations in these rules (@def-derived-rule), so they add no new way to write P(c). What the premise can supply. The only premise is \exists x\, P(x), whose main symbol is \exists. No rule so far looks inside an existential: each elimination rule needs a cited line that is  ot (for ulename{ ot E}) or whose main symbol is \wedge, 	o, \vee, \leftrightarrow, 
eg or  orall, and ulename{\exists I} produces existentials rather than using them. So the premise can enter a derivation only as a whole: copied, built into a larger formula, set against a line 
eg\exists x\, P(x) by ulename{
eg E}, or cited as the side \psi beside a line \psi 	o \chi or \psi \leftrightarrow \chi by ulename{{	o}E} or ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}. None of these reaches the information inside it, and the lines the rules above need (a conjunction containing P(c), an implication ending in it, a biconditional with it as a side, a disjunction for ulename{\vee E}, a universal with it as an instance, a contradiction) have nowhere to come from. A search therefore stalls at once. Why it should stall. The premise says that something has P and does not say what; the conclusion says that the object named c has P. Over 
Z with P as “even” and c as 3, the premise is true and the conclusion false. So no rule for using an existential may give P(c), and the rule of Section 4.6 does not: it names the witness with a fresh variable, about which nothing else is known, instead of with c. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: identifies that P(c) is atomic, so only elimination rules, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{RAA} or ulename{R} can write it, and names what each needs. - 3: observes that no rule so far uses a line whose main symbol is \exists, so the premise cannot supply what those rules need. - 2: says that this explains the stall but is not a proof of non-derivability (that needs a counter-model together with soundness, Sections 4.11–4.12). - 2: gives a reading with the premise true and P(c) false, and the one-sentence reason (the premise does not say which object has P). Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that ulename{\exists I} read backwards gives P(c); claiming that a failed search proves the sequent underivable.

title: 4.6 Using "There Exists": Name a Witness
content:
Using “There Exists”: Name a Witness Section 4.5 gave the rule that proves an existential statement: exhibit a witness, and forget it. This section gives the rule that uses one, ulename{\exists E}. It is the last of the four quantifier rules, and the subtlest, because an existential says that a witness exists without saying which one it is. The rule handles this with a box and a fresh name, as ulename{ orall I} did, but the name now stands for an object that is not arbitrary, and the side condition keeps it from being treated as if it were. With the rule in hand, the section moves an \exists past a  orall, and shows exactly where the reverse move breaks down. Using a witness whose identity is unknown Chapter 2 proved that if n^2 is even then n is even (@thm-square-even-implies-even). One of the facts it rested on, (E3), says that the square of an odd integer is odd, and it was shown by taking “an integer k with n = 2k + 1” and computing with it. Chapter 2 noted that naming the k of (E3) lay outside its derivation: it is a quantifier step, whose rule had to wait. Here is the simplest proof with the same step. If n is even, then n + 2 is even. Since n is even, choose an integer k with n = 2k. Then n + 2 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1), so n + 2 is even. The hypothesis is \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k). The proof does not know which integer k is; it does not need to. It gives the unknown witness a name, uses the one fact it has about it, n = 2k, and reaches a conclusion, “n + 2 is even”, in which the name no longer appears. The witness k + 1 of the last step is forgotten by ulename{\exists I}, as in Section 4.5. Why is this correct? Two tempting shortcuts show what the proof is careful not to do. - It does not name the witness by a term that already means something. From “some integer is even” we may not conclude “3 is even”: the existential does not say that the witness is 3, and, as the warning “ulename{\exists I} runs one way only” of Section 4.5 noted, it cannot be read back as a statement about a named object. - It does not let the conclusion mention the name. If it did, the conclusion would be a statement about k, and outside the argument k refers to nothing; the existential promised only that some k works. So the name must be new, the argument may use only what the existential says about it, and the conclusion must not mention it. Then the argument works for the witness, whichever integer it is, because it never used anything else about it. The long “or” of Section 4.5 gives the same picture from another side. Over a domain with three elements named a, b, c, the line \exists x\, P(x) says P(a) \vee P(b) \vee P(c), and ulename{\vee E} (@def-rules-disjunction) would use it by proving a goal \chi three times, once in each case. The three cases look alike, so they can be done once, with a name that could be any of a, b, c. All three cases must end in the same \chi, so \chi must not say which case it came from. That is the box of the rule, and its side condition. The rule of existential elimination To use “there exists”, give the witness a new name, assume only what the existential says about it, and conclude something that does not mention it. [Rules for the Existential Quantifier] The rule on the left is ulename{\exists E} (existential elimination). It cites a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a flagged box with the name x_0, a variable, whose first line is the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] and whose last line j, a line of that box itself, is \chi; line h and the box must be available at line k (@def-derivation, with the flagged boxes of Section 4.4). The new line k repeats \chi. Side condition, at line k: the name x_0 does not appear - in \chi, - in \exists x\, \varphi, - in any premise, or - in any assumption of a box still open at line k. The rule on the right is ulename{\exists I}, recalled from @def-rule-existential-introduction: t is any term free for x in \varphi. The box of ulename{\exists E} is the flagged box of Section 4.4 with one difference: it opens with an assumption, \varphi[x_0/x], “x_0 is a witness”. The flagged box of ulename{ orall I} had no assumption, because “let x_0 be arbitrary” assumes nothing about x_0. The citation “ulename{\exists E} h, i–j” names the line of the existential and the box, as ulename{\vee E} names its disjunction and its boxes. “Appear” is the word of Section 4.2: written anywhere in the formula, after a quantifier symbol included. Read the rule clause by clause. 1. The assumption. The box assumes \varphi[x_0/x]: the formula of the existential, with the new name in place of x. This is “choose x_0 with \varphi”. It is the only thing the box knows about x_0. 2. The last line. The box ends with \chi, a line of the box itself, not of a box inside it, as for ulename{\vee E} and ulename{ orall I}. It is “whatever the witness is, \chi follows”. The new line k then asserts \chi outside the box, where x_0 is no longer assumed to be anything. 3. x_0 does not appear in \chi. The box shows that \chi follows from “x_0 is a witness”; if \chi mentioned x_0, line k would make a claim about a name that, outside the box, is tied to nothing. The derivation after this list shows the damage. 4. x_0 does not appear in a premise or in an assumption of an open box. The name must be new to everything we know at line k. If a premise or an open assumption already said something about x_0, the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] would add to it a claim that x_0 is the witness, which the existential never made. 5. x_0 does not appear in \exists x\, \varphi. The existential must not itself mention the name chosen for its witness. This clause also makes x_0 free for x in \varphi (Section 4.2: a variable that does not appear in \varphi is free for every variable there), so the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] says of x_0 exactly what \varphi says of x. 6. “Still open at line k”. The box’s own assumption \varphi[x_0/x] is closed at line k, so it is not among the assumptions checked. This matters: read inside the box, “an open assumption” would include \varphi[x_0/x], which contains x_0 whenever x is free in \varphi, and the rule could then never be applied in the cases that matter. Clauses 3, 4 and 5 can each be seen failing. Each derivation below breaks exactly one of them and leads from premises that are true, under the reading given, to a false line. The conclusion clause (3). Over 
N, “some number exceeds 5” is true. Let the ulename{\exists E} box end in the line x_0 > 5, which mentions its own witness: Line 3 breaks clause 3. Every other line is legal: in particular line 5 is a correct ulename{ orall I}, since x_0 appears in no premise and in no open assumption (there is none), and not in line 5. Over 
N the conclusion says that every number exceeds 5, which is false at 0. Once the name leaves its box, it can be generalized over as if it were arbitrary. The premise clause (4). Over 
N, with P read as “even” and the variable x_0 read as 1, both premises below are true: some number is even, and 1 is not even. Line 5 breaks clause 4: x_0 appears in the premise on line 2. The box assumed that x_0, which the premise had already described as odd, is the even witness, and derived a contradiction from that assumption, not from the premises. The existential clause (5). Over 
Z, with R(x, y) read as “x < y”, the premise below says that every integer has a smaller one: true. Line 2 is a legal ulename{ orall E} at the term x_0. Line 5 breaks clause 5: the existential on line 2 is \exists x\, \varphi with \varphi = R(x, x_0), and x_0 appears in it. The assumption \varphi[x_0/x] on line 3 is R(x_0, x_0): the box has assumed that the witness smaller than x_0 is x_0 itself. The conclusion says that some integer is less than itself, which is false. The other clauses hold at line 5: x_0 is not in \exists z\, R(z, z), not in the premise, and no box is open. A fourth illegal pattern, a second witness given a name that an open assumption already uses, is the error of the warning “Two witnesses, one name” below. The witness is not arbitrary. The flagged boxes of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} look alike: both introduce a fresh name. Their names mean opposite things. In a ulename{ orall I} box, x_0 is any object, and what is proved about it holds for all. In an ulename{\exists E} box, x_0 is one particular object, the witness, about which we know \varphi[x_0/x] and nothing else; what is proved about it holds for it alone. From “some integer is even” nothing follows about every integer, and the rules agree: Line 4 is blocked: x_0 appears in the assumption P(x_0) of the ulename{\exists E} box, which is still open at line 4. That clause of ulename{ orall I} is what keeps a witness from being generalized over inside its box; clause 3 of ulename{\exists E}, that x_0 not appear in \chi, keeps it from leaving the box (the derivation for clause 3 above). Using an existential: open the box early When a resource is \exists x\, \varphi, the premise-directed step of the search method is to open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a fresh name x_0, and to make the box’s last line the current goal. Inside the box, the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] is a new resource, and the name x_0 is a new term for later steps to use. Name the witness early: open the ulename{\exists E} box as soon as the existential is available, and aim it at the current goal. Why early? The box takes nothing away: every line available before it opens is available inside it, so every resource is still there, and the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] is one more. And a box aimed at the current goal \chi can always be closed once \chi is reached: x_0 is chosen, when the box opens, to appear in no premise, in no open assumption, not in \exists x\, \varphi and not in the current goal \chi. The assumptions still open at the line that closes the box are the ones that were open when it opened, so every clause of the side condition holds there. (One caution: a ulename{ orall I} inside the box needs a flag that does not appear in the new assumption; a flag that is fresh at that point has this property.) What the early box gives is the witness. The name x_0 is often exactly the term that a postponed \exists goal is waiting for (Section 4.5), and the sooner it exists, the sooner the search can see it. The first result is the derivation that this step writes almost by itself. [Some Distributes Over And, One Way] \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x). The premise is an existential, so open its box first, with a fresh x_0, and aim it at the goal. Inside, the assumption P(x_0) \wedge Q(x_0) splits by ulename{\wedge E}, and each half is an instance of one conjunct of the goal, with the witness x_0. The goal does not mention x_0, so the box closes. The following is a derivation. Line 2 is the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] for \varphi = P(x) \wedge Q(x). Lines 4 and 6 are ulename{\exists I} with the witness x_0. At line 8, x_0 does not appear in line 7, in line 1 (which is also the only premise), or in any assumption of an open box (none is open). So line 8 is a correct ulename{\exists E}, and the derivation has 8 lines. Notice where the witness went. It was used twice inside the box, as the witness of two different existentials, and then forgotten twice. The conclusion records that something has P and something has Q, and no longer that it is the same thing. Is \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr)? Run the search, and say where it stalls. The premise splits by ulename{\wedge E} into \exists x\, P(x) and \exists x\, Q(x). Opening both boxes early gives the assumptions P(x_0) and, for the second box, a different name, Q(y_0): the second box is opened while the first is open, so x_0 appears in an open assumption and may not be reused. The postponed goal \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) needs one term t with P(t) \wedge Q(t), and the resources speak of two names, with nothing to say that they are equal. The search stalls there. It must: over 
Z, with P as “even” and Q as “odd”, the premise is true and the conclusion, “some integer is both even and odd”, is false. Section 4.11 gives a counter-model, and with the soundness statement stated there (proved in Section 4.12) this shows that no derivation exists. Here are three more derivations, each with an Idea saying why each rule was chosen: two for part (a), one for each direction, and one for part (b). [Derivations with existential elimination] Show that: 1. \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \vee Q(x)  igr) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, P(x) \vee \exists x\, Q(x); 2. \exists x\, P(x), \  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)  igr) \vdash 
eg  orall x\, Q(x). (a) (\vdash) Idea. The premise is an existential: open its box first. Inside, the assumption P(x_0) \vee Q(x_0) is a disjunction, and the premise-directed step for \vee (Section 1.7) opens two cases, each ending in the current goal. In each case one side of the goal has an instance with the witness x_0, so ulename{\exists I} and ulename{\vee I} finish it. Line 9 is ulename{\vee E} (@def-rules-disjunction), and it is the last line of the ulename{\exists E} box itself. At line 10, x_0 is in neither line 9 nor line 1, and no box is open. (\dashv) Idea. Now the premise is a disjunction: ulename{\vee E} first, with two cases, each ending in the goal. In each case the resource is an existential, so its box opens at once, and inside it ulename{\vee I} and ulename{\exists I} build the goal. At line 6, the open assumption is line 2, which does not contain x_0; at line 11 it is line 7, which does not either. The name x_0 is used in both cases. That is allowed: when the second box opens, the first has closed, and the side condition looks only at the premises, the boxes still open, the existential and the conclusion. Lines 6 and 11 are lines of the two case boxes themselves, as ulename{\vee E} requires. The two derivations mirror each other: ulename{\exists E} outside and ulename{\vee E} inside in one, the other way round in the other. Over a domain, both sides say that some element has P or Q. Contrast @prp-exists-and, where only one direction holds: \exists passes through \vee in both directions and through \wedge in one. (b) Idea. The goal is a negation, so the goal-directed step of Section 2.2 opens a ulename{
eg I} box on  orall x\, Q(x) (@def-rules-negation), with the goal  ot. Then the premise \exists x\, P(x) opens its box, aimed at  ot. Inside, the witness x_0 is the term at which to instantiate both universal statements: the premise gives 
eg Q(x_0), and the assumption gives Q(x_0), a clash. At line 9, the box of line 3 is still open, so its assumption  orall x\, Q(x) is checked: x_0 does not appear in it. Nor is x_0 in  ot, in line 1, or in line 2. Read over 
Z with P as “odd” and Q as “divisible by 4”: some integer is odd, no odd integer is divisible by 4, so not every integer is divisible by 4. The witness, whichever odd integer it is, is a counterexample to “every integer is divisible by 4”, and the derivation never needs to know which. Moving one quantifier past another Section 4.1 read \exists y\,  orall x\, \varphi and  orall x\, \exists y\, \varphi as games, and observed that the first gives the second: if one y works for every x, then for every x some y works, namely the same one. Here is that observation as a derivation, with the letters of a two-place predicate. It shows, written out in full, a pattern that later derivations of the chapter use again and again and that later exercises leave more and more of to the reader. [Some-All Gives All-Some] \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y). Three moves, read off the goal and the premise. ① Fix. The goal is  orall y: open a flagged box with a fresh y_0 (Section 4.4); the new goal is \exists x\, R(x, y_0). ② Obtain. That goal is an existential: postpone it. The premise is an existential: open its box early, with a fresh x_0, assuming  orall y\, R(x_0, y), and aim it at the current goal \exists x\, R(x, y_0). Instantiate the assumption at the term the goal mentions, y_0: this gives R(x_0, y_0). ③ Choose. That line is an instance of the postponed goal, with the witness x_0: ulename{\exists I}. Before reading on: at the line that closes the ulename{\exists E} box, check each clause of its side condition. Where could x_0 still appear? The following is a derivation. Line 2 is the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] for \varphi =  orall y\, R(x, y). Line 3 is ulename{ orall E} at y_0. Line 4 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi = R(x, y_0) and the witness x_0, which is free for x since R(x, y_0) has no quantifier. Line 5 closes the ulename{\exists E} box, whose last line, line 4, is a line of the box itself. Its side condition holds: x_0 does not appear in \chi = \exists x\, R(x, y_0), nor in the existential \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) of line 1, which is also the only premise; and the one box still open at line 5, the flagged box of y_0, has no assumption. Line 6 closes the flagged box of y_0 by ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal). That box immediately contains the ulename{\exists E} box, so its range starts at line 2 (the convention of Section 4.4), and its last line, line 5, is a line of the box itself, the instance (\exists x\, R(x, y))[y_0/y]. The name y_0 appears neither in the premise nor in line 6, and at line 6 no box is open. This proves the proposition. The two names played opposite parts. The name y_0 is arbitrary: nothing was assumed about it, and line 6 generalizes over it. The name x_0 is the witness: line 2 assumed everything the premise says about it, and line 5 forgets it. The witness x_0 works for y_0 because it works for every y, which line 2 says. This is the shape of a great many proofs in analysis, and it has a name. Fix, obtain, choose: fix the arbitrary objects of the goal (ulename{ orall I}); obtain witnesses from the hypotheses (ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists E}); choose the goal’s witness from what is now available (ulename{\exists I}). Nothing in the proof used that the formula under the quantifiers is R(x, y). For any formula \varphi and different variables x and y, with different names x_0 and y_0, other than x and y, that do not appear in \varphi, the same six lines derive \exists x\,  orall y\, \varphi \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\, \varphi. Line 2 is  orall y\, (\varphi[x_0/x]). Line 3 is (\varphi[x_0/x])[y_0/y], which equals (\varphi[y_0/y])[x_0/x], since the two substitutions put fresh names in for two different variables and so do not interfere; so line 4 is ulename{\exists I} with the formula \varphi[y_0/y] and the witness x_0. The fresh names are free for their variables, since neither appears in \varphi, and the side conditions are checked as before. With the letters x and y exchanged, this is the derivation of \exists y\,  orall x\, \varphi to  orall x\, \exists y\, \varphi promised in Section 4.1. Either nesting works. The derivation opened the flagged box of y_0 first and the ulename{\exists E} box inside it. The other order is just as good. At line 5, y_0 appears neither in the premise, nor in the open assumption  orall y\, R(x_0, y) (its y is a bound variable, not y_0), nor in line 5. At line 6, x_0 is not in line 5, not in line 1, and no box is open. In this order the ulename{\exists E} box is aimed at the whole goal; in the first, at the goal left inside the flagged box. Both are the search method’s “open the box early”: early relative to the goal that the box must reach. The converse search stalls at a side condition. Try  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). The goal is an existential: postpone it; it will need a witness x_0 and a line  orall y\, R(x_0, y). The premise is a universal, and to get an existential out of it we must instantiate it at some term. The natural routes then meet a side condition. Here are two of them. First route: obtain the witness, then try to generalize. Instantiate at a name y_0, open the ulename{\exists E} box on the result, and try to prove  orall y\, R(x_0, y) inside it by ulename{ orall I}: Line 5 is blocked: y_0 appears in the assumption R(x_0, y_0) of the ulename{\exists E} box, which is still open. The witness x_0 was obtained for y_0, and the assumption says so. Choosing a different flag, say z_0, does not help: the goal inside its box would be R(x_0, z_0), and nothing gives it. Second route: fix first, obtain inside, and carry the witness out. Open the flagged box of y_0 first, obtain x_0 inside it, and try to close the ulename{\exists E} box with a line about x_0, so that ulename{ orall I} can then generalize over y_0: Line 4 is blocked: x_0 appears in \chi = R(x_0, y_0). Lines 5 and 6 would be legal on their own; the derivation fails only because the witness escaped its box at line 4. The two blocked lines are the two halves of one fact. The witness x_0 is obtained after y_0 is fixed, so it may depend on y_0; the conclusion asks for an x_0 chosen before any y, which may not. This is the dependence that Section 4.1 read off the order of the quantifiers, now visible as the order of the boxes. A stalled search is not a proof that no derivation exists. Section 4.11 gives a structure on 
Z in which the premise is true and the conclusion false, and the soundness statement stated there (proved in Section 4.12) turns it into a proof that no derivation exists. Renaming the bound variable of an existential Section 4.2 promised that a bound variable at the front of a formula may be renamed, and Section 4.4 derived the renaming for  orall (@exm-universal-introduction-derivations (b)). Here is the derivation for \exists. Let \varphi be a formula and y, z variables, with z not appearing in \varphi. Then \exists y\, \varphi \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists z\, \varphi[z/y] . Take a fresh name z_0, a variable different from y and z that does not appear in \varphi, as in Section 4.4. Both directions use one fact about substitution: since z does not appear in \varphi, each free z of \varphi[z/y] stands where \varphi had a free y, and nowhere else, so putting a term t in for those z’s gives \varphi[t/y]; that is, (\varphi[z/y])[t/z] = \varphi[t/y]. (It is a structural induction of the kind in Section 4.2, one clause at a time.) In the left derivation, line 3 is ulename{\exists I} with the formula \varphi[z/y], the variable z and the witness z_0: by the fact, (\varphi[z/y])[z_0/z] is line 2. The witness is free for z, because the quantifiers of \varphi[z/y] are those of \varphi, and none of them is on z_0. In the right derivation, line 2 is the assumption of the box for the existential \exists z\, \varphi[z/y], which is (\varphi[z/y])[z_0/z], that is \varphi[z_0/y] by the fact, and line 3 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi, y and the witness z_0, which is free for y since it does not appear in \varphi. In both, line 4 is a correct ulename{\exists E}: z_0 does not appear in \varphi, so it is in neither line 1 nor line 3, and no box is open. So \exists y\, (y 
e x) and \exists z\, (z 
e x) can each be derived from the other, as the recipe of Section 4.2 assumed. Two witnesses A proof often obtains several witnesses, one from each existential hypothesis. Each needs its own box and its own name. [The sum of two even integers is even] Over 
Z, with “n is even” written \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k), derive \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k), \ \exists k\, (m = 2 \cdot k) \;\vdash\; \exists k\, (n + m = 2 \cdot k) . Idea. Both premises are existentials: open both boxes early, the second inside the first, with different names k_0 and l_0. The goal is an existential: postpone it. Inside both boxes the resources are n = 2 \cdot k_0 and m = 2 \cdot l_0, and arithmetic gives n + m = 2 \cdot (k_0 + l_0), which shows the witness: the compound term k_0 + l_0. Line 5 is one line of arithmetic: from n = 2k_0 and m = 2l_0, substituting and factoring gives n + m = 2k_0 + 2l_0 = 2(k_0 + l_0). The substitutions are steps of the rule ulename{{=}E}, which arrives only in Section 4.7, so here the whole calculation is one line justified “arith”, citing the two lines it uses. Line 6 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi = (n + m = 2 \cdot k) and the witness k_0 + l_0. At line 7 the only box still open is the outer one, whose assumption is line 3; l_0 appears neither in it, nor in the premises on lines 1 and 2 (line 2 is also the existential cited), nor in line 6. At line 8, k_0 appears neither in line 7, nor in the premises (line 1 is the existential cited), and no box is open. The derivation has 8 lines. The written proof is three sentences: Choose k with n = 2k, and l with m = 2l. Then n + m = 2(k + l). So n + m is even. Why must the second witness in @exm-sum-of-evens be called l_0, and not k_0 again? Name the line and the clause of the side condition that a second k_0 would break. The inner box would then be flagged k_0 with the assumption m = 2 \cdot k_0, and line 7 would close it by ulename{\exists E}. At line 7 the outer box is still open, and its assumption n = 2 \cdot k_0 (line 3) contains k_0. That breaks the clause “x_0 does not appear in any assumption of a box still open at line k”. In words: the second witness would be assumed to be the same integer as the first, so n and m would be forced equal, which the premises never said. How this rule looks in a mathematical proof In a written proof, the ulename{\exists E} box is announced by “choose”, “let x_0 be such a point”, “say n = 2k”, “fix such a k”. The assumption of the box is the property in the sentence, and the rest of the paragraph is the inside of the box. The claim the paragraph ends on, usually the clause after the final “so”, must not mention the chosen name, though the computation leading up to it may. If that claim still mentions the name, the paragraph has not finished: a later step must reach a claim without the name before the box can close, often an ulename{\exists I} that forgets it (as in the example below), or a contradiction  ot (as in @exm-existential-elimination-derivations (b)). Here is an instance from analysis. A sequence (a_n) is bounded if there is an M with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N. A proof says: Since (a_n) is bounded, choose M with \abs{a_n} \le M for all n \in 
N. Then \abs{2a_n} = 2\abs{a_n} \le 2M for all n \in 
N, so (2a_n) is bounded. With the domain 
R, the sequence as a function symbol a, and the bound on n written out by @def-bounded-quantifier, the proof is this derivation. The sentences match the boxes. “Choose M” opens the ulename{\exists E} box (line 2). “For all n \in 
N” in the second sentence is the flagged box of n_0 with its ulename{{	o}I} box (lines 3–7, closed by line 8); the arithmetic \abs{2a_n} = 2\abs{a_n} \le 2M is line 6. “So (2a_n) is bounded” is two steps: ulename{\exists I} with the witness 2 \cdot M_0 (line 9), which forgets the bound 2M, and the close of the box (line 10). The conclusion mentions neither M_0 nor 2 \cdot M_0, as the side condition requires. Section 4.8 shortens the bounded steps. Two witnesses, one name. “Let n and m be even, say n = 2k and m = 2k” is a common error in parity proofs. It gives two unknown witnesses the same name, and the rest of the proof then uses an equation the premises never gave. For instance it “proves” that the sum of two even integers is divisible by 4: Line 7 is blocked: k_0 appears in the assumption n = 2 \cdot k_0 of the outer box, still open at line 7. With n = 2 and m = 4, both premises are true and n + m = 6 is not divisible by 4. What the rule sounds like Here is the row of the rule, phrase and Lean table for ulename{\exists E}; Section 4.7 collects the whole table, and nothing later depends on the last column. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule You write Lean ---------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------------------- ulename{\exists E} “Choose k with n = 2k. Then …”; “let x_0 be such a point.” obtain (or Exists.elim h) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrase “choose” is apt and slightly misleading. We do not choose the witness, since we cannot see it; we choose a name for it. A written proof that says “choose k” promises the reader that nothing more about k will be used than the property stated, and that k will be gone by the end of the argument. The search method: one more step. With this rule, each of the four quantifier rules has added a step, and Section 4.8 collects them with the steps of Section 2.6. - Premise \exists x\, \varphi. Open the ulename{\exists E} box early, as soon as the existential is available, with a fresh name x_0 and the assumption \varphi[x_0/x]; make its last line the current goal, which must not mention x_0. Give every new witness a new name. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the proof of @prp-exists-forall-swap. 1. State ulename{\exists E} as a schema, with every clause of its side condition. 2. The proof opened the flagged box of y_0 first and the ulename{\exists E} box of x_0 inside it. Could they be opened in the other order? If so, does every side condition still hold? 3. Answer the Before reading on prompt of the proof: at line 5, where could x_0 still appear, and does it? 4. In the two attempts at the converse,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), which line is blocked in each, and by which clause of which rule? 5. Give the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) From \exists x\, \varphi on line h and a flagged box with name x_0, from the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] on line i to \chi on line j, a line of the box itself, write \chi on line k, justified “ulename{\exists E} h, i–j”. Side condition at line k: x_0 does not appear in \chi, in \exists x\, \varphi, in any premise, or in any assumption of a box still open at line k. (b) Yes, either order works. In the other order (the derivation under Either nesting works, right after the proof), the ulename{\exists E} box encloses the flagged box. At the ulename{ orall I} line, y_0 appears in no premise, not in the open assumption  orall y\, R(x_0, y), and not in the conclusion; at the ulename{\exists E} line, x_0 is not in  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y), not in the premise, and no box is open. (c) At line 5, the clauses list four places: \chi, which is line 4, \exists x\, R(x, y_0); the existential of line 1, \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y); the premise, which is line 1 again; and the assumptions of boxes open at line 5. The only box open at line 5 is the flagged box of y_0, which has no assumption. The name x_0 appears in none of these, so line 5 is correct. It does appear in lines 2–4, inside the box, which the side condition allows. (d) In the first attempt, line 5 (ulename{ orall I} over y_0) is blocked by the clause “y_0 appears in no assumption of a box still open”, since the ulename{\exists E} box’s assumption R(x_0, y_0) contains y_0. In the second, line 4 (ulename{\exists E}) is blocked by the clause “x_0 does not appear in \chi”, since \chi = R(x_0, y_0). (e) Fix an arbitrary y_0 and obtain the witness x_0 of the premise, which satisfies R(x_0, y) for every y, in particular for y_0. So x_0 is a witness for \exists x\, R(x, y_0), and since y_0 was arbitrary,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) follows. B. Practice [B1] Derive  orall x\, 
eg  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr), \ \exists x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, 
eg Q(x). Read the sequent over 
Z with P as “positive” and Q as “negative”. Idea. The premise \exists x\, P(x) opens its box first, with a witness x_0, aimed at the goal. The goal \exists x\, 
eg Q(x) is postponed; the witness x_0 is the natural candidate, so the new goal inside is 
eg Q(x_0), a negation: a ulename{
eg I} box on Q(x_0). Inside, P(x_0) \wedge Q(x_0) clashes with the first premise at x_0. At line 10, x_0 is not in line 9, not in line 2, not in either premise, and no box is open. Over 
Z: no integer is both positive and negative, and some integer is positive, so some integer is not negative. The witness of the conclusion is the positive witness of the premise. [B2: Fix, obtain, choose, faded] Here is a derivation of  orall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y), \  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( R(x, y) 	o Q(y)  igr) \;\vdash\;  orall x\, \exists y\,  igl( R(x, y) \wedge Q(y)  igr) with its last line missing. Name the move, then complete it. Then mark which lines are the “fix”, which the “obtain”, and which the “choose”. The missing line closes the flagged box of x_0 by ulename{ orall I}; the move is the “fix” of fix, obtain, choose, completed: “since x_0 was arbitrary”. Line 11 cites the flagged box \lines{3}{10}; its last line, line 10, is a line of that box itself and is the instance \psi[x_0/x] for \psi = \exists y\, (R(x, y) \wedge Q(y)). The name x_0 appears in neither premise and not in line 11, and at line 11 no box is open. (At line 10, y_0 is not in line 9, not in line 3, not in the premises, and the only open box, that of x_0, has no assumption.) The moves: fix is the flagged box of x_0 (opened before line 3, closed at line 11); obtain is line 3 (ulename{ orall E} at x_0) and the ulename{\exists E} box of y_0 (lines 4–10), with lines 5–7 using the second premise on the witness; choose is line 9, ulename{\exists I} with the witness y_0. [B3] An integer n is odd when n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Over 
Z, derive \exists k\, (m = 2 \cdot k + 1), \ \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k + 1) \;\vdash\; \exists k\, (m \cdot n = 2 \cdot k + 1), with one line justified “arith”. Then write the proof as three sentences of prose. Idea. As in @exm-sum-of-evens: open both boxes early, with different names, and postpone the goal until the arithmetic shows the witness. Line 5: (2k_0 + 1)(2l_0 + 1) = 4k_0 l_0 + 2k_0 + 2l_0 + 1 = 2(2k_0 l_0 + k_0 + l_0) + 1. Line 6 is ulename{\exists I} with \varphi = (m \cdot n = 2 \cdot k + 1) and the witness 2 \cdot k_0 \cdot l_0 + k_0 + l_0. At line 7, l_0 is in none of line 6, line 2, the premises, and the open assumption on line 3; at line 8, k_0 is in none of line 7, line 1, the premises, and no box is open. In prose: Choose integers k and l with m = 2k + 1 and n = 2l + 1. Then mn = 4kl + 2k + 2l + 1 = 2(2kl + k + l) + 1. Since 2kl + k + l is an integer, mn is odd. C. Going deeper [C1] Derive \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), \  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( R(x, y) 	o R(y, x)  igr) \;\vdash\;  orall y\, \exists x\, R(y, x), and check the side condition of every ulename{\exists E} and ulename{ orall I} line. Then give a reading over 
Z in which both premises are true, and say which integer the derivation’s witness is. [Hint 1] The shape is the one of @prp-exists-forall-swap: fix, obtain, choose. Which line does symmetry have to turn round? [Hint 2] Open a flagged box for y_0, and inside it the ulename{\exists E} box of the first premise, with the assumption  orall y\, R(x_0, y). Idea. The goal is  orall y: fix y_0. The new goal \exists x\, R(y_0, x) is postponed. The first premise is an existential: obtain x_0 with  orall y\, R(x_0, y), and instantiate it at the term the goal mentions, y_0: R(x_0, y_0). The goal needs R(y_0, t), with y_0 first, so the second premise turns the line round, instantiated at x_0 and y_0 in that order (read off the line to be turned). Then choose the witness x_0. Line 9 (ulename{\exists E}): x_0 does not appear in \chi = \exists x\, R(y_0, x), nor in the existential of line 1, nor in either premise; the only box open at line 9 is the flagged box of y_0, which has no assumption. Line 8 is a line of the ulename{\exists E} box itself. Line 10 (ulename{ orall I}): the flagged box immediately contains the ulename{\exists E} box, so its range starts at line 3. Its last line, line 9, is a line of the box itself and is (\exists x\, R(y, x))[y_0/y]. The name y_0 appears in neither premise and not in line 10, and no box is open. A reading. Over 
Z, let R(x, y) mean “x \cdot y = 0”. The second premise holds since x \cdot y = y \cdot x. The first holds with the witness 0, and only with it: for x 
eq 0, the instance y = 1 gives x \cdot 1 = x 
eq 0. The conclusion says that every integer has a partner with product 0, which is true. The derivation’s x_0 names the witness of the first premise, so under this reading it can only be 0, and the derivation gives every y the partner 0; the derivation itself never uses which integer it is. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: opens a flagged box for the goal’s  orall y with a fresh name, and postpones the existential. - 2: opens the ulename{\exists E} box of the first premise with a fresh witness, aimed at the current goal. - 2: instantiates the assumption at y_0 and the symmetry premise at x_0, y_0 in that order, and fires it. - 2: ulename{\exists I} with the witness x_0, inside the ulename{\exists E} box. - 1: checks the side conditions of the ulename{\exists E} and ulename{ orall I} lines clause by clause. - 1: a reading over 
Z in which both premises hold, with the witness identified (or, if the reading does not determine it, correctly described as whichever witness the first premise has). Fatal errors (0 for the step): an ulename{\exists E} box closed on a line containing its witness; ulename{ orall I} over a name in an open assumption; the symmetry premise instantiated in the wrong order and then used as if it fired. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “derivation” of \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge Q(x)  igr) \vdash \exists x\, P(x). 1. Is the conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. 2. Does this derivation prove it? If not, name the exact line that fails, the rule, and the clause of its side condition that is broken. 3. Show that the illegal step itself is unsound: use the same step to “derive”, from a premise true over 
Z, a sentence false over 
Z. [Hint 1] For (a), the conclusion is half of the conclusion of a result proved in this section. [Hint 2] For (c), drop Q: start from the premise \exists x\, P(x) and take the same illegal step as line 4. (a) Yes, the conclusion is derivable: by @prp-exists-and the premise gives \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x), and ulename{\wedge E} gives \exists x\, P(x). Directly, moving the ulename{\exists I} inside the box repairs the derivation: At line 5, x_0 is not in line 4, not in line 1, and no box is open. (b) No. Line 4 fails: it is ulename{\exists E} with \chi = P(x_0), and x_0 appears in \chi, which breaks the clause “x_0 does not appear in \chi” of @def-rules-existential. The witness has escaped its box. Lines 1–3 are correct, and line 5 would be a correct ulename{\exists I} if line 4 were a legitimate line. A true conclusion does not make the argument correct: the conclusion is derivable, but not by this derivation. (c) The same step, from \exists x\, P(x) alone: Line 3 is the illegal step of line 4 above. Line 4 repeats line 3 into a flagged box, and line 5 is a correct ulename{ orall I}: x_0 appears in no premise, in no open assumption, and not in line 5. Over 
Z with P as “even”, the premise “some integer is even” is true and the conclusion “every integer is even” is false. So the step from \exists x\, P(x) to P(x_0) can lead from truth to falsehood; it is a counterexample to the step, while the conclusion of the original sequent has no counterexample at all. (This is the same failure as the derivation after @def-rules-existential that “proves” every natural number exceeds 5.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) says the conclusion is derivable and gives a correct derivation or cites @prp-exists-and with ulename{\wedge E}. - 3: (b) names line 4, the rule ulename{\exists E}, and the clause “x_0 not in \chi”. - 1: (b) says that the other lines are correct, so the error is in that one line. - 4: (c) gives a derivation that uses the same illegal step and is otherwise legal, with a reading in which the premise is true and the conclusion false. Fatal errors (0 for the step): answering (a) “no” because the derivation is wrong; giving a counterexample to the conclusion of the original sequent (there is none); blaming line 5.

title: 4.7 Equality and Unique Existence
content:
Equality and Unique Existence Sections 4.3 to 4.6 gave the four quantifier rules, and with them every logical symbol of the language of Section 4.2 (the connectives,  ot, the quantifiers, and equality) has rules, except one. So far the equals sign has been treated like a predicate symbol: a = b was an atomic formula like P(a), and no rule looked inside it. Yet almost every calculation in mathematics is a chain of equations, and every use of “the” (the limit, the supremum, the inverse) quietly asserts that something is unique. This section adds the two rules for equality, ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E}, which say together that equals may be replaced by equals. Its first application is the phrase “there is exactly one”, which is an existential statement together with an equation. The section ends by completing the table of rules, phrases, and Lean tactics that Chapter 1 began. What the rules so far cannot do with an equation Here is the first line of a calculation any reader has written: Since a = b and a + a = 2a, we have b + b = 2b. Nothing could be simpler, and nothing in Sections 4.3–4.6 derives it. The line a = b is an atomic formula, and so far the rules have treated = exactly as they treat a two-place predicate symbol written between its terms, like the R in front of R(a, b). From the premises R(a, b) and P(a) no rule gives P(b): a relation between a and b says nothing, by itself, about the properties of either. The quantifier rules do not help either, since neither premise begins with a quantifier. As far as the rules of Chapters 1–2 and Sections 4.3–4.6 are concerned, a = b could mean “a is less than b” or “a and b are coprime”, and under those readings the general pattern behind the step, from R(a, b) and P(a) to P(b), fails: reading R(a, b) as a < b and P(x) as x < 1 over 
Z, with a = 0 and b = 5, both premises are true and P(b) is false. What makes the step correct is what = means: a and b are names of the same object. Any statement true of the object is true of it whichever name is used. Two things follow, and they are the two rules of this section. 1. Every term names the same object as itself. Nothing needs to be assumed to write t = t. 2. If t_1 and t_2 name the same object, then a statement about t_1 may be rewritten as the same statement about t_2. The first rule is unusual: it cites no earlier line at all. Chapter 1 anticipated this when it defined rules (Section 1.2): the definition of a rule schema (@def-rule-schema) was worded so that a rule of Chapter 4 could have no given lines at all. This is that rule. The rules for equality Everything is equal to itself, and equals may be replaced by equals. [Rules for Equality] The rule ulename{{=}I} (equality introduction, or reflexivity) writes t = t for any term t, at any line, citing nothing. The rule ulename{{=}E} (equality elimination, or substitution of equals) cites an equation t_1 = t_2 on line i and a line j of the form \varphi[t_1/x], both available at line k, and writes \varphi[t_2/x] on line k. Here \varphi is any formula and x any variable, subject to one side condition: both t_1 and t_2 are free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). In words: ulename{{=}I} says that every term equals itself. ulename{{=}E} says that when t_1 = t_2 is known, a line that says something about t_1 may be rewritten as the same thing said about t_2. The formula \varphi is the “something”: a statement with a hole x, which line j fills with t_1 and line k fills with t_2. Read the definition clause by clause. 1. ulename{{=}I} cites nothing. Its justification is “ulename{{=}I}” alone. It is the first primitive rule of the book with no given lines (derived rules from results with no premises, such as ulename{LEM} of Section 2.5, already cite nothing), and so it may stand anywhere: as the first line of a derivation with no premises, or deep inside a box. 2. The equation is read from left to right. The cited equation t_1 = t_2 licenses replacing t_1 by t_2, and not the other way round. From a = b and P(b), the rule does not give P(a), because P(b) is \varphi[b/x] for \varphi = P(x), and the equation would have to be b = a. The reverse direction needs one more step, symmetry, which we derive below. 3. Some or all occurrences. The choice of \varphi decides which occurrences of t_1 are replaced: exactly those that \varphi marks with x. Occurrences of t_1 that \varphi writes out are left alone. Choosing \varphi is the whole art of using the rule. 4. Free for x. Neither term may have a variable captured by a quantifier of \varphi, the condition of @def-free-for that the rules of Sections 4.3 and 4.5 also carry. The nonexample below shows what goes wrong without it. One line, many readings. Take the equation a = b and the line a + a = 2 \cdot a. The term a occurs three times in the line, and \varphi may mark any of them. Here is a proof from school algebra, read link by link. Claim. If a + b = 0 and a + c = 0, then b = c. Proof. b = b + 0 = b + (a + c) = (b + a) + c = (a + b) + c = 0 + c = c. Unique existence Mathematics says “the limit of the sequence”, “the supremum of A”, “the additive inverse of a”. Each “the” makes two claims. There is such an object, and there is only one, so that the name picks it out. The second claim is the one that is easy to forget, and the one the claim above was about. “There is exactly one x with \varphi”: there is one, and any other is it. Unique Existence Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in \varphi (Section 4.2). Then \exists! x\, \varphi \quad 	ext{abbreviates} \quad \exists x\,  igl( \varphi \wedge  orall y\, (\varphi[y/x] 	o y = x)  igr). We read \exists! x\, \varphi as “there is exactly one x such that \varphi”, or “there is a unique x with \varphi”. In words: there is an x that satisfies \varphi, and every y that satisfies \varphi (that is, satisfies \varphi with y in place of x) is equal to that x. The first conjunct is existence. The second is uniqueness, and it is a statement about the x already found: any other candidate coincides with it. Like the bounded quantifiers of @def-bounded-quantifier, \exists! is not a new symbol of the language but shorthand, and every rule applies to the formula it abbreviates. Well-definedness. The abbreviation seems to depend on the choice of y. It does not, up to renaming a bound variable (Section 4.2). The argument rests on one fact about substitution, used again below: if y does not appear in \varphi, then replacing x by y and then y by a term t is the same as replacing x by t, that is, (\varphi[y/x])[t/y] is \varphi[t/x]. This is a structural induction on \varphi of the kind in Section 4.2. In a term, the y’s of s[y/x] are exactly the former x’s, so (s[y/x])[t/y] = s[t/x]; atomic formulas,  ot and the connectives follow clause by clause. For  orall x\, \psi, both sides are  orall x\, \psi, since substitution for x stops at  orall x and y does not appear in \psi (the second fact of Section 4.2). For  orall z\, \psi with z not x, also z is not y, because y does not appear in \varphi; so both substitutions pass under the quantifier and the induction hypothesis applies, and \exists is the same. Now let y and y' be two admissible choices. If they are the same variable there is nothing to show. Otherwise y' does not appear in \varphi[y/x] 	o y = x, since it is neither x nor y and does not appear in \varphi; so the bound y of  orall y\, (\varphi[y/x] 	o y = x) may be renamed y', which gives  orall y'\,  igl( (\varphi[y/x])[y'/y] 	o y' = x  igr). By the fact with t = y', this is  orall y'\, (\varphi[y'/x] 	o y' = x), the formula written with y'. Why y must not appear in \varphi. How uniqueness is used and proved A proof of “exactly one” rarely follows the shape of @def-unique-existence, which ties the uniqueness clause to the witness just found. It proves two separate statements: there is at least one, and there is at most one. The second is “any two objects with the property are equal”, and it makes no mention of a witness. The next result says that the two shapes say the same thing. [Two Halves of Unique Existence] Let \varphi be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in \varphi. Then \exists! x\, \varphi \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \varphi \wedge  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( \varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] 	o x = y  igr). The right-hand side is “existence and at most one”. Its second conjunct is what a mathematician proves under the heading “uniqueness”: take two objects x and y with the property, and show x = y. Both directions are searches in the style of Section 2.6 with the quantifier steps. For \vdash, the premise is an \exists, so open its ulename{\exists E} box first, with a witness x_0: inside it, \varphi[x_0/x] gives existence at once by ulename{\exists I}, and “at most one” is a  orall orall goal, which opens two flagged boxes u_0, v_0. Two objects u_0, v_0 with the property are each equal to the witness x_0, by the uniqueness clause, and so equal to each other: the witness is the “third point” that links them. For \dashv, open the ulename{\exists E} box on \exists x\, \varphi with a witness x_0; the goal inside is \exists! x\, \varphi, whose witness will be x_0 again, and the uniqueness clause for x_0 comes from “at most one” applied to the pair x_0, y_0. Second, \varphi[y/x] has no free x (every free x became y), so it is unchanged by a substitution for x. Third, for a term t that does not contain y, \varphi[t/x] contains no y, so it is unchanged by a substitution for y. In practice this is how “there is exactly one” is proved: an existence proof, then a separate “suppose x and y both satisfy \varphi; then x = y”. And it is how it is used: from \exists! x\, \varphi we may take a witness, and we may identify any two objects with the property. The claim about additive inverses above was the “at most one” half; existence of an inverse is a field axiom. One more instance: “the maximum”. A maximum of a set A of reals is an element m \in A with a \le m for every a \in A. If m and m' are both maxima, then m' \le m (apply the property of m to the element m' \in A) and m \le m' (apply the property of m' to m \in A), so m = m' by the order fact that a \le b and b \le a give a = b. That is “at most one”; a set may have no maximum at all, such as (0, 1), so existence is a separate question. Only when both halves are known may we write “the maximum of A”.
