In the same derivation, could lines 4 and 5 be replaced by one line? With which \varphi? 4. True or false, with a reason: from the lines a = b and P(b), one application of ulename{{=}E} gives P(a). 5. Write \exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 9) without the symbol \exists!, and decide whether it is true over 
N and over 
Z. (a) ulename{{=}I}: at any line k, write t = t, for any term t, citing nothing. ulename{{=}E}: from t_1 = t_2 on line i and \varphi[t_1/x] on line j, both available at line k, write \varphi[t_2/x] on line k; side condition: t_1 and t_2 are both free for x in \varphi. (b) Line 4: ulename{{=}E} 1, 3, with \varphi = (a \cdot a = z \cdot a), which rewrites the first a on the right. Line 5: ulename{{=}E} 1, 4, with \varphi = (a \cdot a = (b + 1) \cdot z). Line 6: ulename{{=}E} 2, 5, with \varphi = (a \cdot a = (z + 1) \cdot (z + 1)), which rewrites both b’s at once. Line 8: ulename{{=}E} 7, 6, with \varphi = (a \cdot a = z). In each case the left-hand side a \cdot a is written out in \varphi, so it is kept. (c) Yes: ulename{{=}E} 1, 3 with \varphi = (a \cdot a = z \cdot z) gives a \cdot a = (b + 1) \cdot (b + 1) in one step, rewriting both a’s on the right and keeping the two on the left. (d) False. With the equation a = b, ulename{{=}E} passes from \varphi[a/x] to \varphi[b/x]. The line P(b) is \varphi[b/x] for \varphi = P(x), so the rule would need the equation b = a. One application of symmetry first (@prp-equality-symmetric-transitive (a)) gives b = a, and then ulename{{=}E} gives P(a). (e) \exists x\,  igl( x \cdot x = 9 \wedge  orall y\, (y \cdot y = 9 	o y = x)  igr). Over 
N it is true: x = 3 works, and a natural number y with y \cdot y = 9 is 3, since y \le 2 gives y \cdot y \le 4 and y \ge 4 gives y \cdot y \ge 16. Over 
Z it is false: whatever x is proposed, 3 and -3 both satisfy y \cdot y = 9, and they cannot both equal x. B. Practice [B1: The identity is unique] A set with an operation \cdot has an identity e if e \cdot x = x and x \cdot e = x for every x. Derive  orall x\, (e \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e = x), \;\;  orall x\, (e' \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e' = x) \;\vdash\; e = e', where e and e' are constants. Which half of “there is exactly one identity” does this prove? Hint: look at the one element that both premises can say something about. The goal is an equation between e and e', and the only term that both premises can connect to both is the product e \cdot e'. Instantiate the first premise at e' and the second at e (ulename{ orall E}, reading the terms off the goal): Line 7 uses the equation e \cdot e' = e of line 6 to rewrite the left side of line 4, with \varphi = (z = e'): \varphi[e \cdot e'/z] is line 4, and \varphi[e/z] is e = e'. In prose: e = e \cdot e' = e', the first equation because e' is an identity and the second because e is. This is the “at most one” half: any two identities are equal. It says nothing about whether an identity exists. To use it in @prp-unique-existence-use, take \varphi =  orall z\, (x \cdot z = z \wedge z \cdot x = z), and run lines 3–7 again with variables u_0, v_0 in place of e, e': inside flagged boxes for u_0 and v_0 and a ulename{{	o}I} box on \varphi[u_0/x] \wedge \varphi[v_0/x], the two premises (with z as their bound variable) come from that assumption by ulename{\wedge E}, and the same steps give u_0 = v_0. Then ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{ orall I} twice give  orall x\,  orall y\, (\varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] 	o x = y), the second conjunct of the proposition. With the existence of one identity as well, @prp-unique-existence-use gives “there is exactly one”. [B2: A unique square root of zero] Over 
R, write \exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 0) without \exists!, and prove it: existence, then uniqueness in the form “suppose y also satisfies …”. Hint: a product of two nonzero reals is nonzero. Written out, the statement is \exists x\,  igl( x \cdot x = 0 \wedge  orall y\, (y \cdot y = 0 	o y = x)  igr). We take the witness x = 0 and prove the two conjuncts. Existence. 0 \cdot 0 = 0. Uniqueness. Let y be a real number, and suppose y \cdot y = 0. If y 
e 0, then y \cdot y is a product of two nonzero reals and so is nonzero, which contradicts y \cdot y = 0. Hence y = 0, which is the witness. Since y was arbitrary, every y with y \cdot y = 0 equals 0. So 0 witnesses the existential, and \exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 0) holds. The rules behind the words: “we take the witness x = 0” is ulename{\exists I}, postponed to the end as usual; “let y be a real number” is a flagged box for ulename{ orall I}; “suppose y \cdot y = 0” is a ulename{{	o}I} box; “if y 
e 0 … contradicts” is an ulename{RAA} box on y 
e 0. (That box gives y = 0 directly; ulename{
eg I} would give only 
eg(y 
e 0). Since for reals y = 0 or y 
e 0 is also a school fact, a proof by cases would do as well.) [B3: Exactly one fixed point] A fixed point of a function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is a real x with f(x) = x. 1. Formalize “f has exactly one fixed point” over 
R, first with \exists! and then without it. 2. Write a formula without \exists! that says “f does not have exactly one fixed point”, in the form “there is none, or there are two different ones”. 3. Decide the statement of (a) for f(x) = x \cdot x, for f(x) = x + 1 and for f(x) = 2 \cdot x, and check your answer against the formula of (b). (a) With \exists!: \exists! x\, (f(x) = x). Written out, with y as the new variable: \exists x\,  igl( f(x) = x \wedge  orall y\, (f(y) = y 	o y = x)  igr). (b) 
eg\exists x\, (f(x) = x) \vee \exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( f(x) = x \wedge f(y) = y \wedge x 
e y  igr). Read informally over 
R: either no real number is fixed, or two different ones are. That is exactly the failure of “exactly one”. If no x is fixed, the first disjunct holds. If some x is fixed but the uniqueness clause fails for it, then some y is fixed and differs from x. Conversely, either disjunct rules out a unique fixed point: with none there is no witness, and two different fixed points x 
e y would both have to equal any proposed witness w, giving x = y. (Section 4.9 derives such negations mechanically, one quantifier at a time.) (c) For f(x) = x \cdot x: x \cdot x = x holds for x = 0 and for x = 1, so there are two different fixed points; (a) is false, and the second disjunct of (b) is true with x = 0, y = 1. For f(x) = x + 1: x + 1 = x has no solution, so (a) is false and the first disjunct of (b) is true. For f(x) = 2 \cdot x: 2x = x gives x = 0, and 0 is fixed; so (a) is true with the witness 0, and both disjuncts of (b) are false. C. Going deeper [C1: Two unique quantifiers do not commute] Show that \exists! x\, \exists! y\, R(x, y) and \exists! y\, \exists! x\, R(x, y) can have different truth values, by giving a finite domain D and a two-place relation R on it for which the first is true and the second false. Check both, reading \exists! informally. Hint: first say in words what each sentence claims about the rows and columns of a table of R. What any answer must satisfy. Call x single if exactly one y has R(x, y), and call y co-single if exactly one x has R(x, y). The first sentence says that exactly one element is single. The second says that exactly one element is co-single. So an answer needs exactly one single element and a number of co-single elements other than one: none, or two or more. An example. Take D = \{0, 1, 2\} and R = \{(1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 1)\}. - Single elements: 0 has no partner, 1 has exactly one (2), and 2 has two (0 and 1). So 1 is the only single element, and \exists! x\, \exists! y\, R(x, y) is true, with the witness 1. - Co-single elements: y = 0 is reached only from x = 2; y = 1 only from x = 2; y = 2 only from x = 1. All three are co-single, so there is not exactly one, and \exists! y\, \exists! x\, R(x, y) is false. No example exists on one or two elements (there are only 2 + 16 = 18 relations on such domains). On one element, 0 is single and co-single exactly when R(0, 0) holds, so the two sentences agree. On two elements, suppose exactly one element is single; after relabeling, call it 0, and let c be its only partner. Then 1 is not single, so it has no partners or two. If it has none, column c has one entry and the other column has none. If it has two, column c has two entries and the other column has one. Either way exactly one element is co-single. Exchanging the roles of rows and columns gives the converse, so the two sentences have the same truth value. Three elements is therefore the smallest possible domain. The moral: \exists! is not a quantifier that commutes with its own kind, as two \exists’s do. “Exactly one” hides a  orall (the uniqueness clause), and the order of a  orall and an \exists matters. [C2: “At most one”, two ways] Let P be a one-place predicate symbol. Derive both directions of  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( P(x) \wedge P(y) 	o x = y  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; 
eg\exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( (P(x) \wedge P(y)) \wedge x 
e y  igr), and say which of your two derivations uses ulename{RAA}, and at which line. [Hint 1] The right-hand side is a negation: for \vdash, open a ulename{
eg I} box, and inside it two ulename{\exists E} boxes. For \dashv, the goal is  orall orall, then an implication, then an equation. [Hint 2] In the \dashv direction, open flagged boxes for x_0 and y_0 and a ulename{{	o}I} box on P(x_0) \wedge P(y_0). The goal is now the atomic formula x_0 = y_0. Which resources can give it? (\vdash) The goal is a negation, so a ulename{
eg I} box opens on \exists x\, \exists y\, (\dots); inside, the premise-directed step opens an ulename{\exists E} box for each \exists, with the goal  ot as each box’s last line. The premise, instantiated at the two witnesses, gives x_0 = y_0, which clashes with x_0 
e y_0. The brackets in the statement are written out because the default groups a longer conjunction to the right (Section 3.4); with the grouping (P(x_0) \wedge P(y_0)) \wedge x_0 
e y_0 on line 4, ulename{\wedge E} takes out its two halves on lines 5 and 6. At line 11, y_0 is not in  ot, not in line 3, not in the premise, and not in the assumptions still open (lines 2 and 3). At line 12 the same holds for x_0, with line 2 the only open assumption. (\dashv) The goal-directed steps open flagged boxes for x_0 and y_0 and a ulename{{	o}I} box on P(x_0) \wedge P(y_0), leaving the goal x_0 = y_0. No resource gives an equation, so the search is stuck, and step 5 of the method applies: an ulename{RAA} box on x_0 
e y_0. Inside, ulename{\wedge I} and two ulename{\exists I} steps rebuild the formula that the premise denies. The \dashv derivation uses ulename{RAA}, at line 8: the box opens with x_0 
e y_0, that is 
eg(x_0 = y_0), and closes with x_0 = y_0. Closing it by ulename{
eg I} instead would give 
eg
eg(x_0 = y_0), and no rule of Chapter 1 or Sections 2.1–2.4 removes the double negation. (With the derived rule ulename{
eg
eg E} of Section 2.5, that ulename{
eg I} box followed by ulename{
eg
eg E} is an equally good derivation; its classical step is the ulename{
eg
eg E} line, which hides an ulename{RAA}.) The \vdash derivation uses no classical rule. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: \vdash: opens a ulename{
eg I} box on the existential, with the goal  ot. - 2: \vdash: two ulename{\exists E} boxes with fresh witnesses, each ending in  ot, and the premise instantiated at those witnesses. - 2: \dashv: two flagged boxes and a ulename{{	o}I} box, in the order read off the goal. - 2: \dashv: an ulename{RAA} box on x_0 
e y_0, with the clash obtained by ulename{\wedge I} and two ulename{\exists I} steps. - 2: names the \dashv direction as the one using ulename{RAA}, and the line. - A ulename{
eg I} box on x_0 
e y_0 followed by ulename{
eg
eg E}, or an ulename{LEM} split on x_0 = y_0 whose second case reaches  ot the same way (then ulename{ ot E}), earns the 2 points of the ulename{RAA}-box line; for the naming line, the reader names the ulename{
eg
eg E} or ulename{LEM} line as the classical step, a derived rule whose derivation uses ulename{RAA} (Section 2.5). Fatal errors (0 for the step): an ulename{\exists E} box closing on a line that contains its witness; a ulename{ orall I} over a name in an open assumption; ulename{
eg I} claimed to give x_0 = y_0.

title: 4.8 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content:
Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers The calculus is now complete: Sections 4.3–4.7 gave a rule for using and a rule for proving each quantifier, and the two rules for equality. Before any of those rules can act on a definition from analysis, the definition has to be written as a formula, and written correctly. The definitions of analysis have three or four quantifiers stacked in a fixed order, most of them carrying a bound such as \varepsilon > 0 or n \ge N, and every bound costs extra lines in a derivation. This section does three things. It translates the standard definitions into formulas, by a procedure that works from the outside in. It turns each quantifier rule into a bounded rule that handles the bound in the same step. And it collects the steps of Sections 4.3–4.7 into the search method of Section 2.6, extended to quantifiers and equality. Four pieces in one sentence “The sequence (a_n) converges to L” is written a_n 	o L, and a first course defines it in one breath: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for all n \ge N. The sentence has three quantifiers, each with a bound (\varepsilon > 0, N \in 
N, n \in 
N), and a fourth condition, n \ge N, hidden in “for all n \ge N”, which will turn out to sit under an implication. Each piece has a job, and a slip in any piece changes the meaning: - drop the bound \varepsilon > 0, and the challenger may choose \varepsilon = -1; then \abs{a_n - L} < -1 is impossible, and no sequence converges; - swap “for every \varepsilon” and “there is N”, and one N must serve every \varepsilon; then only sequences that are eventually equal to L converge; - read “for all n \ge N” as “for all n”, and the first terms must already be close to L; then 1,  rac12,  rac13, \dots converges to nothing. So translation deserves a procedure, and the rules deserve a form that handles bounds without fuss. We take them in that order. Translation from the outside in Find the outermost claim, name its quantifier and its bound, then translate what it claims about each object, in the same way. The procedure, in three steps: 1. Fix the domain. State what the variables range over. By the one-domain convention of Section 4.1 (after @def-bounded-quantifier), a sentence that mixes kinds of object uses the largest kind as the domain, and each smaller kind enters as a bound: N \in 
N inside the domain 
R. A sequence (a_n) is a function symbol a, with a_n its value at n. 2. Find the outermost claim. Ask what the sentence says first, before any detail: “every \varepsilon > 0 has a property”, “there is an M with a property”, “no prime is largest”. That gives the outermost quantifier (or connective) and its bound. 3. Recurse. Translate the property, which is a sentence about the object just quantified, by the same two steps. Stop at atomic formulas: equations, inequalities, membership, and predicate symbols such as \mathrm{Prime}(p). A bound is attached to its own quantifier with the connective of @def-bounded-quantifier: 	o under  orall, \wedge under \exists. The bounded notation  orall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N \in 
N does this automatically, which is why we use it. [Five definitions, translated] Translate each sentence into a formula, stating the domain. 1. a_n 	o L: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. 2. The set A of real numbers is bounded above. 3. The function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is continuous at a: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. 4. There is no largest prime. 5. Every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor. (a) Domain 
R. The outermost claim is about every \varepsilon > 0:  orall \varepsilon > 0. What it says about \varepsilon is that some natural number N works: \exists N \in 
N. What it says about N is that every natural number n from N on is good:  orall n \in 
N, with the further condition n \ge N under an implication. So  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr). The phrase “for every n \ge N” carries two bounds on n, membership in 
N and n \ge N; the first is a bounded quantifier, the second the hypothesis of the implication. The free variable is L (and the statement is also about the function symbol a, which is not a variable). (b) Domain 
R; A names a set of reals, and x \in A is a one-place predicate of x (Section 4.1). “Bounded above” means that some real number is at least every element of A. Outermost claim: there is an M. Its property: every element of A is at most M: \exists M \;  orall x \in A \; (x \le M). The bound x \in A belongs to the  orall; there is no bound on M, which may be any real number. (c) Domain 
R, with f a one-place function symbol and a a variable, free in the formula:  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \;  igl( \abs{x - a} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon  igr). The last quantifier has no bound of the form “x \in something”, because f is defined on all of 
R; its restriction \abs{x - a} < \delta goes under the implication, like n \ge N in (a). For f defined on a set A, the last quantifier would be  orall x \in A. (d) Domain 
N, with \mathrm{Prime}(p) the predicate “p is prime”. Section 4.1 read the sentence as 
eg\exists p\,  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) \wedge  orall q\, (\mathrm{Prime}(q) 	o q \le p)  igr). A mathematician more often states it positively, “for every prime there is a larger prime”:  orall p \;  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) 	o \exists q \; (\mathrm{Prime}(q) \wedge p < q)  igr). The two forms say the same thing over 
N: the laws of Section 4.9 push the 
eg inside and give  orall p\,  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) 	o \exists q\, (\mathrm{Prime}(q) \wedge 
eg(q \le p))  igr), and the order fact that 
eg(q \le p) is the same as p < q finishes the job. (They are not provably equivalent in logic alone: that last step is a fact about the order of 
N, not a law of logic.) (e) Domain 
Z. Outermost claim: every integer greater than 1 has a property,  orall n > 1. The property: some p is prime and divides n. “Divides” is itself a quantifier: p \mid n means n = p \cdot k for some integer k. So  orall n > 1 \; \exists p \;  igl( \mathrm{Prime}(p) \wedge \exists k \; (n = p \cdot k)  igr). Unfolded, the first bound is  orall n\, (n > 1 	o \dots). The innermost quantifier came from a defined word, “divides”, which is typical: a definition in words often hides quantifiers, and a translation unfolds them. Two remarks on the example. First, the order of the quantifiers in (a) and (c) is the order in which the objects are chosen: \varepsilon first, by a challenger; then N or \delta, by the defender, knowing \varepsilon; then n or x, by the challenger again, knowing both. That is the game reading of @exm-quantifier-order-sum. Second, in (c) the letter a is free, so the formula is a statement about a; “f is continuous at every point” would add  orall a in front. Translate “A has a maximum” (an element of A that is at least every element of A) over 
R. Which quantifier carries the bound x \in A, and does the other quantifier carry a bound too? \exists m \in A \;  orall x \in A \; (x \le m). The bound x \in A belongs to the  orall: “every element of A”. The \exists carries a bound too, m \in A, because a maximum must itself lie in A; dropping it gives \exists m\,  orall x \in A\, (x \le m), which is “A is bounded above”, a weaker statement. For A = (0, 1) the weaker statement is true (m = 1) and the stronger one is false. Three mistranslations to avoid. (1) An \exists with 	o under it, such as \exists x\, (x \in A 	o x > 5): it is true as soon as something lies outside A (Section 4.1). (2) A bound on the wrong quantifier: “f is bounded on A” is \exists M\,  orall x \in A\, (\abs{f(x)} \le M); the form \exists M \in A\,  orall x\, (\abs{f(x)} \le M) asks for a bound that lies in A and works on all of 
R, and it fails for f(x) = x on A = [0, 1], which is bounded on A by 1. (3) “For all large n” read as “for all n”: “a_n > 0 for all large n” is \exists N \in 
N\;  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o a_n > 0), not  orall n \in 
N\, (a_n > 0). The sequence a_n = n - 3 satisfies the first (take N = 4) and not the second (a_0 = -3). Rules for bounded quantifiers Every analysis formula has bounds, and each bound doubles the work of a rule. To use  orall \varepsilon > 0\, \varphi at the term 1, ulename{ orall E} gives 1 > 0 	o \varphi[1/\varepsilon], and a second step, ulename{{	o}E} with a line 1 > 0, gives \varphi[1/\varepsilon]. To prove \exists N \in 
N\, \psi with the witness 7, ulename{\wedge I} builds 7 \in 
N \wedge \psi[7/N] and ulename{\exists I} finishes. Every step is legal and every step is predictable, and a derivation about limits drowns in them. So we fold each pair into one step. A bounded quantifier gets a rule of its own: the bound travels with the quantifier. Rules for Bounded Quantifiers Let A be a fixed set, so that \in A is a one-place predicate symbol (Section 4.2), x a variable and \varphi a formula. The following four rules, the bounded rules, may be used in derivations, with the rule names of the unbounded rules and the same side conditions: in  orall x \in A \; ulename{E} and \exists x \in A \; ulename{I}, the term t is free for x in \varphi; in  orall x \in A \; ulename{I}, the name x_0 appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in  orall x \in A\; \varphi; in \exists x \in A \; ulename{E}, it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in \chi or in \exists x \in A\; \varphi. The last line of each box is a line of that box itself. Every use of a bounded rule can be replaced by a block of steps of the unbounded rules (Sections 4.3–4.6) and of Chapter 1, with the same premises, the same assumptions open, and the same last line. Hence any derivation that uses the bounded rules converts into one that does not. The same holds with x \in A and t \in A replaced by x > a and t > a, or by the bounds \ge a, < a, \le a, for a term a in which x does not occur. In words: to use “every x in A has \varphi”, produce an element t of A and conclude \varphi for t. To prove “some x in A has \varphi”, exhibit an element t of A with \varphi. To prove “every x in A has \varphi”, let x_0 be an arbitrary element of A (the box opens with the assumption x_0 \in A) and prove \varphi for it. To use “some x in A has \varphi”, take such an element x_0, with both facts about it as assumptions, and derive something that does not mention it. These are exactly the sentences a mathematician writes: “let \varepsilon > 0”, “since \delta > 0, the hypothesis applies to \delta”, “take N = 7 \in 
N”, “choose \delta > 0 such that …”. The bounded ulename{ orall I} box is the only flagged box with an assumption that closes by ulename{ orall I}. Its assumption x_0 \in A mentions the flag, and that is allowed: the side condition asks about assumptions of boxes still open at line k, and the box’s own assumption has closed there. Why is this a proposition and not simply a definition? Because the calculus is fixed: its rules are those of Chapters 1–2 and Sections 4.3–4.7, and a new rule is admissible only if it adds no derivable sequents. @def-derived-rule gave one way to show that: a proved sequent, written with statement letters, may be used as one line. It does not cover these rules. The bounded ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I} are one line each, but they are schemas in a formula, a variable and a term, not in statement letters; the bounded ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} close boxes, which no proved sequent can. So the proposition proves admissibility the direct way: each bounded step is shown to be an abbreviation of a block of unbounded steps. In this sense the bounded rules are derived rules, in a looser sense that extends Chapter 2’s: a line citing one abbreviates a block of primitive steps, not a proved sequent. A bounded quantifier is an abbreviation (@def-bounded-quantifier):  orall x \in A\; \varphi is the formula  orall x\, (x \in A 	o \varphi), and \exists x \in A\; \varphi is \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi). So each bounded rule should be an unbounded rule on the unfolded formula, plus the connective rule that handles 	o or \wedge. Write the block, then check two things: the block is a correct piece of derivation wherever the bounded step was, and its side conditions hold exactly when the bounded ones do. We give the replacement block for each rule and check it. In each block, the lines of the bounded version keep their labels, and new lines get new letters. Bounded ulename{ orall E}. Line i is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o \varphi). Replace line k by two lines: Line m is ulename{ orall E} at t: the formula (x \in A 	o \varphi)[t/x] is t \in A 	o \varphi[t/x] by @def-substitution, since A is not a variable. Its side condition asks that t be free for x in x \in A 	o \varphi (@def-free-for), which holds exactly when t is free for x in \varphi, since x \in A has no quantifier. Lines i and j are available at m and k because they were available at k. Bounded ulename{\exists I}. Replace line k by: Line m is the instance at t of x \in A \wedge \varphi, and t is free for x there exactly when it is free for x in \varphi. Bounded ulename{ orall I}. Replace the box and line k by a flagged box with no assumption, which contains a ulename{{	o}I} box holding the old lines: The lines between i and j are unchanged. Each of them lies inside both new boxes, so every line it cited is still available (@def-derivation, with the flagged boxes of Section 4.4): a line outside the old box is outside both new ones, and a line inside the old box is inside the new ulename{{	o}I} box. The side conditions inside the old box are unaffected too: a line inside it has the same open assumptions as before, x_0 \in A (now the assumption of the ulename{{	o}I} box) together with the outer ones, because the flagged box adds none; so every flagged box that closes inside the old box still meets its side condition. Line m is ulename{{	o}I}, and it is the last line of the flagged box, as ulename{ orall I} requires; it is the instance at x_0 of x \in A 	o \varphi. Now the side condition of ulename{ orall I} at line k: the premises are the same as before; the boxes still open at line k are the same as those open at line k in the bounded version, because the ulename{{	o}I} box on x_0 \in A has closed before line k; and the conclusion is the same formula. So the unbounded side condition holds exactly when the bounded one does. Bounded ulename{\exists E}. Line h is \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi). Replace the box’s two assumptions by one assumption and two lines of ulename{\wedge E}: Lines i and j now hold the same formulas as the old assumptions, inside the same box, so every line that cited them may still cite them. At a line inside the box, the open assumptions are now g together with the outer ones, where before they were x_0 \in A and \varphi[x_0/x] together with the outer ones. A name appears in g exactly when it appears in x_0 \in A or in \varphi[x_0/x], so every flagged box that closes inside the box still meets its side condition. The box assumes the instance at x_0 of x \in A \wedge \varphi, as ulename{\exists E} requires. Its side condition at line k names \chi, the formula \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi), the premises and the assumptions open at line k: the same four things as the bounded side condition, with the same result. For the bounds x > a and the others, the same four blocks work with x > a and t > a in place of x \in A and t \in A. One point needs the hypothesis that x does not occur in a: then (x > a)[t/x] is t > a, and the bound contains no bound variable, so free-for conditions are unaffected by it. Replacing the bounded steps one at a time, each by its block, removes them all; the premises and the last line do not change. This proves the proposition. Each block is one line longer than the bounded step it replaces: two lines for one in ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I}; the extra ulename{{	o}I} line in ulename{ orall I}; three lines (an assumption and two ulename{\wedge E}) for two assumptions in ulename{\exists E}. So each bounded step saves exactly one line, and a derivation with many bounds saves many. More than the count, the bounded rules keep the derivation at the level at which a mathematician thinks: “let \varepsilon > 0” is one step, not two. Unfolded, \exists N \in 
N\; \psi is \exists N\, (N \in 
N \wedge \psi). A student uses the bounded ulename{\exists E} on it and writes the box with the single assumption N_0 \in 
N \wedge \psi[N_0/N]. Is that wrong? No, it is the unbounded ulename{\exists E}, which is always available, since the bounded formula is the unfolded one. It costs two ulename{\wedge E} lines inside the box to separate N_0 \in 
N from \psi[N_0/N]. The bounded rule opens the box with the two assumptions already separated. Both are correct; the bounded one is shorter by one line. A limit derivation with bounds Here is the first derivation in the book about a limit. The claim is the school fact “if a_n 	o L, then 2a_n 	o 2L”, with the definition of @exm-translate-limit (a). Claim. Over 
R,  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon  igr) derives the same formula with 2 \cdot a_n and 2 \cdot L in place of a_n and L, using two lines of arithmetic, justified “arith”: \varepsilon_0 > 0 gives \varepsilon_0 / 2 > 0, and \abs{a_{n_0} - L} < \varepsilon_0 / 2 gives \abs{2 \cdot a_{n_0} - 2 \cdot L} < \varepsilon_0 (because \abs{2 u - 2 v} = 2 \abs{u - v}). Run the search. The goal starts with  orall \varepsilon > 0: open a bounded ulename{ orall I} box, “let \varepsilon_0 > 0”. The new goal starts with \exists N \in 
N: postpone it (the step of Section 4.5), since no witness is in sight. Turn to the premise: it starts with  orall \varepsilon > 0, and the step of Section 4.3 says to instantiate it at the term the goal needs. Which term? The goal will need \abs{2 a_n - 2 L} < \varepsilon_0, which follows from \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon_0 / 2: so instantiate at \varepsilon_0 / 2, after an “arith” line \varepsilon_0 / 2 > 0 for the bound. That gives an \exists N \in 
N line: open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness N_0 (the step of Section 4.6), and let the box’s last line be the current goal. Now the postponed goal has its witness: N_0 itself. The remaining goal  orall n \in 
N\, (\dots) opens a bounded ulename{ orall I} box for n_0, and a ulename{{	o}I} box on n_0 \ge N_0 finishes with one ulename{ orall E}, one ulename{{	o}E}, and the second “arith” line. This is the pattern of @prp-exists-forall-swap: fix \varepsilon_0, obtain N_0, choose N_0 as the witness. Check the side conditions at the three lines that close flagged boxes, and the witness line. - Line 13 ( orall n \in 
N \; ulename{I}, flag n_0): n_0 is not in the premise, not in line 13, and not in the assumptions still open at line 13, which are lines 2, 5, and 6. - Line 14 (\exists N \in 
N \; ulename{I}): the witness N_0, with its bound on line 5 and the instance on line 13. - Line 15 (\exists N \in 
N \; ulename{E}, flag N_0): N_0 is not in line 15, the conclusion (the witness has been forgotten by line 14), not in line 4, not in the premise, and not in the open assumption on line 2. - Line 16 ( orall \varepsilon > 0 \; ulename{I}, flag \varepsilon_0): \varepsilon_0 is not in the premise and not in line 16, and no assumption is open at line 16. Line 4 is where N comes to depend on \varepsilon: the witness N_0 is obtained from the premise at \varepsilon_0 / 2, so it depends on \varepsilon_0, exactly as the order  orall \varepsilon\, \exists N allows. Section 4.10 makes this reading of dependence precise. In prose, line by line: Let \varepsilon > 0 [lines 2, 16]. Then \varepsilon / 2 > 0 [3], so, since a_n 	o L, there is N \in 
N with \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N [4]; choose such an N [5, 6, 15]. Let n \in 
N with n \ge N [7, 9]. Then \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon / 2 [8, 10], so \abs{2 a_n - 2 L} = 2 \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon [11]. So this N works [12–14]. Written with the unbounded rules, the same derivation has 22 lines, since each of its six bounded steps (lines 4, 8, 13, 14, 15, and 16) costs one line more. The claim “ rac1n 	o 0” (for n \ge 1) is not derived here: its proof needs a fact about 
N inside 
R, the Archimedean property, which is a theorem of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, not of logic. The search method, extended Section 2.6 put the moves for the connectives in order. Each of Sections 4.3–4.7 added a step. Here is the method with all of them. Searching for a derivation of \Gamma \vdash \varphi in predicate logic. 1. Set up. Write the premises \Gamma at the top and \varphi at the bottom, with one gap between. Translate any definition in words into a formula first, as in @exm-translate-limit. 2. Goal-directed step. Take the current goal’s main symbol and set up its introduction rule: - \wedge, 	o, 
eg, \leftrightarrow: as in Section 2.6; -  orall x\, \psi: open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0; the new goal, the box’s last line, is \psi[x_0/x] (Section 4.4). For  orall x \in A\; \psi, the box opens with the assumption x_0 \in A; - \vee: postpone, as in Section 2.6; - \exists x\, \psi: postpone; work on the premises until an available line shows a term t with \psi[t/x], then use ulename{\exists I} (Section 4.5). For \exists x \in A\; \psi, the line t \in A is needed too. Repeat while the goal is \wedge, 	o, 
eg, \leftrightarrow, or  orall. 3. Premise-directed step. Take the main symbol of a resource and apply its elimination rule: - \wedge, 	o, \vee, \leftrightarrow, and the derived rules: as in Section 2.6; - \exists x\, \psi: open the ulename{\exists E} box early, as soon as the line is available, with a fresh witness x_0, and make its last line the current goal, which must not mention x_0 (Section 4.6). An early box lets the witness serve the goals that come later; -  orall x\, \psi: do not instantiate blindly; instantiate at the term that the goal, or another resource, mentions (Section 4.3). For  orall x \in A\; \psi, the line t \in A is needed too; - an equation t_1 = t_2: use ulename{{=}E} with a \varphi chosen so that one substitution turns an available line into the goal, turning the equation round first if needed (Section 4.7). 4. Clash. As in Section 2.6: for the goal  ot, find or manufacture a pair \chi, 
eg\chi; an impossible case closes itself by ulename{ ot E}. 5. Stuck. As in Section 2.6: ulename{RAA} on the current goal, or ulename{LEM} on a well-chosen statement. When no gap is left, number the lines and check the derivation as @def-derivation, extended in Section 4.4, says: every citation is available, and every side condition holds (t free for x at ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I}, bounded or not; t_1 and t_2 free for x at ulename{{=}E}; a fresh name at each line that closes a flagged box). Two of the new steps deserve a word on their place in the order. The goal step for  orall is safe in the same way as the goal steps for 	o and 
eg (Section 2.6): if  orall x\, \psi is derivable at all, then so is \psi[x_0/x] for a fresh x_0, by one more ulename{ orall E}; so opening the box loses nothing. The goal step for \exists is unsafe in the same way as the one for \vee: a witness chosen too early may be the wrong one, as in @exm-existential-introduction-derivations, where “take y = c” stalled. That is why \exists is postponed and the ulename{\exists E} boxes of the premises are opened early: the witnesses they supply are often the terms the postponed goal is waiting for, as N_0 was in the limit derivation above. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Translate into formulas, stating the domain: (i) every real number has a cube root; (ii) the function f is bounded on A; (iii) between any two different real numbers there is a rational number; (iv) the sequence (a_n) is eventually constant; (v) some natural number divides every natural number. 2. Three students translate “some element of A is larger than every element of B”, over 
R: (i) \exists x \in A \;  orall y \in B \; (x > y); (ii) \exists x\,  igl( x \in A 	o  orall y \in B\; (x > y)  igr); (iii)  orall y \in B \; \exists x \in A \; (x > y). Which are correct? For each wrong one, give sets A, B for which it has the wrong truth value. 3. Which variables are free in your answer to (a)(iv)? 4. Write the bounded rule \exists x \in A \; ulename{I} as a block of two unbounded steps, and name the two rules. (a) (i) Over 
R:  orall x\, \exists y\, (y \cdot y \cdot y = x). (ii) Over 
R: \exists M\,  orall x \in A\, (\abs{f(x)} \le M). (iii) Over 
R, with \in 
Q a one-place predicate symbol:  orall x\,  orall y\,  igl( x < y 	o \exists q \in 
Q\; (x < q \wedge q < y)  igr); “different” is carried by x < y, which names the smaller number x (the case y < x is the same statement with the letters exchanged). (iv) Over 
R, with a a function symbol: \exists N \in 
N\;  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o a_n = a_N). (v) Over 
N: \exists d\,  orall n\, \exists k\, (n = d \cdot k); it is true, with d = 1. (b) Only (i) is correct. (ii) has 	o under \exists: with A = \{0\} and B = \{5\}, the sentence in words is false, but (ii) is true, because x = 7 
otin A makes the implication vacuously true. (iii) has the quantifiers in the wrong order: it lets the element of A depend on y. With A = B = 
N, (iii) is true (for each y, take x = y + 1), and the sentence in words is false, since no natural number exceeds every natural number. (c) None of the variables: N and n are bound. The formula is a statement about the function symbol a, which is not a variable. (d) From t \in A and \varphi[t/x]: first t \in A \wedge \varphi[t/x] by ulename{\wedge I}, then \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi) by ulename{\exists I}, which is \exists x \in A\; \varphi unfolded. B. Practice [B1: Three definitions] Formalize each statement, stating the domain and the kind of each symbol (variable, constant, function symbol, predicate symbol; membership \in A in a fixed set A is a one-place predicate symbol, as in Section 4.2). 1. The set A of real numbers is bounded (above and below). 2. The function f \colon 
R 	o 
R is increasing on A: for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) \le f(y). 3. The sequence (a_n) is bounded: there is a real M with \abs{a_n} \le M for all n. Then, for (c), write the formula with the two quantifiers in the other order, and say why it holds for every sequence. No constants occur in any of the three parts. (a) Domain 
R; m, M, x variables (all bound); \in A a one-place and \le a two-place predicate symbol. \exists m\, \exists M\,  orall x \in A\, (m \le x \wedge x \le M). The two witnesses are chosen before x, so they must work for every element of A. (b) Domain 
R; x, y variables (bound); f a one-place function symbol; \in A a one-place and <, \le two-place predicate symbols.  orall x \in A\;  orall y \in A\;  igl( x < y 	o f(x) \le f(y)  igr). (c) Domain 
R; M, n variables (bound); a a one-place function symbol (the one-domain convention of Section 4.1), and \abs{\cdot} a one-place function symbol; \in 
N a one-place and \le a two-place predicate symbol. \exists M\;  orall n \in 
N\; (\abs{a_n} \le M). Swapped:  orall n \in 
N\; \exists M\; (\abs{a_n} \le M). It holds for every sequence, because the witness may depend on n: take M = \abs{a_n}. The sequence a_n = n, which is not bounded, satisfies it. As in @exm-quantifier-order-sum, the swap turns a statement about one M for all n into a statement about each term separately. [B2: A bounded rehearsal] Using the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules, derive  orall x \in A \; (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \;\; \exists x \in A \; P(x) \;\vdash\; \exists x \in A \; Q(x). Then say how many lines the derivation would have with the unbounded rules only. The goal is an \exists: postpone it. The second premise is an \exists: open its bounded ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness x_0 and the two assumptions x_0 \in A and P(x_0), and aim for the goal as the box’s last line. Inside, the first premise is a  orall x \in A, and the term the box offers is x_0, with its bound on a line. The witness for the goal is x_0 again. At line 8, x_0 is not in line 8, not in line 2, and not in either premise; no other box is open. The derivation uses three bounded steps (lines 5, 7 and 8), each of which costs one more line unbounded, so the unbounded derivation has 8 + 3 = 11 lines: the ulename{\exists E} box assumes x_0 \in A \wedge P(x_0) and splits it with two ulename{\wedge E} lines; line 5 becomes ulename{ orall E} then ulename{{	o}E}; line 7 becomes ulename{\wedge I} then ulename{\exists I}. The bound is the whole point of the exercise: the witness x_0 must carry its membership in A from the premise to the conclusion, and the bounded rules make that one assumption and one citation. C. Going deeper [C1: Where the  orall x stands] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R and A \subseteq 
R. Translate, over 
R: 1. f is uniformly continuous on A: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that for all x, y \in A, \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon; 2. f is continuous at every point of A: for every x \in A and every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that for every y \in A, \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon. Then describe, in one sentence, the only difference between the two formulas, and say what it means for the choice of \delta. (a)  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). (b)  orall x \in A \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). The only difference is the position of  orall x \in A: in (a) it stands after \exists \delta > 0, in (b) before it. In (b) the defender chooses \delta knowing x, so \delta may depend on x and on \varepsilon; in (a) \delta is chosen before any x is given, so one \delta must serve every x \in A at once, and it depends on \varepsilon only. Section 4.10 derives (b) from (a) and shows that x^2 on 
R satisfies (b) but not (a); Section 4.11 turns this example into a counter-model, so (b) does not derive (a). [C2: Six orders, four statements] Fix a formula \mu (the “matrix”) in the variables x, y, z, and consider the six sentences obtained by putting the prefixes  orall x, \exists y,  orall z in front of \mu in the six possible orders:  orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\, \mu,  orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\, \mu, and so on. Call two of these orders essentially the same if the two sentences are provably equivalent (\dashv\vdash) for every matrix \mu, and essentially different if some matrix over 
Z gives them different truth values (read informally, as in Section 4.1). 1. Show that the six orders fall into four groups, with any two orders in one group essentially the same. 2. Using the matrices y > x and y > z over 
Z, show that any two orders from different groups are essentially different. So the six orders say four different things. [Hint 1] Two  orall’s side by side can be exchanged: that was one of the derivations of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations. What is left to decide is where \exists y stands. [Hint 2] List the six orders by the position of \exists y: first, middle or last. When it is first or last, the two  orall’s are side by side. (a) Sort the orders by the position of \exists y. - \exists y first: \exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z\, \mu and \exists y\,  orall z\,  orall x\, \mu. - \exists y last:  orall x\,  orall z\, \exists y\, \mu and  orall z\,  orall x\, \exists y\, \mu. - \exists y in the middle:  orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\, \mu, and  orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\, \mu. Two adjacent  orall’s may be exchanged:  orall x\,  orall z\, \psi \dashv\vdash  orall z\,  orall x\, \psi for every formula \psi, by the derivation of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations that exchanges two universal quantifiers (it uses nothing about its matrix but that it is a formula). This gives the “last” pair at once. For the “first” pair the  orall’s sit under \exists y: open the ulename{\exists E} box on \exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z\, \mu with a witness y_0, exchange the two  orall’s inside it, and close with ulename{\exists I} at y_0; the other direction is the same. So there are at most four groups: \{\exists y\,  orall x\,  orall z, \ \exists y\,  orall z\,  orall x\}, \{ orall x\,  orall z\, \exists y, \  orall z\,  orall x\, \exists y\}, \{ orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z\} and \{ orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x\}. (b) Call the groups F (\exists y first), L (last), M_x ( orall x\, \exists y\,  orall z) and M_z ( orall z\, \exists y\,  orall x). Over 
Z, evaluate each group with the two matrices, reading informally (Section 4.1): ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Group \mu = (y > x) \mu = (y > z) ----------------------- ---------------------------------- ------------------------------- F false: no y exceeds every x false: no y exceeds every z L true: given x, z, take y = x + 1 true: take y = z + 1 M_x true: given x, take y = x + 1 false: no y exceeds every z M_z false: no y exceeds every x true: given z, take y = z + 1 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Every two rows differ in at least one column, so every two groups are separated by one of the two matrices: F from L, from M_x and from M_z by the column in which the other group has “true”; L from M_x by y > z and from M_z by y > x; M_x from M_z by either. So the six orders say four different things: within a group the sentences are provably equivalent by (a), and across groups some matrix over 
Z tells them apart. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: lists the six orders and sorts them by the position of \exists y. - 3: justifies the two collapses, citing the exchange of adjacent  orall’s, and handles the pair under \exists y (by an ulename{\exists E} box, or equivalently). - 3: gives, for each of the six pairs of groups, a matrix and the two truth values, with witnesses for the true sentences. - 2: concludes that the six orders say four different things, combining (a) and (b). Fatal errors (0 for the step): exchanging  orall with \exists; a “separation” in which the two sentences have the same truth value.

title: 4.9 Negating and Moving Quantifiers
content:
Negating and Moving Quantifiers To prove that a sequence does not converge, or that a function is not uniformly continuous, we must use the negation of a definition, and a negation is only usable once the 
eg has been pushed all the way in. “It is not the case that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is an N …” gives a proof nothing to hold. “There is an \varepsilon > 0 such that for every N there is an n \ge N with …” tells it what to find. Section 4.1 read the step from the first form to the second informally, as the challenger and the defender changing sides. This section derives the laws that make it exact, with the rules of Sections 4.3–4.6. Once they are proved, negating a definition is mechanical: one law per symbol, from the outside in. The section also derives the laws that move a quantifier across a connective, and it ends with a short analysis proof in which a negation and a well-chosen \varepsilon do the work. Not every, and some not Section 4.1 called the two quantifiers mirror images: a single counterexample refutes a “for every”, and a single witness confirms a “there exists”. The mirror suggests four sequents. “Not every x satisfies \varphi” should say the same as “some x fails \varphi”, and “no x satisfies \varphi” the same as “every x fails \varphi”. Three of the four directions come straight out of the search method. The fourth does not, and the reason it does not is worth a close look. To negate a quantifier, flip it and move the 
eg inside. In the derivations of this section, 
eg\varphi[x_0/x] means (
eg\varphi)[x_0/x], which is 
eg(\varphi[x_0/x]) by @def-substitution; the two readings give the same formula. The fresh name x_0 is always a variable different from x that does not appear in \varphi (or in \psi, when there is one); so it does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi or \exists x\, \varphi either. The side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} need this, and it also makes x_0 free for x in \varphi (Section 4.2). [Quantifier Negation] Let \varphi be a formula and x a variable. 1. 
eg orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, by a derivation that uses ulename{RAA}; 2. \exists x\, 
eg\varphi \vdash 
eg orall x\, \varphi, by a derivation that does not; 3. 
eg\exists x\, \varphi \dashv\vdash  orall x\, 
eg\varphi, both directions by derivations that do not use ulename{RAA}. Try it first (ten minutes): run the search method of Section 4.8 on (a). Which rule should give the last line, and what would that rule need from the premise? Start with (a), and with the obstacle. The goal \exists x\, 
eg\varphi is an \exists, so the search postpones it until an available line shows an instance 
eg\varphi[t/x]. None ever does. The premise 
eg orall x\, \varphi is a negation, and a negation is used only by clashing it with what it negates,  orall x\, \varphi. It says that a counterexample exists and names none, so ulename{\exists I} has nothing to act on. We are stuck, and the last step of the method applies: assume 
eg\exists x\, 
eg\varphi, “no x fails \varphi”, and hunt for a clash. The clash will be with the premise, so the new goal is  orall x\, \varphi. Open a flagged box for it, with the goal \varphi[x_0/x]. That goal is again stuck (we know nothing about \varphi), so a second ulename{RAA} assumes 
eg\varphi[x_0/x]; and now an instance of 
eg\varphi is on a line, so ulename{\exists I} produces \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, which clashes with the outer assumption. For (b) and (c) the method runs without getting stuck. A negated goal opens a ulename{
eg I} box (Section 2.2); an \exists premise opens an ulename{\exists E} box early (Section 4.6); a  orall goal opens a flagged box (Section 4.4). The clash comes in one of two ways. In (b), and in (c) right to left, the instance assumed in the ulename{\exists E} box clashes with the matching instance that ulename{ orall E} takes from the  orall line. In (c) left to right, ulename{\exists I} turns the instance into \exists x\, \varphi, which meets the premise 
eg\exists x\, \varphi. For (a), the derivation: Line 4 is ulename{\exists I} at the term x_0, which is free for x in 
eg\varphi. At line 7 the side condition of ulename{ orall I} holds: x_0 does not appear in the premise, in the assumption 
eg\exists x\, 
eg\varphi still open at line 7, or in  orall x\, \varphi, since it is not x and does not appear in \varphi; and line 6 is the last line of the flagged box. For (b): At line 6, x_0 does not appear in  ot, in \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, in the premise, or in the assumption  orall x\, \varphi still open there. For (c), left to right and right to left: In the first, line 5 is the instance of

Inside, the premise is an implication whose hypothesis \exists x\, P(x) comes from the assumption P(x_0) by ulename{\exists I}.
