The sequent combines (b) and (a) of @prp-quantifier-passage. Law (b), with \varphi the formula P(x) and \psi the formula  orall y\, Q(y) (in which x is not free), turns the premise into  orall x\,  igl( P(x) 	o  orall y\, Q(y)  igr). Then law (a), applied under  orall x (a provable equivalence may be used under a quantifier, the paragraph after the negation procedure) with \psi the formula P(x), \varphi the formula Q(y) and y as the moving variable (y is not free in P(x)), turns P(x) 	o  orall y\, Q(y) into  orall y\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)). [B3: Choosing \varepsilon from the data] Let a and b be real numbers with a < b + \varepsilon^2 for every \varepsilon > 0. Prove that a \le b, by the method of @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal: suppose not, and choose an \varepsilon built from the data that makes the numbers collide. Then explain why the choice \varepsilon = a - b does not work. Suppose a < b + \varepsilon^2 for every \varepsilon > 0, and suppose, for a contradiction, that a > b (the negation of a \le b). Let \varepsilon \coloneqq \min(1, a - b). Then \varepsilon > 0, since 1 > 0 and a - b > 0. Since 0 < \varepsilon \le 1, \varepsilon^2 = \varepsilon \cdot \varepsilon \le \varepsilon \cdot 1 = \varepsilon, and \varepsilon \le a - b. The hypothesis applies to this \varepsilon and gives a < b + \varepsilon^2 \le b + \varepsilon \le b + (a - b) = a , so a < a, a contradiction. Hence a \le b. The choice \varepsilon = a - b, copied from the text, gives a < b + (a - b)^2, that is, a - b < (a - b)^2. When a - b > 1 this is true (for a - b = 2: 2 < 4), so there is no contradiction. The square shrinks a number only when it is at most 1, and the \min with 1 is what puts \varepsilon there. C. Going deeper [C1: Two prenex forms] A formula is in prenex form when all its quantifiers stand at the front, before a part with no quantifier. Using the laws of @prp-quantifier-passage, bring  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) into prenex form in two ways, ending with \exists x\, \exists y\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)) and with \exists y\, \exists x\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)). Justify each step, and say which directions of the laws are classical. [Hint 1] The formula is an implication with a quantifier on each side. Law (d) moves the quantifier out of the hypothesis, and law (e) moves it out of the conclusion. [Hint 2] For the first route, start with law (d), taking \psi to be the whole conclusion \exists y\, Q(y). First route: x out first. Law (d) of @prp-quantifier-passage, with \varphi the formula P(x) and \psi the formula \exists y\, Q(y), in which x is not free:  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y)  igr). Then law (e) under \exists x, with \psi the formula P(x), \varphi the formula Q(y), and y as the moving variable (y is not free in P(x)): P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \dashv\vdash \exists y\, (P(x) 	o Q(y)). A provable equivalence may be used under a quantifier (the paragraph after the negation procedure), so \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y)  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \exists y\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Second route: y out first. Law (e), with \psi the formula  orall x\, P(x), \varphi the formula Q(y), and y as the moving variable (y is not free in  orall x\, P(x)):  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists y\, Q(y) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists y\,  igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Then law (d) under \exists y, with \varphi the formula P(x) and \psi the formula Q(y) (x is not free in Q(y)): \exists y\,  igl(  orall x\, P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr) \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) 	o Q(y)  igr). Classical steps. Going from the given formula towards the prenex form, every step of both routes uses the direction \dashv of (d) or of (e): the direction from the implication to the \exists. These are exactly the two directions that @prp-quantifier-passage derives with ulename{LEM}. The way back uses only the intuitionistic directions. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: first route, with law (d) then law (e), each with \varphi, \psi and the moving variable named, and the “not free” condition checked. - 3: second route, likewise with (e) then (d). - 2: says why a law may be applied under \exists x or \exists y (an equivalence used under a quantifier, by an ulename{\exists E} box closed with ulename{\exists I}). - 2: identifies the \dashv directions of (d) and (e) as the classical ones, used in every step towards prenex form. Fatal errors (0 for the step): moving  orall x out of the hypothesis as  orall x (it becomes \exists x); applying a passage law when the moving variable is free in \psi. [C2: Exit check: negations] 1. A sequence of functions f_n converges to f uniformly on A when  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \;  orall x \in A \;  igl( n \ge N 	o \abs{f_n(x) - f(x)} < \varepsilon  igr), where f_n(x) is a term in the two variables n and x. Negate this into positive form, citing the laws. 2. Using the negation of uniform continuity in @exm-negating-definitions (c), prove that f(x) = 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1). Give the witnesses that the negation asks for, each as a function of what is chosen before it, and check every condition. [Hint 1] For (b), the negation asks for one \varepsilon first. Near 0, the graph of 1/x is steep: two points close together have values far apart. [Hint 2] Take \varepsilon = 1 and let \delta > 0 be arbitrary. You must now find x, y \in (0, 1), depending on \delta, with \abs{x - y} < \delta and \abs{1/x - 1/y} \ge 1. (a) @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation four times, then @prp-negated-implication and the order fact: \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall N \in 
N \; \exists n \in 
N \; \exists x \in A \;  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{f_n(x) - f(x)} \ge \varepsilon  igr). In words: for some \varepsilon > 0, however far out we start, some later f_n is at least \varepsilon away from f at some point of A. The point may change with n. (b) By @exm-negating-definitions (c), we must prove \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \in (0, 1) \; \exists y \in (0, 1) \; \Bigl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \Bigl\lvert  rac1x -  rac1y \Bigrvert \ge \varepsilon \Bigr). Take \varepsilon = 1, which is positive. Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and let t \coloneqq \min(\delta, 	frac12), so 0 < t \le 	frac12 and t \le \delta; then take x \coloneqq t and y \coloneqq t/2, which depend on \delta. Check: - x, y \in (0, 1): 0 < t/2 < t \le 	frac12 < 1. - \abs{x - y} = t/2 < t \le \delta, since t > 0. - \abs{1/x - 1/y} = \abs{1/t - 2/t} = 1/t \ge 2 \ge 1 = \varepsilon, since t \le 	frac12. Since \delta > 0 was arbitrary, the negation of uniform continuity holds, so 1/x is not uniformly continuous on (0, 1). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) the negation, with every bound kept, \wedge in place of 	o, and the quantifiers in the order \exists \varepsilon\;  orall N\; \exists n\; \exists x \in A. - 2: (b) the witness \varepsilon, stated before \delta is given. - 2: for an arbitrary \delta > 0, points x and y given as functions of \delta. - 3: the three checks: x, y \in (0, 1); \abs{x - y} < \delta; \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \ge \varepsilon. A different correct choice earns full marks (for instance x = t, y = t/3); the scheme rewards the order of the choices and the checks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \varepsilon chosen depending on \delta; points chosen before \delta is given, or not depending on it where they must; a bound negated instead of the quantifier (\exists \varepsilon \le 0, \exists n < N).

title: 4.10 Uniformly Continuous Implies Continuous, Rule by Rule
content:
Uniformly Continuous Implies Continuous, Rule by Rule This chapter opened with a question. Continuity and uniform continuity differ only in where one quantifier stands; why does one imply the other in a few lines, while the converse is false? Section 4.1 gave the informal answer: a variable may depend on the variables quantified to its left, and only on them. @exr-translation-c1 of Section 4.8 asked for both translations into formulas, and Section 4.9 negated uniform continuity (@exm-negating-definitions (c)). This section answers the question with the rules. It derives “uniformly continuous implies continuous” in full, line by line, with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules. It then reads off the derivation the one thing this section adds: which boxes are open where a constant is chosen, and what that says about what the constant may depend on. The same reading locates the exact lines at which the converse breaks down, and the function x^2 shows that the converse is not merely unproved but false. Two definitions that differ in one place Let A be a set of real numbers and f a function defined on A. We work over the domain 
R, with f a one-place function symbol, \in A a one-place predicate symbol (Section 4.2), and \abs{\cdot} the absolute value. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapters 5 and 6 define continuity and uniform continuity properly and develop them. Here the two definitions are only quantifier patterns, and nothing is used about f except that f(x) is a term. (A function symbol has a value at every real number; the values outside A are never used, because f is only applied to variables bounded by \in A, as with sequences in Section 4.1.) f is uniformly continuous on A (UC) when  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). f is continuous at every point of A (C) when  orall x \in A \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon  igr). The two formulas have the same matrix and the same four bounded quantifiers. Only  orall x \in A has moved: in C it stands before \exists \delta > 0, in UC after it. In the game of Section 4.1, the defender chooses \delta in C after seeing x and \varepsilon, and in UC after seeing only \varepsilon. So in UC a single \delta must serve every point of A at once: that is what uniformly means. Swap the first two quantifiers of UC, to get \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; ( \abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon ). What does the new formula say about two points of A closer than \delta? Does f(x) = x on 
R satisfy it? Now \delta is chosen before \varepsilon, so it must work for every \varepsilon > 0 at once. For two points x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, this says \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0, and by @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal, f(x) = f(y). So the formula says: for some \delta > 0, any two points of A closer than \delta have the same value. The function f(x) = x on 
R fails it: whatever \delta > 0 is proposed, the points 0 and \delta/2 are closer than \delta and have different values. Yet f(x) = x is uniformly continuous, with \delta = \varepsilon. Swapping  orall \varepsilon and \exists \delta asks far too much. The derivation [Uniformly continuous implies continuous] Derive C from UC, with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules. Run the search method of Section 4.8. The goal C begins  orall x \in A, then  orall \varepsilon > 0: the goal-directed steps open two bounded ulename{ orall I} boxes, “let x_0 \in A” and “let \varepsilon_0 > 0”, and write the last two lines. The new goal begins \exists \delta > 0, and no witness is in sight, so it is postponed (Section 4.5). Turn to the premise UC. It begins  orall \varepsilon > 0, and the term the goal mentions is \varepsilon_0, whose bound \varepsilon_0 > 0 is on a line: ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon_0 (Section 4.3). That gives an \exists \delta > 0 line, and its ulename{\exists E} box is opened at once, with a witness \delta_0 (Section 4.6), aiming for the postponed goal as its last line. Inside, the premise has become “\delta_0 works for all x, y \in A”; instantiate it at the point we have, x_0. Now the postponed goal has its witness: \delta_0 itself. Before reading on: which lines does the line introducing \delta_0 rest on, and does any of them mention x_0? Every line is tagged with its rule; lines 4, 7 and 8 are the one-line bounded rules, and lines 9, 10 and 11 close bounded boxes. The terms and the side conditions: - Line 4: ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon_0, with its bound on line 3. The term \varepsilon_0 is a variable that does not appear in line 1, so it is free for \varepsilon. - Line 7: ulename{ orall E} at x_0, with its bound on line 2, which is available because the box of line 2 is still open. - Line 8: ulename{\exists I} with the witness \delta_0, its bound on line 5 and the instance on line 7. - Line 9 (ulename{\exists E}, flag \delta_0): \delta_0 does not appear in line 9 (the witness was forgotten at line 8), in line 4, in the premise, or in the assumptions still open at line 9, lines 2 and 3. - Line 10 (ulename{ orall I}, flag \varepsilon_0): \varepsilon_0 does not appear in the premise, in line 10, or in the assumption still open at line 10, line 2. - Line 11 (ulename{ orall I}, flag x_0): x_0 does not appear in the premise or in line 11, and no assumption is open. The answer to the prompt: line 5 is the assumption of the ulename{\exists E} box, so it rests on line 4, which rests on lines 1 and 3. None of the three mentions x_0. The witness \delta_0 was obtained from the premise at \varepsilon_0 alone, before x_0 played any part. That is uniformity, read off the lines. The derivation has 11 lines. Written with the unbounded rules it has 17, since each of its six bounded steps (lines 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11) costs one line more (Section 4.8). The bounded rules keep it at the level at which a mathematician thinks, and the same argument in prose is three sentences, each aligned with the lines it abbreviates: Let x \in A and \varepsilon > 0 [lines 2, 3, 10, 11]. By uniform continuity there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{u - v} < \delta implies \abs{f(u) - f(v)} < \varepsilon for all u, v \in A; choose such a \delta [4, 5, 6, 9]. Applied with u = x, this gives \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon for every y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, so this \delta works for x and \varepsilon [7, 8]. The prose renames the bound variables of UC to u, v, so that “x” can name the fixed point; a derivation needs no such care, because ulename{ orall E} handles bound variables by substitution. Chapter 5 studies this passage from a derivation to prose, at several levels of detail. Reading dependence off the boxes The derivation shows something the informal proof leaves unsaid: the exact place where \delta is chosen, and what surrounds it there. A constant chosen in a box may depend on the names of the boxes open around that box, and it does depend only on the names in the line it comes from. In the derivation above, which flagged boxes surround the box of \delta_0, opened at line 5? What may \delta_0 therefore depend on, and what does it in fact depend on? The boxes of x_0 (opened at line 2) and of \varepsilon_0 (opened at line 3). So \delta_0 may depend on x_0 and on \varepsilon_0, as C allows. In fact it depends only on \varepsilon_0: it comes from line 4, which mentions \varepsilon_0 and not x_0. Why “may”? Inside the boxes of x_0 and \varepsilon_0, every term built from x_0 and \varepsilon_0 is available, so a premise could have been instantiated at such a term, and a witness obtained from the resulting \exists line would depend on both names. The side conditions permit that here, because the goal C puts \exists \delta inside both  orall’s: the witness is forgotten by ulename{\exists I} (line 8) before either box closes. Why “does”? Because everything known about \delta_0 is what its \exists line says, and line 4 mentions \varepsilon_0 alone. So \delta_0 could have been obtained before x_0 entered at all: fix \varepsilon_0, obtain \delta_0, and only then let x_0 \in A. That is the order of UC itself. A derivation in that order nests the boxes as \varepsilon_0, \delta_0, x_0 (the box of \delta_0 rests on line 4, so it stays inside the box of \varepsilon_0), and it ends in  orall \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall x \in A \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \; (\dots), which is C with its first two quantifiers exchanged. C follows by exchanging them back, as in the swap of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (c), here with the bounded rules: boxes for x_1 \in A and \varepsilon_1 > 0, ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon_1 and then at x_1, and two ulename{ orall I} lines. C’s order of choices allows more dependence than this proof uses. The limit derivation of Section 4.8 showed the same thing on a smaller scale: its witness N_0 came from a line obtained at \varepsilon_0 / 2, inside the box of \varepsilon_0 only, and so it depended on \varepsilon_0. The converse breaks at a side condition The converse, from C to UC, is the interesting direction. The search for it fails, and the failure has an exact address. [The search from C to UC] Run the search method on the sequent with premise C and goal UC, and find where it stops. Try it first (ten minutes): start the search. Where does a \delta come from, and at what moment can you get one? The obvious plan copies the derivation above: fix \varepsilon_0, obtain \delta_0 from the premise, choose it as the witness. It runs into an obstacle at the second step. In C, \exists \delta stands behind  orall x \in A, so to reach it the premise must first be instantiated at a point, and the bounded ulename{ orall E} needs a line t \in A. No such line exists until we assume one, in a box for some x_0. The \delta_0 obtained inside that box comes from a line that mentions x_0, and both side conditions then hold it in: it cannot leave its own box while a line about it still mentions it, and x_0 cannot be generalized while a line about \delta_0 still mentions x_0. The goal UC begins  orall \varepsilon > 0, so open a box for \varepsilon_0. The new goal \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; (\dots) is postponed. The premise C begins  orall x \in A, and no line t \in A is available; the only way to get one is to assume it, so open a bounded box “let x_0 \in A”. Then the premise yields a \delta. Here is how far the search gets, every line legal: The goal inside the box of \varepsilon_0 needs a \delta that works for all points: the line  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; (\abs{x - y} < \delta_0 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon_0), so that ulename{\exists I} at \delta_0 could finish. Line 7 says this only for the point x_0. There are two ways to try to generalize it, and each is stopped by a side condition. - Generalize inside the box of \delta_0. After line 7, open a new flagged box with the name x_0 and the assumption x_0 \in A, repeat line 7 in it, and close it by ulename{ orall I} with the conclusion  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; (\abs{x - y} < \delta_0 	o \dots). That line breaks the side condition of ulename{ orall I}: x_0 appears in assumptions still open there, line 3 and line 7. (With a different name x_1 the box is legal, but line 7 says nothing about x_1, so the box cannot reach its last line.) - Leave the box of \delta_0 first, carrying line 7. Close the ulename{\exists E} box with line 7 itself as its conclusion, in order to generalize over x_0 outside it. That line breaks the side condition of ulename{\exists E}: its conclusion mentions the witness \delta_0. The only legal way out of the box of \delta_0 is to forget \delta_0, as line 8 does with ulename{\exists I} before line 9 closes the box. Then ulename{ orall I} on x_0 is legal, and line 10 is what it gives:  orall x \in A \; \exists \delta > 0, with \delta still behind x. That is C at \varepsilon_0 again, not UC, and closing the box of \varepsilon_0 gives line 11, which is C with its first two quantifiers exchanged. The search has gone round in a circle. These are the same two blocks that stopped the converse of @prp-exists-forall-swap: a ulename{ orall I} blocked by an open assumption that mentions its name, and an ulename{\exists E} box that cannot close on a line mentioning its witness. That is no coincidence: with the bounds and the matrix stripped away, C to UC is the swap  orall x\, \exists \delta to \exists \delta\,  orall x. A failed search proves nothing about all derivations: a cleverer route might exist. For this sequent none does. The evidence is a function for which C is true and UC is false, and Section 4.11 explains why such a function settles the question. A function that is continuous and not uniformly continuous [The square function on the real line] Let f(x) = x^2 on A = 
R. Show that f satisfies C and does not satisfy UC. C holds. Let x \in 
R and \varepsilon > 0. Let \delta \coloneqq \min\Bigl( 1, \,  rac{\varepsilon}{2\abs{x} + 1} \Bigr), which is positive, since \varepsilon > 0 and 2\abs{x} + 1 \ge 1 > 0. It depends on \varepsilon and on x. Let y \in 
R with \abs{x - y} < \delta. By the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases), used twice, and since \delta \le 1, \abs{y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y - x} < \abs{x} + 1, so \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} < 2\abs{x} + 1. Hence \abs{x^2 - y^2} = \abs{x - y} \cdot \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x - y} \, (2\abs{x} + 1) < \delta \, (2\abs{x} + 1) \le \varepsilon , where the strict step uses 2\abs{x} + 1 > 0, and the last step uses \delta \le \varepsilon / (2\abs{x} + 1). So this \delta works for x and \varepsilon. UC fails. By the negation of uniform continuity in @exm-negating-definitions (c), with the bounds x \in 
R and y \in 
R dropped because they always hold, we must show \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \; \exists y \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \abs{x^2 - y^2} \ge \varepsilon  igr). Take \varepsilon = 1. Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and take x \coloneqq 1/\delta and y \coloneqq 1/\delta + \delta/2, which depend on \delta. Then \abs{x - y} = \delta/2 < \delta, and, since y > x > 0 (so y - x and y + x are both positive), \abs{x^2 - y^2} = (y - x)(y + x) =  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigl(  rac{2}{\delta} +  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigr) = 1 +  rac{\delta^2}{4} \ge 1 . Since \delta was arbitrary, UC fails. The \delta for C grows smaller as \abs{x} grows, and no single \delta serves the whole line. The proof of failure says why: however small \delta is, far enough out (at x = 1/\delta) the graph is so steep that two points \delta/2 apart have values more than 1 apart. The function is the semantic side of @exm-converse-fails. Read in the real numbers, with f as squaring, the premise C is true and the conclusion UC is false; Section 4.11 calls such a reading a counter-model, and explains why a counter-model rules out every derivation, so that no derivation of UC from C exists. “Depending on \varepsilon” is a claim, and it can be false. When a proof says “choose \delta (depending on \varepsilon)”, the parenthesis records which boxes are open where \delta is chosen, and which names its formula uses. This is the logical origin of the book’s rule that every chosen constant says what it depends on: the dependence is a record of the open boxes, and a reader can check it. A proof of uniform continuity must be able to write “depending on \varepsilon” truthfully. A “proof” that x^2 is uniformly continuous on 
R that takes \delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/(2\abs{x} + 1)) “(depending on \varepsilon)” has a formula for \delta that mentions x: the \delta was chosen inside the box of x, so the proof shows only C, and @exm-square-not-uniform shows that UC is false. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the derivation of @exm-uniform-implies-continuous. 1. Why is line 7 legal? Name the rule, the term, and the lines it cites, and say why those lines are available. 2. At which line is the premise’s “for all x \in A” used, and at which term? 3. State the idea of the derivation in two sentences. 4. Run the derivation for f(x) = 3x + 1 on A = 
R, where UC holds with \delta = \varepsilon/3. For a given x_0 and \varepsilon_0 > 0, which \delta does the derivation hand to C at line 8, and does it depend on x_0? Check that it works. (a) Line 7 is the bounded ulename{ orall E} at the term x_0. It cites line 6,  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \; (\dots), and line 2, x_0 \in A, the bound’s instance. Line 6 is the assumption of the ulename{\exists E} box that contains line 7, and line 2 is the assumption of the box of x_0, which also contains line 7; both boxes are still open at line 7. The term x_0 is a variable not appearing in line 6, so it is free for x. (b) At line 7, at the term x_0. Line 6 says that \delta_0 works for all pairs of points of A, and line 7 uses that for pairs with first point x_0. (c) Uniform continuity at \varepsilon supplies one \delta that works for all points at once, and it is supplied before any point is named. Continuity at a point x then takes that same \delta, specialized to the point x. (d) Line 4 says that some \delta > 0 works at \varepsilon_0, and line 8 hands C that witness \delta_0, whatever it is; the derivation knows only lines 5 and 6 about it. Here \varepsilon_0 / 3 is such a witness (so is any \delta with 0 < \delta \le \varepsilon_0/3). Reading the derivation with the witness the exercise names, \delta_0 = \varepsilon_0 / 3, the \delta handed to C is \varepsilon_0 / 3. It does not depend on x_0. It works: for every real y with \abs{x_0 - y} < \varepsilon_0/3, \abs{f(x_0) - f(y)} = \abs{(3x_0 + 1) - (3y + 1)} = 3\abs{x_0 - y} < 3 \cdot  rac{\varepsilon_0}{3} = \varepsilon_0 . B. Practice [B1: Lipschitz implies uniformly continuous] A function f is Lipschitz on A when \exists L \ge 0 \;  orall x \in A \;  orall y \in A \;  igl( \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \cdot \abs{x - y}  igr). Prove that a function that is Lipschitz on A is uniformly continuous on A, first as a derivation with the bounded rules (lines of arithmetic justified “arith”), then as a short proof in prose. Say what your \delta depends on. (The bound L \ge 0 is part of the definition: if A has at most one point, then x = y in the matrix, and any L, even L = -1, would satisfy it. The bound rules this out, so a proof may use L \ge 0, for instance to divide by L + 1.) The goal UC begins  orall \varepsilon > 0: open a box for \varepsilon_0. The new goal \exists \delta > 0 \dots is postponed until a witness is in hand. The premise begins \exists L \ge 0: open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness L_0, aiming for the postponed goal, which does not mention L_0. Work backwards from what the boxes for x_0 and y_0 will need: from \abs{x_0 - y_0} < \delta we want \abs{f(x_0) - f(y_0)} < \varepsilon_0, and the premise gives \abs{f(x_0) - f(y_0)} \le L_0 \abs{x_0 - y_0} < L_0 \delta when L_0 > 0. So \delta = \varepsilon_0 / L_0 is the natural guess, but L_0 = 0 is allowed and then \varepsilon_0/L_0 is undefined. Take \delta = \varepsilon_0 / (L_0 + 1) instead: L_0 + 1 \ge 1 > 0, and L_0 \delta = \varepsilon_0 \cdot L_0/(L_0 + 1) < \varepsilon_0. Line 11 is arithmetic from lines 2, 3, 8 and 10: \abs{f(x_0) - f(y_0)} \le L_0 \abs{x_0 - y_0} \le L_0 \cdot \varepsilon_0/(L_0 + 1), where the second step uses L_0 \ge 0, and L_0/(L_0 + 1) < 1 with \varepsilon_0 > 0 gives L_0 \varepsilon_0/(L_0 + 1) < \varepsilon_0. Line 15 is the bounded ulename{\exists I} at the term \varepsilon_0/(L_0 + 1), with its bound on line 5. At line 16, L_0 does not appear in line 16 (the witness term was forgotten at line 15), in line 1, which is the premise, or in the assumption \varepsilon_0 > 0 still open there. At lines 13, 14 and 17 the flags y_0, x_0, \varepsilon_0 do not appear in the premise, in the line itself, or in the assumptions then open (among lines 2, 3, 4 and 6). In prose: Let L \ge 0 be a constant with \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \abs{x - y} for all x, y \in A. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon / (L + 1), which is positive and depends on \varepsilon (and on the constant L, which is fixed before \varepsilon), but not on any point. For x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \abs{x - y} \le L\delta = \varepsilon L/(L + 1) < \varepsilon. So f is uniformly continuous on A. The box of L_0 is open where \delta is chosen, so \delta may depend on L_0. That is harmless: L_0 is a constant of the function, not a point, and its box could as well have been opened first, outside the box of \varepsilon_0. [B2: Put the proof in order] Below are ten sentences. Eight of them, in a suitable order, form a proof that a function f uniformly continuous on A is continuous at every point of A; two are distractors. Write down an order for the eight, and say why each distractor is wrong. 1. Since x and y lie in A and \abs{x - y} < \delta, the choice of \delta, applied to u = x and v = y, gives \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon. 2. Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary. 3. Let \varepsilon > 0. 4. Since \varepsilon > 0 and x \in A were arbitrary, f is continuous at every point of A. 5. Suppose f is uniformly continuous on A. 6. By uniform continuity, applied to \varepsilon, choose \delta > 0 such that for all u, v \in A, \abs{u - v} < \delta implies \abs{f(u) - f(v)} < \varepsilon. 7. Choose \delta > 0 for this x and this \varepsilon, and then let x \in A be arbitrary. 8. Let x \in A. 9. So for every y \in A, \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon: this \delta works for x and \varepsilon. 10. Let y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta. An admissible order: (v), (viii), (iii), (vi), (x), (i), (ix), (iv). (v) is the hypothesis of the implication being proved, so it opens the proof (its ulename{{	o}I} box is the outermost one). After it, other orders are admissible as long as each sentence comes after what it uses. (vi) uses the \varepsilon of (iii); (x) uses the \delta of (vi) and the x of (viii); then (i), (ix), (iv) follow in that order. So exactly three orders are admissible: (viii), (iii), (vi); or (iii), (viii), (vi); or (iii), (vi), (viii), each preceded by (v) and followed by (x), (i), (ix), (iv). Only the first matches the derivation of @exm-uniform-implies-continuous directly. The second and the third fix \varepsilon before x; the third even chooses \delta before any point is given, which is possible because uniform continuity supplies \delta from \varepsilon alone. They correspond to variants of that derivation in which the box of \varepsilon_0 (in the third, also that of \delta_0) is opened outside the box of x_0. Both variants end in  orall \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall x \in A \; \exists \delta > 0 \;  orall y \in A \; (\dots), and C follows by exchanging the two bounded universal quantifiers (the swap of @exm-universal-introduction-derivations (c), with the bounded rules); sentence (iv), “since \varepsilon and x were arbitrary”, covers both steps in prose. Distractor (ii) introduces \delta as an arbitrary object, by ulename{ orall I}. But in “continuous at x” the \delta is under \exists: the proof must produce it, by a choice from the hypothesis, not receive it from a challenger. A proof that took \delta arbitrary would have to show that every \delta > 0 works, which is false in general. Distractor (vii) chooses \delta and only afterwards lets x be arbitrary. It looks legitimate, because when (vii) is read after (viii), x is already fixed, and continuity at x does allow \delta to depend on x. But the sentence reverses the order of the two steps: a \delta fitted to one particular x is followed by “let x be arbitrary”, which claims that the same \delta works for every x. In the rules: if \delta really was chosen for this x, its ulename{\exists E} box assumes a line that mentions x, and generalizing over x while that assumption is open breaks the side condition of ulename{ orall I}, the first blocked line of @exm-converse-fails. If \delta does not depend on x, as here, then “for this x” is idle and the sentence should be (vi). [B3: The square root] Prove that f(x) = \sqrt{x} is uniformly continuous on A = [0, \infty). You may use the school inequality \abs{\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}} \le \sqrt{\abs{x - y}} for all x, y \ge 0. State what your \delta depends on. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon^2, which is positive and depends on \varepsilon only. Let x, y \in [0, \infty) with \abs{x - y} < \delta. Then, by the inequality given and because the square root is strictly increasing on [0, \infty), \abs{\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{y}} \le \sqrt{\abs{x - y}} < \sqrt{\varepsilon^2} = \varepsilon . Since x and y were arbitrary, this \delta works for all pairs of points; since \varepsilon was arbitrary, f is uniformly continuous on [0, \infty). The \delta was chosen before the points: in a derivation of this proof, its ulename{\exists I} line would lie inside the box of \varepsilon_0 only. C. Going deeper [C1: Composition, half done] Let f be uniformly continuous on A, with f(x) \in B for every x \in A, and let g be uniformly continuous on B. Here is the start of a proof that the composite x \mapsto g(f(x)) is uniformly continuous on A: Fix \varepsilon > 0. By the uniform continuity of g, choose \eta > 0 such that \abs{u - v} < \eta implies \abs{g(u) - g(v)} < \varepsilon for all u, v \in B. The rest is blank. Name the move, then complete it. [Hint 1] The goal asks for a \delta. Which hypothesis can produce one, and at which positive number should it be applied? [Hint 2] “By the uniform continuity of f, applied to \eta, choose \delta > 0 such that …” The move is fix, obtain, choose: \varepsilon was fixed (ulename{ orall I}), \eta obtained from the hypothesis on g (ulename{ orall E} at \varepsilon, then ulename{\exists E}); now obtain \delta from the hypothesis on f at the term the goal needs, \eta (ulename{ orall E} at \eta, then ulename{\exists E}), and choose that \delta as the witness (ulename{\exists I}). Completion. Since \eta > 0, the uniform continuity of f, applied to \eta, gives \delta > 0 such that \abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta for all x, y \in A; choose such a \delta. It depends on \eta, hence on \varepsilon, and on no point. Let x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta. Then \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta, and f(x), f(y) \in B, so the choice of \eta, applied to u = f(x) and v = f(y), gives \abs{g(f(x)) - g(f(y))} < \varepsilon. Since x, y were arbitrary, this \delta works for all pairs of points of A; since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, x \mapsto g(f(x)) is uniformly continuous on A. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (fix, obtain, choose), or the rules ulename{ orall E} at \eta, ulename{\exists E}, ulename{\exists I}. - 3: applies the uniform continuity of f at \eta (not at \varepsilon), using \eta > 0, and chooses \delta before any point. - 3: for arbitrary x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, gets \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \eta and then \abs{g(f(x)) - g(f(y))} < \varepsilon, using f(x), f(y) \in B. - 2: concludes with the quantifiers in the order \varepsilon, \delta, points, and says \delta depends on \varepsilon only. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \delta chosen after x or depending on x; the uniform continuity of g applied to points not known to lie in B. [C2: Gluing two sets] Let A and B be sets of real numbers and S the set of numbers that lie in A or in B. Suppose f is uniformly continuous on A and uniformly continuous on B. 1. Show that f need not be uniformly continuous on S: take A = (0, 1), B = (1, 2), and f(x) = 0 for x < 1, f(x) = 1 for x \ge 1. 2. Prove that f is uniformly continuous on S when A = [a, b] and B = [b, c] with a < b < c. [Hint 1] For (b), the two sets share the point b. Two points on opposite sides of b are each close to b. [Hint 2] For (b), apply the two hypotheses at \varepsilon/2 and take \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2). (a) On A = (0, 1), f is constantly 0, so every \delta > 0 works for every \varepsilon > 0: \abs{f(x) - f(y)} = 0 < \varepsilon. The same holds on B = (1, 2), where f is constantly 1. On S we prove the negation of uniform continuity (@exm-negating-definitions (c)). Take \varepsilon = 1. Let \delta > 0, and let \eta \coloneqq \min(\delta/4, 	frac12), x \coloneqq 1 - \eta, y \coloneqq 1 + \eta. Then 	frac12 \le x < 1, so x \in A \subseteq S; 1 < y \le 	frac32, so y \in B \subseteq S; \abs{x - y} = 2\eta \le \delta/2 < \delta; and \abs{f(x) - f(y)} = \abs{0 - 1} = 1 \ge \varepsilon. So f is not uniformly continuous on S. The gluing fails because the two sets come arbitrarily close at 1 but have no point in common: points close to 1 on opposite sides are each controlled only by their own set, and no common point links them. (b) Let \varepsilon > 0. By the uniform continuity on A at \varepsilon/2, choose \delta_1 > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2 for all x, y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta_1; likewise choose \delta_2 > 0 for B. Let \delta \coloneqq \min(\delta_1, \delta_2) > 0, which depends on \varepsilon only. Let x, y \in S with \abs{x - y} < \delta. There are three cases. - Case 1: x, y \in A. Then \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon, since \abs{x - y} < \delta \le \delta_1. - Case 2: x, y \in B. The same, with \delta_2. - Case 3: one point in each set, say x \in A and y \in B (the other way round is the same with the letters exchanged). Then x \le b \le y, so \abs{x - b} = b - x \le y - x = \abs{x - y} < \delta \le \delta_1, and b \in A; hence \abs{f(x) - f(b)} < \varepsilon/2. Likewise \abs{b - y} \le \abs{x - y} < \delta_2 and b \in B, so \abs{f(b) - f(y)} < \varepsilon/2. By the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases), \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le \abs{f(x) - f(b)} + \abs{f(b) - f(y)} < \varepsilon . Every point of S lies in A or in B, so the cases cover all pairs. So f is uniformly continuous on S. The common point b is what (a) lacked: there, A and B came arbitrarily close at 1 but had no point in common. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) uniform continuity on A and on B checked, and the negation on S proved: \varepsilon first, then for arbitrary \delta two points depending on \delta, with all three conditions checked. - 2: (b) \delta_1 for A at some \varepsilon_1 > 0 and \delta_2 for B at some \varepsilon_2 > 0 with \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 \le \varepsilon (the solution takes \varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2), and \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2), depending on \varepsilon only. - 2: the cases with both points in one set. - 3: the mixed case, through the point b, with \abs{x - b}, \abs{b - y} \le \abs{x - y} justified and the triangle inequality cited. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a \delta depending on x or y; the mixed case omitted; in (a), points chosen before \delta. [C3: Exit check: a quantifier derivation] 1. Give a full derivation of \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge  orall y\, R(x, y)  igr) \vdash  orall y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr), and check the side condition of every line that closes a flagged box. 2. For the converse,  orall y\, \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge R(x, y)  igr) \vdash \exists x\,  igl( P(x) \wedge  orall y\, R(x, y)  igr), give a domain with two elements and a reading of P and R under which the premise is true and the conclusion false, checking both with the informal reading of Section 4.1. (a) The goal is a  orall: open a flagged box for y_0. The premise is an \exists: open its ulename{\exists E} box at once, with a witness x_0, aiming for the goal’s instance. Inside, take the conjunction apart, instantiate  orall y at y_0, and choose x_0 as the witness: - Line 8 (ulename{\exists E}, flag x_0): x_0 does not appear in line 8, in line 1 (the premise), or in any assumption still open at line 8 (there is none: the box of y_0 has no assumption). Line 7, the last line of the box of x_0, is a line of that box itself and is the formula \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x, y_0)) that line 8 repeats (@def-rules-existential). - Line 9 (ulename{ orall I}, flag y_0): y_0 does not appear in the premise or in line 9, and no assumption is open. Line 8, the last line of the box of y_0, is the instance at y_0 of \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge R(x, y)). The other nesting, with the box of y_0 inside the box of x_0, works too: ulename{ orall I} at the end of the inner box (its name y_0 is in no open assumption, since the assumption on line 2 does not mention it), then ulename{\exists E} on a conclusion without x_0. (b) Take a domain with two elements a, b; let P be true of both, and let R(x, y) mean “x is y”. The premise is true: for y = a the witness x = a has P(a) and R(a, a), and for y = b the witness x = b works. The conclusion is false: x = a fails  orall y\, R(a, y) at y = b, and x = b fails it at y = a. The witness in the premise depends on y; the conclusion asks for one x that serves every y. (Section 4.11 makes this informal reading a structure, and shows that it proves the converse is not derivable.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: a flagged box with a fresh name y_0 for the ulename{ orall I}, closed correctly. - 3: an ulename{\exists E} box with a fresh witness x_0, whose conclusion does not contain x_0, with the side condition checked. - 2: ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{ orall E} at y_0 and ulename{\exists I} with the witness x_0, with the correct terms. - 3: the two-element reading: domain, meaning of P and R, the premise checked for each y and the conclusion refuted for each x. Either nesting of the two boxes earns full marks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): ulename{ orall I} on a name that appears in an open assumption; an ulename{\exists E} conclusion containing the witness.

title: 4.11 Models and Counter-models
content:
Models and Counter-models Sections 4.3 to 4.10 derived a good deal, and some searches stalled. The converse of @prp-exists-forall-swap could not be finished: every attempt ran into a side condition. The converse of @prp-exists-and stalled in the same way, and so did the search for \exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c) in @exr-existential-introduction-c2. But a search that fails proves nothing, since a cleverer derivation might exist. Chapter 3 met the same problem for the connectives and solved it with meaning: a row of a truth table that makes the premises true and the conclusion false rules out every derivation at once (@cor-refuting-row). This section builds the meaning of a quantified formula. A row of \mathrm{T} and \mathrm{F} is replaced by a model: a domain of objects, with a meaning for every symbol. A model that makes the premises true and the conclusion false is a counter-model, and it is the tool that settles the stalled searches. Why a row is not enough Chapter 3’s semantics gave each atom a truth value and computed the rest. Try it on the stalled sequent of @prp-exists-forall-swap’s converse,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) . Neither side has a main connective among 
eg, \wedge, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow: each is a quantified formula, and a truth table would have to treat each as one atom. The sequent would become p \vdash q, refuted by the row p = \mathrm{T}, q = \mathrm{F}. That “refutation” is worthless. The same reading refutes  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x), which is derivable (@prp-forall-implies-exists). Treating a quantified formula as an atom throws away exactly the structure that the quantifier rules use. So what does make  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) true or false? Section 4.1 read such sentences informally, over a domain: “for every y in the domain there is an x in the domain with R(x, y)”. To decide it we need three things. - A domain: the objects the variables range over. Over 
Z the sentence may be true and over a three-element set false. - A meaning for each symbol. R is a predicate symbol, a name with two slots and no meaning of its own (Section 4.2). Read as > on 
Z, the sentence says “every integer has an integer above it”, which is true; read as < on 
N, it says “every natural number has a natural number below it”, which is false at y = 0. - Values for the free variables, if there are any. The formula \exists y\, (y < x) is neither true nor false on 
N until we know which number x is. The first two together are a structure; the third is an assignment. A structure with an assignment decides every formula, by clauses that read the quantifiers as Section 4.1 read them. That is all this section does, and then it uses the result. Structures Situate the notion first. A formula is built from symbols: constants such as c and 0, function symbols such as f and +, predicate symbols such as P, R and <, each function and predicate symbol with its number of argument places, its arity (Section 4.2, @def-term and @def-first-order-formula). The symbol = is special: it is part of the logic, with rules of its own (@def-rules-equality), and it will always mean the same thing. A structure gives every other symbol a meaning. A structure is a non-empty set of objects together with a meaning for each symbol: an object for each constant, an operation for each function symbol, and a relation for each predicate symbol. [Structure] Fix a collection of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols, each function and predicate symbol with its arity n \ge 1. A structure  M (also called a model) for these symbols consists of 1. a non-empty set D, the domain of  M; 2. for each constant c, an element c^{ M} \in D; 3. for each function symbol f of arity n, a function f^{ M} \colon D^n 	o D, defined at every n-tuple of elements of D; 4. for each predicate symbol R of arity n, a set R^{ M} of n-tuples of elements of D. The symbol = is not interpreted by  M: in every structure it means identity, “is the same element of D as”. In words. (M1) says what the variables range over, and insists that there is at least one object. (M2) says which object each name names; two constants may name the same object. (M3) makes each function symbol an operation that can be applied to any objects of the domain and always returns an object of the domain. (M4) makes each predicate symbol a relation: R^{ M} is the set of tuples for which R “holds”. A one-place predicate symbol P becomes a subset P^{ M} \subseteq D, a two-place one a set of ordered pairs, and so on. Here D^n is the set of n-tuples (d_1, \dots, d_n) of elements of D; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 develops sets, pairs and functions properly, and this section uses only their everyday meaning. We usually describe a structure in one line, naming the domain and the meaning of each symbol, and write “ M = (
Z, <)” for the structure with domain 
Z in which the symbol < means the usual order. When a symbol has its usual meaning on a familiar set, we say so and do not write <^{ M}. Examples, simplest first. - One element. D = \{ a \}, with P^{ M} = \{ a \}. This is the degenerate structure. Every variable must take the value a, so “for every element” and “there is an element” both mean “a”. It will reappear as a test case: a sentence true here and false in some other structure cannot be derivable (by the soundness statement at the end of this section), and some of the chapter’s non-derivable sequents need at least two elements to refute. - Two elements, one relation. D = \{ a, b \}, with R^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}: the relation “is the same as”, written out as a set of pairs. A finite structure can be given completely by listing. - The integers with their order. D = 
Z, with R^{ M} = \{ (x, y) \in 
Z^2 : x > y \}. Here the relation is described by a condition rather than a list. - Arithmetic. D = 
R, with the constants 0 and 1 naming zero and one, the function symbols +, \cdot and two-place - meaning addition, multiplication and subtraction, the one-place symbols -, (\cdot)^2 and \abs{\cdot} meaning negation, squaring and absolute value, and <, \le, >, \ge the usual order. Extended by the other familiar symbols with their usual meanings (numerals, halving, the predicates \in A, division with its value at a zero denominator fixed arbitrarily as in the non-example below, and a function symbol for each sequence or function an example uses), this is the structure in which the analysis examples of this chapter have been read all along. Non-example by minimal change. Take the arithmetic structure and add a one-place function symbol g, meant to be read as x \mapsto 1/x. This is not a structure: (M3) asks for a function defined at every element of D, and 1/0 is not defined. Everything else in the description is fine; exactly clause (M3) fails, at the single point 0. There are two repairs. Shrink the domain to (0, \infty), where 1/x is always defined; or keep 
R and give g any value at 0, say g^{ M}(0) \coloneqq 0. The second repair is the one this chapter uses for terms such as 1/n: the value at 0 is fixed arbitrarily and is never looked at, because such terms are used only under a bound n \in 
Z_{>0} (as in @exr-models-c3), exactly as a sequence a_n was read in Section 4.1 as a function symbol whose values off 
N are never used. Why this definition. Each clause earns its place. - Non-empty. This is a genuine choice, and it is made because of @prp-forall-implies-exists. A later subsection explains it. - Total functions. Clause (M3) is what makes every term name an object: the term g(0) must have a value, or the formula g(0) = g(0), which ulename{{=}I} derives from nothing, would have no truth value. - Identity for =. The rule ulename{{=}E} replaces equals by equals everywhere. If a structure could read = as some other relation, ulename{{=}E} would fail. On 
Z, read x = y as “x and y have the same parity” and P as “is positive”: then -2 = 2 and P(2) would both hold, while P(-2), which ulename{{=}E} derives from them, fails. With = fixed as identity, no such reading exists. A structure must interpret every symbol that occurs in the formulas at hand. “Take D = 
Z” is not yet a structure for  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y): until R is given a meaning, the sentence has no truth value, and the same domain makes it true with R read as > and false with R read as “x \cdot x = y” (at y = 2). Always write the domain and the meaning of each symbol. Assignments and the value of a term A structure names the objects that constants stand for. Variables are different: their whole purpose is to range over the domain, so a structure gives them no fixed value. A separate object records what they stand for at a given moment. [Assignment] Let  M be a structure with domain D. An assignment in  M is a function \ell that gives every variable x a value \ell(x) \in D. For an assignment \ell, a variable x and an element d \in D, the assignment \ell[x \mapsto d] is the one that gives x the value d and every other variable the value \ell gives it: \ell[x \mapsto d](y) \coloneqq  egin{cases} d & 	ext{if } y 	ext{ is the variable } x, \ \ell(y) & 	ext{if } y 	ext{ is any other variable.} \end{cases} In words: an assignment is a choice of value for every variable at once, and \ell[x \mapsto d] changes that choice at the one variable x, leaving the others alone. The assignment \ell[x \mapsto d] is what the quantifiers will use: “for every x” will mean “for every d \in D, with x set to d”. Changes can be stacked: \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] first sets x to d and then y to e. When x and y are different variables the order does not matter, since each change touches only its own variable; when they are the same variable, the later change wins. There are always assignments, because D is non-empty: pick any d_0 \in D and let every variable have the value d_0. Like a valuation in Chapter 3 (@def-valuation), an assignment fixes infinitely many values, and a formula will only ever look at finitely many of them. With a structure and an assignment, every term names an element of the domain. Terms are built by the clauses of @def-term, so the value is defined by recursion on terms, in the pattern of @thm-structural-recursion. The value of a term is computed from its variables and constants upwards, one function symbol at a time. For a structure  M and an assignment \ell, the value t^{ M, \ell} \in D of a term t is: - x^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq \ell(x) for a variable x; - c^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq c^{ M} for a constant c; - f(t_1, \dots, t_n)^{ M, \ell} \coloneqq f^{ M} igl( t_1^{ M, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ M, \ell}  igr) for a function symbol f of arity n. The third clause is where (M3) is needed: f^{ M} must accept every tuple the terms t_1, \dots, t_n might produce. For example, in the arithmetic structure on 
R, let \ell(x) = 2 and \ell(y) = -3. The term x \cdot x + y, which is +(\cdot(x, x), y) written in the usual way, has value 2 \cdot 2 + (-3) = 1. Under \ell[y \mapsto 1] it has value 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5, and under \ell[x \mapsto 0] it has value -3. The term 1 + 1 has value 2 under every assignment, since it contains no variable. Satisfaction Now the central definition. We want to say when a structure and an assignment make a formula true. Formulas are built by the clauses of @def-first-order-formula, so we define it by recursion, one clause per way of building a formula, and each clause reads its connective or quantifier as Chapter 3 and Section 4.1 read it. A formula is satisfied when the objects its terms name stand in the relations its predicates name, combined by the connectives as in a truth table, with “for every x” and “there is an x” ranging over the domain. Satisfaction Let  M be a structure with domain D and \ell an assignment in  M. The relation  M, \ell \models \varphi, read “ M satisfies \varphi under \ell”, is defined by recursion on the formula \varphi: 1.  M, \ell \models R(t_1, \dots, t_n) if  igl( t_1^{ M, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{ M, \ell}  igr) \in R^{ M}; 2.  M, \ell \models t_1 = t_2 if t_1^{ M, \ell} and t_2^{ M, \ell} are the same element of D; 3.  M, \ell \models  ot never holds; 4.  M, \ell \models 
eg\varphi if  M, \ell \models \varphi does not hold; 5.  M, \ell \models \varphi \wedge \psi if both  M, \ell \models \varphi and  M, \ell \models \psi;  M, \ell \models \varphi \vee \psi if at least one of them holds;  M, \ell \models \varphi 	o \psi unless  M, \ell \models \varphi holds and  M, \ell \models \psi does not;  M, \ell \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi if both hold or neither does; 6.  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi if  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for every d \in D; 7.  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi if  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for at least one d \in D. When  M, \ell \models \varphi does not hold we write  M, \ell 
ot\models \varphi. For a list \Gamma of formulas,  M, \ell \models \Gamma means that  M, \ell \models \gamma for every formula \gamma of \Gamma. Read it clause by clause. (S1): an atomic formula is satisfied exactly when the values of its terms form a tuple in the relation that interprets its predicate symbol. (S2): an equation is satisfied when both sides name the same object; this is where “= means identity” enters. (S3)–(S5) are the  ot half of (V1) and clauses (V2)–(V6) of Chapter 3’s @def-truth-value, with “is true under v” replaced by “is satisfied by  M under \ell”:  ot is never satisfied, 
eg flips, \wedge needs both, \vee needs one, 	o fails only with a satisfied hypothesis and an unsatisfied conclusion, \leftrightarrow needs agreement. (S6) and (S7) are the new clauses. To decide  orall x\, \varphi, we run through the elements d of the domain, set x to d and leave every other variable alone, and ask whether \varphi is satisfied each time. For \exists x\, \varphi one success is enough. In symbols, for (S6) and (S7):  egin{aligned}  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi \quad &	ext{iff} \quad 	ext{for every } d \in D, \ \  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi , \  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi \quad &	ext{iff} \quad 	ext{there is } d \in D 	ext{ with }  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . \end{aligned} Well defined. The clauses define, for each formula, which pairs ( M, \ell) satisfy it, by recursion on the formula: (S1)–(S3) settle the atomic formulas and  ot, and each of (S4)–(S7) settles a compound formula from its immediate parts. One point needs a word. Clauses (S6) and (S7) consult the immediate part \varphi under other assignments \ell[x \mapsto d], not under \ell. So the recursion must define satisfaction of each formula under all assignments at once, and then (S6) reads off the answer for \varphi at every \ell[x \mapsto d]. The recursion is still on the formula alone, and @thm-structural-recursion, applied to formulas built by the clauses of @def-first-order-formula, gives exactly one such relation. A trace, step by step. Decide  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) in two structures, both with < the usual order:  M_1 with domain 
N, and  M_2 with domain \{ 1, 2, 3 \}. Let \ell be any assignment. In  M_1: by (S6) we must check, for every d \in 
N, that  M_1, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \exists y\, (x < y). Fix d. By (S7) it is enough to find one e \in 
N with  M_1, \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto e] \models x < y. Take e = d + 1. Under \ell[x \mapsto d][y \mapsto d + 1] the terms x and y have the values d and d + 1, and d < d + 1, so (S1) holds. Hence the sentence is satisfied. Notice that the witness e = d + 1 depends on d: (S7) is checked inside (S6), once for each d. In  M_2: (S6) asks the same for d = 1, 2, 3. At d = 1 and d = 2 the witnesses e = 2 and e = 3 work. At d = 3 no e \in \{ 1, 2, 3 \} has 3 < e, so (S7) fails for \ell[x \mapsto 3], and (S6) fails. So  M_2 
ot\models  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y), and the failure has a name: the element 3 has nothing above it. The assignment matters for free variables. In  M_1 = (
N, <), with \le also read as usual, take the formula  orall y\, (x \le y), in which x is free. Under an assignment with \ell(x) = 0 it is satisfied, since every e \in 
N has 0 \le e (recall that 
N = \{ 0, 1, 2, \dots \}). Under an assignment with \ell(x) = 1 it is not: e = 0 gives 1 \le 0, which fails. The same formula in the same structure is satisfied under one assignment and not under another; it is a property of x, “x is least”, not a statement. Degenerate cases. In the one-element structure D = \{ a \}, every assignment gives every variable the value a, so \ell[x \mapsto a] = \ell and (S6) and (S7) both reduce to “ M, \ell \models \varphi”. So  orall x\, \varphi and \exists x\, \varphi are satisfied together or not at all, and every equation x = y is satisfied. In any structure,  orall x\, (x = x) is satisfied, since every d is the same element as itself; and \exists x\, 
eg(x = x) never is. Is  orall x\, \exists y\, (y \cdot y = x) satisfied in 
R, in [0, \infty), and in 
C, each with \cdot the usual product? In 
R, no: at d = -1, (S7) asks for a real e with e \cdot e = -1, and every real square is \ge 0. In [0, \infty), yes: for each d \ge 0, e = \sqrt{d} is in the domain and e \cdot e = d; and [0, \infty) with \cdot is a structure, since a product of non-negative reals is non-negative (M3). In 
C, yes: every complex number has a complex square root (school algebra of complex numbers: r(\cos	heta + i\sin	heta) with r \ge 0 has the square root \sqrt{r}\,(\cos rac{	heta}{2} + i\sin rac{	heta}{2})). The sentence is the same all three times; only the structure changes. Only the free variables matter The example of  orall y\, (x \le y) above showed \ell mattering. In the first example it did not: the verdict on  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) was reached for “any assignment \ell”. That is no accident. A sentence has no free variables (@def-sentence), and every variable it contains is bound, so every value \ell gives is overwritten by (S6) or (S7) before it is looked at. We prove the general fact, which is the first-order version of Chapter 3’s @lem-coincidence: satisfaction depends only on the values of the free variables. Say that two assignments \ell and \ell' agree on a set of variables if \ell(y) = \ell'(y) for every variable y in it. We need the free variables of a formula, recursively defined in @def-free-variable: every variable occurring in an atomic formula is free there; 
eg\varphi has the free variables of \varphi; \varphi \circ \psi, for a binary connective \circ, has those of \varphi and those of \psi; and  orall x\, \varphi and \exists x\, \varphi have those of \varphi other than x. [Free Variables Coincidence Lemma] Let  M be a structure and \varphi a formula, and let \ell and \ell' be assignments in  M that agree on every free variable of \varphi. Then  M, \ell \models \varphi \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad  M, \ell' \models \varphi . Structural induction on \varphi, as for @lem-coincidence, after a first induction on terms: a term’s value depends only on the values of its variables. The connective cases are Chapter 3’s. The quantifier case is the only new one, and it explains why the property must be stated for all pairs of assignments: (S6) compares \ell[x \mapsto d] with \ell'[x \mapsto d], which are new assignments, so the induction hypothesis must apply to them. They agree at x, since both give it d, and at every other free variable of \varphi, since those are free in  orall x\, \varphi. Terms first. We show: if \ell and \ell' agree on every variable occurring in a term t, then t^{ M, \ell} = t^{ M, \ell'}. We use structural induction on terms (@def-term; the pattern of @thm-structural-induction). For a variable x, the variable x occurs in x, so x^{ M, \ell} = \ell(x) = \ell'(x) = x^{ M, \ell'}. For a constant c, both values are c^{ M}. For f(t_1, \dots, t_n), every variable of t_i occurs in f(t_1, \dots, t_n), so the hypothesis for t_i gives t_i^{ M, \ell} = t_i^{ M, \ell'} for each i; applying f^{ M} to equal tuples gives equal values. Formulas. We apply structural induction to the property C(\varphi): for all assignments \ell, \ell' in  M that agree on the free variables of \varphi,  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models \varphi. Atomic formulas. Let \varphi be R(t_1, \dots, t_n), and let \ell, \ell' agree on its free variables. Every variable occurring in \varphi is free in it (@def-free-variable), so \ell and \ell' agree on the variables of each t_i, and by the claim for terms t_i^{ M, \ell} = t_i^{ M, \ell'}. The two tuples in (S1) are equal, so one lies in R^{ M} exactly when the other does. The case t_1 = t_2 is the same with (S2). For  ot, neither side holds, by (S3). Connectives. Assume C(\varphi) and C(\psi), and let \ell, \ell' agree on the free variables of \varphi \wedge \psi. These include the free variables of \varphi and those of \psi, so  M, \ell \models \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models \varphi, and likewise for \psi. By (S5), satisfaction of \varphi \wedge \psi is decided by these two answers through the same rule for \ell and for \ell', so C(\varphi \wedge \psi) holds. The cases 
eg\varphi, \varphi \vee \psi, \varphi 	o \psi, and \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi are the same argument with (S4) and the other parts of (S5), as in the proof of @lem-coincidence. Universal quantifier. Assume C(\varphi), let x be a variable, and let \ell, \ell' agree on the free variables of  orall x\, \varphi. Let d \in D. We claim that \ell[x \mapsto d] and \ell'[x \mapsto d] agree on the free variables of \varphi. At x, both give d. A free variable y of \varphi other than x is a free variable of  orall x\, \varphi (@def-free-variable), so \ell[x \mapsto d](y) = \ell(y) = \ell'(y) = \ell'[x \mapsto d](y). By C(\varphi), applied to these two assignments,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi \quad 	ext{iff} \quad  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . This holds for every d \in D, so by (S6)  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell' \models  orall x\, \varphi. This proves C( orall x\, \varphi). Existential quantifier. The same argument, with (S7) in place of (S6): the displayed equivalence holds for each d, so there is a d making the left side hold exactly when there is one making the right side hold. Every clause of @def-first-order-formula has been covered, so C(\varphi) holds for every formula \varphi. This proves the lemma. The lemma has a consequence that the rest of the section uses constantly. Sentences. If \varphi is a sentence, it has no free variables, so any two assignments agree on its free variables, and the lemma says that  M, \ell \models \varphi either holds for every assignment \ell or for none. We then write  M \models \varphi, and say that \varphi is true in  M (or that  M is a model of \varphi), in the first case, and  M 
ot\models \varphi, \varphi is false in  M, in the second. At least one assignment exists because D is non-empty, so a sentence is always exactly one of true and false in  M. This is the precise form of Section 4.1’s informal “true over a domain”. Only finitely many values matter. A formula has finitely many free variables. To decide  M, \ell \models \varphi, it is enough to know \ell on those. So we describe an assignment by the values that matter (“\ell(x) = 2”), exactly as Chapter 3 described a valuation by the values of a few atoms. The same sentence can be true in one structure and false in another, and “true” without a structure means nothing.  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true in (
N, <) and false in (\{ 1, 2, 3 \}, <), as traced above. A sentence of predicate logic is like a formula of Chapter 3 with atoms: it has a truth value only once the meaning of its symbols has been fixed. Semantic entailment Chapter 3 said that \Gamma entails \psi when every row that makes \Gamma true makes \psi true (@def-valid-argument). The row is now a structure with an assignment. An argument is valid when every structure, under every assignment, that satisfies all the premises also satisfies the conclusion. [Semantic Entailment in Predicate Logic] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \varphi a formula. We say \Gamma semantically entails \varphi, and write \Gamma \models \varphi, if for every structure  M for the symbols occurring in \Gamma and \varphi, and every assignment \ell in  M,  M, \ell \models \Gamma \quad \Rightarrow \quad  M, \ell \models \varphi . We write \models \varphi when \Gamma is empty. If \Gamma \models \varphi fails, we write \Gamma 
ot\models \varphi; a structure  M with an assignment \ell such that  M, \ell \models \Gamma and  M, \ell 
ot\models \varphi is a counter-model to \Gamma \models \varphi. In words: “every structure” means every domain and every meaning of the symbols, so an entailment holds for reasons of form and not because of what R happens to mean. “Every assignment” covers every value of the free variables; when \Gamma and \varphi are sentences, the assignment makes no difference, by @lem-free-coincidence. And a counter-model is the analogue of Chapter 3’s refuting row: one structure, with one assignment, where the premises hold and the conclusion does not. The symbol \models is the one of Chapter 3, and the context always shows which is meant: a sequent of formulas with quantifiers or predicate symbols is read with this definition. A structure may interpret symbols that do not occur in \Gamma or \varphi. The clauses of @def-satisfaction consult only the symbols of the formula at hand, so such extra meanings change nothing. First examples of entailment. The argument Section 4.1 opened with, “every positive real has a square root; 2 is positive; so 2 has a square root”, is  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c), derived in Section 4.3. Truth tables called it invalid, since they saw three unrelated atoms. It is valid in the new sense:  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)), \ P(c) \models Q(c) . Let  M, \ell satisfy both premises, and let a = c^{ M}. By (S6) for the first premise, with d = a, we get  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models P(x) 	o Q(x). Under \ell[x \mapsto a] the term x has value a, and under \ell the term c has value a; so by (S1),  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models P(x) holds if and only if a \in P^{ M} if and only if  M, \ell \models P(c), which is the second premise. So by (S5)  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models Q(x), that is, a \in Q^{ M}, and by (S1) again  M, \ell \models Q(c). Chapter 3’s objection to this argument is gone. Why domains are non-empty Clause (M1) of @def-structure demands a non-empty domain. Here is the reason. @prp-forall-implies-exists derives  orall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) in three lines: ulename{ orall E} at the variable x, then ulename{\exists I}. The matching entailment holds for our structures:  orall x\, P(x) \models \exists x\, P(x) . Let  M, \ell \models  orall x\, P(x). Since D is non-empty, choose some d \in D. By (S6),  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models P(x), and this d is the one element (S7) asks for, so  M, \ell \models \exists x\, P(x). Now suppose empty domains were allowed. In a structure with D = \emptyset, (S6) says  orall x\, P(x) is satisfied, since “for every d \in \emptyset” has nothing to check; and (S7) says \exists x\, P(x) is not, since there is no d at all. So the sequent would be derivable and yet fail in a structure, and the rules would lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. (Worse, no assignment into an empty domain exists, so even the clauses could not be applied as written.) One of two things had to give: the rule ulename{ orall E} at a variable, or empty domains. The book, like most of mathematics, keeps the rules and makes domains non-empty. Nothing is lost. Statements about an empty set are handled by the bounded quantifiers of @def-bounded-quantifier, inside a non-empty domain. The bounded forms  orall x \in \emptyset\ \varphi and \exists x \in \emptyset\ \varphi abbreviate  orall x\, (x \in \emptyset 	o \varphi) and \exists x\, (x \in \emptyset \wedge \varphi), and in a structure with domain 
R in which the one-place predicate symbol \in \emptyset (Section 4.2) is interpreted, by (M4), as the empty subset of 
R, the first is true (every hypothesis d \in \emptyset is false) and the second is false (no d is in \emptyset). Vacuous truth lives in the bound, not in the domain. Counter-models A counter-model is found the way a refuting row was found in Chapter 3, by working backwards from what must fail. The conclusion must be false, so read off what that demands; the premises must be true, so read off what they demand; and then build the smallest structure meeting both. By @cor-refuting-row there is no derivation. (b) Derivable. The goal is an implication, so open a box on q; the premise is waiting for p 	o q, which a box on p produces by repeating q (the goal-directed and premise-directed steps of the search method of Section 2.6). The row method of (a) could not settle (b): no row refutes it, and only a derivation (or @thm-completeness) shows it is derivable. [R2] Derive 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q) \vdash 
eg
eg P \wedge 
eg
eg Q without ulename{RAA} and without derived rules that use it. Which rule would you need to derive P \wedge Q itself? The goal is a conjunction, so derive each conjunct. Each is a negation, so each gets a ulename{
eg I} box, whose goal is  ot. The only way to use the premise 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q) is to clash with it, so inside each box we build P 	o 
eg Q. In the first box, from 
eg P: a ulename{{	o}I} box on P clashes P with 
eg P and uses ulename{ ot E} (the pattern of @prp-vacuous-implication). In the second, from 
eg Q: a ulename{{	o}I} box on P simply repeats 
eg Q. These are the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 (@def-rules-negation, @def-rules-contradiction, @def-rules-implication). No ulename{RAA} is used. To reach P \wedge Q we would need P from 
eg
eg P and Q from 
eg
eg Q, that is, ulename{
eg
eg E}, which is derived with ulename{RAA} (@prp-double-negation), or an ulename{RAA} box directly (@def-rule-raa). The look-alike is @exr-finding-derivations-b1 (b), 
eg(P 	o Q) \vdash P \wedge 
eg Q: there the conjunct P needed ulename{RAA}, while 
eg Q came by ulename{
eg I} alone. Here both conjuncts stop at a double negation. That no derivation of P (or of P \wedge Q) from the premise avoids ulename{RAA} is true, but we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. [R3] Derive 
eg\exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\,  igl( 
eg
eg P(x) \wedge 
eg
eg Q(x)  igr) without ulename{RAA}. The goal is  orall x, so open a flagged box with a fresh name x_0 (@def-rules-universal); the new goal is 
eg
eg P(x_0) \wedge 
eg
eg Q(x_0). Inside, run the derivation of R2 (@exr-models-r2) with P(x_0) and Q(x_0) in place of P and Q. One change: the premise is now 
eg\exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)), not 
eg(P 	o 
eg Q), so each clash first turns P(x_0) 	o 
eg Q(x_0) into \exists x\, (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x)) by ulename{\exists I} at x_0 (@def-rule-existential-introduction). The side condition of ulename{ orall I} at line 18: x_0 does not appear in the premise on line 1, no box is open at line 18, and x_0 does not appear in the conclusion. The flagged box immediately contains the ulename{
eg I} box of line 2, so it is cited from line 2, the first line of that inner box. Lines 7 and 14 are legal ulename{\exists I} steps: P(x_0) 	o 
eg Q(x_0) is (P(x) 	o 
eg Q(x))[x_0/x]. The whole derivation is R2’s, run inside a flagged box, with an ulename{\exists I} before each clash. [R4] Is the sentence  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) 	o \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) true in (
N, <)? Is it derivable? True in (
N, <)? No. The hypothesis  orall x\, \exists y\, (x < y) is true in (
N, <): each d has d + 1 above it. The conclusion \exists y\,  orall x\, (x < y) is false: a candidate e fails at x = e, since e < e is false. By (S5) of @def-satisfaction, an implication with a true hypothesis and a false conclusion is false. Derivable? No. By the soundness statement of this section, a derivable sentence is true in every structure; this one is false in (
N, <), so no derivation exists. Why these tools. A structure settles the question in two lines, while a derivation search could only fail, and a failed search proves nothing. A truth table is the wrong look-alike: it reads the sentence as p 	o q with two atoms, and a refuting row for p 	o q says nothing here, since the sentence  orall x\, P(x) 	o \exists x\, P(x) has the same shape and is derivable (@prp-forall-implies-exists, then ulename{{	o}I}). The soundness statement used here is proved in Section 4.12.

title: 4.12 Soundness for Predicate Logic
content:
Soundness for Predicate Logic This section is optional, and nothing outside it depends on it: Section 4.11 stated soundness for predicate logic without proof, and the rest of the book uses that statement. The results below build on one another, so they carry no optional marker of their own; the section as a whole is the unit a reader may skip. Here is the proof. It is Chapter 3’s proof of @thm-soundness with six new cases, one for each quantifier and equality rule, and it is worth reading for one reason above all: each side condition of Sections 4.3 to 4.7 is used in the case of its own rule, and there one can see what would go wrong without it. The section proves a lemma about substitution and its corollary on renaming bound variables, then the theorem, then the corollary that turns every counter-model of Section 4.11 into a proof that no derivation exists. What carries over, and what is new Chapter 3 proved that whatever the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 derive is true in every row where the premises are true. The proof had four steps (Steps 1–4 of the proof of @thm-soundness). It reduced to derivations in the primitive rules; it proved a claim for every line, not only the last, namely \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k, where \Gamma_k is the context of line k; it did so by strong induction on k, one case per rule; and it read off the claim for the last line. We follow the same four steps. Three things change. The formulas. Lines now carry first-order formulas (@def-first-order-formula), and \models is the entailment of @def-first-order-entailment: \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k says that every structure  M and assignment \ell with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k satisfy \varphi_k. Assignments are not optional here. Lines inside a flagged box can mention the box’s name, a variable such as x_0, free; such a line is then not a sentence, and its truth depends on the value of x_0. This is why Section 4.4 insisted that fresh names are always variables, never constants: the proof below changes their values. The rules. The primitive rules are the thirteen of Chapter 3’s list (Section 3.5) and six new ones: ulename{ orall E} (@def-rule-universal-elimination), ulename{ orall I} (@def-rules-universal), ulename{\exists I} (@def-rule-existential-introduction), ulename{\exists E} (@def-rules-existential), ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E} (@def-rules-equality). Two of the new rules cite a box, the flagged box of ulename{ orall I} and the ulename{\exists E} box, so the box rules are now seven: Chapter 3’s five, and ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E}. The other four new rules cite only lines and join the one-step rules. Derived rules and “arith”. As in Step 1 of @thm-soundness, a line citing a derived rule abbreviates a pasted derivation in primitive rules. This covers Chapter 2’s derived rules (@def-derived-rule), whose derivations have no flagged boxes and apply to first-order formulas as they stand, and the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules, each of which Section 4.8 expanded into a displayed block of unbounded steps whose side conditions hold whenever the bounded ones do, and the one-line “(sym)” and “(trans)” of Section 4.7 (@prp-equality-symmetric-transitive), each of which abbreviates its three-line derivation from ulename{{=}I} and ulename{{=}E} with the given terms pasted in. Those derivations have no boxes, and each \varphi they use is an equation, with no quantifier, so every term is free for its variable and the side conditions of @def-rules-equality hold. A line justified “arith” is not a rule at all: it records an arithmetic fact. Written out, it is a universally quantified arithmetic sentence taken as an extra premise, whose bound variables are distinct and appear nowhere else in the derivation, instantiated by ulename{ orall E} at the terms on the line and applied by ulename{{	o}E}, as Section 4.4 did explicitly when it turned the premises of a Chapter 1 derivation into universal statements. That choice of bound variables means that no fresh name of the derivation appears in the new premise, so the side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} still hold, and that every term on the line is free for the variable it replaces at each ulename{ orall E} step. So a derivation with “arith” lines is a derivation in primitive rules from its premises together with those arithmetic sentences, and soundness speaks about that derivation. Renaming. Section 4.2 took, as a convention, that formulas differing only by renaming bound variables say the same thing, so a derivation may write a line, or apply a rule to a cited line, in a renamed form. This is not a rule either. @cor-renaming-bound-variables below shows that a formula and any renamed form of it are satisfied by exactly the same structures and assignments, so such a step changes nothing in the proof, which may take every line in the form its rule displays. Contexts, once more The context \Gamma_k of line k is still the list of the premises together with the assumptions of every box containing line k (Section 1.5, recalled before @lem-context-inclusion). A flagged box of ulename{ orall I} has no assumption, so it adds nothing to the context of the lines inside it. The ulename{\exists E} box opens with its assumption \varphi[x_0/x], which does join the context. Section 4.4 extended @def-derivation to flagged boxes and kept its scope rule and its notion of availability word for word; two boxes are still disjoint or one inside the other. So @lem-context-inclusion (a), whose proof uses only the scope rule, holds as it stands: if line i is available at line k, then \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k. Part (b) needs one extension, since its statement names “the assumption of that box”.
