It becomes: if line k is justified by a box rule citing the box from line a to line b, then \Gamma_b is \Gamma_k together with the assumption of that box if it has one, and \Gamma_b is \Gamma_k if it is a flagged box without an assumption. The proof of (b) in Section 3.5 is unchanged. It showed that the boxes containing line b are exactly the cited box and the boxes containing line k, and for that it used one fact about box rules: the last line of the cited box is a line of that box itself, not of a box inside it. The two new box rules demand the same: ulename{ orall I} requires \varphi[x_0/x] to be the last line of the flagged box, a line of that box itself (@def-rules-universal), and ulename{\exists E} requires \chi to be the last line of the box itself (@def-rules-existential). So the boxes containing line b are the cited box and those containing line k, and the context of line b adds to \Gamma_k only the cited box’s assumption, if any. When a flagged box immediately contains another box and is cited from the first line of that inner box, as the citation convention of Section 4.4 says, the argument is the same: the cited box runs from that line to its last line, and its last line lies in no box inside it. Here is the derivation of @prp-exists-forall-swap, with its contexts. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Line Boxes containing it Context ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- 1 none \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) 2, 3, 4 flagged y_0 (\lines{2}{5}); ulename{\exists E} box x_0 (\lines{2}{4}) \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), \  orall y\, R(x_0, y) 5 flagged y_0 (\lines{2}{5}) \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) 6 none \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Line 6 cites the flagged box \lines{2}{5}, which has no assumption, and indeed \Gamma_5 = \Gamma_6. Line 5 cites the ulename{\exists E} box \lines{2}{4}, and \Gamma_4 is \Gamma_5 with its assumption  orall y\, R(x_0, y) added. Line 3 mentions x_0 and y_0 free, and line 4 mentions y_0 free, while its context mentions x_0 free, through the assumption  orall y\, R(x_0, y): the claim \Gamma_4 \models \exists x\, R(x, y_0) is about every structure and every value of x_0 and y_0 that makes the context true. Substitution and satisfaction Five of the six new rules write a substitution: ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists I} write \varphi[t/x] for a term t, in their conclusion or premise; ulename{{=}E} writes one in both; and ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} write \varphi[x_0/x] for the fresh name. To handle them we need to know what \varphi[t/x] means in a structure. The natural guess is that substituting the term t for x has the same effect as giving x the value of t. Section 4.2 showed that this can fail: in \exists y\, (y > x), putting y + 1 for x blindly gives \exists y\, (y > y + 1), which is false in 
Z, while giving x the value of y + 1, whatever it is, leaves \exists y\, (y > x) true. The y of the term was captured. The lemma says that capture is the only thing that can go wrong. [Substitution Lemma] Let  M be a structure, \ell an assignment in  M, \varphi a formula, x a variable, and t a term that is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Write a \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}. Then  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] \quad 	ext{if and only if} \quad  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \varphi . First terms: substituting t for x in a term s and then evaluating is the same as evaluating s with x set to the value of t. Then structural induction on \varphi, for all assignments at once, since the quantifier clauses change the assignment. Atomic formulas follow from the claim for terms, and connectives pass straight through. The only real case is  orall y\, \varphi with x free in it. The substitution goes inside, and (S6) sets y to each d in turn. For the induction hypothesis to help, the value of t must not change when y does, and that is exactly what “free for” guarantees: y does not occur in t. Fix  M, x and t. For an assignment \ell, write a_\ell \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}. Terms. We show, for every term s and every assignment \ell, that (s[t/x])^{ M, \ell} = s^{ M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell]}, by structural induction on s (@def-term). If s is the variable x, then s[t/x] is t, with value a_\ell, and s^{ M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell]} = \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell](x) = a_\ell (@def-assignment). If s is another variable y, then s[t/x] is y, and both sides are \ell(y), since \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] changes only x. If s is a constant c, both sides are c^{ M}. If s is f(s_1, \dots, s_n), then s[t/x] is f(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]) (@def-substitution), and applying f^{ M} to the values, which agree by the hypothesis for s_1, \dots, s_n, gives equal results. Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on \varphi, the property B(\varphi): if t is free for x in \varphi, then for every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi. Two facts are used throughout. If t is free for x in 
eg\varphi or in \varphi \circ \psi, it is free for x in the parts, by the recursive description of “free for” after @def-free-for in Section 4.2. And by @def-substitution, substitution passes through connectives: (
eg\varphi)[t/x] is 
eg(\varphi[t/x]), and (\varphi \circ \psi)[t/x] is \varphi[t/x] \circ \psi[t/x]. Atomic formulas. R(s_1, \dots, s_n)[t/x] is R(s_1[t/x], \dots, s_n[t/x]). By the claim for terms, the tuple of values of the s_i[t/x] under \ell is the tuple of values of the s_i under \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell], so (S1) of @def-satisfaction gives the same answer on both sides. Equations s_1 = s_2 are the same with (S2). For  ot,  ot[t/x] is  ot, and neither side holds (S3). Connectives. For \varphi \wedge \psi: by B(\varphi) and B(\psi),  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi, and likewise for \psi; (S5) combines the two answers in the same way on both sides. The cases 
eg, \vee, 	o, \leftrightarrow are the same with (S4) and the other parts of (S5). Universal quantifier, x not free in  orall y\, \varphi. This happens when y is the variable x, or when x is not free in \varphi. Then ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x] is  orall y\, \varphi itself, since there is no free occurrence of x to replace (Section 4.2 proved that \psi[t/x] = \psi whenever x is not free in \psi). The assignments \ell and \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] differ at most at x, which is not free in  orall y\, \varphi; so by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models  orall y\, \varphi, which is B( orall y\, \varphi). Universal quantifier, x free in  orall y\, \varphi. Then y is not x, and x is free in \varphi. Every free occurrence of x in  orall y\, \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, so, as t is free for x in  orall y\, \varphi, the variable y does not occur in t, and t is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for, and its recursive description in Section 4.2). By @def-substitution, ( orall y\, \varphi)[t/x] is  orall y\, (\varphi[t/x]). Let d \in D. Since y does not occur in t, the assignments \ell and \ell[y \mapsto d] agree on every variable of t, so a_{\ell[y \mapsto d]} = a_\ell, by the claim for terms in the proof of @lem-free-coincidence. Since x and y are different variables, \ell[y \mapsto d][x \mapsto a_\ell] = \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell][y \mapsto d]. Hence, using B(\varphi) for the assignment \ell[y \mapsto d] in the second step,  egin{aligned}  M, \ell \models  orall y\, (\varphi[t/x]) &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi[t/x] \ &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[y \mapsto d][x \mapsto a_\ell] \models \varphi \ &\iff 	ext{for every } d \in D, \  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell][y \mapsto d] \models \varphi \ &\iff  M, \ell[x \mapsto a_\ell] \models  orall y\, \varphi , \end{aligned} where the first and last steps are (S6). This is B( orall y\, \varphi). Existential quantifier. The same two subcases, with (S7) in place of (S6) and “for some d” in place of “for every d”. Every clause of @def-first-order-formula is covered, so B(\varphi) holds for every formula. This proves the lemma. The hypothesis “free for” was used once, in the second quantifier case, to get a_{\ell[y \mapsto d]} = a_\ell. The capture example shows what happens without it. In the structure on 
Z with >, +, and 1 as usual, take \varphi = \exists y\, (y > x) and t = y + 1, which is not free for x in \varphi. The blind substitution is \exists y\, (y > y + 1), false under every assignment. But  M, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \exists y\, (y > x) holds for every a \in 
Z, with witness a + 1. The two sides of the lemma disagree, and the reason is visible in the displayed chain: when (S7) sets y to a new value, the value of y + 1 moves with it. Let  M be the structure on 
Z with <, +, and 1 as usual, \varphi =  orall z\, (x < z 	o y < z), t = y + 1, and let \ell(x) = 3, \ell(y) = 5. Is t free for x in \varphi? Compute both sides of @lem-term-substitution. Yes: the only quantifier in \varphi is  orall z, and z does not occur in y + 1. Here a = t^{ M, \ell} = 6. The right side asks whether  M, \ell[x \mapsto 6] \models \varphi: every z > 6 is > 5, so yes. The left side is \varphi[t/x] =  orall z\, (y + 1 < z 	o y < z) under \ell: every z > 6 is > 5, so yes. Both sides hold, as the lemma says. (Under \ell itself, \varphi is false: z = 4 has 3 < 4 and not 5 < 4. The lemma compares \varphi[t/x] with \varphi at the new value of x, not at the old one.) The lemma also pays a debt of Section 4.2, which took renaming of bound variables inside a formula as a convention and left its justification in terms of meaning to this section. [Renaming Keeps Meaning] Let \varphi be a formula and y, z variables, with z not appearing in \varphi (Section 4.2). Let  M be a structure for the symbols of \varphi, with domain D. 1. For every assignment \ell,  M, \ell \models  orall y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell \models  orall z\, \varphi[z/y], and  M, \ell \models \exists y\, \varphi if and only if  M, \ell \models \exists z\, \varphi[z/y]. 2. If \psi' arises from a formula \psi by such a renaming of one quantifier anywhere inside \psi (Section 4.2), then for every structure  M for the symbols of \psi and every assignment \ell in it,  M, \ell \models \psi if and only if  M, \ell \models \psi'. (a) If z is y, then \varphi[y/y] is \varphi and there is nothing to prove. Let z be a variable other than y. Since z does not appear in \varphi, no quantifier of \varphi is on z, so z is free for y in \varphi (@def-free-for). Let d \in D. Under \ell[z \mapsto d] the term z has value d, so @lem-term-substitution gives:  M, \ell[z \mapsto d] \models \varphi[z/y] if and only if  M, \ell[z \mapsto d][y \mapsto d] \models \varphi. The assignments \ell[z \mapsto d][y \mapsto d] and \ell[y \mapsto d] differ at most at z, which does not appear in \varphi; by @lem-free-coincidence, the last statement holds if and only if  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi. So  M, \ell[z \mapsto d] \models \varphi[z/y] if and only if  M, \ell[y \mapsto d] \models \varphi, for every d \in D. Now (S6) gives the statement for  orall, and (S7) the statement for \exists. (b) By structural induction on \psi, for all assignments at once, since the quantifier clauses change the assignment. If the renamed quantifier is the outermost symbol of \psi, this is (a). Otherwise \psi is not atomic, and the renaming takes place inside one immediate part of \psi, which it turns into a formula satisfied by the same assignments, by the induction hypothesis; the other parts are unchanged. If \psi is 
eg\alpha or \alpha \circ  eta, (S4) or (S5) then gives the same answer for \psi and \psi' under every \ell. If \psi is  orall w\, \alpha or \exists w\, \alpha, with the renaming inside \alpha, then \psi' is  orall w\, \alpha' or \exists w\, \alpha', and \alpha, \alpha' are satisfied by the same assignments \ell[w \mapsto d], so (S6) or (S7) gives the same answer for \psi and \psi'. Several renamings one after another are covered by applying (b) once for each. The soundness theorem We can now state the theorem that Section 4.11 took on trust. Soundness for Predicate Logic Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If \Gamma \vdash \psi with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 and the quantifier and equality rules of Sections 4.3 to 4.7, then \Gamma \models \psi (@def-first-order-entailment). The steps are those of Chapter 3’s proof (Steps 1–4 of @thm-soundness). ① Reduce to derivations in the primitive rules. ② Prove \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k for every line k, by strong induction on k (@thm-strong-induction): fix a structure  M and an assignment \ell satisfying \Gamma_k, and show that they satisfy \varphi_k. ③ The cases. Premises, assumptions, and the thirteen propositional rules go through word for word, because (S3)–(S5) are Chapter 3’s clauses. ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists I}, and ulename{{=}E} are @lem-term-substitution, used once or twice. ulename{{=}I} is (S2). The two box rules are the heart of the proof, and they both use the same trick: change the value of the fresh name. In ulename{ orall I}, to show  orall x\, \varphi under \ell, take any d, and set x_0 to d; the context does not notice, because x_0 is not in it, so the box’s last line \varphi[x_0/x] holds there, and moving d from x_0 to x gives \varphi under \ell[x \mapsto d]. In ulename{\exists E}, set x_0 to the witness d that \exists x\, \varphi provides; the box’s assumption holds there, so its last line \chi holds there, and since \chi does not mention x_0, it holds under \ell as well. ④ The last line lies in no box, so its context is the premises. Before reading on: in the ulename{ orall I} case below, the assignment \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] must still satisfy the context \Gamma_k, and at the end the conclusion must come back from \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] to \ell[x \mapsto d]. Which clause of the side condition of ulename{ orall I} does each step use? Step 1 (reduction). Suppose \Gamma \vdash \psi. By the subsection “What carries over, and what is new”, there is a derivation of \psi in the primitive rules whose premises all belong to \Gamma. (A derivation with “arith” lines is of this kind only for the list of its premises together with the arithmetic sentences A those lines stand for, as explained there. The theorem applies to it with the list \Gamma, A in place of \Gamma, and gives \Gamma, A \models \psi: truth in every structure that satisfies \Gamma and A. The sentences A hold, for instance, when the arithmetic symbols have their usual meaning on 
R, as in Section 4.11.) Fix one, with lines 1, \dots, n, formulas \varphi_k, and contexts \Gamma_k. Let \Sigma be the finite set of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols that occur in some line of it. A line may contain symbols that occur neither in \Gamma nor in \psi, as c does in the line P(c) between  orall x\, P(x) and \exists x\, P(x); so the induction is run over structures that interpret every symbol of \Sigma, and Step 4 returns to the structures of @def-first-order-entailment. Step 2 (the induction). For k \in 
N, let S(k) be: if 1 \le k \le n, then every structure  M that interprets every symbol of \Sigma and every assignment \ell in  M with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k satisfy  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. In Steps 2 and 3, “structure” means a structure that interprets every symbol of \Sigma, and possibly more. We prove S(k) for all k by @thm-strong-induction. For k = 0 and k > n, S(k) holds vacuously. Let 1 \le k \le n and assume S(j) for every j < k. Every line and box that line k cites is available at line k, so lies before it (@def-derivation); hence the hypothesis holds for every cited line and for the last line of every cited box. Let  M be a structure, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. We show  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. Two consequences of the hypothesis do the bookkeeping, as in the proof of @thm-soundness. If line k cites line i, then \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), so  M, \ell \models \Gamma_i, and S(i) gives  M, \ell \models \varphi_i \quad 	ext{for every line } i 	ext{ cited by line } k . 	ag{$\ast$} If line k cites, by a box rule, the box from line a to line b, then by @lem-context-inclusion (b), extended in the subsection “Contexts, once more”, and S(b): 	ext{every structure and assignment satisfying } \Gamma_k 	ext{ and the box's assumption, if any, satisfy } \varphi_b . 	ag{$\ast\ast$} Step 3 (the cases). If line k is a premise, an assumption, or justified by one of the thirteen primitive rules of Chapters 1 and 2, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. Claims 1–3 in the proof of @thm-soundness treat these cases. Each step there uses only (\ast), (\ast\ast), the fact that a premise or an assumption belongs to its own context, and the clauses (V1)–(V6) of @def-truth-value. Clauses (S3)–(S5) of @def-satisfaction are (V1)–(V6) with “v makes \varphi true” replaced by “ M, \ell \models \varphi”. Making that replacement throughout, the proofs of those claims prove this one, case by case. If line k is justified by ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists I}, ulename{{=}I}, or ulename{{=}E}, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. ulename{ orall E}. Line k is \varphi[t/x], citing a line holding  orall x\, \varphi, with t free for x in \varphi. By (\ast),  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi, so by (S6),  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi for every d \in D, in particular for d = t^{ M, \ell}. By @lem-term-substitution, which applies because t is free for x in \varphi,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. ulename{\exists I}. Line k is \exists x\, \varphi, citing a line holding \varphi[t/x], with t free for x in \varphi. By (\ast),  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. By @lem-term-substitution,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi with d = t^{ M, \ell} \in D. So d is the element (S7) asks for, and  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi. ulename{{=}I}. Line k is t = t. The two sides have the same value t^{ M, \ell}, so (S2) holds. ulename{{=}E}. Line k is \varphi[t_2/x], citing lines holding t_1 = t_2 and \varphi[t_1/x], with t_1 and t_2 free for x in \varphi. By (\ast) and (S2), t_1^{ M, \ell} and t_2^{ M, \ell} are the same element d; and  M, \ell \models \varphi[t_1/x]. By @lem-term-substitution for t_1,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. By @lem-term-substitution for t_2, read from right to left,  M, \ell \models \varphi[t_2/x]. If line k is justified by ulename{ orall I} or ulename{\exists E}, then  M, \ell \models \varphi_k. ulename{ orall I}. Line k is  orall x\, \varphi, citing a flagged box with name x_0 and no assumption, whose last line b holds \varphi[x_0/x]. The side condition of @def-rules-universal says that at line k the name x_0 appears in no premise and in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in  orall x\, \varphi. The premises and the assumptions of the boxes open at line k are exactly the formulas of \Gamma_k, so (i) x_0 appears in no formula of \Gamma_k; and (ii) x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi, so x_0 is not the variable x, and x_0 does not appear in \varphi. The flagged box has no assumption, so (\ast\ast) says: every structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k satisfy \varphi[x_0/x]. Let d \in D; we show  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Put \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. It differs from \ell at most at x_0, which by (i) is free in no formula of \Gamma_k; so by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k. This is where the fresh-name condition is used: changing the value of x_0 cannot disturb anything we assumed. By (\ast\ast),  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. By (ii), x_0 does not appear in \varphi, so no quantifier of \varphi is on x_0, and the term x_0 is free for x in \varphi (@def-free-for). Its value under \ell' is d, so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] \models \varphi . The assignments \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] agree at x, where both give d, and at every variable other than x and x_0, where both give the value \ell gives. They can differ only at x_0, which by (ii) does not appear in \varphi. By @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Since d \in D was arbitrary, (S6) gives  M, \ell \models  orall x\, \varphi. ulename{\exists E}. Line k is \chi, citing a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a box with name x_0 that opens with the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] and ends with \chi. The side condition of @def-rules-existential says that x_0 appears neither in \chi, nor in \exists x\, \varphi, nor in any premise, nor in any assumption of a box still open at line k. So (i) x_0 appears in no formula of \Gamma_k; (ii) x_0 is not x, and does not appear in \varphi; (iii) x_0 does not appear in \chi. By (\ast\ast), every structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k and \varphi[x_0/x] satisfy \chi. By (\ast) for line h,  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi; by (S7), choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Put \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. First,  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k, by (i) and @lem-free-coincidence, as in the ulename{ orall I} case. Second,  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. Indeed, \ell'[x \mapsto d] = \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] differ at most at x_0, which by (ii) does not appear in \varphi, so  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi by @lem-free-coincidence; the term x_0 is free for x in \varphi by (ii), and has value d under \ell', so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. This is where “x_0 not in \exists x\, \varphi” is used. By (\ast\ast),  M, \ell' \models \chi. Finally, \ell' and \ell differ at most at x_0, which by (iii) does not appear in \chi, so  M, \ell \models \chi by @lem-free-coincidence. This is where “x_0 not in \chi” is used. The three claims cover every way a line can be justified, so S(k) holds, and by @thm-strong-induction S(k) holds for every line k of the derivation. Step 4 (the last line). The last line n lies in no box (@def-derivation), so \Gamma_n consists of premises only, and \varphi_n = \psi. Let  M be a structure for the symbols occurring in \Gamma and \psi, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma. Expand  M to a structure  M' with the same domain and the same meanings, which also interprets the symbols of \Sigma that  M does not, so that  M' interprets every symbol of \Sigma: fix some e \in D, which exists because D is non-empty (M1), and give each new constant the value e, each new function symbol, of arity m say, the function D^m 	o D with constant value e, and each new predicate symbol the empty relation. Then \ell is an assignment in  M', and by the remark after @def-first-order-entailment (the clauses of @def-satisfaction consult only the symbols of the formula at hand), each formula of \Gamma, and \psi, is satisfied by  M', \ell exactly when it is satisfied by  M, \ell. Every premise belongs to \Gamma, so  M', \ell \models \Gamma_n; by S(n),  M', \ell \models \psi; and so  M, \ell \models \psi. This proves \Gamma \models \psi. The answer to the prompt: the first step uses the clauses “no premise” and “no open assumption”, which together say that x_0 is not in \Gamma_k; the second uses “not in  orall x\, \varphi”. The last line \varphi[x_0/x] of the box, which may mention x_0 as often as it likes, plays no part in either. That is the precise sense in which “let x_0 be arbitrary” works: whatever value x_0 is given, what we know still holds, so what we proved about x_0 holds at that value. The ulename{\exists E} case uses the same move with the opposite purpose. There the value of x_0 is not arbitrary; it is set to the witness d. What makes that legitimate is that nothing else knows about x_0 (condition (i)), that the assumption \varphi[x_0/x] then holds at the witness (condition (ii)), and that the result \chi forgets it again (condition (iii)). Counter-models prove nonderivability The corollary is the one Section 4.11 used, now with a proof. [Counter-models] Let \Gamma be a list of formulas and \psi a formula. If some structure  M and assignment \ell satisfy every formula of \Gamma and do not satisfy \psi, then \Gamma 
vdash \psi. The pair  M, \ell shows that \Gamma \models \psi fails (@def-first-order-entailment). If \Gamma \vdash \psi held, @thm-first-order-soundness would give \Gamma \models \psi. So \Gamma \vdash \psi does not hold. If the derivations in question may use “arith” lines, a counter-model must also satisfy the arithmetic sentences those lines stand for (Step 1 of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness), for instance by giving the arithmetic symbols their usual meaning. Every counter-model of Section 4.11 is now a proof that no derivation exists. - By @exm-counter-model-swap,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) 
vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). The converse search of @prp-exists-forall-swap stalled at two lines, a ulename{ orall I} blocked by an open assumption and an ulename{\exists E} blocked by its conclusion; now we know that no other route could have succeeded. - The two-element structure with P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \} gives \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x) 
vdash \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) and  orall x\, (P(x) \vee Q(x)) 
vdash  orall x\, P(x) \vee  orall x\, Q(x): the one-way laws of @prp-quantifier-distribution are one-way. - \exists x\, P(x) 
vdash P(c), which @exr-existential-introduction-c2 could only explain informally. - P(x_0) 
vdash  orall x\, P(x), by the structure on 
Z with P^{ M} the even integers and \ell(x_0) = 2: generalizing over a name in a premise is not merely forbidden, it would be unsound. - The passage laws of @prp-quantifier-passage need x not free in \psi: with x free, 
vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x), by the counter-model of @exr-models-b1 (iii), which names an assignment. The converse of @thm-first-order-soundness is also true: if \Gamma \models \psi, then \Gamma \vdash \psi. This is the completeness theorem for predicate logic, proved by Gödel in 1929. Its proof needs to build a structure out of the formulas themselves, and it is beyond this book; nothing here depends on it. One difference from Chapter 3 remains even with completeness: there is no truth table to check. Whether a sentence of predicate logic is derivable cannot, in general, be decided by any mechanical procedure (Church and Turing, 1936). A failed search and a missing counter-model can both go on for ever. Every side condition is a case of the proof The side conditions of Sections 4.3 to 4.7 were introduced one at a time, each with a counterexample. The proof above shows that they are all the same kind of thing: each is used in the case of its own rule, and dropping it breaks a step of that case. Each counterexample of Sections 4.3 to 4.7 can be read as a failed case: - generalizing over a name in a premise, as in “P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x)” (Section 4.4): the ulename{ orall I} case fails at “ M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] \models \Gamma_k”, since changing x_0 changes the premise P(x_0); - generalizing over a name in an open assumption, as in “from x_0 > 0,  orall x\, (x > 0)” (Section 4.4): the same step, with the assumption x_0 > 0 in \Gamma_k; - a name that leaks into the conclusion of ulename{ orall I}, as in @exr-existential-introduction-c1: the last step of the ulename{ orall I} case, since x_0 now occurs in \varphi; - treating the witness as arbitrary, by ulename{ orall I} over its name inside its ulename{\exists E} box (Section 4.6): the ulename{ orall I} case again, since the box’s assumption is in \Gamma_k; - letting the witness escape its box, or giving a second witness a name already in an open assumption (Section 4.6): the ulename{\exists E} case, at condition (iii) or (i); - a capture in ulename{ orall E} (Section 4.3) or ulename{\exists I} (Section 4.5): the ulename{ orall E} or ulename{\exists I} case, where @lem-term-substitution does not apply; Exercise C2 and the solution to Exercise B1 give false conclusions; - a capture in ulename{{=}E}, as in a = y, \ \exists y\, (y < a) \vdash \exists y\, (y < y) (Section 4.7): the ulename{{=}E} case, where @lem-term-substitution does not apply to t_2. A side condition is not mere bookkeeping: a derivation that breaks one is not covered by @thm-first-order-soundness, and it can reach a false line, as the counter-model to P(x_0) \vdash  orall x\, P(x) in the previous subsection shows for the first item of the list. @exr-existential-elimination-c2 gives a derivation of \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) whose ulename{\exists E} box ends in P(x_0); the line after the box is P(x_0) by ulename{\exists E}, and the last line is \exists x\, P(x) by ulename{\exists I}. Which case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness fails, at which step, and for which line? Give a structure and an assignment showing that the claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k is false for that line. The ulename{\exists E} case fails, at its last step: \chi = P(x_0) contains x_0, so condition (iii) is false, and “ M, \ell' \models \chi” cannot be carried back from \ell' = \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] to \ell. The line concerned is the illegal ulename{\exists E} line P(x_0), whose context is the premise alone. Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = Q^{ M} = \{ a \} and \ell(x_0) = b: the premise \exists x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) holds (witness a), and P(x_0) fails, since b 
otin P^{ M}. The final conclusion \exists x\, P(x) is still true in this structure, as it is in every structure satisfying the premise; the fault is in the line before it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness. 1. In the ulename{ orall I} case, name the two places where the side condition of ulename{ orall I} is used, and say which clause each uses. 2. The derivation below breaks the side condition of ulename{\exists E}: its conclusion P(x_0) contains the fresh name. Which step of the ulename{\exists E} case fails? Give a structure and an assignment in which the premise holds and line 3 does not. 3. Give the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. Why does the claim \Gamma_k \models \varphi_k quantify over assignments, and not only over structures? Point to a line of the derivation of @prp-exists-forall-swap printed in this section. (a) First, to show that \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] still satisfies \Gamma_k: this uses “x_0 appears in no premise and in no assumption of a box open at line k”, which together say that x_0 is in no formula of \Gamma_k, so @lem-free-coincidence applies. Second, to pass from \ell[x_0 \mapsto d][x \mapsto d] to \ell[x \mapsto d] (and, before that, to know that x_0 is free for x in \varphi): this uses “x_0 does not appear in  orall x\, \varphi”. (b) The last step: from  M, \ell[x_0 \mapsto d] \models \chi to  M, \ell \models \chi, which needs x_0 not in \chi. Take D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, \ell(x_0) = b. The premise \exists x\, P(x) holds, with witness a; line 3, P(x_0), fails, since \ell(x_0) = b 
otin P^{ M}. Inside the box, under \ell[x_0 \mapsto a], line 2 holds; the proof would carry it back to \ell, and that is exactly what fails. (c) Every line of a derivation is satisfied by every structure and assignment that satisfy its context, by strong induction on the line, with one case per rule. The quantifier box rules are handled by changing the value of the fresh name, which the side conditions guarantee the context and the conclusion cannot notice. (d) Lines inside boxes contain free variables, the fresh names, and their truth depends on the values of those variables. Line 3, R(x_0, y_0), is not a sentence: in the structure on 
Z with R read as <, it is satisfied when \ell(x_0) = 1, \ell(y_0) = 2, and not when \ell(x_0) = 2, \ell(y_0) = 1. The ulename{ orall I} and ulename{\exists E} cases work precisely by changing such values. B. Practice [B1: The ulename{\exists I} case] Write out the ulename{\exists I} case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness in full: state what is known about the cited line, and show  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi, naming the reason for each step. Where is “t free for x in \varphi” used? Line k is \exists x\, \varphi, by ulename{\exists I} citing a line i holding \varphi[t/x], where t is free for x in \varphi (@def-rule-existential-introduction). Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation (as in Step 2), with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. Line i is available at line k, so \Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k by @lem-context-inclusion (a), and  M, \ell \models \Gamma_i. Since i < k, the induction hypothesis S(i) gives  M, \ell \models \varphi[t/x]. Let d \coloneqq t^{ M, \ell}, an element of D. Because t is free for x in \varphi, @lem-term-substitution applies and gives  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. By (S7) of @def-satisfaction, with the element d,  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi. “Free for” is used exactly once, to apply @lem-term-substitution. Without it the step fails: from  orall y\, R(y, y), read as ( orall y\, R(x, y))[y/x], an “ulename{\exists I}” would give \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y), and in the structure on 
Z with R read as \le the first is true and the second (“there is a least integer”) false. [B2: Three nonderivability results] Use the following counter-models from Section 4.11 to state three nonderivability results, citing @cor-counter-model, and check in each case that the structure (and assignment) satisfy every premise and not the conclusion. 1. The two-element structure of @exm-counter-model-swap. 2. The counter-model of @exr-models-b3. 3. The counter-model of @exr-models-b1 (iii). (a) D = \{ a, b \}, R^{ M} = \{ (a, a), (b, b) \}. The premise  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) holds (for y = a take x = a, for y = b take x = b); the conclusion \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y) fails (x = a fails at y = b, x = b at y = a). Both are sentences, so any assignment will do. By @cor-counter-model,  orall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) 
vdash \exists x\,  orall y\, R(x, y). (b) D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, Q^{ M} = \{ b \}. The premise  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) holds, since its hypothesis fails at b; the conclusion  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) fails at a. By @cor-counter-model,  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) 
vdash  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)). (c) D = \{ a, b \}, P^{ M} = \{ a \}, with an assignment \ell(x) = b. There are no premises, so the condition on premises holds trivially. The formula \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x) fails under \ell: its hypothesis holds (witness a) and its conclusion, with x free, has value b 
otin P^{ M}. By @cor-counter-model, with \Gamma empty, 
vdash \exists x\, P(x) 	o P(x). Here the assignment is essential: under \ell(x) = a the formula holds, and the structure alone would not have been a counter-model. C. Going deeper [C1: The ulename{\exists E} case] Write out the ulename{\exists E} case of the proof of @thm-first-order-soundness in full, from memory: the data of line k, the side condition, what the induction hypothesis gives for the cited line and the cited box, and the argument, naming at each step which clause of the side condition it uses. [Hint 1] The tool is the assignment \ell[x_0 \mapsto d], where d is a witness for \exists x\, \varphi under \ell. You will need @lem-free-coincidence three times and @lem-term-substitution once. [Hint 2] Start: “Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation, with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. By the induction hypothesis for line h and @lem-context-inclusion (a),  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi, so choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi.” Data. Line k is \chi, by ulename{\exists E} citing a line h holding \exists x\, \varphi and a box with name x_0, from line a (the assumption \varphi[x_0/x]) to line b (the formula \chi). Side condition (@def-rules-existential): x_0 appears neither in \chi, nor in \exists x\, \varphi, nor in a premise, nor in an assumption of a box still open at line k. What the hypothesis gives. Line h is available at line k, so \Gamma_h \subseteq \Gamma_k (@lem-context-inclusion (a)), and S(h) holds: every structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation, and every assignment satisfying \Gamma_h, satisfy \exists x\, \varphi. The box is cited by a box rule, so its last line has context \Gamma_k, \varphi[x_0/x] (@lem-context-inclusion (b), extended in the subsection “Contexts, once more”), and S(b) says that every such structure and assignment satisfying \Gamma_k and \varphi[x_0/x] satisfy \chi. The argument. Let  M be a structure interpreting every symbol of the derivation (as in Step 2), with domain D, and \ell an assignment with  M, \ell \models \Gamma_k. Then  M, \ell \models \Gamma_h, so  M, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi; by (S7), choose d \in D with  M, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi. Let \ell' \coloneqq \ell[x_0 \mapsto d]. 1.  M, \ell' \models \Gamma_k. The formulas of \Gamma_k are the premises and the assumptions of the boxes open at line k; by the side condition, x_0 appears in none of them. \ell' differs from \ell only at x_0, so @lem-free-coincidence applies to each formula of \Gamma_k. 2.  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. Since x_0 does not appear in \exists x\, \varphi, it is not x and does not appear in \varphi. So \ell'[x \mapsto d] and \ell[x \mapsto d] differ at most at x_0, which is not in \varphi, and  M, \ell'[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi by @lem-free-coincidence. The term x_0 is free for x in \varphi, as no quantifier of \varphi is on x_0, and x_0^{ M, \ell'} = d; so @lem-term-substitution gives  M, \ell' \models \varphi[x_0/x]. 3. By 1, 2 and the hypothesis for the box,  M, \ell' \models \chi. 4. \ell' and \ell differ only at x_0, which does not appear in \chi; by @lem-free-coincidence,  M, \ell \models \chi. Since  M and \ell were arbitrary, this proves S(k). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: states the data and the full side condition, and the context \Gamma_k, \varphi[x_0/x] of the box’s last line. - 2: obtains a witness d from the cited line through the induction hypothesis and (S7), and sets x_0 to d. - 2: shows the new assignment still satisfies \Gamma_k, using “x_0 in no premise and no open assumption”. - 2: shows the new assignment satisfies \varphi[x_0/x], using “x_0 not in \exists x\, \varphi” and the substitution lemma. - 2: applies the hypothesis for the box, and returns to \ell using “x_0 not in \chi”. A proof that treats the box’s assumption and the context in the other order earns the same points. Fatal errors (0 for the step): setting x_0 to an arbitrary element rather than the witness; concluding  M, \ell \models \chi directly from  M, \ell' \models \chi without the condition on \chi. [C2: “Free for” is needed] Show that the side condition “t is free for x in \varphi” of ulename{ orall E} cannot be dropped. Give a two-line “derivation” that uses ulename{ orall E} with a term that is not free for x, a structure in which its premise is true and its conclusion false, and the step of the proof of @lem-term-substitution that fails. [Hint 1] Look for a premise  orall x\, \varphi in which \varphi contains a quantifier  orall y and x occurs free inside its scope; instantiate at t = y. [Hint 2] Try \varphi = 
eg orall y\, (y \le x), “x is not an upper bound of everything”, in a structure with no largest element. Take \varphi = 
eg orall y\, (y \le x) and t = y. The free occurrence of x in \varphi lies in the scope of  orall y, and y occurs in t, so t is not free for x in \varphi. Ignoring this, ulename{ orall E} would allow: In (
Z, \le), the premise says “for every integer x, not every integer y is \le x”, that is, no integer is largest: for each x, the integer x + 1 is not \le x. It is true. The conclusion says “not every integer y has y \le y”, which is false, since \le is reflexive. So the premise is true and the conclusion false, and a rule allowing this step would be unsound. The step of @lem-term-substitution that fails is the second quantifier case, applied to  orall y\, (y \le x): it needs y not in t, so that the value of t does not change when (S6) sets y to each d. Here t = y, and its value is the new d each time:  orall y\, (y \le y) compares each d with itself, while  orall y\, (y \le x) at the value a of t compares each d with the fixed a. The legal route renames first (Section 4.2):  orall x\, 
eg orall z\, (z \le x), and then ulename{ orall E} at y gives 
eg orall z\, (z \le y), which is true in (
Z, \le) under every assignment. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: a premise and a ulename{ orall E} step at a term that is not free for x, with the capture identified. - 4: a structure, with the premise checked true and the conclusion checked false. - 3: names the quantifier case of @lem-term-substitution and the fact it needs (y not in t). Fatal errors (0 for the step): a “counter-model” in which the premise is false; a step in which t is in fact free for x.

title: From Derivations to Mathematical Prose
content: From Derivations to Mathematical Prose Here is a complete proof, as a textbook of analysis would print it, that a function uniformly continuous on a set A is continuous at every point of A: Let x \in A and \varepsilon > 0. By uniform continuity, choose \delta > 0 (depending on \varepsilon only) such that \abs{f(u) - f(v)} < \varepsilon for all u, v \in A with \abs{u - v} < \delta. In particular \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon for every y \in A with \abs{x - y} < \delta, so this \delta works for x and \varepsilon. Section 4.10 proved the same fact as an eleven-line derivation (@exm-uniform-implies-continuous), with three nested boxes: one for the point x_0, one for \varepsilon_0, one for the chosen \delta_0. The paragraph has no boxes and no line numbers. Where did the boxes go? Nowhere. “Let x \in A and \varepsilon > 0” opens the first two, “choose” opens the third, and the parenthesis “(depending on \varepsilon only)” records that \delta came from a line that mentions \varepsilon and not x, which is exactly where uniform continuity and continuity differ. Words such as “let”, “choose”, “suppose” and “in either case” are the boxes, spoken. This chapter makes that correspondence exact in both directions. Learning to hear the boxes is what lets a reader working alone check a proof, by restoring the derivation underneath wherever a step is in doubt; learning to speak them is what makes a proof checkable by someone else. The chapter builds a dictionary from rules to phrases, writes two proofs at four levels from full derivation to plain prose, fixes once and for all which steps plain prose may leave unsaid, and turns all of this into habits for reading, writing and checking proofs, with a catalogue of the errors that recur. From Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, the start of Part I, proofs are written in plain prose, and a rule tag appears only where the rule is itself the point, as in a review exercise that looks back at Part 0; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3 may still tag some proofs. The chapter ends with the one rule that mathematicians have seriously argued about: reductio ad absurdum, the rule behind excluded middle, what analysis would lose without it, and where this book stands. What you need. Chapters 1–4. From Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for every connective, derivations with their boxes and scope rule (@def-derivation), derived rules (@def-derived-rule), the classical rules of Section 2.5 and their interderivability (@thm-classical-rules-interderivable), and the two running examples @thm-square-even-implies-even and @thm-sqrt2-irrational. From Chapter 3: induction (@ax-induction), the cut rule (@lem-weakening-cut), truth tables and refuting rows (@exm-backwards-from-f, @def-valid-argument, @cor-refuting-row), soundness (@thm-soundness), completeness and the proof of @lem-atom-splitting (@thm-completeness, @cor-derivable-iff-valid), and, for Section 5.7 only, the optional @thm-raa-independent. From Chapter 4: the quantifier rules and their side conditions (@def-rules-universal, @def-rules-existential), the bounded rules (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), definitions of analysis translated into formulas (Section 4.8), the laws for negating quantifiers (@prp-quantifier-negation), and the derivation that uniform continuity implies continuity together with the place where its converse breaks down (@exm-uniform-implies-continuous, @exm-converse-fails, and the counter-model @exm-square-not-uniform). School arithmetic and the order of \nR are used in examples as facts. Time. About 35 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - The connective rules in prose. The dictionary rows for the connectives and the classical rules, each with an analysis proof annotated phrase by phrase; the three faces of “proof by contradiction”; and the contradiction proofs that are direct or contrapositive proofs in costume. - The quantifier rules in prose. The rows for “for every”, “there exists”, equality and unique existence, and for induction, “it suffices to show” and “without loss of generality”; the dependency parenthesis; and the quantifiers that English leaves unwritten or puts in the wrong place. - Four levels of one proof. Full derivation, skeleton, annotated prose and plain prose; the convention that says which steps plain prose may leave silent; the irrationality of \sqrt 2 and “uniformly continuous implies continuous”, each written four times; and how to check a doubtful sentence by expanding it. - Reading a proof: self-explanation. The book’s training passage for the habit of naming, at each line, what makes it true; four questions to ask of every line; and five strategies that good readers apply to a proof as a whole. - Writing a proof. A seven-step procedure from the statement to plain prose, the conventions of written mathematics as rules made audible, and three worked examples: labeling a proof, turning a derivation into a paragraph, and writing a new proof from its goal. - Checking proofs, and what is not allowed. Two questions for every line, the catalogue (N1)–(N11) of errors with the rule each one breaks, and four student proofs checked line by line. - The dispute over excluded middle. Intuitionistic logic as the rules without reductio; why excluded middle cannot be refuted; what a proof provides under the BHK reading; an irrational power of an irrational number that is rational, with and without a witness; a short history; what analysis would lose; proofs as programs; and the book’s position. Named moves - Hear the rule in the phrase. “Let x \in A” opens a \rulename{\forall I} box and “suppose” an assumption; “choose” is \rulename{\exists E}; “take” and “let \delta \coloneqq \dots” are \rulename{\exists I}; “suppose, for contradiction” is \rulename{RAA} or \rulename{\neg I}; both boxes end in \bot, and what the box assumes and the line written after it closes tell which. - Expand to check. When a sentence is doubtful, rewrite that stretch, and only that stretch, as a skeleton, and look for the line that breaks a rule. - Skeleton first. Write the first and the last sentence of every box before filling any. - Self-explain each line by earlier lines, definitions and named results, and the rule that combines them; never by paraphrase. - Two columns when checking: is the line true? and does it follow, and by which rule? The first column finds where to look; the second decides. - Say what depends on what. Every chosen object carries its dependencies: the names in the line it comes from, among the boxes open when it was chosen.

title: 5.1 The Connective Rules in Prose
5.2 The Quantifier Rules in Prose
content:
The Quantifier Rules in Prose Section 5.1 read the connective rules in the sentences of written proofs. The statements of analysis, though, are made of “for every” and “there exists”, and most of the words in an analysis proof carry a quantifier rule: “let”, “fix”, “choose”, “take”, “will do”. This section completes the dictionary with the rows for the quantifiers, equality and unique existence, and for the three patterns that are not single rules but are written as if they were: induction, the lemma (“it suffices to show”), and symmetry (“without loss of generality”). It also makes exact one habit of analysis prose, the parenthesis “(depending on \varepsilon)”. Three sentences, three rules Section 4.8 derived “if a_n 	o L, then 2a_n 	o 2L” in sixteen lines. In a proof in Part I the same argument takes three sentences: Let \varepsilon > 0. Since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0, we may choose N \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N. Then for every n \ge N, \abs{2a_n - 2L} = 2\abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon. Each sentence opens a box, and the boxes are nested in the order of the sentences. - “Let \varepsilon > 0” opens the bounded ulename{ orall I} box of lines 2–15 in the derivation of Section 4.8, with the fresh name \varepsilon_0. Its closing line, line 16, is not written: the paragraph simply ends, and a reader who heard “let” knows that the box closes there. - “Choose N …” is two rules. The words “since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0” are the ulename{ orall E} of line 4, at the term \varepsilon_0/2, with its bound from line 3. The word “choose” opens the ulename{\exists E} box of lines 5–14, with the fresh name N_0. - “Then for every n \ge N” opens the ulename{ orall I} box of n_0 and the ulename{{	o}I} box of n_0 \ge N_0 (lines 7 and 9), and the computation is lines 8, 10 and 11. The words “for every n \ge N” also announce the lines that close these two boxes, 12 and 13. - The ulename{\exists I} of line 14, which writes “some N works” from “this N works”, and the closing line 15 of the ulename{\exists E} box, are silent. They are the end of the paragraph. The one word in the paragraph that no rule asks for is the parenthesis “(depending on \varepsilon)”. It is the subject of a subsection below. First, the rows. The quantifier rows --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Rule Phrases Silent in plain prose? ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------- ulename{ orall I} “let x \in A”; “fix \varepsilon > 0”; “let \varepsilon > 0 be given”; “since x was arbitrary” never the introduction; “since x was arbitrary” may be silent ulename{ orall E} “in particular, for x = \dots”; “applying … with \varepsilon/2 in place of \varepsilon” the instance must be named when it is not the obvious one ulename{\exists I} “take N = \dots”; “let \delta \coloneqq \dots; then …”; “… will do” never; its dependencies are stated ulename{\exists E} “choose N such that”; “by hypothesis there is k with n = 2k”; “let x_0 be such a point” never; the name must be fresh --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The phrases in the table are mostly the bounded forms of the rules (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules): “let x \in A” opens a ulename{ orall I} box whose assumption is x \in A, and “choose N \in 
N such that …” opens an ulename{\exists E} box with the two assumptions N \in 
N and “…”. A bound is part of the phrase: “let \varepsilon > 0” is one step, not “let \varepsilon” followed by “suppose \varepsilon > 0”. In analysis, ulename{ orall I} is the first sentence of every limit proof: “Let \varepsilon > 0.” ulename{ orall E} is “apply the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon/2”: the instance \varepsilon/2 is not the obvious one, so it is named. ulename{\exists I} is the line that places a constant, “let \delta \coloneqq \min\{1, \varepsilon/10\}”, written before the computation that shows it works. ulename{\exists E} is “choose N (depending on \varepsilon) such that …”, in which the name N has not been used before in the proof. [A constant sequence] Let c be a real number and let a_n \coloneqq c for every n \in 
N. Prove that a_n 	o c, and annotate each phrase with its rule. Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. Take N \coloneqq 0 [ulename{\exists I}]. Let n \in 
N with n \ge N [ulename{ orall I}, ulename{{	o}I}, opening]. Then \abs{a_n - c} = \abs{c - c} = 0 < \varepsilon , where the first equality substitutes a_n = c [ulename{{=}E}] and the last step uses \varepsilon > 0, the assumption of the first box. This proves a_n 	o c. The last sentence stands for three closing lines, all silent: the ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{ orall I} for n (“for every n \ge N”), and the ulename{ orall I} for \varepsilon (“since \varepsilon was arbitrary”). The witness “take N \coloneqq 0” is placed before the work that justifies it. Two things here are degenerate, and both are worth seeing once. The witness N depends on nothing: any N \in 
N works. And the assumption n \ge N is never used. The box is still opened, because the goal  orall n \in 
N\; (n \ge N 	o \dots) asks for it; without “let n \ge N”, the line “\abs{a_n - c} = 0” would not say which n it is about. The dependency parenthesis In the paragraph that opened this section, N was chosen “(depending on \varepsilon)”. Section 4.10 read off a derivation the rule behind the parenthesis: A constant chosen in a box may depend on the names of the boxes open around that box, and it does depend only on the names in the line it comes from. In the derivation of Section 4.8, the witness N_0 is obtained at line 5 from line 4, which mentions \varepsilon_0, inside the box of \varepsilon_0 only. So N_0 may depend on \varepsilon_0, and it does. In the derivation of @exm-uniform-implies-continuous, the witness \delta_0 is obtained inside the boxes of x_0 and \varepsilon_0, so it may depend on both; but it comes from a line that mentions \varepsilon_0 alone, so it does depend only on \varepsilon_0, and that is uniformity. The parenthesis is the prose record of this. “Choose N (depending on \varepsilon)” says: the boxes open here are those of \varepsilon (besides the data of the theorem, such as the sequence), and the line from which N comes mentions \varepsilon. “Choose \delta (depending on \varepsilon and on x)” says that \delta came from a line mentioning both, inside both boxes. A witness that came from a line mentioning neither is a constant, and the proof may say “(depending on neither)” or simply “a fixed \delta”. This is why proofs in analysis say what each chosen constant depends on. A missing parenthesis is not a wrong step, but it hides the one fact a reader most needs in order to check the quantifier order, and many false proofs in analysis go wrong exactly there. [The reciprocals tend to zero] Prove that 1/n 	o 0, for the sequence (1/n)_{n \ge 1}. Annotate each phrase with its rule, and state what the chosen constant depends on. The sequence starts at n = 1, so the definition of Section 4.8 is read with N and n in 
Z_{>0} instead of 
N: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
Z_{>0} such that \abs{1/n - 0} < \varepsilon for every n \in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N. We use one school fact about the real numbers: for every real number u there is an integer greater than u. (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it from the axioms of 
R.) Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. It suffices to find N \in 
Z_{>0} with  rac{1}{N} < \varepsilon , 	ag{$\ast$} since then every n \in 
Z_{>0} with n \ge N has 0 < 1/n \le 1/N < \varepsilon, so \abs{1/n - 0} < \varepsilon [cut: the claim (\ast) displayed, then used]. By the school fact, applied to u = 1/\varepsilon [ulename{ orall E}], there is an integer greater than 1/\varepsilon; choose such an integer N [ulename{\exists E}], which depends on \varepsilon. Since \varepsilon > 0, we have 1/\varepsilon > 0, so N > 0 and N \in 
Z_{>0}. From N > 1/\varepsilon > 0, taking reciprocals reverses the inequality: 1/N < \varepsilon, which is (\ast). So this N will do [ulename{\exists I}], and 1/n 	o 0. Read the proof as a skeleton. The first sentence opens the box of \varepsilon. The second is a cut, in the sense of the row below: it states a simpler claim (\ast), shows on the spot that (\ast) is enough, and leaves (\ast) to be proved. The next paragraph proves (\ast). It contains two different quantifier steps that both concern N: “choose” is the ulename{\exists E} on the school fact, which hands over some integer beyond 1/\varepsilon and calls it N; “will do” is the ulename{\exists I} that offers this N as the witness the definition asks for. Between them, the clause “so N > 0 and N \in 
Z_{>0}” checks the bound N \in 
Z_{>0} of the witness, which the bounded ulename{\exists I} needs as a line. The constant N depends on \varepsilon only: it came from the school fact at 1/\varepsilon, inside the box of \varepsilon. For instance, \varepsilon = 0.03 has 1/\varepsilon = 33.3\ldots, and N = 34 is a choice that works; so is any larger integer. “For every \varepsilon > 0, \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for all large n.” Where is the hidden \exists N, and between which two quantifiers does it stand? “For all large n” is “there is an N such that for every n \ge N” (Section 4.8): the hidden \exists N stands after  orall \varepsilon > 0 and before  orall n \ge N. Written out, the sentence is  orall \varepsilon > 0 \; \exists N \in 
N \;  orall n \in 
N \; (n \ge N 	o \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon), the definition of a_n 	o L. Since \exists N comes after  orall \varepsilon, the N may depend on \varepsilon. Equality and unique existence ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Rule Phrases Silent in plain prose? ---------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------ ulename{{=}I}, ulename{{=}E} “substituting”; chains “\dots = \dots = \dots”; “by (1)” yes, inside chains \exists! “there is exactly one”; “existence … uniqueness …”; “suppose y also …” never either half ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ In analysis, ulename{{=}E} is at work in every chain of equalities and inequalities, such as \abs{x^2 - 4} = \abs{x - 2}\, \abs{x + 2} \le 5 \abs{x - 2} \quad 	ext{for } \abs{x - 2} < 1 , where each = link substitutes equals for equals and each inequality link applies one fact about order (Section 4.7). (Here \abs{x - 2} < 1 gives 1 < x < 3, so 3 < x + 2 < 5.) The ulename{{=}I} lines t = t that such chains rest on are never written. Unique existence (@def-unique-existence) has two halves, which @prp-unique-existence-use separates: “2x + 3 = 7 has exactly one real solution: x = 2 is one, and if 2y + 3 = 7, then y = 2”. The first clause is existence, by ulename{\exists I}; the second is uniqueness, a ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I} box on a second candidate. Neither half implies the other, so neither may be silent. The uniqueness half often stands alone, when existence is not claimed or is proved elsewhere. Uniqueness of limits is a case of this kind. [A sequence has at most one limit] Let (a_n) be a sequence of real numbers with a_n 	o L and a_n 	o M. Prove that L = M, and annotate each phrase with its rule. Let \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, opening]. Then \varepsilon/2 > 0, so, applying the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon/2 in place of \varepsilon [ulename{ orall E}], we may choose N_1 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1 [ulename{\exists E}, fresh name N_1]. Likewise, from a_n 	o M, choose N_2 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2 [ulename{ orall E}, ulename{\exists E}, fresh name N_2]. Let n \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. Then n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2, so both bounds apply at n [ulename{ orall E} at n, twice, with ulename{{	o}E}], and  egin{aligned} \abs{L - M} &= \abs{(L - a_n) + (a_n - M)} \ &\le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{a_n - M} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon , \end{aligned} where the inequality is the triangle inequality of @exm-triangle-inequality-cases, with \abs{L - a_n} = \abs{a_n - L}. Since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, \abs{L - M} < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0 [ulename{ orall I}, closing], and @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal gives L = M [ulename{{	o}E}, citing it]. Four things in this proof are never silent, and each is visible. The instance \varepsilon/2 is named twice, because it is not the obvious instance. The two witnesses get two names, N_1 and N_2: the hypotheses promise a threshold for L and a threshold for M, and nothing says they are the same number, so calling both N would assert an equality nobody proved (Section 5.6 catalogues the error). The point n = \max\{N_1, N_2\} is named, since the bounds are applied at it. And the closing result is cited by name. What is silent is the bookkeeping of the two ulename{\exists E} boxes. The line \abs{L - M} < \varepsilon mentions neither N_1, N_2 nor n, so the side condition of ulename{\exists E} lets it leave both boxes, and then the box of \varepsilon closes on it. The calculation chain hides its ulename{{=}E} steps, as the row allows. The proof shows that a sequence has at most one limit: the uniqueness half of \exists!. Whether a given sequence has a limit at all is a separate question, which this proof does not touch. Induction, lemmas and symmetry The last three rows are not rules of the calculus. Each is a pattern of rules that proofs announce with a phrase of its own. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Pattern Phrases Silent in plain prose? -------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- induction (@ax-induction, @thm-strong-induction) “we argue by induction on n”; “base case”; “suppose the claim holds for n” never either the base case or the step; the induction hypothesis is stated cut, lemma (@lem-weakening-cut) “we first show (Claim)”; “it suffices to show”; “we claim” never the claim itself; “it suffices” may be dropped if the claim is displayed and then used symmetry “without loss of generality”; “similarly”; “by symmetry” allowed only when the swap turns the statement and the hypotheses into themselves, up to identities such as \abs{b - a} = \abs{a - b} ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- An induction is ulename{{	o}E} applied to @ax-induction, whose hypothesis is a conjunction: the base case P(0), and the step “for every n \in 
N, if P(n) then P(n + 1)”. So the step is a ulename{ orall I} box with a ulename{{	o}I} box inside it, and the phrase “suppose the claim holds for n” opens the inner box; its assumption is the induction hypothesis, and it must be stated, because the step uses it. A lemma is a cut: @lem-weakening-cut (b) says that once \varphi is derived, it may be used as a premise. “It suffices to show \varphi” is the same cut seen from the goal, as Section 1.4 observed: it promises a derivation of the goal from \varphi and leaves \varphi to be proved. In analysis, “it suffices to show \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for n \ge N” is the cut that reduces a limit to a single estimate; @exm-rhetoric-existential made one with the claim (\ast). Symmetry is a case split ulename{\vee E} whose second box is the first with two letters exchanged, up to identities such as \abs{b - a} = \abs{a - b}; “without loss of generality x \le y” writes the first box and leaves that check to the reader. [An induction, and a legitimate symmetry] (a) Let a be a real number with 0 < a \le 1. Prove that 0 < a^n \le 1 for every n \in 
N, and annotate each phrase with its rule. (b) Let a and b be real numbers. Prove that \abs{a - b} = \max\{a, b\} - \min\{a, b\}, with a “without loss of generality”, and write out the case split it abbreviates. (a) For n \in 
N, let P(n) be the statement “0 < a^n and a^n \le 1”. We argue by induction on n, using @ax-induction. Base case. a^0 = 1, and 0 < 1 and 1 \le 1, so P(0) holds [ulename{\wedge I}]. Step. Let n \in 
N [ulename{ orall I}, opening], and suppose P(n) holds, that is, 0 < a^n and a^n \le 1 [ulename{{	o}I}, opening: the induction hypothesis]. Then a^{n+1} = a^n a. Since a^n > 0 [ulename{\wedge E}] and a > 0, the product a^n a is positive, so 0 < a^{n+1}. Since a \le 1 and a^n > 0, multiplying gives a^n a \le a^n, and a^n \le 1 [ulename{\wedge E}], so a^{n+1} \le 1. Hence P(n + 1) holds [ulename{\wedge I}]. By induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N [\( ulename{{	o}E} \) on @ax-induction]. The base case is the first hypothesis of @ax-induction, written as its own paragraph. The step is the second: “let n \in 
N” and “suppose P(n) holds” open its two boxes, and “hence P(n + 1)” is the last line of the inner one; the closing lines “so P(n) 	o P(n + 1), for every n” are silent. The induction hypothesis is stated in full, and each of its halves is taken out by ulename{\wedge E} and used: a^n > 0 twice (for the sign of a^{n+1}, and to multiply a \le 1 by a^n without reversing it), and a^n \le 1 once, at the end. The statement was chosen with care: the tempting “a^n \le a” fails at n = 0 whenever a < 1, since a^0 = 1, and an induction for it would have to start at n = 1. (b) Without loss of generality, a \le b. Then \max\{a, b\} = b and \min\{a, b\} = a, and since b - a \ge 0, \abs{a - b} = \abs{b - a} = b - a = \max\{a, b\} - \min\{a, b\} . The phrase abbreviates a ulename{\vee E} on “a \le b or b \le a”, which holds for all real a, b by trichotomy. The first box is the paragraph above. The second box, on b \le a, reads: then \max\{a, b\} = a and \min\{a, b\} = b, and since a - b \ge 0, \abs{a - b} = a - b = \max\{a, b\} - \min\{a, b\}. That is the first box with a and b exchanged throughout, read through three identities: \abs{b - a} = \abs{a - b}, \max\{b, a\} = \max\{a, b\}, and \min\{b, a\} = \min\{a, b\}. These say that the statement is unchanged when a and b are exchanged, and there are no hypotheses to check. This is what makes the swap exact, and so what licenses “without loss of generality”. “Without loss of generality” needs a statement and hypotheses that are unchanged by the swap. Here is a false “proof” that \max\{a, b\} = b for all real a, b: “Without loss of generality a \le b; then \max\{a, b\} = b.” Exchanging a and b turns the claim into \max\{b, a\} = a, which is a different claim, so the second case is not the first one in disguise; and indeed a = 2, b = 1 gives \max\{a, b\} = 2 
e 1. Before writing “without loss of generality”, swap the letters in the statement and the hypotheses, and check that each comes back unchanged, up to identities such as \abs{b - a} = \abs{a - b}. What the sentence does not say Some quantifiers in mathematical English are not written at all, and some are written where they do not apply. Four habits of mathematical English cover most of them. The hidden universal closure. A theorem stated as “if n is even, then n^2 is even” means “for every integer n, if n is even, then n^2 is even”. Section 4.1 introduced this convention: a letter that is not introduced anywhere, in the statement of a theorem, is read with a “for every” in front of the whole statement. It applies to the statement of a theorem, lemma or exercise, not to a line inside a proof: inside a proof every letter has been introduced by a “let” or a “choose”, and its box tells the reader which. The proof of such a theorem begins by opening the hidden box: “let n be an integer”. “For all large n” hides an \exists N and a bound, as the Quick check above found. “Eventually” means the same. The negation of “P(n) for all large n” is “for every N there is an n \ge N for which P(n) fails”, usually said “P(n) fails for infinitely many n”. “Any” can mean “every” or “some”, and only the rest of the sentence decides (Section 4.1). “Any x \in A is positive” means every element of A is positive. “If any x \in A is positive, then A is non-empty” means: if some element of A is positive. When “any” appears, rewrite the sentence once with “every” and once with “some”, and keep the one that was meant. Quantifiers at the end of a sentence. English lets a writer put “for some x” or “for all y” after the formula they govern, and then the order of two such phrases is unclear. “x^2 > y for some x for all y”, over 
R, has two readings:  orall y\, \exists x\; (x^2 > y) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \exists x\,  orall y\; (x^2 > y) . The first is true (for y \ge 0 take x = y + 1, since (y + 1)^2 = y^2 + 2y + 1 > y; for y < 0 take x = 0). The second is false (whatever x is proposed, y = x^2 refutes it). The remedy is to write the quantifiers of such a statement in front, in the order in which they apply. A trailing phrase such as “for every n \ge N” is safe only when it is the last quantifier of the sentence, as in the definition of a_n 	o L. Moving “for all x” to the end of a sentence can change continuity into uniform continuity. “\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon whenever \abs{x - y} < \delta, for all x”, written after “for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that”, does not say whether  orall x comes before \exists \delta (continuity at every point) or after it (uniform continuity). The two formulas of Section 4.10 differ exactly there, and @exm-square-not-uniform shows that the difference is real: f(x) = x^2 on 
R satisfies the first and not the second. Write the quantifiers in front. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let (a_n) be a sequence of real numbers and L a real number. Here is a proof that if a_n 	o L and L > 0, then a_n > 0 for all large n. Its sentences are numbered. (1) Suppose a_n 	o L and L > 0. (2) Then L/2 > 0. (3) Choose N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < L/2 for every n \ge N. (4) Let n \in 
N with n \ge N. (5) Then L - a_n \le \abs{a_n - L} < L/2, so a_n > L/2 > 0. (6) Hence a_n > 0 for every n \ge N, that is, a_n > 0 for all large n. 1. Name the rule or rules carried by each sentence. 2. Sentence (3) has no dependency parenthesis. What should it say, and why does N not depend on n? 3. Which instance of ulename{ orall E} in the proof is not the obvious one? 4. Which closing lines are silent? (a) (1) ulename{{	o}I}, opening: the hypothesis of the theorem is assumed (its two conjuncts are then available by ulename{\wedge E}). (2) An arithmetic step from L > 0. (3) ulename{ orall E} on the definition of a_n 	o L at L/2, with its bound from (2), then ulename{\exists E}, opening a box with the fresh name N. (4) ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I}, opening the boxes of n and of n \ge N. (5) ulename{ orall E} at n and ulename{{	o}E} on the line from (3), giving \abs{a_n - L} < L/2; then the school fact -u \le \abs{u} with u = a_n - L, and arithmetic. (6) ulename{{	o}I} and ulename{ orall I}, closing (“for every n \ge N”), then ulename{\exists I} with the witness N (“for all large n” is \exists N\,  orall n \ge N), and the ulename{\exists E} box of (3) closes, since the conclusion does not mention N. (b) “Choose N \in 
N (depending on L) such that …”. N is obtained at line (3), from the definition instantiated at L/2, a term that mentions L (and the sequence, which is data). The box of n is opened only at (4), after N is chosen, so N cannot depend on n. (c) The instance \varepsilon = L/2 in (3). It is the instance the proof is built around: any \varepsilon with 0 < \varepsilon \le L would do, and L/2 leaves the margin a_n > L/2. (d) The closing lines of the ulename{\exists E} box (3) and of the ulename{{	o}I} box (1), “hence, if a_n 	o L and L > 0, then …”. Sentence (6) writes the closings of the boxes of (4) in words, and the ulename{\exists I} through “that is”. B. Practice [B1: Ambiguous English] Each sentence has a quantifier phrase at its end. Write both readings in symbols, with the quantifiers in front, and decide whether each reading is true for the function given. 1. “f(x) \le M for every real x, for some real M”, for f(x) = x. 2. “x + y = 0 for some real y, for every real x.” 3. “\abs{x - y} < \delta implies \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < 1 for all real x, y, for some \delta > 0”, for f(x) = x^2. (a) \exists M\,  orall x\; (f(x) \le M), “f is bounded above”, and  orall x\, \exists M\; (f(x) \le M). For f(x) = x the first is false: whatever M is proposed, x = M + 1 has f(x) = M + 1 > M. The second is true for every function: given x, take M = f(x). (b)  orall x\, \exists y\; (x + y = 0) and \exists y\,  orall x\; (x + y = 0). The first is true: given x, take y = -x. The second is false: for any y, the two values x = -y and x = 1 - y give x + y = 0 and x + y = 1, so not every x works. (c) \exists \delta > 0\;  orall x\,  orall y\; (\abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < 1) and  orall x\,  orall y\; \exists \delta > 0\; (\abs{x - y} < \delta 	o \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < 1). For f(x) = x^2 the first is false: it is the uniform continuity condition at \varepsilon = 1, and @exm-square-not-uniform refutes it with x = 1/\delta, y = 1/\delta + \delta/2, for which \abs{x - y} < \delta and \abs{x^2 - y^2} = 1 + \delta^2/4 \ge 1. The second is true for every function: given x and y, if x = y then \abs{f(x) - f(y)} = 0 < 1 for any \delta, say \delta = 1; if x 
e y, take \delta = \abs{x - y}, so that \abs{x - y} < \delta is false and the implication holds vacuously. In (a) and (c), the reading with \exists in front is the one a writer means; the other is true of every function, so it says nothing about f. In (b), the intended reading is  orall x\, \exists y. Written with the quantifiers in front, the sentences say what they mean: “there is M such that f(x) \le M for every x”, “for every x there is y with x + y = 0”, “there is \delta > 0 such that for all x, y, …”. [B2: An induction, annotated] Prove that 5^n - 1 is divisible by 4 for every n \in 
N. Annotate each phrase of your proof with its rule, and say which hypothesis of @ax-induction each part of the proof establishes. For n \in 
N, let P(n) be “4 \mid 5^n - 1”, that is, “there is an integer k with 5^n - 1 = 4k”. We argue by induction on n. Base case. 5^0 - 1 = 0 = 4 \cdot 0, so P(0) holds, with the witness k = 0 [ulename{\exists I}]. This is hypothesis (i) of @ax-induction. Step. Let n \in 
N [ulename{ orall I}, opening], and suppose P(n) holds [ulename{{	o}I}, opening: the induction hypothesis]. By the induction hypothesis there is an integer k with 5^n - 1 = 4k; choose such a k (depending on n) [ulename{\exists E}, fresh name k]. Then 5^{n+1} - 1 = 5 \cdot 5^n - 1 = 5(5^n - 1) + 4 = 5 \cdot 4k + 4 = 4(5k + 1) , where the third equality substitutes 5^n - 1 = 4k [ulename{{=}E}]. Since 5k + 1 is an integer, P(n + 1) holds, with the witness 5k + 1 [ulename{\exists I}]. The step is hypothesis (ii) of @ax-induction: the ulename{ orall I} on n and the ulename{{	o}I} on P(n). By induction, 4 \mid 5^n - 1 for every n \in 
N [\( ulename{{	o}E} \) on @ax-induction]. The ulename{\exists E} box of k closes on “P(n + 1)”, which does not mention k, as its side condition requires; its closing line, and those of the two boxes of the step, are silent. C. Going deeper [C1: When “similarly” is honest] 1. Prove that \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y for all real x and y, with a “without loss of generality”. Then write out the ulename{\vee E} it abbreviates, and check that its second box is the first with the letters exchanged. 2. Let x \ge 0 and y be real numbers. A student proves x \max\{x, y\} \ge xy as follows: “Without loss of generality x \le y. Then \max\{x, y\} = y, and xy \ge xy.” Explain why “without loss of generality” is not legitimate here, prove the case the student skipped, and show by an example that the hypothesis x \ge 0 cannot be dropped from the statement. [Hint 1] In (b), exchange x and y in the statement and in the hypothesis, and compare with the original. [Hint 2] In the case y \le x, \max\{x, y\} = x, and the claim becomes x^2 \ge xy. (a) Without loss of generality x \le y. Then \max\{x, y\} = y and \min\{x, y\} = x, so \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = y + x = x + y. The phrase abbreviates ulename{\vee E} on “x \le y or y \le x”, true for all real x, y by trichotomy. Box 1, on x \le y, is the paragraph above. Box 2, on y \le x: then \max\{x, y\} = x and \min\{x, y\} = y, so \max\{x, y\} + \min\{x, y\} = x + y. Exchanging x and y in box 1 gives “y \le x; \max\{y, x\} = x, \min\{y, x\} = y; \max\{y, x\} + \min\{y, x\} = x + y = y + x”, which is box 2 read through \max\{y, x\} = \max\{x, y\}, \min\{y, x\} = \min\{x, y\} and y + x = x + y. These identities say that the statement is unchanged by the exchange, and there are no hypotheses, so the swap is exact. (b) Exchanging x and y changes both the hypothesis and the claim: it gives “y \ge 0, and y \max\{y, x\} \ge yx”, which is not the original statement. So the case y \le x is not the case x \le y in disguise, and it needs its own argument. Case y \le x. Then \max\{x, y\} = x, and multiplying x \ge y by x \ge 0 gives x \max\{x, y\} = x^2 \ge xy. With the student’s case (x \le y: x \max\{x, y\} = xy \ge xy), this proves the claim in either case. The hypothesis x \ge 0 is used only in the skipped case. It cannot be dropped: x = -1, y = -2 has \max\{x, y\} = -1, so x \max\{x, y\} = 1, while xy = 2, and 1 \ge 2 is false. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) a correct computation in the case x \le y. - 3: (a) the ulename{\vee E} written out, with its disjunction justified, and the exchange checked against the statement. - 2: (b) the reason: the exchange changes the hypothesis and the claim. - 2: (b) the case y \le x proved, using x \ge 0. - 1: (b) a counterexample without x \ge 0, checked. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (b), “the other case is similar” without computing it; a counterexample that satisfies x \ge 0. [C2: Moving a quantifier changes the meaning] Give an example of a sentence of analysis, in English, that begins “for every x …”, whose meaning changes when the phrase “for every x” is moved to the end of the sentence. Write both readings in symbols and show that one is true and the other false. An example. “For every real x > 0, there is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x.” Moved: “There is n \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < x, for every real x > 0.” The readings are  orall x > 0\; \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\; (1/n < x) \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad \exists n \in 
Z_{>0}\;  orall x > 0\; (1/n < x) . The first is true: given x > 0, there is an integer n > 1/x (the school fact of @exm-rhetoric-existential), and n > 1/x > 0 gives n \in 
Z_{>0} and 1/n < x. The second is false: whatever n \in
