Z_{>0} is proposed, x = 1/n is positive and 1/n < x fails. (It is natural to read the moved sentence as the second formula, since its “for every x” now comes after “there is n”; whichever reading a reader picks, the sentence no longer says one thing.) What a different answer must have, so that it can be checked against this one: - the sentence contains “for every x” and at least one existential quantifier (“there is”, “for some”) whose scope contains a formula mentioning x; - moved to the end, “for every x” can be read as coming after the existential quantifier, so that the witness may no longer depend on x; - both readings are written in symbols with all quantifiers in front, and there is a specific interpretation (here 
R with its usual order) in which one reading is true and the other false, each claim checked; - the false reading is refuted by naming, for each candidate witness, a value of x that defeats it. Another correct answer, for f(x) = x^2 on 
R, is “for every x, for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon whenever \abs{x - y} < \delta” (continuity, true); with “for every x” moved to the end, it becomes the sentence of the warning, whose uniform-continuity reading @exm-square-not-uniform refutes.

title: 5.3 Four Levels of One Proof
5.4 Reading a Proof: Self-Explanation
content:
Reading a Proof: Self-Explanation Section 5.3 showed that a level-3 proof leaves steps unsaid by a fixed convention, and that any doubtful stretch can be expanded and checked. That presupposes a reader who notices the doubtful stretch. This section is about becoming that reader. It teaches one habit, self-explanation: for each line of a proof, say what makes it true. The habit is taught here once, on one short proof, and the rest of the book relies on it. When a later proof ends its Idea with “Before reading on: …” or “Self-explain lines 3–5”, this is the passage it means. Two readers of one proof Two people read the same proof, line by line, to the end. Both say they understood it. Asked afterwards whether it was correct, one can answer and point to the reason each line holds; the other can only repeat the proof in other words. What separates them is not intelligence or background. It is what each did at every line. The first asked, at each line, what makes this true? and answered by pointing: to earlier lines, to a definition, to a named result, and to the rule that combines them. The second asked what does this say? and answered by restating it. Only the first answer can come out wrong, and that is exactly why it is useful. A restatement always succeeds, so it tests nothing. To self-explain a line is to name its warrant: the earlier lines, definitions and results it comes from, and the rule that gets it from them. The answer has the shape of a justification column in a derivation. In the derivations of Chapters 1–4 that column was printed beside every line. In level-3 prose it is gone, and self-explanation is the reader writing it back in, at level 1 or 2 of @def-levels-of-proof, one line at a time. The training passage Here is a short proof. Read it once, then read the two explanations that follow. [Explaining a proof, well and badly] Claim. For every real number x > 0, x + 1/x \ge 2. Proof. Let x > 0. 1. (x - 1)^2 \ge 0. 2. So x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0. 3. Dividing by x, x - 2 + 1/x \ge 0. 4. Hence x + 1/x \ge 2. Self-explain each line of the proof. Explained well. - The opening. “Let x > 0” opens a box for an arbitrary x with the assumption x > 0: the claim is  orall x > 0 \; (x + 1/x \ge 2), and this is its bounded ulename{ orall I}. Everything below may use x > 0; so far nothing has. - Line 1 is an instance of the school fact that the square of every real number is at least 0, at the term x - 1 (a ulename{ orall E}). It uses no earlier line, and in particular not x > 0: it holds for every real x. - Line 2 follows from line 1 because (x - 1)^2 and x^2 - 2x + 1 are the same number, by expanding the square; one is replaced by the other (ulename{{=}E}). - Line 3 follows from line 2 by dividing both sides by x. Two things need x > 0 here. Dividing by x needs x 
e 0, and dividing both sides of an inequality by a number is guaranteed to keep its direction only when that number is positive. Both come from the assumption x > 0, and this is the only place in the proof where the assumption is used. The left side becomes (x^2 - 2x + 1)/x = x - 2 + 1/x, and the right side 0/x = 0. - Line 4 follows from line 3 by adding 2 to both sides, which keeps any inequality. It is the claim for this x; since x was arbitrary, the claim holds for every x > 0 (the closing ulename{ orall I}, silent in the proof as written). Explained badly. - Line 1: we start with a square, which is positive. - Line 2: multiply it out. - Line 3: now we divide by x and it still works. - Line 4: rearranging gives the answer. Both explanations follow the order of the proof, and the second is not even wrong everywhere; it is shorter, and every sentence after the first describes what happened (the first we return to below). But compare what each one did with line 3. The first says why the inequality survives the division, and in saying it, finds the one place where the hypothesis x > 0 earns its keep. The second says “it still works”, which is a description of the outcome, not a reason. The difference shows as soon as the proof is wrong. Change the claim to “for every real x 
e 0, x + 1/x \ge 2”, and keep all four lines. The bad explanation reads the new proof exactly as happily as the old one: we start with a square, multiply out, divide by x and it still works, rearrange. The good explanation stops at line 3. It needs “the inequality keeps its direction because x > 0”, and the hypothesis now says only x 
e 0; for negative x, division by x reverses the inequality, and line 3 does not follow. The claim is in fact false: at x = -1, x + 1/x = -2 < 2. A reader who explains warrants finds the gap; a reader who paraphrases cannot, because a paraphrase of a wrong step reads exactly like a paraphrase of a right one. The bad explanation also slipped in its first line. A square is not always positive, only at least 0: (x - 1)^2 = 0 at x = 1, where the claim holds with equality. Restating invites such slips, because nothing is being checked. Explaining a warrant forces the exact fact, “every square is at least 0”, because the explanation has to cite it. So the first kind of reading does three things the second does not. It checks each step, since a warrant can fail to exist. It locates the hypotheses, since every use of a hypothesis is a warrant. And it prepares the reader to reuse the proof, since the warrants, not the restatements, are what transfer to the next problem. How to explain a line For each line, ask four questions, in this order. 1. What kind of line is it? An assumption that opens a box (“let”, “suppose”, “choose … such that”), a line derived from earlier ones, or the closing of a box (“hence”, “so”, “since x was arbitrary”). 2. Where does it come from? Name the earlier lines, the definitions and the results it uses. “Line 2”, “the definition of even”, “@thm-square-even-implies-even”, “the hypothesis x > 0”. A result is named, not paraphrased. 3. By which step? A rule of Chapters 1–4, or a piece of arithmetic that you can say in one clause (“divide both sides by x”, “expand the square”). 4. Is it legitimate here? Is every cited line still available, inside the boxes that are open (@def-derivation)? Is a chosen name fresh? Does a division have a non-zero divisor, and does an inequality keep its direction? You do not need to write out a derivation; a phrase per line is enough, at the level of the “explained well” column above. When you cannot answer one of the four questions, you have found what to look at: either a step you do not yet understand, or a gap in the proof. Section 5.3 says what to do next: expand that stretch to level 1. Self-explanation is not re-reading, and not summarizing. Reading a proof twice more makes it familiar, not checked: familiarity is what makes the bad explanation of @exm-self-explanation feel adequate. A summary (“the proof expands a square and divides by x”) is useful afterwards, but it skips exactly the warrants that matter, such as why the division by x is allowed and keeps the inequality’s direction. Self-explanation is local and backward-looking: each line, against what came before it. Here is a six-line proof that for real numbers x and y, if x + y > 2, then x > 1 or y > 1. 1. We prove the contrapositive: if it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1, then x + y > 2 fails. 2. Suppose it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1. 3. Then x \le 1 and y \le 1. 4. Adding these, x + y \le 2. 5. So x + y > 2 fails. 6. This proves the contrapositive, and hence the claim. Self-explain lines 2–4. Line 2 is an assumption: it opens the ulename{{	o}I} box for the contrapositive announced in line 1, whose hypothesis is 
eg(x > 1 \vee y > 1). Line 3 comes from line 2 in two steps. First @prp-de-morgan (a), 
eg(P \vee Q) \vdash 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q, gives “not x > 1, and not y > 1”. Then the order fact that 
eg(u > 1) means u \le 1, for every real u, turns each conjunct into the form written. Line 4 uses both conjuncts of line 3 (ulename{\wedge E}, twice) and the order fact that inequalities may be added: x \le 1 and y \le 1 give x + y \le 1 + y \le 1 + 1 = 2. (For the record: line 5 is the order fact x + y \le 2 means 
eg(x + y > 2); line 6 closes the box by ulename{{	o}I} and then passes from the contrapositive to the claim by @prp-contrapositive-converse, a classical step.) Strategies of good readers Self-explanation is the habit for single lines. Readers who are good at proofs also do a few things with a proof as a whole. Here are five, shown on one short proof. Claim. For real numbers x > 0 and y > 0, \sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2. Proof. Let x > 0 and y > 0. Since x = (\sqrt x)^2, y = (\sqrt y)^2 and \sqrt{xy} = \sqrt x \, \sqrt y, x + y - 2\sqrt{xy} = (\sqrt x - \sqrt y)^2 \ge 0 . Hence 2\sqrt{xy} \le x + y, and dividing by 2 gives the claim. 1. Try it first. Before reading the proof, spend a few minutes on the claim yourself. A natural attempt squares both sides: xy \le (x + y)^2/4 is 4xy \le x^2 + 2xy + y^2, that is, 0 \le (x - y)^2, which is true. Already you know what the difficulty is (the square root) and what your attempt rests on (that a square is at least 0). 2. Identify the framework. Find the skeleton, level 1 of @def-levels-of-proof. Here: a bounded ulename{ orall I} on x and y (opened by “Let”, closed silently) with the bounds x > 0, y > 0, then a direct chain. There is no case split, no contradiction, and no chosen witness. Knowing that tells you where to look: every line is a computation, so every warrant is an algebraic fact. 3. Break it into sub-proofs. The proof has one claim inside it, the displayed identity, and then a short finish. A claim inside a proof is a cut (the cut row of Section 5.2’s dictionary): it is proved once and then used. Here the claim is proved inside the box on x and y, so it is simply a line that later lines of the box may cite (@def-derivation); @lem-weakening-cut (b) is the same move for sequents proved outside every box. Read the claim on its own: it needs \sqrt{xy} = \sqrt x \sqrt y (true for x, y \ge 0) and (\sqrt x)^2 = x. 4. Illustrate a hard line with an example. If the identity is not clear, try numbers. With x = 1 and y = 4: the left side is 1 + 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 1, the right side (1 - 2)^2 = 1. An example checks nothing in general, but it shows what the line claims. 5. Compare with your own attempt. Your squaring route proves the claim too, and it hides a warrant the given proof avoids: passing back from xy \le (x + y)^2/4 to \sqrt{xy} \le (x + y)/2 uses the converse of “squaring preserves order”: from a^2 \le b^2 conclude a \le b. This holds when b \ge 0, because then \abs{a} \le b; here b = (x + y)/2 > 0. Without that hypothesis it fails: a = 1, b = -2. Comparing the two routes shows why the given proof introduces \sqrt x and \sqrt y: it never has to undo a squaring. The comparison also links this claim to @exm-self-explanation: put y = 1/x, and \sqrt{xy} = 1, so the claim becomes x + 1/x \ge 2. The five strategies work at the level of the whole proof and self-explanation at the level of the line, and they support each other. Trying first tells you which line will be the hard one; the framework tells you which boxes are open at each line, which is what the fourth question of self-explanation needs. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Here is a proof that if a > 0, b > 0 and a^2 = b^2, then a = b. (1) a^2 - b^2 = 0. (2) (a - b)(a + b) = 0. (3) a + b > 0. (4) Hence a - b = 0, that is, a = b. Classify each explanation as one that justifies its line or one that paraphrases it. 1. “Line 1 follows from the hypothesis a^2 = b^2 by subtracting b^2 from both sides.” 2. “Line 2: then the factored form is zero as well.” 3. “Line 2 is line 1 rewritten with the identity u^2 - v^2 = (u - v)(u + v), at u = a and v = b.” 4. “Line 3: now we know that a + b is positive.” 5. “Line 3 holds because a > 0 and b > 0 are hypotheses, and a sum of two positive numbers is positive.” 6. “Line 4: so a - b is zero, which is what we wanted.” (a) Justifies: it names the source (the hypothesis) and the step (subtracting b^2). (b) Paraphrases: “is zero as well” restates line 2 without saying why the product equals the left side of line 1. (c) Justifies: it names the identity and the instance. (d) Paraphrases: it restates line 3 and gives no reason. (e) Justifies: it names both hypotheses and the fact that combines them. (f) Paraphrases: it gives no warrant. A justification would say: by line 2 a product is zero, so one of its factors is zero; line 3 says the factor a + b is not zero, being positive; so a - b = 0 (@prp-disjunctive-syllogism, applied to “a + b = 0 or a - b = 0” and a + b 
e 0). B. Practice [B1: Self-explain a counterexample] Here, with its lines numbered, is the half of @exm-square-not-uniform that shows f(x) = x^2 is not uniformly continuous on 
R. (1) By the negation of uniform continuity, with the bounds x \in 
R and y \in 
R dropped because they always hold, we must show \exists \varepsilon > 0 \;  orall \delta > 0 \; \exists x \; \exists y \;  igl( \abs{x - y} < \delta \wedge \abs{x^2 - y^2} \ge \varepsilon  igr). (2) Take \varepsilon = 1. (3) Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and take x \coloneqq 1/\delta and y \coloneqq 1/\delta + \delta/2, which depend on \delta. (4) Then \abs{x - y} = \delta/2 < \delta, (5) and, since y > x > 0, \abs{x^2 - y^2} = (y - x)(y + x) =  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigl(  rac{2}{\delta} +  rac{\delta}{2} \Bigr) = 1 +  rac{\delta^2}{4} \ge 1 . (3) Since \delta was arbitrary, uniform continuity fails. Self-explain each line, citing labels where a line uses an earlier result. Say at which lines \delta > 0 is used. (1) A cut: the goal “f is not uniformly continuous” is replaced by the displayed formula, and the proof then proves the formula. The formula is the positive form of the negation of uniform continuity, @exm-negating-definitions (c), read with A = 
R; there the two are shown interderivable, by @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @prp-negated-implication and the order fact 
eg(u < \varepsilon) iff u \ge \varepsilon. The direction used here is from the displayed formula to the negation. The bounds can be dropped because a bounded quantifier \exists x \in 
R abbreviates \exists x\, (x \in 
R \wedge \dots) (@def-bounded-quantifier), and over the domain 
R the conjunct x \in 
R always holds. (2) The witness for \exists \varepsilon > 0: a bounded ulename{\exists I} at the term 1, with its bound 1 > 0. It is written first, but as a rule it is applied last: the instance it needs, the formula after \exists \varepsilon > 0 with 1 for \varepsilon, is what lines (3)–(6) prove. (3) “Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary” opens a bounded ulename{ orall I} box flagged \delta_0 with the assumption \delta_0 > 0. As in Section 4.4, the prose uses the letter \delta both for the flag and for the bound variable; below, \delta in the arithmetic is the flag \delta_0. The terms 1/\delta and 1/\delta + \delta/2 are the witnesses for \exists x and \exists y (two ulename{\exists I}, applied at the end of the box). They may mention \delta because \delta’s box is open; the clause “which depend on \delta” records this. The term 1/\delta exists because \delta 
e 0, from \delta > 0. (4) Arithmetic: y - x = \delta/2, which is positive since \delta > 0, so \abs{x - y} = \delta/2; and \delta/2 < \delta since \delta > 0. This is the first conjunct. (5) Arithmetic. Since \delta > 0, x = 1/\delta > 0 and y = x + \delta/2 > x. Then x^2 < y^2, so \abs{x^2 - y^2} = y^2 - x^2 = (y - x)(y + x), with y - x = \delta/2 and y + x = 2/\delta + \delta/2; multiplying out gives 1 + \delta^2/4, which is at least 1 because \delta^2/4 \ge 0. This is the second conjunct; with (4) it gives the conjunction (ulename{\wedge I}), and the two ulename{\exists I} of (3) then give \exists x\, \exists y\, (\dots). (6) The closing line of the bounded ulename{ orall I} box flagged \delta_0 (@prp-bounded-quantifier-rules). The side condition holds: the proof has no premises; the only assumption mentioning \delta_0 is \delta_0 > 0, the assumption of the box this line closes, and no outer box is open; and \delta_0 does not appear in the conclusion  orall \delta > 0\, \exists x\, \exists y\, (\dots), whose \delta is a bound variable different from the flag. With (2) this proves the displayed formula, and by the cut (1) uniform continuity fails. \delta > 0 is used in (3) (so that 1/\delta exists), in (4) (twice) and in (5) (for y > x > 0). [B2: The unjustified line] Here is a proof that for real numbers x < y, x^3 < y^3. (1) Let x < y. (2) Then y^3 - x^3 = (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2). (3) Since x < y, y - x > 0. (4) Also y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0. (5) So y^3 - x^3 > 0, as a product of two positive numbers. (6) Hence x^3 < y^3. Every line is true. Line 1 opens the box; of the rest, all but one are instances of a routine algebra or order fact, cited or not; one line is not an instance of any fact stated so far, and it needs an argument of its own. Self-explain the proof line by line to find it, and supply that argument as its warrant. Line 1 opens the box, with the assumption x < y. Line 2 is the identity (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2) = y^3 - x^3, checked by multiplying out. Line 3 cites line 1 and the order fact u < v iff v - u > 0. Line 5 cites lines 2, 3 and 4 and the fact that a product of two positive numbers is positive. Line 6 is line 5 rearranged by the same order fact. Line 4 is the one without a warrant: it cites nothing, and it is not an instance of any fact stated so far. It is not obvious either, since xy can be negative. A warrant: complete the square, y^2 + xy + x^2 = \Bigl( y +  rac{x}{2} \Bigr)^2 +  rac{3x^2}{4} \ge 0 , with equality only if x = 0 and y + x/2 = 0, that is, only if x = y = 0. Line 1 rules that out, since x < y gives x 
e y. So y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0. The repaired line 4 uses the hypothesis x < y a second time, which the proof as printed hides; a reader who explains only “the bracket is positive” has paraphrased line 4 and missed this. C. Going deeper [C1: A longer proof] Self-explain the proof of @lem-atom-splitting in Section 3.6: for each of its five numbered steps, and for each claim in the paragraph that follows them, say what it uses and why that is legitimate. Then state the idea of the proof in two sentences. [Hint 1] Keep @def-derivation open beside you: the paragraph after the five steps checks, in turn, the premises, the scope rule for the transplanted citations, the rule schemas, the last line of each box, and the availability of what the last line cites. [Hint 2] Start with step 2. Which result supplies p \vee 
eg p, what is substituted for its letter, and why may that line cite nothing? Step 1. The premises of the new list are the members of \Delta that D or E uses. Clause (D1) of @def-derivation places premises first, above every box, and puts no restriction on which statements they are. The conclusion will be \Delta \vdash \psi, so only members of \Delta are taken. The premises p, 
eg p of D and E are therefore left out, unless they also belong to \Delta, which does no harm. Step 2. The line p \vee 
eg p is @prp-excluded-middle with the atom p for the letter P, used as a derived rule (@def-derived-rule) with no premises, so it cites nothing. This is the one classical step, through ulename{LEM}. Step 3. The box opened by p contains the non-premise lines of D with their own boxes; every citation of the premise p is redirected to the assumption, and every citation of a premise in \Delta to the premise line of step 1. The two degenerate cases (the last line of D is a premise) are handled separately so that the box still ends in \psi, by repetition (ulename{R}, clause (D3)) where needed. Step 4. The same, for E with the assumption 
eg p. Step 5. The last line \psi is ulename{\vee E} (@def-rules-disjunction), citing the disjunction of step 2 and the two boxes, each opened by one disjunct and ending in \psi. The verification paragraph. It checks that the list is a derivation. (i) Premises are first and in no box, so they are available everywhere. (ii) Inside each new box, a line of D cites the same lines and boxes as before, renumbered, or a premise line, or the assumption, and each of those is available by the scope rule of @def-derivation: the old boxes have simply been placed inside one new box, which contains both the citing line and the cited one. (iii) Each line is still an instance of its rule’s schema, since its statement and the statements it cites are unchanged, as in the proof of @lem-weakening-cut. (iv) The last line of each new box is \psi, as a line of that box itself, which ulename{\vee E} requires. (v) The disjunction and the two boxes are available at the last line, which lies in no box. So the last line is a correct ulename{\vee E}, and \Delta \vdash \psi. The idea in two sentences. The lemma is proof by cases on p \vee 
eg p: excluded middle supplies the disjunction, and the two given derivations, with their premise p or 
eg p turned into the assumption of a box, are the two cases of ulename{\vee E}. All the work is in checking that the transplanted lines still cite only available lines. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: step 2 explained: @prp-excluded-middle as a derived rule at the atom p, citing nothing, and identified as the classical step. - 2: steps 3 and 4 explained: the redirection of citations of p (or 
eg p) to the assumption and of members of \Delta to the premise lines, and the degenerate cases. - 1: step 5 named as ulename{\vee E} with its three citations. - 3: the verification paragraph explained against @def-derivation: availability by the scope rule, schemas unchanged, each box ending in \psi as its own line. - 2: an idea in two sentences that names both the case split on p \vee 
eg p and the transplanting of D and E into the two boxes. Fatal errors (0 for the step): explanations that restate the steps without naming what they use; calling the case split ulename{
eg I} or ulename{RAA}.

title: 5.5 Writing a Proof
content:
Writing a Proof Section 5.4 trained a reader to say what licenses each line of a proof, as @exm-self-explanation did line by line. This section turns to the writer. A proof is written for a reader who will check it in exactly that way, so the writer’s job is to make each line’s warrant visible. The section gives a procedure that leads from a statement to plain prose, the conventions of written mathematics, each a rule of Chapters 1–4 made audible, and three worked examples. A procedure A reader checks a proof forwards, one line at a time. A writer finds a proof mostly backwards, from the goal. The two directions are not in conflict: Section 2.6 showed that the search for a derivation is goal-directed, and @def-derivation says that the derivation found is a list in which each line cites only lines above it. The procedure below keeps both, the search in scratch work and the derivation on the page. Its steps 3 and 6 use the levels of @def-levels-of-proof and the convention of @def-silent-steps from Section 5.3. Writing a proof of a statement. 1. Write the goal in symbols. Translate the statement, its hypotheses and its conclusion into a formula, as in Section 4.8, with every quantifier and its bound. Read a letter that is not introduced as universally quantified (Section 4.1). 2. Unwind the definitions. Replace each defined word (“bounded”, “converges”, “irrational”, “\subseteq”) by its definition, in the hypotheses and in the goal. This is ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} on a definition. 3. Read the skeleton off the goal (Section 2.6, extended in Section 4.8), and write it at level 1: the boxes, their first lines and their last lines. Open the ulename{\exists E} boxes of existential hypotheses early. 4. Fill the boxes: backwards in scratch, forwards on the page. The search runs from the goal; the written proof runs from the hypotheses, each line citing lines above it. What the search found goes into the Idea, not into the Proof. 5. Choose constants last in the search, and write them first on the page, each with what it depends on. 6. Write level 3, leaving silent exactly the steps that @def-silent-steps allows, and no others. 7. Reread as a checker: for each line, is it true, and by which rule does it follow from which available lines? (Section 5.6 makes this a two-column check.) Steps 1–3 involve no mathematics, only logical form, and they fix the first and last sentence of every box before anything is invented (“skeleton first”). Steps 4 and 5 need a remark each. Step 4 as a logical fact. The search of Section 2.6 opens a box for the goal before it knows how the box will be filled, and it postpones an existential goal until a witness appears; that is why it works backwards. But a derivation is a list in which line k cites only lines available at k (@def-derivation), and a written proof is that list in sentences. So the order of the page is forced by the rules, not by taste: “\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon holds if \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2” points from a later line to an earlier one. The backward reasoning lives in the Idea block. Step 5 as a logical fact. A chosen constant, such as “let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/2”, is the witness of an ulename{\exists I} line. The search finds it last, because only the end of the search shows what it must do. On the page it comes first, right after the names it is built from, because later lines use it. Those names are its dependencies; they must be among the names of the boxes open where it is chosen (Section 4.10). Which step of the procedure produces the sentence “Let \varepsilon > 0” at the start of a proof that a_n 	o L, and which step keeps it at level 3? Step 3. Unwound in step 2, the goal begins  orall \varepsilon > 0, so its skeleton is a bounded ulename{ orall I} box whose assumption is \varepsilon_0 > 0; “Let \varepsilon > 0” is the first line of that box. Step 6 keeps it, because the opening of a ulename{ orall I} box is never silent (@def-silent-steps). The closing “since \varepsilon was arbitrary” may be silent. Conventions of written mathematics A handful of conventions make a proof checkable. Each is a rule of Chapters 1–4 heard in a sentence. - Announce the skeleton. “We prove the contrapositive”, “by induction on n”, “we consider two cases”, “suppose, for a contradiction, that …”. An announcement tells the reader which box is opening, and so what its last line must be. - Name every object when it is introduced, by “let” (an arbitrary object, ulename{ orall I}), “choose” (a witness, ulename{\exists E}, with a fresh name), or “let … \coloneqq …” (a constant, the witness of ulename{\exists I}), and say what a chosen object depends on. - One claim per sentence. A sentence carries one line, or a short chain of lines joined by “so”, each step of which the reader can name. Two unrelated claims joined by “and” hide which one is used later. - End with what was shown. The last sentence of a proof is the last line of the derivation, outside every box. If it is not the statement to be proved, the reader should be told how the two are related. - Label displayed claims that will be cited, (\ast) or (1), and cite them by the label. A citation is a line number in prose. None of these is a matter of style. An object used without being introduced is a line citing nothing, and an announcement that does not match its box (assuming the conclusion of an implication) proves the converse; these are entries (N9) and (N5) of the catalogue in Section 5.6. Matching sentences and rules The first two examples go in opposite directions. [Label every sentence] Here is a short proof. Label each sentence with the rule it uses. Claim. For a real number x, if \abs{x - 1} < 1, then x > 0. Proof. (1) Assume \abs{x - 1} < 1. (2) Either x \ge 1 or x < 1. (3) Suppose first that x \ge 1. (4) Then x \ge 1 > 0. (5) Suppose instead that x < 1. (6) Then x - 1 < 0, so \abs{x - 1} = 1 - x. (7) Hence 1 - x < 1, that is, x > 0. (8) In either case x > 0, which proves the claim. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence What it does Rule ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) opens a box with the hypothesis assumption for ulename{{	o}I} (2) states a fact about real numbers a school fact, entered as a line (3) opens the first case box assumption for ulename{\vee E} (4) x \ge 1 and 1 > 0 give x > 0 ulename{{	o}E}, with the fact “a \ge b and b > c imply a > c” (5) opens the second case box assumption for ulename{\vee E} (6) computes \abs{x - 1} ulename{{	o}E} twice, with the facts “x < 1 implies x - 1 < 0” and “a < 0 implies \abs{a} = -a” (7) uses the assumption of (1) ulename{{=}E}, putting (6) into (1), then ulename{{	o}E} with “1 - x < 1 implies x > 0” (8) combines the cases, then closes the outer box ulename{\vee E} on (2), (3)–(4), (5)–(7); then ulename{{	o}I} on (1)–(8) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence (7) uses the assumption made in (1), and it may: that box is still open. The facts of school algebra enter as implications, each used by ulename{{	o}E}. Sentence (8) closes two boxes, which is normal. Measured against @def-silent-steps, the proof leaves out nothing that must be written: the split in (2) is on the page, and the disjunction it splits is a school fact (every real number is at least 1 or below it), so it covers every case; each case box opens with its assumption; and every step it leaves unwritten is of a kind that may be silent, for instance the ulename{ orall E} instances of the school facts at the obvious terms, the conclusion x > 0 of case 1, which is left to the chain x \ge 1 > 0 of (4), the ulename{\wedge I} behind (4), whose conjuncts are displayed, the ulename{{=}E} of (7), and the closing of the ulename{{	o}I} box, for which “which proves the claim” stands. Labeling also shows where the work is. The case split exists only because \abs{\cdot} is defined by cases (Chapter 1); the school fact -\abs{u} \le u, used with u = x - 1, gives -1 < x - 1 in one step, and a proof written that way would have no ulename{\vee E} at all. The second direction starts from a derivation whose premises are facts about integers. [From a derivation to a paragraph] Let n be an integer. Write E for “n is even”, O for “n is odd”, F for “n + 1 is even”, and G for “n(n + 1) is even”. The derivation below uses four facts about integers as premises. Write the paragraph a mathematician would write for it. Every integer is even or odd, so we consider two cases. If n is even, then n(n + 1) has an even factor, and so it is even. If n is odd, then n + 1 is even, since an odd number plus one is even; so again n(n + 1) has an even factor and is even. In either case n(n + 1) is even. Compare the two. The paragraph keeps one sentence for each box and each rule that matters: line 1 becomes “we consider two cases”, with its reason; the two boxes become the two “if” sentences; line 10 becomes “in either case”. It drops the line numbers and the rule names, and it merges the two ulename{{	o}E} steps of lines 8 and 9 into one sentence joined by “so”. It never skips a box: the reader still sees both cases and sees them combined. By @def-silent-steps, the closing “in either case …” could be dropped at level 3; the split of line 1, with the reason it covers every integer, could not. The paragraph leaves the premises unproved. Premises 2–4 are one line of algebra each (for instance, n = 2k gives n(n + 1) = 2 igl(k(n + 1) igr)), and a careful write-up includes them; premise 1, that every integer is even or odd, is not, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 2 proves it. From the goal to prose The third example runs all seven steps on a statement not seen before. Sets of reals are used here as Chapter 4 used them, with “a \in A” a one-place predicate and A \subseteq B read as “every element of A is an element of B”; Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1 develops sets properly. [A subset of a bounded set] Let A and B be sets of real numbers with A \subseteq B. Prove that if B is bounded above, then A is bounded above. Steps 1 and 2: the goal in symbols, unwound. Over the domain 
R, “B is bounded above” is \exists M \;  orall b \in B \; (b \le M) (Section 4.8), and A \subseteq B is  orall x \in A \; (x \in B). The statement is an implication, so the derivation below is the inside of a ulename{{	o}I} box: its assumption is the first formula (line 2), the hypothesis is the second, and its goal is \exists M \;  orall a \in A \; (a \le M). Step 3: the skeleton. The goal is an existential, so it is postponed: no witness is in sight yet. The assumption “B is bounded above” (line 2) is an existential, so its ulename{\exists E} box opens at once, with a fresh name M_0 and the assumption  orall b \in B \; (b \le M_0); the box’s last line is the goal. Step 4: filling the box. Backwards: the goal needs a witness M and a proof of  orall a \in A \; (a \le M). The only bound in sight is M_0, so try it. Then the new goal is a bounded universal: a box “let a_0 \in A” whose last line is a_0 \le M_0. That line comes from the bound on B, instantiated at a_0, which needs a_0 \in B; and a_0 \in B comes from A \subseteq B instantiated at a_0. Forwards, the same lines in the order of the list are the derivation below (with the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules; each bounded ulename{ orall E} abbreviates a ulename{ orall E} and a ulename{{	o}E}, and the bounded ulename{ orall I} box a ulename{ orall I} box with a ulename{{	o}I} box inside). The side conditions hold: a_0 appears in neither line 1 nor line 2, not in line 7 and not in the open assumption on line 3; M_0 appears in none of lines 1, 2 and 9. Step 5: the constant. The witness for the goal is the bound M_0. The search could choose it only once the ulename{\exists E} box supplied M_0, and confirm it only at line 6; the page writes it first, in the sentence that chooses it. It depends on B only: its box is opened before the box of a_0, so it cannot depend on a_0, and it must not, because a single bound has to serve every element of A. Step 6: level 3. Suppose B is bounded above, and choose an upper bound M of B (depending on B only). Let a \in A. Since A \subseteq B, we have a \in B, and so a \le M. Hence M is an upper bound of A, and A is bounded above. The two instances of ulename{ orall E} (lines 5 and 6) are at the obvious term a, and each appears only as the citation that licenses it (“since A \subseteq B”, “so”, which cites the choice of M). The closing of the ulename{ orall I} box, “since a was arbitrary”, is silent. Two steps that are never silent are on the page: the ulename{\exists E} with its fresh name (“choose an upper bound M”), and the ulename{\exists I} with its witness and dependence (“M is an upper bound of A”; “depending on B only”). “Suppose B is bounded above” opens the ulename{{	o}I} box; its closing is silent. Step 7: reread. The order of the first two sentences matters. With “let a \in A” first and M chosen inside, the ulename{\exists I} would fall inside the box of a_0, giving only  orall a \in A \; \exists M \; (a \le M), which says nothing. The example used A \subseteq B once, at line 5, and “B is bounded above” once, at line 9, by ulename{\exists E}, whose box assumption is used at line 6. The two warnings below concern steps 4 and 5. The search is not the proof. A page that reads “we want x^2 < 4; this holds if x < 2; so let x < 2” has copied the search, and each “holds if” points backwards. A backward step can be false, and the page hides it: “x < 2 implies x^2 < 4” fails at x = -3. In scratch work every backward step must be checked as an implication pointing forwards; on the page only the forward chain appears, each line citing lines above it. A constant without its dependencies is a claim nobody can check. In a proof that x^2 is uniformly continuous on 
R, the sentence “let \delta \coloneqq \min\{1, \varepsilon/(2\abs{x} + 1)\}” looks innocent. Asked “what does \delta depend on?”, the formula answers: on \varepsilon and on x, so the \delta was chosen inside the box of x, and the proof shows only continuity at every point. Uniform continuity is false here (@exm-square-not-uniform). Writing “(depending on \varepsilon only)” after the constant is what lets a reader catch the error. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Here is a proof. Claim. For real numbers x and y, if x + y > 2, then x > 1 or y > 1. (1) Assume x + y > 2. (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that it is not the case that x > 1 or y > 1. (3) Then x > 1 fails and y > 1 fails. (4) So x \le 1 and y \le 1. (5) Adding, x + y \le 2. (6) This contradicts x + y > 2. (7) Hence x > 1 or y > 1, which proves the claim. 1. Label each sentence with the rule it uses, as in @exm-annotate-abs. 2. Which sentence closes an ulename{RAA} box, and which uses one of De Morgan’s laws (@prp-de-morgan)? Which law? 3. Everything inside the box of (2) follows from (2) alone, until the clash in (6). Which face of “by contradiction” (Section 5.1) does the proof wear, and which face is it really? Write the first sentence of the rewritten proof. 4. Sentence (7) closes two boxes. Which of the two closings may be silent at level 3, by @def-silent-steps? (a) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Sentence Rule ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) assumption, opening the ulename{{	o}I} box (2) assumption 
eg(x > 1 \vee y > 1), opening an ulename{RAA} box (3) @prp-de-morgan (a), 
eg(P \vee Q) \vdash 
eg P \wedge 
eg Q, applied to (2) (4) ulename{\wedge E} on (3), twice; ulename{{	o}E} with the order fact “
eg(a > 1) implies a \le 1”, twice; then ulename{\wedge I} (5) ulename{\wedge E} on (4), then ulename{{	o}E} with “a \le 1 and b \le 1 imply a + b \le 2” (6) ulename{{	o}E} with the order fact “a \le 2 implies 
eg(a > 2)” on (5), then ulename{
eg E} on (1) and the result (7) ulename{RAA} on the box (2)–(6); then ulename{{	o}I} on (1)–(7) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (b) Sentence (7) closes the ulename{RAA} box: the box opened with the negation of the goal x > 1 \vee y > 1 and closes with the goal itself. Sentence (3) uses De Morgan’s law (a), a direction derived without ulename{RAA}. (c) It wears face (iii), genuine ulename{RAA}, but it is a contrapositive in costume, as in @exm-costume-contrapositive: the hypothesis (1) is used only at the clash, and everything else derives x + y \le 2 from x \le 1 and y \le 1. The rewrite opens: “We prove the contrapositive: if x \le 1 and y \le 1, then x + y \le 2.” The rewrite is clearer, but it does not remove the classical step: passing from the contrapositive back to the claim is @prp-contrapositive-converse, which uses ulename{RAA}. (d) The closing of the ulename{{	o}I} box (“so if x + y > 2, then …”) may be silent. The conclusion of the ulename{RAA} box, “hence x > 1 or y > 1”, may not. B. Practice [B1: From skeleton to prose] Each part gives a statement and a level-1 skeleton of its proof. Write the proof at level 3, keeping every step that @def-silent-steps says is never silent. 1. For every integer n, if n is odd, then 3n + 5 is even. (Domain 
Z.) 2. No real number x satisfies x^2 + 1 = 2x - 1. (Domain 
R.) 3. For a real number x: x^3 = x if and only if x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. (Here x is fixed; “or” chains group to the right.) Hint: line 3 of (c) uses the school fact that a product of real numbers is zero only if one of its factors is zero. (a) Let n be an integer, and suppose n is odd. Choose an integer k with n = 2k + 1. Then 3n + 5 = 6k + 3 + 5 = 2(3k + 4), and 3k + 4 is an integer, so 3n + 5 is even. “Choose an integer k” is the ulename{\exists E} box, with a fresh name; the witness 3k + 4 of line 4 is on the page, and it depends on k, hence on n. Lines 5, 6 and 7 close boxes and are silent. (b) Suppose, to the contrary, that some real x satisfies x^2 + 1 = 2x - 1, and fix such an x. Rearranging, x^2 - 2x + 2 = 0, that is, (x - 1)^2 + 1 = 0. But (x - 1)^2 \ge 0, since a square is non-negative, so 1 \le 0, which is false. Hence no real x satisfies the equation. “Suppose, to the contrary” opens the ulename{
eg I} box of line 1 (the goal is a negation, so no classical rule is used), and “fix such an x” the ulename{\exists E} box. The clash of lines 5–7 is named, and the conclusion of the ulename{
eg I} box is written; line 8 is silent. (c) Let x be real. (\Rightarrow) Suppose x^3 = x. Then (x + 1)\,x\,(x - 1) = x^3 - x = 0. A product of real numbers is zero only if a factor is zero, so x + 1 = 0, x = 0 or x - 1 = 0; that is, x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. (\Leftarrow) Suppose x = -1, x = 0 or x = 1. In the three cases, x^3 = -1 = x, x^3 = 0 = x and x^3 = 1 = x. This proves the equivalence. Both directions are written, and the citation in line 3 is visible. The two splits of (\Leftarrow) are merged into “in the three cases”; the disjunction split is the hypothesis itself, and the closing lines 12 and 13 are silent. [B2: Put the proof in order] Let (a_n) and (b_n) be sequences of real numbers with a_n 	o L and b_n 	o M, where “a_n 	o L” is the pattern of Section 4.8: for every \varepsilon > 0 there is N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. Eight of the ten sentences below, in a suitable order, form a level-3 proof that a_n + b_n 	o L + M; two are distractors. Write down an order for the eight, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each distractor is wrong. 1. Let n \in 
N with n \ge N. 2. Since b_n 	o M and \varepsilon/2 > 0, choose N_2 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_2. 3. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}, where N_1 and N_2 serve every \varepsilon at once. 4. Then n \ge N_1 and n \ge N_2. 5. Let \varepsilon > 0. 6. Since n \ge N and \varepsilon > 0 were arbitrary, a_n + b_n 	o L + M. 7. Choose N_1 \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N_1. 8. Let N \coloneqq \max\{N_1, N_2\}. 9. So \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)} \le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{b_n - M} < \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. 10. Since a_n 	o L and \varepsilon/2 > 0, choose N_1 \in 
N (depending on \varepsilon) such that \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon/2 for every n \ge N_1. An admissible order: (v), (x), (ii), (viii), (i), (iv), (ix), (vi). The only other admissible order swaps (x) and (ii), which use only \varepsilon and one hypothesis each. Nothing else moves: (viii) uses N_1 and N_2; (i) uses N; (iv) uses n \ge N and the definition of N; (ix) uses (iv), (x) and (ii) at this n, and the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases); (vi) closes the boxes of n and \varepsilon, with the ulename{\exists I} of the witness N inside “a_n + b_n 	o L + M”. The maximum exists because there are finitely many numbers. Distractor (iii) claims that N_1 and N_2 serve every \varepsilon at once. They were chosen from  orall \varepsilon \, \exists N, inside the box of \varepsilon, so they depend on \varepsilon and serve only the \varepsilon they were chosen for; a uniform N would need \exists N \,  orall \varepsilon, which the hypothesis does not give. This is the error that Section 5.6 catalogues as (N2). For a_n = 1/(n + 1), L = 0, no single N_1 serves every \varepsilon > 0: at \varepsilon = 1/(N_1 + 2) the term a_{N_1} = 1/(N_1 + 1) is too far from 0. Distractor (vii) applies the hypothesis at \varepsilon instead of \varepsilon/2. It is a legal step, but with it in place of (x), the bound in (ix) becomes \abs{(a_n + b_n) - (L + M)} < \varepsilon + \varepsilon/2, not < \varepsilon, so (ix) would no longer follow. It is an \varepsilon of the wrong kind for the goal. [B3: The last step] Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “for real numbers x and y, if x is rational and y is irrational, then x + y is irrational”, with x and y fixed: and its level-3 prose, with the closing sentence of the ulename{
eg I} box left blank: Let x be rational and y irrational. Suppose x + y is rational. Then y = (x + y) - x is a difference of two rational numbers, so y is rational. This contradicts the irrationality of y. \underline{\qquad\qquad} Name the move, then complete it. The move is skeleton first: the blank is line 8, the line written after the ulename{
eg I} box of lines 4–7 closes, a line the skeleton fixes before any arithmetic. That box assumed “x + y is rational” and reached  ot at line 7, so line 8 concludes its negation. It is the first face of “by contradiction” (Section 5.1), proof of a negative statement, and uses no classical rule: “irrational” means “not rational”, so the goal of the outer box, line 8, is a negation, and the inner box is opened on x + y \in 
Q with goal  ot. Completion. “Hence x + y is not rational, that is, x + y is irrational.” The conclusion of a ulename{
eg I} box is never silent (@def-silent-steps), so this sentence must be written even though the reader can guess it. Line 9, the closing of the ulename{{	o}I} box, may stay silent. The sentence before the blank, “this contradicts the irrationality of y”, is line 7, the clash of ulename{
eg E}, which names both lines it cites. C. Going deeper [C1: A constant found backwards] Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and let a be a fixed real number. Prove that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is \delta > 0 such that \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon for every real x with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Write your answer as an Idea, which finds \delta backwards, followed by a Proof, which runs forwards. Say what \delta depends on. [Hint 1] Compute \abs{f(x) - f(a)} in terms of \abs{x - a} before choosing anything. [Hint 2] The Proof begins: “Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq …”. Idea. We want \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon. Compute: f(x) - f(a) = (2x + 3) - (2a + 3) = 2(x - a), so \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = 2\abs{x - a}. This is below \varepsilon exactly when \abs{x - a} < \varepsilon/2. So \delta = \varepsilon/2 should work, and it does not involve x or a. Proof. Let \varepsilon > 0, and let \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/2, which is positive and depends on \varepsilon only. Let x be a real number with \abs{x - a} < \delta. Then \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = \abs{2(x - a)} = 2\abs{x - a} < 2\delta = \varepsilon . Since x was arbitrary, \delta works for \varepsilon; since \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, this proves the claim. The Idea reads the computation from the goal back to \abs{x - a}; the Proof places \delta right after \varepsilon, before any x appears, and justifies it by the final display. Because \delta does not depend on a either, the same proof shows that one \delta serves every point: f is uniformly continuous on 
R, in the sense of Section 4.10. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: an Idea that computes \abs{f(x) - f(a)} = 2\abs{x - a} and reads off \delta from the goal. - 2: the Proof opens with \varepsilon > 0 arbitrary and introduces \delta before any x, with \delta > 0 checked. - 2: says what \delta depends on (\varepsilon only, or \varepsilon and a if the choice involves a). - 3: for arbitrary x with \abs{x - a} < \delta, the forward chain to \abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon, each step justified. - 1: a closing sentence with the quantifiers in the order \varepsilon, \delta, x. Any \delta with 0 < \delta \le \varepsilon/2 earns full marks. Fatal errors (0 for the step): \delta depending on x; a Proof that runs backwards (“this holds if …”). [C2: Rewrite it properly] A sequence (a_n) is bounded if there is M \in 
R with \abs{a_n} \le M for every n \in 
N (Section 4.6). The following proof that a sequence (a_n) with a_n 	o L is bounded is correct in substance but badly written. We want some M with \abs{a_n} \le M. For big n, a_n is near L, so \abs{a_n} is less than \abs{L} + 1 if we use 1 for \varepsilon. The small n are only finitely many, so take the biggest. So M is the max of all of them and it works. 1. Name three faults of the text, each by the convention it breaks (this section) or the step that is not written. 2. Rewrite the proof at level 3. [Hint 1] Which objects does the text use without introducing them, and what does each depend on? [Hint 2] The rewrite begins: “Apply the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon = 1, and choose N \in 
N such that …”. (a) (i) It writes the search: “we want some M” and “if we use 1 for \varepsilon” describe what is being looked for, not lines that follow. (ii) It uses objects without introducing them: “big n” hides an N, obtained from the hypothesis at \varepsilon = 1 by ulename{ orall E} and ulename{\exists E}, which is never named; “the biggest” does not say of which numbers. (iii) It never says what M is or what it depends on: M is built from the finitely many terms before N, so it depends on N. (Also acceptable: the split into small and big n has no stated reason; the last sentence does not say what was shown.) (b) Apply the definition of a_n 	o L with \varepsilon = 1, and choose N \in 
N such that \abs{a_n - L} < 1 for every n \ge N. Let M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{a_0}, \abs{a_1}, \dots, \abs{a_{N-1}}, \abs{L} + 1 \}, the largest of finitely many numbers, so it exists; it depends on N (when N = 0 the list is just \abs{L} + 1). Let n \in 
N. Either n < N or n \ge N, since every natural number is one or the other. If n < N, then \abs{a_n} is in the list, so \abs{a_n} \le M. If n \ge N, then by the triangle inequality (@exm-triangle-inequality-cases) \abs{a_n} = \abs{(a_n - L) + L} \le \abs{a_n - L} + \abs{L} < 1 + \abs{L} \le M . In either case \abs{a_n} \le M. Hence (a_n) is bounded. The ulename{ orall E} instance \varepsilon = 1 is named, because it is not the obvious one; the witness M of the final ulename{\exists I} is defined before it is used, with its dependence; the split on n < N or n \ge N carries its reason (every natural number is one or the other). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) three genuine faults, each tied to a convention or an unwritten step (1 each). - 2: (b) applies the hypothesis at a named positive \varepsilon and chooses N from it. - 2: defines M before using it, with its dependence on N, bounding the early terms and \abs{L} + \varepsilon (a maximum or a sum). - 2: the two cases n < N and n \ge N, the second by the triangle inequality (cited) or an equivalent estimate from \abs{a_n - L} < \varepsilon, such as L - \varepsilon < a_n < L + \varepsilon and a split on the sign of a_n. - 1: ends with what was shown. Fatal errors (0 for the step): M chosen before N or as a maximum or sum of infinitely many numbers; the early terms omitted.

title: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
5.7 The Dispute over Excluded Middle
content:
The Dispute over Excluded Middle Chapter 2 found that one rule stands apart. ulename{RAA} belongs to no connective, and over the other primitive rules it derives ulename{
eg
eg E} and ulename{LEM} and is derived by each of them (@thm-classical-rules-interderivable). Chapter 3’s optional @thm-raa-independent showed that the other propositional rules cannot derive it. Some mathematicians have refused to use it, for a century now and for reasons that are mathematical rather than merely fussy. This section asks what those reasons are, what can still be proved without the rule, and what analysis would lose. One extra rule Recall what Section 2.5 established. Over the primitive rules other than ulename{RAA}, the three rules ulename{RAA}, ulename{
eg
eg E}, and ulename{LEM} each derive the other two, so adding any one of them gives the same derivable sequents. There is one classical principle, and it has three faces. Nothing needs re-proving here; what is new is the decision to leave the principle out and see what remains. Call a derivation intuitionistic if no line is justified by ulename{RAA} and no line uses a derived rule or a cited result whose own derivation uses ulename{RAA}. Intuitionistic logic is the system of these derivations. Its rules are the introduction and elimination rules for \wedge, 	o, and \vee (Chapter 1); ulename{
eg I}, ulename{
eg E}, ulename{ ot E}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}, and ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (Chapter 2); the rules for  orall, \exists, and = (Chapter 4); and repetition. Classical logic, the logic of Chapters 1–4, is the same list with ulename{RAA} added. This is why Chapter 2 kept ulename{ ot E} as a primitive rule although ulename{RAA} and repetition derive it (the remark after @thm-classical-rules-interderivable). Had ulename{ ot E} been dropped, striking ulename{RAA} would have taken it away too, and the remaining system would be weaker than the one intuitionists actually use: it could no longer derive  ot \vdash P. That is a claim about all derivations, and we state it without proof; nothing depends on it. With ulename{ ot E} kept, the rules without ulename{RAA} are exactly intuitionistic logic. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- System Rules \vdash P \vee 
eg P? ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- intuitionistic the primitive rules other than ulename{RAA} not derivable (@thm-raa-independent for the propositional rules; the rules for  orall, \exists and = do not change this, stated without proof) classical the same rules and ulename{RAA} derivable (@prp-excluded-middle) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every intuitionistic derivation is a derivation, so everything intuitionistic logic derives, classical logic derives too, and soundness applies to it: @thm-soundness, and, for derivations whose lines contain quantifiers or equations, the soundness statement for predicate logic in Section 4.11. The difference is a list of sequents that only the classical system reaches. Chapters 2–4 flag the derivations that use ulename{RAA} as they go, so the results on that list can be read off the text; the Quick check asks for them. (a) Which labeled results of Chapter 2 (propositions and theorems) were derived with ulename{RAA}, directly or through ulename{
eg
eg E}, ulename{LEM}, or a cited result that uses one of them? (b) The same question for Chapters 3 and 4. (a) Seven: @prp-double-negation (b); @prp-contrapositive-converse; @prp-excluded-middle; @prp-de-morgan (d); @prp-implication-as-disjunction (b), through ulename{LEM}; @thm-classical-rules-interderivable, whose proof uses all three: ulename{RAA} in ①, ulename{
eg
eg E} in ②, ulename{LEM} in ③; and @prp-peirce. Every other proposition and theorem of Chapter 2 uses no classical rule, including @thm-sqrt2-irrational, whose box closes by ulename{
eg I}. (b) In Chapter 3: @lem-atom-splitting, through ulename{LEM}, and with it @thm-completeness and the direction (\Leftarrow) of @cor-derivable-iff-valid. In Chapter 4: @prp-quantifier-negation (a); the direction \vdash of @prp-negated-implication; the direction \vdash of @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (a); the two directions \dashv of @prp-quantifier-passage, in (d) and in (e), both through ulename{LEM}; and @prp-arbitrarily-close-equal, as proved, since its box assumes a 
e b and concludes a = b. Excluded middle cannot be refuted If intuitionists do not assert P \vee 
eg P, perhaps they deny it. They do not, and they could not: its double negation needs no classical rule at all. Excluded Middle Cannot Be Refuted For every statement P, \vdash 
eg
eg(P \vee 
eg P), by a derivation that uses neither ulename{RAA} nor ulename{ ot E}. Try it first (ten minutes): the goal is a negation. Open the box that the goal asks for, hunt for a clash, and note which rule closes each box you open. An attempt that starts from P \vee 
eg P stalls at once: ulename{\vee I} needs one side, and neither side is in hand. But the goal is not P \vee 
eg P. It is 
eg(
eg(P \vee 
eg P)), a negation, so the goal-directed move of Section 2.2 opens a ulename{
eg I} box on 
eg(P \vee 
eg P) with the goal  ot. That assumption can clash only with P \vee 
eg P, which ulename{\vee I} builds from either side, so we manufacture a side as in @exm-manufactured-clash. A box on P gives P \vee 
eg P, a clash, and ulename{
eg I} closes it with 
eg P. Then ulename{\vee I} builds P \vee 
eg P from 
eg P, and that is the second clash. Every box ends in  ot and closes by ulename{
eg I}. Before reading on: self-explain lines 5 and 6. The derivation is: The two boxes close by ulename{
eg I}, at lines 5 and 8. The other rules used are ulename{\vee I} (lines 3 and 6) and ulename{
eg E} (lines 4 and 7). The derivation has no premises. This proves the proposition. Set it beside the derivation of @prp-excluded-middle. Lines 1–7 are the same, line for line. Only line 8 differs: there ulename{RAA} closed the outer box and wrote P \vee 
eg P; here ulename{
eg I} closes it and writes the negation of its assumption. So the whole classical content of @prp-excluded-middle sits in its last line. Non-example by minimal change. Keep lines 1–7, and write P \vee 
eg P at line 8 with the justification ulename{
eg I}\ \lines{1}{7}. The box still checks. What fails is the conclusion of ulename{
eg I}, which must be the negation of the box’s assumption, 
eg
eg(P \vee 
eg P). Writing P \vee 
eg P there needs ulename{RAA}. What the proposition says is this: nobody can refute excluded middle. Suppose some derivation, intuitionistic or not, gave 
eg(P \vee 
eg P) from no premises. Then ulename{
eg E} against the line 
eg
eg(P \vee 
eg P) would give  ot from no premises, and soundness forbids that: @thm-soundness, or the soundness statement for predicate logic in Section 4.11 when P or the derivation involves quantifiers or equality, since no valuation, and no structure and assignment, makes  ot true. The intuitionist does not claim that excluded middle fails. The intuitionist declines to assert it, because asserting it would mean having a proof of one side, and for many statements P, an open conjecture for instance, nobody has one. The proposition is one instance of a general fact, due to Glivenko (1929) and stated here without proof: if a statement built from letters by the connectives is derivable with all the rules, then its double negation is derivable without ulename{RAA}. Classical propositional logic survives inside intuitionistic logic, behind two negations. The fact fails once quantifiers are allowed; 
eg
eg orall x\, (\varphi \vee 
eg\varphi) is in general not derivable without ulename{RAA} (also stated without proof). Intuitionistic logic does not say that excluded middle is false. No instance P \vee 
eg P can be refuted, since 
eg
eg(P \vee 
eg P) is derivable without ulename{RAA}; dropping a rule is not adding its negation. (Brouwer’s own analysis adds axioms about the real numbers under which the universal statement “every real number is 0 or not 0” is refuted, but no single instance is.) What a proof provides Chapter 3 gave the connectives a meaning through truth values: every letter is true or false, and a table computes the rest. That semantics already takes a side, since a row decides every letter. The intuitionist explains a statement instead by saying what counts as a proof of it. The resulting clauses are called the BHK reading, after Brouwer, Heyting, and Kolmogorov. To know a statement is to have a proof of it, and a proof of a compound statement is built from proofs of its parts. - There is no proof of  ot. - A proof of P \wedge Q is a pair: a proof of P and a proof of Q. - A proof of P \vee Q is a proof of P or a proof of Q, with a label saying which. - A proof of P 	o Q is a method that takes any proof of P and returns a proof of Q. - A proof of 
eg P is a method that takes any proof of P and returns a proof of  ot. So 
eg P is read as P 	o  ot, exactly the reading that the table in Section 2.2, after @def-rules-negation, found row by row. - A proof of \exists x\, \varphi is an object t together with a proof of \varphi[t/x]. - A proof of  orall x\, \varphi is a method that produces, for every object t, a proof of \varphi[t/x]. In words: a disjunction must say which side, an existence claim must name the object, and an implication or a universal statement must come with a method that works on every input. A proof of a negation provides no object at all; it is a guarantee that no proof of the negated statement will ever arrive. Each intuitionistic rule builds exactly what its clause asks for. ulename{\vee I} writes P \vee Q from a line P, so it knows which side it used. ulename{\exists I} writes \exists x\, \varphi from an instance \varphi[t/x], so the witness t is on the page. A ulename{{	o}I} box is a method: given the assumption, it produces the conclusion. ulename{RAA} is the exception. Its box shows that 
eg\varphi leads to  ot, which is a proof of 
eg
eg\varphi, and then it writes \varphi. Under the BHK reading a method for refuting every refutation of \varphi is not a proof of \varphi. Excluded middle under BHK. A proof of P \vee 
eg P for every statement P would be a single method that decides each statement, says which side holds, and proves that side. Nobody has such a method. Take Goldbach’s conjecture, that every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes: nobody has proved it and nobody has refuted it, so nobody can produce a labeled proof of “Goldbach’s conjecture or its negation”. The proposition under BHK. The derivation of @prp-not-not-excluded-middle is such a method, and it decides nothing. Its conclusion asks for a method that takes any f, a method sending proofs of P \vee 
eg P to proofs of  ot, and returns a proof of  ot. Here is one. Given a proof p of P, label it “left” and apply f: that turns proofs of P into proofs of  ot, which is a proof g of 
eg P (lines 2–5). Now label g “right” and apply f once more (lines 6–7). At no point did the method need to know whether P holds. Not every, and some not. Chapter 4 derived 
eg orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, 
eg\varphi (@prp-quantifier-negation (a)) with two ulename{RAA} boxes, and noted that the derivation never says which x fails \varphi. The BHK reading says why that matters. A proof of the premise is a method that refutes every proof of  orall x\, \varphi; a proof of the conclusion must name an object. Nothing in the first produces the second, and the derivation does not try: its conclusion comes from ulename{RAA}, not from an ulename{\exists I} applied to an available instance. Classical mathematics accepts the step, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses it at the end of its proof of the Archimedean property. A constructive mathematician accepts that conclusion only with an object in hand. Describe a BHK proof of 
eg(P \wedge 
eg P). Does it decide whether P holds? We need a method that takes any proof of P \wedge 
eg P and returns a proof of  ot. A proof of P \wedge 
eg P is a pair: a proof p of P and a method f turning proofs of P into proofs of  ot. Apply f to p. That is the whole method, and it never decides P: it only uses a pair that someone else supplies. (It is the BHK reading of a ulename{
eg I} box on P \wedge 
eg P whose clash is ulename{
eg E} on its two halves.) Irrational powers, with and without a witness Here is the standard example of a proof that establishes existence without saying what exists. [An Irrational Power of an Irrational Number Can Be Rational] There are irrational numbers a and b such that a^b is rational. Try it first (ten minutes): find such a and b explicitly, and prove that your a and b are irrational and that a^b is rational. The first candidates anyone tries are a = b = \sqrt 2. Then the question is whether \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is rational, and the attempt stalls there: nothing in this book decides it. There are two ways out. The classical one splits on the undecided question with ulename{LEM}. If \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is rational, the first candidates work. If not, use it as the new a and raise it to \sqrt 2 once more, which turns the exponent into \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 = 2. The proof below takes this way. The other way chooses an exponent that undoes the square root, and the proposition after the proof takes it. Let s \coloneqq \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}, a positive real number. By excluded middle, s is rational or s is not rational [ulename{LEM}], and we argue by cases [ulename{\vee E}]. Case 1: s is rational. Take a \coloneqq \sqrt 2 and b \coloneqq \sqrt 2. Both are irrational by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and a^b = s is rational [ulename{\exists I}]. Case 2: s is not rational. Take a \coloneqq s and b \coloneqq \sqrt 2. Then a is irrational by the case assumption and b by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and a^b =  igl( \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}  igr)^{\sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2} = \sqrt 2^{\,2} = 2, which is rational [ulename{\exists I}]. In either case there are irrational a and b with a^b rational. This proves the theorem. The classical step is the first line, ulename{LEM} on the statement “s is rational”. Every other step is intuitionistic. The proof does not tell us which pair works. It hands over two candidate pairs, (\sqrt 2, \sqrt 2) and (\sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2}, \sqrt 2), and a guarantee that one of them succeeds. Under the BHK reading a proof of an existence claim must name the object, so this proof is not one. Section 2.5 described excluded middle as making a decision; here the decision about “s is rational” is made, and nobody learns its outcome. In fact the second case holds: \sqrt 2^{\sqrt 2} is transcendental, so in particular irrational, by the Gelfond–Schneider theorem, proved independently by Gelfond and by Schneider in 1934. That theorem lies far beyond this book, and nothing here uses it. It also does not repair the proof above, which never needed to know the answer. The other way out finds the witness. Since \sqrt 2^{\,b} = 2^{b/2}, the exponent b = 2\log_2 m = \log_2(m^2) gives \sqrt 2^{\,b} = m for every integer m \ge 2. The choice m = 2 gives b = 2, which is rational, so m must avoid the powers of 2; the first choice left is m = 3. [A Witness for an Irrational Power] The number \log_2 9 is irrational. Consequently a \coloneqq \sqrt 2 and b \coloneqq \log_2 9 are irrational numbers with a^b = 3. The irrationality goes as for \sqrt 2: suppose \log_2 9 is a fraction p/q, clear the denominator, and look at parity. Here the clash is quicker than for \sqrt 2: a power of 2 would equal a power of 9, and one is even while the other is odd. The positivity of \log_2 9 is what makes the power of 2 even. Suppose that \log_2 9 = p/q for integers p and q with q 
e 0; replacing p, q by -p, -q if necessary, we may take q \ge 1. Since 2^0 = 1 < 9 and t \mapsto 2^t is increasing, \log_2 9 > 0, so p > 0, that is, p \ge 1. From 2^{p/q} = 9, raising both sides to the power q gives 2^p = 9^q . The left side is even, since 2^p = 2 \cdot 2^{p-1} with p - 1 \ge 0. The right side is odd, being a product of q odd factors. No integer is both even and odd, by (E2) of Section 2.1, so this is a contradiction. Hence \log_2 9 is not rational [ulename{
eg I}]. For the consequence, a = \sqrt 2 is irrational by @thm-sqrt2-irrational, and b = \log_2 9 is irrational by what was just shown. Since \log_2 9 = \log_2 (3^2) = 2\log_2 3, a^b =  igl( 2^{1/2}  igr)^{\log_2 9} = 2^{(\log_2 9)/2} = 2^{\log_2 3} = 3 . This proves the proposition. This proof uses no classical rule. The irrationality of \log_2 9 is a negative statement, “no fraction equals \log_2 9”, and its box closes by ulename{
eg I}, like the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational. The witness (\sqrt 2, \log_2 9) is written down. So @prp-log2-9-irrational gives a second proof of @thm-irrational-power-rational, and this one provides what the BHK reading asks for. (The exponent laws for real exponents are school facts here; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 10 defines a^x for irrational x and proves them.) A short history The dispute has dates. In 1908 L. E. J. Brouwer published “De onbetrouwbaarheid der logische principes” (“The unreliability of the logical principles”) in the Tijdschrift voor Wijsbegeerte. His point was that excluded middle had been abstracted from reasoning about finite collections, where every case can in principle be checked, and then applied without justification to infinite ones, where it cannot. Over the next two decades he rebuilt parts of analysis on this view, and the movement took the name intuitionism. In 1925 A. N. Kolmogorov showed that classical reasoning can be imitated inside a logic without excluded middle by putting a double negation in front of every subformula: the first double-negation translation (Exercise C2 below checks one step of it). In July 1927 David Hilbert lectured in Hamburg on “Die Grundlagen der Mathematik”, printed in 1928. He defended excluded middle in a much-repeated comparison: to take it from the mathematician would be like forbidding the astronomer the telescope or the boxer the use of his fists. The quarrel between his program and Brouwer’s became known as the Grundlagenstreit, the dispute over foundations. It turned personal in 1928, when Hilbert had Brouwer removed from the editorial board of the Mathematische Annalen; the board was then dissolved and re-formed without him. In 1929 V. Glivenko proved the theorem of the remark above: classical propositional logic sits inside intuitionistic logic behind a double negation. In 1930 Arend Heyting published “Die formalen Regeln der intuitionistischen Logik” in the Sitzungsberichte der Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. It wrote down rules for intuitionistic logic, in a format different from ours, and from then on the logic could be studied as a formal system like any other. In 1933 Kurt Gödel published a double-negation translation of arithmetic, which shows that classical arithmetic is consistent if intuitionistic arithmetic is. Gerhard Gentzen had found an equivalent translation independently and withdrew his paper of 1933 when Gödel’s appeared. In 1967 Errett Bishop published Foundations of Constructive Analysis. It developed a large part of analysis without excluded middle, and also without Brouwer’s philosophy and his special axioms about the real numbers. Most of what is now called constructive analysis descends from it. What analysis would lose What does analysis look like without the rule? Here are four previews, stated informally and without proof. The book takes the first as an axiom and proves the classical versions of the other three; each is a place where classical reasoning, by the rule or by an axiom, does work that a constructive proof cannot. - The supremum. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes as an axiom that every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum. Constructively, a non-empty set A bounded above has a supremum if and only if it is order-located: for all real numbers x < y, either y is an upper bound of A or some element of A exceeds x (Bishop’s form of the least upper bound principle). The classical axiom asserts the supremum without requiring anyone to make these decisions. - Monotone sequences. E. Specker (1949) gave an increasing, bounded sequence of rational numbers that a computer program can list term by term, but whose limit is not a computable real number: no program can print its decimal digits. So the convergence of bounded monotone sequences, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 2 proves from the axiom, cannot come with a method for computing the limit. - The intermediate value theorem. Let f be continuous on [a, b] with f(a) < 0 < f(b). Classically, Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 6 proves that f(x) = 0 for some x \in [a, b]. Constructively, what holds in general is the approximate version: for every \varepsilon > 0 some x \in [a, b] has \abs{f(x)} < \varepsilon. The exact version holds under extra hypotheses, for example when f is strictly increasing. A bisection needs the sign of f at a midpoint m, and finitely many digits of f(m) cannot always tell whether f(m) is negative, zero, or positive: the digits of a value equal to 0 begin like those of a tiny positive or negative one. - Bolzano–Weierstrass. A bisection proof of the theorem (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 2 proves it by another route) says: one of the two halves of an interval contains infinitely many terms of the sequence; continue with that half. That step is ulename{LEM} on “the left half contains infinitely many terms”, a statement that nobody can decide in general, and the proof does not say which half. Proofs as programs The BHK clauses read like the description of a programming language. A proof of P \wedge Q is a pair; a proof of P \vee Q is a value tagged “left” or “right”; a proof of P 	o Q is a function; a proof of \exists x\, \varphi is a pair of an object and a proof; a proof of  orall x\, \varphi is a function that accepts any object. This match between propositions and types, and between proofs and programs, is the Curry–Howard correspondence. It is what a proof assistant such as Lean is built on: checking a proof is checking that a program has the right type. Intuitionistic logic fits this picture exactly. ulename{LEM} does not, since no program decides every proposition. Lean adds classical logic by an axiom, Classical.choice, a form of the axiom of choice. Excluded middle, Classical.em, is then a theorem, derived from choice together with two extensionality principles by Diaconescu’s theorem. Lean draws one line with care. A definition that uses classical logic to produce data, for instance a number chosen by deciding an arbitrary proposition, must be marked noncomputable, since no program computes it. A proof that uses Classical.em needs no mark, because proofs carry no data. -- excluded middle is a theorem, proved from the axiom of choice example (p : Prop) : Or p (Not p) := Classical.em p -- a number defined by deciding an arbitrary proposition open Classical in noncomputable def indicator (p : Prop) : Nat := if p then 1 else 0 “Constructive” does not mean “computable in practice”. A constructive proof provides a method, and the method may be hopeless. Deciding whether a whole number is prime by trying every smaller divisor is constructive, and for a number with a thousand digits no computer could finish it. Constructive mathematics asks whether a method exists, not whether it is fast. The book’s position The main line of this book stays classical. The decision is made once, in the axioms. The ordered-field axioms of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 include trichotomy: for real numbers a and b, exactly one of a < b, a = b, b < a holds. Constructive analysis does not accept trichotomy for real numbers, because it would decide the sign of every real number. So a case split such as “x \ge 0 or x < 0” rests on an axiom, and the book does not flag it. What the book does flag is a genuinely non-constructive step of the kind discussed above, such as the bisection step of Bolzano–Weierstrass, and every use of the axiom of choice. One clause says so, and nothing more. Such a step is never silent anyway: by @def-silent-steps, a ulename{

title: Definition 1.1.2 (Main Connective)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: The main connective of a compound statement is the connective applied last when the statement is built up from its parts. An atomic statement has no main connective.

title: Definition 1.1.3 (Sequent)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: Let \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) and \(Q\) be statements, where \(n \ge 0\) . The sequent \[ P_1, \dots, P_n \vdash Q \] is the claim that \(Q\) can be derived from \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) by the rules of logic. The statements \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) are its premises and \(Q\) is its conclusion . When \(n = 0\) we write \(\vdash Q\) .

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Statement)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: A statement is a declarative sentence that is either true or false , and not both.

title: Example (Statements and nonstatements)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: Decide which of the following are statements. \(7\) is a prime number. \(0.999 > 1\) . There are infinitely many primes \(p\) for which \(p + 2\) is also prime. Is \(2^{11} - 1\) prime? \(x > 2\) . \(3 > 2\) .
