content: State the definition of a statement. Is “ \(10^{100} + 1\) is prime” a statement? For a real number \(x\) , is “ \(x^2 - 1 = 0\) ” a statement? Is “ \(0^2 - 1 = 0\) ”? With \(P\) : “ \(n\) is even” and \(Q\) : “ \(n\) is prime”, write “ \(n\) is prime but not even” in symbols. Find the main connective of \(P \wedge Q \to \neg R\) , and write the statement with all its parentheses. True or false, with a reason: if \(P\) and \(Q\) are both true, then \(P \vee Q\) is false. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Write the form of the argument “ \(x > 0\) and \(y > 0\) ; so \(y > 0\) and \(x > 0\) ” as a sequent, saying what each letter stands for. Which of \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) , \(\to\) is the main connective of \((P \vee Q) \wedge (Q \to R)\) ? Using the preview table of “Each connective, two rules”, say what a proof of this statement must do, and name the rule that Section 1.3 will state for it.

title: Exercise (B1: Translating analysis)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: Translate each sentence into symbols, using the atomic statements given. You do not need to know what the words mean; only the grammar matters. “ \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) but not differentiable there”, with \(C\) : “ \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) ” and \(D\) : “ \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\) ”. “If the sequence \((a_n)\) converges, it is bounded”, with \(V\) : “ \((a_n)\) converges” and \(B\) : “ \((a_n)\) is bounded”. “ \(x\) is rational or irrational”, with \(R\) : “ \(x\) is rational”. (A real number is irrational when it is not rational.) “The set \(F\) is closed if and only if its complement is open”, with \(K\) : “ \(F\) is closed” and \(U\) : “the complement of \(F\) is open”.

title: Exercise (C1: “Only if” and “unless”)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be statements. Explain why “ \(P\) only if \(Q\) ” means \(P \to Q\) , and not \(Q \to P\) . (Ask: which situation would make “ \(P\) only if \(Q\) ” false?) Explain why “ \(P\) unless \(Q\) ” means \(\neg Q \to P\) . Let \(x\) be a real number. Decide whether each sentence is true for every real \(x\) . Justify your answer, giving a value of \(x\) that makes it false where there is one. “ \(x^2 = 4\) if \(x = 2\) .” “ \(x^2 = 4\) only if \(x = 2\) .” “ \(x^2 > 0\) unless \(x = 0\) .”

title: Exercise (C2: Necessary and sufficient)
page: 1.1 Statements, Connectives and the Form of an Argument
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Write “ \(x > 1\) is sufficient for \(x^2 > 1\) ” and “ \(x > 1\) is necessary for \(x^2 > 1\) ” as implications. Decide which of the two is true for every real \(x\) , and give a value of \(x\) that makes the other false. Find a condition on \(x\) , written with \(\vee\) , that is both necessary and sufficient for \(x^2 > 1\) . You may use that \(x^2 > 1\) exactly when \(\abs{x} > 1\) , where \(\abs{x}\) is \(x\) if \(x \ge 0\) and \(-x\) if \(x < 0\) .

title: Definition 1.2.2 (Box-Free Derivation)
content: Fix a list of rules, each given by schemas. A box-free derivation is a finite list of numbered lines \(1, 2, \dots, n\) , where \(n \ge 1\) , each carrying one statement and a justification, such that: the first lines, possibly none and possibly all, are premises , justified by nothing; a short horizontal rule is drawn under the last premise; every later line is justified by one rule of the list, citing earlier lines, and it and the cited lines form an instance of a schema of that rule. The premises of the derivation are its premise lines, and its conclusion is its last line.

title: Definition 1.2.3 (Derivable)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of statements \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , where \(n \ge 0\) , and let \(\psi\) be a statement. We say \(\psi\) is derivable from \(\Gamma\) , and write \[ \Gamma \vdash \psi , \] if there is a derivation, using the rules of logic, whose premises all belong to \(\Gamma\) and whose last line is \(\psi\) . We write \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi\) for \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) , and \(\vdash \psi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty.

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Rule Schema)
content: A rule schema is a pattern of lines: given lines and boxes at the top, possibly none, and exactly one new line at the bottom, whose justification names the rule and cites the given lines and boxes. Line numbers in a schema are written \(i, j, k\) . The letters in the pattern stand for arbitrary expressions of the right kind, and a use of the rule replaces them consistently : the same letter by the same expression, symbol for symbol , everywhere it occurs. A line is justified by the rule when it and the lines it cites, with their numbers, are an instance of a schema of the rule: the pattern with every letter replaced in this way. The schema of \(\mathrm{Tr}\) is Here \(a\) , \(b\) , \(c\) stand for expressions for numbers.

title: Example (Chaining)
content: Let \(x\) , \(y\) , \(u\) , \(v\) , \(w\) , \(z\) be real numbers. Using the rule \(\mathrm{Tr}\) only, write a box-free derivation of each conclusion from the given premises. Premises \(0 < x\) , \(x < y\) , \(y < 1\) ; conclusion \(0 < 1\) . The same premises in the order \(y < 1\) , \(0 < x\) , \(x < y\) ; the same conclusion. Premises \(u < v\) , \(w < z\) , \(v < w\) ; conclusion \(u < z\) .

title: Example (Derivations, simplest first)
content: Decide whether each of the following is a derivation, and if so, what it shows. The single line \(1 \quad P \quad \text{premise}\) . The empty list, with no lines at all. The derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation , for the list of rules consisting of \(\mathrm{Tr}\) alone.

title: Example (Not a derivation)
content: Each list below is the derivation of part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation with one change. Say which of the three questions of “Reading a derivation” fails, and at which line. The statements of lines 4 and 5 are swapped, and each keeps its justification. Line 5 is justified “ \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 3, 4\) ” instead of “ \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 4, 3\) ”.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the definition of a box-free derivation, and of \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) . Fill in the justifications of the following derivation, which uses \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) . Is the following list a derivation with \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) ? If not, name the line and the clause of @def-box-free-derivation that fails. “1. \(0 < x\) , premise. 2. \(x < 1\) , premise. 3. \(0 + 1 < 1 + 1\) , \(\mathrm{Sh} \ 4\) . 4. \(0 < 1\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2\) .” What sequent “with \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) ” does the derivation of (b) show? True or false, with a reason: if \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) with \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) , and every statement in \(\Gamma\) is true, then \(\psi\) is true.

title: Exercise (B1: Shift, then chain)
content: Let \(x\) , \(y\) , \(z\) be real numbers. Using \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) , derive \(x + 1 < z\) from the premises \(x < y\) and \(y + 1 < z\) . Remember that \(\mathrm{Sh}\) writes \(a + c < b + c\) literally: no simplification of an expression is a step of the derivation. Then say in one sentence how you found the step that uses \(\mathrm{Sh}\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Instances)
content: A derivation begins with the premises \[ 1.\ \ 0 < x, \qquad 2.\ \ x < 3, \qquad 3.\ \ 3 < y . \] Determine which of the following candidate lines 4 are justified. Justify your answer: for each justified one, give the replacement of the letters; for each other one, say which clause of @def-rule-schema fails. \(0 < 3\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 2\) . \(x < y\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 2, 3\) . \(0 < y\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 3\) . \(0 + 2 < x + 2\) , \(\mathrm{Sh} \ 1\) . \(x + 1 < 3 + 2\) , \(\mathrm{Sh} \ 2\) . \(x + y < 3 + y\) , \(\mathrm{Sh} \ 2\) .

title: Exercise (B3: How many steps a chain takes)
content: Write the chain \(0 < \tfrac14 < \tfrac13 < \tfrac12\) as a derivation, with its three links as premises and the conclusion \(0 < \tfrac12\) , using \(\mathrm{Tr}\) , forwards from the first link as in part (a) of @exm-chaining-derivation . A chain \(e_0 < e_1 < \dots < e_m\) has \(m \ge 1\) links. Forward chaining, as in (a), writes the links as premises and then joins the first link with the next, again and again. How many applications of \(\mathrm{Tr}\) does it use to reach \(e_0 < e_m\) ?

title: Exercise (C1: A bad rule)
content: Add to \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) a third rule, \(\mathrm{Flip}\) : from \(a < b\) , write \(b < a\) . Derive \(1 < 0\) from the premise \(0 < 1\) , using \(\mathrm{Flip}\) . Explain why a checker following “Reading a derivation” would accept your derivation. What property do \(\mathrm{Tr}\) and \(\mathrm{Sh}\) have that \(\mathrm{Flip}\) lacks?

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: A student offers the following list as a derivation of \(0 < 4\) with \(\mathrm{Tr}\) . Is \(0 < 1, \ 1 < 2, \ 2 < 3, \ 3 < 4 \vdash 0 < 4\) with \(\mathrm{Tr}\) ? Is the list a derivation? If not, name the line that fails and the clause of @def-box-free-derivation it breaks. The two lines “1. \(0 < 0\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 2, 2\) ” and “2. \(0 < 0\) , \(\mathrm{Tr} \ 1, 1\) ” would each pass the first two questions of “Reading a derivation”. Use them to explain why a line may cite only earlier lines.

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Rules for Conjunction)
content: The first schema is the rule \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) ( and-introduction ). The second and third are the two forms of the rule \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) ( and-elimination ), one writing the left conjunct and one the right.

title: Example (Three warm-ups)
content: Give a derivation of each sequent. \(P, \ Q \vdash Q \wedge P\) . \(P \vdash P \wedge P\) . \(P \wedge Q \vdash Q\) .

title: Example (A product of numbers in the unit interval)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers with \(0 < x < 1\) and \(0 < y < 1\) . Show that \(0 < xy < 1\) , and name the rule behind each logical step.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the three schemas of @def-rules-conjunction from memory, and name the rule of each. Which statements does one application of \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) give from the line \(P \wedge (Q \wedge R)\) ? True or false, with a reason: \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) may be applied to the line \(P \wedge Q \to R\) . In the derivation in the proof of @prp-and-associative , why must line 2 come before line 4? Fill in the justifications (i)–(iv) of the following derivation.

title: Exercise (B1: The other grouping)
content: Give a derivation of \(P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \wedge R\) . For each line, say whether you found it from the goal or from the premise.

title: Exercise (B2: Annotating a proof)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Here is a proof. Let \(1 < x < 2\) and \(3 < y < 4\) . Then \(4 < x + y < 6\) . Write out the proof in full, naming each use of \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) and \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) , and marking the steps that are school algebra rather than logic.

title: Exercise (B3: Which lines are instances?)
content: A derivation begins as follows. Determine which of the following candidates for line 4 are correct. Justify your answer. \(P\) — \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) 1. \(R\) — \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) 1. \((Q \wedge R) \wedge S\) — \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) 3, 2. \(S \wedge (Q \wedge R)\) — \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) 3, 2. \(Q\) — \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) 3.

title: Exercise (C1: What conjunction cannot do)
content: Show that no box-free derivation whose only premise is \(P \wedge Q\) , and whose only rules are \(\rulename{\wedge I}\) and \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) , has a line whose statement contains the letter \(R\) . Deduce that, with these two rules, \(P \wedge Q \vdash P \wedge R\) cannot be shown.

title: Exercise (C2: A shortcut through two layers)
content: A student offers the following derivation of \(P \wedge (Q \wedge R) \vdash Q \wedge P\) . Is line 2 an instance of a schema of \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) ? Justify your answer. Is the conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. The step at line 2 never leads from a true line to a false one. Why must a checker still reject it? State, as a schema, a rule \(\wedge\mathrm{E}^{*}\) that would allow line 2. Show that every use of \(\wedge\mathrm{E}^{*}\) in a derivation can be replaced by two uses of \(\rulename{\wedge E}\) .

title: Proposition 1.3.2 (Conjunction Is Associative)
content: \((P \wedge Q) \wedge R \vdash P \wedge (Q \wedge R)\) .

title: Proposition 1.3.1 (Conjunction Commutes)
content: \(P \wedge Q \vdash Q \wedge P\) .

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Implication Elimination)
content: This rule is called \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) ( implication-elimination , or modus ponens ).

title: Example (Chains of implications)
content: Give a derivation of each sequent. \(P \to Q, \ P \vdash Q\) . \(P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash R\) . \(P \wedge Q, \ P \to (Q \to R) \vdash R\) . \((P \wedge Q) \to R, \ P, \ Q \vdash R\) . \((P \to Q) \wedge (R \to S), \ P \wedge R \vdash Q \wedge S\) .

title: Example (Four cards)
content: Each of four cards has a whole number on one side and a color on the other. They lie on a table showing \[ 6, \qquad 7, \qquad \text{red}, \qquad \text{green} . \] Someone claims: if a card shows an even number on one side, then its other side is red. Which cards must be turned over to find out whether the claim is true of these four cards? Decide before reading the solution.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schema of \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) from memory. Lines 1 and 2 of a derivation are \(P \to (Q \wedge R)\) and \(P\) . Which of the following can line 3 be, by one application of \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) ? \(Q \wedge R\) ; \(Q\) ; \(R \wedge Q\) ; \(P \to Q\) . In @exm-wason-selection , why is the red card not worth turning? True or false, with a reason: from lines \(P \to Q\) and \(Q \to R\) , \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) gives \(P \to R\) .

title: Exercise (B1: Two chains)
content: Give a derivation of each sequent. For each, say which step you found first, and whether it came from the goal or from a premise. \(P, \ P \to Q, \ Q \to (R \wedge S) \vdash S \wedge Q\) . \((P \wedge Q) \to R, \ Q \wedge P \vdash R\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Two facts and a number)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Take as premises the two facts “if \(0 < x < 1\) , then \(x^2 < x\) ” and “if \(x^2 < x\) , then \(x^3 < x^2\) ”, and the hypothesis \(0 < x < 1\) . Derive \(x^3 < x^2\) , naming the rule on each line. Then write the argument as one or two sentences of prose.

title: Exercise (B3: Which premises are needed?)
content: Find a derivation of \[ P, \ P \to Q, \ P \to R, \ R \to S, \ S \to U, \ Q \to T \ \vdash \ T , \] and list the premises it uses. Explain why a backward search finds the needed premises faster than a forward one here.

title: Exercise (C1: Find the error)
content: Here is an argument, followed by the derivation its author offers for it. If \(10\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(10\) is even. And \(10\) is even. So \(10\) is divisible by \(6\) . With \(D\) : “ \(10\) is divisible by \(6\) ” and \(E\) : “ \(10\) is even”: Name the line that fails, and say why it is not an instance of the schema of \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) . Show that the step can lead from true premises to a false conclusion. What new statement about divisibility can be correctly derived from the two premises with the rules so far?

title: Exercise (C2: Both ends)
content: Consider the sequent \[ P \to (Q \to R), \ S \to P, \ S \wedge Q \ \vdash \ R \wedge S . \] Describe a search for a derivation in words, in three parts: what the goal asks for; what the premises give; where the two meet. Write the derivation, naming the rule on every line.

title: Definition 1.5.2 (Derivation)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Fix a list of rules. A derivation is a finite list of numbered lines \(1, 2, \dots, n\) , each carrying one statement and a justification, together with a set of boxes . A box is a block of consecutive lines whose first line is an assumption. Any two boxes are either disjoint or one inside the other . A box ends at one of its lines and is closed after it. The last line of the derivation lies outside every box. The scope rule. Line \(i\) is available at line \(k\) if \(i < k\) and every box containing line \(i\) also contains line \(k\) . A box is available at line \(k\) if it ends before line \(k\) and the boxes other than itself that contain it are exactly the boxes containing line \(k\) . A line may cite only lines and boxes available at it. Every line is exactly one of the following: a premise ; the premises are the first lines, above every box, with a short rule under the last of them; an assumption , which may be any statement, and opens a new box; a repetition of the statement on a line available at this one, justified “R” and the line repeated; the conclusion of one rule of the list, applied to lines and boxes available at this one, such that this line and the cited lines and boxes form an instance of the rule’s schema. Clause (D3) is the rule \(\rulename{R}\) ( repetition ), whose schema is where line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) .

title: Definition 1.5.1 (Rules for Implication)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: The left schema is the rule \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) ( implication-introduction ); the right one is \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) ( @def-rule-implication-elimination ). In \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) , the line \(\varphi\) is an assumption , which opens the box, and the assumption is discharged when the box closes. The line \(\psi\) is a line of that box itself , not of a box inside it.

title: Example (First boxes)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Find a derivation of each sequent. \(\vdash P \to P\) . \(\vdash P \to (Q \to P)\) . \(P \to (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (P \to R)\) .

title: Example (A line cited from a closed box)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Is the following a derivation? If it were, what would it show?

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Consider the following derivation, whose justifications are missing. Write the schema of \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) from memory, and state the condition that the drawing cannot show. Fill in the justifications (i), (ii), (iii), and say what the derivation shows, written with \(\vdash\) . Which of lines 1–5 are available at line 6? What is the context of line 5? Someone extends the derivation by a line 7, the statement \(R\) justified by \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) 6, 3. Is the result a derivation? If not, name the clause of @def-derivation that line 7 breaks. In the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry , why is line 4 available at line 5? And why is the inner box closed before the outer one? In the same derivation, which rule produces line 5, and which lines does it cite?

title: Exercise (B1: Swapping inside an implication)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Show that \(\vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (Q \wedge P)\) by a derivation. Then write the argument as a paragraph of prose, one sentence per line.

title: Exercise (B2: An assumption that is not used)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Show that \(Q \vdash P \to Q\) , and say which line needs repetition. Show that \(\vdash (P \wedge Q) \to (R \to Q)\) . Let \(x\) be a real number. Write the instance of (a) with \(Q\) : “ \(x^2 \ge 0\) ” and \(P\) : “ \(x > 5\) ” as an English sentence, and say which hypothesis its proof never uses.

title: Exercise (B3: Unwinding an absolute value)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Show that \(P \to Q, \ P \to R \vdash P \to (Q \wedge R)\) . Let \(x\) be a real number. Use (a) to deduce “if \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) , then \(1 < x < 3\) ” from the two facts “if \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) , then \(x > 1\) ” and “if \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) , then \(x < 3\) ”. Write the resulting argument as prose.

title: Exercise (B4: Putting a derivation in order)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Here are nine lines, each a statement with its justification. Seven of them, in the right order and with the right boxes, form a derivation of \(P \to (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (P \to R)\) . Give the order, and say where each box opens and closes. Then say why each of the other two lines cannot be used. \(P \to R\) , by \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) on the box from \(P\) to \(R\) . \(Q\) , assumption. \(R\) , by \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) from \(Q \to R\) and \(Q\) . \(R\) , by \(\rulename{R}\) , repeating the line \(R\) of (iii), written directly below (i). \(P \to (Q \to R)\) , premise. \(Q \to (P \to R)\) , by \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) on the box from \(Q\) to \(P \to R\) . \(R\) , assumption, opening the box for the \(\rulename{{\to}I}\) that proves \(P \to R\) . \(Q \to R\) , by \(\rulename{{\to}E}\) from \(P \to (Q \to R)\) and \(P\) . \(P\) , assumption.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: a line from a closed box)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: A student wants to show \((P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash (P \to (Q \to R)) \wedge (Q \to (P \to R))\) , and offers the following derivation. Lines 1–7 are the first derivation in the proof of @prp-curry . Find the first illegal line, and name the clause of @def-derivation that it breaks. Is the student’s conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. The student defends line 10: “at line 10, both \(P\) and \(Q\) are assumed, exactly as they were at line 5, so \(R\) holds there too.” Explain why @def-derivation does not accept this defense, and show by an instance with real numbers that the move “repeat a line of a closed box” cannot be allowed.

title: Exercise (C2: A hypothesis inside a hypothesis)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Show that \((P \to Q) \to (P \to R) \vdash P \to (Q \to R)\) . Then say, in one sentence, why the premise cannot be used until a third box is opened.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: a derivation and its prose)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: Write a derivation of \(P \to Q, \ (Q \to R) \wedge (R \to S) \vdash P \to S\) , with every line justified. Let \(x\) be a real number, and take \(P\) : “ \(x > 5\) ”, \(Q\) : “ \(x > 4\) ”, \(R\) : “ \(x^2 > 16\) ”, \(S\) : “ \(x^2 > 9\) ”. Say why each premise is true for every real \(x\) . Then write your derivation as fluent prose about \(x\) , one sentence per step.

title: Proposition 1.5.2 (Two Hypotheses or One at a Time)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: \((P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \to R)\) , and \(P \to (Q \to R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.1 (Implication Is Transitive)
page: 1.5 Proving an Implication: the Rule of the Box
content: \(P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to R\) .

title: Definition 1.6.1 (Or-Introduction)
content: The rule given by these two schemas is called \(\rulename{\vee I}\) ( or-introduction ).

title: Example (Derivations with or-introduction)
content: Show that: \(P \vdash P \vee Q\) , and \(P \vdash Q \vee P\) ; \(P \wedge Q \vdash P \vee Q\) ; \(P \to Q \vdash P \to (Q \vee R)\) ; \((P \wedge Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \to (R \vee S))\) .

title: Example (A disjunctive hypothesis splits into two implications)
content: Show that \((P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R)\) .

title: Example (A product with a zero factor)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers, and take as known the school fact “if \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) , then \(a \cdot b = 0\) ”. Prove that if \(a = 0\) , then \(a \cdot b = 0\) , naming the rule behind each step. Then write the step from \(x > 0\) to \(x \ge 0\) as a derivation.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the two schemas of @def-rule-disjunction-introduction from memory, and say which letter in them may stand for a statement that appears in no earlier line. Which of the following sentences, taken from proofs about a real number \(x\) or real numbers \(a\) , \(b\) , use \(\rulename{\vee I}\) ? For each of the others, name the rule it uses. “We have \(x < 3\) , so \(x \le 3\) .” “We found that \(a = 0\) . So \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) , and therefore \(a \cdot b = 0\) .” “Since \(0 < x < 1\) , in particular \(x < 1\) .” “Since \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) implies \(1 < x < 3\) , and \(\abs{x - 2} < 1\) , we get \(1 < x < 3\) .” True or false, with a reason: \(\rulename{\vee I}\) may introduce a side that is false. To show \(Q, \ (P \vee Q) \to (Q \to R) \vdash R\) , which rule writes the first line after the premises, and what is that line? Why is that rule used, although the goal is not a disjunction?

title: Exercise (B1: Committing to a side)
content: Show that \(P \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash Q \to (R \vee S)\) , and that \(P \vdash (Q \vee P) \vee R\) . For each derivation, say at which line you committed to a side of a disjunctive goal, and why that was safe.

title: Exercise (B2: The last line)
content: A search for \(P \to Q, \ Q \to R \vdash P \to (S \vee R)\) has reached the stage below; only the last line is missing. Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B3: A theorem with a weaker hypothesis)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number, and take as known the school fact “if \(x \ge 1\) , then \(x^2 \ge x\) ”. Prove that if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 \ge x\) . Write the proof as a derivation whose premise is the school fact, with \(x \ge 1\) written out as a disjunction, and then as two or three sentences of prose.

title: Exercise (C1: Which new rules are safe?)
content: Suppose someone proposes new rules for the derivations of this chapter. Let \(x\) be a real number. Take the rule “from \(\varphi \vee \psi\) , write \(\varphi\) ”. Starting from the premise “ \(x \ge 0\) or \(x < 0\) ”, which is true for every real \(x\) , derive with it a line that is false at \(x = -1\) . \(\rulename{\vee I}\) adds a side \(\psi\) that may be any statement at all. Explain why it can never lead from a true line to a false one. Is the rule “from \(\varphi\) , write \(\varphi \wedge \psi\) , for any statement \(\psi\) ” safe in the same sense? Justify your answer with an instance.

title: Exercise (C2: Predicting the manufacture)
content: Show that \((P \vee Q) \to (R \wedge S) \vdash P \to S\) . Show that \((P \vee Q) \to R \vdash (P \wedge Q) \to R\) . In each derivation, which rule built the hypothesis of the premise? Could you have predicted, from the premise’s main connective and the shape of its hypothesis alone, that this rule would be needed?

title: Definition 1.7.1 (Rules for Disjunction)
content: The first schema is the rule \(\rulename{\vee E}\) ( or-elimination , or proof by cases ); the other two are \(\rulename{\vee I}\) , as in @def-rule-disjunction-introduction . In \(\rulename{\vee E}\) , each line \(\chi\) (line \(k\) and line \(m\) ) is a line of its box itself, not of a box inside it.

title: Example (A number is at most its absolute value)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Prove that \(\abs{x} \ge x\) , by cases, labeling each step with its rule.

title: Example (The absolute value of a product)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove that \(\abs{xy} = \abs{x}\abs{y}\) .

title: Example (Cases on a hypothesis are two implications)
content: Show that \((P \to R) \wedge (Q \to R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \to R\) .

title: Example (First derivations with “or”)
content: Show that \(P \vee Q \vdash Q \vee P\) , and that \(P \vee P \vdash P\) .

title: Example (Regrouping a disjunction)
content: Show that \(P \vee (Q \vee R) \vdash (P \vee Q) \vee R\) .

title: Example (The triangle inequality by cases)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove that \(\abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State the rule \(\rulename{\vee E}\) as a schema, and name the three things its justification cites. For each sentence, taken from a proof, name the disjunction that supplies the cases and the statement both cases end in. “If \(n\) is even, then \(n^2 + n = n(n + 1)\) is even; if \(n\) is odd, then \(n + 1\) is even and so is \(n(n + 1)\) . Either way, \(n^2 + n\) is even.” “Both possibilities for the sign of \(t\) give \(t^2 \ge 0\) .” Let \(n\) be an integer. True or false, with a reason: “If \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even. Since every integer is even or odd, \(n^2\) is even” is a correct proof by cases that \(n^2\) is even. The following is offered as a derivation of \(P \vee Q, \; P \to R \vdash R\) . Name the line that is not justified and the clause of @def-rules-disjunction it violates. In the first derivation of @prp-distributivity , which line is the disjunction that \(\rulename{\vee E}\) cites at line 10, and where did it come from? Why does each box end in \((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)\) rather than in \(P \wedge Q\) and \(P \wedge R\) ? In the same derivation, why does line 6 use \(\rulename{\vee I}\) to put \(P \wedge Q\) on the left ? Could line 6 have been \((P \wedge R) \vee (P \wedge Q)\) ?

title: Exercise (B1: The other distributive law)
content: Show that \((P \vee Q) \wedge (P \vee R) \vdash P \vee (Q \wedge R)\) . Hint: after taking the premise apart, you will need a case split inside a case.

title: Exercise (B2: The larger of two numbers)
content: For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) , let \(\max(a, b) \coloneqq a\) if \(a \ge b\) , and \(\max(a, b) \coloneqq b\) if \(a < b\) . Prove that \(\max(a, b) \ge a\) and \(\max(a, b) \ge b\) . Hence deduce that \(\max(a, b) \ge \frac{1}{2}(a + b)\) : the larger of two numbers is at least their average.

title: Exercise (B3: Two cases, two conclusions)
content: Show that \(P \vee Q, \; P \to R, \; Q \to S \vdash R \vee S\) . Use (a) to prove: for every integer \(n\) , \(n^2\) is a multiple of \(4\) or \(n^2\) is one more than a multiple of \(4\) . You may use that every integer is even or odd.

title: Exercise (C1: The reverse triangle inequality)
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove that \[ \bigl\lvert \abs{x} - \abs{y} \bigr\rvert \le \abs{x - y} \] by splitting into the two cases \(\abs{x} \ge \abs{y}\) and \(\abs{x} < \abs{y}\) , using in each case the triangle inequality of @exm-triangle-inequality-cases . Then explain why these two cases exhaust all possibilities, and why a split on the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) would need four cases.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a proof, by four cases, that \(\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) . Case 1: \(x \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{x} = x\) . Case 1a: \(y \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = y\) , and \(\abs{x - y}\) is \(x - y\) or \(y - x\) . Since \(x - y \le x \le x + y\) and \(y - x \le y \le x + y\) , we get \(\abs{x - y} \le x + y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Case 1b: \(y < 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = -y\) , and \(x - y > 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = x - y = \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Case 2: \(x < 0\) . Then \(\abs{x} = -x\) . Case 2a: \(y \ge 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = y\) , and \(x - y < 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = y - x = \abs{y} + \abs{x}\) . Case 2b: \(y < 0\) . Then \(\abs{y} = -y\) . Since \(x \ge 0\) and \(y < 0\) , we have \(x - y > 0\) , so \(\abs{x - y} = x - y \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) , because \(x \le \abs{x}\) and \(-y = \abs{y}\) . All four cases give \(\abs{x - y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}\) . Is the statement true? Find the line that is not justified, and name the rule whose conditions it breaks. Show with specific numbers that the step fails. Repair Case 2b.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: a distributive law, rule by rule)
content: Derive \((P \wedge Q) \vee (R \wedge Q) \vdash (P \vee R) \wedge Q\) , naming the rule and the cited lines on every line. Then say which steps would change if the premise were \((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)\) and the goal \(P \wedge (Q \vee R)\) , and which would stay the same.

title: Exercise (C4: The second half)
content: A search for \(Q \vee R, \ Q \to (P \to S), \ R \to S \vdash P \to S\) has written the premises and opened one box; the rest is blank. The finished derivation has 11 lines. Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (R1)
content: Let \(f\) be a function and \([a, b]\) an interval. Take the atomic statements \(C\) : “ \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) ”, \(B\) : “ \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\) ” and \(I\) : “ \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) ”; you need not know what the words mean. Translate the argument “If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and bounded there, then \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) . \(f\) is bounded on \([a, b]\) . \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) . So \(f\) is integrable on \([a, b]\) and bounded there.” into a sequent, and derive it.

title: Exercise (R2)
content: Show that \((P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to R), \ P \wedge S \vdash R \wedge S\) , and say in one sentence which step you found by working backwards from the goal.

title: Exercise (R3)
content: Is \(\vdash (P \wedge (P \to Q)) \to (Q \vee R)\) ? Justify your answer.

title: Proposition 1.7.1 (Distributivity)
content: \(P \wedge (Q \vee R) \vdash (P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R)\) , and \((P \wedge Q) \vee (P \wedge R) \vdash P \wedge (Q \vee R)\) .

title: Definition 2.1.1 (Rules for Contradiction)
content: The left schema is \(\rulename{\neg E}\) ( not-elimination ): if \(\varphi\) and \(\neg\varphi\) stand on lines \(i\) and \(j\) available at line \(k\) , write \(\bot\) , citing both, the unnegated line first. The right schema is \(\rulename{\bot E}\) ( contradiction-elimination , or ex falso ): if \(\bot\) stands on a line \(i\) available at line \(k\) , write any statement \(\varphi\) , citing line \(i\) .

title: Example (The first clashes)
content: Show that (a) \(\bot \vdash P\) , and (b) \(P \wedge Q, \ \neg Q \vdash R\) .

title: Example (An impossible case)
content: Show that \(P \vee Q, \ P \to R, \ \neg R \vdash Q\) .

title: Example (Manufacturing the other half of a clash)
content: Show that \(\neg(P \vee Q) \vdash P \to R\) .

title: Example (An implication with an impossible hypothesis)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Show that if \(x^2 < 0\) , then \(x = 7\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schemas of \(\rulename{\neg E}\) and \(\rulename{\bot E}\) from memory. Match each sentence, taken from proofs, with the rule it uses, \(\rulename{\neg E}\) or \(\rulename{\bot E}\) : “But \(n\) was assumed odd, and we have just shown it is even”; “In this case \(x^2 < 0\) , which is impossible, so there is nothing to prove”. True or false, with a reason: \(\rulename{\bot E}\) lets us write \(\bot\) from any line. In @exm-impossible-case , why is the second box only one line long? In the derivation after @thm-square-even-implies-even , why does line 8 need line 4, and why may it cite it?

title: Exercise (B2: An even successor)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Prove that if \(n + 1\) is even, then \(n\) is odd, by cases on (E1) with one case shown impossible. Tag each step with its rule, as in the proof of @thm-square-even-implies-even .

title: Exercise (B3: Two vacuous promises)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Prove that if \(x^2 + 1 \le 0\) , then \(x > 100\) ; and that if \(x^2 + 1 \le 0\) , then \(x < -100\) . Write each as a derivation with one premise, a school fact, and explain why the two statements together are no paradox.

title: Exercise (C1: A disjunct that cannot hold)
content: Show that \(P \vee (Q \wedge \neg Q) \vdash P\) . What does (a) say about the statement “ \(x > 0\) , or \(x = 1\) and \(x \ne 1\) ”, for a real number \(x\) ?

title: Exercise (C2: A clash that escaped its box)

Find the first line that is not justified, and name the clause of @def-derivation it breaks. Show that the move made at that line can lead from a true premise to a false conclusion. Write a correct derivation.

content: \(P, \ \neg P \vdash Q\) .

content: \(\neg P \vdash P \to Q\) .

title: Theorem 2.1.3 (Even Square, Even Number)
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. If \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

The right schema is \(\rulename{\neg E}\) , recalled from @def-rules-contradiction , so that the rule that proves a negation and the rule that uses one stand together.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schema of \(\rulename{\neg I}\) from memory, and say which statement opens its box. Which rule does this sentence use, and which box does it close? “Suppose \(0\) had a reciprocal \(y\) . Then \(1 = 0 \cdot y = 0\) , which is absurd. So \(0\) has no reciprocal.” In the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational , the sentence “ \(p\) is even” follows from “ \(p^2\) is even”. Which result and which rule justify it? Where in the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational is (L) used, and what would go wrong if (L) said only “ \(r = p/q\) with \(q \ne 0\) ”? Run the proof of @thm-sqrt2-irrational with \(4\) in place of \(2\) : assume \(r^2 = 4\) and write \(r = p/q\) as in (L). Which step can no longer be justified? (The conclusion “no rational number has square \(4\) ” is false, so some step must fail.)

title: Exercise (B1: A box inside a box)
content: Show that \(P \to \neg Q \vdash Q \to \neg P\) . Name the move that opens each box.

title: Exercise (B2: A quadratic with no zero)
content: Let \(x\) be a real number. Prove that \(x^2 - x + 1 \ne 0\) , naming the rules. Hint: complete the square.

title: Exercise (B3: The square root of three)
content: You may use that every integer can be written as \(3k\) , \(3k + 1\) or \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer, in one way only, and that every rational number can be written as \(p/q\) with integers \(p\) , \(q\) , \(q \ne 0\) , and \(p\) , \(q\) not both divisible by \(3\) . Prove that if \(n\) is an integer and \(n^2\) is divisible by \(3\) , then \(n\) is divisible by \(3\) . Hence prove that no rational number has square \(3\) .

title: Exercise (B4: A premise that turns on itself)
content: Show that \(P \to Q, \ Q \to \neg P \vdash \neg P\) . Then say in one sentence what the sequent means.

title: Exercise (C1: The square root of six)
content: Prove that no rational number has square \(6\) . Use only the facts (E1)–(E3) of Section 2.1, (L), and @thm-square-even-implies-even , and name the rule at each logical step.

title: Exercise (C2: A proof that proves too much)
content: Here is a “proof” that \(\sqrt{4}\) is irrational, modeled on @thm-sqrt2-irrational . Suppose \(r\) is rational and \(r^2 = 4\) . Write \(r = p/q\) with \(p\) , \(q\) integers, \(q \ne 0\) , not both divisible by \(4\) . Then \(p^2 = 4q^2\) , so \(4\) divides \(p^2\) . Since \(n^2\) divisible by \(4\) implies \(n\) divisible by \(4\) , we get \(p = 4m\) . Then \(16m^2 = 4q^2\) , so \(q^2 = 4m^2\) , and as before \(4\) divides \(q\) . This contradicts the choice of \(p\) and \(q\) . Hence no rational number has square \(4\) . Explain why the conclusion must be false. Find the step that fails, and show that it fails with a specific integer. Every other step is a correct use of a rule. Which rule turns the “contradiction” into the conclusion, and why is the argument still wrong?

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Irrationality of the Square Root of Two)
content: There is no rational number whose square is \(2\) . In other words, \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Derived Rule)
page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: Let \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \vdash \psi\) be a sequent, written with statement letters, that has already been derived earlier in the book. In a later derivation, replace each letter in \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n, \psi\) by a statement, the same statement for every occurrence of the same letter. If lines \(i_1, \dots, i_n\) , all available at line \(k\) , hold the resulting instances of \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , we may write the resulting instance of \(\psi\) on line \(k\) . The justification names the result and cites \(i_1, \dots, i_n\) . A sequent used in this way is a derived rule . For example, @prp-modus-tollens becomes the rule \(\rulename{MT}\) :

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: labeling a proof)
page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: Here is a proof that for an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is odd, then \(n\) is odd. Suppose \(n^2\) is odd. If \(n\) were even, \(n = 2k\) , then \(n^2 = 2(2k^2)\) would be even; so, by contraposition, since \(n^2\) is not even (it is odd, and no integer is both), \(n\) is not even. As every integer is even or odd, \(n\) is odd. Label each sentence, or part of a sentence, with the rule or rules it uses, primitive or derived. Take as premises the facts (E1) and (E2) of Section 2.1 and the school computation “if \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even”.

page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules
content: \(P \to Q \vdash \neg Q \to \neg P\) .

page: 2.3 Derived Rules: Proved Sequents as New Rules

title: Definition 2.4.2 (Provable Equivalence)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Statements \(P\) and \(Q\) are provably equivalent , written \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) , if \(P \vdash Q\) and \(Q \vdash P\) .

title: Definition 2.4.1 (Rules for the Biconditional)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says

The two schemas below it are the two forms of \(\rulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}\) ( iff-elimination ).

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: State the rules \(\rulename{{\leftrightarrow}I}\) and \(\rulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}\) , and the definition of \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) . For a real number \(x \ge 0\) , consider “ \(x^2 = x\) if and only if \(x = 0\) or \(x = 1\) ”. Write the directions \((\Rightarrow)\) and \((\Leftarrow)\) as implications. Which one would a proof begin with “Suppose \(x^2 = x\) ”? True or false, with a reason: from the definition “an integer \(n\) is even if there is an integer \(k\) with \(n = 2k\) ” and the fact that \(10\) is even, we may conclude that \(10 = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) . True or false, with a reason: from the theorem “if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > 1\) ” and the fact that \(x^2 > 1\) , we may conclude that \(x > 1\) .

page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says

title: Exercise (B3: Strict inequalities)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\) . Deduce from @thm-squares-order and @exm-iff-negations that \(x < y\) if and only if \(x^2 < y^2\) . You may use that, for real numbers \(a\) and \(b\) , \(a < b\) holds exactly when \(b \le a\) fails.

title: Exercise (C1: Divisibility by six)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: For integers \(d\) and \(n\) , write \(d \mid n\) if \(n = dk\) for some integer \(k\) . Let \(n\) be an integer. Which steps of its proof use \(y \ge 0\) , and why is \(x \ge 0\) never needed? Refute \((\Rightarrow)\) with a new pair. title: Proposition 2.4.5 (Proving Equivalence by a Cycle)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: \(P \to Q, \; Q \to R, \; R \to P \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) . Likewise, from the same three premises, \(Q \leftrightarrow R\) and \(R \leftrightarrow P\) are derivable.

title: Proposition 2.4.1 (An Iff Is Two Implications)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: \(P \leftrightarrow Q \vdash (P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to P)\) , and \((P \to Q) \wedge (Q \to P) \vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) .

title: Proposition 2.4.2 (Provable Equivalence and the Biconditional)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: For all statements \(P\) , \(Q\) , \(R\) : \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) if and only if \(\vdash P \leftrightarrow Q\) ; \(P \dashv\vdash P\) ; if \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) , then \(Q \dashv\vdash P\) ; and if \(P \dashv\vdash Q\) and \(Q \dashv\vdash R\) , then \(P \dashv\vdash R\) .

title: Theorem 2.4.3 (Odd Square, Odd Number)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Let \(n\) be an integer. Then \(n\) is odd if and only if \(n^2\) is odd.

title: Theorem 2.4.4 (Squaring Preserves Order)
page: 2.4 Iff, Equivalence, and What a Definition Says
content: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\) . Then \[ x \le y \iff x^2 \le y^2 . \]

title: Definition 2.5.1 (Reductio ad Absurdum)

page: 2.5 Proof by Contradiction and the Classical Rules

title: Definition 2.6.1 (Partial Derivation)
content: A partial derivation is a list of lines laid out as a derivation ( @def-derivation ), except that some stretches of lines are still missing. Each missing stretch is a gap , drawn as a row \(\vdots\) . The line just below a gap is its current goal ; it is already written, but it has no justification yet, since the lines of the gap are to supply one. The lines available at the current goal, in the sense of @def-derivation , are the gap’s resources .

title: Definition 3.1.1 (Formula)
content: The formulas are the strings given by the following clauses. Every atom is a formula, and \(\bot\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) is a formula, then \(\neg\varphi\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are formulas, then \((\varphi \wedge \psi)\) , \((\varphi \vee \psi)\) , \((\varphi \to \psi)\) and \((\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)\) are formulas. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a formation sequence . A formation sequence is a finite list of strings \(\chi_1, \dots, \chi_m\) , with \(m \ge 1\) , in which every entry \(\chi_i\) is an atom or \(\bot\) , or is \(\neg\chi_j\) for some earlier entry \(\chi_j\) (so \(j < i\) ), or is \((\chi_j \circ \chi_l)\) for some earlier entries \(\chi_j\) and \(\chi_l\) (so \(j, l < i\) ; \(j = l\) is allowed) and some binary connective \(\circ\) .

title: Definition 3.1.4 (Height)
content: The height of a formula \(\varphi\) , written \(\hgt(\varphi)\) , is the number of nodes on a longest branch of its parse tree.

title: Definition 3.1.2 (Parse Tree)
content: A parse tree for a formula is defined along the clauses of @def-formula . For an atom or \(\bot\) : a single node, labeled by that atom or by \(\bot\) . If \(T\) is a parse tree for \(\varphi\) , then the tree whose root is labeled \(\neg\) and has \(T\) hanging below it as its only subtree is a parse tree for \(\neg\varphi\) . If \(T\) and \(T'\) are parse trees for \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) , then the tree whose root is labeled \(\circ\) , with \(T\) hanging below it on the left and \(T'\) on the right , is a parse tree for \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) . The leaves are the nodes with nothing below them; a branch is a path from the root down to a leaf.

title: Definition 3.1.3 (Subformula)
content: The subformulas of a formula \(\varphi\) are the formulas whose parse trees hang from the nodes of a parse tree for \(\varphi\) : for each node, the formula of which the part of the tree from that node downwards is a parse tree. The formulas at the children of the root are the immediate subformulas of \(\varphi\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 3.2 Induction on Numbers and on Formulas
content: The following argument claims to prove that every formula contains an even number of parentheses. We prove, by strong induction on \(n\) , that every formula with \(n\) symbols has an even number of parentheses. Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(\chi\) be a formula with \(n\) symbols, and suppose that every formula with fewer than \(n\) symbols has an even number of parentheses. If \(\chi\) is an atom or \(\bot\) , it has no parentheses, and \(0\) is even. If \(\chi = \neg\varphi\) , then \(\varphi\) is a formula with \(n - 1\) symbols, so by hypothesis it has an even number of parentheses; and \(\chi\) has the same parentheses as \(\varphi\) . If \(\chi = (\varphi \circ \psi)\) , remove the outer pair of parentheses. The string \(\varphi \circ \psi\) has \(n - 2\) symbols, so by hypothesis it has an even number of parentheses. Putting the outer pair back adds \(2\) , so \(\chi\) has an even number of parentheses. By @thm-strong-induction , every formula has an even number of parentheses. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why? Show that the move made in that line is illegal by applying the same move to a different property that every formula has, and reaching a false statement. Repair the argument.

title: Lemma 3.2.4 (Parenthesis Count)
page: 3.2 Induction on Numbers and on Formulas
content: Let \(\chi\) be a formula. \(\operatorname{ex}(\chi) = 0\) : \(\chi\) has as many left as right parentheses. Every initial segment \(u\) of \(\chi\) has \(\operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 0\) . If moreover \(\chi\) has the form \((\varphi \circ \psi)\) and \(u\) is proper and nonempty, then \(\operatorname{ex}(u) \ge 1\) . For every occurrence of a binary connective in \(\chi\) , the initial segment of \(\chi\) that ends just before that occurrence has excess at least \(1\) .

title: Theorem 3.2.2 (Strong Induction)

title: Theorem 3.2.3 (Structural Induction)
page: 3.2 Induction on Numbers and on Formulas
content: Let \(P(\varphi)\) be a property of formulas. Suppose that \(P(p)\) holds for every atom \(p\) , and \(P(\bot)\) holds; for every formula \(\varphi\) , if \(P(\varphi)\) holds, then \(P(\neg\varphi)\) holds; for all formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) and each binary connective \(\circ\) , if \(P(\varphi)\) and \(P(\psi)\) hold, then \(P((\varphi \circ \psi))\) holds. Then \(P(\varphi)\) holds for every formula \(\varphi\) .

title: Theorem 3.2.5 (Unique Readability)
page: 3.2 Induction on Numbers and on Formulas
content: Let \(\chi\) be a formula that is neither an atom nor \(\bot\) . Then exactly one of the following holds: \(\chi = \neg\varphi\) for a formula \(\varphi\) ; \(\chi = (\varphi \circ \psi)\) for formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) and a binary connective \(\circ\) . In case (i), \(\varphi\) is uniquely determined by \(\chi\) ; in case (ii), \(\circ\) , \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are uniquely determined by \(\chi\) .

title: Definition 3.3.3 (Truth Table)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and let \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) be a list of distinct atoms that includes every atom of \(\varphi\) . A row is an assignment of a truth value to each of \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) . The truth table of \(\varphi\) (on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) ) lists, for each of the \(2^n\) rows, the value \(v(\varphi)\) for a valuation \(v\) that agrees with the row on \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) . We say \(\varphi\) is true (or false) in the row.

title: Definition 3.3.2 (Truth Value of a Formula)
content: Let \(v\) be a valuation. The truth value \(v(\varphi)\) of a formula \(\varphi\) under \(v\) is defined by recursion on \(\varphi\) : for an atom \(p\) , \(v(p)\) is the value the valuation assigns to \(p\) ; and \(v(\bot) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\neg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) , and \(v(\neg\varphi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; \(v(\varphi \wedge \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\varphi \vee \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) or \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) (or both); otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) ; \(v(\varphi \to \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{F}\) if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{F}\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{T}\) ; \(v(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi) \coloneqq \mathrm{T}\) if \(v(\varphi) = v(\psi)\) ; otherwise \(\mathrm{F}\) . We say \(\varphi\) is true under \(v\) , or \(v\) makes \(\varphi\) true, if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ; otherwise \(\varphi\) is false under \(v\) .

title: Definition 3.3.1 (Valuation)
content: A valuation \(v\) assigns to every atom \(p\) exactly one of the two truth values \(\mathrm{T}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) . We write \(v(p)\) for the value it assigns to \(p\) , and say that \(p\) is true under \(v\) if \(v(p) = \mathrm{T}\) , false under \(v\) if \(v(p) = \mathrm{F}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The rows of implication are forced)
content: Pretend we do not know the table of \(\to\) . Say only that there is some table: a rule \(t\) giving a truth value \(t(a, b)\) for each pair of truth values \(a, b\) , with \[ v(\varphi \to \psi) = t\bigl( v(\varphi), v(\psi) \bigr) \] for every valuation \(v\) and all formulas \(\varphi\) , \(\psi\) . (The other connectives keep their clauses.) Suppose the two rules for implication preserve truth in the following sense. For every valuation \(v\) and all formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) : if \(v(\varphi \to \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) . For every list of formulas \(\Gamma\) and all formulas \(\varphi, \psi\) : if every valuation that makes all of \(\Gamma\) and \(\varphi\) true makes \(\psi\) true, then every valuation that makes all of \(\Gamma\) true makes \(\varphi \to \psi\) true. Prove that \(t\) is the table of (V5): \(t(\mathrm{T}, \mathrm{F}) = \mathrm{F}\) , and \(t(a, b) = \mathrm{T}\) for the other three pairs.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Let \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) be the all-T valuation. Every formula built from atoms by \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) and \(\to\) only is true under \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) . Proof. By @thm-structural-induction , with the property “if \(\varphi\) is built from atoms by \(\wedge\) , \(\vee\) , \(\to\) only, then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) ”. The formulas \(\bot\) , \(\neg\varphi\) and \(\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) are not built in this way, so the property holds for them. If a formula built in this way is \(\varphi \wedge \psi\) , \(\varphi \vee \psi\) or \(\varphi \to \psi\) , then \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are built in this way too, so the hypothesis applies to them. (1) For an atom \(p\) , \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(p) = \mathrm{T}\) by the definition of \(v_{\mathrm{T}}\) . (2) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \wedge \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V3). (3) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V4), since at least one part is true. (4) If \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi \to \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) by (V5), because \(v_{\mathrm{T}}(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) and an implication with a false hypothesis is true. This covers every clause, and proves the claim. Is the claim true? Name the line that fails and say exactly what is wrong with it. Give a formula on which the reason given in that line is false. Repair the line.

title: Lemma 3.3.1 (Coincidence Lemma)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, and let \(v\) and \(w\) be valuations that agree on \(\atoms(\varphi)\) . Then \(v(\varphi) = w(\varphi)\) .

title: Definition 3.4.2 (Satisfiable)
content: A formula \(\varphi\) is satisfiable if there is a valuation \(v\) with \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) . A list of formulas \(\Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) , where \(n \ge 0\) , is satisfiable if there is a valuation that makes every \(\varphi_i\) true. A formula or list that is not satisfiable is unsatisfiable .

title: Definition 3.4.4 (Semantic Equivalence)
content: Formulas \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are semantically equivalent , written \(\varphi \equiv \psi\) , if \(\varphi \models \psi\) and \(\psi \models \varphi\) .

title: Definition 3.4.1 (Tautology and Contradiction)
content: A formula \(\varphi\) is a tautology if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) for every valuation \(v\) . It is a contradiction if \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{F}\) for every valuation \(v\) .

title: Definition 3.4.3 (Semantic Entailment)
content: Let \(\Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) be a list of formulas, where \(n \ge 0\) , and let \(\psi\) be a formula. We say \(\Gamma\) semantically entails \(\psi\) , and write \[ \Gamma \models \psi , \] if every valuation that makes all of \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) true also makes \(\psi\) true. We then also call the argument from \(\Gamma\) to \(\psi\) valid . We write \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n \models \psi\) for \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , and \(\models \psi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty. If \(\Gamma \models \psi\) fails, we write \(\Gamma \not\models \psi\) , and a valuation that makes every formula of \(\Gamma\) true and \(\psi\) false is a refuting valuation , or refuting row .

title: Example (Affirming the consequent is not valid)

content: Decide whether \((p \to q) \to r \models p \to (q \to r)\) , and whether \(p \to (q \to r) \models (p \to q) \to r\) .

A substitution \(\sigma\) of \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) for \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) is defined by the clauses in the text, with \(\sigma(\chi \mathbin{|} \theta) \coloneqq \sigma(\chi) \mathbin{|} \sigma(\theta)\) added. title: Lemma 3.4.2 (Replacement)
content: Let \(\varphi \equiv \varphi'\) . If \(\chi'\) is obtained from a formula \(\chi\) by replacing one occurrence of \(\varphi\) in \(\chi\) by \(\varphi'\) , then \(\chi' \equiv \chi\) .

content: Let \(\sigma\) be the substitution of \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n\) for the distinct atoms \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) . If \(\models \chi\) , then \(\models \sigma(\chi)\) . If \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , then \(\sigma(\Gamma) \models \sigma(\psi)\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Ordering the \veeE case)
content: Here are nine lines. Seven of them, in the right order, form the \(\rulename{\vee E}\) case of the proof of @thm-soundness . Line \(k\) is \(\chi\) , by \(\rulename{\vee E}\) citing line \(i\) (holding \(\varphi \vee \psi\) ), the box from line \(a\) to line \(b\) (opening with \(\varphi\) , ending with \(\chi\) ), and the box from line \(c\) to line \(d\) (opening with \(\psi\) , ending with \(\chi\) ). Give an admissible order, and say why each of the other two lines cannot be used. (i) By the induction hypothesis for lines \(b\) and \(d\) , which come before line \(k\) , \(\Gamma_b \models \chi\) and \(\Gamma_d \models \chi\) . Hence \(v(\chi) = \mathrm{T}\) in either case; since \(v\) was arbitrary, \(\Gamma_k \models \chi\) . Let \(v\) be a valuation making every formula of \(\Gamma_k\) true. If \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v\) makes every formula of \(\Gamma_d\) true, so \(v(\chi) = \mathrm{T}\) . (v) By @lem-context-inclusion (a), \(\Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k\) , so \(v\) makes every formula of \(\Gamma_i\) true; by the induction hypothesis for line \(i\) , \(v(\varphi \vee \psi) = \mathrm{T}\) , so \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) or \(v(\psi) = \mathrm{T}\) . By the induction hypothesis for line \(k\) , \(\Gamma_k \models \chi\) . By @lem-context-inclusion (b), \(\Gamma_b\) is \(\Gamma_k\) with \(\varphi\) added, and \(\Gamma_d\) is \(\Gamma_k\) with \(\psi\) added. If \(v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T}\) , then \(v\) makes every formula of \(\Gamma_b\) true, so \(v(\chi) = \mathrm{T}\) . Line \(b\) is inside the box, and the box was cited at line \(k\) , so the context of line \(b\) is \(\Gamma_k\) ; the induction hypothesis for line \(b\) then gives \(\Gamma_k \models \chi\) directly.

title: Lemma 3.5.1 (Contexts in a Derivation)
content: Let lines \(i\) , \(k\) and \(a \le b\) belong to a derivation, and let \(\Gamma_j\) denote the context of line \(j\) . If line \(i\) is available at line \(k\) , then \(\Gamma_i \subseteq \Gamma_k\) . If line \(k\) is justified by a box rule citing the box whose first line is \(a\) and whose last line is \(b\) , then the formulas of \(\Gamma_b\) are exactly those of \(\Gamma_k\) together with \(\varphi_a\) , the assumption of that box. We write this \(\Gamma_b = \Gamma_k, \varphi_a\) .

title: Theorem 3.5.2 (Soundness)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \models \psi\) .

title: Corollary 3.6.6 (Derivable Means Valid)
content: For every list of formulas \(\Gamma\) and every formula \(\psi\) , \[ \Gamma \vdash \psi \iff \Gamma \models \psi . \] In particular, whether \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) holds can be decided by checking the \(2^n\) rows of a truth table, where \(n\) is the number of atoms occurring in \(\Gamma\) and \(\psi\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These questions are about @lem-truth-table-line and @thm-completeness . In the conjunction case of the proof of @lem-truth-table-line , suppose \(v(\alpha) = \mathrm{F}\) and \(v(\beta) = \mathrm{T}\) . Which sequent of @lem-connective-rows is used, and which induction hypotheses? Where is \(\rulename{RAA}\) used in the proof of @thm-completeness , including inside the results it cites? Step 1 lists the atoms without repetition . Where in the proof is that used? Which step of the proof fails if \(\Gamma\) is allowed to be an infinite collection of formulas, each with its own atoms?

title: Lemma 3.6.3 (One Row of the Truth Table Is Derivable)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, let \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) ( \(n \ge 0\) ) be atoms among which are all the atoms of \(\varphi\) , and let \(v\) be a valuation. Then \[ p_1^{v}, \dots, p_n^{v} \vdash \varphi^{v} . \]

title: Lemma 3.6.1 (Weakening and Cut)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\) be lists of formulas, and let \(\varphi\) , \(\psi\) , \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m\) ( \(m \ge 1\) ), and \(\beta\) be formulas. Weakening. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) and every member of \(\Gamma\) is a member of \(\Delta\) , then \(\Delta \vdash \psi\) . In particular, \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) implies \(\Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi\) . Cut. If \(\Gamma \vdash \varphi\) and \(\Gamma, \varphi \vdash \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) . Chaining. If \(\Gamma \vdash \alpha_i\) for every \(i = 1, \dots, m\) , and \(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_m \vdash \beta\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \beta\) .

title: Theorem 3.6.5 (Completeness)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \models \psi\) , then \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) .

title: Definition 3.7.5 (Adequate Set of Connectives)
content: A set \(S\) of connectives is adequate if every truth function, with any number \(n \ge 1\) of inputs, is expressed by some formula in \(S\) .

title: Definition 3.7.3 (Conjunctive Normal Form)
content: A formula has conjunctive normal form (CNF), or is in CNF , when it has the shape \(K_1 \wedge \dots \wedge K_k\) , with \(k \ge 1\) , where every \(K_i\) joins one or more literals by \(\vee\) .

title: Definition 3.7.2 (Disjunctive Normal Form)
content: A formula has disjunctive normal form (DNF), or is in DNF , when it has the shape \(C_1 \vee \dots \vee C_k\) , with \(k \ge 1\) , where every \(C_i\) joins one or more literals by \(\wedge\) .

title: Definition 3.7.1 (Literal)
content: A literal is an atom or the negation of an atom.

title: Definition 3.7.4 (Truth Function)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . A truth function with \(n\) inputs assigns to each list \((a_1, \dots, a_n)\) of truth values (each \(a_i\) is \(\mathrm{T}\) or \(\mathrm{F}\) ) a truth value \(f(a_1, \dots, a_n)\) . A formula \(\varphi\) expresses \(f\) if \[ v(\varphi) = f\bigl(v(p_1), \dots, v(p_n)\bigr) \quad \text{for every valuation } v . \]

title: Proposition 3.7.3 (Validity of a CNF)
content: A formula in CNF is a tautology exactly when every clause contains some atom together with its negation. A formula in DNF is satisfiable exactly when some conjunct contains no atom together with its negation.

title: Theorem 3.7.4 (Adequate Sets)
Theorem 3.7.2 (Conjunctive Normal Form)
content: Every formula \(\varphi\) is equivalent to a formula in CNF. If \(\varphi\) has at least one atom, the CNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \(\varphi\) .

title: Theorem 3.7.1 (Disjunctive Normal Form)
content: Every formula \(\varphi\) is equivalent to a formula in DNF. If \(\varphi\) has at least one atom, the DNF can be chosen so that every atom in it is an atom of \(\varphi\) .

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Bounded Quantifier)
content: Let \(A\) be a set, \(x\) a variable, and \(\varphi\) an open sentence. The bounded quantifiers are the abbreviations \[ \begin{aligned} \forall x \in A \; \varphi \quad &\text{stands for} \quad \forall x\, (x \in A \to \varphi), \\ \exists x \in A \; \varphi \quad &\text{stands for} \quad \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge \varphi). \end{aligned} \] In the same way, for a term \(a\) in which \(x\) does not occur, \(\forall x > a \; \varphi\) stands for \(\forall x\, (x > a \to \varphi)\) and \(\exists x > a \; \varphi\) for \(\exists x\, (x > a \wedge \varphi)\) , and likewise with \(\ge\) , \(<\) , \(\le\) in place of \(>\) .

title: Definition 4.2.2 (First-Order Formula)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: The formulas (of predicate logic, or first-order formulas ) are the strings given by the following clauses. Atomic formulas. If \(R\) is a predicate symbol of arity \(n\) and \(t_1, \dots, t_n\) are terms, then \(R(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) is a formula. If \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) are terms, then \(t_1 = t_2\) is a formula. And \(\bot\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) is a formula, then \(\neg\varphi\) is a formula. If \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are formulas, then \((\varphi \wedge \psi)\) , \((\varphi \vee \psi)\) , \((\varphi \to \psi)\) , and \((\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi)\) are formulas. If \(\varphi\) is a formula and \(x\) is a variable , then \(\forall x\, \varphi\) and \(\exists x\, \varphi\) are formulas. Nothing else is a formula: a string is a formula only if it is the last entry of a finite list in which every entry is an atomic formula, or is built by (Fm2), (Fm3) or (Fm4) from earlier entries.

title: Definition 4.2.6 (Free For)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Let \(t\) be a term, \(x\) a variable, and \(\varphi\) a formula. The term \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) if no free occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) lies in the scope of a quantifier \(\forall y\) or \(\exists y\) such that \(y\) is a variable of \(t\) .

title: Definition 4.2.3 (Free and Bound Variables)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and \(x\) a variable. An occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) is an appearance of \(x\) inside one of the terms of an atomic formula of \(\varphi\) . (The \(x\) written just after a quantifier symbol, as in \(\forall x\) , is part of the quantifier node and is not an occurrence.) An occurrence of \(x\) is bound if the path from its leaf up to the root of the parse tree passes through a quantifier node \(\forall x\) or \(\exists x\) , with the same variable \(x\) . The lowest such node binds the occurrence. An occurrence that is not bound is free . The scope of a quantifier node is the part of the tree below it: the formula it governs. The variable \(x\) is a free variable of \(\varphi\) , or is free in \(\varphi\) , if at least one occurrence of \(x\) in \(\varphi\) is free.

title: Definition 4.2.4 (Sentence)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: A sentence is a formula with no free variables.

title: Definition 4.2.1 (Term)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: The terms are the strings given by the following clauses. Every variable is a term, and every constant symbol is a term. If \(f\) is a function symbol of arity \(n\) and \(t_1, \dots, t_n\) are terms, then \(f(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) is a term. Nothing else is a term: a string is a term only if it is the last entry of a finite list of strings in which every entry is a variable, a constant symbol, or \(f(s_1, \dots, s_n)\) for some function symbol \(f\) of arity \(n\) and earlier entries \(s_1, \dots, s_n\) .

title: Exercise (B2: The set of free variables)
page: 4.2 Terms, Formulas, Free Variables and Substitution
content: For a term \(t\) , let \(\mathrm{Var}(t)\) be the set of variables of \(t\) , and for a formula \(\varphi\) , let \(\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)\) be the set of its free variables. content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable and \(t\) a term, with \(t\) free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) , and with \(x\) free in \(\varphi\) . Prove that the free variables of \(\varphi[t/x]\) are the free variables of \(\varphi\) other than \(x\) , together with the variables of \(t\) : \[ \mathrm{FV}(\varphi[t/x]) = \bigl( \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\} \bigr) \cup \mathrm{Var}(t), \] with the notation of B2. Show, with the capture example \(\exists y\, (y > x)\) , \(t = y + 1\) , that the conclusion can fail when \(t\) is not free for \(x\) . Show also, with an example of your own, that it can fail when \(x\) is not free in \(\varphi\) .
