title: Definition 4.3.1 (Universal Elimination)
content: Here \(\varphi\) is a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(t\) any term, subject to one side condition: \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) (the scope rule of @def-derivation ). This rule is called \(\rulename{\forall E}\) ( universal elimination , or instantiation ), and \(\varphi[t/x]\) is an instance of \(\forall x\, \varphi\) .

title: Example (Instantiation at work)
content: Give a derivation of each sequent. \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)), \ P(c) \vdash Q(c)\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(c, c)\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, (R(x, y) \to R(y, x)), \ R(a, b) \vdash R(b, a)\) . \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to P(f(x))), \ P(c) \vdash P(f(f(c)))\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the schema of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) and its side condition from memory. For each pair, decide whether line 2 follows from line 1 by one application of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) . If not, name the clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination that fails. Line 1: \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (y > x)\) ; line 2: \(\exists y\, (y > y)\) . Line 1: \(\forall x\, (x \cdot x \ge 0)\) ; line 2: \(3 \cdot x \ge 0\) . Line 1: \(\forall x\, P(x) \to P(c)\) ; line 2: \(P(a) \to P(c)\) . Line 1: \(\forall x\, (P(x) \to P(f(x)))\) ; line 2: \(P(f(c)) \to P(f(f(c)))\) . True or false, with a reason: from \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)\) , one application of \(\rulename{\forall E}\) gives \(\forall x\, R(x, c)\) . Why does \(\rulename{\forall E}\) not need a line saying that the term \(t\) names an element of the domain?

title: Exercise (B1: Two links)
content: Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)), \ \forall x\, (Q(x) \to R(x)), \ P(a) \vdash R(a), \] and say, for each \(\rulename{\forall E}\) line, which line of the search asked for its term.

title: Exercise (B2: An increasing function)
content: Read \(f\) as a function from \(\nR\) to \(\nR\) and \(a, b, c\) as real numbers. Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, \forall y\, (x \le y \to f(x) \le f(y)), \ a \le b, \ b \le c \ \vdash \ f(a) \le f(b) \wedge f(b) \le f(c) , \] and then write the argument as one sentence of prose.

title: Exercise (B3: Squares are not negative)
content: Let \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers. Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (x^2 \ge 0) \vdash (a + b)^2 \ge 0 \wedge (a - b)^2 \ge 0 . \] Then extend it by one line justified “arith” to a derivation of \(a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab\) from the same premise, and say which earlier line the arith line uses.

title: Exercise (C1: A partner makes a loop)
content: A relation \(R\) is symmetric if \(R(x, y)\) gives \(R(y, x)\) , and transitive if \(R(x, y)\) and \(R(y, z)\) give \(R(x, z)\) . Show that in a symmetric and transitive relation, every element that is related to something is related to itself, by giving a derivation of \[ \begin{aligned} &\forall x\, \forall y\, (R(x, y) \to R(y, x)), \\ &\forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, ((R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z)) \to R(x, z)), \ R(a, b) \ \vdash \ R(a, a) . \end{aligned} \] Explain how each term of each \(\rulename{\forall E}\) was chosen.

title: Exercise (C2: Instantiating at the variable itself)
content: Show that \(\forall x\, P(x) \vdash P(x)\) , by a derivation whose one \(\rulename{\forall E}\) line you check against every clause of @def-rule-universal-elimination . The reverse step, from a line \(P(x)\) to \(\forall x\, P(x)\) , is an instance of no rule so far. Show that it must not be allowed without restriction: give a reading over \(\nZ\) , with \(x\) naming one particular integer, in which \(P(x)\) is true and \(\forall x\, P(x)\) is false. Section 4.4 will allow the step from a line \(P(x_0)\) to \(\forall x\, P(x)\) under conditions on the name \(x_0\) : the line \(P(x_0)\) must close a special box opened for \(x_0\) , and \(x_0\) must appear in no premise, in no assumption still in force, and not in the conclusion \(\forall x\, P(x)\) . Using this description, explain why the route “ \(\forall x\, P(x)\) , so \(P(x)\) , so \(\forall x\, P(x)\) ” cannot use the letter \(x\) as the name, what it must do instead, and why no name at all will do when \(P(x)\) is itself the premise.

title: Definition 4.4.1 (Rules for the Universal Quantifier)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: The rule on the left is \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ( universal introduction , or generalization ). It cites a flagged box, with flag \(x_0\) , from its first line \(i\) to its last line \(j\) , and writes \(\forall x\, \varphi\) on line \(k\) . The flag \(x_0\) is a variable . The box’s last line \(j\) is \(\varphi[x_0/x]\) , and it is a line of the flagged box itself , not of a box inside it. The side condition is on the name: at line \(k\) , \(x_0\) appears in no premise , \(x_0\) appears in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and \(x_0\) does not appear in \(\forall x\, \varphi\) . The rule on the right is \(\rulename{\forall E}\) , as in @def-rule-universal-elimination : \(t\) is any term free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) .

title: Example (Flagged boxes at work)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: Give a derivation of each sequent; in (b), of each direction. \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash \forall x\, R(x, x)\) . \(\forall y\, \varphi \dashv\vdash \forall z\, \varphi[z/y]\) , for a formula \(\varphi\) and variables \(y\) , \(z\) with \(z\) not appearing in \(\varphi\) . \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash \forall y\, \forall x\, R(x, y)\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: Three derivations, D1, D2 and D3, are used in part (b). D1: D2: D3: Write the schema of \(\rulename{\forall I}\) with its side condition. For each of D1, D2, D3, decide whether its \(\rulename{\forall I}\) line is legal. If not, name the clause of the side condition that fails. True or false, with a reason: “fresh” means that \(x_0\) appears nowhere in the derivation outside its flagged box. In the derivation of the \((\vdash)\) half of @prp-forall-and , the name \(x_0\) flags two boxes. Why does the side condition allow this?

title: Exercise (B1: A chain, for every x)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: Give a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (P(x) \to Q(x)), \ \forall x\, (Q(x) \to R(x)) \vdash \forall x\, (P(x) \to R(x)), \] and check the side condition at its \(\rulename{\forall I}\) line.

title: Exercise (B2: Contraposition under a quantifier)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content:
Give a derivation of \( orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x)) \vdash  orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x)\) . Try to derive the converse, \( orall x\, 
eg Q(x) 	o  orall x\, 
eg P(x) \vdash  orall x\, (P(x) 	o Q(x))\) . Say where the search stalls, and which side condition stops it.

title: Exercise (B3: A number is at most its absolute value, for every number)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: @exm-abs-at-least-x (Section 1.7) derived \(\abs{x} > x \vee \abs{x} = x\) for one fixed real \(x\) from three premises about that \(x\) : \(x \ge 0 \vee x < 0\) , \(x \ge 0 \to \abs{x} = x\) , and \(x < 0 \to \abs{x} > x\) . Turn it into a derivation of \[ \forall x\, (\abs{x} > x \vee \abs{x} = x) \] from premises that are universal statements. Explain why the premises of @exm-abs-at-least-x , copied with \(x_0\) in place of \(x\) , will not do.

title: Exercise (C1: How fresh is fresh?)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: Give a derivation of \(\forall x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash R(x_0, x_0) \wedge \forall x\, R(x, x)\) in which the line \(R(x_0, x_0)\) is written before a flagged box that uses the same name \(x_0\) . Check every clause of the side condition at the \(\rulename{\forall I}\) line. A stronger condition is sometimes proposed: “ \(x_0\) occurs nowhere in the derivation outside its box”. Does your derivation meet it? Explain why the conclusion of your derivation is nonetheless correct, so that the stronger condition forbids more than it needs to. Could the last line of the flagged box in (a) be obtained by \(\rulename{R}\) , repeating the earlier line \(R(x_0, x_0)\) ? Is the result a derivation?

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: A student offers this proof. Claim. For every real number \(x\) , \(x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0\) . Proof. (1) Let \(x\) be a real number. (2) At \(x = 0\) : \(0 - 0 + 1 = 1 \ge 0\) . (3) At \(x = 1\) : \(1 - 2 + 1 = 0 \ge 0\) . (4) At \(x = 2\) : \(4 - 4 + 1 = 1 \ge 0\) . (5) So \(x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0\) , and since \(x\) was arbitrary, the claim holds for every real \(x\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? Name the step that fails and the rule it misuses. Show that the step can lead to a false conclusion: give a polynomial \(p\) for which the same checks at \(x = 0, 1, 2\) succeed and \(p(x) \ge 0\) fails for some real \(x\) . Point to a correct proof.

title: Proposition 4.4.1 (Universal Quantifier and Conjunction)
page: 4.4 Proving "For Every": Let x Be Arbitrary
content: \[ \forall x\, (P(x) \wedge Q(x)) \dashv\vdash \forall x\, P(x) \wedge \forall x\, Q(x) . \]

title: Definition 4.5.1 (Existential Introduction)
content: The rule given by this schema is called \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ( existential introduction ). Here \(\varphi\) is any formula, \(x\) any variable, and \(t\) any term, subject to one side condition: \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Line \(i\) must be available at line \(k\) ( @def-derivation ).

title: Example (Derivations with existential introduction)
content: Show that: \(P(c) \wedge Q(c) \vdash \exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \wedge Q(x) \bigr)\) ; \(R(c, c) \vdash \exists x\, R(x, c) \wedge \exists x\, R(x, x)\) ; and decide whether one \(\rulename{\exists I}\) step leads from \(\exists x\, R(x, x)\) to \(\exists x\, R(x, c)\) ; \(\forall x\, R(x, x) \vdash \forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y)\) ; \(\forall x\, \bigl( P(x) \to Q(f(x)) \bigr), \ P(c) \vdash \exists y\, Q(y)\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State \(\rulename{\exists I}\) as a schema, with its side condition. Line 1 of a derivation is \(R(c, f(c))\) . Which of the following may line 2 be, by one application of \(\rulename{\exists I}\) to line 1? For each that may, give \(\varphi\) and the witness \(t\) ; for each that may not, say why. \(\exists x\, R(x, f(c))\) ; (ii) \(\exists x\, R(c, x)\) ; (iii) \(\exists x\, R(x, f(x))\) ; (iv) \(\exists x\, R(x, x)\) ; (v) \(\exists x\, R(f(c), x)\) . Line 1 of a derivation is \(\forall y\, (y \le y \cdot y)\) . Is \(\exists x\, \forall y\, (y \le x \cdot x)\) a legal \(\rulename{\exists I}\) step from line 1? Read both lines over \(\nZ\) : which is true? True or false, with a reason: from the line \(\exists x\, P(x)\) , one application of \(\rulename{\exists I}\) gives \(P(c)\) . The current goal of a search is \(\exists x\, \varphi\) and no available line is an instance of \(\varphi\) . What does the search method say to do, and why not choose a witness now?

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Derive \(\forall x\, \bigl( P(x) \to Q(x) \bigr), \ P(a) \vdash \exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \wedge Q(x) \bigr)\) . In the Idea, say which rule each line was chosen by: the goal or a premise.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Over \(\nR\) , with the premise \(\forall x\, \bigl( x + (-x) = 0 \bigr)\) , derive \(\forall x\, \exists y\, (x + y = 0)\) , the true sentence (i) of @exm-quantifier-order-sum . Say what the witness is, and what it depends on.

title: Exercise (B3)
content: Over \(\nZ\) , prove “there is an integer \(n\) with \(n^2 = n + 2\) ” as a derivation whose only line not justified by a rule is one line of arithmetic justified “arith”; write \(n^2\) as \(n \cdot n\) . Then write the proof as one sentence.

title: Exercise (C1: The conclusion clause of for-all-introduction)
content: The side condition of \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ( @def-rules-universal ) has three clauses about the flag \(x_0\) : it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at the \(\rulename{\forall I}\) line, and not in the conclusion \(\forall x\, \varphi\) . Show that the third clause is needed: give a “derivation” that breaks only that clause, from a premise that is true over \(\nN\) to a sentence ( @def-sentence ) that is false over \(\nN\) . Check that every other step is legal.

title: Exercise (C2: A witness is not a name)
content: Explain why the rules so far (Chapters 1–2 and \(\rulename{\forall E}\) , \(\rulename{\forall I}\) , \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ) cannot derive \(\exists x\, P(x) \vdash P(c)\) . Go through the rules that could produce the last line \(P(c)\) , and say what each would need. Then say, in one sentence, why no rule for using \(\exists\) should give \(P(c)\) .

title: Proposition 4.5.1 (Every Implies Some)
content: \(\forall x\, P(x) \vdash \exists x\, P(x)\) .

title: Definition 4.6.1 (Rules for the Existential Quantifier)
content: The rule on the left is \(\rulename{\exists E}\) ( existential elimination ). It cites a line \(h\) holding \(\exists x\, \varphi\) and a flagged box with the name \(x_0\) , a variable, whose first line is the assumption \(\varphi[x_0/x]\) and whose last line \(j\) , a line of that box itself, is \(\chi\) ; line \(h\) and the box must be available at line \(k\) ( @def-derivation , with the flagged boxes of Section 4.4). The new line \(k\) repeats \(\chi\) . Side condition, at line \(k\) : the name \(x_0\) does not appear in \(\chi\) , in \(\exists x\, \varphi\) , in any premise, or in any assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) . The rule on the right is \(\rulename{\exists I}\) , recalled from @def-rule-existential-introduction : \(t\) is any term free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) .

title: Example (Derivations with existential elimination)
content: Show that: \(\exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \vee Q(x) \bigr) \dashv\vdash \exists x\, P(x) \vee \exists x\, Q(x)\) ; \(\exists x\, P(x), \ \forall x\, \bigl( P(x) \to \neg Q(x) \bigr) \vdash \neg \forall x\, Q(x)\) .

title: Example (The sum of two even integers is even)
content: Over \(\nZ\) , with “ \(n\) is even” written \(\exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k)\) , derive \[ \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k), \ \exists k\, (m = 2 \cdot k) \;\vdash\; \exists k\, (n + m = 2 \cdot k) . \]

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These parts are about the proof of @prp-exists-forall-swap . State \(\rulename{\exists E}\) as a schema, with every clause of its side condition. The proof opened the flagged box of \(y_0\) first and the \(\rulename{\exists E}\) box of \(x_0\) inside it. Could they be opened in the other order? If so, does every side condition still hold? Answer the Before reading on prompt of the proof: at line 5, where could \(x_0\) still appear, and does it? In the two attempts at the converse, \(\forall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y) \vdash \exists x\, \forall y\, R(x, y)\) , which line is blocked in each, and by which clause of which rule? Give the idea of the proof in two sentences.

Derive \( orall x\,

title: Exercise (B2: Fix, obtain, choose, faded)
content: Here is a derivation of \[ \forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y), \ \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( R(x, y) \to Q(y) \bigr) \;\vdash\; \forall x\, \exists y\, \bigl( R(x, y) \wedge Q(y) \bigr) \] with its last line missing. Name the move, then complete it. Then mark which lines are the “fix”, which the “obtain”, and which the “choose”.

title: Exercise (B3)
content: An integer \(n\) is odd when \(n = 2k + 1\) for some integer \(k\) . Over \(\nZ\) , derive \[ \exists k\, (m = 2 \cdot k + 1), \ \exists k\, (n = 2 \cdot k + 1) \;\vdash\; \exists k\, (m \cdot n = 2 \cdot k + 1), \] with one line justified “arith”. Then write the proof as three sentences of prose.

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Derive \[ \exists x\, \forall y\, R(x, y), \ \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( R(x, y) \to R(y, x) \bigr) \;\vdash\; \forall y\, \exists x\, R(y, x), \] and check the side condition of every \(\rulename{\exists E}\) and \(\rulename{\forall I}\) line. Then give a reading over \(\nZ\) in which both premises are true, and say which integer the derivation’s witness is.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a “derivation” of \(\exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \wedge Q(x) \bigr) \vdash \exists x\, P(x)\) . Is the conclusion derivable from the premise? Justify your answer. Does this derivation prove it? If not, name the exact line that fails, the rule, and the clause of its side condition that is broken. Show that the illegal step itself is unsound: use the same step to “derive”, from a premise true over \(\nZ\) , a sentence false over \(\nZ\) .

title: Proposition 4.6.1 (Some Distributes Over And, One Way)
content: \(\exists x\, \bigl( P(x) \wedge Q(x) \bigr) \vdash \exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x)\) .

title: Proposition 4.6.2 (Some-All Gives All-Some)
content: \(\exists x\, \forall y\, R(x, y) \vdash \forall y\, \exists x\, R(x, y)\) .

title: Definition 4.7.1 (Rules for Equality)
content: The rule \(\rulename{{=}I}\) ( equality introduction , or reflexivity) writes \(t = t\) for any term \(t\) , at any line, citing nothing. The rule \(\rulename{{=}E}\) ( equality elimination , or substitution of equals) cites an equation \(t_1 = t_2\) on line \(i\) and a line \(j\) of the form \(\varphi[t_1/x]\) , both available at line \(k\) , and writes \(\varphi[t_2/x]\) on line \(k\) . Here \(\varphi\) is any formula and \(x\) any variable, subject to one side condition: both \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) are free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ).

title: Definition 4.7.2 (Unique Existence)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(y\) a variable other than \(x\) that does not appear in \(\varphi\) (Section 4.2). Then \[ \exists! x\, \varphi \quad \text{abbreviates} \quad \exists x\, \bigl( \varphi \wedge \forall y\, (\varphi[y/x] \to y = x) \bigr). \] We read \(\exists! x\, \varphi\) as “there is exactly one \(x\) such that \(\varphi\) ”, or “there is a unique \(x\) with \(\varphi\) ”.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State \(\rulename{{=}I}\) and \(\rulename{{=}E}\) as schemas, with the side condition of \(\rulename{{=}E}\) . In the derivation below, name for each of lines 4, 5, 6, and 8 the rule, the cited lines, and the formula \(\varphi\) (with a variable \(z\) as its hole). In the same derivation, could lines 4 and 5 be replaced by one line? With which \(\varphi\) ? True or false, with a reason: from the lines \(a = b\) and \(P(b)\) , one application of \(\rulename{{=}E}\) gives \(P(a)\) . Write \(\exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 9)\) without the symbol \(\exists!\) , and decide whether it is true over \(\nN\) and over \(\nZ\) .

title: Exercise (B1: The identity is unique)
content: A set with an operation \(\cdot\) has an identity \(e\) if \(e \cdot x = x\) and \(x \cdot e = x\) for every \(x\) . Derive \[ \forall x\, (e \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e = x), \;\; \forall x\, (e' \cdot x = x \wedge x \cdot e' = x) \;\vdash\; e = e', \] where \(e\) and \(e'\) are constants. Which half of “there is exactly one identity” does this prove? Hint: look at the one element that both premises can say something about.

title: Exercise (B2: A unique square root of zero)
content: Over \(\nR\) , write \(\exists! x\, (x \cdot x = 0)\) without \(\exists!\) , and prove it: existence, then uniqueness in the form “suppose \(y\) also satisfies …”. Hint: a product of two nonzero reals is nonzero.

title: Exercise (B3: Exactly one fixed point)
content:
A fixed point of a function \(f \colon 
R 	o 
R\) is a real \(x\) with \(f(x) = x\) . Formalize “ \(f\) has exactly one fixed point” over \(
R\) , first with \(\exists!\) and then without it. Write a formula without \(\exists!\) that says “ \(f\) does not have exactly one fixed point”, in the form “there is none, or there are two different ones”. Decide the statement of (a) for \(f(x) = x \cdot x\) , for \(f(x) = x + 1\) and for \(f(x) = 2 \cdot x\) , and check your answer against the formula of (b).

title: Exercise (C1: Two unique quantifiers do not commute)
content: Show that \(\exists! x\, \exists! y\, R(x, y)\) and \(\exists! y\, \exists! x\, R(x, y)\) can have different truth values, by giving a finite domain \(D\) and a two-place relation \(R\) on it for which the first is true and the second false. Check both, reading \(\exists!\) informally. Hint: first say in words what each sentence claims about the rows and columns of a table of \(R\) .

title: Exercise (C2: “At most one”, two ways)
content: Let \(P\) be a one-place predicate symbol. Derive both directions of \[ \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( P(x) \wedge P(y) \to x = y \bigr) \;\dashv\vdash\; \neg\exists x\, \exists y\, \bigl( (P(x) \wedge P(y)) \wedge x \ne y \bigr), \] and say which of your two derivations uses \(\rulename{RAA}\) , and at which line.

title: Proposition 4.7.1 (Equality Is Symmetric and Transitive)
content: For all terms \(s\) , \(t\) , \(u\) : \(s = t \vdash t = s\) ; \(s = t, \; t = u \vdash s = u\) .

title: Proposition 4.7.2 (Two Halves of Unique Existence)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(y\) a variable other than \(x\) that does not appear in \(\varphi\) . Then \[ \exists! x\, \varphi \;\dashv\vdash\; \exists x\, \varphi \wedge \forall x\, \forall y\, \bigl( \varphi \wedge \varphi[y/x] \to x = y \bigr). \]

content:
Translate each sentence into a formula, stating the domain. \(a_n 	o L\) : for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(N \in

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.8 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content: Translate into formulas, stating the domain: (i) every real number has a cube root; (ii) the function \(f\) is bounded on \(A\) ; (iii) between any two different real numbers there is a rational number; (iv) the sequence \((a_n)\) is eventually constant; (v) some natural number divides every natural number. Three students translate “some element of \(A\) is larger than every element of \(B\) ”, over \(\nR\) : \(\exists x \in A \; \forall y \in B \; (x > y)\) ; (ii) \(\exists x\, \bigl( x \in A \to \forall y \in B\; (x > y) \bigr)\) ; (iii) \(\forall y \in B \; \exists x \in A \; (x > y)\) . Which are correct? For each wrong one, give sets \(A\) , \(B\) for which it has the wrong truth value. Which variables are free in your answer to (a)(iv)? Write the bounded rule \(\exists x \in A \; \rulename{I}\) as a block of two unbounded steps, and name the two rules.

title: Exercise (B1: Three definitions)
page: 4.8 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content: Formalize each statement, stating the domain and the kind of each symbol (variable, constant, function symbol, predicate symbol; membership \(\in A\) in a fixed set \(A\) is a one-place predicate symbol, as in Section 4.2). The set \(A\) of real numbers is bounded (above and below). The function \(f \colon \nR \to \nR\) is increasing on \(A\) : for all \(x, y \in A\) , \(x < y\) implies \(f(x) \le f(y)\) . title: Proposition 4.8.1 (Rules for Bounded Quantifiers)
page: 4.8 Translating Mathematics: Nested and Bounded Quantifiers
content: Let \(A\) be a fixed set, so that \(\in A\) is a one-place predicate symbol (Section 4.2), \(x\) a variable and \(\varphi\) a formula. The following four rules, the bounded rules , may be used in derivations, with the rule names of the unbounded rules and the same side conditions: in \(\forall x \in A \; \rulename{E}\) and \(\exists x \in A \; \rulename{I}\) , the term \(t\) is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ; in \(\forall x \in A \; \rulename{I}\) , the name \(x_0\) appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and not in \(\forall x \in A\; \varphi\) ; in \(\exists x \in A \; \rulename{E}\) , it appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line \(k\) , and not in \(\chi\) or in \(\exists x \in A\; \varphi\) . The last line of each box is a line of that box itself. Every use of a bounded rule can be replaced by a block of steps of the unbounded rules (Sections 4.3–4.6) and of Chapter 1, with the same premises, the same assumptions open, and the same last line. Hence any derivation that uses the bounded rules converts into one that does not. The same holds with \(x \in A\) and \(t \in A\) replaced by \(x > a\) and \(t > a\) , or by the bounds \(\ge a\) , \(< a\) , \(\le a\) , for a term \(a\) in which \(x\) does not occur.

Since \(x\) and \(y\) lie in \(A\) and \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) , the choice of \(\delta\) , applied to \(u = x\) and \(v = y\) , gives \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon\) . Suppose \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(A\) . By uniform continuity, applied to \(\varepsilon\) , choose \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(u, v \in A\) , \(\abs{u - v} < \delta\) implies \(\abs{f(u) - f(v)} < \varepsilon\) . Choose \(\delta > 0\) for this \(x\) and this \(\varepsilon\) , and then let \(x \in A\) be arbitrary. Let \(x \in A\) . So for every \(y \in A\) , \(\abs{x - y} < \delta\) implies \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} < \varepsilon\) : this \(\delta\) works for \(x\) and \(\varepsilon\) . title: Definition 4.11.2 (Assignment)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure with domain \(D\) . An assignment in \(\fM\) is a function \(\ell\) that gives every variable \(x\) a value \(\ell(x) \in D\) . For an assignment \(\ell\) , a variable \(x\) and an element \(d \in D\) , the assignment \(\ell[x \mapsto d]\) is the one that gives \(x\) the value \(d\) and every other variable the value \(\ell\) gives it: \[ \ell[x \mapsto d](y) \coloneqq \begin{cases} d & \text{if } y \text{ is the variable } x, \\ \ell(y) & \text{if } y \text{ is any other variable.} \end{cases} \]

title: Definition 4.11.4 (Semantic Entailment in Predicate Logic)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\varphi\) a formula. We say \(\Gamma\) semantically entails \(\varphi\) , and write \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) , if for every structure \(\fM\) for the symbols occurring in \(\Gamma\) and \(\varphi\) , and every assignment \(\ell\) in \(\fM\) , \[ \fM, \ell \models \Gamma \quad \Rightarrow \quad \fM, \ell \models \varphi . \] We write \(\models \varphi\) when \(\Gamma\) is empty. If \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) fails, we write \(\Gamma \not\models \varphi\) ; a structure \(\fM\) with an assignment \(\ell\) such that \(\fM, \ell \models \Gamma\) and \(\fM, \ell \not\models \varphi\) is a counter-model to \(\Gamma \models \varphi\) .

title: Definition 4.11.3 (Satisfaction)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure with domain \(D\) and \(\ell\) an assignment in \(\fM\) . The relation \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) , read “ \(\fM\) satisfies \(\varphi\) under \(\ell\) ”, is defined by recursion on the formula \(\varphi\) : \(\fM, \ell \models R(t_1, \dots, t_n)\) if \(\bigl( t_1^{\fM, \ell}, \dots, t_n^{\fM, \ell} \bigr) \in R^{\fM}\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models t_1 = t_2\) if \(t_1^{\fM, \ell}\) and \(t_2^{\fM, \ell}\) are the same element of \(D\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \bot\) never holds; \(\fM, \ell \models \neg\varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) does not hold; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \wedge \psi\) if both \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) and \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \vee \psi\) if at least one of them holds; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \to \psi\) unless \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) holds and \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) does not; \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi \leftrightarrow \psi\) if both hold or neither does; \(\fM, \ell \models \forall x\, \varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi\) for every \(d \in D\) ; \(\fM, \ell \models \exists x\, \varphi\) if \(\fM, \ell[x \mapsto d] \models \varphi\) for at least one \(d \in D\) . When \(\fM, \ell \models \varphi\) does not hold we write \(\fM, \ell \not\models \varphi\) . For a list \(\Gamma\) of formulas, \(\fM, \ell \models \Gamma\) means that \(\fM, \ell \models \gamma\) for every formula \(\gamma\) of \(\Gamma\) .

title: Definition 4.11.1 (Structure)
content: Fix a collection of constants, function symbols and predicate symbols, each function and predicate symbol with its arity \(n \ge 1\) . A structure \(\fM\) (also called a model ) for these symbols consists of a non-empty set \(D\) , the domain of \(\fM\) ; for each constant \(c\) , an element \(c^{\fM} \in D\) ; for each function symbol \(f\) of arity \(n\) , a function \(f^{\fM} \colon D^n \to D\) , defined at every \(n\) -tuple of elements of \(D\) ; for each predicate symbol \(R\) of arity \(n\) , a set \(R^{\fM}\) of \(n\) -tuples of elements of \(D\) . The symbol \(=\) is not interpreted by \(\fM\) : in every structure it means identity , “is the same element of \(D\) as”.

title: Lemma 4.11.1 (Free Variables Coincidence Lemma)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure and \(\varphi\) a formula, and let \(\ell\) and \(\ell'\) be assignments in \(\fM\) that agree on every free variable of \(\varphi\) . Then \[ \fM, \ell \models \varphi \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \fM, \ell' \models \varphi . \]

title: Corollary 4.12.4 (Counter-models)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If some structure \(\fM\) and assignment \(\ell\) satisfy every formula of \(\Gamma\) and do not satisfy \(\psi\) , then \(\Gamma \nvdash \psi\) .

title: Corollary 4.12.2 (Renaming Keeps Meaning)
content: Let \(\varphi\) be a formula and \(y, z\) variables, with \(z\) not appearing in \(\varphi\) (Section 4.2). Let \(\fM\) be a structure for the symbols of \(\varphi\) , with domain \(D\) . For every assignment \(\ell\) , \(\fM, \ell \models \forall y\, \varphi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \forall z\, \varphi[z/y]\) , and \(\fM, \ell \models \exists y\, \varphi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \exists z\, \varphi[z/y]\) . If \(\psi'\) arises from a formula \(\psi\) by such a renaming of one quantifier anywhere inside \(\psi\) (Section 4.2), then for every structure \(\fM\) for the symbols of \(\psi\) and every assignment \(\ell\) in it, \(\fM, \ell \models \psi\) if and only if \(\fM, \ell \models \psi'\) .

title: Lemma 4.12.1 (Substitution Lemma)
content: Let \(\fM\) be a structure, \(\ell\) an assignment in \(\fM\) , \(\varphi\) a formula, \(x\) a variable, and \(t\) a term that is free for \(x\) in \(\varphi\) ( @def-free-for ). Write \(a \coloneqq t^{\fM, \ell}\) . Then \[ \fM, \ell \models \varphi[t/x] \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \fM, \ell[x \mapsto a] \models \varphi . \]

title: Theorem 4.12.3 (Soundness for Predicate Logic)
content: Let \(\Gamma\) be a list of formulas and \(\psi\) a formula. If \(\Gamma \vdash \psi\) with the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 and the quantifier and equality rules of Sections 4.3 to 4.7, then \(\Gamma \models \psi\) ( @def-first-order-entailment ).

title: Example (A contrapositive in costume)
content: Here is a proof that, for an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even then \(n\) is even. Decide what it really uses, and rewrite it. Suppose \(n^2\) is even. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(n\) is not even. Then \(n\) is odd, say \(n = 2k + 1\) with \(k\) an integer. Then \(n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1\) is odd, so \(n^2\) is not even. This contradicts the fact that \(n^2\) is even. Hence \(n\) is even.

title: Example (A direct proof in costume)
content: Here is a proof that \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) for every real \(x > 3\) . Decide what it really uses, and rewrite it. Let \(x > 3\) . Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x^2 - 2x \le 3\) . Since \(x > 3\) , both \(x - 3\) and \(x + 1\) are positive, so \((x - 3)(x + 1) > 0\) , that is, \(x^2 - 2x - 3 > 0\) . So \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) . This contradicts our assumption. Hence \(x^2 - 2x > 3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Euclid without the contradiction)
content: Here is a common proof that there are infinitely many primes. It uses two facts about integers that we take as known here: every integer \(m \ge 2\) has a prime divisor ( Sets, Relations, and Cardinality , Chapter 2 proves it); and if an integer \(d\) divides two integers, it divides their difference (if \(u = dk\) and \(v = dl\) , then \(u - v = d(k - l)\) ). Suppose, for a contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) . Let \(N \coloneqq p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1\) . Then \(N \ge 2\) , so \(N\) has a prime divisor \(p\) . Since \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) are all the primes, \(p = p_i\) for some \(i\) . Then \(p_i\) divides both \(N\) and \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) , so it divides their difference \(1\) , which is impossible for a prime. This is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. “There are infinitely many primes” means “the set of primes is not finite”. Is the last step of the proof \(\rulename{RAA}\) or \(\rulename{\neg I}\) ? Where is the assumption “ \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) are all the primes” used? Which smell from this section does that suggest? Rewrite the argument as a direct proof of: for every finite list \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) of primes, with \(k \ge 1\) , there is a prime not in the list. Say what the rewrite gains over the original.

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x \ne 0\) . Then \(x^2 > 0\) , so we may take \(\varepsilon = x^2\) , and the hypothesis gives \(x^2 < x^2\) , which is impossible. Hence \(x = 0\) . title: Definition 5.3.1 (Levels of Proof)
content: A proof can be written at four levels . Level 0, the full derivation. A derivation in the sense of @def-derivation , with the rules of Chapters 1, 2 and 4: every line is a premise, an assumption, or one rule applied to available lines. A derived rule used as one line ( @def-derived-rule ), such as the bounded rules of @prp-bounded-quantifier-rules , counts as one rule. Facts about numbers enter as premises, or as lines justified “arith”, each of which records one such fact applied to the lines it cites. Level 1, the skeleton. The boxes and the logical lines only: every assumption, every flagged name, every line that opens or closes a box, with the rule that closes it, and every line that such a closing line cites. Each stretch of mathematics between them is compressed into one line, justified “arith”, “by def”, or by a cited result; a stretch of routine logical steps inside one box is compressed into one line justified by the names of its rules in order, such as “ \(\rulename{\forall E}\) , \(\rulename{\exists I}\) ”. Level 2, annotated prose. Sentences, each tagged in brackets with the rule or rules it carries, such as [ \(\rulename{\forall I}\) ] or [ \(\rulename{\exists E}\) ]. Level 3, plain prose. Sentences without tags, in which some steps are left unsaid. Which steps may be left unsaid is fixed by the convention that follows, not by the writer.

title: Exercise (B2: Back from prose to a skeleton)
content: Here is a level-3 proof. Claim. If \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(8 \mid n^2 - 1\) . Let \(n\) be odd, say \(n = 2k + 1\) with \(k\) an integer. Then \(n^2 - 1 = 4k(k + 1)\) , so it suffices to show that \(k(k + 1)\) is even. If \(k = 2j\) for an integer \(j\) , then \(k(k + 1) = 2 \cdot j(2j + 1)\) ; if \(k = 2j + 1\) , then \(k(k + 1) = 2 \cdot (2j + 1)(j + 1)\) . Either way \(k(k + 1) = 2i\) for an integer \(i\) , and then \(n^2 - 1 = 8i\) . Reconstruct its level-1 skeleton. Work over the domain \(\nZ\) , with “ \(n\) is odd” as \(\exists k\, (n = 2k + 1)\) and \(8 \mid m\) as \(\exists t\, (m = 8t)\) . Name the rule that closes each box, and say where the proof uses the fact (E1) of Section 2.1, that every integer is even or odd.

Write its proof at level 1, as a skeleton in which school facts about \(\abs{\cdot}\) and \(<\) are lines justified “arith”. Write it at level 3. Which lines of your skeleton are silent at level 3? title: Example (Explaining a proof, well and badly)
content: Claim. For every real number \(x > 0\) , \(x + 1/x \ge 2\) . Proof. Let \(x > 0\) . \((x - 1)^2 \ge 0\) . So \(x^2 - 2x + 1 \ge 0\) . Dividing by \(x\) , \(x - 2 + 1/x \ge 0\) . Hence \(x + 1/x \ge 2\) . Self-explain each line of the proof.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Here is a proof that if \(a > 0\) , \(b > 0\) and \(a^2 = b^2\) , then \(a = b\) . \(a^2 - b^2 = 0\) . (2) \((a - b)(a + b) = 0\) . (3) \(a + b > 0\) . (4) Hence \(a - b = 0\) , that is, \(a = b\) . Classify each explanation as one that justifies its line or one that paraphrases it. “Line 1 follows from the hypothesis \(a^2 = b^2\) by subtracting \(b^2\) from both sides.” “Line 2: then the factored form is zero as well.” “Line 2 is line 1 rewritten with the identity \(u^2 - v^2 = (u - v)(u + v)\) , at \(u = a\) and \(v = b\) .” “Line 3: now we know that \(a + b\) is positive.” “Line 3 holds because \(a > 0\) and \(b > 0\) are hypotheses, and a sum of two positive numbers is positive.” “Line 4: so \(a - b\) is zero, which is what we wanted.”

title: Exercise (B2: The unjustified line)
content: Here is a proof that for real numbers \(x < y\) , \(x^3 < y^3\) . Let \(x < y\) . (2) Then \(y^3 - x^3 = (y - x)(y^2 + xy + x^2)\) . (3) Since \(x < y\) , \(y - x > 0\) . (4) Also \(y^2 + xy + x^2 > 0\) . (5) So \(y^3 - x^3 > 0\) , as a product of two positive numbers. (6) Hence \(x^3 < y^3\) . Every line is true. Line 1 opens the box; of the rest, all but one are instances of a routine algebra or order fact, cited or not; one line is not an instance of any fact stated so far, and it needs an argument of its own. title: Example (Label every sentence)
content: Here is a short proof. Label each sentence with the rule it uses. Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(\abs{x - 1} < 1\) , then \(x > 0\) . Proof. (1) Assume \(\abs{x - 1} < 1\) . (2) Either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x < 1\) . (3) Suppose first that \(x \ge 1\) . (4) Then \(x \ge 1 > 0\) . (5) Suppose instead that \(x < 1\) . (6) Then \(x - 1 < 0\) , so \(\abs{x - 1} = 1 - x\) . (7) Hence \(1 - x < 1\) , that is, \(x > 0\) . (8) In either case \(x > 0\) , which proves the claim.

title: Example (A subset of a bounded set)

title: Example (From a derivation to a paragraph)

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Here is a proof. Claim. For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , if \(x + y > 2\) , then \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) . Assume \(x + y > 2\) . (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that it is not the case that \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) . (3) Then \(x > 1\) fails and \(y > 1\) fails. (4) So \(x \le 1\) and \(y \le 1\) . (5) Adding, \(x + y \le 2\) . (6) This contradicts \(x + y > 2\) . (7) Hence \(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\) , which proves the claim. Label each sentence with the rule it uses, as in @exm-annotate-abs . Which sentence closes an \(\rulename{RAA}\) box, and which uses one of De Morgan’s laws ( @prp-de-morgan )? Which law? Everything inside the box of (2) follows from (2) alone, until the clash in (6). title: Exercise (B3: The last step)
content: Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “for real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , if \(x\) is rational and \(y\) is irrational, then \(x + y\) is irrational”, with \(x\) and \(y\) fixed: and its level-3 prose, with the closing sentence of the \(\rulename{\neg I}\) box left blank: Let \(x\) be rational and \(y\) irrational. Suppose \(x + y\) is rational. Then \(y = (x + y) - x\) is a difference of two rational numbers, so \(y\) is rational. This contradicts the irrationality of \(y\) . \(\underline{\qquad\qquad}\) Name the move, then complete it.

title: Exercise (C1: A constant found backwards)
content: Let \(f(x) = 2x + 3\) and let \(a\) be a fixed real number. Prove that for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . Write your answer as an Idea, which finds \(\delta\) backwards, followed by a Proof, which runs forwards. Say what \(\delta\) depends on.

title: Exercise (C2: Rewrite it properly)
content: A sequence \((a_n)\) is bounded if there is \(M \in \nR\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) for every \(n \in \nN\) (Section 4.6). The following proof that a sequence \((a_n)\) with \(a_n \to L\) is bounded is correct in substance but badly written. We want some \(M\) with \(\abs{a_n} \le M\) . For big \(n\) , \(a_n\) is near \(L\) , so \(\abs{a_n}\) is less than \(\abs{L} + 1\) if we use \(1\) for \(\varepsilon\) . The small \(n\) are only finitely many, so take the biggest. So \(M\) is the max of all of them and it works. Name three faults of the text, each by the convention it breaks (this section) or the step that is not written. Rewrite the proof at level 3.

title: Example (What is not allowed)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content:
Each entry names the error, the rule it breaks and where that rule lives, and a failing instance whose conclusion is marked true or false : a wrong argument can reach either. Verifying instances and concluding “for all”. Breaks \(ulename{ orall I}\) , which needs one proof about a fresh name ( @def-rules-universal , Section 4.4). Instance: \(n^2 - n + 11\) is prime for \(n = 0, 1, \dots, 10\) (the values are \(11, 11, 13, 17, 23, 31, 41, 53, 67, 83, 101\) ), “so it is prime for every \(n \in 
N\) ”. False: at \(n = 11\) the value is \(121 = 11^2\) . A witness that depends on a variable introduced later, while uniformity is claimed. Breaks the side conditions of \(ulename{\exists E}\) and \(ulename{ orall I}\) : a witness \(\delta_0\) obtained inside the box of \(x_0\) may not leave it (Section 4.10, @exm-converse-fails ). Instance: “ \(x^2\) is continuous at every \(x\) , with \(\delta = \min\{1, \varepsilon/(2\abs{x} + 1)\}\) ; so one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\) serves every \(x\) , and \(x^2\) is uniformly continuous on \(
R\) ”. False ( @exm-square-not-uniform ). Treating the name from \(ulename{\exists E}\) as arbitrary. Breaks the side condition of \(ulename{ orall I}\) : the witness appears in the open assumption of its box ( @def-rules-existential , Section 4.6). Instance: “Some element of \(A\) is positive; let \(x\) be such an element. Since \(x\) was arbitrary, every element of \(A\) is positive.” False for \(A = \{-1, 1\}\) . Reusing one witness name for two \(ulename{\exists E}\) ’s. Breaks the fresh-name condition: the second name may not appear in an open assumption, and the first box’s assumption mentions it (Section 4.6, @exm-sum-of-evens ). Sibling boxes may share a name. Instance: “ \(m\) and \(n\) are even, so \(m = 2k\) and \(n = 2k\) for an integer \(k\) ; hence \(m = n\) ”. False: \(m = 2\) , \(n = 4\) . Proving the converse. Breaks \(ulename{{	o}I}\) , whose box opens with the hypothesis, not the conclusion ( @def-rules-implication , Section 1.5). Instance: “If \(x^2 > 1\) , then \(x > 1\) : suppose \(x > 1\) ; then \(x^2 > x > 1\) .” False: \(x = -2\) . Argument B of Section 1.1 makes the same move with a true conclusion. Affirming the consequent; denying the antecedent. Breaks @def-derivation (Section 1.5), being no rule: \(P 	o Q\) with \(Q\) gives no \(P\) , and with \(
eg P\) gives no \(
eg Q\) . Each pattern has a refuting row, so no derivation exists ( @cor-refuting-row , Section 3.5): @exm-affirming-the-consequent , and for denying the row \(P\) false, \(Q\) true. Instances: “a multiple of \(4\) is even and \(6\) is even, so \(6\) is a multiple of \(4\) ”; “… and \(6\) is not a multiple of \(4\) , so \(6\) is not even”. Both false . A missing case. Breaks \(ulename{\vee E}\) , which needs one box for each disjunct ( @def-rules-disjunction , Section 1.7). Instance: “ \(\abs{x} > 0\) for every real \(x\) : every real \(x\) has \(x > 0\) , \(x = 0\) or \(x < 0\) ; if \(x > 0\) , \(\abs{x} = x > 0\) ; if \(x < 0\) , \(\abs{x} = -x > 0\) ”. False: the case \(x = 0\) was dropped, and \(\abs{0} = 0\) . Cases that do not exhaust. Breaks \(ulename{\vee E}\) , whose first input must be a disjunction already derived (Section 1.7). Instance: “ \(x^2 \ge x\) for every real \(x\) : either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x \le 0\) ; in the first case \(x^2 = x \cdot x \ge x\) , in the second \(x^2 \ge 0 \ge x\) ”. False: \(x = 1/2\) satisfies neither case, and \(1/4 < 1/2\) . Citing a line that is not available: the goal itself (circular reasoning), a result proved later, or a general “fact” neither proved nor a true school fact (a false “fact” never qualifies). Breaks @def-derivation : every line is a premise, an assumption, or a rule applied to available lines (Section 1.5). Instances: “if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even: suppose \(n^2\) is even; since \(n\) is even, …” ( true , and circular); “ \(x < 1\) , so \(x^2 < 1\) , since squaring preserves \(<\) ” ( false: \(x = -2\) ). Using an assumption after its box has closed. Breaks the scope rule of @def-derivation (Section 1.5). Instance: “Suppose \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2k\) ; then \(n^2 = 4k^2\) . Hence if \(n\) is even, \(4 \mid n^2\) . Now \(n^2 = 4k^2\) , so \(4 \mid n^2\) for every integer \(n\) .” False: \(n = 1\) . Proof D below makes the same move with a true conclusion. A wrong negation. An \(ulename{RAA}\) box opened with a statement that is not the negation of the goal; a bound negated instead of a quantifier ( @prp-bounded-quantifier-negation ); the negation of \(\varphi 	o \psi\) written as an implication, \(
eg\varphi 	o 
eg\psi\) or \(\varphi 	o 
eg\psi\) , instead of \(\varphi \wedge 
eg\psi\) ( @prp-negated-implication ). Breaks \(ulename{RAA}\) , which closes only a box opened with \(
eg\varphi\) (Section 2.5), or the laws of Section 4.9. Instances: “if \(x > 2\) , then \(x^2 > 4\) ” is “refuted” because “if \(x \le 2\) , then \(x^2 \le 4\) ” holds at \(x = 0\) ( false : both are true at \(x = 0\) , so one is not the negation of the other); “ \(a_n = 0\) does not converge to \(0\) , since some \(\varepsilon \le 0\) has \(\abs{a_n - 0} \ge \varepsilon\) for all \(n\) ” ( false ).

title: Example (Proof A)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0\) , then \(1 < x < 2\) . Assume \(x^2 - 3x + 2 < 0\) . (2) Then \((x - 1)(x - 2) < 0\) . (3) A product of two real numbers is negative only when one factor is positive and the other negative, so either \(x - 1 > 0\) and \(x - 2 < 0\) , or \(x - 1 < 0\) and \(x - 2 > 0\) . (4) In the first case, \(1 < x < 2\) . (5) In the second case, \(x < 1\) and \(x > 2\) , which is impossible. (6) Hence \(1 < x < 2\) .

title: Example (Proof B)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For an integer \(n\) , if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even. Suppose \(n\) is even. (2) Then \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) . (3) So \(n^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)\) . (4) Hence \(n^2\) is even. (5) Therefore, if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

title: Example (Proof C)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For an integer \(n\) , the number \(n^2 - 2\) is not divisible by \(4\) . Suppose \(n^2 - 2\) is divisible by \(4\) , say \(n^2 - 2 = 4k\) with \(k\) an integer. (2) Then \(n^2 = 4k + 2 = 2(2k + 1)\) , so \(n^2\) is even. (3) By @thm-square-even-implies-even , \(n\) is even, say \(n = 2m\) with \(m\) an integer. (4) Then \(n^2 = 4m^2\) , so \(4m^2 = 4k + 2\) , and hence \(1 = 2(m^2 - k)\) . (5) So \(1\) is even. (6) But \(1\) is odd, and no integer is both even and odd; this is a contradiction. (7) Hence \(n^2 - 2\) is not divisible by \(4\) .

title: Example (Proof D)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Claim. For a real number \(x\) : if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > x\) ; and \(x^2 + 1 > x\) . Suppose \(x > 1\) . (2) Multiplying both sides by \(x\) , which is positive, gives \(x^2 > x\) . (3) Hence if \(x > 1\) , then \(x^2 > x\) . (4) For the second part, \(x^2 + 1 > x^2\) , and \(x^2 > x\) by (2), so \(x^2 + 1 > x\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Each line below comes from a proof. Name the catalogue entry of @exm-not-allowed-catalogue that it commits, and the rule it breaks. “We checked \(3^n > n^2\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\) , so it holds for every \(n \in \nN\) .” “By hypothesis some \(x \in A\) has \(f(x) = 0\) ; fix such an \(x\) . Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(f(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in A\) .” “To prove that \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) , suppose \(x_1 = x_2\) ; then \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) .” “To prove \(x \ge 0\) , suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x \le 0\) .” “If \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) , then \(n\) is even. Since \(n\) is even, \(n\) is divisible by \(6\) .” “Every real \(x\) satisfies \(x > 0\) or \(x < 0\) ; we consider the two cases.”

title: Exercise (B1: Two proofs in two columns)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Check each proof in two columns. For a wrong proof, name the first line that fails and its catalogue entry, and say whether the claim is true. Claim. For integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are odd, then \(m + n\) is even. (1) Assume \(m\) and \(n\) are odd. (2) Choose integers \(k\) and \(l\) with \(m = 2k + 1\) and \(n = 2l + 1\) . (3) Then \(m + n = 2k + 2l + 2 = 2(k + l + 1)\) . (4) Since \(k + l + 1\) is an integer, \(m + n\) is even. Claim. For a real number \(x\) , if \(x^2 < 1\) , then \(x < 1\) . (1) Assume \(x^2 < 1\) . (2) Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(x > 1\) . (3) Then \(x > 0\) , so \(x^2 = x \cdot x > x > 1\) . (4) This contradicts \(x^2 < 1\) . (5) Hence \(x < 1\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Find the error)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Find the error in the following proof, name its catalogue entry, and decide whether the claim is true. Claim. For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) , \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}\) . Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. (2) Either \(x\) and \(y\) are both \(\ge 0\) , or they are both \(< 0\) . (3) If both are \(\ge 0\) , then \(x + y \ge 0\) , so \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = x + y = \abs{x + y}\) . (4) If both are \(< 0\) , then \(x + y < 0\) , so \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = -x - y = -(x + y) = \abs{x + y}\) . (5) In either case \(\abs{x} + \abs{y} = \abs{x + y}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The second half)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Let \(f \colon \nR \to \nR\) be continuous at \(a\) , as the quantifier pattern of Section 4.8: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < \varepsilon\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . Suppose \(f(a) > 0\) . Here is a level-1 skeleton for the statement “there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f(x) > 0\) for every \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) ”: Its level-3 prose begins: Since \(f(a) > 0\) , the number \(f(a)/2\) is positive. By the continuity of \(f\) at \(a\) , applied with \(\varepsilon = f(a)/2\) , choose \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\abs{f(x) - f(a)} < f(a)/2\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x - a} < \delta\) . The rest is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Say which skeleton lines your sentences carry, and what \(\delta\) depends on.

title: Exercise (C2: A true conclusion)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Here is a proof that \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3\) is irrational, a true conclusion. Find the line that fails and its catalogue entry, give a counterexample to the illegal step, and write a correct proof. Suppose \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3 = r\) for some rational number \(r\) . (2) Squaring, \(r^2 = 2 + 2\sqrt 6 + 3 = 5 + 2\sqrt 6\) . (3) Hence \(\sqrt 6 = (r^2 - 5)/2\) , which is rational, since \(r\) is. (4) But \(\sqrt 6 = \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 3\) is irrational, being a product of two irrational numbers. (5) This contradiction shows that \(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3\) is irrational.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: four student proofs)
page: 5.6 Checking Proofs, and What Is Not Allowed
content: Judge each proof. If it is wrong, give the line that fails, its entry in @exm-not-allowed-catalogue , and a counterexample to the illegal step. If it is correct, name the rule of its most delicate step and check that step. Claim. For every integer \(n\) , if \(n\) is a multiple of \(4\) or a multiple of \(6\) , then \(n\) is even. (1) Let \(n\) be an integer that is a multiple of \(4\) or of \(6\) . (2) Case 1: \(n\) is a multiple of \(4\) . Choose an integer \(k\) with \(n = 4k\) ; then \(n = 2(2k)\) , so \(n\) is even. (3) Case 2: \(n\) is a multiple of \(6\) . Choose an integer \(k\) with \(n = 6k\) ; then \(n = 2(3k)\) , so \(n\) is even. (4) In either case, \(n\) is even. Claim. For integers \(m\) and \(n\) , if \(m\) and \(n\) are even, then \(mn\) is divisible by \(4\) . (1) Assume \(m\) and \(n\) are even. (2) Then \(m = 2k\) and \(n = 2k\) for an integer \(k\) . (3) So \(mn = 4k^2\) , which is divisible by \(4\) . Claim. For every real \(x\) , \(\abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1\) . (1) Either \(x \ge 1\) or \(x \le 0\) . (2) If \(x \ge 1\) , then \(\abs{x - 1} = x - 1 \le x + 1 = \abs{x} + 1\) . (3) If \(x \le 0\) , then \(\abs{x - 1} = 1 - x = 1 + \abs{x}\) . (4) In either case, \(\abs{x - 1} \le \abs{x} + 1\) . Claim. For every real \(x\) , if \(x^2 = 2x\) , then \(x = 2\) . (1) Assume \(x^2 = 2x\) . (2) Canceling \(x\) from both sides, \(x = 2\) . (3) Hence if \(x^2 = 2x\) , then \(x = 2\) .
